**Sūrat Āl ʿImrān**
Medinan, with 200 verses. It was revealed after Sūrat al-Anfāl.

In the name of God, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

﴿Alif, Lām, Mīm.﴾ ﴿God! There is no god but Him, the Living, the Self-Subsisting.﴾

In the name of God, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

﴿Alif, Lām, Mīm.﴾ ﴿God! There is no god but Him, the Living, the Self-Subsisting.﴾

As for the explanation of ﴿Alif, Lām, Mīm﴾, it has already been discussed in Sūrat al-Baqara. In this verse there are several issues:

**The first issue:** Abu Bakr, on the authority of ʿĀṣim, read "Al-Lām Allāh" with a sukūn (vowel-less) on the mīm and a naṣb (fatḥa) on the hamza, as "Allāh" (with the hamza pronounced). The rest of the readers read it connected (mawṣūl), with a fatḥa on the mīm. The reading of ʿĀṣim has two possible explanations:

The first: the intention of pausing, and then pronouncing the hamza because of the beginning of a new utterance.

The second: that this is in accordance with the dialect of those who cut off the hamzat al-waṣl (the connecting hamza). Whoever separates and pronounces the hamza does so for emphasis and magnification. As for the one who puts a naṣb on the mīm, there are two opinions:

The first opinion, which is the view of al-Farrāʾ and the choice of many of the Basran grammarians, is that the names of the letters end with a pause. One says: "Alif," "Lām," "Mīm," just as one says: "Wāḥid," "Ithnān," "Thalātha." On this assumption, it is necessary to begin with the word "Allāh." When we begin with it, we keep the hamza vowelled. However, they dropped the hamza for ease, and then its vowel was transferred to the mīm, so that its vowel would indicate that it is in the status of being retained, because this word is the beginning of the utterance.

If it is said: if the assumption is the separation of one of the two words from the other, then dropping the hamza is impossible; and if the assumption is the connection, then the retention of the hamza with its vowel is impossible. And if its retention is impossible, its vowel is impossible, and transferring its vowel to the mīm is impossible.

We reply: Why is it not permissible that it be dropped in its form but retained in its meaning, so that its vowel is kept to indicate its continued existence in meaning? This is the complete explanation of al-Farrāʾ's view.

The second opinion is the view of Sībawayh, namely that the reason for the vowel on the mīm is the meeting of two sukūns (unvowelled letters). This view has been rejected by many people, and it is subtle and refined, and discussing its summary at length is long.

I say: there are two investigations here. One is the cause of the original vowel. The second is that this vowel is a fatḥa.

As for the first investigation, it is built on several premises:

**The first premise:** When two sukūns come together, if the first of them is one of the letters of elongation and softness (ḥurūf al-madd wa al-līn), vowelling is not required, because it is easy to pronounce such two sukūns, as in your saying: "Hādhā Ibrāhīm wa Isḥāq wa Yaʿqūb" (with pause on the last). But if it is not so, vowelling is required, because it is not easy to pronounce such two, since pronunciation is impossible without a vowel.

**The second premise:** Sībawayh's view is that the definite article is the lām, and it is unvowelled, and an unvowelled letter cannot be begun with. So they placed before it the hamzat al-waṣl and vowelled it, so that they could reach the pronunciation of the lām through it. Accordingly, if they find before the definite-article lām another letter, then if it is vowelled they reach the pronunciation of this unvowelled lām through it; and if it is unvowelled, they vowel it and reach the pronunciation of this lām through it. On this assumption, the need for the hamzat al-waṣl is eliminated, because the need for it is that its vowel is used to reach the pronunciation of the lām. When another letter exists, they reach the pronunciation of this lām through its vowel, so this hamza is dropped in form and in meaning, in reality and in legal status. And if this is so, it is impossible to say that its vowel was transferred to the mīm so that that vowel would indicate that it remains in legal status, because this is only resorted to where a legal ruling or an effect depends on its existence. But we have shown that the matter is not so. Thus we know that this hamza fell out entirely, both in itself and in its effects. By this, al-Farrāʾ's view is refuted.

**The third premise:** The names of these letters end with a pause, and this is agreed upon.

Having understood these premises, we say: the mīm in our saying "Alif Lām Mīm" is unvowelled, and the lām of the definite article in our saying "Allāh" is unvowelled. The two have come together, so the mīm must be vowelled, and the hamza must necessarily fall out completely in form and meaning. By this explanation Sībawayh's view is correct and al-Farrāʾ's view is refuted.

As for the second investigation: someone may say: when an unvowelled letter is vowelled, it is vowelled with a kasra. Why was fatḥa chosen here? Al-Zajjāj answered this by saying: a kasra is not suitable here, because the mīm in our saying "Alif Lām Mīm" is preceded by a yāʾ. So if you make the mīm kasra, the kasra would come together with the yāʾ, and that is heavy. Therefore the kasra was abandoned and the fatḥa was chosen.

Abu ʿAlī al-Fārisī criticised al-Zajjāj's statement and said: his statement is refuted by our saying "Jayr," for the rāʾ is kasra although it is preceded by a yāʾ. In my view this criticism is weak, because the kasra is a vowel in which there is some heaviness, and the yāʾ is its sister. When the two come together, the heaviness becomes great. Then there is a transition from it to pronouncing the alif in your saying "Allāh," and that is in the extreme of lightness. So the tongue moves from the heaviest vowels to the lightest vowels, and moving from one opposite to another in a single step is difficult for the tongue. But if we make the mīm fatḥa, the tongue moves from the fatḥa of the mīm to the alif in our saying "Allāh," and so its pronunciation is easy. This is the explanation of Sībawayh's view, and God knows best.

* * *

**The second issue:** Concerning the cause of the revelation of the beginning of this sūra, there are two opinions:

The first opinion, which is the view of Muqātil ibn Sulaymān, is that part of the beginning of this sūra concerns the Jews, and we have mentioned this in the explanation of ﴿Alif, Lām, Mīm﴾ ﴿That is the Book﴾ [al-Baqara 2:1].

The second opinion: from the beginning of the sūra to the verse of mubāhala (mutual invocation of curses) concerns the Christians. This is the view of Muḥammad ibn Isḥāq, who said: "The delegation of Najrān came to the Messenger of God (ﷺ), sixty riders, among them fourteen men of their nobles, and three of them were the greatest of the people. The first of them was their commander, whose name was ʿAbd al-Masīḥ. The second was their adviser and the man of their opinion; they used to call him 'the Lord,' and his name was al-Ayham. The third was their scholar (ḥabr), their bishop (usquf), and the master of their school (midrās); he was called Abū Ḥāritha ibn ʿAlqama, one of the Banū Bakr ibn Wāʾil. The kings of Rome had honoured him, granted him stipends and treated him generously because of the knowledge and diligence in their religion that had reached them about him. When they came from Najrān, Abū Ḥāritha rode his mule, and beside him was his brother Kurz ibn ʿAlqama. While Abū Ḥāritha's mule was walking, it stumbled. Kurz, his brother, said: 'May the far one perish,' meaning the Messenger of God (ﷺ). Abū Ḥāritha said: 'Rather may your mother perish.' He said: 'Why, my brother?' He said: 'By God, he is the Prophet whom we used to await.' His brother Kurz said to him: 'What then prevents you from following him, when you know this?' He said: 'Because these kings have given us much wealth and honoured us, and if we believed in Muḥammad (ﷺ), they would take all these things from us.' This thought entered the heart of his brother Kurz, and he kept concealing it until he became a Muslim, and then he used to speak about it.

Then those three, the commander, the lord and the scholar, spoke with the Messenger of God (ﷺ), while differing in their religious views: at times they said ʿĪsā is God; at times they said he is the son of God; at times they said he is the third of three. They argued for their saying that he is God by his bringing the dead to life, healing the blind and the leper, healing diseases, informing of the unseen, and creating from clay a form like a bird, then breathing into it so that it flew. They argued for their saying that he is the son of God by his having no known father. And they argued for the third-of-three view by God's saying ﴿We did, and We made﴾, and had he been one he would have said 'I did.' Then the Messenger of God (ﷺ) said to them: 'Submit.' They said: 'We have submitted.' He (ﷺ) said: 'You lie. How can your submission be valid when you attribute a son to God, worship the cross, and eat pork?' They said: 'Then who is his father?' The Messenger of God (ﷺ) was silent, and God revealed concerning that the beginning of Sūrat Āl ʿImrān, up to some eighty-odd verses of it."

Then the Messenger of God (ﷺ) began to debate with them. He said: "Do you not know that God is living and does not die, and that ʿĪsā will come to extinction?" They said: "Yes." He said: "Do you not know that there is no child except that it resembles its father?" They said: "Yes." He said: "Do you not know that our Lord is the Sustainer (qayyim) over everything, who protects it, guards it and provides for it, and does ʿĪsā possess any of that?" They said: "No." He said: "Do you not know that nothing on earth or in heaven is hidden from God, and does ʿĪsā know any of that except what He has taught him?" They said: "No." He said: "Our Lord fashioned ʿĪsā in the womb however He willed. Do you know that our Lord does not eat food, does not drink drink, and does not eliminate waste, while you know that ʿĪsā was carried by a woman as a woman carries, and gave birth to him as a woman gives birth, and then he ate food, drank drink and eliminated waste?" They said: "Yes." He (ﷺ) said: "Then how can he be as you claim?" They recognised it, but then refused except to deny. Then they said: "O Muḥammad, do you not claim that he is the Word of God and a spirit from Him?" He said: "Yes." They said: "Then that is enough for us." So God revealed: ﴿As for those in whose hearts is deviation, they follow what is ambiguous﴾ and the rest of the verse.

Then God commanded Muḥammad (ﷺ) to invoke a curse upon them (mulāʿana) when they rejected that from him. The Messenger of God (ﷺ) invited them to the mutual cursing. They said: "O Abū al-Qāsim, let us consider our affair, and then we will come to you with what you want us to do." They departed, and then one of those three said to the others: "What do you think?" He said: "By God, O company of Christians, you know that Muḥammad is a Prophet sent, and he has brought you the decisive account of your companion's affair. You know that no people has ever cursed a prophet without their great and small being destroyed, and that will be your annihilation if you do it. You have refused except your religion and remaining upon what you are upon. So make peace with the man and go back to your lands."

They came to the Messenger of God (ﷺ) and said: "O Abū al-Qāsim, we have decided not to curse you, and to leave you upon your religion and to return ourselves to our religion. Send with us a man of your companions to judge between us in matters about which we have disagreed concerning our property, for you are trusted by us." He (peace be upon him) said: "Come to me in the evening, and I will send with you the strong and trustworthy arbiter." ʿUmar used to say: "I never loved leadership (imāra) except on that day, hoping that I would be its holder. When we prayed the noon prayer with the Messenger of God (ﷺ), he gave the salam, then looked to his right and to his left, and I began stretching myself up so that he would see me. He kept moving his gaze until he saw Abū ʿUbayda ibn al-Jarrāḥ, and he called him and said: 'Go out with them and judge between them with truth concerning what they dispute.' ʿUmar said: 'So Abū ʿUbayda took it.'"

Know that this narration indicates that debate in establishing the religion and removing doubts is the craft of the Prophets, peace be upon them, and that the view of the Ḥashwiyya (a term for literalist extremists) who deny inquiry and reflection is utterly false. And God knows best.

* * *

**The third issue:** Know that the opening of this sūra has a subtle and wonderful arrangement (naẓm). That is because those Christians who disputed with the Messenger of God (ﷺ) were as if told: either you dispute with him concerning knowledge of God, or concerning prophethood. If the dispute is about knowledge of God, namely that you attribute a son to Him and that Muḥammad does not attribute a son to Him, then the truth is with him by decisive rational proofs, for it has been established by demonstration that He is the Living, the Self-Subsisting, and it is rationally impossible for the Living, the Self-Subsisting to have a son. And if the dispute is about prophethood, that too is false, for by the same means by which you know that God sent down the Torah and the Gospel to Moses and Jesus, it is precisely present in Muḥammad (ﷺ). That is only through a miracle, and it is present here. So how can his prophethood be disputed? This is the manner of the arrangement, and it is very well-ordered and excellent. Let us now look here at two investigations:

**Part 2 of 2**

**The First Discussion:** This concerns matters of divine theology (al-Ilahiyyat). We say that He, exalted is He, is *al-Hayy al-Qayyum* (the Ever-Living, the Self-Subsisting), and whoever is ever-living and self-subsisting cannot have a son. We have said that He is ever-living and self-subsisting because He is *wajib al-wujud* (necessary of existence) in His essence, while everything other than Him is *mumkin al-wujud* (contingent of existence) in its essence, originated, and its creation, fashioning, and bringing into being have occurred. We have explained all of this in the commentary on His, exalted is He, words: ﴿Allah! There is no god but He, the Ever-Living, the Self-Subsisting.﴾ [Al-Baqarah: 255]. Since all of creation is originated and created, it is impossible for any of it to be a son of Allah or a god, as He said: ﴿There is none in the heavens and the earth but that he comes to the Most Merciful as a servant.﴾ [Maryam: 93]

Furthermore, since it has been established that God must be ever-living and self-subsisting, and it has been established that Jesus (ʿIsa) was not ever-living and self-subsisting, because he was born, ate, drank, and excreted, and the Christians claim that he was killed and could not defend himself against the killing, it follows that he was not ever-living and self-subsisting. This necessitates the certain and definite conclusion that he was not a god. Thus this phrase, His words ﴿the Ever-Living, the Self-Subsisting﴾, comprehends all the aspects of the proofs against the Christian doctrine of the Trinity (al-Tathlith).

**The Second Discussion:** This concerns prophethood (al-Nubuwwah). Allah, exalted is He, has mentioned it here in the utmost beauty and the highest excellence. He said: ﴿He has sent down to you the Book with truth﴾ [Ali ʿImran: 3]. This functions as a claim. Then He, exalted is He, established evidence for the validity of this claim, saying: "O Jews and Christians, you agree with us that Allah, exalted is He, sent down the Torah and the Gospel
[Page 136]
before (this) as guidance for mankind." You only recognized that the Torah and the Gospel are two divine books because He, exalted is He, coupled their revelation with a miracle (*muʿjizah*) that distinguishes between the speech of the one who is right (*al-muhiqq*) and the speech of the one who is false (*al-mubtil*). Since the miracle is that by which a distinction is made between a true claim and a false claim, it is necessarily a distinction. Moreover, the criterion (*al-furqan*), which is the miracle, has provided the evidence that the Torah and the Gospel were sent down from Allah, and likewise it provides the evidence that the Qur'an was sent down from Allah. Since the method is shared, either it is obligatory to reject all of them, as the position of the Brahmins (*al-Barahimah*) holds, or to affirm all of them, as the position of the Muslims holds. As for accepting some and rejecting others, that is ignorance and blind imitation (*taqlid*).

Then, when He, exalted is He, mentioned what is the foundation of knowing God as brought by Muhammad, peace and blessings be upon him, and what is the foundation of establishing the prophethood of Muhammad (ﷺ), no excuse remained for anyone who disputes with him regarding his religion. Therefore He inevitably followed this with a threat and warning, saying: ﴿Indeed, those who disbelieve in the signs of Allah will have a severe punishment, and Allah is Exalted in Might, the Owner of Retribution.﴾ [Ali ʿImran: 4]. It has thus become clear that no statement can be more precise, more well-ordered, or more excellent in composition than this statement. All praise is due to Allah for guiding this humble one to it, and to Him belongs thanks for His blessings, which have no limit and no end.

Having summarized the overall aim of the discourse, let us now return to the explanation of each of the words.

As for His words ﴿Allah! There is no god but He﴾, this is a refutation of the Christians, because they used to worship ʿIsa, peace be upon him. Allah, exalted is He, made clear that no one deserves worship besides Him.

Then He followed this with what serves as an indication of it, saying: ﴿the Ever-Living, the Self-Subsisting﴾. As for *al-Hayy* (the Ever-Living), it is the one who acts and perceives. As for *al-Qayyum* (the Self-Subsisting), it is the one who subsists by His own essence, and the one who manages the affairs of creation and their interests in what they need for their livelihood, from night and day, heat and cold, winds and rains, and the blessings which none other than Him can provide and none other than Him can count, as He, exalted is He, said: ﴿And if you should count the favor of Allah, you could not enumerate them﴾ [Ibrahim: 34].

ʿUmar, may Allah be pleased with him, recited ﴿al-Hayy al-Qayyum﴾. Qatadah said: *al-Hayy* is the One who does not die, and *al-Qayyum* is the One who stands over His creation with respect to their deeds, their terms, and their provisions. It is related from Saʿid ibn Jubayr: *al-Hayy* is the One who was before every living being, and *al-Qayyum* is the One who has no equal. We have mentioned in the Surah of al-Baqarah that our saying "al-Hayy al-Qayyum" encompasses all the attributes that are considered in divinity.

Since it has been established that the one worshipped must be ever-living and self-subsisting, and since reason (*al-badihah*) and the senses indicate that ʿIsa, peace be upon him, was not ever-living and self-subsisting, and how could he be, when they themselves claim that he was killed and showed fear of death, we know with certainty that ʿIsa was neither a god nor a son of the God, exalted is He and far above what the wrongdoers say, a great exaltation.

They said: 'We have submitted.' He (ﷺ) said: 'You lie. How can your submission be valid when you attribute a son to God, worship the cross, and eat pork?' They said: 'Then who is his father?' The Messenger of God (ﷺ) was silent, and God revealed concerning that the beginning of Sūrat Āl ʿImrān, up to some eighty-odd verses of it."

Then the Messenger of God (ﷺ) began to debate with them. He said: "Do you not know that God is living and does not die, and that ʿĪsā will come to extinction?" They said: "Yes." He said: "Do you not know that there is no child except that it resembles its father?" They said: "Yes." He said: "Do you not know that our Lord is the Sustainer (qayyim) over everything, who protects it, guards it and provides for it, and does ʿĪsā possess any of that?" They said: "No." He said: "Do you not know that nothing on earth or in heaven is hidden from God, and does ʿĪsā know any of that except what He has taught him?" They said: "No." He said: "Our Lord fashioned ʿĪsā in the womb however He willed. Do you know that our Lord does not eat food, does not drink drink, and does not eliminate waste, while you know that ʿĪsā was carried by a woman as a woman carries, and gave birth to him as a woman gives birth, and then he ate food, drank drink and eliminated waste?" They said: "Yes." He (ﷺ) said: "Then how can he be as you claim?" They recognised it, but then refused except to deny. Then they said: "O Muḥammad, do you not claim that he is the Word of God and a spirit from Him?" He said: "Yes." They said: "Then that is enough for us." So God revealed: ﴿As for those in whose hearts is deviation, they follow what is ambiguous﴾ and the rest of the verse.

Then God commanded Muḥammad (ﷺ) to invoke a curse upon them (mulāʿana) when they rejected that from him. The Messenger of God (ﷺ) invited them to the mutual cursing. They said: "O Abū al-Qāsim, let us consider our affair, and then we will come to you with what you want us to do." They departed, and then one of those three said to the others: "What do you think?" He said: "By God, O company of Christians, you know that Muḥammad is a Prophet sent, and he has brought you the decisive account of your companion's affair. You know that no people has ever cursed a prophet without their great and small being destroyed, and that will be your annihilation if you do it. You have refused except your religion and remaining upon what you are upon. So make peace with the man and go back to your lands."

They came to the Messenger of God (ﷺ) and said: "O Abū al-Qāsim, we have decided not to curse you, and to leave you upon your religion and to return ourselves to our religion. Send with us a man of your companions to judge between us in matters about which we have disagreed concerning our property, for you are trusted by us." He (peace be upon him) said: "Come to me in the evening, and I will send with you the strong and trustworthy arbiter." ʿUmar used to say: "I never loved leadership (imāra) except on that day, hoping that I would be its holder. When we prayed the noon prayer with the Messenger of God (ﷺ), he gave the salam, then looked to his right and to his left, and I began stretching myself up so that he would see me. He kept moving his gaze until he saw Abū ʿUbayda ibn al-Jarrāḥ, and he called him and said: 'Go out with them and judge between them with truth concerning what they dispute.' ʿUmar said: 'So Abū ʿUbayda took it.'"

Know that this narration indicates that debate in establishing the religion and removing doubts is the craft of the Prophets, peace be upon them, and that the view of the Ḥashwiyya (a term for literalist extremists) who deny inquiry and reflection is utterly false. And God knows best.

* * *

**The third issue:** Know that the opening of this sūra has a subtle and wonderful arrangement (naẓm). That is because those Christians who disputed with the Messenger of God (ﷺ) were as if told: either you dispute with him concerning knowledge of God, or concerning prophethood. If the dispute is about knowledge of God, namely that you attribute a son to Him and that Muḥammad does not attribute a son to Him, then the truth is with him by decisive rational proofs, for it has been established by demonstration that He is the Living, the Self-Subsisting, and it is rationally impossible for the Living, the Self-Subsisting to have a son. And if the dispute is about prophethood, that too is false, for by the same means by which you know that God sent down the Torah and the Gospel to Moses and Jesus, it is precisely present in Muḥammad (ﷺ). That is only through a miracle, and it is present here. So how can his prophethood be disputed? This is the manner of the arrangement, and it is very well-ordered and excellent. Let us now look here at two investigations:

**Part 2 of 2**

**The First Discussion:** This concerns matters of divine theology (al-Ilahiyyat). We say that He, exalted is He, is *al-Hayy al-Qayyum* (the Ever-Living, the Self-Subsisting), and whoever is ever-living and self-subsisting cannot have a son. We have said that He is ever-living and self-subsisting because He is *wajib al-wujud* (necessary of existence) in His essence, while everything other than Him is *mumkin al-wujud* (contingent of existence) in its essence, originated, and its creation, fashioning, and bringing into being have occurred. We have explained all of this in the commentary on His, exalted is He, words: ﴿Allah! There is no god but He, the Ever-Living, the Self-Subsisting.﴾ [Al-Baqarah: 255]. Since all of creation is originated and created, it is impossible for any of it to be a son of Allah or a god, as He said: ﴿There is none in the heavens and the earth but that he comes to the Most Merciful as a servant.﴾ [Maryam: 93]

Furthermore, since it has been established that God must be ever-living and self-subsisting, and it has been established that Jesus (ʿIsa) was not ever-living and self-subsisting, because he was born, ate, drank, and excreted, and the Christians claim that he was killed and could not defend himself against the killing, it follows that he was not ever-living and self-subsisting. This necessitates the certain and definite conclusion that he was not a god. Thus this phrase, His words ﴿the Ever-Living, the Self-Subsisting﴾, comprehends all the aspects of the proofs against the Christian doctrine of the Trinity (al-Tathlith).

**The Second Discussion:** This concerns prophethood (al-Nubuwwah). Allah, exalted is He, has mentioned it here in the utmost beauty and the highest excellence. He said: ﴿He has sent down to you the Book with truth﴾ [Ali ʿImran: 3]. This functions as a claim. Then He, exalted is He, established evidence for the validity of this claim, saying: "O Jews and Christians, you agree with us that Allah, exalted is He, sent down the Torah and the Gospel
[Page 136]
before (this) as guidance for mankind." You only recognized that the Torah and the Gospel are two divine books because He, exalted is He, coupled their revelation with a miracle (*muʿjizah*) that distinguishes between the speech of the one who is right (*al-muhiqq*) and the speech of the one who is false (*al-mubtil*). Since the miracle is that by which a distinction is made between a true claim and a false claim, it is necessarily a distinction. Moreover, the criterion (*al-furqan*), which is the miracle, has provided the evidence that the Torah and the Gospel were sent down from Allah, and likewise it provides the evidence that the Qur'an was sent down from Allah. Since the method is shared, either it is obligatory to reject all of them, as the position of the Brahmins (*al-Barahimah*) holds, or to affirm all of them, as the position of the Muslims holds. As for accepting some and rejecting others, that is ignorance and blind imitation (*taqlid*).

Then, when He, exalted is He, mentioned what is the foundation of knowing God as brought by Muhammad, peace and blessings be upon him, and what is the foundation of establishing the prophethood of Muhammad (ﷺ), no excuse remained for anyone who disputes with him regarding his religion. Therefore He inevitably followed this with a threat and warning, saying: ﴿Indeed, those who disbelieve in the signs of Allah will have a severe punishment, and Allah is Exalted in Might, the Owner of Retribution.﴾ [Ali ʿImran: 4]. It has thus become clear that no statement can be more precise, more well-ordered, or more excellent in composition than this statement. All praise is due to Allah for guiding this humble one to it, and to Him belongs thanks for His blessings, which have no limit and no end.

Having summarized the overall aim of the discourse, let us now return to the explanation of each of the words.

As for His words ﴿Allah! There is no god but He﴾, this is a refutation of the Christians, because they used to worship ʿIsa, peace be upon him. Allah, exalted is He, made clear that no one deserves worship besides Him.

Then He followed this with what serves as an indication of it, saying: ﴿the Ever-Living, the Self-Subsisting﴾. As for *al-Hayy* (the Ever-Living), it is the one who acts and perceives. As for *al-Qayyum* (the Self-Subsisting), it is the one who subsists by His own essence, and the one who manages the affairs of creation and their interests in what they need for their livelihood, from night and day, heat and cold, winds and rains, and the blessings which none other than Him can provide and none other than Him can count, as He, exalted is He, said: ﴿And if you should count the favor of Allah, you could not enumerate them﴾ [Ibrahim: 34].

ʿUmar, may Allah be pleased with him, recited ﴿al-Hayy al-Qayyum﴾. Qatadah said: *al-Hayy* is the One who does not die, and *al-Qayyum* is the One who stands over His creation with respect to their deeds, their terms, and their provisions. It is related from Saʿid ibn Jubayr: *al-Hayy* is the One who was before every living being, and *al-Qayyum* is the One who has no equal. We have mentioned in the Surah of al-Baqarah that our saying "al-Hayy al-Qayyum" encompasses all the attributes that are considered in divinity.

Since it has been established that the one worshipped must be ever-living and self-subsisting, and since reason (*al-badihah*) and the senses indicate that ʿIsa, peace be upon him, was not ever-living and self-subsisting, and how could he be, when they themselves claim that he was killed and showed fear of death, we know with certainty that ʿIsa was neither a god nor a son of the God, exalted is He and far above what the wrongdoers say, a great exaltation.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 3, verse 3:

As for His saying, may He be exalted, ﴿He has sent down to you the Book with truth, confirming what was before it, and He sent down the Torah and the Gospel﴾.

Know that "the Book" here is the Qur'an, and we have already mentioned its derivation (ishtiqaq) at the beginning of Surat al-Baqarah. The Qur'an was specifically described with tanzil (sending down in stages), while the Torah and the Gospel were described with inzal (sending down all at once), because tanzil implies repetition and multiplicity: God, exalted is He, sent down the Qur'an piece by piece, so the sense of repetition was present in it. As for the Torah and the Gospel, God, exalted is He, sent them down in a single instance, and therefore He described them with inzal. But one may object: this is problematic in light of His saying, ﴿Praise be to God who sent down the Book to His servant﴾ [al-Kahf: 1] and His saying ﴿And with truth We sent it down, and with truth it descended﴾ [al-Isra': 105].

Know that He, exalted is He, described the Qur'an that was sent down with two attributes:

The first attribute: His saying "with truth." Abu Muslim said: it admits of several meanings.

One: that it is true in what it contains of reports about the earlier nations.

Two: that what it contains of promise and threat compels the responsible person to remain upon the true path in beliefs and deeds, and prevents him from following the path of falsehood.

Three: that it is true in the sense that it is a decisive word, and not jest.

Four: al-Asamm said: the meaning is that He sent it down with the truth that is due to Him from His creation, namely worship, thankfulness for blessing, and the manifestation of humility, and what is due among them one to another of justice and fairness in dealings.

Five: that He sent it down with truth, not with corrupt and contradictory meanings, as He said: ﴿He sent down to His servant the Book and did not make in it any crookedness﴾ [al-Kahf: 1], and He said: ﴿And if it had been from other than God, they would have found in it much discrepancy﴾ [al-Nisa': 82].

The second attribute of this Book is His saying ﴿confirming what was before it﴾. The meaning is that it confirms the books of the prophets, upon them be prayers and peace, and what they were informed of from God, mighty and majestic.

Then, in the verse there are two interpretations:

The first: that God, exalted is He, indicated by this the soundness of the Qur'an, for if it had been from other than God it would not have agreed with the rest of the books, since he was unlettered, did not mix with any of the scholars, did not become a disciple of anyone, and did not read anything under anyone. A fabricator in such a state cannot be free of falsehood and distortion; since this was not the case, it is established that he came to know these stories only through the revelation of God, exalted is He.

The second: Abu Muslim said: what is meant is that God, exalted is He, never sent a prophet except with the call to His unity, belief in Him, exalting Him above what is unfitting for Him, commanding justice and goodness, and with the laws that are the welfare of every age. So the Qur'an confirms those books in all of that. There remain two questions concerning the verse:

The first question: how did He call what has passed "before it" (bayna yadayhi)?

The answer: because those reports, by the extent of their manifestation, He named by this name.

The second question: how can it confirm the books that preceded it, when the Qur'an abrogates most of those rulings (naskh)?

The answer: if those books gave good news of the Qur'an and of the Messenger, and indicated that their rulings remain in force until his sending, and that they become abrogated upon the descent of the Qur'an, then they were in agreement with the Qur'an, and so the Qur'an confirmed them. As for what lies outside the rulings, there is no doubt that the Qur'an confirms them, because the proofs of the divine investigations do not differ in this, so it confirms them in the reports found in the Torah and the Gospel.

* *

Then God, exalted is He, said: ﴿and He sent down the Torah and the Gospel﴾, and concerning it there are issues:

The first issue: the author of al-Kashshaf said: "al-Tawrah" and "al-Injil" are two non-Arabic (a'jamiyyan) names, and occupying oneself with their derivation is not beneficial. al-Hasan read "wal-Anjil" with a fatha on the hamza, and this is evidence of their being non-Arabic, because the pattern af'il with a fatha on the hamza is absent from the patterns of the Arabs. Know that this statement is the truth from which there is no escape; nevertheless, we shall transmit the words of the men of letters concerning it.

As for the word "al-Tawrah," there are three investigations:

The first investigation: concerning its derivation. al-Farra' said: "al-Tawrah" means light and radiance, from the Arab saying: warā al-zand yarī when it strikes and the fire appears. God, exalted is He, said: ﴿By the strikers, striking sparks﴾ [al-'Adiyat: 2], and they say: "waraytu bika zanadi," meaning: good appeared to me through you. So the Torah was named by this name because the truth became manifest through it. And His saying, exalted is He, confirms this meaning: ﴿And We gave Moses and Aaron the Criterion and a light﴾ [al-Anbiya': 48].

The second investigation: concerning its pattern, they have three opinions:

The first opinion: al-Farra' said: the origin of "al-Tawrah" is tawriyah, on the pattern taf'alah with a fatha on the ta', a sukun on the waw, and a fatha on the ra' and the ya'; but the ya' became an alif because it was vocalized and what preceded it was open.

The second opinion: al-Farra' said: it is also permissible that it be tif'alah on the pattern of tawfiyah and tawsiyah, so its origin would be tiriyah, except that the ra' was transferred from kasra to fatha according to the dialect of Tayy, for they say, of jariyah: jara'ah, and of nasiyah: nasa'ah. The poet said:

fa-ma al-dunya bi-baqatin li-hayyin wa-ma hayyun 'ala al-dunya bi-baqi
(So the world does not endure for a living thing, nor does any living thing remain upon the world.)

The third opinion, which is the opinion of al-Khalil and the Basrans: its origin is wawriyah, on the pattern fawalah, then the first waw was changed to a ta', and this change is frequent in their speech, such as: tujah, turath, tukhamah, and tuklan. Then the ya' was changed to an alif because it was vocalized and what preceded it was open, so it became "tawrah," and it was written with a ya' according to the original form of the word.

Then they criticized al-Farra's opinion. As for the first: they said: this pattern is rare, whereas fawalah is common, such as sawma'ah, hawsalah, and dawsarah, and reliance on the more common is preferable. As for the second: it is only complete by reading the word according to the dialect of Tayy, and the Qur'an was not revealed in it at all.

The third investigation: concerning "al-Tawrah," there are two readings, imalah (inclination) and tafkhim (emphasis). Whoever emphasizes does so because the ra' is a letter that prevents imalah due to the trilling (takrir) in it. And God knows best.

As for "al-Injil," there are several opinions:

The first: al-Zajjaj said: it is if'il from al-najl, which is the origin: it is said, "God curse his najilayh," meaning his parents. That book was named by this name because it is the origin to which that religion is referred.

The second: some people said: al-Injil is derived from the Arab saying: najaltu al-shay' when you extract it and make it manifest, and water that comes out of a well is called najl, and it is said: istanjala al-wadi, when water came out of the seep. So the Gospel was named Injil because God made the truth manifest through it.

The third: Abu 'Amr al-Shaybani said: al-tanajul is al-tanazu' (dispute), so that book was named al-Injil because the people disputed concerning it.

The fourth: that it is from al-najl, which is the breadth of the eye, and from it comes "ta'natun najla'" (a wide wound). It was named by this because it is breadth, light and radiance that He brought forth for them.

I say: the matter of these men of letters is strange, as if they required that every word be derived from something else. Were that so, it would necessarily lead either to an infinite regress (tasalsul) or to circularity (dawr). Since both are invalid, it must be acknowledged that there must be words established by primary imposition (wad' awwal), so that all other words are derived from them. And if that is so, why should it not be permissible, regarding this word which they have made derived from that other, that the origin be this and the branch be that other? And who informed them that this is the branch and that is the origin? Perhaps what they make a branch and derivative is most famous, and what they make the origin is most obscure. Furthermore, if the Torah was only named "Torah" because of its manifestness, and the Gospel was only named "Injil" because it is an origin, then it would be necessary that everything that becomes manifest be named Torah, and so all events would have to be named Torah; and it would be necessary that everything that is the origin of something else be named Injil, so clay would be the origin of the jug and thus would have to be Injil, and gold is the origin of the ring, and thread the origin of the garment, so these things would have to be named Injil; and it is known that this is not the case. Moreover, when these objections are raised against them, they must have recourse to imposition, and say: the Arabs specified these two words for these two things by way of imposition. And if the intended purpose is only attained in the end by returning to the imposition of the language, why do we not rely upon it at the outset and relieve ourselves of plunging into these words? Also, al-Tawrah and al-Injil are two non-Arabic names, one of which is in Hebrew and the other in Syriac; how is it fitting for a sensible person to occupy himself with fitting them to the patterns of the Arabic language? Thus it becomes clear that the better course for the sensible person is not to turn to these investigations. And God knows best.

**Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 3, verse 4:**

As for His words, exalted is He, ﴿before this, as guidance for mankind﴾.

Know that He, exalted is He, stated that He sent down the Torah and the Gospel before He sent down the Qur'an, and then stated that He sent them down only as guidance for mankind. Al-Ka'bi said: This verse refutes the view of those who claim that the Qur'an is blindness for the disbelievers and is not guidance for them. The meaning of His words ﴿and it is blindness for them﴾ [Fussilat: 44] is that, at the time of its revelation, they chose blindness, in a figurative sense, like the words of Noah, peace be upon him, ﴿but my call only increased them in flight﴾ [Nuh: 6], when they fled from him.

Know that His words ﴿guidance for mankind﴾ admit of two interpretations. The first is that this refers only to the Torah and the Gospel. On this reading, He has described the Qur'an as truth and described the Torah and the Gospel as guidance, and the two descriptions are close in meaning.

If it is said: He described the Qur'an at the beginning of Surat al-Baqarah as guidance for the God-conscious, so why does He not describe it as guidance here?

We say: There is a subtle point in this. We mentioned in Surat al-Baqarah that He said ﴿a guidance for the God-conscious﴾ [al-Baqarah: 2] because they are the ones who benefit from it, so in that respect it is guidance for them and not for others. Here, however, the debate was with the Christians, and they do not take guidance from the Qur'an. Therefore He did not say here that the Qur'an is guidance, but rather said that it is truth in itself, whether or not they accept it. As for the Torah and the Gospel, they believe in their authenticity and claim that we only fabricate about our religion based upon them. Therefore God, exalted is He, described them as guidance, for the sake of this argument. This is what came to mind, and God knows best.

[Page 140]

The second view, which is the view of most scholars, is that God, exalted is He, described the three Books as guidance. This description refers to everything mentioned before and is not restricted to the Torah and the Gospel. God knows best what He intends.

* *
* * *

Then He said: ﴿and He sent down the Criterion﴾.

Among the majority of the exegetes (tafsir scholars) there are several opinions concerning it. The first is that what is meant is the Psalms (Zabur), as He said: ﴿and We gave David the Psalms﴾ [al-Nisa': 163]. The second is that what is meant is the Qur'an, and He repeated it to glorify its status and to praise it for being that which distinguishes between truth and falsehood. Or it may be said that He repeated its mention to show that He sent it down after the Torah and the Gospel, so that it would be a criterion between what the Jews and Christians disagreed about, of truth and falsehood. On this reading, there is no repetition.

The third view, which is the view of most scholars, is that what is meant is that God, exalted is He, just as He made the three Books guidance and proof, also made them a distinguishing criterion between the lawful and the unlawful and the rest of the laws. Thus this statement indicates that God, exalted is He, through these Books, clarified what is required by reason and by revelation. This is the sum of what the people of tafsir have said regarding this verse. In my view, however, it is problematic. As for interpreting it as referring to the Psalms, that is far-fetched, because the Psalms contain none of the laws and rulings; in fact, they contain nothing but exhortations. Describing the Torah and the Gospel as the Criterion, given that they include proofs and clarifications of rulings, is more fitting than describing the Psalms with it. As for the second view, interpreting it as referring to the Qur'an, that is far-fetched because His words ﴿and He sent down the Criterion﴾ are a conjunction upon what precedes them, and the conjoined element must differ from that to which it is conjoined. The Qur'an has already been mentioned before this, so this indicates that this Criterion must be different from the Qur'an. For this same reason the weakness of the third view becomes apparent, because the description of these Books as distinguishing between truth and falsehood is an attribute of these Books, and conjoining an attribute to the thing described, although it has occurred in some rare poetry, is weak and far from the eloquence fitting to the speech of God, exalted is He. The view I prefer in interpreting this verse is a fourth view, namely that what is meant by this Criterion is the miracles that God, exalted is He, attached to the sending down of these Books. This is because, when they brought these Books and claimed that they were books sent down to them from God, exalted is He, they needed proof for this claim so that a distinction would arise between their claim and the claim of liars. When God, exalted is He, manifested miracles in accordance with their claim, the distinction between the claim of the truthful and the claim of the liar was established. Thus the miracle is the Criterion. When God, exalted is He, mentioned that He had sent down the Book with truth, and that He had sent down the Torah and the Gospel before that, He clarified that He had sent down along with them that which is the true Criterion, namely the overpowering miracle that testifies to their authenticity and makes the distinction between them and all other differing books. This is what I hold regarding the tafsir of this verse. Even if none of the exegetes had mentioned it, interpreting the words of God, exalted is He, in this way yields strength of meaning, eloquence of expression, and soundness of arrangement and composition, whereas the views they mentioned contradict all of that. Therefore what we have mentioned is more fitting, and God knows best what He intends.

Know that when He, glory be to Him and exalted is He, established in these few words everything related to knowing God and everything related to establishing prophethood, He followed this with a warning, as a deterrent to those who turn away from these dazzling proofs, and said:

* *
﴿Indeed, those who disbelieve in the signs of God will have a severe punishment, and God is Mighty, Owner of Retribution.﴾

Know that some exegetes restricted this to the Christians, thereby confining the general wording to its occasion of revelation. But the scholarly exegetes said: The specificity of the occasion of revelation does not prevent the generality of the wording, so it encompasses everyone who turns away from the proofs of God, exalted is He.

* * *
Then He said: ﴿and God is Mighty, Owner of Retribution﴾.

Al-'Aziz (the Mighty) is the Overpowering who cannot be overpowered, and al-intiqam (retribution) is punishment. It is said: "intaqama minhu intiqaman," meaning he punished him. Al-Layth said: It is said, "I was not pleased with him until I took retribution from him (naqamtu minhu) and avenged myself (intaqamtu)," when one repays him with punishment for what he did. Al-'Aziz is an indication of complete power over punishment, and Dhu'l-intiqam (Owner of Retribution) is an indication of His being the one who actually inflicts the punishment. The first is an attribute of the Essence, and the second is an attribute of action. God knows best.

﴿Indeed, nothing on earth or in heaven is hidden from Allah﴾ ﴿It is He who forms you in the wombs however He wills. There is no god but Him, the Almighty, the All-Wise﴾. Know that this statement admits of two interpretations.

The first interpretation: when He mentioned that He is the Qayyum (the Sustainer, the One who stands by Himself and sustains all else), and the Qayyum is the One who manages the welfare and affairs of creation, this status is not complete except through the combination of two matters:

The first: that He knows their needs in every quantity and quality.

The second: that He is such that whenever He knows the aspects of their needs, He is able to meet them.

The first is not complete unless He knows all that is knowable, and the second is not complete unless He is able over all that is possible. So His saying ﴿Indeed, nothing on earth or in heaven is hidden from Allah﴾ points to the perfection of His knowledge, which encompasses all that is knowable. Then He necessarily knows the measures of needs and the degrees of necessities. No question distracts Him from another question, and the matter is not confused for Him because of the multitude of questions of those who ask. Then His saying ﴿It is He who forms you in the wombs however He wills﴾ points to His being able over all that is possible. Then He is able to secure the welfare and benefits of all creation. When these two matters are established, His being the one who stands by justice and sustains all possible and existing things becomes evident.

Then there is another subtle point in it: His saying ﴿Indeed, nothing on earth or in heaven is hidden from Allah﴾, as we have mentioned, points to the perfection of His knowledge, glorified is He. The path to establishing that He is knowing cannot be transmitted testimony (sam‘, i.e., revelation or report), because knowing the soundness of transmitted testimony depends on knowing that He is knowing of all that is knowable. Rather, the only path to it is the rational proof (dalil ‘aqli). That is, we say: the acts of Allah are firm and perfectly made, and a firm and perfectly made act indicates that its doer is knowing. Since the proof that He is knowing is what we have mentioned, then when He claimed that He knows all that is knowable with His saying ﴿Indeed, nothing on earth or in heaven is hidden from Allah﴾, He followed it with the rational proof that indicates this, which is that He is the One who formed in the darkness of the wombs this wondrous structure and strange composition, and assembled it from organs differing in shape, nature and quality: some are bones, some are cartilage, some are arteries, some are veins, and some are muscles. Then He joined some of them to others in the best arrangement and the most perfect composition. This indicates the perfection of His power, in that He is able to create from a drop of semen these organs differing in natures, shapes and colours. It also indicates that He is knowing, since a firm act does not proceed except from one who knows. When it is established that He, exalted is He, knows all that is knowable and is able over all that is possible, it is established that He is the Sustainer of all originated and possible things. Thus it becomes clear that this is like a confirmation of what He mentioned first, that He is the Ever-Living, the Sustainer. Whoever reflects on these subtleties knows that no statement can be conceived that is more beneficial, better arranged, or more effective in hearts than these words.

The second interpretation: these verses are understood in light of their occasion of revelation (sabab al-nuzul). The Christians claimed the divinity of ‘Isa (Jesus), peace be upon him, and relied in that on two kinds of doubts (shubah, pl. shubah). One kind is doubts derived from observed premises, and the second kind is doubts derived from premises of argumentation (ilzami, i.e., premises imposed by the opponent's own position).

As for the first kind of doubts: their reliance in that is on two matters. One of them relates to knowledge, and the second relates to power.

As for what relates to knowledge: ‘Isa, peace be upon him, used to inform of hidden matters, and he would say to this one: "You ate such-and-such in your house," and to that one: "You made such-and-such in your house." This kind of Christian doubt relates to knowledge.

As for the second of their doubts, it relates to power: ‘Isa, peace be upon him, used to give life to the dead, heal the blind and the leper, and create from clay something like the shape of a bird, then breathe into it, and it would become a bird by the permission of Allah. This kind of Christian doubt relates to power. The Christians have no doubts on the question other than these two kinds. As for the first doubt, which relates to knowledge, namely their saying that he informed of hidden matters and therefore must be a god, Allah answered it with His saying ﴿Indeed, nothing on earth or in heaven is hidden from Allah﴾. The explanation of the answer is that being knowing of some unseen matters does not necessarily entail being a god, because it is possible that he knew that only through revelation from Allah to him and Allah's teaching him that. But his lack of encompassing some unseen matters decisively indicates that he is not a god, because the god is the One to whom nothing on earth or in heaven is hidden. The god is the one who is a creator, and the creator must necessarily know what he creates. It is known by necessity that ‘Isa, peace be upon him, was not knowing of all knowable and hidden matters. How so, when the Christians say that he displayed dread of death? If he had known all the unseen, he would have known that the people wanted to seize and kill him, and that this would harm and pain him, so he would have fled from them before they reached him. Since he did not know this unseen matter, it became clear that he did not know all knowable and hidden matters, while the god is the One to whom none of the knowable things is hidden. So it is necessary to conclude with certainty that ‘Isa, peace be upon him, was not a god. Thus it is established that deducing from knowing some of the unseen does not indicate the attainment of divinity, whereas ignorance of some of the unseen decisively indicates the absence of divinity. This is the answer to the first kind of doubts related to knowledge.

The meaning is that the occurrence of giving life and causing death in accordance with his word in some forms does not indicate that he is a god, since it is possible that Allah, exalted is He, honoured him with that giving of life to display His miracle and to honour him.

As for the inability to give life and cause death in some forms, it indicates the absence of divinity. This is because the god is the One who is able to form in the wombs, from a small drop of semen, this wondrous structure and strange composition. It is known that ‘Isa, peace be upon him, was not able to give life and cause death in this manner. And how could he be, since if he had been able to do so, he would have caused those who seized him, according to the Christians' claim, and killed him, to die? Thus it is established that the occurrence of giving life and causing death in accordance with his word in some forms does not indicate that he is a god, whereas the non-occurrence of these two in accordance with his will in all forms indicates that he was not a god. It became clear from what has been mentioned that this second doubt too is invalid.

As for the second kind of doubts, these are doubts built on premises of argumentation (ilzami), and their outcome returns to two kinds.

**Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 3, verse 7 (part 1 of 4)**

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿He it is who has sent down to you the Book. In it are verses that are decisive (muhkamat), they are the foundation of the Book, and others are ambiguous (mutashabihat). As for those in whose hearts is deviation, they follow what is ambiguous in it, seeking discord and seeking its interpretation. None knows its interpretation except God, and those firm in knowledge say: "We believe in it; all of it is from our Lord." And none takes heed except people of understanding.﴾

Know that in this verse there are several issues.

The first issue: We have mentioned, regarding the connection of His saying ﴿Indeed, nothing on earth or in heaven is hidden from God﴾ with what precedes it, two possibilities. The first is that it serves as an affirmation of His being al-Qayyum (the Self-Subsisting Sustainer). The second is that it is a reply to the doubts of the Christians. On the first possibility, we say: He, Exalted is He, intended to show that He is al-Qayyum and that He sustains the interests of creation. The interests of creation are of two kinds: bodily and spiritual. As for the bodily, the most noble of them is the proper balancing of the physical constitution and the harmonious ordering of temperament in the best forms and most perfect shapes. This is what is meant by His saying ﴿He it is who fashions you in the wombs﴾. As for the spiritual, the most noble of them is knowledge, by which the soul becomes like a polished mirror in which the forms of all existing things are reflected. This is what is meant by His saying ﴿He it is who has sent down to you the Book﴾. On the second possibility, we have mentioned that among the Christians' doubts is their reliance on what came in the Qur'an, in His saying, Exalted is He, describing Jesus, peace be upon him: "He is the Spirit of God and His Word." So God, Exalted is He, showed through this verse that the Qur'an contains the decisive and the ambiguous, and that relying on the ambiguous is not permissible. This is what relates to the manner of the composition, and it is in the utmost beauty and soundness.

The second issue: Know that the Qur'an indicates that it is decisive in its entirety, and indicates that it is ambiguous in its entirety, and indicates that some of it is decisive and some of it is ambiguous.

As for what indicates that it is decisive in its entirety, it is His saying ﴿Alif, Lam, Ra. These are the verses of the Wise Book﴾ [Yunus: 1] and ﴿Alif, Lam, Ra. A Book whose verses have been made firm﴾ [Hud: 1]. In these two verses He mentioned that all of it is decisive. The meaning of "decisive" in this sense is that it is a true speech, eloquent in its wording and sound in its meanings. Every saying and speech that exists, the Qur'an is superior to it in eloquence of expression and strength of meaning, and no one is able to produce a speech that equals the Qur'an in these two qualities. The Arabs say of a sound structure and a firm knot that cannot be untied: "muhkam" (firm). This is the meaning of describing all of it as decisive.

As for what indicates that it is ambiguous in its entirety, it is His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿A Book whose parts resemble one another, oft-repeated﴾ [Az-Zumar: 23]. The meaning is that some of it resembles the rest in excellence and confirms the rest. To this refers His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Had it been from other than God, they would have found in it much contradiction﴾ [An-Nisa: 82], meaning that some of it would have been contrary to the other, and the arrangement of the speech would have varied in eloquence and weakness.

As for what indicates that some of it is decisive and some of it is ambiguous, it is this verse which we are now interpreting. We must explain the decisive (muhkam) and the ambiguous (mutashabih) according to the original linguistic usage, and then according to their usage in the terminology of the Shari'ah. As for the decisive (muhkam), the Arabs say: "hakamtu," "hakkamtu," and "ahkamtu," meaning "I repelled" or "I prevented." The judge (hakim) prevents the wrongdoer from wrongdoing. The "hakama" (bridle ring) of the bridle is that which prevents the horse from agitation. In the hadith of al-Nakha'i: "Restrain the orphan as you restrain your child," meaning prevent him from corruption. Jarir said: "Restrain your foolish ones," meaning prevent them. A "muhkam" structure is one that is firm and prevents whoever approaches it. Wisdom (hikmah) was named "hikmah" because it prevents one from what is not fitting. As for the ambiguous (mutashabih), it is that one of two things resembles the other in such a way that the mind is unable to distinguish between them. God, Exalted is He, said: ﴿Indeed, the cows have become confused for us﴾ [Al-Baqarah: 70]. He also said, describing the fruits of Paradise: ﴿And they will be given something resembling it﴾ [Al-Baqarah: 25], meaning similar in appearance and different in taste. And God, Exalted is He, said: ﴿Their hearts have become alike﴾ [Al-Baqarah: 118]. From this one says: "The matter became confused for me (ishtabaha 'alayya) when I did not differentiate between the two." People who perform tricks with toys are called "the people of doubts (shubhah)." And the Prophet, peace be upon him, said: "The lawful is clear and the unlawful is clear, and between them are matters that are ambiguous (mutashabihat)." In another narration it is "mushtabihat" (doubtful).

Then, since it is in the nature of two similar things that a person is unable to distinguish between them, everything that a person cannot be guided to has been called "ambiguous," by applying the name of the cause to the effect. Similarly, the "mushkil" (difficult) was so named because it has become "ashkala," meaning it entered into the form of something else, resembling it and being like it. Then the term is applied to anything obscure, even if its obscurity is not from this aspect. It may also be said that it is that of which one does not know whether its truth is affirmed or denied, and the judgment of its affirmation is equal to the judgment of its negation in reason and understanding, resembling it, and not distinguished from the other by any greater preponderance. Therefore, what is not known has rightly been called "ambiguous." This is the explanation of the decisive and the ambiguous according to the original linguistic usage. Now we say:

People have multiplied the aspects of interpreting the decisive and the ambiguous. We shall mention the summarized aspect on which most verifiers agree, and then after it we shall mention the sayings of people on the matter. We say:

[Page 146]

A word that is set to a meaning either admits of something other than that meaning or does not. If the word is set to a meaning and does not admit of anything else, this is the explicit text (nass). If it admits of something else, then either its admission of one of the two meanings is preponderant over the other, or it is not so, but its admission of both is equal. If its admission of one is preponderant over the other, that word is called "apparent" (zahir) with respect to the preponderant meaning and "interpreted" (mu'awwal) with respect to the less probable meaning. If its admission of both is equal, the word is called "shared" (mushtarak) with respect to both together, and "ambiguous" (mujmal) with respect to each one of them specifically. It has thus emerged from the division we have described that a word is either an explicit text (nass), or apparent (zahir), or interpreted (mu'awwal), or shared (mushtarak), or ambiguous (mujmal). The explicit text and the apparent share the feature of having a preponderance, except that the explicit text is a strong preponderance that excludes the other, while the apparent is a preponderance that does not exclude the other. This shared element is what is called the decisive (muhkam).

As for the ambiguous (mujmal) and the interpreted (mu'awwal), they share the feature that the word's indication of it is not preponderant. Even if it is not preponderant, it is not less probable. The interpreted, although not preponderant, is less probable, but not according to the individual proof alone. This shared element is what is called the ambiguous (mutashabih), because the lack of understanding is present in both categories. We have explained that this is called ambiguous either because what is not known has a negation that resembles the affirmation in the mind, or because what becomes ambiguous ceases to be known. So the term "ambiguous" is applied to what is not known, by applying the name of the cause to the effect. This is the established discussion of the decisive and the ambiguous.

Then know that when a word is equal with respect to two concepts, the mind pauses there, like the word "qur'" (which means both menstruation and purity) with respect to menstruation and purity. Difficulty arises only when a word, by its original setting, is preponderant in one of two meanings and less probable in the other, and then the preponderant meaning proves to be false while the less probable meaning proves to be true. An example from the Qur'an is His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿When We intend to destroy a town, We command its affluent ones, and they commit wickedness therein, and the word takes effect against it﴾ [Al-Isra: 16]. The apparent meaning of this speech is that they are commanded to commit wickedness. Its decisive meaning is His saying: ﴿Indeed, God does not command immorality﴾ [Al-A'raf: 28], as a refutation of the disbelievers in what is reported of them: ﴿And when they commit an immorality, they say: "We found our fathers doing it, and God commanded us to do it."﴾ [Al-A'raf: 28]. Likewise His saying: ﴿They forgot God, so He forgot them﴾ [At-Tawbah: 67]. The apparent meaning of forgetting is that which is the opposite of knowledge, and its less probable meaning is abandonment. The decisive verse concerning it is His saying: ﴿And your Lord is not forgetful﴾ [Maryam: 64] and His saying: ﴿My Lord neither errs nor forgets﴾ [Ta-Ha: 52].

Know that this is a great matter. Each of the adherents of the schools claims that the verses agreeing with his doctrine are decisive, and that the verses agreeing with the view of his opponent are ambiguous. The Mu'tazili says that His saying ﴿So whoever wills, let him believe, and whoever wills, let him disbelieve﴾ [Al-Kahf: 29] is decisive, and His saying ﴿And you do not will except that God wills, the Lord of the worlds﴾ [At-Takwir: 29] is ambiguous. The Sunni reverses the matter in this regard. Therefore, there must be a principle here to which one refers in this chapter. We say: When a word admits of two meanings, and is preponderant with respect to one and less probable with respect to the other, if we interpret it according to the preponderant meaning and do not interpret it according to the less probable meaning, this is the decisive. But if we interpret it according to the less probable meaning and do not interpret it according to the preponderant meaning, this is the ambiguous. We say: Turning a word from the preponderant to the less probable meaning requires a separate proof, and that separate proof is either verbal or rational.

As for the first kind: We say that this holds only if there is a conflict between those two verbal proofs. When a conflict occurs between them, abandoning the apparent meaning of one in favor of the apparent meaning of the other is no more justified than the reverse, unless it is said that one of them is definitive in its indication and the other is not definitive, in which case preponderance is achieved; or it is said that each of them, although preponderant, one of them is more preponderant, in which case preponderance is achieved. However, we say:

As for the first, it is invalid, because verbal indications are never absolutely definitive. Every verbal proof depends on the transmission of languages, and the transmission of the forms of grammar and morphology, and depends on the absence of homonymy, the absence of metaphor, the absence of specification, the absence of ellipsis, and the absence of a transmitted or rational counter-proof. All of this is presumed, and what depends on the presumed is more fitting to be presumed. Thus it is established that none of the verbal proofs is definitive.

Part 2 of the commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 3, verse 7:

As for the second point, which is to say: one of the two proofs is stronger than the second proof, even though the basic possibility of figurative meaning exists in both of them together. This is correct. But on this assumption, turning the verbal proof away from its apparent meaning towards the less probable meaning becomes merely conjectural (ẓanniyyan), and such a thing is not permissible to rely upon in usul (fundamental doctrinal) matters. Rather, it is permissible to rely upon it in furu' (legal) matters. Thus it is established by what we have mentioned that turning a word away from its preponderant meaning towards its less probable meaning in definitive (qat'i) matters is not permissible except when there is a definitive rational proof that what the apparent wording indicates is impossible. We know in general that using a word in its less probable meaning is permissible when it is impossible to take it in its apparent sense. At this point, interpretation (ta'wil) becomes necessary. It is thus clear that there is no way to turn a word away from its preponderant meaning towards its less probable meaning except by means of establishing a decisive rational indication that its preponderant meaning is rationally impossible. Then, once this indication has been established and the responsible person (mukallaf) knows that the meaning intended by God Most High from this word is not what its apparent sense indicates, at this point he does not need to know what that less probable meaning which is the intended one is, because the way to that is only by preferring one figurative meaning over another figurative meaning and preferring one interpretation over another interpretation. Such preference is not possible except through verbal indications, and verbal indications, as we have explained, are conjectural, especially the indications used to prefer one less probable meaning over another less probable meaning, which are in an extremely weak state. All of this yields only weak conjecture, and relying on such indications in definitive matters is impossible. Therefore, on the basis of this firm verification, our position is that after establishing definitive proofs that taking the word in its apparent sense is impossible, it is not permissible to engage in specifying the interpretation. This is the final point of what we have gathered on this subject, and God is the guardian of guidance and right direction.
* * *
The third issue: on relating the opinions of people concerning the muhkam and the mutashabih. The first: what is transmitted from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him and his father, that he said: The muhkamat are the three verses in Surat al-An'am, ﴿Say: Come, I will recite﴾ [al-An'am: 151] to the end of the three verses. The mutashabihat are those that were confusing to the Jews, and they are the names of the letters of the alphabet mentioned at the beginnings of the surahs. That is because they calculated them by the abjad (jummal) reckoning, seeking to extract from them the duration of this community's existence, so the matter became confused and ambiguous for them. I say: The obligations sent down from God Most High are divided into two categories. Among them are those that cannot differ from one revealed law to another, such as the command to obey God Most High, and refraining from injustice, lying, ignorance and killing a soul without right. And among them are those that differ from one law to another, such as the numbers of prayers, the measures of zakat, the conditions of sale and marriage, and other such things. The first category is what Ibn 'Abbas called the muhkam, because the three verses in Surat al-An'am comprise this category. As for the mutashabih, it is what we have named the mujmal (ambiguous), namely that where the indication of the word, in relation to it and to other than it, is equal, for the indication of these words towards all the aspects by which these words are explained is equal, without a separate indicator, as we summarized at the beginning of Surat al-Baqarah.
Page 148
The second opinion, which is also transmitted from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him and his father: the muhkam is the nasikh (abrogating), and the mutashabih is the mansukh (abrogated).
The third opinion: al-Asamm said: The muhkam is that whose indication is clear and manifest, such as what God Most High has informed of concerning the creation of humans, in His saying: ﴿We made the drop a clot﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 14], and His saying ﴿And We made from water every living thing﴾ [al-Anbiya': 30], and His saying ﴿And He sent down from the sky water, and brought forth thereby fruits as provision for you﴾ [al-Baqarah: 22]. And the mutashabih is that which requires reflection and contemplation to be known, such as the judgment that He will resurrect them after they have become dust. Had they reflected, the mutashabih would have become muhkam for them, because whoever is able to originate creation first is able to restore it a second time.
Know that al-Asamm's statement is not condensed. If by his saying "the muhkam is that whose indications are clear" he means that the muhkam is that whose word's indication of its meaning is determinate and preponderant, and the mutashabih is that which is not so, and it is either the ambiguous (mujmal) of equal probability or the interpreted (mu'awwal) of lesser probability, then this is what we mentioned first. But if he means that the muhkam is that whose meaning is known to be correct without a proof, then on his view the muhkam becomes what is known to be correct by necessity of reason, and the mutashabih becomes what is known to be correct by a proof of reason. On this view, the entire Qur'an would become mutashabih, because His saying ﴿We made the drop a clot﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 14] is a matter whose correctness requires rational proofs to know. The people of nature say: the cause of that is the natures and the elements, or the influences of the stars, and the combinations and mixtures of the elements. Just as establishing resurrection and gathering requires proof, so too attributing these events to God Most High requires proof. Perhaps al-Asamm means: although all these things require proof, they are divided into those in which the proof is manifest, such that its premises are few, arranged and clear, with error being safe from it except rarely, and those in which the proof is hidden, with many premises not arranged. The first category is the muhkam and the second is the mutashabih.
The fourth opinion: that everything whose knowledge can be attained, whether by a clear proof or a hidden proof, is the muhkam, and everything for which there is no way to knowledge is the mutashabih. Such is the knowledge of the time of the Hour, and the knowledge of the measures of reward and punishment concerning the responsible persons. A parallel to this is His saying Most High: ﴿They ask you about the Hour, when it will take place﴾ [al-A'raf: 187].
