The fourth issue: on the benefits for which some of the Qur'an was made muhkam and some of it mutashabih.
Know that among the heretics (mulhidah) is one who criticized the Qur'an because of its containing mutashabihat, and said: You say that the obligations of creation are tied to this Qur'an until the Hour arrives. Then we see it such that every possessor of a doctrine clings to it for his doctrine. The Jabri (determinist) clings to verses of compulsion, such as His saying Most High: ﴿And We have placed over their hearts coverings lest they understand it, and in their ears deafness﴾ [al-An'am: 25]. The Qadari (libertarian) says: rather this is the doctrine of the disbelievers, by the proof that He Most High related that of the disbelievers in the context of blaming them, in His saying ﴿And they said: Our hearts are in coverings from what you call us to, and in our ears is deafness﴾ [Fussilat: 5], and in another place ﴿And they said: Our hearts are uncircumcised﴾ [al-Baqarah: 88]. Likewise, the affirmer of the vision (of God) clings to His saying ﴿Faces on that day will be radiant, looking at their Lord﴾ [al-Qiyamah: 22-23], and the negator clings to His saying ﴿Eyesight does not perceive Him﴾ [al-An'am: 103]. The affirmer of direction clings to His saying ﴿They fear their Lord above them﴾
Page 149
[al-Nahl: 50], and His saying ﴿The Merciful is established upon the Throne﴾ [Ta-Ha: 5]. The negator clings to His saying ﴿There is nothing like unto Him﴾ [al-Shura: 11]. Then each one names the verses agreeing with his doctrine "muhkam" and the verses disagreeing with his doctrine "mutashabih." Often the matter, in preferring some over others, ends in hidden preferences and weak aspects. So how is it fitting for the Wise to make the Book, which is the reference for the whole religion until the Hour, to be like this? Would it not be closer to achieving the purpose if He had made it manifest and clear, free of these mutashabihat?
Know that the scholars have mentioned several aspects regarding the benefits of the mutashabihat:
The first aspect: when the mutashabihat exist, reaching the truth becomes harder and more difficult, and increased hardship necessitates greater reward. God Most High said: ﴿Or do you think that you will enter Paradise while Allah has not yet known those of you who strove and known the patient﴾ [Al 'Imran: 142].
The second aspect: if the Qur'an were entirely muhkam, it would conform only to one doctrine, and its explicit statement would invalidate everything other than that doctrine, and this would repel the adherents of the other doctrines from accepting it and from examining it. Benefit from it was attained only because it contains both the muhkam and the mutashabih. In that case, each adherent of a doctrine hopes to find in it what strengthens his doctrine and supports his view. Thus all the adherents of the doctrines look into it, and each adherent of a doctrine strives to reflect upon it. When they exert themselves in this, the muhkamat become explainers of the mutashabihat. By this means the one in error is freed from his falsehood and reaches the truth.
The third aspect: when the Qur'an contains both the muhkam and the mutashabih, the one who examines it needs to seek help from rational proof, and at that point he is freed from the darkness of imitation (taqlid) and reaches the light of inference and clear evidence. But if it were entirely muhkam, he would not need to hold to rational proofs, and in that case he would remain in ignorance and imitation.
The fourth aspect: since the Qur'an contains both the muhkam and the mutashabih, people needed to learn the methods of interpretation and to prefer some over others, and learning this required acquiring many sciences, including the science of language, grammar, and the science of the principles of jurisprudence. Had the matter not been so, a person would not need to acquire these many sciences. So the presence of these mutashabihat was for these many benefits.
The fifth aspect, which is the strongest reason in this matter: the Qur'an is a book that comprehensively addresses both the elite and the common people, and the natures of the common people generally recoil from grasping realities. Whoever hears from the common people at first the affirmation of an existent that is neither a body, nor located in space, nor pointed to, supposes that this is non-existence and negation, and falls into negation of attributes (ta'til). So it was most fitting that they be addressed with words indicating some aspects that correspond to what they imagine and conceive, mixed with what indicates the clear truth. The first category, which they are addressed with at the beginning, is among the mutashabihat, and the second category, which is revealed to them at the end, is the muhkamat. This is what occurred to us on this subject, and God knows best His intent.
Having understood these discussions, let us return to the exegesis.
As for His saying Most High: ﴿It is He who has sent down to you the Book﴾, what is meant by it is the Qur'an. ﴿Among it are muhkam verses﴾, and they are those

whose indicated meanings are confirmed either by decisive rational proofs, which is the case in definitive matters, or whose indicated meanings are free from stronger counter-arguments.

Then He said: ﴿They are the mother of the Book﴾, and concerning this there are two questions.
The first question: what is the meaning of the muhkam being a "mother" to the mutashabih?

al-Jawab: The umm (أُمّ, "mother") in the true sense of the language is the origin from which a thing comes into being. Since the muhkamat are understood in and of themselves, while the mutashabihat become understood only with the help of the muhkamat, the muhkamat are therefore like the mother of the mutashabihat. It has also been said: what occurred in the Gospel concerning the mention of the Father, namely that He said: the Eternal Creator, the One who brings things into being, by whom creatures subsist and by whom they remain until He resurrects them, so He expressed this meaning by the term "Father," from the standpoint that the father is the one from whom the begetting of the son occurs. Then in the translation there occurred something that suggested the fatherhood arising from the standpoint of birth. Thus His saying ﴿It is not for God to take a son﴾ [Maryam: 35] became muhkam, because its meaning is confirmed by decisive rational proofs, while His saying "Jesus is the Spirit of God and His Word" is among the mutashabihat which must be referred back to that muhkam.

The second question: Why did He say ﴿Umm al-Kitab﴾ and not "ummahat al-Kitab" (mothers of the Book)?

al-Jawab: The totality of the muhkamat is considered as one thing, and the totality of the mutashabihat as another thing, and one of them is the mother of the other. A parallel to this is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And We made the son of Mary and his mother a sign﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 50], and He did not say "two signs." He said that in the sense that their totality is one sign. Likewise here.
* * *
Then He said: ﴿And others are mutashabihat﴾. You have already known the reality of the mutashabihat. Al-Khalil and Sibawayh said: "Ukhar" (أُخَرُ, "others") differs from its sisters in one ruling, because ukhar is the plural of ukhra, and ukhra is the feminine of akhar, and akhar is on the pattern of af'al. Whatever is on the pattern of af'al is used either with "min" or with al (the definite article). One says: Zayd is afdal than 'Amr, or Zayd al-afdal. So al and min are interchangeable in the pattern af'al. The analogy would have been to say: Zayd akhar min 'Amr, or to say: Zayd al-akhar. But they omitted the word "min" from it, because its form implied the meaning of "min," so they dropped it, being satisfied with the indication of the word upon it. And al is interchangeable with min, so al also dropped. Then, when it became permissible to use it without al, it became ukhar, and ukhar is its plural. Thus this word became exceptional with respect to the rule of its counterparts in dropping al from its plural and singular forms.

Then He said: ﴿As for those in whose hearts is deviation﴾. Know that when He, exalted is He, made clear that the Book divides into two parts, one of which is muhkam and the other mutashabih, He made clear that the people of deviation cling only to the mutashabih. Zaygh (زَيْغ) is inclination away from the truth; one says: zaagha zaygh, i.e., he inclined inclination. The commentators differed about those who are meant by His saying ﴿in whose hearts is deviation﴾. Al-Rabi' said: "They are the delegation of Najran, when they disputed with the Messenger of God (ﷺ) concerning the Messiah. They said: Is he not the Word of God and a Spirit from Him? He said: Yes. They said: That is enough for us. So God revealed this verse, then He revealed ﴿Indeed, the likeness of Jesus with God is like the likeness of Adam﴾ [Al 'Imran: 59]." Al-Kalbi said: "They are the Jews, who sought to know the duration of this community's lifespan and to extract it from the disjointed letters at the beginnings of the surahs." Qatadah and al-Zajjaj said: "They are the disbelievers who deny the Resurrection, because He said at the end of the verse ﴿and none knows its interpretation except God﴾, and that is only the time of the Resurrection, since He concealed it from all creation, even from the angels and the prophets, peace be upon them."

The scholars who investigate (al-Muhaqqiqun) said: This encompasses all the falsifiers, and everyone who argues for his falsehood with the mutashabih, because the wording is general, and the specificity of the occasion of revelation does not prevent the generality of the wording. It includes everything in which there is ambiguity and confusion. Among its components is what God promised His Messenger of victory, and what He threatened the disbelievers of vengeance, and they say ﴿Bring us the punishment of God﴾ [al-'Ankabut: 29], and ﴿The Hour will not come upon us﴾ [Saba': 3], and ﴿Why do you not bring us the angels?﴾ [al-Hijr: 7]. Thus they confused the matter upon the weak. This category includes the argument of the anthropomorphists (al-Mushabbihah) with His saying: ﴿The Most Merciful is established upon the Throne﴾ [Taha: 5]. For since it has been established by clear reason that everything which is particular to a place is either in smallness, like the indivisible particle, which is false by consensus, or greater, in which case it is divisible and composite, and everything composite is contingent and originated, by this clear proof it is impossible that God be in a place; so His saying ﴿The Most Merciful is established upon the Throne﴾ is mutashabih, and whoever clings to it is clinging to the mutashabihat. Among this is the argument of the Mu'tazilah from the apparent texts indicating the complete delegation of the act to the servant. For since it has been established by rational demonstration that the emergence of an act depends on the arising of the motive, and it has been established that the arising of that motive is from God, exalted is He, and it has been established that whenever the matter is so, the occurrence of the act at the presence of that motive is necessary, and its non-occurrence at the absence of that motive is necessary, then that delegation is invalidated, and it is established that all is by the decree of God, His destiny and His will. So the Mu'tazilah's argument from those apparent texts, however numerous they are, becomes an argument from the mutashabihat. Thus God made clear that all those who turn away from the decisive proofs and confine themselves to the misleading apparent texts, cling to the mutashabihat because there is deviation from the truth in their hearts and a desire to establish falsehood.

Know that you will not see any group in this world that does not call the verses agreeing with its doctrine muhkam, and the verses agreeing with the doctrine of its opponent mutashabih. Then it is the same in that. Do you not see al-Jubba'i? He says: The Mujbirah, who attribute injustice, lying and the imposition of what is beyond capacity to God, exalted is He, are the ones who cling to the mutashabihat.

Abu Muslim al-Isfahani said: The deviant seeker of sedition is one who attaches himself to verses of misguidance and does not interpret them in light of the muhkam which God made clear by His saying ﴿And the Samiri misled them﴾ [Taha: 85], ﴿And Pharaoh misled his people, and did not guide﴾ [Taha: 79], ﴿And He misleads thereby none but the defiantly disobedient﴾ [al-Baqarah: 26]. They also interpreted His saying ﴿And when We intend to destroy a town, We command its affluent ones, and they commit sin therein﴾ [al-Isra': 16] as meaning that He destroyed them and willed their sinfulness, and that God seeks pretexts against His creatures in order to destroy them, although He said: ﴿God intends for you ease and does not intend for you hardship﴾ [al-Baqarah: 185], ﴿God intends to make clear to you and guide you﴾ [al-Nisa': 26]. And they interpreted His saying ﴿We made their deeds appealing to them, so they wander blindly﴾ [al-Naml: 4] as meaning that He made the blessing appealing to them, and by this they contradicted what is in the Qur'an, such as His saying: ﴿Indeed, God does not change what is with a people until they change what is with themselves﴾ [al-Ra'd: 11], ﴿And We never destroyed the towns except while their people were wrongdoers﴾ [al-Qasas: 59]. And He said: ﴿As for Thamud, We guided them, but they preferred blindness over guidance﴾ [Fussilat: 17], and He said: ﴿Whoever is guided, is guided only for himself﴾ [Yunus: 108], and He said: ﴿But God has endeared to you faith and made it beautiful in your hearts﴾ [al-Hujurat: 7]. So how does He make the blessing appealing? This is what Abu Muslim said. I wonder why he judged the verses agreeing with his doctrine to be muhkamat, and the verses opposing his doctrine to be mutashabihat? And why did he make it obligatory to take those agreeing with his doctrine according to their apparent meaning, and to turn those opposing his doctrine away from their apparent meaning? It is known that this cannot be accomplished except by returning to the overwhelming rational proofs. So when the rational proofs indicate the invalidity of the Mu'tazilite doctrine, their doctrine cannot be sustained unless we say that it proceeded from one of two acts without a preponderant factor, and that is an explicit denial of the Creator. And it cannot be sustained unless we say

that the emergence of the firm, perfected act from the servant does not indicate the knowledge of its doer about it. In that case that number would have been specified for occurrence rather than more or less, without a specifier, and that is a denial of the Creator. It also follows from this that the emergence of a firm act does not indicate that the doer is knowing; and then the door of inference from the rulings of God's acts to the knowing of their doer is closed. Even if the people of the heavens and the earth gathered together against these rational proofs, they would not be able to repel them. When these overwhelming rational proofs are apparent, how is it permissible for any intelligent person to call the verses indicating qada' and qadar mutashabihah? Thus it has become clear from what we have mentioned that the prevailing rule among most people is that every verse agreeing with their doctrine is muhkamah, and every verse opposing them is mutashabihah.

As for the investigating, impartial scholar (al-Muhaqqiq al-Munsif), he handles the matter of the verses in three categories:

The first: that whose apparent meaning is confirmed by rational proofs; that is the muhkam in truth.

The second: that for which decisive proofs have established the impossibility of its apparent meaning; that is what is judged to mean other than its apparent meaning.

The third: that for which no such proofs exist on either side of its affirmation or negation; it is incumbent to suspend judgment on it, and that is mutashabih in the sense that the matter is confused in it, and neither side is distinguished from the other, except that the stronger assumption exists in taking it according to its apparent meaning. This is what I hold on this subject, and God knows best His intent.

* * *

Know that when He, exalted is He, made clear that the deviators follow the mutashabih, He made clear that they have two aims in it. The first is His saying: ﴿seeking sedition﴾, and the second is His saying ﴿and seeking its interpretation﴾.

As for the first: know that fitnah in the language means being infatuated with a thing and going to excess in it. One says: So-and-so is maftun with seeking the world, meaning he has gone to excess in seeking it and exceeded the measure. The commentators mentioned several meanings for this fitnah:

First: al-Asamm said: When they introduce those mutashabihat into the religion, some of them come to oppose others in religion, and that leads to killing, chaos and turmoil, and that is the fitnah.

Second: clinging to that mutashabih establishes innovation and falsehood in the heart, so he becomes infatuated with that falsehood, devoted to it, and does not detach from it by any stratagem whatsoever.

Third: fitnah in religion is deviation from it, and it is known that there is no greater fitnah or corruption than fitnah in religion and corruption in it.

As for the second aim of theirs, His saying ﴿and seeking its interpretation﴾: know that ta'wil in the language is tafsir (explanation), and its origin in the language is return and destination, from your saying: the matter returned to such-and-such (ala amr ila kadha) when it reached it, and I interpreted it (awwaltuhu ta'wilan) when I made it reach it. This is the meaning of ta'wil in the language. Then tafsir is called ta'wil. God, exalted is He, said: ﴿I will inform you of the interpretation of that over which you could not be patient﴾ [al-Kahf: 78], and He said: ﴿and better in interpretation﴾ [al-Nisa': 59]. That is because it is information about what the wording returns to in meaning. Know that what is meant by it is that they seek the interpretation for which there is no proof or clarification in the Book of God, such as their seeking when the Hour will occur, and how great are the measures of reward and punishment for each obedient and disobedient person.

The judge (al-Qadi) said: These deviators have sought the mutashabih in two ways:

One of them: that they interpret it in other than the truth; this is what is meant by His saying ﴿seeking sedition﴾.

The second: that they pass judgment on a matter where there is no proof; this is what is meant by His saying ﴿and seeking its interpretation﴾. Then God, exalted is He, made clear what would be an addition in censure of the way of these deviators, and He said: ﴿And none knows its interpretation except God﴾. People differed about this point. Some said: the speech ends here, and then the waw in His saying ﴿and those firmly rooted in knowledge﴾ is the waw of beginning (wa al-ibtida'). According to this view, none knows the mutashabih

Page 153
except God. This is the view of Ibn 'Abbas, 'A'ishah, Malik ibn Anas, al-Kisa'i and al-Farra', and among the Mu'tazilah, the view of Abu 'Ali al-Jubba'i, and it is the one we prefer.

**The second view:** the sentence is complete at His words ﴿and those firmly grounded in knowledge﴾. On this view, knowledge of the ambiguous (*mutashabih*, the verses whose meaning is not immediately clear) is possessed both by Allah the Exalted and by those firmly grounded in knowledge. This view is also narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid, al-Rabi' ibn Anas, and most of the theologians (*mutakallimun*).

The proofs for the soundness of the first view are several:

**The first proof:** When a word has a dominant meaning, and then a stronger proof shows that this apparent meaning is not intended, we know that Allah's intended meaning is one of the figurative meanings (*majazat*) of that literal meaning. Figurative meanings are numerous, and preferring one over another can only be done by linguistic preponderances (*tarjihat lughawiyya*). Linguistic preponderances yield only weak conjecture. So when a matter is definitive and certain, it is impermissible to argue about it on the basis of weak conjectural evidence. An example: Allah the Exalted said ﴿Allah does not burden a soul beyond its capacity﴾ [al-Baqarah: 286], then a decisive proof established that such a burden has in fact occurred, as we explained in the five demonstrations in the commentary on this verse. So we know that Allah's intended meaning is not what the apparent sense of this verse indicates. It is therefore necessary to turn the word to one of its figurative meanings. Figurative meanings are numerous, and preferring one over another can only be done by linguistic preponderances, which yield only weak conjecture. This matter is not one of the conjectural matters, so it is required that arguing about it on the basis of conjectural proofs be invalid.

Also, Allah the Exalted said ﴿The Most Merciful is established upon the Throne﴾ [Ta-Ha: 5]. A proof has established that the deity cannot be in a place. So we know that Allah's intended meaning from this verse is not what its apparent sense suggests. Yet the figurative meanings of this expression are numerous, so turning the word to one meaning rather than another can only be done by conjectural linguistic preponderances. And to speak by conjecture about the Essence and Attributes of Allah the Exalted is impermissible by the consensus of the Muslims. This is a decisive argument on the matter. A heart free of partisanship inclines to it, and the original disposition (*fitra*) bears witness to its soundness. And success is from Allah.

**The second proof:** What precedes this verse indicates that seeking the interpretation (*ta'wil*) of the ambiguous is blameworthy, where He said ﴿As for those in whose hearts is deviation, they follow what is ambiguous of it, seeking discord and seeking its interpretation.﴾ Had seeking the interpretation of the ambiguous been permissible, Allah the Exalted would not have censured it.

If it is said: why can it not be that what is meant is seeking the time of the Hour, as in His words ﴿They ask you about the Hour: when will it occur? Say: its knowledge is only with my Lord﴾ [al-A'raf: 187]? Also, seeking the measures of reward and punishment, and seeking the appearance of victory and support, as they said ﴿Why do you not bring us the angels?﴾ [al-Hijr: 7].

We say: When He divided the Book into two parts, the clear (*muhkam*, the verses whose meaning is definite) and the ambiguous (*mutashabih*), and reason indicates the soundness of this division, since carrying a word on its dominant meaning is the clear, while carrying it on a meaning that is not dominant is the ambiguous, then He censured the path of one who seeks the interpretation of the ambiguous. Restricting that censure to some ambiguous matters and not others would be abandoning the apparent sense, and that is impermissible.

**The third proof:** Allah praised those firmly grounded in knowledge by saying that they say, "We believe in it." And at the beginning of Surat al-Baqarah He said ﴿As for those who believe, they know that it is the truth from their Lord﴾ [al-Baqarah: 26]. If these firmly grounded ones knew the detailed interpretation of that ambiguity, there would be no praise for them in believing in it. For whoever knows something in detail must believe in it. Rather, those firmly grounded in knowledge are those who know by definitive proofs that Allah the Exalted is knowing of the objects of knowledge, which have no end, and who know that the Qur'an is the speech of Allah the Exalted, and that He does not speak falsehood or vanity. So when they hear a verse, and definitive proofs indicate that its apparent sense cannot be the intended meaning of Allah the Exalted, but His intended meaning is other than that apparent sense, then they delegate the determination of that intended meaning to His knowledge. They are certain that whatever that meaning is, it is the truth and the correct view. These are the ones firmly grounded in knowledge of Allah, for their certainty about abandoning the apparent sense does not shake them, nor does their not knowing the specific intended meaning turn them away from believing in Allah and from affirming the soundness of the Qur'an.

**The fourth proof:** If His words ﴿and those firmly grounded in knowledge﴾ were coordinated with His words "except Allah," then His words ﴿they say, "We believe in it"﴾ would become a new sentence. That is far from the taste of eloquence. Rather, the better phrasing would be: "and they say, 'We believe in it,'" or "and they say, 'We believe in it.'"

If it is said: there are two ways to correct this:

The first: His words "they say" are a new independent sentence, the implied sense being: "These who know the interpretation say, 'We believe in it.'"

The second: "they say" is a circumstantial clause (*hal*) referring to "those firmly grounded."

We say: As for the first, it is rejected, because interpreting the speech of Allah the Exalted in a way that requires no supplied words is better than interpreting it in a way that requires supplied words. As for the second: the one in the circumstantial position is the one previously mentioned, and here both Allah the Exalted and those firmly grounded in knowledge have been mentioned. So it is necessary to make His words "they say, 'We believe in it'" a circumstantial clause for "those firmly grounded," not for Allah the Exalted, and this involves abandoning the apparent sense. Thus it is established that this view does not hold without deviating from the apparent sense, while our view does not need that. So this view is preferable.

**The fifth proof:** His words ﴿Each is from our Lord﴾ mean that they believe in what they know in detail and in what they do not know the detail and interpretation of. If they knew the detail of everything, this statement would serve no purpose.

**The sixth proof:** It is related from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, that he said: "The exegesis of the Qur'an is of four kinds: an exegesis that no one is excused for being ignorant of; an exegesis that the Arabs know through their tongues; an exegesis that the scholars know; and an exegesis that none knows except Allah the Exalted."

Malik ibn Anas, may Allah have mercy on him, was asked about the Istiwa' (the Establishment upon the Throne), and he said: "The Istiwa' is known, the modality (*kayfiyya*) is unknown, believing in it is obligatory, and asking about it is an innovation (*bid'a*)." We have mentioned part of this matter at the beginning of Surat al-Baqarah. When what we have mentioned here is combined with what we mentioned there, the discussion of this matter is complete. And success is from Allah.

\* \* \*

Then He, the Exalted, said: ﴿And those firmly grounded in knowledge say, "We believe in it; each is from our Lord."﴾ And in this are several issues.

**The first issue:** *Rusukh* (firm grounding) in the lexicon means firm establishment in a thing.

Know that the one firmly grounded in knowledge is the one who knows the Essence and Attributes of Allah through certain, definitive proofs, and who knows through certain proofs that the Qur'an is the speech of Allah the Exalted. So when he sees something ambiguous, and a definitive proof indicates that the apparent sense is not the intended meaning of Allah the Exalted, he then knows with certainty that Allah's intended meaning is something other than what its apparent sense indicates, and that this intended meaning is true. And the fact that its apparent sense has been rejected does not become a doubt that casts aspersions on the soundness of the Qur'an.

Then He related about them also that they say ﴿each is from our Lord﴾. The meaning is that each of the clear and the ambiguous is from our Lord. And here there are two questions.

**The first question:** If He had said "each is from our Lord," it would have been correct. So what is the benefit of the word "from-with" (*'inda*)?

Answer: Believing in the ambiguous requires greater emphasis, so He used the word *'inda* for added emphasis.

**The second question:** Why was it permissible to omit the genitive complement of "each" (*kull*)?

Answer: Because the indication of the complement by the context is strong, and after the omission there is safety from ambiguity.

\* \* \*

Then He said ﴿And none takes heed except those of sound minds﴾. This is praise from Allah the Exalted for those who said, "We believe in it." And the meaning is: none is admonished by what is in the Qur'an except those with complete intellects. So this expression serves as an indication that they employ their intellects in understanding the Qur'an, so they know the meaning whose apparent sense agrees with the proofs of reason, and that is clear (*muhkam*). As for the meaning whose apparent sense contradicts the proofs of reason, that is ambiguous (*mutashabih*). Then they know that the whole is the speech of One in whose speech there is no contradiction or falsehood. So they know that this ambiguous must have a sound meaning with Allah the Exalted. This verse indicates the high standing of the theologians (*mutakallimun*) who investigate the rational proofs and use them to arrive at knowledge of the Essence, Attributes and Acts of Allah the Exalted, and who interpret the Qur'an only in ways that agree with the proofs of reason and accord with the language and the *i'rab* (grammatical inflection).

Know that whatever is more noble, its opposite is more base. Likewise, the exegete of the Qur'an, whenever he is characterized by this attribute, his rank is this supreme rank whose praise Allah has magnified. And whenever he speaks about the Qur'an without being thoroughly versed in the science of the principles (*usul*), and in the science of the language and grammar, he is at the furthest distance from Allah. For this reason the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Whoever explains the Qur'an by his own opinion, let him take his seat in the Fire."

[Page 154]

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 3, verse 8:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Our Lord, do not let our hearts deviate after You have guided us, and grant us from Yourself mercy. Indeed, You are the Bestower.﴾

Know that He, exalted is He, just as He related about those firmly grounded in knowledge that they say, "We have believed in it," related about them that they say, ﴿Our Lord, do not let our hearts deviate after You have guided us, and grant us,﴾ and the omission of (yaqulun, "they say") is because the first indicates it, as in His saying, ﴿And they contemplate the creation of the heavens and the earth, [saying], "Our Lord, You did not create this aimlessly"﴾ [Al 'Imran: 191]. In this verse, the statements of the People of the Sunnah (Ahl al-Sunnah) and the Mu'tazilah differ.

As for the statement of the People of the Sunnah, it is evident, because the heart is capable of inclining toward faith and capable of inclining toward disbelief, and it is impossible for it to incline to one of the two sides except at the occurrence of a motive and a will that Allah, exalted is He, creates. If that motive is a motive toward disbelief, then it is abandonment (al-khidhlan), deviation (al-izaghah), turning away (al-sadd), sealing (al-khatm), stamping (al-tab'), rust (al-rayn), hardness (al-qaswah), heaviness (al-waqr), covering (al-kinan), and other terms occurring in the Qur'an. If that motive is a motive of faith, then it is: success (al-tawfiq),

Page 156
guidance to right conduct (al-rashad), guidance (al-hidayah), making firm (al-taysid), steadfastness (al-tathbit), protection (al-‘ismah), and other terms occurring in the Qur'an. The Messenger of Allah ﷺ used to say: "The heart of the believer is between two fingers of the fingers of the Most Merciful." The intended meaning of these two fingers is the two motives. Just as the thing that is between the two fingers of a man turns as the man turns it by means of those two fingers, so too the heart, by being between the two motives, turns as the Truth turns it by means of those two motives. Whoever is fair and does not force the matter, and tests himself, finds this meaning like a perceptible thing. And if one permits the occurrence of one of the two motives without a producer and an effective agent, it necessarily entails the denial of the Creator. The Prophet ﷺ used to say: "O Turner of the hearts and the sights, make my heart firm upon Your religion." Its meaning is what we have mentioned. So when those firmly grounded in knowledge believed in everything Allah, exalted is He, sent down of the decisive (muhkam) and the ambiguous (mutashabih) verses, they humbly implored Him, glorified and exalted is He, not to make their hearts inclined toward falsehood after He had made them inclined toward the truth. This is a demonstrative argument reinforced by a Qur'anic confirmation.

Among what confirms what we have mentioned is that Allah, exalted is He, praised these believers for not following the ambiguous verses, but believing in them in a general manner, and refraining from delving into them. Therefore it is unlikely that they would speak of the ambiguous at this time; it must be that they spoke this supplication because they believed it to be of the decisive verses. Then Allah, exalted is He, related that about them in the context of praising them and commending them because they said it. This indicates that this verse is among the strongest of the decisive verses. This is a sound argument.

As for the Mu'tazilah, they said: Since the proofs indicate that deviation (al-zaygh) cannot be by the act of Allah, exalted is He, it is necessary to interpret this verse. As for their proofs, we have mentioned them in the explanation of His saying, exalted is He: ﴿It is the same for them whether you warn them or do not warn them; they will not believe﴾ [Al-Baqarah: 6].

Among what they argued with specifically in this place is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿So when they deviated, Allah caused their hearts to deviate﴾ [As-Saff: 5], which is explicit that the beginning of the deviation is from them. As for their interpretations of this verse, they are of several aspects. The first, which al-Jubba'i said and al-Qadi chose: that what is meant by His saying ﴿do not let our hearts deviate﴾ is: do not withhold from them the favors (al-alutaf) by which their hearts remain upon the attribute of faith. This is because when He withholds His favors from them upon their deserving, withholding them is permissible to be called "causing to deviate." This is indicated by His saying, exalted is He: ﴿So when they deviated, Allah caused their hearts to deviate.﴾ The second: al-Asamm said: Do not test us with a trial at which our hearts would deviate. It is like His saying: ﴿And if We had decreed upon them, "Kill yourselves or leave your homes," few of them would have done it﴾ [An-Nisa': 66], and His saying: ﴿And We would have made for those who disbelieve in the Most Merciful silver roofs for their houses﴾ [Az-Zukhruf: 33]. The meaning is: do not burden us with acts of worship with which we are not secure from deviation. A speaker may say, "Do not compel me to harm you," meaning: do not do what makes me, in that state, one who harms you. The third: al-Ka'bi said, "Do not let our hearts deviate" means: do not name us with the name of the deviant, just as one says, "So-and-so declares so-and-so a disbeliever" when he names him a disbeliever. The fourth: al-Jubba'i said: meaning, do not let our hearts deviate from Your Paradise and Your reward after You have guided us. This is close to the first aspect, except that it may be understood as something else, namely that if He, exalted is He, knows that he is a believer now, and knows that if he remained until the second year he would disbelieve, then His saying "do not let our hearts deviate" is understood as: that He cause him to die before he becomes a disbeliever, because keeping him alive until the second year is akin to what would be if He had caused him to deviate from the path to Paradise. The fifth: al-Asamm said: "Do not let our hearts deviate" from the perfection of reason through madness, after You have guided us by the light of reason. The sixth: Abu Muslim said: Guard us from Satan and from the evils of our own souls, so that we do not deviate. This is the sum of what they have mentioned in interpreting this verse, and all of it is weak.

Page 157
As for the first: because it is among their doctrines that whatever is within Allah's power to do for them as a favor, He is obligated to do it, an obligation such that if He abandoned it, His divinity would be nullified and He would become ignorant and needy. Something that is like this, what need is there to supplicate for it? Rather, this view continues on the position of Bishr ibn al-Mu'tamir and his companions, who do not make it obligatory upon Allah to perform all the favors.

As for the second: it is weak, because the imposition of hardship in obligation, if Allah, exalted is He, knows it has an effect in driving the accountable person toward wrongdoing, it would be ugly on Allah's part; and if Allah, exalted is He, knows that it has absolutely no effect in driving the accountable person toward committing wrongdoing, then its existence is like its non-existence with regard to the servant being obedient or disobedient, so there is no benefit in directing the supplication toward it.

As for the third: it is that naming with deviation and disbelief revolves with disbelief in existence and non-existence, and disbelief and deviation are by the choice of the servant, so there is no benefit in His saying, "Do not name us with the name of deviation and disbelief."

As for the fourth: it is that if His knowledge, exalted is He, that he will disbelieve in the second year necessitated that He cause him to die, then His knowledge that he would never believe and would disbelieve throughout his life would necessitate that He not create him.

As for the fifth: which is to interpret it as preserving the intellect, it is weak, because this is connected to what He said before this verse: ﴿As for those in whose hearts is deviation﴾.

As for the sixth: which is that guarding from Satan and from the evils of the self, if it is within capacity, it is obligatory to do it, so there is no benefit in supplication; and if it is not within capacity, its doing is impossible, so there is no benefit in supplication. From what we have mentioned, the invalidity of these aspects has become clear, and that the truth is what we have gone to.

If it is said: On that view, how is the discussion regarding the explanation of His saying, exalted is He: ﴿So when they deviated, Allah caused their hearts to deviate﴾ [As-Saff: 5]?

We say: It is not far-fetched to say that Allah, exalted is He, causes them to deviate at the outset, and at that point they deviate; then upon this deviation there follows another causing to deviate, other than the first, from Allah, exalted is He, and all of that involves no contradiction.

As for His saying, exalted is He: ﴿after You have guided us﴾, that is: after You made us guided. This is also explicit that the attainment of guidance in the heart is by the creation of Allah, exalted is He.

* * *

Then He said: ﴿and grant us from Yourself mercy.﴾ Know that the purification of the heart from what is not fitting takes precedence over its illumination with what is fitting. These believers first asked their Lord that He not make their hearts inclined toward falsehood and corrupt beliefs; then they followed that by asking their Lord to illuminate their hearts with the lights of knowledge, and their limbs and members with the adornment of obedience. He said "mercy" (rahmah) so that this would include all kinds of mercy. The first of them: that there come to be in the heart the light of faith, monotheism, and knowledge. The second: that there come to be in the limbs and members the light of obedience, servitude, and service. The third: that there come to be in this world ease of the means of livelihood, of security, health, and sufficiency. The fourth: that there come to be at death ease of the agonies of death. The fifth: that there come to be in the grave ease of questioning and ease of the darkness of the grave. The sixth: that there come to be on the Day of Resurrection ease of punishment and reckoning, forgiveness of misdeeds, and the weighing of good deeds in favor. So His saying ﴿from Yourself mercy﴾ encompasses all these divisions.

Page 158
And since it has been established by overwhelming and compelling proofs that there is no Merciful except Him, and no Generous except Him, He therefore emphasized that with His saying ﴿from Yourself﴾, as an alert to the intellect, the heart, and the spirit that the intended thing is attained only from Him, glorified is He. And since this sought thing is of utmost greatness relative to the servant, he therefore mentioned it in indefinite form, as though he were saying: "I ask for mercy—and what mercy!—I ask for mercy from You, which befits You." That entails utmost greatness.

* * *

Then He said: ﴿Indeed, You are the Bestower.﴾ It is as if the servant says: "My God, this which I have asked of You in this supplication is great relative to me, but it is small relative to the perfection of Your generosity and the extent of Your bounty and mercy. You are the Bestower, from whose gift the realities of things, their essences, their quiddities, and their existences have come into being. Everything other than You is by Your bounty, Your kindness, and Your generosity. O Ever-Constant in Kindness, O Ancient in Benevolence, do not disappoint the hope of this poor one, do not turn away his supplication, and make him, by Your grace, worthy of Your mercy, O Most Merciful of the merciful and Most Generous of the generous."

**Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 3, verse 9:**

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Our Lord, You are the gatherer of mankind for a Day about which there is no doubt. Indeed, Allah does not fail in His promise.﴾

Know that this supplication is part of the speech of those firmly rooted in knowledge (al-rasikhun fi al-'ilm), because when they asked Allah, exalted is He, to preserve them from deviation (al-zaygh) and to single them out with guidance and mercy, it is as though they said: The purpose of this request is not what relates to the interests of this world, for it is transient and passing away. Rather, the greatest purpose of it is what relates to the Hereafter. For we know, O our God, that You are the gatherer of mankind for recompense on the Day of Resurrection, and we know that Your promise will not be broken and Your word will not be false. Whoever's heart has deviated will remain there in punishment forever and ever, and whoever You grant success, guidance and mercy, and make among the believers, will remain there in happiness and honour forever and ever. Therefore, the greatest purpose of that supplication is what relates to the Hereafter. There remain in the verse several issues:

The first issue: His saying ﴿Our Lord, You are the gatherer of mankind for a Day about which there is no doubt﴾. Its implied sense is: "gatherer of mankind for recompense on a Day about which there is no doubt," and it has been omitted because the intended meaning is evident.

The second issue: Al-Jubba'i (Abu 'Ali al-Jubba'i) said: The speech of the believers was complete at His saying ﴿for a Day about which there is no doubt﴾. As for His saying ﴿Indeed, Allah does not fail in His promise﴾, it is the speech of Allah, mighty and majestic. It is as though the people, when they said ﴿You are the gatherer of mankind for a Day about which there is no doubt﴾, Allah, exalted is He, affirmed what they said and confirmed their speech with His saying ﴿Indeed, Allah does not fail in His promise﴾, just as He said, relating the words of the believers at the end of this surah: ﴿Our Lord, grant us what You promised us through Your messengers and do not disgrace us on the Day of Resurrection. Indeed, You do not fail in the promise﴾ [Al 'Imran: 194]. Some people said: It is not far-fetched that this occurs according to the stylistic shift in speech from the third person to the second person (al-'udul min al-ghayba ila al-huduri), and similar instances are numerous in the Book of Allah, exalted is He. He said: ﴿Until, when you are in the ship and they sail with them by a good wind﴾ [Yunus: 22].

If it is asked: Why did they say in this verse ﴿Indeed, Allah does not fail in His promise﴾, and in that verse ﴿You do not fail in the promise﴾ [Al 'Imran: 194]?

[p. 159]

I say: The distinction, and Allah knows best, is that this verse is in the station of awe (maqam al-hayba), meaning that divinity (al-ilahiyya) requires gathering and resurrection so that the oppressed may be given justice against the oppressors. Therefore, mentioning Him by His greatest name (al-ism al-a'zam) is more fitting in this station. As for His saying at the end of the surah ﴿You do not fail in the promise﴾, that station is the station of the servant asking his Lord to bestow upon him His grace and to overlook his misdeeds. It was not a station of awe, so necessarily He said: ﴿You do not fail in the promise﴾.

* * *

The third issue: Al-Jubba'i used this verse as proof for the certainty of the threat against sinners (wa'id al-fussaq). He said: That is because the threat (al-wa'id) falls under the wording of the promise (al-wa'd), as evidenced by His saying: ﴿Have we found what our Lord promised us to be true? Have you found what your Lord promised to be true?﴾ [Al-A'raf: 44]. The words al-wa'd, al-mawid and al-mi'ad are one and the same. He has informed in this verse that He does not fail in the promise (al-mi'ad), so this is evidence that He does not fail in the threat.

The answer: We do not accept that He threatens sinners absolutely. Rather, that threat, according to us, is conditional upon the condition of non-pardon (shart 'adam al-'afw), just as it is by consensus conditional upon the condition of non-repentance. Just as you affirmed that condition by a separate proof, so we affirm the condition of non-pardon by a separate proof. Even if we grant that He threatens them, we do not grant that the threat falls under the wording of the promise.

As for His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Have you found what your Lord promised to be true?﴾ [Al-A'raf: 44].

We say: Why should it not be like His saying ﴿So give them the good news of a painful punishment﴾ [Al 'Imran: 21] and His saying ﴿Taste it! Indeed, you are the mighty, the noble﴾ [al-Dukhan: 49]? Furthermore, why should it not be that what is meant by it is that they used to expect from their idols that they would intercede for them with Allah, so the promise meant by it was those benefits? The complete discussion of the issue of the threat has already passed in surah al-Baqarah, in the commentary on His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Yes, whoever earns an evil deed and his sin has encompassed him, those are the companions of the Fire; they will abide therein eternally﴾ [al-Baqarah: 81]. Al-Wahidi, in al-Basit, mentioned another approach, saying: Why should this not be taken to refer to the promise of allies (mi'ad al-awliya'), rather than the threat against enemies (wa'id al-a'da'), because failing to carry out a threat is considered generosity (karam) among the Arabs? He said: The evidence for this is that they praise a person for it. The poet said:

*When he promises good fortune, he fulfils his promise, and if he threatens hardship, then pardon is what restrains him.*

And he related the debate that took place between Abu 'Amr ibn al-'Ala' and 'Amr ibn 'Ubayd. Abu 'Amr ibn al-'Ala' said to 'Amr ibn 'Ubayd: What do you say about the people of major sins? He said: I say that Allah made a promise and issued a threat; He fulfils His threat just as He fulfils His promise. Abu 'Amr ibn al-'Ala' said: You are a man who is non-Arab (a'jam), not in terms of tongue, but in terms of heart. The Arabs consider going back on a promise to be baseness (luwm), and going back on a threat to be generosity (karam). And he recited:

*Indeed I, whether I threaten him or promise him, am one who denies my threat and fulfils my promise.*

The Mu'tazila (al-Mu'tazila) related that when Abu 'Amr ibn al-'Ala' said this speech, 'Amr ibn 'Ubayd said to him: O Abu 'Amr, is God then called "the one who denies His own self"? He said: No. 'Amr ibn 'Ubayd said: Then your argument has collapsed. They said: Abu 'Amr ibn al-'Ala' was silenced.

In my view, Abu 'Amr ibn al-'Ala' could have answered this question by saying: You have analogised the threat to the promise, whereas I only mentioned this to clarify the difference between the two categories. That is because the promise is a right owed by the one who promises, and the threat is a right belonging to the one who threatens. Whoever waives his own right has shown generosity and nobility, and whoever waives the right of another has committed baseness. Thus the difference between promise and threat becomes clear, and your analogy is invalid. I only mentioned this poetry to explain this difference. As for your saying: If He did not do it, He would become a liar and one who denies His own self, the answer is that this would only follow if the threat were established as definite without any condition. In my view, all threats are conditional upon the non-occurrence of pardon. Therefore, it does not follow that leaving it out would introduce falsehood into the speech of Allah, exalted is He. This is what relates to this report, and Allah knows best.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 3, verse 10:

His saying, may He be exalted, ﴿Indeed, those who disbelieve, their wealth will not avail them, nor their children, against Allah at all. And they are the fuel of the Fire﴾.

Know that when Allah, glorified and exalted is He, related the supplication and humility of the believers, He related the condition of the disbelievers and the severity of their punishment. This is the connection of the arrangement (wajh al-nazm), and in the verse there are several issues:

The first issue: Regarding His saying ﴿Indeed, those who disbelieve, their wealth will not avail them, nor their children, against Allah at all﴾ there are two opinions. The first: what is meant by them is the delegation of Najran. This is because we have related, in some account of their story, that Abu Harithah ibn Alqamah said to his brother: "Indeed I know that he is the Messenger of Allah ﷺ in truth, but if I make that manifest, the kings of Rome will take from me what they have given me of wealth and rank." So Allah, the Exalted, made clear that their wealth and their children would not repel from them the punishment of Allah in this world and the Hereafter.

The second opinion: the wording is general, and the specificity of the occasion of revelation does not prevent the generality of the wording.

The second issue: Know that the completeness of punishment is that every means by which one benefits is removed from him, and then all the painful causes gather upon him.

As for the first: it is what is meant by His saying ﴿their wealth will not avail them, nor their children﴾. This is because a person, in the calamities and misfortunes of this world, turns for refuge to wealth and children, for they are the nearest of things a person turns to in repelling calamities. So Allah, the Exalted, made clear that the nature of that Day is contrary to the nature of this world, because if the nearest paths to repelling harms are not available on that Day, then what lies beyond them is all the more unavailable. A parallel to this verse is His saying, the Exalted: ﴿The day when neither wealth nor children will benefit, except one who comes to Allah with a sound heart﴾ [al-Shu'ara': 88-89], and His saying ﴿Wealth and children are the adornment of the worldly life, but the enduring good deeds are better with your Lord in reward﴾ [al-Kahf: 46], and His saying ﴿And We will inherit from him what he says, and he will come to Us alone﴾ [Maryam: 80], and His saying ﴿And you have certainly come to Us alone, as We created you the first time, and you have left behind what We bestowed upon you﴾ [al-An'am: 94].

As for the second part of the causes of the completeness of punishment, it is that the painful causes gather upon him, and to this the reference is in His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And they are the fuel of the Fire﴾. This is the ultimate in describing punishment, for there is no punishment greater than that the Fire should blaze among them as it blazes in dry firewood. The wuquud (fuel), with a fatha on the waw, is the firewood with which the fire is kindled; with a damma, it is the verbal noun of "waqadati al-nar" (the fire blazed), like His saying: "waradat wurudan" (she came to water).

The third issue: Regarding His saying (min Allah, "from Allah") there are two opinions. One: the implied meaning is "their wealth will not avail them, nor their children, against the punishment of Allah," so the modified noun was omitted, since the context indicates it. The second: Abu 'Ubaydah said that "min" here means "inda" (with/in the sight of), and the meaning is: "will not avail them anything in the sight of Allah."

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 3, verse 11:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿As was the case of the people of Pharaoh and those before them, who denied Our signs, so Allah seized them for their sins. And Allah is severe in punishment.﴾

It is said: "daʾabtu al-shayʾa, adʾabu, daʾban and duʾūban," when one exerts oneself in a matter and becomes weary of it. Allah, exalted is He, said: ﴿seven years in succession (daʾban)﴾ [Yusuf: 47], meaning with diligence, striving and continuity. It is also said: "So-and-so traveled a day of daʾib," when he exerted himself in travel the whole day. This is its meaning in the lexicon. Then al-daʾb became an expression for affair, matter and custom. It is said: "This is so-and-so's daʾb," meaning his custom. Some have said: al-duʾūb and al-daʾb mean continuity.

Having known this, we say: There are several aspects concerning the manner of the comparison.

The first: al-daʾb is interpreted as striving (ijtihād), as is its meaning in the origin of the language. This is the view of al-Aṣamm and al-Zajjāj. The aspect of comparison is that the daʾb of the disbelievers, i.e., their diligence and striving in denying Muhammad (ﷺ) and rejecting his religion, is like the daʾb of the people of Pharaoh with Musa (peace be upon him). Then We destroyed those people for their sins, so likewise We will destroy these.

The second aspect: al-daʾb is interpreted as affair and conduct (ṣunʿ). There are several views on this. The first: ﴿as was the case of the people of Pharaoh﴾, meaning the affair and conduct of these people in denying Muhammad (ﷺ) is like the affair of the people of Pharaoh in denying Musa. There is no difference between this aspect and the one before it, except that in the first aspect we took the word to mean striving, and in this aspect to mean conduct and custom. The second: the sense of the verse is: Indeed those who disbelieve, their wealth and their children will not avail them anything against Allah, and Allah will make them fuel for the Fire, according to His custom and conduct regarding the people of Pharaoh, for when they denied their messenger, He seized them for their sins. The verbal noun is sometimes attributed to the agent and sometimes to the object, and what is meant here is: as Allah's daʾb regarding the people of Pharaoh, for when they denied their messenger, He seized them for their sins. A parallel to this is His saying: ﴿They love them as they love Allah﴾ [al-Baqarah: 165], meaning as they love Allah, and His saying: ﴿The custom of those whom We sent before you of Our messengers﴾ [al-Isra: 77], meaning My custom regarding those whom We sent before you. The third: al-Qaffal, may Allah have mercy on him, said: It is possible that the verse encompasses both the custom attributed to Allah, exalted is He, and the custom attributed to the disbelievers, as if it were said: The custom and way of these disbelievers in harming Muhammad (ﷺ) is like the custom of those before them in harming their messengers, and Our custom too in destroying these is like Our custom in destroying those earlier disbelievers. The intended meaning, in all these interpretations, is the support of the Prophet (ﷺ) against the harm of the disbelievers and the glad tidings that Allah will take vengeance upon them.

The third aspect: concerning the interpretation of al-daʾb and al-duʾūb, which is lingering, continuity and long remaining in a thing. The sense of the verse is: And those are the fuel of the Fire, as was the case of the people of Pharaoh, i.e., their lasting in the Fire is like the lasting of the people of Pharaoh.

The fourth aspect: al-daʾb is striving, as we have mentioned, and among its necessary implications is fatigue and hardship, so that the meaning is: their hardship and fatigue from the punishment are like the hardship and fatigue of the people of Pharaoh from the punishment. For Allah, exalted is He, explained that their punishment occurs at the closest point, which is His saying: ﴿They are drowned and then made to enter a fire﴾ [Nuh: 25], and at the utmost severity as well, which is His saying: ﴿The Fire; they are exposed to it morning and evening, and on the day the Hour arises: "Cause the people of Pharaoh to enter the most severe punishment."﴾ [Ghafir: 46].

The fifth aspect: the thing compared is that their wealth and children do not benefit them in removing the punishment. So the comparison with the people of Pharaoh is achieved in these two aspects. The meaning is: You have known what befell the people of Pharaoh and those before them of the messenger-deniers, of the hastened punishment, in the face of which wealth and children did not benefit them, rather they became compelled to what descended upon them. Likewise is your condition, O disbelievers who deny Muhammad (ﷺ): that there will descend upon you the like of what descended upon the people before, whether earlier or later, and wealth and children will not avail you.

The sixth aspect: it is possible that the aspect of comparison is that just as the hastened punishment of annihilation descended upon those before, so likewise it descends upon you, O disbelievers, against Muhammad (ﷺ), and that is by killing, captivity and the seizure of wealth. And His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Say to those who disbelieve: "You will be overcome and gathered into Hell"﴾ serves as an indication of this. It is as if He, exalted is He, explained that just as the hastened punishment descended upon those people, and then they proceed to lasting punishment, so there will descend upon those who deny Muhammad (ﷺ) two matters: the first is the hastened trials, which are killing, captivity and humiliation; then after that will be the proceeding to the painful, everlasting punishment. These last two aspects were mentioned by al-Qadi, may Allah, exalted is He, have mercy on him.

As for His saying: ﴿and those before them﴾, the meaning is: and those before them among the deniers of the messengers. And His saying ﴿who denied Our signs﴾: by the signs is meant the miracles, and whenever they denied them, they have certainly denied the prophets.

* * *
Then He said: ﴿So Allah seized them for their sins﴾. He used the word seizure (akhdh) here because one upon whom punishment descends becomes like one seized and captured, who cannot free himself.

* * *
Then He said: ﴿And Allah is severe in punishment﴾, which is evident.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 3, verse 12:

His saying, may He be exalted, ﴿Say to those who disbelieve: You will be overcome and gathered to Hell, and it is an evil resting-place﴾. In this verse there are several issues:

The first issue: Hamzah and al-Kisa'i recited "sa-yughlabuna wa-yuhsharuna" with the letter ya' (y) in both places, while the rest recited them with the letter ta' (t) at the top in both places. As for the one who recites with ya' dotted from below, the meaning is: convey to them that they will be overcome. What confirms the soundness of the ya' is His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Say to those who believe that they should forgive those who do not expect the Days of Allah﴾ [al-Jathiyah: 14], and ﴿Say to the believing men that they should lower their gaze﴾ [al-Nur: 30], and He did not say "ghuddu" (lower, in the imperative addressed to the second person). As for the one who recites with ta', it is for direct address, and what confirms the goodness of the ta' is His saying: ﴿And when Allah took the covenant of the Prophets: that which I have given you of the Book﴾ [Al 'Imran: 81]. The difference between the two recitations in meaning is that the recitation with ta' is a command to inform them of what will befall them of overcoming and of being gathered to Hell, while the recitation with ya' is a command to relate it to them. And Allah knows best.

The second issue: They mentioned several explanations concerning the occasion of revelation of this verse. The first: "When the Messenger of Allah ﷺ fought Quraysh on the Day of Badr and came to Madinah, he gathered the Jews in the market of Banu Qaynuqa' and said: O assembly of Jews, embrace Islam before there befalls you the like of what befell Quraysh. They said: O Muhammad, do not let yourself deceive you that you killed a group of Quraysh who do not know fighting; if you had fought us, you would have known." So Allah, may He be exalted, revealed this verse.

The second narration: When the Jews of Madinah witnessed the event of the people of Badr, they said: By Allah, he is the Unlettered Prophet whom Moses gave us good tidings of in the Torah, and described him, and that his banner is never turned back. Then some of them said to others: Do not hasten! But when the Day of Uhud came and his companions were struck with misfortune, they said: This is not that one. Wretchedness overcame them, so they did not embrace Islam. So Allah, may He be exalted, revealed this verse.

The third narration: This verse concerns a group of disbelievers by their specific persons, whom Allah, may He be exalted, knew would die in their disbelief, and there is nothing in the verse that indicates who they are.

The third issue: Whoever argues for the obligation of what is beyond one's capacity (taklif ma la yutaq) relies on this verse, saying: Allah, may He be exalted, has informed of that group of disbelievers that they will be gathered to Hell. So if they believed and obeyed, this report would turn into a falsehood, and that is impossible; and what entails an impossibility is impossible. Therefore belief and obedience were impossible for them, while they were commanded to it. So they were commanded with the impossible and with what cannot be borne. The full exposition of this has already passed in the commentary on His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿It is the same for them whether you warn them or do not warn them; they will not believe﴾ [al-Baqarah: 6].

* * *

The fourth issue: His saying "sa-tughlabun" (you will be overcome) is a report about a matter that will occur in the future, and its reporting was in accordance with its occurrence. So this is a report of the unseen, and it is a miracle. Its parallel is His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿The Romans have been overcome in the nearest land, and they, after their defeat, will overcome﴾ [al-Rum: 2–3], and its parallel regarding 'Isa, peace be upon him: ﴿And I inform you of what you eat and what you store in your houses﴾ [Al 'Imran: 49].

The fifth issue: The verse indicates the occurrence of resurrection on the Day of Judgment, the occurrence of gathering and dispersal, and that the return of the disbelievers is to the Fire.

* * *

Then He said: ﴿And it is an evil resting-place﴾. This is because, when He, may He be exalted, mentioned their being gathered to Hell, He described it, saying: ﴿and it is an evil resting-place﴾. Al-mihad (resting-place) is the place which is prepared and on which one sleeps, like a bed. Allah, may He be exalted, said: ﴿And the earth – We have spread it out, and how excellent are the ones who spread it out﴾ [al-Dhariyat: 48]. So when Allah, may He be exalted, mentioned the destiny of the disbelievers to Hell, He reported of it with evil, because "bi'sa" is derived from "al-ba'sa'" which is evil and hardship. Allah, may He be exalted, said: ﴿And We seized those who did wrong with a severe punishment (ba'is)﴾ [al-A'raf: 165], meaning severe. And Hell is well known; may Allah protect us from it by His grace.

﴿قَدْ كانَ لَكم آيَةٌ في فِئَتَيْنِ التَقَتا فِئَةٌ تُقاتِلُ في سَبِيلِ اللَّهِ وأُخْرى كافِرَةٌ يَرَوْنَهم مِثْلَيْهِمْ رَأْيَ العَيْنِ واللَّهُ يُؤَيِّدُ بِنَصْرِهِ مَن يَشاءُ إنَّ في ذَلِكَ لَعِبْرَةً لِأُولِي الأبْصارِ﴾ .

Know that there are several issues concerning this verse.

**The first issue:** He did not say *qad kānat lakum āyatun* (with the feminine verb), but said ﴿qad kāna lakum āyatun﴾ (with the masculine verb). On this there are two views.

The first: it is construed according to the meaning. The intended sense is: "The occurrence of this has been a sign for you."

The second: al-Farrā' (the grammarian) said: the verb was made masculine because of the separation between the verb and its subject, which is the phrase *lakum* ("for you").

**The second issue:** The connection (*wajh al-naẓm*, the link with what precedes). We have mentioned that the preceding verse, His saying ﴿sa-tughlabūna wa-tuḥsharūn﴾ ("You will be overcome and gathered [to Hell]"), was revealed concerning the Jews, and that when the Messenger of Allah ﷺ invited them to Islam, they showed defiance and said: "Are we not like the Quraysh in weakness and lack of knowledge of fighting? Rather, we have strength and knowledge of war, which will overcome anyone who opposes us." So Allah the Exalted said to them: "Even though you are strong and possessors of equipment and numbers, you will indeed be overcome." Then Allah the Exalted mentioned what serves as evidence for the truth of these judgments, and said: ﴿qad kāna lakum āyatun fī fi'atayni iltaqat fi'atun﴾ ("There has been a sign for you in the two armies that met"). He means the event of Badr, which served as evidence for this, because the multitude and equipment were on the side of the disbelievers, while the few and the lack of weapons were on the side of the Muslims. Then Allah the Exalted subdued the disbelievers and made the Muslims victorious and triumphant. This indicates that that victory was by the support and aid of Allah. Whoever is thus supported will overcome all adversaries, whether they are strong or not. This is what serves as evidence that he (peace be upon him) will defeat and subdue these Jews, even if they possess weapons and power. Thus this verse became like evidence for the truth of His saying ﴿qul lilladhīna kafarū sa-tughlabūn﴾ ("Say to those who disbelieve: you will be overcome") and so on. This is the discussion of the connection of the verses.

**The third issue:** *al-fi'ah* means a group. The commentators unanimously agree that the two groups are: the Messenger of Allah ﷺ and his companions on the day of Badr, and the polytheists of Mecca. It is reported that the polytheists on the day of Badr numbered nine hundred and fifty men, among them Abū Sufyān and Abū Jahl. They brought one hundred horses, and they had seven hundred camels with them. All the horsemen were armored, and they were one hundred men; and among the infantry there was armor besides that. The Muslims were three hundred and thirteen men, with one camel for every four of them, and among them were six suits of armor and two horses. There is no doubt that the victory of the Muslims over the disbelievers in this condition is a clear sign and an overwhelming miracle.

Know that the scholars have mentioned several explanations of why that event was a clear sign:

**The first:** The Muslims had gathered several causes of weakness that prevented resistance. Among them: the small number; that they went out without intending to fight, so they had not prepared; the lack of weapons and horses; and that this was the beginning of a raid in war, since it was the first of the expeditions of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ. The polytheists, on the other hand, possessed the opposites of these qualities: a large number; they went out fully prepared for war; a great quantity of weapons and horses; and that those peoples had been practiced in fighting and battle in past times. Given this, it is not the custom that a group so small, so weak, without weapons, and with little knowledge of warfare, would defeat such a large host with abundant weapons and readiness for battle. And since that was outside the normal course of events, it was a miracle.

**The second:** The event was a sign in that he (peace and blessings be upon him) had informed his people that Allah would grant him victory over the Quraysh, by His saying ﴿wa-idh ya'idukumu llāhu iḥdā al-ṭā'ifatayni annahā lakum﴾ ("And when Allah promised you one of the two groups, that it would be yours") [al-Anfal: 7], meaning either the army of the Quraysh or the caravan of Abū Sufyān. He had also been informed before the battle that "this is the place where so-and-so will fall, and this is where so-and-so will fall." When the content of his report was found in the future exactly as he had said, that was a report of the unseen, and so it was a miracle.

**The third:** Regarding how this event was a clear sign: it is what He mentioned after this verse, namely His saying ﴿yarawnahum mithlayhim ra'y al-'ayn﴾ ("they saw them as twice their number with their own eyes"). The more correct interpretation of this verse is that the ones who see are the polytheists and the ones seen are the believers. The meaning is that the polytheists saw the believers as twice the number of the polytheists, about two thousand; or twice the number of the Muslims, which was six hundred. And that is a miracle.

If it is said: allowing the seeing of what does not exist leads to sophistry (*sufsaṭah*).

We reply: we take the seeing to mean supposition and estimation. This is because whoever is greatly afraid may suppose a small group to be very numerous. Or we may say that Allah the Exalted sent down the angels so that the Muslim army appeared numerous. The first answer is closer, because the discussion is limited to the two groups, and the story of the angels is not included in them.

**The fourth:** Regarding how this story is a sign. Al-Ḥasan said: Allah the Exalted reinforced His Messenger ﷺ in that battle with five thousand angels, because He said ﴿fa-stajāba lakum annī mumiddukum bi-alf﴾ ("So He answered you: I will reinforce you with a thousand") [al-Anfal: 9], and He said ﴿balā in taṣbirū wa-tattaqū wa-ya'tūkum min fawrihim hādhā yumdidkum rabbukum bi-khamsati ālāfin mina al-malā'ikah﴾ ("Yes, if you are patient and mindful of Allah, and they come upon you suddenly, your Lord will reinforce you with five thousand angels") [Āl ʿImrān: 125]. The thousand together with the four thousand make five thousand angels. Their distinguishing mark was that upon the tails and forelocks of their horses was white wool. This is what is meant by His saying ﴿wa-llāhu yu'ayyidu bi-naṣrihi man yashā'﴾ ("And Allah supports with His help whom He wills"). And Allah knows best.

* * *

Then Allah the Exalted said: ﴿fi'atun tuqātilu fī sabīli llāh wa-ukhrā kāfirah﴾ ("One fighting in the way of Allah, and another disbelieving"). On this there are two issues.

**The first issue:** The well-known recitation (*qirā'ah*, a mode of Qur'anic recitation) is *fi'atun* in the nominative (*raf'*), and likewise *ukhrā kāfirah*. It was also recited *fi'atin tuqātilu wa-ukhrā kāfirah* in the genitive (*jarr*), as an apposition (*badal*) to *fi'atayn*. It was also recited in the accusative (*naṣb*), either by way of specification (*ikhtiṣāṣ*) or as a circumstantial clause (*ḥāl*) from the pronoun in *iltaqat*. Al-Wāḥidī, may Allah have mercy on him, said: The nominative is the preferred reading, because the meaning is "one of them fights in the way of Allah," so it is in the nominative as a resumption of speech (*istiʾnāf*).

**The second issue:** The group that fights in the way of Allah is the Muslims, because they fought to support the religion of Allah.

As for His saying ﴿wa-ukhrā kāfirah﴾ ("and another disbelieving"), it refers to the disbelievers of Quraysh.

* * *

Then the Exalted said: ﴿yarawnahum mithlayhim ra'y al-'ayn﴾ ("they saw them as twice their number with their own eyes"). On this there are two issues.

**The first issue:** Nāfi' and Abān on the authority of ʿĀṣim recited *tarawnahum* with a *tā'* (second person) above the line, while the rest recited it with a *yā'* (third person). Whoever recites with *tā'* does so because what precedes is an address to the Jews, and the meaning is: "You, O Jews, see the Muslims as twice what they were," or "as twice the disbelieving group." Or the verse is an address to the polytheists of Quraysh, and the meaning is: "You, O polytheists of Quraysh, see the Muslims as twice your disbelieving group." Whoever recites with *yā'* does so because of the shift from address (*mughālabah*, the change from direct address to third person), which came after the address in His saying ﴿fi'atun tuqātilu fī sabīli llāh wa-ukhrā kāfirah yarawnahum mithlayhim﴾. So His saying *yarawnahum* refers back to the report about one of the two groups.

**The second issue:** Know that in this verse the disbelieving group has been mentioned, and the Muslim group has been mentioned. So His saying ﴿yarawnahum mithlayhim﴾ may allow that the seers are the disbelieving group and the seen are the Muslim group, and it may allow the reverse. These are two possibilities. Also, His saying *mithlayhim* may mean "twice the number of the seers" or "twice the number of the seen." So this verse allows four meanings:

**The first:** The intended meaning is that the disbelieving group saw the Muslims as twice the number of the polytheists, about two thousand.

**The second possibility:** The disbelieving group saw the Muslims as twice the number of the Muslims, which was six hundred and a bit more than twenty. The wisdom in this is that Allah increased the number of the Muslims in the eyes of the polytheists despite their small number, so that they would be awed and refrain from fighting them.

If it is said: this contradicts His saying in Sūrat al-Anfāl ﴿wa-yuqalliluhum fī a'yunihim﴾ ("and He made them appear few in their eyes") [al-Anfal: 44].

The answer: the reducing and the increasing happened in two different states. They were made to appear few in their eyes at first, so that they dared to engage them; then, when they met, Allah increased them in their eyes until they became overcome. Moreover, their reduction at the beginning of the matter and their increase at its end is more eloquent in demonstrating power and manifesting the sign.

**The third possibility:** The seers are the Muslims and the seen are the polytheists. So the Muslims saw the polytheists as twice the number of the Muslims, six hundred and more. The reason for this is that Allah the Exalted commanded one Muslim to confront the disbelievers. Allah the Exalted said: ﴿fa-in yakun minkum mi'atun ṣābirah yaghlibū mi'atayn﴾ ("If there are among you a hundred patient ones, they will overcome two hundred") [al-Anfal: 66].

If it is said: how could they see them as twice their number with their own eyes, when they were three times their number?

The answer: Allah the Exalted only showed the Muslims from the number of the polytheists the amount by which the Muslims knew they would overcome them. This is because He said: ﴿fa-in yakun minkum mi'atun ṣābirah yaghlibū mi'atayn﴾, so He showed the Believers that number of polytheists to strengthen their hearts and remove fear from their breasts.

**The fourth possibility:** The seers are the Muslims, and they saw the polytheists as double the number of the polytheists. This is a view that no one can hold, because it would necessitate supporting the polytheists by casting fear into the hearts of the believers, and the verse contradicts that.

There is a fifth possibility in the verse. It is that, at the beginning of the verse, we have shown that the address is to the Jews. So the meaning would be: "You, O Jews, see the polytheists as twice the believers in strength and might."

If it is said: how could they see them as twice their number when they were three times their number? The answer to this has already been given.

* * *

Two matters remain to be discussed concerning this point.

**The first discussion:** The first and second possibilities require that something non-existent became visible, whereas the third possibility requires that what existed and was present did not become visible. As for the first: it is rationally impossible, because what does not exist cannot be seen. Therefore it is necessary to interpret seeing as strong supposition. As for the second: it is permissible according to our companions (the Ash'arites), because according to us, when the conditions are met and the sense is sound, perception is permissible but not necessary. That time was a time of the manifestation of miracles and extraordinary events, so it is not far-fetched to say that this miraculous thing occurred. But the Mu'tazilah hold that perception must occur when the conditions are met and the sense is sound. For this reason, al-Qāḍī (ʿAbd al-Jabbār) offered several explanations for this point:

**The first:** During fighting and combat, a person may not have the leisure to turn his eyeball around the army and look at them in complete contemplation. Thus he sees some but not others.

**The second:** Dust may arise during the battle, which becomes an obstacle to perceiving some of them.

**The third:** It is permissible to say that Allah the Exalted created in the air something that became an obstacle to perceiving a third of the army. All of this is possible.

**The second discussion:** Although the wording allows that the seers be the polytheists and that they be the Muslims, which of the two possibilities is more apparent?

It has been said that the polytheist being the seer is preferable, and this is indicated by several considerations:

**The first:** The connection of a verb to its subject is stronger than its connection to its object. So making the nearer of the two previously mentioned items the subject and the more distant one the object is preferable to the reverse. And the nearer of the two mentioned items is His saying ﴿wa-ukhrā kāfirah﴾.

The second point: the introduction of the verse, which is His saying ﴿There has already been a sign for you﴾, is addressed to the disbelievers. So the reading of Nafi' with the ta' (ت) makes it an address to those disbelievers, and the meaning is: "You, O polytheists of Quraysh, see the Muslims as twice their number." This reading supports only the view that the seer is a polytheist.

The third point: Allah, exalted is He, made this situation a sign for the disbelievers, when He said ﴿There has already been a sign for you in the two hosts that met﴾. Therefore this situation must be something the disbeliever witnesses, so that it may serve as a proof against him.
