As for if this situation were occurring for the believer, it would not be correct to make it a proof for the disbeliever. And Allah knows best.

Those who argued that the seers are the Muslims said: if the seers were the polytheists, it would follow that they saw what does not exist, which is impossible; but if the seers were the believers, it would follow that what exists is not seen, and this is not impossible. So the latter is preferable. And Allah knows best.

* * *

Then He said: ﴿seeing with their own eyes (ra'y al-'ayn)﴾. It is said: "I saw him (ra'aytuhu) ra'yan and ru'yah," and "I saw in a dream a good vision (ru'ya hasanah)." So ru'yah is specific to dreams. And one says: "He is in my sight (mar'a al-'ayn), where my gaze falls upon him." So His saying ﴿ra'y al-'ayn﴾ may be in the accusative as a verbal noun (masdar), or it may be an adverb of place, as you say: "You see them in front of you." Similar to it is: "He is close to me (mana't al-'unuq) and at the place where the dog is driven away (mazjar al-kalb)."

* * *

Then He said: ﴿And Allah supports with His help whom He wills﴾. The help of Allah to the Muslims is of two kinds: help through victory, like the help on the day of Badr, and help through proof. For this meaning, even if we supposed that a group of believers were defeated, it would be correct to say: they are the ones who are helped, because they are the ones helped with proof and with the good end. The purpose of the verse is that victory and triumph are achieved only through the support and help of Allah, not through the multitude of numbers, strength, or weapons.

* * *

Then He said: ﴿Indeed in that is a lesson﴾. The 'ibrah (lesson) is consideration (i'tibar), and it is the sign by which one passes (ya'bur) from the station of ignorance to knowledge. Its root is from 'ubur (crossing), which is passing through from one side to the other. From it comes 'ibarah (expression), which is speech that conveys (ya'bur) the meaning to the addressee, and 'ibarat al-ru'ya (interpretation of a dream) is of this kind, because it is an explanation (ta'bir) of it. And His saying ﴿for those of insight (li-ulil-absar)﴾ means for those of intellect (ulil-'uqul), as one says: "So-and-so has insight (basar) into this matter," meaning knowledge and understanding. And Allah knows best.

This is the first part of al-Razi's commentary on Surah Al ʿImran 3:14, so I'll translate it as it stands.

Allah the Exalted says: ﴿Beautified for people is the love of desires: of women, sons, heaped-up piles of gold and silver, branded horses, cattle and tilled land. That is the enjoyment of the worldly life, but with Allah is the best return.﴾ There are several issues concerning this verse.

**The first issue: concerning the manner of its arrangement (naẓm), there are two opinions.**

The first: it relates to a story. We have been told that Abu Ḥārithah ibn ʿAlqamah, a Christian, admitted to his brother that he knew the truth of Muḥammad (ﷺ) in what he said, but he would not acknowledge it out of fear that the kings of Rome would take from him wealth and status. We have also been told that when the Prophet (ﷺ) invited the Jews to Islam after the Battle of Badr, they displayed in themselves strength, vigour, and reliance on wealth and weapons. So Allah the Exalted explained in this verse that these things, and others of the enjoyments of this world, are transient and vain, and that the Hereafter is better and more lasting.

The second opinion, which is the general interpretation: when Allah the Exalted said in the preceding verse ﴿Allah supports with His help whom He wills. Indeed in that is a lesson for those endowed with vision﴾, He then mentioned after this verse what serves as an explanation and clarification of that lesson. That is, He explained that He has beautified for people the love of bodily desires and worldly pleasures, which are themselves perishable and come to an end, their pleasures passing away while their consequences remain. Then He urged desire for the Hereafter by His saying ﴿Say: Shall I inform you of something better than that?﴾. Then He explained that the good things of the Hereafter are prepared for those who persevere in worship, among the patient and the truthful, to the end of the verse.

* * *

**The second issue: they differed over who it is that beautified these things.** As for our companions (the Ashʿarites), their position is clear, because in their view the Creator of all actions is Allah the Exalted. They also said: if the one who beautifies were Satan, then who beautified disbelief and innovation to Satan? If that was another Satan, it leads to an infinite regress; and if it came from that same Satan into the human being, then let it be so with the human being; and if it came from Allah the Exalted, which is the truth, then let it be so regarding the human being. The Qur'an alludes to this point in Surah al-Qaṣaṣ in His saying ﴿Our Lord, these are the ones whom we led astray; we led them astray as we ourselves went astray﴾ [al-Qaṣaṣ: 63], meaning: if anyone believes that We led them astray, then who led us astray? This argument is very clear.

As for the Muʿtazilah, al-Qāḍī (ʿAbd al-Jabbār) reported three opinions from them:

The first: it is related from al-Ḥasan that he said: "Satan beautified it for them," and he would swear by Allah to that. al-Qāḍī argued for them with several points:

The first of them: He, the Exalted, stated the love of desires without restriction, so it includes forbidden desires, and the one who beautifies forbidden desires is Satan.

The second: He, the Exalted, mentioned heaped-up piles of gold and silver; and love of such a great amount of wealth to this degree befits only one who has made the world the direction of his seeking and the end of his aim, for the people of the Hereafter are content with sufficiency.

The third: His saying, the Exalted, ﴿That is the enjoyment of the worldly life﴾, and there is no doubt that Allah the Exalted mentioned this in the context of disparaging the world, and disparagement of a thing precludes it from being what beautifies it.

The fourth: His saying after this verse ﴿Say: Shall I inform you of something better than that?﴾, and the purpose of this speech is to turn the servant away from the world and make it repugnant in his eyes, and that does not befit one who beautifies the world in his eyes.

The second opinion: the saying of another group of the Muʿtazilah, namely that the one who beautifies these things is Allah, and they argued for it with several points:

The first of them: just as He, the Exalted, encouraged the benefits of the Hereafter, He also created the delights of this world and permitted them to His servants; and permitting them to the servants is an embellishing of them. For when He, the Exalted, creates desire and the object desired, and creates for the one who desires knowledge of the pleasure in partaking of the object desired, and then permits him that partaking, He is then the one who beautifies it.

The second: the benefiting from these desired things is a means to the benefits of the Hereafter, and Allah the Exalted has urged toward them, so He is the one who beautifies them. We only said that benefiting from them is a means to the reward of the Hereafter for several reasons:

The first: that one gives charity from them.

The second: that one strengthens oneself with them for obedience to Allah the Exalted.

The third: that when one benefits from them and knows that those benefits were made easy by the creation and help of Allah the Exalted, this becomes a cause for the servant to occupy himself with great gratitude. For this reason al-Ṣāḥib ibn ʿAbbād used to say: drinking cold water in summer draws out praise from the depths of the heart; and he recited verse of similar meaning.

The fourth: that one who is able to enjoy these pleasures and good things, when he leaves them and occupies himself with worship and bears the hardship in them, has greater reward. Thus it is established by these points that benefiting from these good things is a means to the reward of the Hereafter.

The fifth: His saying, the Exalted, ﴿He it is who created for you all that is on the earth﴾ [al-Baqarah: 29], and He said ﴿Say: Who has forbidden the adornment of Allah which He brought forth for His servants, and the good things of provision?﴾ [al-Aʿrāf: 32], and He said ﴿Indeed We have made what is on the earth an adornment for it﴾ [al-Kahf: 7], and He said ﴿Take your adornment at every place of prayer﴾ [al-Aʿrāf: 31], and He said in Surah al-Baqarah ﴿And He sent down water from the sky and brought forth with it fruits as provision for you﴾ [al-Baqarah: 22], and He said ﴿Eat of what is on the earth, lawful and good﴾ [al-Baqarah: 168]. All of this indicates that the beautification is from Allah the Exalted. Confirming this is the reading of Mujāhid, "زَيَّنَ لِلنّاسِ" with the subject named as the agent (i.e., "He beautified for people").

The third opinion: this is the choice of Abū ʿAlī al-Jubbāʾī and al-Qāḍī: it is a detailed distinction. Every matter of this kind that is obligatory or recommended, the beautification in it is from Allah the Exalted; and every matter that is forbidden, the beautification in it is from Satan. This is what al-Qāḍī mentioned, but there remains a third category, which is the permissible (mubāḥ), whose doing or leaving carries neither reward nor punishment. Al-Qāḍī did not mention this category, and it was incumbent upon him to mention it and explain whether the beautification in it is from Allah the Exalted or from Satan.

* * *

**The third issue: concerning His saying ﴿the love of desires﴾, there are three discussions.**

The first discussion: the desires (shahawāt) here are the objects desired. They are so called by way of metaphor for attachment and connection, just as what is willed is called a "power" (qudrah), what is hoped for a "hope" (rajāʾ), and what is known a "knowledge" (ʿilm). This is a well-known metaphor in the language; one says "this is so-and-so's shahwah," meaning his object of desire. The author of al-Kashshāf said: in calling them by this name there are two benefits:

The first: he made the things he mentioned into desires, as an intensification of their being desired and eagerly sought for enjoyment.

The second: desire (shahwah) is a quality regarded as base and blameworthy by the wise; whoever follows it bears witness against himself to animality, so the purpose of mentioning this term is to create aversion to it.

The second discussion: the speakers on theology said: this verse indicates that love is other than desire, because He attributed love to desire, and the attributed is other than that to which it is attributed. Desire is from the act of Allah the Exalted, while love is from the acts of the servants, and it is an expression for a person making his whole purpose and life the pursuit of pleasures and good things.

The third discussion: the philosophers said: a person may love something yet wish that he did not love it, like a Muslim whose nature inclines toward some forbidden things but who wishes he did not love them. As for one who loves something and loves to love it, that is the perfection of love; if this is in the direction of good, it is the perfection of happiness, as in His saying, the Exalted, relating about Solomon, peace be upon him, ﴿Indeed I have loved the love of good﴾ [Ṣād: 32], meaning: I love good and I love to be a lover of good. If it is in the direction of evil, it is as He said in this verse, for His saying ﴿Beautified for people is the love of desires﴾ indicates three ordered matters:

The first: that he desires the kinds of desired things.

The second: that he loves his desire for them.

The third: that he believes that this love is good and a virtue. When these three levels come together in this matter, it reaches the utmost extreme of intensity and strength, and it scarcely unravels except by a great grace from Allah the Exalted. Then He attributed this to people, and it is a general term with the definite article, which gives comprehensiveness, so the apparent meaning requires that this condition applies to all people. Reason also indicates this, namely that whatever is pleasurable and beneficial is loved and sought for its own sake; and the pleasurable and beneficial is of two kinds: bodily and spiritual. The bodily kind is available to everyone at the outset, while the spiritual kind is found only in a single person by way of rarity; and that person attains this spiritual pleasure only after the soul has grown accustomed to bodily pleasures. So the soul's attraction to bodily pleasures is like a firmly established, consolidated disposition, while its attraction to spiritual pleasures is like a passing state that disappears with the slightest cause. Therefore the predominant tendency among creatures is indeed the strong inclination toward bodily pleasures, while the inclination toward seeking spiritual pleasures is found only in the rare individual, and his attaining it happens only at rare times. For this reason Allah generalized this judgment, saying ﴿Beautified for people is the love of desires﴾.

* * *

As for His saying, the Exalted, ﴿of women and sons﴾, there are two discussions:

The first discussion: the "min" in His saying ﴿of women and sons﴾ is like His saying ﴿so shun the abomination of idols﴾ [al-Ḥajj: 30]. Just as the meaning there is "shun the idols which are an abomination," so too the meaning of this verse is: beautified for people is the love of women and such-and-such which are desired.

The second discussion: know that He, the Exalted, enumerated here seven matters among the desired things:

The first of them: women. He placed them before all others because enjoyment of them is greater and companionship with them is more complete. For this reason He, the Exalted, said ﴿He created for you mates from yourselves that you may find rest in them, and He placed between you affection and mercy﴾ [al-Rūm: 21]. Confirming this is that the intense, consuming, destructive passion of love occurs only in this kind of desire.

The second level: love of children. Since love of male children is greater than love of female children, Allah the Exalted singled him out by mention. The benefit of enjoying them is evident in terms of joy and multiplication through them, among other things.

Know that Allah the Exalted has in creating love of spouse and child in the human heart a far-reaching wisdom, for were it not for this love, procreation and reproduction would not occur and would lead to the cutting off of progeny. This love is like an innate disposition, and for this reason it is found in all animals, and its wisdom is what we have mentioned: the continuation of offspring.

The third and fourth levels: ﴿and heaped-up piles of gold and silver﴾, and there are discussions concerning this:

Research Point 1: Al-Zajjaj said: al-qintar (a large weight or sum of wealth) is derived from the tying and securing of a thing, and al-qantarah (bridge) is derived from this because of its being secured by the arch. So al-qintar is a large amount of wealth by which a person secures himself against all kinds of calamities. Abu 'Ubayda related from the Arabs that they say: it is a weight that has no limit. Know that this is the correct view. Some people have tried to define it, and there are reports about this. Abu Hurayrah related from the Prophet ﷺ that he said: "The qintar is twelve thousand uqiyyah." Anas also related from him that "the qintar is a thousand dinars." Ubayy ibn Ka'b related that he (peace be upon him) said: "The qintar is one thousand and two hundred uqiyyah." Ibn 'Abbas said: the qintar is a thousand dinars or twelve thousand dirhams, which is the measure of the diyah (blood money). Al-Hasan also said this. Al-Kalbi said: the qintar in the language of the Romans is the filling of a bull's hide with gold or silver. There are other opinions besides what we have mentioned, but we have omitted them because they are not supported by any proof whatsoever.

Research Point 2: (al-muqantarah) is a passive participle derived from al-qintar, and it is for emphasis, like their saying: alfun mu'allafah (a thousand gathered), badrah mubaddarah (a purse scattered), ibil mu'abbalah (camels gathered in herds), and darahim mudarhamah (dirhams in heaps). Al-Kalbi said: al-qanatir are three, and al-muqantarah is the doubled one, so the total was six.

Research Point 3: Gold and silver are loved only because they have become the price of all things, so their owner is like the owner of all things. The attribute of ownership is power, and power is an attribute of perfection, and perfection is loved for its own sake. Since gold and silver are the most perfect means of attaining this perfection, which is loved for its own sake, and what the beloved is attained only through is itself beloved, therefore they are inevitably loved.

* * *

Fifth Issue: ﴿wal-khayli al-musawwamah﴾ (and the branded horses). Al-Wahidi said: al-khayl (horses) is a collective noun with no singular from its own form, like al-qawm (people), al-nisa' (women), and al-rahṭ (group). Mares were called khayl because of their proud gait (khuyala'), and a person's movement in a free-roaming manner was called ikhtiyal (strutting), and the imagination was called khayal, and imagining was called takhayyul, because this faculty roams in summoning that image. Al-akhyal is the shiqrraq (magpie), because it appears at times green and at times red. Scholars differed about the meaning of al-musawwamah in three opinions.

The first: they are the grazing ones. It is said: asamtu al-dabbah and sawwamtuha when you release it into its pastures to graze, just as it is said aqamtu al-shay' and qawwamtuhu, and ajadtu and jawwadtu, and anamtu and nawwamtu. The intended meaning is that when they graze they grow in beauty. From this is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿fihi tusimun﴾ (in which you pasture) [al-Nahl: 10].

The second opinion: al-musawwamah means the marked ones. Abu Muslim al-Isfahani said: it is derived from al-simা (with short alif) and al-sima' (with long alif), and their meaning is one, which is a good appearance. God, exalted is He, said: ﴿sima-hum fi wujuhihim min athari al-sujud﴾ (their mark is on their faces from the trace of prostration) [al-Fath: 29]. Then those who held this view differed about that mark. Abu Muslim said: the intended meaning of these marks is the white spots and blazes that appear on horses, namely that the mares are blazed and white-socked. Al-Asamm said: they are only the piebald markings. Qatadah said: the shiyah (distinctive coloring). Al-Mu'arrij said: the branding. Abu Muslim's view is the best, because the reference in this verse is to the noblest of wealth, and that is for the horse to be blazed and white-socked. As for the other aspects they mentioned, they do not add any nobility to the horse.

The third opinion, which is the view of Mujahid and 'Ikrimah: they are the fine, handsome horses. Al-Qaffal said: al-mutahhamah is a beautiful woman.

Sixth Rank: (al-an'am), which is the plural of na'am, and these are camels, cattle and sheep. The single animal of each kind is not called na'am except for camels specifically, since the term came to be applied predominantly to them.

Seventh Rank: (wal-harth), the tilth, and we have already mentioned its derivation in His saying ﴿wa-yuhlika al-harth wal-nasl﴾ (and destroy the crops and the offspring) [al-Baqarah: 205].

Then, when He, exalted is He, enumerated these seven, He said: ﴿dhalika matā' al-hayah al-dunya﴾ (that is the enjoyment of the worldly life). The judge said: It is known that the enjoyment of this world was created only to be enjoyed, so how can it be said that it is not permissible to attribute adornment to God, exalted is He?

Then he said: There are aspects to enjoying the enjoyments of this world:
Among them is that one monopolizes it, the one whom God has singled out with these blessings, and thus he is blameworthy.
Among them is that one abstains from benefiting from it while in need of it, and so he is also blameworthy.
Among them is that one benefits from it in a permissible way without thereby reaching the interests of the Hereafter, and that is neither praiseworthy nor blameworthy.
Among them is that one benefits from it in a way by which he reaches the interests of the Hereafter, and this is the praiseworthy one.

* * *

Then He, exalted is He, said: ﴿wallahu 'indahu husn al-ma'ab﴾ (and with God is the best place of return). Know that al-ma'ab in the language means the return place. It is said: aba al-rajul iyaban, awbatan, ayabatan and ma'aban. God, exalted is He, said: ﴿inna ilayna iyabahum﴾ (indeed, to Us is their return) [al-Ghashiyah: 25]. The purpose of this statement is to explain that whoever God has granted worldly provision, it is obligatory upon him to spend it on what will cultivate his afterlife, and to reach through it the felicity of his Hereafter. Then, since the aim is to encourage the return, He described the return as good.

If it is said: the return is of two kinds: Paradise, which is at the utmost of goodness, and Hell, which is devoid of goodness, so how does He describe the absolute return as good?

We say: the return intended in essence is Paradise, whereas Hell is intended only incidentally, because He, glorified is He, created creation for mercy, not for punishment, as He said: "My mercy precedes My wrath." And this is a secret from which obscure secrets are disclosed.

[Page 173]

The words of the Most High: ﴿Say: Shall I inform you of something better than that? For those who are conscious of God, with their Lord are gardens beneath which rivers flow, abiding therein forever, and pure spouses, and the good pleasure of God. And God is Seeing of His servants.﴾

In this verse there are several issues.

**The first issue:** Ibn 'Amir, 'Asim, Hamza and al-Kisa'i read ﴿أؤُنَبِّئُكُمْ﴾ (*a-unabbi'ukum*) with two hamzas. The transmission from Nafi' and Abu 'Amr differs.

**The second issue:** Scholars have mentioned three possibilities for what the interrogative (*al-istifham*) is connected to:

The first: the meaning is "Shall I inform you of something better than that?", and then a new sentence begins: "For those who are conscious of God, with their Lord are such-and-such."

The second: "Shall I inform you of something better than that for those who are conscious of God?", and then a new sentence begins: "With their Lord are gardens which flow..."

The third: "Shall I inform you of something better than that for those who are conscious of God with their Lord?", and then a new sentence begins: "Gardens which flow..."

**The third issue:** Regarding the arrangement (*wajh al-nazm*) of the verse, there are several explanations:

The first: When He said, ﴿And with God is the best return﴾, He clarified in this verse that this return, just as it is good in itself, is better and more excellent than this world. So He said, ﴿Say: Shall I inform you of something better than that?﴾

The second: When He enumerated the blessings of this world, He clarified that the benefits of the Hereafter are better than them, as He said in another verse, ﴿But the Hereafter is better and more lasting﴾ [al-A'la: 17].

The third: It is as if He, the Most High, drew attention to the fact that your affair in this world, though good and orderly, is less than your affair in the Hereafter, which is better and more excellent. The purpose of this is that the servant should know that just as this world is more pleasant, wider and more spacious than the womb of the mother, so the Hereafter is more pleasant, wider and more spacious than this world.

**The fourth issue:** We say that the blessings of the Hereafter are better than the blessings of this world because the blessings of this world are mixed with harm, while the blessings of the Hereafter are entirely free from any admixture of harm. Also, the blessings of this world are inevitably terminated, while the blessings of the Hereafter are inevitably everlasting.

As for His saying, ﴿For those who are conscious of God﴾: we have already explained, in the commentary on His saying, ﴿a guidance for those who are conscious of God﴾ [al-Baqarah: 2], what piety (*al-taqwa*) is. In general, a person is not "conscious of God" unless he performs the obligations and guards himself against what is forbidden. Some of our companions said: piety is an expression for guarding oneself against polytheism (*shirk*). This is because piety has, in the usage of the Qur'an, become specific to faith, as He, the Most High, said: ﴿And He made the word of piety binding upon them﴾ [al-Fath: 26]. The apparent meaning of the expression also agrees with this, because guarding oneself against polytheism is more general than guarding oneself against all forbidden things, and more general than guarding oneself against some of the forbidden things, since the essence of commonality does not indicate the essence of distinction. Thus the reality and essence of piety is present when one guards oneself against polytheism, and the usage of the Qur'an agrees with this, so it is necessary to interpret it accordingly. Therefore His saying, ﴿For those who are conscious of God﴾, is taken to refer to everyone who guards himself against disbelief in God.

As for His saying, ﴿For those who are conscious of God, with their Lord﴾, there are two possibilities:

The first: that this is a qualifier of the good (*khayr*), and the meaning is: "Shall I inform you of something better than that, with their Lord, for those who are conscious of God?"

The second: that this is a qualifier of those who are conscious of God, and the meaning is: "For those who are conscious of God, with their Lord, is something better than the benefits of this world." This indicates that this great reward is not attained except by one who is conscious of God in the sight of God, so the hypocrite is excluded from it, and whoever is a believer in the knowledge of God is included in it.

As for His saying (*jannat*, "gardens"): the implied reading is "they are gardens." Some read *jannatin* in the genitive, as an apposition (*badal*) to *khayr*. Know that His saying, ﴿gardens beneath which rivers flow﴾, is a description of the goodness of Paradise, and everything in it of blessings is included under it: food, drink, clothing, furnishings and scenery. In general, Paradise comprises all desires, as He, the Most High, said: ﴿And therein is what the souls desire and what the eyes delight in﴾ [al-Zukhruf: 71].

* * *

Then He said: ﴿abiding therein﴾, and what is meant is that those blessings are lasting.

* * *

Then He said: ﴿and pure spouses, and the good pleasure of God﴾. We have mentioned their subtleties at His saying in Surat al-Baqarah: ﴿and for them therein are pure spouses﴾ [al-Baqarah: 25]. The fullest statement on this is that blessing, however great it may be, will not be complete except through spouses, with whom intimacy is not attained except through them. Then He described the spouses with one attribute that encompasses every desired quality, saying *"pure"* (*muṭahharah*). This includes purity from menstruation, post-natal bleeding, and all the conditions that appear in women in this world and from which natural disposition recoils. It also includes their being pure of blameworthy character traits, of ugliness, and of disfigurement of form; and it includes their being pure of bad companionship.

* * *

Then the Most High said: ﴿and the good pleasure of God﴾. On this there are two issues:

**The first issue:** ʿĀsim read *wa-rudwānun* with a *ḍamma* on the *rāʾ*, while the rest read it with a *kasra*. As for the *ḍamma*, it is the dialect of Qays and Tamim. al-Farra' said: it is said *raḍītu riḍan wa-riḍwānan*. Like *ridwān* with a *kasra* are *al-ḥirmān* and *al-qirbān*; and with a *ḍamma* are *al-ṭughyān*, *al-rujḥān*, *al-kufrān* and *al-shukrān*.

**The second issue:** The theologians (*al-mutakallimūn*) said: reward has two pillars. One is benefit, which is what we have mentioned. The second is honour, and this is what is meant by *riḍwān*. This is because the knowledge of the people of Paradise, together with this lasting bliss, that He, the Most High, is pleased with them, approves of them and praises them, is more effective in producing joy than those benefits. As for the philosophers (*al-ḥukamā'*), they said: "the gardens with what is in them" refer to the physical Paradise, and "the good pleasure" refers to the spiritual Paradise, and the highest stations are only the spiritual Paradise. It is an expression for the manifestation of the light of God's majesty in the spirit of the servant and the servant's absorption in knowledge of Him. Then at the beginning of these stations he becomes content with God, and at their end he becomes one with whom God is content. To this refers His saying, ﴿content, well-pleasing﴾ [al-Fajr: 28]. A parallel to this verse is His saying: ﴿God has promised the believing men and believing women gardens beneath which rivers flow, abiding therein, and good dwellings in gardens of perpetual residence. But the good pleasure of God is greater. That is the great achievement﴾ [al-Tawbah: 72].

* * *

Then He said: ﴿And God is Seeing of His servants﴾, that is, He is Knowing of their interests. Therefore they must be content with what He has chosen for them of the blessings of the Hereafter, and must renounce what He has made them renounce of the affairs of this world.

**Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on Surah 3, Verse 16**

His words, exalted is He: ﴿Those who say, "Our Lord, indeed we have believed, so forgive us our sins and protect us from the punishment of the Fire."﴾

On this verse there are several issues:

**The first issue:** On the grammatical analysis (i'rab, the study of case endings and sentence function) of the position of ﴿الَّذِينَ يَقُولُونَ﴾ (alladhina yaqulun, "those who say"), there are several views:

The first: it is in the genitive (khafd) as an adjective (sifah) of ﴿لِلَّذِينَ اتَّقَوْا﴾ (for those who have been mindful of God). The construction would be: "for those who have been mindful, those who say..." It may also be an adjective of ﴿الْعِبَادِ﴾ (the servants), and the sense would be: "God is seeing of the servants, and those are the mindful ones, those for whom with their Lord are gardens... they are those who say such-and-such."

The second: it is in the accusative (nasb) by way of praise (madh).

The third: it is in the nominative (raf') by way of specification (takhsis), and the sense is: "They are those who say such-and-such."

**The second issue:** Know that God, exalted is He, related of them that they said, ﴿Our Lord, indeed we have believed﴾, and then they said after that, ﴿so forgive us our sins﴾. This indicates that they sought forgiveness by means of faith alone (mujarrad al-iman) as a means (tawassul). God related this about them in the context of praising them and commending them. This shows that a servant, by faith alone, deserves mercy and forgiveness from God, exalted is He.

If they (the opponents) say: "Faith is an expression for all acts of obedience," we refute this for them by the proofs mentioned in the explanation of His words, ﴿those who believe in the unseen﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:3].

Furthermore: whoever obeys God, exalted is He, in all matters and repents of all sins, then for them, his being cast into the Fire would be an ugly act on God's part. And the ugly (qabih) is that which arises from the one who does it, either from ignorance (jahl) or from need (hajah). Both of these are impossible, and what entails the impossible is impossible. Therefore, God's casting them into the Fire is impossible. And whatever is rationally impossible to occur, the supplication and humble entreaty that God not do it is a futile and ugly thing.

A parallel to this verse is His words at the end of this surah: ﴿Our Lord, indeed we heard a caller calling to faith, "Believe in your Lord," so we believed. Our Lord, forgive us our sins, expiate from us our misdeeds, and cause us to die with the righteous﴾ [Al 'Imran 3:193].

If it is said: Did not God take the totality of acts of obedience into account for attaining forgiveness, since He followed this verse with His words, ﴿the patient and the truthful﴾ [Al 'Imran 3:17]?

We say: The interpretation of this verse confirms what we have mentioned. This is because He made faith alone a means to seeking forgiveness, then mentioned after it the attributes of the obedient, which are that they are patient and truthful. Had these attributes been conditions for attaining this forgiveness, mentioning them before seeking forgiveness would have been more fitting. Since He ordered the seeking of forgiveness upon faith alone, and then mentioned these attributes after that, we know that these attributes are not considered in the attainment of the basic forgiveness, and that they are considered only in the attainment of the perfection of ranks.

**Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on Surah 3, verse 17:**

Allah's words, ﴿the patient, the truthful, the obedient, those who spend, and those who seek forgiveness at dawn﴾.

Concerning this there are several issues:

**First issue:** *al-Sabirin* (الصابرين, "the patient") is said to be in the accusative case by way of praise, with the implied meaning "I mean the patient." It is also said that *al-Sabirin* is in the genitive case as an apposition (*badal*) to *alladhina* (الذين, "those who").

**Second issue:** Know that Allah, exalted is He, mentions here five attributes.

**The first attribute:** that they are patient (*sabirun*). What is meant is that they are patient in performing the obligatory and recommended acts, and in abstaining from what is forbidden, and that they are patient in everything that befalls them of trials and hardships. This means that they do not complain but remain content in their hearts with Allah, exalted is He, as He said: ﴿Those who, when a calamity afflicts them, say, "Indeed we belong to Allah, and indeed to Him we will return"﴾ [al-Baqarah: 156]. Sufyan ibn 'Uyayna, concerning His words ﴿And We made from among them leaders guiding by Our command when they were patient﴾ [al-Sajdah: 24], said: this verse indicates that they deserved those high ranks from Allah, exalted is He, only because of patience.

It is narrated that a man stood before al-Shibli and asked: "What patience is the most difficult for the patient?" He said: "Patience in Allah, exalted is He." The man said: "No." He said: "Patience for Allah, exalted is He." The man said: "No." He said: "Patience with Allah, exalted is He." The man said: "No." He said: "Then what?" He said: "Patience away from Allah, exalted is He." Then al-Shibli let out a cry that nearly destroyed his soul.

[Page 176]

Allah, exalted is He, has often praised the patient, as He said: ﴿And the patient in misfortune and adversity and during battle﴾ [al-Baqarah: 177].

**The second attribute:** that they are truthful (*sadiqun*). Know that the word *sidq* (صدق, "truthfulness") may apply to speech, action, and intention. Truthfulness in speech is well known, and it is avoiding lying. Truthfulness in action is carrying the act out and not turning away from it before completing it. It is said: "So-and-so was truthful in the fighting," and "was truthful in general." The opposite is said: "He lied in the fighting," and "lied in general." Truthfulness in intention is carrying out the resolve and persisting in it until it reaches the act.

**The third attribute:** that they are obedient (*qanitun*). We have explained this in His words: ﴿And stand before Allah in obedience﴾ [al-Baqarah: 238]. In summary, it is an expression for constancy in worship and persistence in it.

**The fourth attribute:** that they spend (*munfiqun*). This includes a person's spending on himself, his family, and his relatives, maintaining ties of kinship, zakat, jihad, and all other forms of righteousness.

**The fifth attribute:** that they seek forgiveness at dawn (*bil-asḥar*). *Saḥar* (السحر, "the pre-dawn period") is the time before the break of dawn, and *tasahhara* means he ate during that time. Know that what is meant is one who prays at night and then follows it with seeking forgiveness and supplication, because a person does not occupy himself with supplication and seeking forgiveness unless he has prayed before that. So His words ﴿and those who seek forgiveness at dawn﴾ indicate that they had prayed at night. Know also that seeking forgiveness at the pre-dawn has a greater effect in strengthening faith and in perfecting servitude, in several respects:

*First:* At the time of pre-dawn, the light of morning rises after darkness had covered everything. Because of the rising of the morning light, it is as if the dead become living, so that is a time of general generosity and complete outpouring. It is therefore not far-fetched that when the morning of the greater world rises, the morning of the lesser world rises as well, which is the appearance of the light of Allah's majesty in the heart.

*Second:* The pre-dawn is the most pleasant time for sleep. So when the servant turns away from that pleasure and devotes himself to servitude, his obedience is more perfect.

*Third:* It is reported from Ibn 'Abbas concerning ﴿and those who seek forgiveness at dawn﴾ that he meant those who pray the dawn prayer.

**Third issue:** His words *al-sabirin wa al-sadiqin* (الصابرين والصادقين) are more complete than saying *alladhina yasbiruna wa yasdiquna* (الذين يصبرون ويصدقون, "those who are patient and truthful"), because His words *al-sabirin* indicate that this quality is their habit and their character, and that they do not part from it.

* * *

**Fourth issue:** Know that Allah, exalted is He, has imposed upon His servants various kinds of obligations, and the patient one is the one who is patient in performing all of them. Then the servant may bind himself, of his own accord, to other kinds of acts of obedience, either by way of beginning them. The perfection of this rank is that when he binds himself to an act of obedience, he is truthful to himself in that commitment, by carrying it out for the one to whom he committed it without any deficiency whatsoever. Since this rank comes after the first, He, glorified is He, therefore mentioned the patient first and then said *al-sadiqin* second. Then Allah, exalted is He, urged persistence in these two kinds of obedience, saying *wal-qanitin* (والقانتين, "and the obedient"). So these three words are an encouragement to persist in all kinds of obedience. After that He mentioned specific acts of obedience. The two greatest in rank among acts of obedience are:

*One:* service with wealth, to which the Prophet, peace be upon him, alluded in his saying: "And compassion toward the creatures of Allah." So He mentioned it here with His words *wal-munfiqin* (والمنفقين, "and those who spend").

*Second:* service with the self, to which he alluded in his saying: "Glorifying the command of Allah." So He mentioned it here with His words ﴿and those who seek forgiveness at dawn﴾.

[Page 177]

If it is asked: Why did He here put the mention of those who spend before the mention of those who seek forgiveness, while in the Prophet's saying "Glorifying the command of Allah and compassion toward the creatures of Allah" the order is reversed?

We say: Because this verse describes the servant's ascent from the lower to the higher. Therefore the conclusion was with the mention of those who seek forgiveness at dawn. The saying "Glorifying the command of Allah" appears in the description of the servant's descent from the higher to the lower. Therefore the order was reversed.

**Fifth issue:** These five are an enumeration of attributes for one described subject. So it would have been required to omit the conjunction *waw* (واو, "and") between them, as in His words ﴿He is Allah, the Creator, the Originator, the Fashioner﴾ [al-Hashr: 24]. However, here He mentioned the conjunction *waw*. I think, and Allah knows best, that everyone who possesses any one of these qualities enters under great praise and deserves this abundant reward. And Allah knows best.

[Page 178]

The Exalted said: ﴿God bears witness that there is no god but He, and the angels and those of knowledge, standing firm in justice. There is no god but He, the Mighty, the Wise.﴾

Know that when the Exalted praised the believers and commended them by His saying ﴿Those who say, "Our Lord, we have believed"﴾, He followed this by explaining that the proofs of faith are manifest and clear, and so He said: ﴿God bears witness﴾. On this there are several issues.

The first issue: Know that everything on which knowledge of the prophethood of Muhammad (ﷺ) depends, that knowledge cannot be established by the revealed (sam'i) proofs. As for what is not of this kind, it is permissible to establish it by revealed proofs. This applies to the case of the angels and to the case of those of knowledge. However, knowledge of the validity of the prophethood of Muhammad (ﷺ) does not depend on knowledge that God the Exalted is one. Therefore, it is permissible to establish that God the Exalted is one solely by the revealed Qur'anic proofs.

Having understood this, we say: The commentators have mentioned two views regarding His saying ﴿God bears witness that there is no god but He, and the angels and those of knowledge﴾:

The first: that the witnessing comes from God the Exalted, from the angels, and from those of knowledge in one and the same sense.

The second: that it is not so.

As for the first view, it can be established in two ways:

The first way: that you take witnessing to mean declaration accompanied by knowledge. This meaning is one concept, and it is present in the case of God the Exalted, in the case of the angels, and in the case of those of knowledge. As for God the Exalted, He has declared in the Qur'an concerning His being one, with no god besides Him. We have already explained that relying on revealed proof in this matter is permissible. As for the angels and those of knowledge, they all also declare that God the Exalted is one, with no partner. Thus it is established on this explanation that the understanding of witnessing is one meaning in the case of God, in the case of the angels, and in the case of those of knowledge.

[Page 178 continues]

The second way: that we take witnessing to mean manifestation and clarification. Then we say: He, the Exalted, manifested and clarified that by creating what indicates it. As for the angels and those of knowledge, they manifested and clarified it by setting out proofs and demonstrations. As for the angels, they clarified this to the messengers, peace be upon them; the messengers clarified it to the scholars; and the scholars clarified it to the common people. Thus the difference lies only in the means by which manifestation and clarification occurred. The concept, therefore, is manifestation and clarification, which is one concept in the case of God, glorified and exalted is He, and in the case of those of knowledge. It becomes clear that the understanding of witnessing is one on these two explanations. The purpose of this, as if He were saying to the Messenger (ﷺ): The oneness of God the Exalted is a matter established by the witness of God the Exalted and the witness of all the reliable among His creation. A religion this firm and a path this upright does not weaken, unlike the view of some ignorant people among the Christians and the idol-worshippers. So persist, you and your people, O Muhammad, in this, for it is Islam, and "the religion with God is Islam."

The second view: the view of those who say that God the Exalted's witnessing to His oneness is an expression of His having created the proofs indicating His oneness, and the witnessing of the angels and those of knowledge is an expression of their affirmation of that. Since each of these two matters is called witnessing, there is no impropriety in gathering both under one word. A parallel to this is His saying: ﴿Indeed, God and His angels send blessings upon the Prophet. O you who have believed, send blessings upon him and greet him with a worthy greeting﴾ [al-Ahzab: 56]. It is known that the blessing from God is other than the blessing from the angels, and the blessing from the angels is other than the blessing from people, yet He has gathered them in one word.

If it is said: The one who claims oneness is God, so how can the one who claims be a witness?

The answer has several aspects:

The first: The true witness is none other than God, because He is the One who created things and made them indicators of His oneness. Had those indicators not existed, witnessing would not be valid. Then, after that, the establishing of those indicators is what enabled the scholars to know them. Had it not been for the indicators that God established and guided them to, they would have been unable to reach knowledge of oneness through them. Since this is the case, the true witness to oneness is none other than God alone. Therefore He said: ﴿Say, "What thing is greatest in testimony?" Say, "God"﴾ [al-An'am: 19].

The second answer: He is the One who exists eternally and everlastingly, and everything other than Him was, in eternity, pure non-existence and absolute negation. Non-existence resembles the absent, and existence resembles the present. Thus everything other than Him was absent, and by the witness of the Truth it became present. So the Truth became a witness over all. Therefore He said: ﴿God bears witness that there is no god but He﴾.

The third answer: Although this has the form of witnessing, it carries the sense of affirmation, because when He declared that there is no god besides Him, all beings became His servants. A noble master is not fitting to neglect the interests of his servants. So this statement works as an affirmation that it is incumbent upon Him, as the Noble, to look after the affairs of all creation.

The fourth answer: Ibn 'Abbas recited "God bears witness that indeed there is no god but He," with the particle "inna" in the kasra form, and then recited "Indeed the religion with God is Islam," with "anna" in the fatha form. On this reading the meaning becomes: God bears witness that the religion with God is Islam, and His saying "indeed there is no god but He" is then a parenthetical insertion in the speech. Know that this answer is not to be relied upon, because this reading is not accepted by the scholars. And even supposing it were accepted, the first reading is agreed upon, so the difficulty that arises from it is not resolved by the other reading.

[Page 179]

The second issue: What is meant by ﴿those of knowledge﴾ in this verse are those who came to know His oneness through decisive proofs, because witnessing is only acceptable when the declaration is accompanied by knowledge. For this reason the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "When you know as clearly as the sun, then bear witness." This indicates that this high rank and this noble station belong only to the scholars of the foundations (of religion).

* * *

As for His saying ﴿standing firm in justice﴾, there are several issues:

The first issue: ﴿standing firm in justice﴾ is in the accusative case, and there are several explanations of it:

The first explanation: it is in the accusative as a circumstantial state (hal). Here there are several possibilities: One is that the implied sense is: God bears witness, standing firm in justice. Second: it may be a circumstantial state of the pronoun in "huwa," with the implied sense: there is no god but He, standing firm in justice. This is called an emphatic circumstantial state, like your saying: "Abdullah came to us bravely," and like your saying: "There is no man except Abdullah, bravely."

The second explanation: that it is an adjective of the negated noun, as if it were said: "There is no god standing firm in justice except He." This is not far-fetched, because they separate between the adjective and the noun it describes.

The third explanation: that it is in the accusative as a term of praise.

If it is said: Is it not the case that praise should be definite, as in your saying "All praise is for God, the Praiseworthy"?

We reply: It has also come indefinite. Sibawayh recited:

"And he resorts to women, idle and disheveled,
nursing mothers like the ghouls."

The second issue: His saying ﴿standing firm in justice﴾ has two explanations:

The first: that it is a circumstantial state of the believers, and the sense is: "and those of knowledge," in the state of each one of them standing firm in justice in the performance of this witnessing.

The second, which is the view of the majority of the exegetes: that it is a circumstantial state of ﴿God bears witness﴾.

The third issue: The meaning of His being ﴿standing firm in justice﴾ is standing firm in justice, as one says: "So-and-so is in charge of the management," meaning he carries it out on a correct course.

Know that this justice of His is partly connected with the affairs of this world and partly connected with the affairs of religion. As for what is connected with religion, consider first the way in which the parts of the human body were created, so that you may know God's justice in them. Then look at the variation in the conditions of creation in beauty and ugliness, wealth and poverty, health and sickness, long life and short life, pleasure and pain, and be certain that all of this is justice from God, and wisdom, and right. Then look at the way He created the elements and the bodies of the celestial spheres, and His determining each of them by a specific measure and a specific property, and be certain that all of this is wisdom and right. As for what is connected with the matter of religion, consider the variation among creatures in knowledge and ignorance, intelligence and dullness, guidance and misguidance, and be certain that all of this is justice and equity.

Here the author of the Kashshaf (al-Zamakhshari) plunged into partisanship for Mu'tazilism (the rationalist school that held God's justice and oneness as central principles), and claimed that the verse indicates that Islam is justice and monotheism. That poor fellow was far from knowledge of these matters, yet he was a meddler who delved much into what he did not know. He claimed that the verse indicates that whoever permits the vision of God, or adheres to determinism (jabr, the doctrine that human beings have no real power over their actions), is not upon the religion of God, which is Islam. The wonder is that the leading Mu'tazilites and their great men spent their lives seeking a proof that if God were visible He would have to be a body, and they found in it nothing but reasoning from the observed to the unobserved without a decisive rational common ground. So how did this poor man, who never smelled a whiff of knowledge, find that!

[Page 180]

As for the matter of determinism, plunging into it by that poor man is plunging into what does not concern him, because he admitted that God the Exalted knows all particulars, and he admitted that the servant cannot turn God's knowledge into ignorance. Therefore he has already admitted this determinism. So how can he, and delving into such discussions!

Then God the Exalted said: ﴿There is no god but He﴾. The benefit of repeating it has several aspects:

The first: the sense of the verse is: God bears witness that there is no god but He, and when He bears witness to that, it is established that there is no god but He. A parallel to this is the saying of one who says: "The proof has indicated the oneness of God the Exalted, and when this is so, the affirmation of the oneness of God the Exalted is established."

The second: when He, the Exalted, informed us that God bears witness that there is no god but He, and the angels and those of knowledge bear witness to that, the sense becomes as if He said: O community of Muhammad, then you too say, in accordance with the witness of God, the witness of the angels, and those of knowledge: ﴿There is no god but He﴾. So the purpose of the repetition is the command to utter this word in accordance with those testimonies.

The third: the benefit of this repetition is to inform that the Muslim must always be repeating this word, for the noblest word a person can mention is this word. When he is occupied most of the time with mentioning it and repeating it, he is occupied with one of the greatest kinds of worship. So the purpose of the repetition in this verse is to urge the servants to repeat it.

The fourth: He mentioned ﴿There is no god but He﴾ first to make known that worship is due only to God the Exalted, and He mentioned it a second time to make known that He is the One standing firm in justice, who does not oppress and does not wrong.

As for His saying ﴿the Mighty, the Wise﴾: "the Mighty" points to perfection of power, and "the Wise" points to perfection of knowledge. These are the two attributes without which divinity cannot be realized, because His standing firm in justice is not complete unless He knows the measures of needs and is able to accomplish the great affairs. He placed "the Mighty" before "the Wise" in mention, because knowledge that God the Exalted is powerful precedes knowledge that He is knowing, in the path of inferential knowledge. Since it precedes in inferential knowledge, and this address is with those who reason, He necessarily mentioned "the Mighty" before "the Wise."

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 3, verse 19:

His saying, may He be exalted, ﴿Indeed, the religion with Allah is Islam﴾. On this verse there are several issues:

**The first issue:** The reciters agreed on reading *inna* (إنَّ) with a kasra, except al-Kisa'i (al-Kisā'ī), who read *anna* (أنَّ) with a fatha. The reading of the majority is clear, because the speech before it is complete. As for al-Kisa'i's reading, the grammarians mention three possibilities concerning it:

The first: the implied meaning is, "Allah has borne witness that there is no god but He, that the religion with Allah is Islam." This is because His being One necessitates that the true religion be Islam, since the religion of Islam is the one that includes this oneness.

The second: the implied meaning is, "Allah has borne witness that there is no god but He, and that the religion with Allah is Islam."

The third, which is the view of the Basrans, is that the second clause is a *badal* (substitution) for the first. Then, if we say that the religion of Islam includes monotheism itself, this is of the type of your saying, "I struck Zayd himself" (*daraba Zaydan nafsahu*). If we say that the religion of Islam includes monotheism, this is of the type of *badal al-ishtimal* (substitution of inclusion), like your saying, "I struck Zayd his head" (*daraba Zaydan ra'sahu*).

If it is objected: On this view, the name of Allah, may He be exalted, should not be repeated, just as one would not say, "I struck Zayd the head of Zayd."

We reply: They sometimes show the noun explicitly in a place where a pronoun would be expected. The poet said:

> *I do not see death preceding death, anything...*

And there are many similar examples.

**The second issue:** Regarding the arrangement of the construction: whoever reads *anna al-dīna* with the fatha of *anna* means: "Allah bore witness, on account of the fact that there is no god but He, that the religion with Allah is Islam." For if Islam is the religion that includes monotheism, and Allah, may He be exalted, has borne witness to this oneness, then what necessarily follows is that the religion with Allah is Islam. As for whoever reads *inna al-dīna* with a kasra on the hamza, the point of connection is that He, may He be exalted, has made clear that monotheism is a matter whose correctness Allah has witnessed, and the angels and those possessing knowledge have also witnessed to it. When this is the case, it necessarily follows that it be said: ﴿Indeed, the religion with Allah is Islam﴾.

**The third issue:** The root meaning of *dīn* (religion) in the language is recompense. Then obedience is called *dīn* because it is the cause of recompense. As for *Islam*, there are several meanings for it in the original linguistic usage:

The first: it is an expression for entering into Islam, that is, into submission and obedience. He, may He be exalted, said: ﴿And do not say to one who offers you peace...﴾ [an-Nisa': 94], meaning: to one who has become submissive to you and obedient to you.

The second: "*man aslama*" means he entered into peace (*salm*), like their saying *asnā* (he entered the summer) and *aqhaṭa* (he entered a year of drought). The root of *salm* is safety.

The third: Ibn al-Anbari said: the meaning of *muslim* is one who makes his worship sincere to Allah, from their saying, "The thing became *salima* for so-and-so," that is, it became pure for him. So the meaning of *Islam* is the sincere devotion of religion and creed to Allah, may He be exalted. This is what relates to the explanation of the word *Islam* in the original language. As for in the usage of the Sharia (religious law), *Islam* is *iman* (faith). The evidence for this is two-fold:

The first: this verse itself. For His saying, ﴿Indeed, the religion with Allah is Islam﴾ requires that the religion accepted with Allah is nothing but Islam. So if *iman* were other than *Islam*, then *iman* would not be an accepted religion with Allah. There is no doubt that this is false.

The second: His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And whoever seeks other than Islam as a religion, it will never be accepted from him﴾ [Al 'Imran: 85]. So if *iman* were other than *Islam*, then *iman* would not be a religion accepted with Allah, may He be exalted.

If it is objected: His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿The Bedouins say, "We have believed." Say, "You have not believed; but say, 'We have submitted'"﴾ [al-Hujurat: 14]. This is explicit that *Islam* is different from *iman*.

We reply: *Islam* in the original language is an expression for submission, as we have explained. The hypocrites submitted outwardly out of fear of the sword, so *Islam* was inevitably present in the judgment of the outward, and *iman* was also present in the judgment of the outward, because He, may He be exalted, said: ﴿And do not marry polytheistic women until they believe﴾ [al-Baqarah: 221]. And the *iman* upon which the ruling can be based is the outward declaration. So, on this basis, *Islam* and *iman* are sometimes considered in the outward and sometimes in reality. The hypocrite obtained outward *Islam* but did not obtain inward *Islam*, because his inner self was not submissive to the religion of Allah. Thus the implied meaning of the verse is: "You have not submitted in the heart and inwardly, but say, 'We have submitted' outwardly." And Allah knows best.

* *

As for His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And those who were given the Book did not differ except after knowledge had come to them, out of envy among themselves. And whoever disbelieves in the signs of Allah, then indeed Allah is swift in reckoning﴾, on it there are several issues:

**The first issue:** The purpose of the verse is to explain that Allah, may He be exalted, has made the proofs clear and removed the doubts, and the people did not disbelieve except due to negligence. So His saying, ﴿And those who were given the Book did not differ﴾ has several interpretations:

The first: the intended people are the Jews. Their difference was that when the death of Musa, peace be upon him, drew near, he handed over the Torah to seventy rabbis (*ahbar*), and appointed them as its trustees, and he appointed Yusha' (Joshua) as his successor. Then, when one generation after another had passed, the descendants of the seventy differed after knowledge of the Torah had come to them, out of envy among themselves in the pursuit of the world.

The second: the intended people are the Christians, and their difference concerned the matter of 'Isa (Jesus), peace be upon him, after knowledge had come to them that he was the servant of Allah and His messenger.

The third: the intended people are the Jews and the Christians, and their difference is that the Jews said, "'Uzayr is the son of Allah," and the Christians said, "The Messiah is the son of Allah," and they denied the prophethood of Muhammad (ﷺ), and said, "We have more right to prophethood than the Quraysh, because they are unlettered (*ummiyyun*) and we are the People of the Book."

**The second issue:** His saying, ﴿except after knowledge had come to them﴾ means: except after the proofs had come to them, which, if they had reflected upon them, knowledge would have been attained for them. For if we interpreted it as knowledge, they would be stubborn deniers, and stubbornness cannot be attributed to a great multitude. And this verse was revealed concerning all the People of the Book, and they are a great multitude.

**The third issue:** Concerning the case of His saying *(baghyan)* there are two views:

The first: the view of al-Akhfash, that it is in the accusative as an object of purpose (*maf'ul lahu*), i.e., for the sake of transgression, like your saying, "I came to you seeking good and preventing evil."

The second: the view of al-Zajjaj, that it is in the accusative as an absolute object (*masdar*) in terms of meaning, for His saying ﴿And those who were given the Book did not differ﴾ is equivalent to His saying: "Those who were given the Book did not transgress," so he made *baghyan* a verbal noun. The difference between the object of purpose and the verbal noun is that the object of purpose is the aim of the verb, whereas the verbal noun is the absolute object that the doer brings about.

**The fourth issue:** Al-Akhfash said: His saying ﴿out of envy among themselves﴾ is related to His saying *(ikhtalafa)* (differed), and the meaning is: "They did not differ out of envy among themselves except after knowledge had come to them, out of envy among themselves." Others said: The meaning is: "They did not differ except after knowledge had come to them, except for envy among themselves," so this is an information that they only differed for the sake of envy. Al-Qaffal said: This is better than the first, because the first gives the impression that they differed because of the knowledge that had come to them, whereas the second indicates that they only differed for the sake of envy and transgression.

* * *

Then He, may He be exalted, said: ﴿And whoever disbelieves in the signs of Allah, then indeed Allah is swift in reckoning﴾. This is a threat, and on it there are two views:

The first: the meaning is that he will surely come to Allah, may He be exalted, swiftly, and He will call him to account, that is, He will recompense him for his disbelief.

The second: that Allah, may He be exalted, will make him aware of his deeds, his sins, and the various kinds of his disbelief, by a swift enumeration despite the multitude of the deeds.

[Page 183]

Commentary of al-Razi (*Mafatih al-Ghayb*) on surah 3, verse 20:

God, exalted is He, says: ﴿So if they argue with you, say: I have submitted my face to God, and so have those who follow me. And say to those who were given the Book and to the unlettered: Have you submitted? If they submit, then they are guided; but if they turn away, your duty is only to convey [the message]. God is Seeing of [His] servants.﴾

Know that when God, exalted is He, mentioned earlier that the People of the Book differed after knowledge had come to them, and that they persisted in disbelief despite this, God instructed the Messenger (ﷺ) on what to say in disputing with them. He said: ﴿So if they argue with you, say: I have submitted my face to God, and so have those who follow me.﴾ There are two ways of understanding how this statement is presented.

The first way: this is a turning away from argument. The reason is that he (ﷺ) had already shown them the proof of his truthfulness many times and in various ways before this verse was revealed, since this surah is Medinan. He had shown them miracles through the Qur'an, the calling of the tree, the speech of the wolf, and others. Also, before this verse, God mentioned verses indicating the soundness of his religion. The first of these is that God established the argument with His words ﴿The Living, the Self-Subsisting﴾ [al-Baqarah: 255], against the Christian claim of the divinity of Jesus, peace be upon him. And with His words ﴿He has sent down to you the Book with truth﴾ [Al 'Imran: 3], He established the soundness of prophethood. He also mentioned the doubts of the people and answered all of them, as we established previously. Then He mentioned to them another miracle, which is the miracles they witnessed on the day of Badr, as we explained in the commentary on His words, exalted is He: ﴿There has been for you a sign in the two armies that met﴾ [Al 'Imran: 13]. Then He demonstrated the soundness of the doctrine of monotheism and denied any equal, rival, consort, or offspring with His words ﴿God bears witness that there is no deity except Him﴾ [Al 'Imran: 18]. Then God, exalted is He, explained that the departure of these Jews and Christians from the truth, and their differing in religion, was only due to rebellion and envy. This is what would have led them to submit to the truth and to reflect on the proofs, had they been sincere. Thus it became clear that no means of establishing the argument against the various groups of disbelievers remained except that it had been accomplished. After this, He said: ﴿So if they argue with you, say: I have submitted my face to God, and so have those who follow me.﴾ That is, "We have gone to great lengths in establishing the proofs and clarifying the evidences. If you abandon arrogance and envy and hold fast to them, you will be the guided ones. If you turn away, then God is behind your recompense." This interpretation is a common method in speech. When the righteous one is tested by an obstinate falsifier and presents him with proof after proof, he may say at the end: "As for me and those who follow me, we submit to the truth, surrender to it, and devote ourselves to the worship of God, exalted is He. If you agree and follow the truth that I hold after these proofs I have mentioned, you will be guided; but if you turn away, God is on watch." This method may be mentioned by the righteous arguer with the persistent falsifier at the end of his speech.

The second way: we say that His words ﴿I have submitted my face to God﴾ constitute an argument and a display of proof. Its explanation is in several aspects.

The first aspect: the people admitted the existence of the Creator and that He deserves worship. So it is as if he (peace be upon him) said to the people: "This is agreed upon by all. I hold firmly to this agreed-upon matter and call people to it. The disagreement lies in matters beyond this, and you are the claimants, so the burden of proof is on you. The Jews claim anthropomorphism and corporeality, the Christians claim the divinity of Jesus, and the polytheists claim the obligation of worshipping idols. These are the claimants of these things, so the proof is upon them. As for me, I claim nothing except the obligation of obeying God, exalted is He, and worshipping Him, and this matter is agreed upon." A parallel to this verse is His words, exalted is He: ﴿O People of the Book, come to a word that is equitable between us and you, that we will not worship except God and not associate anything with Him﴾ [Al 'Imran: 64].

The second aspect, concerning the manner of reasoning: what Abu Muslim al-Isfahani mentioned, namely that the Jews, the Christians, and the idol-worshippers all acknowledged the greatness of Abraham, peace be upon him, and affirmed that he was righteous in his speech and truthful in his religion, except for additions of laws and rulings. So God commanded Muhammad (ﷺ) to follow his creed, saying: ﴿Then We revealed to you, [saying], "Follow the religion of Abraham, inclining toward truth"﴾ [al-Nahl: 123]. Then God commanded Muhammad (ﷺ) in this place to say what Abraham (peace be upon him) said when he said: ﴿Indeed, I have turned my face toward He who originated the heavens and the earth﴾ [al-An'am: 79]. So the statement of Muhammad (ﷺ), ﴿I have submitted my face﴾, is like the statement of Abraham (peace be upon him), ﴿I have turned my face﴾ [al-An'am: 79]. That is, I have turned away from every object of worship other than God, exalted is He, directed myself to Him in worship, and devoted myself sincerely to Him. The meaning of the verse, then, is as if He, exalted is He, said: "If they dispute with you, O Muhammad, over these details, then say: I hold firmly to the way of Abraham, and you acknowledge that his way is true and far from every doubt and accusation. This is then a case of holding firmly to what is binding upon the opponent, and it falls under His words ﴿And argue with them in a way that is best﴾ [al-Nahl: 125]."

The third aspect, concerning the manner of reasoning: what occurred to my mind when writing this section, namely that before this verse He claimed that the religion with God is Islam alone. Then He said: ﴿So if they argue with you﴾, meaning: if they dispute with you regarding your statement ﴿Indeed, the religion with God is Islam﴾, then say: the proof of it is that I have submitted my face to God. This is because the purpose of religion is only the fulfilment of the requirements of lordship. When I have submitted my face to God, I do not worship other than Him, I do not expect good except from Him, and I do not fear except His subjugation and might, and I do not associate anything with Him. This is the complete fulfilment of the requirements of lordship and servitude. Thus it is established that the complete religion is Islam. This aspect fits the verse.

The fourth aspect, concerning the manner of reasoning: what occurred to my mind is that this verse corresponds to His words, exalted is He, quoting Abraham, peace be upon him: ﴿Why do you worship that which does not hear and does not see and does not avail you at all?﴾ [Maryam: 42]. That is, worship is not permissible except for one who is beneficial and harmful, and whose affairs are in His hands, and whose judgment is in the grip of His power. If everyone knows that Jesus was not capable of these things, it is rationally impossible for me to submit to him or to obey him. Rather, I submit my face to the One from whom comes good and evil, benefit and harm, governance and decree.

The fifth aspect: it may also be that this statement is an allusion to the way of Abraham, peace be upon him, in His words: ﴿When his Lord said to him, "Submit," he said, "I have submitted to the Lord of the worlds"﴾ [al-Baqarah: 131]. This is related from Ibn 'Abbas.

As for His words ﴿I have submitted my face to God﴾, there are several interpretations. The first: al-Farra' said, "I have submitted my face to God" means: I have made my deed sincere for God. It is said: "I submitted the thing to so-and-so," meaning: I made it sincerely his, and no one else shared it with him. He said: "By 'face' here is meant the deed, as in His words ﴿seeking His face﴾ [al-An'am: 52], meaning His worship. It is said, 'This is the face of the matter,' meaning its pure essence. When a man intends someone else for a need, he says, 'I have turned my face to you.' And it is said of one absorbed in something from which he does not turn back: 'He passed on his face.'" The second: "I have submitted my face to God" means: I have submitted the face of my deed to God, and the meaning is that whatever deeds proceed from me, the direction in performing them is the worship of God, exalted is He, and submission to His divinity and His judgment. The third: "I have submitted my face to God" means: I have submitted my self to God, and there is no station in worship higher than the submission of the self to God, such that it becomes as if it is devoted to His worship, turning away from everything else.

As for His words ﴿and those who follow me﴾, there are two issues:

The first issue: 'Asim, Hamzah, and al-Kisa'i omitted the *ya'* from *ittaba'anī* (the pronoun "me"), relying on the kasrah and following the Mushaf, while the others wrote it according to the original form.

[Page 184]

The second issue: *man* (مَن, "those who") is in the nominative position, conjoined to the *tā'* in His words "*aslamtu*" (I have submitted). That is, "and those who follow me have submitted likewise."

If it is asked: why did He say "I have submitted, and those who follow me," and not "I have submitted, I and those who follow me"?

We say: the speech was lengthened by His words ﴿my face to God﴾, so it became a substitute for emphasizing the attached pronoun. If one said, "I have submitted and Zayd," it would not be good until one says, "I have submitted, I and Zayd." But if one said, "I have submitted today with an open heart, and whoever came with me," it would be permissible and good.

* * *

Then God, exalted is He, said: ﴿And say to those who were given the Book and to the unlettered: Have you submitted?﴾ There are issues concerning this:

The first issue: this verse encompasses all who oppose the religion of Muhammad (ﷺ). This is because among them are those who belong to the People of the Book, whether they were truthful in that claim, such as the Jews and Christians, or lying in it, such as the Magians. And among them are those who are not People of the Book, namely the idol-worshippers.

The second issue: He described the Arab polytheists as "unlettered" for two reasons:

The first: since they did not claim a divine Book, they were described as "unlettered," in comparison to one who neither reads nor writes.

The second: it may be meant that they were not among the people of reading and writing. This was the characteristic of most of them, and if there were some among them who could write, they were rare. And God knows best.

The third issue: this verse indicates that what is meant by His words ﴿if they argue with you﴾ is general to all disbelievers, because everyone who claims a Book is included under His words ﴿those who were given the Book﴾, and whoever has no Book is included under His words "the unlettered."

Then God, exalted is He, said: ﴿Have you submitted?﴾ This is an interrogative in the form of affirmation, and its intended meaning is a command. The grammarians said: it came in the form of a question with the sense of a command, because it has the same function as a command in demanding an action and calling to it. However, in expressing the meaning of a command with the wording of a question there is an additional benefit, namely expressing that the addressee is obstinate and far from fairness, because the fair person, when the proof becomes clear to him, does not hesitate but accepts at once. A parallel to this is your saying to one to whom you have explained the matter in the utmost clarity, disclosure, and exposition: "Have you understood it?" This indicates that the addressee is dull and slow to understand. God, exalted is He, said in the verse about wine: ﴿So will you not desist?﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 91], which indicates reluctance to refrain and an intense eagerness to engage in what is forbidden.

Then God, exalted is He, said: ﴿If they submit, then they are guided﴾, because this submission is holding fast to what He has guided to, and one who holds fast to God's guidance is guided. It may also be meant: "then they are guided to success and salvation in the Hereafter, if they remain steadfast in it." Then He said: ﴿But if they turn away﴾ from submission and following Muhammad (ﷺ), ﴿then your duty is only to convey [the message]﴾. The purpose of this is to console the Messenger (ﷺ) and to inform him that what is incumbent upon him is nothing but conveying the proofs and displaying the argument. When he has conveyed what he was sent with, he has discharged his obligation, and it is not incumbent upon him that they accept it. Then He said: ﴿God is Seeing of [His] servants﴾, and this implies both promise and warning, which is evident.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 3, verse 21–22:

His saying, may He be exalted, ﴿Indeed, those who disbelieve in the signs of Allah and kill the prophets without right and kill those who enjoin justice among the people – give them tidings of a painful punishment.﴾ ﴿Those are the ones whose deeds have become worthless in this world and the Hereafter, and they will have no helpers.﴾

Know that when He, may He be exalted, mentioned earlier the state of the one who turns away and refuses, by His saying ﴿But if they turn away, then upon you is only the conveyance (of the message)﴾, He followed it with the description of this one who turns away, and He mentioned three kinds of attributes:

The first attribute: His saying ﴿Indeed, those who disbelieve in the signs of Allah﴾.

If it is said: the apparent meaning of the verse requires that they be disbelievers in all the signs of Allah, while the Jews and Christians were not like that, for they affirmed the Creator, His knowledge, His power and the Return.

We say: the answer is in two respects:

The first: that we turn "the signs of Allah" to the previously known referent, which is the Qur'an and Muhammad (ﷺ).

The second: that we take it in its generality, and say that whoever denies the prophethood of Muhammad (ﷺ) is necessarily one who denies all the signs of Allah, Exalted, because whoever is inconsistent does not believe in any of the signs; for if he believed in any of them, he would believe in all of them.

The second attribute: His saying, may He be exalted, ﴿and kill the prophets without right﴾, and in it are issues:

The first issue: al-Hasan read ﴿wa yuqattiluna al-nabiyyina bi-ghayri haqq﴾ (with the intensive form), and it is for emphasis (mubalaghah).

The second issue: It is narrated from Abu 'Ubaydah ibn al-Jarrah that he said: "I said, 'O Messenger of Allah, who among people will have the most severe punishment on the Day of Resurrection?' He said: 'A man who killed a prophet, or a man who enjoined what is good and forbade what is evil.' Then he recited this verse, and then said: 'O Abu 'Ubaydah, the Children of Israel killed forty-three prophets at the beginning of the day in a single hour, then a hundred men and twelve men from the worshippers of the Children of Israel arose, and they enjoined those who had killed them to do good and forbade them from evil, so they were all killed at the end of that day. They are the ones whom Allah, may He be exalted, mentioned.'" Also, that people killed Yahya ibn Zakariyya, and they claimed that they killed 'Isa ibn Maryam. So according to their claim, it is established that they used to kill the prophets.

* * *
And in the verse there are questions:

The first question: If His saying ﴿Indeed, those who disbelieve in the signs of Allah﴾ is in the sense of the future, since it is a threat to those who were in the time of the Messenger, peace be upon him, and killing of the prophets and of those who uphold justice did not occur from them, then how is that correct?

The answer is in two respects:

The first: that since this path was the path of their forefathers, this attribution to them is correct, for they approved of it and were pleased with their way. Indeed, the deed of the father may be attributed to the son if he is pleased with it and follows his path. The second: that these people intended to kill the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and the believers, but Allah, may He be exalted, protected him from them.
