When they were in extreme eagerness for that, this name was correctly applied to them in a figurative sense, as one says: "Fire burns, and poison kills," meaning that this is its nature when the receptive object is present. Likewise here, it can only be so.

The second question: What is the benefit in His saying ﴿and kill the prophets without right﴾, when the killing of prophets can only be without right?

The answer: We have mentioned the aspects of this in Surat al-Baqarah. Its purpose is to explain the magnitude of their sin. Also, it is possible that what is meant is that by the path of injustice in their killing they intended the path of justice.

The third question: His saying ﴿and kill the prophets﴾, its apparent sense suggests that they killed all of them, while it is known that they did not kill all of them, nor the majority, nor half.

The answer: the alif and lam are taken to refer to a known referent, not to totality (al-istighraq).

* * *
The third attribute: His saying ﴿and kill those who enjoin justice among the people﴾, and in it are issues:

The first issue: Hamzah alone read ﴿wa yuqatiluna﴾ with an alif, and the rest read ﴿wa yaqtulun﴾; both are equivalent, for they may fight and thereby kill through fighting, and they may kill directly without fighting. Ubayy read ﴿wa yaqtulun al-nabiyyina wa al-ladhina ya'murun﴾.

The second issue: al-Hasan said: this verse indicates that one who stands up to enjoin good and forbid evil in fear holds a rank in greatness close to the rank of the prophets. And it is narrated that a man came to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and said: "Which jihad is best?" He, peace be upon him, said: "The best jihad is a word of truth before an oppressive ruler."

Know that He, may He be exalted, as He described them with these three attributes, also mentioned their threat in three aspects:

The first: His saying ﴿give them tidings of a painful punishment﴾, and in it are two issues:

The first issue: the particle fa' entered into His saying "fa-bashshirhum" even though it is the predicate of inna, because it carries the meaning of a conditional, and the implied sense is: "whoever disbelieves, then give them tidings."

The second issue: this is taken in a figurative sense, namely that warning these people of punishment stands in the place of giving the good news of bliss to the righteous. The discussion of the true meaning of glad tidings has preceded in His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And give good tidings to those who believe and do righteous deeds﴾ [al-Baqarah: 25].

The second kind of threat: His saying ﴿Those are the ones whose deeds have become worthless in this world and the Hereafter.﴾

Know that He, may He be exalted, made clear by this that the good deeds of the disbelievers are nullified (muhbatah, from habt) in this world and the Hereafter. As for this world, it is by replacing praise with blame and commendation with curse, and it includes what befalls them of killing, captivity, the taking of their wealth as spoils, enslavement, and other forms of manifest humiliation among them. As for their nullification in the Hereafter, it is by the removal of reward and its replacement with punishment.

The third kind of their threat: His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿and they will have no helpers.﴾

Know that He, may He be exalted, by the first kind of threat made clear the gathering of the causes of pain and hardship against them, and by the second kind made clear the complete cessation of the causes of benefit from them, and by this third aspect made clear the necessity of that for them, in such a way that they will have no helper and no one to repel (harm). And Allah knows best.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 3, verse 23–25 (part 1 of 2):

The saying of the Exalted: ﴿Have you not seen those who were given a portion of the Book? They are invited to the Book of God so that it may judge between them, then a faction of them turns away while they are refusing.﴾ ﴿That is because they said: "The Fire will not touch us except for numbered days," and what they used to fabricate deceived them in their religion.﴾ ﴿So how will it be when We gather them for a Day about which there is no doubt, and every soul is paid in full what it has earned, and they will not be wronged?﴾

Know that when the Exalted drew attention to the obstinacy of the people by His saying ﴿And if they argue with you, say: I have submitted myself to God﴾, He clarified in this verse the extent of their obstinacy, which is that they are invited to the Book that they claim they believe in, namely the Torah, and then they rebel and turn away, and this indicates the extent of their obstinacy. In the verse there are issues:

The first issue: The apparent meaning of His saying ﴿Have you not seen those who were given a portion of the Book﴾ encompasses all of them. There is no doubt that this is mentioned in the context of blame, but another proof has indicated that not all of the People of the Book are like that, because He, the Exalted, says ﴿Among the People of the Book is an upright community that recites the signs of God in the hours of the night while they prostrate﴾ [Al 'Imran: 113].

The second issue: The Exalted's saying ﴿were given a portion of the Book﴾ is meant to refer to other than the Qur'an, because He attributed the Book to the disbelievers, who are the Jews and the Christians. If that is so, it is necessary to take it to mean the Book which they acknowledged to be true and from God.

The third issue: They mentioned several explanations of the occasion of revelation. One of them: "It is narrated from Ibn 'Abbas that a man and a woman from the Jews committed adultery, and they were people of nobility, and in their Book there was stoning, so they disliked stoning them because of their nobility, and they returned regarding their matter to the Prophet ﷺ, hoping that he would have a concession for abandoning stoning. The Messenger ﷺ ruled for stoning, so they denied that. Then he (peace be upon him) said: 'Between me and you is the Torah, for in it is stoning. So who is your most knowledgeable?' They said: 'Abdullah ibn Suriya al-Fadaki.' So they brought him and produced the Torah. When he came to the verse of stoning, he placed his hand upon it. Then Ibn Salam said: 'He has passed its place, O Messenger of God.' So he lifted his palm from it, and they found the verse of stoning. Then the Prophet ﷺ commanded that the two be stoned, and the Jews, may God curse them, became exceedingly angry because of that. So God the Exalted revealed this verse."

The second narration: "That he ﷺ entered the house of study of the Jews, and there was a group of them in it. He invited them to Islam, and they said: 'On what religion are you?' He said: 'On the religion of Abraham.' They said: 'Abraham was a Jew.' He ﷺ said: 'Come to the Torah.' They refused that, so God the Exalted revealed this verse."

The third narration: That the signs of the mission of Muhammad ﷺ are mentioned in the Torah, and the proofs indicating the soundness of his prophethood
صفحة ١٨٩
are present in it. The Prophet ﷺ invited them to the Torah and to those signs indicating his prophethood, but they refused, so God the Exalted revealed this verse. The meaning is that when they refuse to respond to judgement by their Book, then do not be surprised at their opposition to your Book. Therefore God the Exalted said: ﴿Say: Bring the Torah and recite it, if you are truthful﴾ [Al 'Imran: 93]. This verse, according to this narration, indicates that there were found in the Torah indications of the soundness of his prophethood, for if they knew that there was nothing in the Torah indicating the soundness of his prophethood, they would have hastened to declare what is in it, but they concealed that.

The fourth narration: That this ruling is general to the Jews and the Christians, because the indications of the prophethood of Muhammad ﷺ were present in the Torah and the Gospel, and they were invited to the judgement of the Torah and the Gospel, and they refused.

Then He said: ﴿while they are refusing﴾, and in it are two views:

The first: "Those who turn away" are the leaders and scholars, and "those who refuse" are the rest of them, as if it was said: Then the scholars and the followers turn away, refusing to accept from the Prophet ﷺ because of the turning away of their scholars.

The second: The one who turns away and the one who refuses is that same faction, and the meaning is that he turns away from hearing the proof in that situation and refuses to hear all the other proofs on all the other issues and matters, as if it was said: Do not think that he turned away only from this issue; rather he refuses all of it.

* * *

As for the Exalted's saying ﴿That is because they said: "The Fire will not touch us except for numbered days"﴾, the discussion of its interpretation has already passed in Surat al-Baqara. The connection of the arrangement is that when He said in the first verse ﴿then a faction of them turns away while they are refusing﴾, He said in this verse: that turning away and refusal occurred because they said: "The Fire will not touch us except for numbered days." Al-Jubba'i said: In it is an indication of the falsity of the view of one who says that the people of the Fire will come out of the Fire. He said: For if that were valid for this community, it would be valid for all other nations, and if that were established for all other nations, the report of it would not be false, and they would not deserve blame. So when God the Exalted mentioned that in the context of blame, we know that the claim that the people of the Fire will come out is a false claim.

I say: It should not have been his place to mention such a statement, because his doctrine is that pardon is good and permissible from God the Exalted, and if that is so, the occurrence of pardon for this community does not necessitate its occurrence for all other nations.

Suppose we concede that it necessitates that. But why did you say that these people only deserved blame for merely reporting that the sinner comes out of the Fire? Rather, there are other aspects here. The first: They deserved blame because they were certain that the period of punishment of the sinner is short and brief, for it is narrated that they used to say: "Our punishment period is seven days," and some of them said: "Rather forty nights, according to the length of the worship of the calf." The second: They were lax regarding the foundations of religion, saying: "Even supposing an error from us, our punishment is little"; and this is an error, because according to us, the one who errs regarding monotheism, prophethood and the resurrection, his punishment is everlasting, for he is a disbeliever, and the punishment of the disbeliever is everlasting. The third: When they said ﴿The Fire will not touch us except for numbered days﴾, they belittled the denial of Muhammad ﷺ and believed that it had no effect in intensifying the punishment, so that was an explicit denial of Muhammad ﷺ, and that is disbelief, and the disbeliever who persists in his disbelief, there is no doubt that his punishment is everlasting. Since the matter is as we have stated, it is established that al-Jubba'i's argument with this verse is weak. The complete discussion in full detail is mentioned in Surat al-Baqara.

As for the Exalted's saying ﴿and what they used to fabricate deceived them in their religion﴾, know that they differed regarding what is meant by His saying ﴿what they used to fabricate﴾. It was said: it is their saying ﴿We are the sons of God and His beloved﴾ [al-Ma'ida: 18]. It was said: it is their saying ﴿The Fire will not touch us except for numbered days﴾. It was said: what deceived them was their saying: We are upon the truth and you are upon falsehood.

As for the Exalted's saying ﴿So how will it be when We gather them for a Day about which there is no doubt﴾, the meaning is that when the Exalted related their deception by what they were upon of ignorance, He made clear that a day will come in which that ignorance will vanish and that delusion will be uncovered, so He said ﴿So how will it be when We gather them for a Day about which there is no doubt﴾. There is an ellipsis in the speech, and the estimate is: So how will their form and condition be? The condition is often omitted with "how" because it is indicated by it. You say: "I used to honour him, and he did not visit me; so how would it be if he visited me?" meaning: how would his condition be if he visited me. Know that this ellipsis brings additional eloquence, because it stirs the soul to call to mind every kind of honour in the speaker's words "if he visited me," and every kind of punishment in this verse.

As for the Exalted's saying ﴿when We gather them for a Day﴾ and not "in a Day," because the meaning is: for the recompense of a Day or for the reckoning of a Day, so the noun in apposition was omitted and the lam indicated it. Al-Farra' said: the lam is for a hidden verb. When you say "they were gathered for Thursday," the meaning is they were gathered for an action that occurs on Thursday; but when you say "they were gathered on Thursday," you do not imply a verb. Also, it is known that that Day has no benefit except recompense and the manifestation of the distinction between the rewarded and the punished. And His saying ﴿about which there is no doubt﴾ means: about which there is no doubt.

* * *

Then He said: ﴿and every soul is paid in full what it has earned﴾. If you take "what it has earned" as the deeds of the servant, an ellipsis is made in the speech, and the estimate is: every soul is paid in full the recompense of what it has earned of reward or punishment. If you take "what it has earned" as the reward and punishment, you are free of this supposition.

* * *

Then He said: ﴿and they will not be wronged﴾, so nothing is reduced from the reward of the acts of obedience, and nothing is added to the punishment of the misdeeds.

Know that His saying ﴿and every soul is paid in full what it has earned﴾ is used as evidence by those who hold the doctrine of threat (wa'id), and our companions also use it as evidence for the view that the one guilty of a grave sin among the people of prayer will not be abiding in the Fire. As for the first group, they say: because the one guilty of a grave sin, there is no doubt that he deserves punishment for that grave sin, and the verse indicates that every soul is paid in full its deed and what it has earned, and that requires the arrival of punishment at the one guilty of a grave sin.

Our answer: this is among the general statements, and we have already spoken about the Mu'tazila's reliance on general statements.

As for our companions, they say: the believer has deserved the reward of faith, so that reward must be paid to him in full, by His saying ﴿and every soul is paid in full what it has earned﴾. Then either he is rewarded in Paradise and then transferred to the abode of punishment, and that is false by consensus; or it is said: he is punished in the Fire and then transferred to the abode of reward forever and everlasting, which is what is sought.

If it is said: Why is it not permissible to say that the reward of their faith is nullified by the punishment of their disobedience?

We say: this is false, because we have already shown that the doctrine of mutual cancellation (al-muhabatah) is impossible in Surat al-Baqarah. Furthermore, we know by necessity that the reward for affirming the divine oneness for seventy years is greater than the punishment for drinking one sip of wine, and whoever disputes this is being obstinate. Therefore, even granting the validity of mutual cancellation, it is impossible that the entire reward of faith should be cancelled by the punishment for drinking one sip of wine. Yahya ibn Mu'adh (may Allah have mercy on him) used to say: "The reward of faith for a single moment cancels the disbelief of seventy years, so how can the reward of faith for seventy years be conceivably cancelled by the punishment for the sin of a single moment!" There is no doubt that this is a clear argument.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 3, verses 26–27 (part 1 of 3):

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Say: O Allah, Owner of sovereignty, You give sovereignty to whom You will and You take sovereignty away from whom You will. You endue with honour whom You will and You humble whom You will. In Your hand is [all] good. Indeed, You are over all things competent.﴾ ﴿You cause the night to enter the day and You cause the day to enter the night. And You bring the living out of the dead and You bring the dead out of the living. And You provide for whom You will without account.﴾

Know that when He, exalted is He, mentioned the proofs of monotheism (tawhid), of prophethood, and of the soundness of the religion of Islam, then said to His Messenger: ﴿And if they argue with you, say: I have submitted myself entirely to Allah, and [so have] those who follow me﴾, then mentioned among the attributes of the opponents their disbelief in Allah and their killing of the prophets and the righteous without right, and mentioned the severity of their obstinacy and rebellion in His saying: ﴿Have you not considered those who were given a portion of the Scripture?﴾, then mentioned the severity of their delusion in His saying: ﴿They say: The Fire will not touch us except for numbered days﴾, then mentioned their threat in His saying: ﴿So how [will it be] when We gather them for a Day about which there is no doubt?﴾, He commanded the Messenger of Allah ﷺ with a supplication and glorification that indicates the divergence of his way and the way of his followers from the way of these disbelieving, obstinate, and averse people. So He said, teaching His Prophet how he should glorify, magnify, supplicate, and ask: ﴿Say: O Allah, Owner of sovereignty﴾. In the verse there are issues:

The first issue: The grammarians differed concerning His saying (Allahumma). Al-Khalil and Sibawayh said: "Allahumma" means "Ya Allah" (O Allah), and the doubled mim is a substitute for "ya." Al-Farra' said: its original form was "Ya Allah, umma bi-khayr" (O Allah, aim for good), and when it was frequent in speech they dropped the vocative particle and dropped the hamza from "umma," so it became "Allahumma." Its parallel is the Arabs' saying "hallumma" (come here), whose origin is "hal," so "umma" was added to it.

The arguments of the first group against the invalidity of al-Farra's view are several:

The first: If the matter were as al-Farra said, it would not be correct to say "Allahumma if'al kadha" (O Allah, do such-and-such) except with the conjunctive particle, because the implied meaning would be "Ya Allah, umma-na wa-ghfir lana" (O Allah, aim for us and forgive us), and we do not find anyone mentioning this conjunctive particle.

The second, which is the argument of al-Zajjaj: If the matter were as he said, it would be permissible to use it in its original form, so one would say "Allahu umma" just as one says "waylamma," and then one would use it in the original form, saying "waylu ummihi" (woe to his mother).

The third: If the matter were as al-Farra said, the vocative particle would be elided, so it would be permissible to say "Ya Allahumma," but since this is not permissible, we know the invalidity of al-Farra's view. Rather, we say: the vocative particle ought to be obligatory, as one says "Ya Allahu, ighfir li" (O Allah, forgive me).

Al-Farra' answered these arguments, saying: As for the first, it is weak, because his saying "Ya Allah, umma" means "Ya Allah, intend," so if he said "wa-ghfir" (and forgive), the conjoined would be different from the conjoined-to, and then the request would become two requests: one of them is his saying "umma-na," and the second is his saying "wa-ghfir lana" (Al-Baqarah: 286). But when we omit the conjunction, his saying "ghfir lana" becomes an explanation of his saying "umma-na," so the sought object in both cases is one thing, and that is more emphatic. Its parallels in the Qur'an are numerous. As for the second, it is also weak, because its original form, according to us, is to say "Ya Allah, umma-na." And who denies the permissibility of speaking with that? Also, many words do not permit putting the derived form in place of the original, do you not see that the view of al-Khalil and Sibawayh is that his saying "ma akramahu" means "ayyu shay'in akramahu" (what a thing it is that made him so noble), yet this expression they claim to be the original is never used in a context of wonder. So it is likewise here.

As for the third: who has conceded to you that it is not permissible to say "Ya Allahumma"? And al-Farra' recited:

"As for what is incumbent on you, that you say whenever you glorify or pray: Ya Allahumma."

And the saying of the Basrans: this poetry is not known. Its outcome is the denial of the transmission. If we opened this door, nothing of the language and grammar would remain free from criticism. As for his saying that the mention of the vocative particle would have to be obligatory, its answer is that the vocative particle may be elided, as in His saying: ﴿Joseph, O man of truth, give us an interpretation﴾ (Yusuf: 46). So it is not far-fetched that this name is specifically bound to this elision. Then al-Farra' argued against the view of the Basrans from several aspects:

The first: If we make the mim stand in place of the vocative particle, we would have postponed the vocative particle from the mention of the one called, and this is absolutely impermissible, for one never says "Allah ya" at all, yet on your view the matter would be so.

The second: If this particle stood in place of the vocative, its like would be permissible in all other names, so that one would say "Zaydumma" and "Bakrumma," just as one says "Ya Zayd" and "Ya Bakr."

The third: If the mim were a substitute for the vocative particle, the two would not be combined, but they are combined in the poetry we have related.

The fourth: We do not find the Arabs adding this mim to complete nouns to convey the meaning of some particles that are distinct from the word they are attached to. So resorting to it in this single word would be a judgment contrary to the general induction in the language, and it is impermissible. This is the summary of the discussion on this point.

The second issue: In the case of His saying "Owner of sovereignty" (malika al-mulk) there are two possibilities of its grammatical case. The first, which is the view of Sibawayh, is that it is in the accusative as a vocative, and likewise His saying: ﴿O Allah, Originator of the heavens and the earth﴾ (Al-Zumar: 46). It is not permissible for it to be a qualifier of "Allahumma," because our saying "Allahumma" is a compound of the noun and the particle, and this compound cannot be described. The second, which is the view of al-Mubarrad and al-Zajjaj, is that "malika" is an adjective of the singular addressed noun, because this name together with the mim is like it together with "ya," and the adjective is not barred with the mim, just as it is not barred with the ya.

The third issue: It is related that "when the Prophet ﷺ conquered Makkah, he promised his community the sovereignty of Persia and Byzantium, and the hypocrites and the Jews said: Far-fetched, far-fetched! From where would Muhammad have the sovereignty of Persia and Byzantium, when they are mightier and more fortified than that?" And it is related that when he, peace be upon him, dug the trench in the year of the Confederates, and allotted to every ten men forty cubits, and they began digging, a rock emerged from the belly of the trench like a great hill, which the pickaxes did not affect. They directed Salman to the Prophet ﷺ, and he informed him. He took the pickaxe from Salman, and when he struck it a blow he split it, and a flash came out of it that illuminated what lay between its two stony tracts, as if it were a lamp in the depth of a dark night. He exclaimed "Allahu akbar," and the Muslims exclaimed "Allahu akbar" too. He, peace be upon him, said: "The palaces of al-Hirah have been illuminated for me from it, as if they were the fangs of dogs." Then he struck the second blow and said: "The red palaces of the land of the Romans have been illuminated for me from it." Then he struck the third and said: "The palaces of San'a have been illuminated for me from it, and Jibril, peace be upon him, has informed me that my community will prevail over all of them, so rejoice." The hypocrites then said: "Do you not marvel at your Prophet, who promises you falsehood and tells you that from Yathrib he sees the palaces of al-Hirah and the cities of Kisra, and that they will be opened to you while you are digging the trench out of fear, unable to go out?" Then this verse was revealed. And Allah knows best.

Al-Hasan said: Allah, exalted is He, commanded His Prophet to ask Him to give him the sovereignty of Persia and Byzantium and to return the humiliation of the Arabs upon them. His command to him with this is evidence that He would respond to this supplication for him, and thus is the rank of the prophets, peace be upon them, when they are commanded to supplicate, their supplication is answered.

* * *

The fourth issue: "Al-mulk" is power, and "al-malik" is the one who is capable, so His saying "malika al-mulk" means the one capable over power. The meaning is that the power of creatures over whatever they are capable of is only by Allah's empowerment; He is the One who empowers every capable one over what he can do, and makes every owner an owner of what he owns. The author of al-Kashshaf said: "Malika al-mulk" means "He owns the genus of sovereignty and disposes of it as owners dispose of what they own." Know that when He, exalted is He, made clear that He is "Owner of sovereignty" absolutely, He then detailed it afterwards and mentioned five kinds:

The first kind: His saying, exalted is He: ﴿You give sovereignty to whom You will and You take sovereignty away from whom You will﴾. They have mentioned several aspects regarding it:

The first: What is meant by it is the sovereignty of prophethood and messengership, as He, exalted is He, said: ﴿We had already given the family of Abraham the Scripture and wisdom, and We gave them a great kingdom﴾ (An-Nisa: 54). Prophethood is the greatest rank of sovereignty, because scholars have a great authority over the inner states of creatures, and tyrants have authority over their outward affairs, while the prophets' command is effective in both the inner and the outer. As for the inner, it is obligatory on everyone to accept their religion and law and to believe that it is the truth. As for the outer, if they were to rebel and be arrogant, they would deserve to be killed. What confirms this interpretation is that some of them found it improbable that Allah would make a human a messenger, so Allah relates their saying: [﴿Has Allah sent a human as a messenger?﴾ (Al-Isra: 94) and Allah, exalted is He, said: ﴿And if We had made him an angel, We would have made him a man﴾ (Al-An'am: 9)]. Other groups allowed from Allah, exalted is He, that He send a human messenger, but they used to say: Muhammad is poor and an orphan, so how does this great station befit him, as Allah relates of them that they said: ﴿Why was this Qur'an not sent down upon a great man of the two cities?﴾ (Az-Zukhruf: 31). As for the Jews, they used to say: prophethood was in our fathers and forefathers, and as for the Quraysh, they were not people of prophethood and Scripture, so how does prophethood befit Muhammad ﷺ? As for the hypocrites, they used to envy him for prophethood, as Allah relates of them in His saying: ﴿Or do they envy the people for what Allah has given them of His bounty?﴾ (An-Nisa: 54).

Also, we have mentioned in the commentary on His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Say to those who disbelieved: You will be overcome and gathered to Hell, and wretched is the resting place﴾ (Al 'Imran: 12) that the Jews were arrogant toward the Prophet ﷺ because of their large numbers, their weapons, and their strength. Then He, exalted is He, answered all these groups by making clear that He, glorified is He, is the Owner of sovereignty, so He gives His sovereignty to whom He wills, saying: ﴿You give sovereignty to whom You will and You take sovereignty away from whom You will﴾.

If it is said: When you interpret His saying "You give sovereignty to whom You will" as giving the sovereignty of prophethood, it is necessary that you interpret His saying "and You take sovereignty away from whom You will" as meaning that He may remove from prophethood one whom He made a prophet, and it is known that this is not permissible.

We say: The answer is in two respects:

The first: When Allah places prophethood in the lineage of a man, then removes it from his lineage and honours another person with it from outside that lineage, it is correct to say that He took it away from them. The Jews believed that prophethood must be among the Children of Israel, so when Allah honoured Muhammad ﷺ with it, it is correct to say that He takes the sovereignty of prophethood away from the Children of Israel and gives it to the Arabs.

The second answer: The meaning of His saying "and You take sovereignty away from whom You will" may be: You deprive them and do not give them this sovereignty, not in the sense that He strips it from them after He had given it. A parallel is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Allah is the Guardian of those who believe; He brings them out of darkness into light﴾ (Al-Baqarah: 257), although this statement includes one who was never in the darkness of disbelief at all. And Allah, exalted is He, related of the disbelievers that they said to the prophets, peace be upon them: ﴿Or you will return to our religion﴾ (Al-A'raf: 88), and those prophets said: ﴿It is not for us to return to it unless Allah wills﴾ (Al-A'raf: 89), although they had never been in it at all. This is the full discussion in establishing the view of one who interprets His saying, exalted is He, ﴿You give sovereignty to whom You will﴾ as the sovereignty of prophethood.

The second view: What is meant by sovereignty is what is called sovereignty in common usage, which is an expression for a collection of things:

I shall translate this passage faithfully.

First: the increase of wealth and of standing (jah). As for the increase of wealth, it includes ownership of minted and unminted property (al-samit wa al-natiq, i.e. gold and silver and livestock/goods), houses and estates, cultivated land, and offspring. As for the increase of standing, it is that a person be held in awe by people, have his word accepted, and be obeyed by creation.

The second: that he be in such a position that others are obliged to be under his obedience and under his command and prohibition.

The third: that he be in such a position that if anyone disputes his dominion, he is able to overpower that disputant and defeat him. And it is known that all of this is obtained only from God, the Exalted. As for the increase of wealth, we see people of great shrewdness who, despite severe toil and great hardship, obtain only a little wealth, while we see the foolish and heedless sometimes obtain wealth whose amount he does not know. As for standing, the matter is clearer, for we have seen many kings who spent great wealth for the sake of standing, and who every day became more contemptible and humiliated in the eyes of their subjects. And it may be the reverse of that: a person is esteemed in hearts, held in awe in minds, and the young and old submit to him, and the far and near humble themselves before him.

As for the second category, namely that he is owed obedience, it is known that this is an honour which God, the Exalted, bestows upon some of His servants.

As for the third category, namely the attainment of victory and triumph, it is known that this is something obtained only from God, the Exalted. For how often have we witnessed a small group overcome a large group by God's permission. At this point, by rational proof, the correctness of what God, the Exalted, mentioned becomes evident in His saying: ﴿You give sovereignty to whom You will﴾.

Know that the Mu'tazilah have a discussion here. Al-Ka'bi said: His saying ﴿You give sovereignty to whom You will and You take sovereignty away from whom You will﴾ is not in the manner of arbitrary choice, but by merit: He gives it to whoever is fit for it, and does not take it away except from one who has transgressed the command of his Lord. This is indicated by His saying: ﴿My covenant does not reach the wrongdoers﴾ [al-Baqarah: 124], and He said concerning the righteous servant: ﴿Indeed, God has chosen him over you and increased him broadly in knowledge and physique﴾ [al-Baqarah: 247], so He made it a cause of kingship.

Al-Jubba'i said: this ruling is specific to just kings. As for unjust kings, it is not permissible that their kingship be by God's giving, for how could that be by God's giving when He has obligated them not to possess it and forbade them from it? Thus it is established by what we have mentioned that the just kings are the ones specifically meant by God's giving them that kingship, whereas the unjust are not. They said: The parallel of this is what we have said regarding provision: that it does not include the unlawful, which God forbade benefiting from and commanded to be returned to its owner; so likewise here. They said: As for removal, it is different, because just as kingship is removed from just kings for a benefit that requires it, kingship may also be removed from unjust kings. Removal of kingship occurs in several ways:

Among them: by death, by the removal of reason, by the removal of strengths, power and the senses. Among them: by the coming of destruction and loss upon wealth. Among them: that God, the Exalted, commands the rightful to strip the kingship that is in the hand of the usurping wrongdoer and grants him strength and victory; then when the rightful fights him, overpowers him and strips his kingship, it is permissible that this stripping and removal be attributed to Him, the Exalted, because it occurred by His command. In this manner God, the Exalted, removed the kingship of Persia at the hand of the Messenger. This is the sum of the Mu'tazilah's words on this subject.

Know that this place is the site of an important investigation, because the attainment of kingship by the unjust either: it is said that it occurred without an agent, and was brought about only by the action of that usurper; or that it occurred by divine causes. The first is a denial of the Creator, and the second is false, because everyone wishes to attain rule and dominion for himself, and it is by no means easy for him. So nothing remains but to say that the kingship of the unjust came about by God's giving, and this statement is evident. What confirms this is that a man may be such that souls fear him and hearts incline to him, victory is his companion and triumph his sitting-companion, so wherever he turns he attains his aim; and it may be the opposite of that. Whoever reflects on the condition of kings is compelled to know that this is none other than by God's decree. For this reason the wisest of poets said:

If wealth were attained by stratagems, you would find me clinging to the most exalted causes of the sky,
But whoever is given intellect is deprived of wealth — two opposites, sharply separated, what a separation!
And from the proof of predestination and its being: the misery of the intelligent and the pleasant life of the fool.

The second opinion: His saying ﴿You give sovereignty to whom You will﴾ is taken to cover all kinds of sovereignty, so it includes the sovereignty of prophethood, the sovereignty of knowledge, the sovereignty of reason, health and good character, the sovereignty of effectiveness and power, the sovereignty of love, and the sovereignty of wealth; for the wording is general, and specification without evidence is not permissible.

* * *

As for His saying: ﴿And You exalt whom You will and You abase whom You will﴾, know that honour may be in religion and may be in the world. As for honour in religion, the most noble kind of honour is faith. God, the Exalted, said: ﴿Honour belongs to God, and to His Messenger, and to the believers﴾ [al-Munafiqun: 8]. Given this, we say: since the most honourable of things that cause honour is faith, and the most abased of things that cause abasement is disbelief, if the attainment of faith and disbelief were by the mere will of the servant, then the servant's honouring of himself through faith and his abasing of himself through disbelief would be greater than God's honouring of His servant by everything by which He honours him, and His abasing of His servant by everything by which He abases him. And if the matter were so, the servant's share of this attribute would be more complete and perfect than God's share of it. It is known that this is absolutely false. So we know that honour through faith and truth is only from God, and abasement through disbelief and falsehood is only from God. This is a strong argument on the question.

The Qadi said: The honour attributed to God may be in religion and may be in the world. As for that which is in religion, it is that reward must include honour, praise and dignity in this world and the next; and also that He supplies them with increased kindnesses and raises them over their enemies according to what is beneficial. As for what concerns the world, it is by giving abundant wealth of both minted and unminted kinds, increasing cultivation and increasing offspring among livestock, and casting awe into the hearts of creation.

We say: our discourse rejects this, because whatever honour God does in the matter of reward is a right incumbent upon God; and if He did not do it, He would be removed from divinity and would cease to be God for creation. So by granting these honours He preserves the divinity of His own self from zawal. As for the servant, since he himself chose faith, which necessitates these honours, it is he who honoured himself; so his honouring of himself is greater than God's honouring of him. Thus we know that this statement is binding upon the people.

As for His saying: ﴿And You abase whom You will﴾, al-Jubba'i said in its interpretation: God abases only His enemies in this world and the next, and does not abase any of His friends, even if He makes them poor, sick, and in need of others; because God, the Exalted, does these things only to honour them in the Hereafter, either through reward or through compensation. So this is like cupping and bloodletting: though they cause pain in the present, since they lead to great benefit, it is not said of them that they are punishment. He said: when poverty is described as abasement, it is in a figurative sense, just as God, the Exalted, called the gentleness of the believers abasement in His saying: ﴿humble towards the believers﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 54].

Having known this, we say: God's abasing of His false servant occurs in several ways: among them by blame and cursing; among them by leaving them without support in argument and victory; among them by making them servants to the people of His religion and making their wealth spoils for them; and among them by punishment for them in the Hereafter. This is the sum of the Mu'tazilah's words.

Our position is that He honours some through faith and knowledge, and abases some through disbelief and misguidance; and the greatest kinds of honour and abasement are this, and what indicates it are several points.

The first: the honour of Islam and the abasement of disbelief necessarily require an agent; that agent is either the servant or God, the Exalted. The first is false, because no one chooses disbelief for himself; rather he wills faith, knowledge and guidance. When the servant wanted faith and it did not come to him, but ignorance came to him, we know that its coming is from God, the Exalted, and not from the servant.

The second: the ignorance that arises in the servant either arises through some doubt, or it is said that the servant does it originally. The first is false, for if every ignorance arose through another ignorance preceding and prior to it, an infinite regress would follow, which is impossible. So it remains that those chains end in an ignorance the servant does originally, without any prior cause at all. But we find within ourselves that the intelligent person does not accept for himself to fall into ignorance originally without a cause; so we know that this is through God's abandoning His servant and forsaking him.

The third: we have shown that an act necessarily requires a motive and a determinant, and that determinant is from God, the Exalted. If it lies on the side of good, it is honour; if it lies on the side of ignorance, evil and misguidance, it is abasement. Thus it is established that the one who honours and the one who abases is God, the Exalted.

* * *

As for His saying, the Exalted: ﴿In Your hand is the good﴾.

Know that the intended meaning of "hand" is power, and the meaning is: by Your power is the good. The definite article in "al-khayr" (the good) implies generality, so the meaning is: by Your power all blessings and goods are obtained. Also, His saying ﴿In Your hand is the good﴾ conveys restriction, as if He said: in Your hand is the good, not in the hand of another than You, just as His saying: ﴿For you is your religion and for me is my religion﴾ [al-Kafirun: 6], i.e., for you is your religion, meaning not for others; and such restriction excludes the good being in another's hand. Thus the indication of this verse from these two aspects is established that all good is from Him, and by His making, creating, originating and bringing into being. Having known this, we say: the best of goods is belief in God, the Exalted, and knowledge of Him; so it must be that good is by God's creation, the Exalted, not by the servant's creation, and this is a clear inference. Among the companions (of al-Ash'ari) some have added to this reasoning and said: whenever of two agents the act of one is more noble and excellent than the act of the other, that agent is more noble and more perfect than the other. And there is no doubt that faith is more excellent than good and than everything other than faith. So if faith were by the servant's creation and not by God's creation, the servant would have to be greater in goodness than God, the Exalted, and in excellence and perfection; and that is a hideous disbelief. Thus this verse, from these two aspects, indicates that faith is by God's creation, the Exalted.

If it is said: this verse is an argument against you from another aspect, because when He, the Exalted, said ﴿In Your hand is the good﴾, its meaning is that there is in Your hand nothing but good; and this requires that disbelief and disobedience not occur by God's creation.

The answer: His saying ﴿In Your hand is the good﴾ indicates that the good is in His hand, not in the hand of another; and this excludes its being in another's hand, but it does not exclude that the good is in His hand and that what is other than good is also in His hand. Only, He singled out the good for mention, because it is the matter that is benefited from, so it was explicitly stated for this reason. The Qadi said: every good that comes from the servants, were it not that He enabled them to do it...

Wa-hadāhum ilayhi lammā tamakkanū minhu, fa-li-hādhā s-sabab kāna muḍāfan ilā Llāh taʿālā, illā anna hādhā ḍaʿīf; li-anna ʿalā hādhā t-taqdīr yaṣīru baʿḍ al-khayr muḍāfan ilā Llāh taʿālā, wa-yaṣīru ashraf al-khayrāt muḍāfan ilā al-ʿabd, wa-dhālika ʿalā khilāf hādhā n-naṣṣ.

Wa-ammā qawluhu: ﴿Innaka ʿalā kulli shayʾin qadīr﴾ fa-hādhā ka-t-taʾkīd li-mā taqaddama min kawnihi mālikan li-ītāʾi l-mulk wa-naziʿihi wa-l-iʿzāz wa-l-idhlāl.

Wa-ammā qawluhu taʿālā: ﴿Tūlijul-layla fi n-nahār wa-tūlijun-nahāra fi l-layl﴾ fīhi wajhān:

al-Awwal: an yajʿala al-layl qaṣīran wa-yajʿala dhālika l-qadr az-zāʾid dākhilan fi n-nahār, wa-tāratan ʿalā l-ʿaks min dhālik. Wa-innamā faʿala subḥānahu wa-taʿālā dhālika li-annahu ʿallaqa qiwām al-ʿālam wa-niẓāmahu bi-dhālik.

wa-th-thānī: anna l-murād huwa annahu taʿālā yaʾtī bi-l-layl ʿaqība n-nahār, fa-yulbisu d-dunyā ẓulmatan baʿda an kāna fīhā ḍawʾ an-nahār, thumma yaʾtī bi-n-nahār ʿaqība al-layl fa-yulbisu d-dunyā ḍawʾahu, fa-kāna al-murād min īlāj aḥadihimā fi l-ākhar ījād kull wāḥidin minhumā ʿaqība al-ākhar, wa-l-awwal aqrab ilā l-lafẓ, li-annahu idhā kāna n-nahār ṭawīlan fa-jaʿala mā naqaṣa minhu ziyādatan fi l-layl kāna mā naqaṣa minhu dākhilan fi l-layl.

* * *

Wa-ammā qawluhu: ﴿Wa-tukhriju l-ḥayya mina l-mayyiti wa-tukhriju l-mayyita mina l-ḥayy﴾ fa-fīhi masāʾil:

Al-Masʾala al-Ūlā: qaraʾa Nāfiʿ wa-Ḥamzah wa-l-Kisāʾī "al-mayyita" bi-t-tashdīd, wa-l-bāqūna bi-t-takhfīf, wa-humā lughatān bi-maʿnan wāḥid. Qāla al-Mubarrad: ajmaʿa al-Baṣriyyūna ʿalā annahumā sawāʾ, wa-ansadū:

innamā l-maytu mayyitu l-aḥyāʾ

wa-huwa mithlu qawlihi: hayyinun wa-hayn, wa-layyinun wa-layn. Wa-qad dhahaba dhāhibūna ilā anna al-mayta man qad māta, wa-l-mayyita man lam yamut.

Al-Masʾala al-Thāniya: dhakara al-mufassirūna fīhi wujūhan:

Aḥaduhā: yukhriju al-muʾmina mina l-kāfir ka-Ibrāhīma min Āzar, wa-l-kāfira mina l-muʾmin mithla Kanʿān min Nūḥ ʿalayhi s-salām.

wa-th-thānī: yukhriju aṭ-ṭayyiba mina l-khabīth wa-bi-l-ʿaks.

wa-th-thālith: yukhriju al-ḥayawān mina n-nuṭfa, wa-ṭ-ṭayra mina l-bayḍa wa-bi-l-ʿaks. Wa-r-rābiʿ: yukhriju as-sunbulata mina l-ḥabba wa-bi-l-ʿaks, wa-n-nakhlata mina n-nawā wa-bi-l-ʿaks. Qāla al-Qaffāl, raḥimahu Llāh: wa-l-kalima muḥtamilatun li-l-kull. Ammā al-kufr wa-l-īmān fa-qāla taʿālā: ﴿Awa-man kāna maytan fa-aḥyaynāhu﴾ [al-Anʿām: 122] yurīdu kāna kāfiran fa-hadaynāhu, fa-jaʿala al-mawta kufran wa-l-ḥayāta īmānan. Wa-sammā ikhrāja n-nabāti mina l-arḍi iḥyāʾan, wa-jaʿala qablu dhālika maytatan fa-qāla: ﴿Wa-yuḥyī l-arḍa baʿda mawtihā﴾ [ar-Rūm: 50] wa-qāla: ﴿Fa-suqnāhu ilā baladin mayyitin fa-aḥyaynā bihi l-arḍa baʿda mawtihā﴾ [Fāṭir: 9] wa-qāla: ﴿Kayfa takfurūna bi-Llāhi wa-kuntum amwātan fa-aḥyākum thumma yumītukum thumma yuḥyīkum﴾ [al-Baqarah: 28].

Ammā qawluhu: ﴿Wa-tarzuqu man tashāʾu bi-ghayri ḥisāb﴾ fa-fīhi wujūh:

al-Awwal: annahu yuʿṭī man yashāʾu mā yashāʾu, lā yuḥāsibuhu ʿalā dhālika aḥad, idh laysa fawqahu malikun yuḥāsibuhu, bal huwa al-Malik, yuʿṭī man yashāʾu bi-ghayri ḥisāb.

wa-th-thānī: tarzuqu man tashāʾu [rizqan] ghayra maqdūrin wa-lā maḥdūd, bal tabsuṭuhu lahu wa-tuwassiʿuhu ʿalayhi, kamā yuqālu: fulānun yunfiqu bi-ghayri ḥisāb idhā wuṣifa ʿaṭāʾuhu bi-l-kathra, wa-naẓīruhu qawluhum fī takthīr māl al-insān: ʿindahu mālun lā yuḥṣā.

wa-th-thālith: tarzuqu man tashāʾu bi-ghayri ḥisāb, yaʿnī ʿalā sabīl at-tafaḍḍul min ghayri istiḥqāq, li-anna man aʿṭā ʿalā qadr al-istiḥqāq fa-qad aʿṭā bi-ḥisāb. Wa-qāla baʿḍu man dhahaba ilā hādhā l-maʿnā: innaka lā tarzuqu ʿibādaka ʿalā maqādīr aʿmālihim, wa-llāhu aʿlam.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 3, verses 26–27 (part 1 of 3):

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Say: O Allah, Owner of sovereignty, You give sovereignty to whom You will and You take sovereignty away from whom You will. You endue with honour whom You will and You humble whom You will. In Your hand is [all] good. Indeed, You are over all things competent.﴾ ﴿You cause the night to enter the day and You cause the day to enter the night. And You bring the living out of the dead and You bring the dead out of the living. And You provide for whom You will without account.﴾

Know that when He, exalted is He, mentioned the proofs of monotheism (tawhid), of prophethood, and of the soundness of the religion of Islam, then said to His Messenger: ﴿And if they argue with you, say: I have submitted myself entirely to Allah, and [so have] those who follow me﴾, then mentioned among the attributes of the opponents their disbelief in Allah and their killing of the prophets and the righteous without right, and mentioned the severity of their obstinacy and rebellion in His saying: ﴿Have you not considered those who were given a portion of the Scripture?﴾, then mentioned the severity of their delusion in His saying: ﴿They say: The Fire will not touch us except for numbered days﴾, then mentioned their threat in His saying: ﴿So how [will it be] when We gather them for a Day about which there is no doubt?﴾, He commanded the Messenger of Allah ﷺ with a supplication and glorification that indicates the divergence of his way and the way of his followers from the way of these disbelieving, obstinate, and averse people. So He said, teaching His Prophet how he should glorify, magnify, supplicate, and ask: ﴿Say: O Allah, Owner of sovereignty﴾. In the verse there are issues:

The first issue: The grammarians differed concerning His saying (Allahumma). Al-Khalil and Sibawayh said: "Allahumma" means "Ya Allah" (O Allah), and the doubled mim is a substitute for "ya." Al-Farra' said: its original form was "Ya Allah, umma bi-khayr" (O Allah, aim for good), and when it was frequent in speech they dropped the vocative particle and dropped the hamza from "umma," so it became "Allahumma." Its parallel is the Arabs' saying "hallumma" (come here), whose origin is "hal," so "umma" was added to it.

The arguments of the first group against the invalidity of al-Farra's view are several:

The first: If the matter were as al-Farra said, it would not be correct to say "Allahumma if'al kadha" (O Allah, do such-and-such) except with the conjunctive particle, because the implied meaning would be "Ya Allah, umma-na wa-ghfir lana" (O Allah, aim for us and forgive us), and we do not find anyone mentioning this conjunctive particle.

The second, which is the argument of al-Zajjaj: If the matter were as he said, it would be permissible to use it in its original form, so one would say "Allahu umma" just as one says "waylamma," and then one would use it in the original form, saying "waylu ummihi" (woe to his mother).

The third: If the matter were as al-Farra said, the vocative particle would be elided, so it would be permissible to say "Ya Allahumma," but since this is not permissible, we know the invalidity of al-Farra's view. Rather, we say: the vocative particle ought to be obligatory, as one says "Ya Allahu, ighfir li" (O Allah, forgive me).

Al-Farra' answered these arguments, saying: As for the first, it is weak, because his saying "Ya Allah, umma" means "Ya Allah, intend," so if he said "wa-ghfir" (and forgive), the conjoined would be different from the conjoined-to, and then the request would become two requests: one of them is his saying "umma-na," and the second is his saying "wa-ghfir lana" (Al-Baqarah: 286). But when we omit the conjunction, his saying "ghfir lana" becomes an explanation of his saying "umma-na," so the sought object in both cases is one thing, and that is more emphatic. Its parallels in the Qur'an are numerous. As for the second, it is also weak, because its original form, according to us, is to say "Ya Allah, umma-na." And who denies the permissibility of speaking with that? Also, many words do not permit putting the derived form in place of the original, do you not see that the view of al-Khalil and Sibawayh is that his saying "ma akramahu" means "ayyu shay'in akramahu" (what a thing it is that made him so noble), yet this expression they claim to be the original is never used in a context of wonder. So it is likewise here.

As for the third: who has conceded to you that it is not permissible to say "Ya Allahumma"? And al-Farra' recited:

"As for what is incumbent on you, that you say whenever you glorify or pray: Ya Allahumma."

And the saying of the Basrans: this poetry is not known. Its outcome is the denial of the transmission. If we opened this door, nothing of the language and grammar would remain free from criticism. As for his saying that the mention of the vocative particle would have to be obligatory, its answer is that the vocative particle may be elided, as in His saying: ﴿Joseph, O man of truth, give us an interpretation﴾ (Yusuf: 46). So it is not far-fetched that this name is specifically bound to this elision. Then al-Farra' argued against the view of the Basrans from several aspects:

The first: If we make the mim stand in place of the vocative particle, we would have postponed the vocative particle from the mention of the one called, and this is absolutely impermissible, for one never says "Allah ya" at all, yet on your view the matter would be so.

The second: If this particle stood in place of the vocative, its like would be permissible in all other names, so that one would say "Zaydumma" and "Bakrumma," just as one says "Ya Zayd" and "Ya Bakr."

The third: If the mim were a substitute for the vocative particle, the two would not be combined, but they are combined in the poetry we have related.

The fourth: We do not find the Arabs adding this mim to complete nouns to convey the meaning of some particles that are distinct from the word they are attached to. So resorting to it in this single word would be a judgment contrary to the general induction in the language, and it is impermissible. This is the summary of the discussion on this point.

The second issue: In the case of His saying "Owner of sovereignty" (malika al-mulk) there are two possibilities of its grammatical case. The first, which is the view of Sibawayh, is that it is in the accusative as a vocative, and likewise His saying: ﴿O Allah, Originator of the heavens and the earth﴾ (Al-Zumar: 46). It is not permissible for it to be a qualifier of "Allahumma," because our saying "Allahumma" is a compound of the noun and the particle, and this compound cannot be described. The second, which is the view of al-Mubarrad and al-Zajjaj, is that "malika" is an adjective of the singular addressed noun, because this name together with the mim is like it together with "ya," and the adjective is not barred with the mim, just as it is not barred with the ya.

The third issue: It is related that "when the Prophet ﷺ conquered Makkah, he promised his community the sovereignty of Persia and Byzantium, and the hypocrites and the Jews said: Far-fetched, far-fetched! From where would Muhammad have the sovereignty of Persia and Byzantium, when they are mightier and more fortified than that?" And it is related that when he, peace be upon him, dug the trench in the year of the Confederates, and allotted to every ten men forty cubits, and they began digging, a rock emerged from the belly of the trench like a great hill, which the pickaxes did not affect. They directed Salman to the Prophet ﷺ, and he informed him. He took the pickaxe from Salman, and when he struck it a blow he split it, and a flash came out of it that illuminated what lay between its two stony tracts, as if it were a lamp in the depth of a dark night. He exclaimed "Allahu akbar," and the Muslims exclaimed "Allahu akbar" too. He, peace be upon him, said: "The palaces of al-Hirah have been illuminated for me from it, as if they were the fangs of dogs." Then he struck the second blow and said: "The red palaces of the land of the Romans have been illuminated for me from it." Then he struck the third and said: "The palaces of San'a have been illuminated for me from it, and Jibril, peace be upon him, has informed me that my community will prevail over all of them, so rejoice." The hypocrites then said: "Do you not marvel at your Prophet, who promises you falsehood and tells you that from Yathrib he sees the palaces of al-Hirah and the cities of Kisra, and that they will be opened to you while you are digging the trench out of fear, unable to go out?" Then this verse was revealed. And Allah knows best.

Al-Hasan said: Allah, exalted is He, commanded His Prophet to ask Him to give him the sovereignty of Persia and Byzantium and to return the humiliation of the Arabs upon them. His command to him with this is evidence that He would respond to this supplication for him, and thus is the rank of the prophets, peace be upon them, when they are commanded to supplicate, their supplication is answered.

* * *

The fourth issue: "Al-mulk" is power, and "al-malik" is the one who is capable, so His saying "malika al-mulk" means the one capable over power. The meaning is that the power of creatures over whatever they are capable of is only by Allah's empowerment; He is the One who empowers every capable one over what he can do, and makes every owner an owner of what he owns. The author of al-Kashshaf said: "Malika al-mulk" means "He owns the genus of sovereignty and disposes of it as owners dispose of what they own." Know that when He, exalted is He, made clear that He is "Owner of sovereignty" absolutely, He then detailed it afterwards and mentioned five kinds:

The first kind: His saying, exalted is He: ﴿You give sovereignty to whom You will and You take sovereignty away from whom You will﴾. They have mentioned several aspects regarding it:

The first: What is meant by it is the sovereignty of prophethood and messengership, as He, exalted is He, said: ﴿We had already given the family of Abraham the Scripture and wisdom, and We gave them a great kingdom﴾ (An-Nisa: 54). Prophethood is the greatest rank of sovereignty, because scholars have a great authority over the inner states of creatures, and tyrants have authority over their outward affairs, while the prophets' command is effective in both the inner and the outer. As for the inner, it is obligatory on everyone to accept their religion and law and to believe that it is the truth. As for the outer, if they were to rebel and be arrogant, they would deserve to be killed. What confirms this interpretation is that some of them found it improbable that Allah would make a human a messenger, so Allah relates their saying: [﴿Has Allah sent a human as a messenger?﴾ (Al-Isra: 94) and Allah, exalted is He, said: ﴿And if We had made him an angel, We would have made him a man﴾ (Al-An'am: 9)]. Other groups allowed from Allah, exalted is He, that He send a human messenger, but they used to say: Muhammad is poor and an orphan, so how does this great station befit him, as Allah relates of them that they said: ﴿Why was this Qur'an not sent down upon a great man of the two cities?﴾ (Az-Zukhruf: 31). As for the Jews, they used to say: prophethood was in our fathers and forefathers, and as for the Quraysh, they were not people of prophethood and Scripture, so how does prophethood befit Muhammad ﷺ? As for the hypocrites, they used to envy him for prophethood, as Allah relates of them in His saying: ﴿Or do they envy the people for what Allah has given them of His bounty?﴾ (An-Nisa: 54).

Also, we have mentioned in the commentary on His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Say to those who disbelieved: You will be overcome and gathered to Hell, and wretched is the resting place﴾ (Al 'Imran: 12) that the Jews were arrogant toward the Prophet ﷺ because of their large numbers, their weapons, and their strength. Then He, exalted is He, answered all these groups by making clear that He, glorified is He, is the Owner of sovereignty, so He gives His sovereignty to whom He wills, saying: ﴿You give sovereignty to whom You will and You take sovereignty away from whom You will﴾.

If it is said: When you interpret His saying "You give sovereignty to whom You will" as giving the sovereignty of prophethood, it is necessary that you interpret His saying "and You take sovereignty away from whom You will" as meaning that He may remove from prophethood one whom He made a prophet, and it is known that this is not permissible.

We say: The answer is in two respects:

The first: When Allah places prophethood in the lineage of a man, then removes it from his lineage and honours another person with it from outside that lineage, it is correct to say that He took it away from them. The Jews believed that prophethood must be among the Children of Israel, so when Allah honoured Muhammad ﷺ with it, it is correct to say that He takes the sovereignty of prophethood away from the Children of Israel and gives it to the Arabs.

The second answer: The meaning of His saying "and You take sovereignty away from whom You will" may be: You deprive them and do not give them this sovereignty, not in the sense that He strips it from them after He had given it. A parallel is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Allah is the Guardian of those who believe; He brings them out of darkness into light﴾ (Al-Baqarah: 257), although this statement includes one who was never in the darkness of disbelief at all. And Allah, exalted is He, related of the disbelievers that they said to the prophets, peace be upon them: ﴿Or you will return to our religion﴾ (Al-A'raf: 88), and those prophets said: ﴿It is not for us to return to it unless Allah wills﴾ (Al-A'raf: 89), although they had never been in it at all. This is the full discussion in establishing the view of one who interprets His saying, exalted is He, ﴿You give sovereignty to whom You will﴾ as the sovereignty of prophethood.

The second view: What is meant by sovereignty is what is called sovereignty in common usage, which is an expression for a collection of things:

I shall translate this passage faithfully.

First: the increase of wealth and of standing (jah). As for the increase of wealth, it includes ownership of minted and unminted property (al-samit wa al-natiq, i.e. gold and silver and livestock/goods), houses and estates, cultivated land, and offspring. As for the increase of standing, it is that a person be held in awe by people, have his word accepted, and be obeyed by creation.

The second: that he be in such a position that others are obliged to be under his obedience and under his command and prohibition.

The third: that he be in such a position that if anyone disputes his dominion, he is able to overpower that disputant and defeat him. And it is known that all of this is obtained only from God, the Exalted. As for the increase of wealth, we see people of great shrewdness who, despite severe toil and great hardship, obtain only a little wealth, while we see the foolish and heedless sometimes obtain wealth whose amount he does not know. As for standing, the matter is clearer, for we have seen many kings who spent great wealth for the sake of standing, and who every day became more contemptible and humiliated in the eyes of their subjects. And it may be the reverse of that: a person is esteemed in hearts, held in awe in minds, and the young and old submit to him, and the far and near humble themselves before him.

As for the second category, namely that he is owed obedience, it is known that this is an honour which God, the Exalted, bestows upon some of His servants.

As for the third category, namely the attainment of victory and triumph, it is known that this is something obtained only from God, the Exalted. For how often have we witnessed a small group overcome a large group by God's permission. At this point, by rational proof, the correctness of what God, the Exalted, mentioned becomes evident in His saying: ﴿You give sovereignty to whom You will﴾.

Know that the Mu'tazilah have a discussion here. Al-Ka'bi said: His saying ﴿You give sovereignty to whom You will and You take sovereignty away from whom You will﴾ is not in the manner of arbitrary choice, but by merit: He gives it to whoever is fit for it, and does not take it away except from one who has transgressed the command of his Lord. This is indicated by His saying: ﴿My covenant does not reach the wrongdoers﴾ [al-Baqarah: 124], and He said concerning the righteous servant: ﴿Indeed, God has chosen him over you and increased him broadly in knowledge and physique﴾ [al-Baqarah: 247], so He made it a cause of kingship.

Al-Jubba'i said: this ruling is specific to just kings. As for unjust kings, it is not permissible that their kingship be by God's giving, for how could that be by God's giving when He has obligated them not to possess it and forbade them from it? Thus it is established by what we have mentioned that the just kings are the ones specifically meant by God's giving them that kingship, whereas the unjust are not. They said: The parallel of this is what we have said regarding provision: that it does not include the unlawful, which God forbade benefiting from and commanded to be returned to its owner; so likewise here. They said: As for removal, it is different, because just as kingship is removed from just kings for a benefit that requires it, kingship may also be removed from unjust kings. Removal of kingship occurs in several ways:

Among them: by death, by the removal of reason, by the removal of strengths, power and the senses. Among them: by the coming of destruction and loss upon wealth. Among them: that God, the Exalted, commands the rightful to strip the kingship that is in the hand of the usurping wrongdoer and grants him strength and victory; then when the rightful fights him, overpowers him and strips his kingship, it is permissible that this stripping and removal be attributed to Him, the Exalted, because it occurred by His command. In this manner God, the Exalted, removed the kingship of Persia at the hand of the Messenger. This is the sum of the Mu'tazilah's words on this subject.

Know that this place is the site of an important investigation, because the attainment of kingship by the unjust either: it is said that it occurred without an agent, and was brought about only by the action of that usurper; or that it occurred by divine causes. The first is a denial of the Creator, and the second is false, because everyone wishes to attain rule and dominion for himself, and it is by no means easy for him. So nothing remains but to say that the kingship of the unjust came about by God's giving, and this statement is evident. What confirms this is that a man may be such that souls fear him and hearts incline to him, victory is his companion and triumph his sitting-companion, so wherever he turns he attains his aim; and it may be the opposite of that. Whoever reflects on the condition of kings is compelled to know that this is none other than by God's decree. For this reason the wisest of poets said:

If wealth were attained by stratagems, you would find me clinging to the most exalted causes of the sky,
But whoever is given intellect is deprived of wealth — two opposites, sharply separated, what a separation!
And from the proof of predestination and its being: the misery of the intelligent and the pleasant life of the fool.

The second opinion: His saying ﴿You give sovereignty to whom You will﴾ is taken to cover all kinds of sovereignty, so it includes the sovereignty of prophethood, the sovereignty of knowledge, the sovereignty of reason, health and good character, the sovereignty of effectiveness and power, the sovereignty of love, and the sovereignty of wealth; for the wording is general, and specification without evidence is not permissible.

* * *

As for His saying: ﴿And You exalt whom You will and You abase whom You will﴾, know that honour may be in religion and may be in the world. As for honour in religion, the most noble kind of honour is faith. God, the Exalted, said: ﴿Honour belongs to God, and to His Messenger, and to the believers﴾ [al-Munafiqun: 8]. Given this, we say: since the most honourable of things that cause honour is faith, and the most abased of things that cause abasement is disbelief, if the attainment of faith and disbelief were by the mere will of the servant, then the servant's honouring of himself through faith and his abasing of himself through disbelief would be greater than God's honouring of His servant by everything by which He honours him, and His abasing of His servant by everything by which He abases him. And if the matter were so, the servant's share of this attribute would be more complete and perfect than God's share of it. It is known that this is absolutely false. So we know that honour through faith and truth is only from God, and abasement through disbelief and falsehood is only from God. This is a strong argument on the question.

The Qadi said: The honour attributed to God may be in religion and may be in the world. As for that which is in religion, it is that reward must include honour, praise and dignity in this world and the next; and also that He supplies them with increased kindnesses and raises them over their enemies according to what is beneficial. As for what concerns the world, it is by giving abundant wealth of both minted and unminted kinds, increasing cultivation and increasing offspring among livestock, and casting awe into the hearts of creation.

We say: our discourse rejects this, because whatever honour God does in the matter of reward is a right incumbent upon God; and if He did not do it, He would be removed from divinity and would cease to be God for creation. So by granting these honours He preserves the divinity of His own self from zawal. As for the servant, since he himself chose faith, which necessitates these honours, it is he who honoured himself; so his honouring of himself is greater than God's honouring of him. Thus we know that this statement is binding upon the people.

As for His saying: ﴿And You abase whom You will﴾, al-Jubba'i said in its interpretation: God abases only His enemies in this world and the next, and does not abase any of His friends, even if He makes them poor, sick, and in need of others; because God, the Exalted, does these things only to honour them in the Hereafter, either through reward or through compensation. So this is like cupping and bloodletting: though they cause pain in the present, since they lead to great benefit, it is not said of them that they are punishment. He said: when poverty is described as abasement, it is in a figurative sense, just as God, the Exalted, called the gentleness of the believers abasement in His saying: ﴿humble towards the believers﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 54].

Having known this, we say: God's abasing of His false servant occurs in several ways: among them by blame and cursing; among them by leaving them without support in argument and victory; among them by making them servants to the people of His religion and making their wealth spoils for them; and among them by punishment for them in the Hereafter. This is the sum of the Mu'tazilah's words.

Our position is that He honours some through faith and knowledge, and abases some through disbelief and misguidance; and the greatest kinds of honour and abasement are this, and what indicates it are several points.

The first: the honour of Islam and the abasement of disbelief necessarily require an agent; that agent is either the servant or God, the Exalted. The first is false, because no one chooses disbelief for himself; rather he wills faith, knowledge and guidance. When the servant wanted faith and it did not come to him, but ignorance came to him, we know that its coming is from God, the Exalted, and not from the servant.

The second: the ignorance that arises in the servant either arises through some doubt, or it is said that the servant does it originally. The first is false, for if every ignorance arose through another ignorance preceding and prior to it, an infinite regress would follow, which is impossible. So it remains that those chains end in an ignorance the servant does originally, without any prior cause at all. But we find within ourselves that the intelligent person does not accept for himself to fall into ignorance originally without a cause; so we know that this is through God's abandoning His servant and forsaking him.

The third: we have shown that an act necessarily requires a motive and a determinant, and that determinant is from God, the Exalted. If it lies on the side of good, it is honour; if it lies on the side of ignorance, evil and misguidance, it is abasement. Thus it is established that the one who honours and the one who abases is God, the Exalted.

* * *

As for His saying, the Exalted: ﴿In Your hand is the good﴾.

Know that the intended meaning of "hand" is power, and the meaning is: by Your power is the good. The definite article in "al-khayr" (the good) implies generality, so the meaning is: by Your power all blessings and goods are obtained. Also, His saying ﴿In Your hand is the good﴾ conveys restriction, as if He said: in Your hand is the good, not in the hand of another than You, just as His saying: ﴿For you is your religion and for me is my religion﴾ [al-Kafirun: 6], i.e., for you is your religion, meaning not for others; and such restriction excludes the good being in another's hand. Thus the indication of this verse from these two aspects is established that all good is from Him, and by His making, creating, originating and bringing into being. Having known this, we say: the best of goods is belief in God, the Exalted, and knowledge of Him; so it must be that good is by God's creation, the Exalted, not by the servant's creation, and this is a clear inference. Among the companions (of al-Ash'ari) some have added to this reasoning and said: whenever of two agents the act of one is more noble and excellent than the act of the other, that agent is more noble and more perfect than the other. And there is no doubt that faith is more excellent than good and than everything other than faith. So if faith were by the servant's creation and not by God's creation, the servant would have to be greater in goodness than God, the Exalted, and in excellence and perfection; and that is a hideous disbelief. Thus this verse, from these two aspects, indicates that faith is by God's creation, the Exalted.

If it is said: this verse is an argument against you from another aspect, because when He, the Exalted, said ﴿In Your hand is the good﴾, its meaning is that there is in Your hand nothing but good; and this requires that disbelief and disobedience not occur by God's creation.

The answer: His saying ﴿In Your hand is the good﴾ indicates that the good is in His hand, not in the hand of another; and this excludes its being in another's hand, but it does not exclude that the good is in His hand and that what is other than good is also in His hand. Only, He singled out the good for mention, because it is the matter that is benefited from, so it was explicitly stated for this reason. The Qadi said: every good that comes from the servants, were it not that He enabled them to do it...

Wa-hadāhum ilayhi lammā tamakkanū minhu, fa-li-hādhā s-sabab kāna muḍāfan ilā Llāh taʿālā, illā anna hādhā ḍaʿīf; li-anna ʿalā hādhā t-taqdīr yaṣīru baʿḍ al-khayr muḍāfan ilā Llāh taʿālā, wa-yaṣīru ashraf al-khayrāt muḍāfan ilā al-ʿabd, wa-dhālika ʿalā khilāf hādhā n-naṣṣ.

Wa-ammā qawluhu: ﴿Innaka ʿalā kulli shayʾin qadīr﴾ fa-hādhā ka-t-taʾkīd li-mā taqaddama min kawnihi mālikan li-ītāʾi l-mulk wa-naziʿihi wa-l-iʿzāz wa-l-idhlāl.

Wa-ammā qawluhu taʿālā: ﴿Tūlijul-layla fi n-nahār wa-tūlijun-nahāra fi l-layl﴾ fīhi wajhān:

al-Awwal: an yajʿala al-layl qaṣīran wa-yajʿala dhālika l-qadr az-zāʾid dākhilan fi n-nahār, wa-tāratan ʿalā l-ʿaks min dhālik. Wa-innamā faʿala subḥānahu wa-taʿālā dhālika li-annahu ʿallaqa qiwām al-ʿālam wa-niẓāmahu bi-dhālik.

wa-th-thānī: anna l-murād huwa annahu taʿālā yaʾtī bi-l-layl ʿaqība n-nahār, fa-yulbisu d-dunyā ẓulmatan baʿda an kāna fīhā ḍawʾ an-nahār, thumma yaʾtī bi-n-nahār ʿaqība al-layl fa-yulbisu d-dunyā ḍawʾahu, fa-kāna al-murād min īlāj aḥadihimā fi l-ākhar ījād kull wāḥidin minhumā ʿaqība al-ākhar, wa-l-awwal aqrab ilā l-lafẓ, li-annahu idhā kāna n-nahār ṭawīlan fa-jaʿala mā naqaṣa minhu ziyādatan fi l-layl kāna mā naqaṣa minhu dākhilan fi l-layl.

* * *

Wa-ammā qawluhu: ﴿Wa-tukhriju l-ḥayya mina l-mayyiti wa-tukhriju l-mayyita mina l-ḥayy﴾ fa-fīhi masāʾil:

Al-Masʾala al-Ūlā: qaraʾa Nāfiʿ wa-Ḥamzah wa-l-Kisāʾī "al-mayyita" bi-t-tashdīd, wa-l-bāqūna bi-t-takhfīf, wa-humā lughatān bi-maʿnan wāḥid. Qāla al-Mubarrad: ajmaʿa al-Baṣriyyūna ʿalā annahumā sawāʾ, wa-ansadū:

innamā l-maytu mayyitu l-aḥyāʾ

wa-huwa mithlu qawlihi: hayyinun wa-hayn, wa-layyinun wa-layn. Wa-qad dhahaba dhāhibūna ilā anna al-mayta man qad māta, wa-l-mayyita man lam yamut.

Al-Masʾala al-Thāniya: dhakara al-mufassirūna fīhi wujūhan:

Aḥaduhā: yukhriju al-muʾmina mina l-kāfir ka-Ibrāhīma min Āzar, wa-l-kāfira mina l-muʾmin mithla Kanʿān min Nūḥ ʿalayhi s-salām.

wa-th-thānī: yukhriju aṭ-ṭayyiba mina l-khabīth wa-bi-l-ʿaks.

wa-th-thālith: yukhriju al-ḥayawān mina n-nuṭfa, wa-ṭ-ṭayra mina l-bayḍa wa-bi-l-ʿaks. Wa-r-rābiʿ: yukhriju as-sunbulata mina l-ḥabba wa-bi-l-ʿaks, wa-n-nakhlata mina n-nawā wa-bi-l-ʿaks. Qāla al-Qaffāl, raḥimahu Llāh: wa-l-kalima muḥtamilatun li-l-kull. Ammā al-kufr wa-l-īmān fa-qāla taʿālā: ﴿Awa-man kāna maytan fa-aḥyaynāhu﴾ [al-Anʿām: 122] yurīdu kāna kāfiran fa-hadaynāhu, fa-jaʿala al-mawta kufran wa-l-ḥayāta īmānan. Wa-sammā ikhrāja n-nabāti mina l-arḍi iḥyāʾan, wa-jaʿala qablu dhālika maytatan fa-qāla: ﴿Wa-yuḥyī l-arḍa baʿda mawtihā﴾ [ar-Rūm: 50] wa-qāla: ﴿Fa-suqnāhu ilā baladin mayyitin fa-aḥyaynā bihi l-arḍa baʿda mawtihā﴾ [Fāṭir: 9] wa-qāla: ﴿Kayfa takfurūna bi-Llāhi wa-kuntum amwātan fa-aḥyākum thumma yumītukum thumma yuḥyīkum﴾ [al-Baqarah: 28].

Ammā qawluhu: ﴿Wa-tarzuqu man tashāʾu bi-ghayri ḥisāb﴾ fa-fīhi wujūh:

al-Awwal: annahu yuʿṭī man yashāʾu mā yashāʾu, lā yuḥāsibuhu ʿalā dhālika aḥad, idh laysa fawqahu malikun yuḥāsibuhu, bal huwa al-Malik, yuʿṭī man yashāʾu bi-ghayri ḥisāb.

wa-th-thānī: tarzuqu man tashāʾu [rizqan] ghayra maqdūrin wa-lā maḥdūd, bal tabsuṭuhu lahu wa-tuwassiʿuhu ʿalayhi, kamā yuqālu: fulānun yunfiqu bi-ghayri ḥisāb idhā wuṣifa ʿaṭāʾuhu bi-l-kathra, wa-naẓīruhu qawluhum fī takthīr māl al-insān: ʿindahu mālun lā yuḥṣā.

wa-th-thālith: tarzuqu man tashāʾu bi-ghayri ḥisāb, yaʿnī ʿalā sabīl at-tafaḍḍul min ghayri istiḥqāq, li-anna man aʿṭā ʿalā qadr al-istiḥqāq fa-qad aʿṭā bi-ḥisāb. Wa-qāla baʿḍu man dhahaba ilā hādhā l-maʿnā: innaka lā tarzuqu ʿibādaka ʿalā maqādīr aʿmālihim, wa-llāhu aʿlam.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 3, verse 28:

Concerning the composition (naẓm) of the verse there are two views. The first: when He, exalted is He, mentioned what the believer must uphold in glorifying God, He then mentioned what the believer must uphold in dealing with people, because perfection of the matter lies in nothing but two things: glorifying the command of God, and compassion toward the creatures of God. He said: ﴿Let not the believers take the disbelievers as allies (awliyā') instead of the believers﴾. The second: when He explained that He is the Owner of this world and the Hereafter, He explained that the desire should be for what is with Him and with His allies, not with His enemies.

In the verse there are issues:

The first issue: regarding the occasion of revelation (sabab al-nuzūl), there are several reports:

The first: a group of Jews came to a group of Muslims to seduce them from their religion. Rifā'ah ibn al-Mundhir, 'Abd al-Raḥmān ibn Jubayr, and Sa'īd ibn Khaythamah said to those men among the Muslims: "Avoid these Jews, and beware lest they seduce you from your religion." So this verse was revealed.

The second: Muqātil said: it was revealed concerning Ḥāṭib ibn Abī Balta'ah and others, who used to take the Jews and the polytheists as allies, informing them of news and hoping that victory over the Messenger of God (ﷺ) would be theirs. So this verse was revealed.

The third: that it "was revealed concerning 'Ubādah ibn al-Ṣāmit, who had allies among the Jews. On the day of the Confederates he said: 'O Prophet of God, I have five hundred Jews with me, and I think they should go out with me.' So this verse was revealed."
