Then God, exalted is He, sometimes answers and sometimes does not answer, and this is not a deficiency in the station of the prophets (peace and blessings be upon them), for they are seekers at the door of God's mercy. If He answers them, it is by His grace and kindness; and if He does not answer them, it is from the creation, so that they would have a station at the door of the Creator.

As for the saying of God, exalted is He, quoting Zakariyya (peace be upon him): ﴿Grant me from Yourself a good offspring﴾, there are issues:

**The first issue:** As for the discussion of the word "ladun" (from Yourself), it will come in Surat al-Kahf. The benefit of mentioning it here is that the occurrence of a child, by customary norms, has specific causes. When he requested a child while those causes were absent, the meaning was: "I ask of You, my God, to suspend the causes in this matter and to bring about this child by sheer power from You, without the intermediation of any of these causes."

**The second issue:** "Dhurriyya" means offspring. It is a word that applies to the singular and the plural, and the masculine and the feminine. What is meant here is one child, like His saying: ﴿So grant me from Yourself an heir﴾ [Maryam: 5]. Al-Farra' said: "tayyiba" (good) is feminine because "dhurriyya" is feminine in outward form. Feminine and masculine forms sometimes follow the wording and sometimes follow the meaning. This is what we say regarding common nouns (asma' al-ajnas). But regarding proper names (asma' al-a'lam), no; it is not permissible to say "jaa'at Talha" (Talha came, feminine), because proper names only refer to that specific person, so if that person is masculine, only the masculine form is permissible.

**The third issue:** His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, You are the Hearer of supplication﴾ does not mean that He hears the sound of the supplication, for that is known. Rather, it means that He answers his supplication and does not disappoint his hope. This is like the saying of worshippers: "Allah hears whoever praises Him" (sami'a Allahu liman hamidah), meaning He accepts the praise of whoever among the believers praises Him. This is confirmed by what God, exalted is He, quoted from Zakariyya (peace be upon him) in Surat Maryam: ﴿And I have never been, in my supplication to You, my Lord, unblessed﴾ [Maryam: 4].

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 3, verse 39:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Then the angels called to him while he stood praying in the sanctuary, "Indeed, Allah gives you good tidings of Yahya, confirming a word from Allah, and a leader, and chaste, and a prophet from among the righteous."﴾ ﴿He said, "My Lord, how can I have a boy when old age has already reached me and my wife is barren?" He said, "Thus Allah does what He wills."﴾ In it are two issues:

Page 31

The first issue: Hamzah and al-Kisa'i recited (فَناداهُ المَلائِكَةُ), with the masculine form and imalah (fa-nadahu al-mala'ikah), while the rest recited it in the feminine, following the wording. It was said: whoever used the masculine did so because the verb precedes the noun, and whoever used the feminine did so because the verb belongs to the angels. Ibn 'Amir recited "al-mihrab" with imalah, and the rest with tafkhim (the full, velarized vowel). In the recitation of Ibn Mas'ud: "fa-nadahu Jibril" (then Jibril called to him).

The second issue: The apparent wording indicates that the calling was from the angels, and there is no doubt that this is greater in honour. If a separate proof indicates that the one calling was Jibril (peace be upon him) alone, we turn to it and interpret this wording figuratively. It is said: "So-and-so eats good foods and wears precious garments," meaning he eats from this category and wears from this category, although it is known that he did not eat all foods nor wear all garments. So it is here. A similar example in the Qur'an is ﴿Those to whom the people said﴾ [Al 'Imran: 173], and they were Nu'aym ibn Mas'ud; "the people" here means Abu Sufyan. Al-Mufaddal ibn Salamah said: when the speaker is a leader, it is permissible to report about him with the plural, because his companions are with him. Since Jibril is the leader of the angels, and he is rarely sent except with a group, this is valid.

* * *

As for His saying: ﴿while he stood praying in the sanctuary﴾, it indicates that prayer was prescribed in their religion, and we have already explained the meaning of al-mihrab.

As for His saying: ﴿Indeed, Allah gives you good tidings of Yahya﴾, there are issues:

The first issue: As for the glad tidings (bishara), we have explained it in His saying: ﴿And give glad tidings to those who believe and do righteous deeds﴾ [al-Baqarah: 25]. In ﴿gives you good tidings of Yahya﴾ there are two views: The first: that Allah had informed Zakariyya that among the prophets there would be a man named Yahya, who would have a lofty offspring; so when it was said that this prophet named Yahya is your son, that was glad tidings to him of Yahya (peace be upon him). The second: that Allah gives you glad tidings of a son named Yahya.

The second issue: Ibn 'Amir and Hamzah recited "inna" with a kasrah on the hamzah, while the rest recited it with a fatha. The kasrah is based on the intention of speech, or because calling is a type of speech; the fatha is by the estimate: "the angels called to him that Allah gives you good tidings."

The third issue: Hamzah and al-Kisa'i recited "yabshuruka" with a fatha on the yaa', sukun on the baa', and damma on the shin; the rest recited "yubashshiruka". It was also read "yubshiruka". Abu Zayd said: one says bashara yabshuru bashran, and bashsharа yubashshiru tabshiran, and abshara yubshiru: three dialects.

The fourth issue: Hamzah and al-Kisa'i recited "Yahya" with imalah because of the yaa', and the rest with tafkhim. As for why he was named Yahya, we have mentioned it in the surah of Maryam. Know that He mentioned three types of Yahya's attributes:

The first attribute: His saying: ﴿confirming a word from Allah﴾, and in it are two issues:

The first issue: al-Wahidi said: His saying ﴿confirming a word from Allah﴾ is in the accusative as a circumstantial state (hal), because it is indefinite, and Yahya is definite.

The second issue: Regarding the meaning of ﴿a word from Allah﴾ there are two views:

The first: the view of Abu 'Ubaydah: that it is a Book from Allah, and he cited the saying of people: "So-and-so recited a word (kalimah)," meaning a long qasidah (ode).

Page 32

The second view, which is the choice of the majority: that what is meant by His saying ﴿a word from Allah﴾ is 'Isa (peace be upon him). Al-Suddi said: The mother of 'Isa met the mother of Yahya (peace be upon them both), and the latter was pregnant with Yahya and the former with 'Isa. She said: "O Maryam, did you feel that I am pregnant?" Maryam said: "I too am pregnant." The wife of Zakariyya said: "I have found that what is in my womb prostrates to what is in your womb." That is His saying: ﴿confirming a word from Allah﴾. Ibn 'Abbas said: Yahya was six months older than 'Isa, and Yahya was the first to believe and confirm that he was a word of Allah and His spirit. Then Yahya was killed before the raising of 'Isa (peace be upon them both). If it is asked: why was 'Isa called a word in this verse, and in His saying ﴿The Messiah, 'Isa son of Maryam, is only a messenger of Allah and His word﴾ [al-Nisa': 171]? We say: there are aspects:

The first: he was created by the word of Allah, which is His saying "Be," without the intermediary of a father. Since his bringing into existence was by the mere word of Allah "Be," and by the mere bringing into being and creating without the intermediary of a father or seed, he was therefore called a word, just as the created is called a creation, the decreed a decree, the hoped-for a hope, and the desired a desire. This is a well-known usage in the language.

The second: he spoke in infancy, and Allah gave him the Book in the time of infancy, so his being a speaker reached a great level; he was thus called a word by this interpretation, as one says "So-and-so is generosity and munificence" when he is perfect in both.

The third: just as a word conveys meanings and realities, so 'Isa guided to realities and divine secrets; he was thus called a word by this interpretation. This is like calling him a spirit, since Allah gave life through him from error as a human lives by the spirit. Allah also called the Qur'an a spirit, saying: ﴿And thus We revealed to you a spirit from Our command﴾ [al-Shura: 52].

The fourth: the glad tidings of him had come in the books of the prophets before him; when he came, it was said: "this is that word." He was thus called a word by this interpretation. They said: the metaphor here is that whoever reports the occurrence of a matter, when that matter happens, says: "my word has come and my speech has come," meaning what I used to say and speak of. A parallel is His saying: ﴿And thus the word of your Lord has been justified against those who disbelieved, that they are the companions of the Fire﴾ [Ghafir: 6], and His saying: ﴿But the word of punishment has come due upon the disbelievers﴾ [al-Zumar: 71].

The fifth: a person may be named by Allah's grace and kindness; so also 'Isa (peace be upon him) had as his proper name: "the word of Allah" and "the spirit of Allah." Know that the word of Allah is His speech, and His speech, according to the people of the Sunnah, is an eternal attribute subsisting in His essence; according to the Mu'tazilah, it is sounds which Allah creates in a specific body, indicating by convention specific meanings. Necessary knowledge establishes that the eternal attribute, or the sounds which are accidents that do not endure, cannot be said to be the very essence of 'Isa (peace be upon him). Since that is false by the self-evident judgment of minds, only interpretation remains.

* * *

The second attribute of Yahya (peace be upon him): His saying: (and a leader). The exegetes gave several views on it:

The first: Ibn 'Abbas said: the leader is the forbearing. Al-Jubba'i said: he was a leader of the believers, a chief for them in religion, meaning in knowledge, forbearance, worship and piety. Mujahid said: the honoured before Allah. Ibn al-Musayyab said: the jurist, the learned. 'Ikrimah said: the one whom anger does not overcome. Al-Qadi said: the leader is the one who is foremost and to whom one returns. Since he was a leader in religion, he was one to whom people returned in religion and an example in religion; thus all the mentioned attributes are included in it: knowledge, forbearance, generosity, chastity, asceticism and piety.

* * *

The third attribute: His saying: (and chaste). In it are two issues:

The first issue: on the interpretation of ḥaṣūr. In language, ḥaṣr means confinement; one says ḥaṣarahu yaḥṣuruhu ḥaṣran, and ḥuṣira al-rajul, meaning his belly was constricted. Al-ḥaṣūr is one who keeps a secret and restrains it, and al-ḥaṣūr is the narrow, the miserly. As for the exegetes:

Page 33

They have two views. One: that he was incapable of approaching women. Then some said that this was due to the smallness of the organ; some said it was due to the impossibility of ejaculation; some said it was due to lack of ability. According to this, ḥaṣūr is fa‘ūl in the sense of maf‘ūl, as if it said maḥṣūr ‘anhunna, meaning confined, like rakūb in the sense of markūb and ḥalūb in the sense of maḥlūb. This view, in our opinion, is false, because this is an attribute of deficiency, and mentioning an attribute of deficiency in the context of praise is not permissible; and because on this assumption he would deserve no reward or honour.

The second view, which is the choice of the verifiers: that he is one who does not approach women, not out of incapacity but out of chastity and asceticism. This is because al-ḥaṣūr is one who frequently restrains and withholds himself, like the one who eats much (akūl), the one who drinks much (sharūb), the tyrant (ẓalūm), and the oppressor (ghashūm). Restraint occurs only when the motive is present; were the ability and the desire not both present, he would not be restraining himself, let alone being ḥaṣūr, because the need to frequently restrain and repel arises only when desire, drive and ability are strong. According to this, ḥaṣūr means ḥāṣir, fa‘ūl in the sense of fā‘il.

The second issue: Our companions (the Ash'arites) cited this verse to show that abandoning marriage is better. That is because He praised him for abandoning marriage, and this indicates that abandoning marriage is better in that law. If it is established that abandonment is better in that law, it must be so in this law too, by text and reason. As for the text, it is His saying: ﴿Those are the ones whom Allah guided, so follow their guidance﴾ [al-An'am: 90]. As for reason, the original principle regarding what is established is that it remains as it was, and abrogation is contrary to the original principle.

* * *

The fourth attribute: His saying: (and a prophet). Know that leadership points to two matters: one, his capacity to regulate the interests of creation in what concerns teaching religion; and two, regulating their interests in what concerns discipline, enjoining good and forbidding evil. As for chastity, it points to complete asceticism. When these two were combined, prophethood followed after them, since beyond them there is nothing but prophethood.

The fifth attribute: His saying: ﴿from among the righteous﴾, and in it there are three aspects:

The first: its meaning is that he was among the offspring of the righteous.

The second: that he was good, as one says of a good man, "he is one of the righteous."

The third: that his righteousness was more complete than the righteousness of all the other prophets, based on the saying of the Prophet (peace and blessings be upon him): "There is no prophet but that he has disobeyed or intended a disobedience, except Yahya, for he did not disobey and did not intend it."

If it is asked: since prophethood is a higher rank than righteousness, what is the benefit of describing him with righteousness after describing him with prophethood? We say: Did not Sulayman (peace be upon him), after attaining prophethood, say: ﴿And admit me by Your mercy among Your righteous servants﴾ [al-Naml: 19]? The full answer: prophets possess a degree of righteousness such that if it were diminished, prophethood would be cancelled; that degree, relative to them, functions like the preservation of obligations relative to us. Then, after sharing in that degree, their ranks vary in the increase above it, and whoever has a greater share of it has a higher rank. And Allah knows best.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 3, verse 40:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿He said: "My Lord, how can I have a son?"﴾ There are several questions concerning this verse.

Page 34

The first question: His saying "My Lord" (rabbi) is addressed either to God or to the angels. It is possible that it is addressed to God, because the preceding verse indicated that those who called out to him were the angels, and this speech must be addressed to that caller and not to anyone else. It is not possible that it be addressed to an angel, because it is not permissible for a human to say to an angel, "My Lord."

The answer: the exegetes have two opinions on this.

The first: when the angels called out to him with this and gave him the good news, Zakariyya (peace be upon him) was astonished, and to remove that astonishment he turned back to God exalted.

The second: it is addressed to the angels, and "rabb" (lord) is a reference to one who nurtures, and it is permissible to describe a created being with it, as one says: "So-and-so nurtures me and is good to me."

The second question: since Zakariyya (peace be upon him) is the one who asked for a child, and then God answered him, why was he astonished at it and why did he consider it unlikely?

The answer: this statement was not due to his doubting God's power to do that. The evidence for this is two aspects:

The first: everyone knows that the creation of a child from a drop of semen occurs by way of habit, because if there were no semen except from a created being, and no created being except from semen, there would follow an infinite regress and the occurrence of events in eternity, which is impossible. So we know that one must end at a created being that God created not from semen, or from semen that God created not from a human.

The second aspect: Zakariyya (peace be upon him) asked this from God exalted, and if that were impossible and unattainable, he would not have asked it from God exalted. Thus it is established by these two aspects that his saying ﴿How can I have a son?﴾ is not for the sake of considering it unlikely. Rather, the scholars mentioned several aspects regarding it:

The first: his saying "how" (anna) means "from where?" It may mean: how will You give a child, in the first manner or in the second? This is because the occurrence of a child may involve two possibilities:

One of them: that God restores his youth and then gives him a child while he is old. So his saying ﴿How can I have a son?﴾ means: how will You give a child in the first manner or in the second? It was said to him: thus, that is, in this state, and God does what He wills. This view was mentioned by al-Hasan and al-Asamm.

The second: whoever is in despair of something and considers its attainment unlikely, if it happens to him that this aim is achieved, he may sometimes become like one dazed from intense joy, and says: how did this happen, and from where did this come about? Like someone who sees a person give him great wealth and says: how did you give these riches, and from where did your soul permit giving them? Likewise here: since Zakariyya (peace be upon him) considered that unlikely, and then God's answer happened to him, he said that statement from the greatness of his joy and delight.

The third: when the angels gave him the good news of Yahya, he did not know whether he would be given a child from a female or from his own loins, so he made this statement because of that possibility.

The fourth: when a slave is in extreme longing for something and asks it from his master, and then the master promises him that he will give it to him afterward, the one asking takes pleasure in hearing that statement, and he may repeat the question so as to hear that answer again, and then he takes pleasure in hearing that answer once more. The cause of Zakariyya's repeating this statement may be of this kind.

The fifth: Sufyan ibn 'Uyayna reported that he said: his supplication had been sixty years before the good news, until he had forgotten that request at the time of the good news. So when he heard the good news in old age, he undoubtedly considered that unlikely according to the course of habit, not out of doubt about God's power, and so he said what he said.

The sixth: it is reported from al-Suddi that when Zakariyya (peace be upon him) heard the good news, Satan came to him and said: this voice is from Satan, and he has mocked you. So the matter became confused for Zakariyya (peace be upon him), and he said: ﴿My Lord, how can I have a son?﴾ His intention in this statement was that God would show him a sign indicating that this speech was revelation and from the angels, not from Satan's insinuation.

Page 35

Al-Qadi said: it is not permissible that the speech of the angels be confused with the speech of Satan during revelation to the prophets, peace and blessings be upon them, for if we allowed that, trust in all the laws would be lost. It may be said: since miracles established the truthfulness of revelation in everything related to religion, trust was therefore secured there, that revelation is from God exalted through the angels, and Satan has no part in it. As for what relates to the worldly interests and to a child, perhaps that miracle was not confirmed, so the possibility remained that it was from Satan; therefore he turned to God exalted to remove that possibility from his mind.

* * *

As for His saying exalted: ﴿and old age has already reached me﴾, there are several issues:

First issue: "kibar" (old age) is the verbal noun of "kabira al-rajul yakbaru," when a man grows old. Ibn 'Abbas said: on the day he was given the good news of a child he was one hundred and twenty years old, and his wife was ninety-eight years old.

Second issue: the people of the meanings (ahl al-ma'ani) said: whatever you encounter and reach, it has encountered you and reached you. Whatever may be said "I reached old age" may also be said "old age reached me." What indicates this is the saying of the Arabs: "I met the wall," and "the wall met me."

If it is said: may one say "the city reached me" in place of "I reached the city"? We say: this is not permissible. The difference between the two positions is that old age is like a thing seeking the person, so it comes to him by its occurrence in him, and the person also comes to it by the passing of years over him. As for the city, it is not like something seeking the person who goes; thus the difference is clear.

As for his saying: ﴿and my wife is barren﴾.

Know that "'aqir" among women is one who does not bear children. It is said: "'aqara yi'qiru 'aqran," and it is also said: "'aqara al-rajul" and "'aqura" with all three vowel forms on the qaf, when he has not had offspring; and "raml 'aqir" is sand that grows nothing. Know that Zakariyya (peace be upon him) mentioned his own old age together with his wife being barren in order to emphasize the state of unlikelihood.

As for his saying: ﴿He said: "So it is; God does what He wills."﴾ there are two discussions:

The first: his saying "He said" refers to a previously mentioned party, namely the Lord mentioned in His saying ﴿My Lord, how can I have a son?﴾ We have mentioned that this may be God exalted, and it may be Gabriel.

The second discussion: the author of al-Kashshaf said: ﴿Thus, God﴾ is a subject and predicate, meaning: in the manner of this attribute is God, and "yaf'alu ma yasha'" (He does what He wills) is an explanation of it, that is, He does what He intends of extraordinary acts that break the habit.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 3, verse 41:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿He said, "My Lord, appoint for me a sign." He said, "Your sign is that you will not speak to the people for three days except by gestures. And remember your Lord much and glorify Him in the evening and the morning."﴾

Know that Zakariyya, peace be upon him, out of his great joy at what he had been given good news of, and his certainty in the generosity of his Lord and His favour upon him, wished to have for himself

[Page 36]

a sign indicating that conception had taken place. This is because conception does not become apparent at the very beginning. So he said: ﴿My Lord, appoint for me a sign.﴾ Then God, exalted is He, said: ﴿Your sign is that you will not speak to the people for three days except by gestures.﴾ On this verse there are several issues.

The first issue: Here He mentioned three days, while in Surat Maryam He mentioned three nights. The combination of the two verses indicates that the sign was present during the three days together with their nights.

The second issue: The scholars have mentioned several interpretations of this verse.

The first: God restrained his tongue for three days, so that he could not speak to the people except by gestures. In this there are two benefits.

One of them: that this be a sign of the child's conception.

The second: that God restrained his tongue from worldly affairs and enabled him to remember, glorify and declare the oneness of God (tahlil), so that during that period he would be occupied with the remembrance of God, exalted is He, and with obedience and gratitude for that great blessing. On this reading, one thing becomes both a sign of the intended matter and an expression of gratitude for that blessing, so it combines all the aims.

Then know that this event contained a miracle in several respects.

The first: his ability to speak in glorification and remembrance, while being unable to speak about worldly matters, is among the greatest miracles.

The second: that this miraculous state occurred during those days of restricted speech while his body remained sound and his temperament balanced, is also among the miracles.

The third: that his report that when this state occurred the child had been conceived, and then the matter came out in accordance with this report, is also among the miracles.

The second interpretation, the view of Abu Muslim (al-Isfahani): the meaning is that when Zakariyya, peace be upon him, asked God for a sign indicating that conception had taken place, He said: "Your sign is that you will not speak." That is, you will be commanded not to speak to the creation for three days and nights. That is, you will be occupied with remembrance, glorification and the declaration of God's oneness, turning away from the creation and the world, thanking God, exalted is He, for granting such a gift. If you have any need, indicate it by gesture. When you are commanded to this obedience, know that the sought matter has been achieved. In my view this interpretation is good and reasonable, and Abu Muslim had fine expression in tafsir and frequently delved into subtleties and fine points.

The third interpretation: it is related from Qatada that he, peace be upon him, was punished by this because he asked for a sign after the good news from the angels, so his tongue was seized and made such that he could not speak.

* * *

As for His saying ﴿except by gestures﴾, there are two issues.

The first issue: The root of ramz is movement. It is said: "irtamaza" when he moved. From this the sea is called "al-Ramus." The scholars differed about the intended meaning of ramz here, in several views.

One of them: it is an expression for signalling in any form, by the hand, the head, the eyebrow, the eye, or the lip.

The second: it is an expression for moving the two lips with the words without uttering or voicing them. They said: understanding ramz in this sense is preferable, because signalling with the lips can be such that the movements of the two lips at the time of the gesture correspond to their movements when speaking, so that inferring the mental meanings from those movements is easier.

The third: he was able to speak in a quiet voice, but raising the voice in speech was forbidden to him.

If it is said: ramz is not of the same kind as speech, so how is it excepted from it?

We reply: when it fulfilled the purpose of speech, it was called speech. It is also permissible that this be a disjunctive exception (istithna' munqati', an exception not of the same category). But if we take ramz to mean quiet speech, the difficulty disappears.

The second issue: Yahya ibn Wathhab read ﴿ruMuzan﴾ with two dammas, the plural of ramuz, like rasul and rusul. It is also read ﴿ramazan﴾ with a fatha on the ra' and the mim, the plural of ramiz, like khadim and khadam. It is a circumstantial accusative (hal) referring to him and to the people. The meaning of ﴿except by gestures﴾ is except while exchanging gestures, as people speak with a mute person by signs and he speaks to them.

* * *

Then God, exalted is He, said: ﴿And remember your Lord much﴾. On this there are two views. One: God restrained his tongue from worldly affairs, "except by gestures." But as for remembrance and glorification, his tongue was sound, and this was among the manifest miracles. The second: the intended meaning is remembrance of the heart. This is because those immersed in the oceans of knowledge of God, exalted is He, are accustomed at first to persist in remembrance with the tongue for a period. When the heart is filled with the light of the remembrance of God, the tongue falls silent and the remembrance remains in the heart. For this reason they said: "Whoever knows God, his tongue is rendered speechless." So it is as if Zakariyya, peace be upon him, was commanded to be silent and to call up the meanings of remembrance and knowledge and to sustain them.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And glorify Him in the evening and the morning﴾. On this there are two issues.

The first issue: al-'ashiyy (the evening) is from the time the sun declines until it sets. The poet said:

Neither can the shade bear the chill of the forenoon, nor does the afternoon shade taste the chill of the evening.

The afternoon shade (fay') occurs only from the time the sun passes its zenith until its setting is complete. As for al-ibkar, it is the verbal noun of bakkara, yubakkiru, meaning to set out for a matter at the beginning of the day. Similar are bakara, ibtakara and bakkara, and from it comes al-bakurah, the first of the fruit. This is the original linguistic sense. Then what lies between the break of dawn and the forenoon was called ibkar, just as it was called isbah (morning). Some read ﴿wal-abkar﴾ with a fatha on the hamza, the plural of bakar, like sahar and asjar (sahar, pl. ashar). It is said: "atituhu bakaran," with two fathas.

The second issue: Regarding His saying ﴿wa-sabbih﴾ (and glorify), there are two views. One: the intended meaning is "and pray," because prayer is called tasbih. God, exalted is He, said: ﴿So glorify God when you enter the evening and when you enter the morning﴾. Also, prayer includes glorification, so it is permissible to call prayer tasbih. Here, the evidence indicates that this possibility is intended, and this is shown in two ways:

The first: if we took it to mean glorification and declaring God's oneness, there would be no distinction between this verse and what precedes it, namely His saying ﴿and remember your Lord﴾, and then the distinction would disappear, since it is not permissible to conjoin a thing to itself.

The second: this reading is strongly consistent with His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And establish the prayer at the two ends of the day﴾ (Hud 11:114).

The second view: His saying ﴿and remember your Lord﴾ is taken to mean remembrance with the tongue.

**The Third Story**

**His description of Mary's purity, may God's blessings be upon her**

﴿And when the angels said, "O Mary, indeed God has chosen you and purified you, and chosen you above the women of the worlds. O Mary, be devoutly obedient to your Lord, prostrate yourself, and bow with those who bow."﴾

His statement, glorified and exalted is He: ﴿And when the angels said, "O Mary, indeed God has chosen you and purified you, and chosen you above the women of the worlds. O Mary, be devoutly obedient to your Lord, prostrate yourself, and bow with those who bow."﴾ There are several issues concerning this verse:

**First issue:** The grammatical governor (*'amil al-i'rab*, the word that determines the case endings, or grammatical analysis, *i'rab*) of "*idh*" ("when") here is what we mentioned in His statement, ﴿When the wife of 'Imran said...﴾ [Al 'Imran: 35], from His statement, "All-Hearing, All-Knowing." Then "when the angels said" is joined to it by conjunction. It has also been said that its implied sense is: "Remember when the angels said."

**Second issue:** They said that by "the angels" here is meant Gabriel alone. This is like His statement, ﴿He sends down the angels with the Spirit by His command﴾ [al-Nahl: 2], meaning Gabriel. Although this is a departure from the apparent meaning, it must be adopted, because the Surah of Maryam indicates that the one who spoke with Mary, peace be upon her, was Gabriel, peace be upon him, as in His statement, ﴿So We sent to her Our Spirit, and it appeared to her as a man in full form﴾ [Maryam: 17].

**Third issue:** Know that Mary, peace be upon her, was not one of the prophets, because of His statement, ﴿We sent before you only men, to whom We revealed, from among the people of the cities﴾ [Yusuf: 109]. Given this, the sending of Gabriel, peace be upon him, to her was either a miracle (*karamah*) for her, which is the view of those who allow the miracles of the saints (*karamat al-awliya'*), or a foundation-miracle (*irhas*) for 'Isa (Jesus), peace be upon him, which is permissible according to us and according to al-Ka'bi of the Mu'tazilah, or a miracle for Zakariyya, peace be upon him, which is the view of the majority of the Mu'tazilah. Some people said that this was by way of a breathing into the heart (*naft fi al-ru'*), inspiration (*ilham*), and casting into the heart, as it was in the case of the mother of Musa, peace be upon him, in His statement, ﴿And We revealed to the mother of Musa﴾ [al-Qasas: 7].

**Fourth issue:** Know that what is mentioned in this verse, first, is the choosing (*istifa'*); second, the purifying; and third, the choosing above the women of the worlds. It is not permissible that the first choosing be part of the second choosing, since explicitly stating repetition is inappropriate. Therefore the first choosing must be understood as referring to the good matters that befell her in the early part of her life, and the second choosing as referring to what befell her in the latter part of her life.

**The first type of choosing** comprises several matters:

First: He, exalted, accepted her consecration (*tahrir*), although she was a female, and no such status had been granted to any other female.

Second: al-Hasan said: When her mother gave birth to her, she did not nourish her even for the blink of an eye, but rather placed her with Zakariyya, and her provision came to her from Paradise.

Third: He, exalted, freed her for His worship and singled her out in this respect with various kinds of gentleness (*lutf*), guidance, and protection (*'isma*).

Fourth: He sufficed her with the matter of her livelihood, so her provision came to her from God, exalted, as God said: ﴿"Where has this come to you?" She said, "It is from God."﴾

Fifth: He, exalted, made her hear the speech of the angels directly, face to face, which did not happen to any other female. This is what is meant by the first choosing.

As for the purifying, it has several aspects:

First: He, exalted, purified her from disbelief and disobedience, like His statement, exalted, concerning the wives of the Prophet ﷺ: ﴿and to purify you with a thorough purification﴾ [al-Ahzab: 33].

Second: He, exalted, purified her from being touched by men.

Third: He purified her from menstruation. They said: Mary did not menstruate.

Fourth: "And purified you" from blameworthy actions and vile customs.

Fifth: "And purified you" from the claims of the Jews, their accusation, and their lies.

As for the second choosing, it means that He, exalted, granted her 'Isa, peace be upon him, without a father, and made 'Isa speak at the moment of his separation from her, until he testified to what indicates her innocence from the accusation. He also made her and her son a sign for the worlds. This is what is meant by these three expressions.

**Fifth issue:** It is reported that he, peace and blessings be upon him, said: "Four are sufficient for you from among the women of the worlds: Mary, Asiya the wife of Pharaoh, Khadijah, and Fatimah, peace be upon them." It was said: This hadith indicates that these four are superior to other women, and this verse indicates that Mary, peace be upon her, is superior to all of them. As for the view of those who said that what is meant is that she was chosen above the worlds of her own time, this abandons the apparent meaning.

* * *

Then He, exalted, said: ﴿O Mary, be devoutly obedient to your Lord, prostrate yourself﴾. The meaning of *qunut* has already been explained in the Surah of al-Baqarah, in His statement: ﴿And stand before God in devout obedience﴾ [al-Baqarah: 238]. In summary, when He, exalted, made clear that she was specially favoured with greater bestowals and gifts from God, He made obligatory upon her greater acts of obedience, in gratitude for those noble blessings. There are questions concerning the verse:

**The first question:** Why was mention of prostration (*sujud*) placed before mention of bowing (*ruku'*)?

The answer has several aspects:

The first: the conjunction *wa* indicates joining, not sequence.

The second: the utmost nearness of the servant to God is to be prostrate. He, peace and blessings be upon him, said: "The closest a servant is to his Lord is when he prostrates." Since prostration is specific to this rank and excellence, it was rightly placed before the other acts of obedience.

Then He said: ﴿and bow with those who bow﴾. This is a reference to the command to pray. It is as if He, exalted, commanded her to persevere in prostration at most times, while prayer she would perform at its specified times.

The third: Ibn al-Anbari said: His statement, exalted, "*iqnuti*" (be devoutly obedient) is a command to worship in general. Then after that He said, "*wa-sjudi wa-rka'i*" (prostrate yourself and bow), meaning: use prostration at its fitting time, and use bowing at its fitting time. The intention is not that they be combined, with prostration then placed before bowing. And God knows best.

The fourth: Prayer is called prostration, as has been said in His statement: ﴿and during the times of prostration﴾ [Qaf: 40]. And in the hadith: "When one of you enters the mosque, let him prostrate twice." Also, the mosque (*masjid*) is named by a word derived from prostration (*sujud*), and what is meant by it is the place of prayer. Also, the most noble part of prayer is prostration, and naming a thing by the name of its most noble part is a well-known type of figurative usage (*majaz*).

Having established this, we say: His statement, "*Yā Maryam, iqnuti*," means: O Mary, stand. His statement, "*wa-sjudi*," means: pray. So what is meant by this prostration is prayer. Then He said: ﴿and bow with those who bow﴾. This may be a command to pray in congregation, so that "*wa-sjudi*" is a command to pray individually, and "*wa-rka'i ma'a al-raki'in*" is a command to pray in congregation. Or what is meant by bowing is humility, and "*wa-sjudi*" is an apparent command to pray, while "*wa-rka'i ma'a al-raki'in*" is a command to humility and lowliness of heart.

The fifth aspect of the answer: Perhaps prostration in that religion came before bowing.

**The second question:** What is meant by His statement, ﴿and bow with those who bow﴾?

The answer: It has been said that its meaning is: do as they do. It has also been said that what is meant is prayer in congregation. She was commanded to pray in Bayt al-Maqdis with those who lived there, even though she did not mix with them.

**The third question:** Why did He not say "*wa-rka'i ma'a al-raki'at*" (with the female worshippers who bow)?

The answer: Because following men while remaining hidden from men is better than following women.

Know that the commentators said: When the angels spoke these words to Mary, peace be upon her, face to face, Mary stood in prayer until her feet swelled and blood and pus flowed from her feet.

**Verse 3:44:** ﴿That is of the news of the unseen which We reveal to you. You were not with them when they cast their pens, [to see] which of them would take charge of Maryam, nor were you with them when they disputed.﴾ And in it are several issues:

**First issue:** "That" refers to what has preceded, and the meaning is that the account already mentioned of Hannah, Zakariyya, Yahya and 'Isa son of Maryam is of the news of the unseen. You could not know it except through revelation (wahy).

If it is asked: why was this witnessing negated, when its absence is known beyond any doubt, while the negation of hearing these things from those who memorized them, which is a mere supposition, was omitted?

We say: it was known to them with certain knowledge that he was not one who had heard or read, and they denied revelation. So only witnessing remained. Although it was extremely unlikely, it was negated sarcastically toward those who denied revelation, given that they knew he had neither heard nor read. Its parallels are ﴿You were not on the western side﴾ [al-Qasas: 44], ﴿nor were you on the side of the Mount﴾ [al-Qasas: 46], ﴿nor were you with them when they agreed on their plan﴾ [Yusuf: 102], and ﴿Neither you nor your people knew it before this﴾ [Hud: 49].

**Second issue:** *al-inba'* (informing) is informing about what is absent from you. As for *al-iya'* (revelation, wahy), the Book uses it in various meanings, which share the notion of making the one addressed aware of a hidden matter by a sign, writing or other means. By this definition, *al-ilham* (inspiration) is also called wahy, as in His saying: ﴿And your Lord inspired the bee﴾ [al-Nahl: 68]; He said of the devils that they inspire their allies; and He said: ﴿So He inspired them to glorify [Him] morning and evening﴾ [Maryam: 11]. Since God, glory be to Him, conveyed these matters to the Messenger ﷺ through Jibril (peace be upon him) in a manner hidden from others, He called it wahy.

* * *

As for His saying: ﴿when they cast their pens, [to see] which of them would take charge of Maryam﴾, there are several issues:

**First issue:** They mentioned several interpretations of those pens:

The first: the pens meant are those with which they used to write the Torah and the rest of God's books. The casting of lots was on the basis that whoever's pen moved against the direction of the flow of water, the truth was with him. When they did this, Zakariyya's pen moved in that way, so they submitted the matter to him. This is the view of most scholars.

The second: when they threw their staves into the flowing water, Zakariyya's staff moved against the direction of the water's flow and so prevailed over them. This is the view of al-Rabi'.

The third: Abu Muslim said: the meaning of "they cast their pens" is what nations used to do in *al-musahama* (drawing lots) when disputing. They would throw down objects on which they had written their names, and whoever's arrow came out was granted the matter. God, the Exalted, said: ﴿Then he cast lots and was among the losers﴾ [al-Saffat: 141]. This resembles the *qidah* arrows by which the Arabs divided the meat of a slaughtered camel. These arrows were called *aqlam* (pens) because they are trimmed (*tuqallam*) and shaved, and whatever you cut from something piece by piece, you have *qallamtahu*. For this reason, that with which one writes is called a *qalam* (pen).

Al-Qadi said: although applying the word *qalam* to these things is correct when considering the root derivation (*ishtiqaq*), custom (*'urf*) has made *qalam* specific to that with which one writes, so the word *qalam* must be understood in that sense.

**Second issue:** The apparent sense of the verse indicates that they used to cast their pens in a way by which one of them could be distinguished from another in entitlement to that claim. The verse does not state the manner of this casting. However, it is reported in a report that they would cast them into water on the condition that whoever's pen moved against the direction of the water, the guardianship belonged to him. This meaning was realized for Zakariyya (peace be upon him), so he was indeed more entitled to her guardianship. And God knows best.

**Third issue:** They differed about the reason why they desired her guardianship so strongly that this desire led them to dispute. Some said: her father 'Imran was their chief and leader, so because of the right of her father they desired her guardianship. Some said: her mother had dedicated her to the worship of God and the service of the House of God, and for this reason they eagerly sought to take charge of her. Others said: rather, because the divine books contained the explanation of her matter and the matter of 'Isa (peace be upon him), they sought nearness through this, to the point that they disputed.

**Fourth issue:** They differed about who those disputing people were. Some said they were the servants of the House, and some said they were the scholars, the rabbis and the scribes of revelation. There is no doubt that they were among the elite, people of excellence in religion and of eagerness in the path.

As for His saying ﴿[to see] which of them would take charge of Maryam﴾, there is an ellipsis, and the implied meaning is: "they cast their pens so that they might see which of them would take charge of Maryam." It was fine to omit this because it was understood.

As for His saying ﴿nor were you with them when they disputed﴾, the meaning is: "you were not there when they cast lots for her guardianship and when they disputed over her cause." It is possible that the dispute meant is what happened before the casting of lots, and it is possible that it is another dispute which occurred after the casting. In sum, the purpose of the verse is the intensity of their desire to take charge of her affairs and to attend to the improvement of her needs. This was due only to the supplication of her mother, when she said: ﴿So accept it from me; indeed You are the Hearing, the Knowing﴾ [Al 'Imran: 35], and she said: ﴿I seek refuge for her in You, and for her offspring, from Satan, the expelled﴾ [Al 'Imran: 36].

[Page 42]

His saying, glorified and exalted is He: ﴿When the angels said, "O Mary, indeed Allah gives you good tidings of a word from Him, whose name is the Messiah, Jesus, son of Mary, distinguished in this world and the Hereafter and among those brought near."﴾ ﴿"And he will speak to the people in the cradle and in maturity, and he will be among the righteous."﴾

Know that when He, exalted is He, had explained the condition of Mary, peace be upon her, at the beginning and at the end of her affair, and explained the manner of her giving birth to Jesus, peace be upon him, He said: ﴿When the angels said﴾. In this there are two issues.

The first issue: They differed about what governs "idh" (when). It was said: what governs it is "And you were not with them when the angels said" (3:44). It was also said: it is "they were disputing when the angels said." It was said: it is connected to the first "idh" in His saying: ﴿When the wife of 'Imran said﴾ (3:35). It was also said that the meaning is: what I have described of the affairs of Zakariyya and Allah's granting him Yahya was at the time when the angels said, "O Mary, indeed Allah gives you good tidings." As for Abu 'Ubayda, he takes this in his well-known school of thought, which is that "idh" here is a filler and an addition in speech. Know that the first two opinions have some weakness, because when they were casting their pens and when they were disputing, Mary had not reached the stage at which she would be given good tidings of Jesus, peace be upon him. The exception is the saying of al-Hasan, for he says that she was intelligent in her childhood, and that this was among her miracles. If that is correct, then it is possible in that state for the good tidings from the angels to come to her. Otherwise, the good tidings must have been delayed until the time of her reaching maturity. Some of them undertook to answer, saying: It is possible to say that the disputing and the good tidings occurred over a long span of time, just as you say, "I met him in such-and-such a year." This answer is far-fetched. The most correct is the third and fourth opinion. As for Abu 'Ubayda's saying, you already know its weakness. And Allah knows best.

The second issue: The apparent meaning of His saying ﴿When the angels said﴾ indicates plurality, but the well-known view is that this caller was Jibril (ﷺ), and we have established this earlier. As for the good tidings, we have explained its meaning in Surat al-Baqara in His saying: ﴿And give good tidings to those who believe and do righteous deeds﴾ (2:25).

* * *

As for His saying, exalted is He: ﴿a word from Him﴾, we have explained the meaning of "word" in several ways, and the most fitting of them for this place are two:

The first: Every conception, even though it is created through the word, which is His saying "Be!" (kun), nevertheless the usual cause was absent in the case of Jesus, peace be upon him, namely the father. Therefore, attributing his coming into being to the word was more complete and perfect. Thus, by this interpretation, he was made as if he were the very word, just as one who is overwhelmed by generosity, magnanimity, and kindness is described, in hyperbole, as being pure generosity, unmixed magnanimity, and clear kindness. So it is likewise here.

The second: A just ruler may be described as "the shadow of Allah on His earth," and as "the light of Allah," because he is the cause of the manifestation of the shadow of justice and the light of benevolence. Likewise, Jesus, peace be upon him, was a cause of the manifestation of the speech of Allah, mighty and majestic, through the abundance of his clarifications and the removal of doubts and distortions concerning it. So it is not far-fetched that he be called "the word of Allah, exalted is He," according to this interpretation.

If it is said: Why do you say that the coming into being of a person without the father's sperm is possible? We reply: As for the principles of the Muslims, the matter in this is clear, and two proofs indicate it:

The first: The composition of bodies and their assembly in a manner by which life, understanding, and speech come about in them is a possible matter. It has been established that He, exalted is He, is capable of all possible things. And He, glorified and exalted is He, was capable of bringing about a person not from the father's sperm. And when possibility is established, then, since the miracle has attested to the truthfulness of the Prophet, it is obligatory that he be truthful. Then he reported the occurrence of that possible thing, and when a truthful one reports the occurrence of a possible thing, it is necessary to be certain that it is so. Thus the soundness of what we have mentioned is established.

The second: What Allah, exalted is He, mentioned in His saying: ﴿Indeed, the likeness of Jesus with Allah is like the likeness of Adam﴾ (3:59). Since the creation of Adam without a father was not far-fetched, then the creation of Jesus without a father is even more fitting not to be far-fetched. This is a clear argument.

As for the principles of the philosophers, the matter of allowing it is also clear, and several things indicate it:

The first: The philosophers agreed that it is not impossible for a human to come into being by way of reproduction without generation. They said: The human body was only prepared to receive the rational soul, which is governed through the presence of a specific temperament in that body. That temperament was only made for the mixing of the four elements in a fixed measure within a fixed period. So the obtaining of the parts of the elements in that measure which suits the human body is not impossible, and their mixing is not impossible. Therefore, their mixing is necessary when the temperamental quality comes into being, and when the temperamental quality comes into being, the attachment of the soul to that body is necessary. Thus it is established that the coming into being of a human by way of generation is intelligible and possible. And if this is the case, then the coming into being of a human not from a father is even more deserving of being possible.

The second: We observe the coming into being of many animals by way of spontaneous generation, such as the generation of mice from clods of earth, of snakes from hair, and of scorpions from bādharūj (a substance once believed to produce scorpions). If this is so, then the generation of a child not from a father is even more deserving of not being impossible.

The third: Mental imaginings often become causes for the occurrence of many events. Does not the imagining of an opposite produce the state of anger, and produce intense heat in the body? Is it not the case that a long plank laid on the ground can be walked upon by a person, but if it is placed like a bridge over a pit, the person cannot walk on it? Rather, whenever he walks on it he falls, and this is nothing but because the imagining of falling brings about the falling. The philosophers have mentioned many examples of this kind, and they made them like the basis for explaining the possibility of miracles and marvels (karamat). So what prevents one from saying that when his image (peace be upon him) was imagined, that was enough for the child to be conceived in her womb? And when all these aspects are possible and admissible, the claim that Jesus, peace be upon him, came into being without a father's intermediary is not an impossible claim.

And if you were to ask all the first and last of the masters of natures, medicine, and philosophy to establish a persuasive proof that the coming into being of a child without a father is impossible, they would not find a way to it except by returning to the inductive study of common custom and habit. The scholars of the philosophers have agreed that such induction does not yield strong conjecture, let alone certain knowledge. So we know that this matter is possible. And when the servants were informed of its occurrence, it became obligatory to affirm it firmly and to be certain of its truth.

As for His saying, exalted is He: ﴿a word from Him﴾, the particle "min" (from) here is not partitive, for if it were, Allah, exalted is He, would be divisible, subdividable, capable of aggregation and separation. And whoever is like that is originated, and Allah is exalted above that. Rather, what is meant by "min" here is the beginning of the end (ibtida' al-ghaya). That is because, in the case of Jesus, peace be upon him, since the intermediary of the father was not present, the effect of the word of Allah, exalted is He, in his formation and creation became more complete and more evident. So his being the "word of Allah" became the source of his manifestation and his coming into being in a more complete way. Thus the meaning is in accordance with what we have mentioned, not what the Christians and the Incarnationists (hulooliyya, those who believe in divine indwelling) imagine.

* * *

As for His saying, exalted is He: ﴿whose name is the Messiah, Jesus, son of Mary﴾, there are questions concerning it:

First question: Is "al-Masih" (the Messiah) a derived name or a established name?

The answer: There are two opinions:

The first: Abu 'Ubayda and al-Layth said: Its origin in Hebrew is mashih, and the Arabs arabized it and changed its form. As for "'Isa," its origin is Yashu', just as they said for "Musa" that its origin is Mushā or Mīshā in Hebrew. According to this view, it has no derivation.

[Page 44]

The second opinion: It is derived, and this is the view of most scholars. Then they mentioned several interpretations of it:

The first: Ibn 'Abbas said: Jesus, peace be upon him, was called "masih" only because he would not pass his hand over anyone afflicted with a disease without that person being cured of his illness.

The second: Ahmad ibn Yahya said: He was called "masih" because he would traverse the earth (yamsahu al-ard), that is, cross it, and from this comes "misaha" (the measuring) of the parts of the land. According to this meaning, it is permissible to say that Jesus is "massih" with a doubled letter, as an intensive form, just as one says "fassiq" (very wicked) and "sharrib" (great drinker) of a man.

The third: That he was "masih" because he would wipe (yamsah) the heads of orphans for the sake of Allah, exalted is He. According to these sayings, the form is fa'il in the sense of fa'il (active), like rahim in the sense of rahim (merciful).

The fourth: That he was wiped clean (musih) of sins and transgressions.

The fifth: He was called "masih" because there was no flatness (khamas) in his foot, so he was smooth-footed (mamsuh al-qadamayn).

The sixth: He was called "masih" because he was anointed with a pure and blessed oil with which prophets are anointed, and with which no one else is anointed. Then they said: This oil may be a sign that Allah, exalted is He, made, so that the angels would know that whoever is anointed with it at the time of birth would be a prophet.

The seventh: He was called "masih" because Jibril (ﷺ) wiped him with his wing at the time of his birth, so that this would protect him from the touch of Satan.

The eighth: He was called "masih" because he came out of his mother's womb anointed with oil.

According to these sayings, "al-Masih" means "the one who is wiped" (al-mamsuh), the form being fa'il in the sense of maf'ul (passive). Abu 'Amr ibn al-'Ala' said: "al-Masih" means "the angel." And al-Nakha'i said: "al-Masih" means "the truthful one (al-siddiq)." And Allah knows best. Perhaps these two said that from the standpoint that it is praise, not because the language indicates it.

As for "al-Masih al-Dajjal" (the false Messiah), he was called "masih" for one of two reasons:

One of them: Because one of his eyes is wiped (blind).

The second: Because he traverses (yamsah) the earth, that is, crosses it in a short period. They said: For this reason he is called "dajjal," because of his roaming (darb) in the earth and his crossing most of its regions. It is said: "qad dajala al-dajjal" (the deceiver has deceived) when he does that. It was also said: He was called "dajjal" from the saying "dajjala al-rajul," when a man covers over and mixes up (things).

Second question: "al-Masih" was like a title for him, and "Isa" like a name. Why was the title placed before the name?

The answer: "Al-Masih" is like a title that indicates he is noble and of high rank, like "al-Siddiq" (the Truthful) and "al-Faruq" (the Discriminator). So Allah, exalted is He, mentioned him first by his title, to indicate the loftiness of his rank, and then mentioned him by his specific name.

Third question: Why did He say "Jesus, son of Mary," while the address was to Mary?

The answer: Because the prophets are attributed to their fathers, not to their mothers. So when Allah, exalted is He, attributed him to the mother and not to the father, this was an announcement to her that he had been brought into being without a father. Thus this was a cause of increasing his excellence and the loftiness of his rank.

Fourth question: The pronoun in His saying "whose name" refers to "word," which is feminine. Why is the pronoun masculine?

The answer: Because the one named by it is masculine.

Fifth question: Why did He say "whose name is the Messiah, Jesus, son of Mary," when the name is only "Isa," "al-Masih" is a title, and "son of Mary" is a descriptive attribute?

The answer: The name is a sign of the named and identifies it. So it is as if it were said: What he is identified by is the totality of these three.

* * *

As for His saying, exalted is He: ﴿distinguished in this world and the Hereafter﴾, there are two issues in it:

First issue: The meaning of "wajih" (distinguished) is one who possesses standing, nobility, and rank. It is said: "wajuha al-rajul, yawjuhu, wajaha," so he is "wajih," when he attains an elevated position among people and the ruler. Some of the lexicographers said: "wajih" means noble, because the most noble part of a human being is his face, so "face" was used metaphorically for nobility and perfection.

Know that Allah, exalted is He, described Moses (ﷺ) as being "wajih," as Allah, exalted is He, said: ﴿O you who believe, do not be like those who harmed Moses, but Allah cleared him of what they said, and he was distinguished in the sight of Allah﴾ (33:69). Then there are sayings of the exegetes:

The first view: al-Hasan said: he was a dignitary (wajih) in this world by virtue of prophethood, and in the Hereafter by virtue of his high standing with God, exalted be He.

The second view: he is a dignitary with God, exalted be He. As for Jesus, peace be upon him, he is a dignitary in this world because his supplication is answered, and he gives life to the dead and cures the blind man born blind and the leper by his supplication; and he is a dignitary in the Hereafter because God will make him an intercessor for the righteous members of his community, and will accept his intercession on their behalf, just as He accepts the intercession of the greatest of the prophets, peace be upon them.

The third view: God made him a dignitary in this world because he was free from the defects with which the Jews described him, and he is a dignitary in the Hereafter by virtue of the abundance of his reward and the loftiness of his rank with God, exalted be He.

If it is asked: how was he a dignitary in this world when the Jews treated him as they did? We say: we have mentioned that God called Moses, peace be upon him, "wajih" (dignitary), although the Jews slandered him and harmed him until God cleared him of what they said. That did not detract from Moses' dignity, peace be upon him, and so it is here.

Second issue: al-Zajjaj said: "wajihan" (dignitary) is in the accusative as a circumstantial qualifier (hal). The meaning: God gives you good news of this son as a dignitary in this world and the Hereafter. Al-Farra' calls this qat' (a shift from the definite form), as if he had said: "Isa son of Maryam the dignitary," and the definite article was dropped from it.

As for His words: ﴿And of those brought near﴾ [Al 'Imran: 45], there are several interpretations:

First: God made this like a great praise for the angels, so He joined him to their station and rank through this attribute.

Second: this description is an indication that he, peace be upon him, will be raised up to heaven and accompanied by the angels.

Third: not every dignitary in the Hereafter is necessarily among those brought near, because the people of Paradise are of different stations and ranks. For this reason God, exalted be He, said: ﴿And you will be three kinds﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 7], up to His words: ﴿And the foremost, the foremost. Those are the ones brought near﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 10–11].

[Page 46]

As for His saying, ﴿And he will speak to the people in the cradle and in maturity﴾, there are several issues.

**First issue:** The conjunction "wa" (and) is coordinating with His saying "distinguished" (wajihan). The sense is as if He had said: "distinguished and speaking to the people." In my view this is weak, because coordinating a verbal sentence (al-jumla al-fi'liyya) with a nominal sentence (al-jumla al-ismiyya) is not permitted except out of necessity or for a benefit. The better view is that the meaning of the verse is: ﴿Indeed, Allah gives you good news of a word from Him, whose name is the Messiah, Jesus son of Mary﴾ [Ali 'Imran: 45], "distinguished in this world and the Hereafter and counted among those brought near." This whole phrase is a single sentence. Then He said: ﴿and he will speak to the people﴾, so His saying ﴿and he will speak to the people﴾ is coordinated with His saying ﴿Indeed, Allah gives you good news﴾.

**Second issue:** Regarding "in the cradle" (al-mahd), there are two views:

One: it is the lap of his mother.

Two: it is the well-known object, the bed where the infant lies during nursing.

Whichever is meant, the point is that he speaks to the people in the state in which the infant needs a cradle. This meaning does not change whether he is in his mother's lap or in a cradle.

**Third issue:** His saying "and in maturity" (wa kahlan) is coordinated with the adverbial phrase in His saying "in the cradle." It is as if it were said: "He will speak to the people as an infant and in maturity." Here there are questions:

**First question:** What is al-kahl (the man in maturity)?

Answer: In the language, al-kahl is one whose strength has gathered and whose youth is complete. It is derived from the saying of the Arabs, "the plant reached its kahal (maturity)," when it became strong and complete. Al-A'sha said:

*It laughs at the sun through it, a bright star,*
*Wrapped in a cloak of thick plant growth, mature.*

By "mature" (al-muktahil) he meant one who is perfect in beauty and completeness.

**Second question:** His speaking while in the cradle is one of the miracles, but his speaking in maturity is not a miracle. So what is the benefit of mentioning it?

The answer has several aspects:

First: The purpose is to show that he passes through states, from childhood to maturity, and change is impossible for God, the Exalted. The purpose is also to refute the delegation of Najran in their claim that Jesus was a god.

Second: The purpose is that he speaks to the people only once, in the cradle, to show the purity of his mother, and then in maturity he speaks by revelation and prophethood.

Third: Abu Muslim said: its meaning is that he speaks while in the cradle and while mature, in one manner and one attribute, and there is no doubt that this is the utmost in being a miracle.

Fourth: al-Asamm said: the purpose is that he reaches the state of maturity.

**Third question:** It is reported that the age of 'Isa (peace be upon him) until he was raised was thirty-three years and six months, and according to this he did not reach maturity.

The answer has two aspects:

First: We have explained that al-kahl in the original language refers to the complete and perfect one, and the most perfect state of a person is when he is between thirty and forty. So it is correct to describe him as kahl at this time.

Second: This is the view of al-Husayn ibn al-Fadl al-Bajali: the meaning of His saying "and in maturity" is that he will be mature after he descends from the heaven at the end of time, speaks to the people, and kills the Dajjal (the Antichrist). Al-Husayn ibn al-Fadl said: in this verse there is a clear text that he (peace be upon him) will descend to the earth.

**Fourth issue:** The Christians denied the speech of the Messiah (peace be upon him) in the cradle, and they argued for the soundness of their view by saying that his speech in the cradle is among the most astonishing and strange of matters. There is no doubt that if this event had occurred, it would have been necessary for it to take place in the presence of a great multitude, which would produce certainty and conviction in their report, because restricting such a miracle to one or two people is not permissible. When an extraordinarily strange event occurs in the presence of a great multitude, the motives to transmit it must be strong, so it becomes reported by mass transmission (tawatur). Concealing what has reached the level of tawatur is impossible. Moreover, if it had occurred, concealment would be impossible here, because the Christians went to extremes in their love for him, to the point that they said he was a god, and one who is like this cannot be expected to strive to hide his virtues and merits, but rather he may make one into a thousand. Thus it is established that if this event had existed, the people most likely to know it would be the Christians. When they unanimously denied it, we know that it never existed at all.

The theologians (al-mutakallimun) answered this doubt and said: the speech of 'Isa (peace be upon him) in the cradle was only to show the innocence of Maryam (peace be upon her) from immorality. The people present were few, so the listeners to that speech were a small group, and in such a case it is not unlikely that they agreed together to conceal it. Even if they had mentioned it, the Jews used to deny it to them and attribute to them slander. They also kept silent for this reason. For these reasons the matter remained hidden and concealed until Allah, glorified and exalted, informed Muhammad (ﷺ) of it. Moreover, not all Christians deny it. It is reported from Ja'far ibn Abi Talib that when he recited to al-Najashi the chapter of Maryam, al-Najashi said: "There is not the slightest difference between the event of 'Isa and what is mentioned in this speech."

* * *

Then He, exalted, said: ﴿and among the righteous﴾.

If it is said: That 'Isa is a word from Allah, that he is ﴿distinguished in this world and the Hereafter﴾, that he is among those brought near to Allah, and that he speaks to the people in the cradle and in maturity, each of these attributes is greater and more noble than being righteous. So why did Allah end the attributes of 'Isa with His saying ﴿and among the righteous﴾?

We say: There is no rank greater than a person being righteous, because one is not righteous except that he is constant in all his actions and abstentions, adhering to the most upright path and the most perfect way. It is known that this includes all stations in this world and in religion, in the actions of the heart and in the actions of the limbs. So when Allah mentioned some of the details, He followed them with this statement, which indicates the highest of ranks.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 3, verse 47–48:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿She said, "My Lord, how can I have a child when no man has touched me?" He said, "Thus Allah creates what He wills. When He decrees a matter, He only says to it, 'Be,' and it is."﴾ ﴿And He will teach him the Book and wisdom and the Torah and the Gospel.﴾

The exegetes said: She only said that because the giving of glad tidings of him entails wonder at what occurs contrary to custom. We have established something similar in the story of Zakariyya, peace be upon him. As for His saying, ﴿When He decrees a matter, He only says to it, "Be," and it is,﴾ its explanation has already passed in Surat al-Baqarah.

As for His saying, exalted is He, ﴿And He will teach him the Book and wisdom and the Torah and the Gospel,﴾ there are two issues concerning it:

The first issue: Nafi' and 'Asim read "wayu'allimuhu" (and He will teach him) with the letter ya', while the rest read it with nun. As for the ya', it is coordinated with His saying, "what He wills." Al-Mubarrad said: it is coordinated with "yubashshiruki" (He gives you glad tidings) in the phrase "with a word from Him," and so on, "and He will teach him the Book." As for the one who reads with nun, he says the sense of the verse is that she said, "My Lord, how can I have a child?" and Allah said to her, "Thus Allah creates what He wills. When He decrees a matter, He only says to it, 'Be,' and it is." So this, although it is a report in the third person, says "wanu'allimuhu" (and We will teach him), because the meaning of His saying, "Thus Allah creates what He wills," is: thus We create what We will, "and We will teach him the Book and wisdom." And Allah knows best.

The second issue: In this verse there are four matters, some coordinated with others by the conjunction waw. The closest to me is that it may be said: what is meant by "the Book" is teaching writing and penmanship. Then what is meant by "wisdom" is teaching the sciences and refining the character, because human perfection lies in knowing the truth for its own sake and the good for the sake of acting upon it, and the combination of both is what is called wisdom. Then, after he has become knowledgeable in writing and penmanship, and encompassing the rational and legal sciences, "He will teach him the Torah." The teaching of the Torah has been placed after the teaching of writing and wisdom because the Torah is a divine book, and in it are great secrets, and a person who has not learned many sciences cannot delve into investigating the secrets of the divine books. Then in the fourth rank He said, "and the Gospel." The mention of the Gospel has been placed after the mention of the Torah because whoever learns writing, then learns the sciences of truth, then comprehends the secrets of the Book that Allah, exalted is He, sent down to those prophets before him, his rank in knowledge has become great. When Allah, exalted is He, then sends down to him another book after that and makes him aware of its secrets, that is the ultimate goal and the highest rank in knowledge and understanding and comprehension of the rational and legal secrets, and awareness of the sublime and lowly wisdoms. This is what I have in mind regarding the ordering of these four words.
