Then what is meant by "wisdom" is teaching the sciences and refining the character, because human perfection lies in knowing the truth for its own sake and the good for the sake of acting upon it, and the combination of both is what is called wisdom. Then, after he has become knowledgeable in writing and penmanship, and encompassing the rational and legal sciences, "He will teach him the Torah." The teaching of the Torah has been placed after the teaching of writing and wisdom because the Torah is a divine book, and in it are great secrets, and a person who has not learned many sciences cannot delve into investigating the secrets of the divine books. Then in the fourth rank He said, "and the Gospel." The mention of the Gospel has been placed after the mention of the Torah because whoever learns writing, then learns the sciences of truth, then comprehends the secrets of the Book that Allah, exalted is He, sent down to those prophets before him, his rank in knowledge has become great. When Allah, exalted is He, then sends down to him another book after that and makes him aware of its secrets, that is the ultimate goal and the highest rank in knowledge and understanding and comprehension of the rational and legal secrets, and awareness of the sublime and lowly wisdoms. This is what I have in mind regarding the ordering of these four words.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 3, verse 49:

Then He, exalted is He, said: ﴿And a messenger to the Children of Israel, [saying]: "Indeed, I have come to you with a sign from your Lord."﴾ Concerning this there are several issues:

The first issue: regarding this verse there are several views.

The first: the sense of the verse is: "And We teach him the Book, the wisdom, the Torah and the Gospel, and We send him as a messenger to the Children of Israel, saying: 'Indeed, I have come to you with a sign from your Lord.'" Omission is good when it does not lead to confusion.

The second: al-Zajjaj said: "My preference is that its implied meaning is: 'and he speaks to the people as a messenger,' and we supplied this because of His saying: ﴿Indeed, I have come to you﴾. The meaning is: 'and he speaks to them as a messenger, [saying] that I have come to you.'"

The third: al-Akhfash said: "If you wish, you may take the waw (and) as extra, and the sense is: 'And He teaches him the Book, the wisdom, the Torah and the Gospel, [and makes him] a messenger to the Children of Israel, saying: Indeed I have come to you with a sign.'"

The second issue: this verse indicates that he (ﷺ) was a messenger to all the Children of Israel, contrary to the view of some Jews that he was sent only to a particular group among them.

The third issue: the meaning of "a sign" here is the category, not the single instance, because He, exalted is He, enumerated here several kinds of signs: raising the dead, healing the blind and the leper, and informing about unseen matters. Therefore what is meant by His saying ﴿I have come to you with a sign from your Lord﴾ is the category, not a single instance.

* * *

Then He said: ﴿Indeed, I shall create for you from clay [the form] of a bird; then I shall breathe into it, and it will be a bird by the permission of Allah﴾.

Know that He, exalted is He, here relates five kinds of the miracles (mu'jizat) of 'Isa (peace be upon him):

The first kind

This is what He mentioned here in this verse, and concerning it there are several issues:

The first issue: Hamzah recited ﴿Anni﴾ with a fatha on the hamzah, while Nafi' recited it with a kasra. Whoever reads it with a fatha has made it a substitute (badal)

[p. 49]

for "sign," as if he had said: "and I have come to you with [the sign] that I create for you from clay." As for whoever reads it with a kasra, he has two possibilities:

One of them: the istinaf (resumption), cutting off the speech from what precedes it.

The second: that he explains the sign by His saying: ﴿that I create for you﴾. It is also permissible to explain the preceding clause by what is in the form of a fresh beginning. Allah, exalted is He, said: ﴿Allah has promised those who believe and do righteous deeds﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 9], then explained what was promised by His saying: ﴿for them is forgiveness﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 9]. And He said: ﴿Indeed, the likeness of 'Isa with Allah is like the likeness of Adam﴾ [Al 'Imran: 59], then explained the likeness by His saying: ﴿He created him from dust﴾ [Al 'Imran: 59]. This second view is better, because in meaning it is like the reading of the one who read ﴿Anni﴾ with a fatha, by making it a substitute for "sign."

The second issue: ﴿I create for you from clay﴾ means: I shape and form. We have already explained, in the commentary on His saying, exalted is He: ﴿O mankind, worship your Lord who created you﴾ [al-Baqarah: 21], that creation (khalq) is measuring/determining. There is no harm in mentioning it here too, so we say: what the Qur'an, poetry and lexical usage indicate is as follows. As for the Qur'an, there are verses:

One of them: His saying, exalted is He: ﴿So blessed is Allah, the best of creators﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 14], meaning the best of those who determine. This is because it is established that a servant is not a creator in the sense of bringing into existence and originating, so it is necessary to interpret his being a creator as determining and arranging.

The second: the word khalq is applied to lying. He, exalted is He, said in Surat ash-Shu'ara': ﴿This is nothing but the fabrication (khuluq) of the former peoples﴾ [ash-Shu'ara': 137]; in al-'Ankabut: ﴿and you fabricate (takhluqun) a falsehood﴾ [al-'Ankabut: 17]; and in Surat Sad: ﴿This is nothing but a fabrication (ikhtilaq)﴾ [Sad: 7]. The liar is called a creator only because he determines the lie in his mind and forms it.

The third: this verse we are commenting on, namely His saying: ﴿Indeed, I create for you from clay﴾, i.e., I form and determine. And He, exalted is He, said in al-Ma'idah: ﴿and when you create from clay [the form] of a bird﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 110]. All of this indicates that creation is forming and determining.

The fourth: His saying, exalted is He: ﴿It is He who created for you all that is on the earth﴾ [al-Baqarah: 29]. The word "created" (khalaqa) refers to the past. If we take His saying "created" to mean bringing into existence and originating, the meaning would be that everything on earth was brought into existence by Him in the past, and that is false by consensus. Therefore it is necessary to interpret creation as determining, so that the statement is sound, namely that He determined in the past everything that now exists on earth.

As for poetry, there is the verse:

"Indeed you cut what you have fashioned (khalaqta), and some people fashion and do not cut."

And the verse:

"Nor does he give to the hands of the creator (al-khaliq), nor to the hands of the fabricators (al-khawaliq), except the finest of hides."

As for lexical usage: it is said "khalaqa the sandal" when he measured and shaped it by standard measure. Al-khallaq means the measure of good. And "fulan is khalaq (fit) for such-and-such," i.e., he has this measure of deserving. And "al-sakhrah al-khalqa'" means the smooth rock, because smoothness is evenness, whereas roughness involves irregularity. Thus it is established that khalq is an expression for determining and arranging.

Having known this, we say: the people differed over the word "creator" (khaliq). Abu 'Abdullah al-Basri said: it is not permissible to apply it to Allah in the literal sense, because determining and arranging are an expression for supposition and reckoning, and that is impossible for Allah. Our companions said: the Creator is none other than Allah, and they argued for it with His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Allah is the Creator of everything﴾ [ar-Ra'd: 16]. Some of them argued with His saying: ﴿Is there any creator other than Allah who provides for you from the sky?﴾ [Fatir: 3]. This is weak, because He, exalted is He, said: ﴿Is there any creator other than Allah who provides for you from the sky?﴾ [Fatir: 3]. So the meaning is: "Is there any creator other than Allah described by the attribute of being a provider from the sky?" And it does not follow from the truth of our statement "the Creator is the one whose state is this, and none but Allah is such" that the truth of our statement "there is no creator except Allah" is established.

[p. 50]

They answered Abu 'Abdullah's statement by saying that determining and arranging are an expression for knowledge and opinion, but although opinion is impossible with respect to Allah, knowledge is established.

Having known this, we say: ﴿Indeed, I create for you from clay﴾ means: I form and determine. As for His saying ﴿[the form] of a bird﴾, the hay'ah (form) is the shaped image, from the expression "I prepared (hayya'tu) the thing," when you determined it. As for His saying ﴿then I breathe into it﴾, it means into that shaped clay.

* * *

As for His saying ﴿then it will be a bird by the permission of Allah﴾, concerning it there are several issues:

The first issue: Nafi' recited ﴿fa-yakunu ta'iran﴾ with an alif, as a singular, while the rest recited ﴿tayran﴾ as a plural. The same is in al-Ma'idah. The word tayr is a collective noun which applies to the singular and to the plural.

It is related that when 'Isa (peace be upon him) claimed prophethood and displayed miracles, they began to challenge him and demanded that he create a bat. So he took clay and shaped it, then breathed into it, and behold, it was flying between heaven and earth. Wahb said: it kept flying as long as the people were looking at it, and when it disappeared from their eyes it fell dead. Then the people differed: some said he had created only a bat, and this was the recitation of Nafi'. Others said he created various kinds of birds, and this was the recitation of the rest.

The second issue: some of the theologians (mutakallimun) said: the verse indicates that the spirit (ruh) is a subtle body like wind, and for this reason it is described as being blown. Here there is a discussion: is it permissible to say that Allah placed in the very self of 'Isa (peace be upon him) a special property, such that whenever he breathed into a thing, his breathing into it would necessarily cause that thing to become living? Or is it said: the matter is not like that, but rather Allah, by His power, used to create life in that body at the moment of the breath of 'Isa (peace be upon him) into it, as a manifestation of miracles? This second is the truth, because of His saying, exalted is He: ﴿He who created death and life﴾ [al-Mulk: 2]. And it is related of Ibrahim (peace be upon him) that in his debate with the king he said: ﴿My Lord is He who gives life and causes death﴾ [al-Baqarah: 258]. If this attribute were to occur to another, that argument would be invalid.

* * *

The third issue: the Qur'an indicates that he (peace be upon him) came into being only from the breath of Jibril (peace be upon him) into Maryam, and Jibril (ﷺ) is a pure spirit and purely spiritual; therefore the breath of 'Isa (peace be upon him) was necessarily for life and spirit.

The fourth issue: His saying ﴿by the permission of Allah﴾ means by the bringing into being and creation of Allah, exalted is He, in accordance with His saying: ﴿And it is not for any soul to die except by the permission of Allah﴾ [Al 'Imran: 145], i.e., except that Allah brings death into existence. 'Isa (peace be upon him) mentioned this qualification only to remove doubt, and to alert that I perform this shaping, but as for the creation of life, it is from Allah, exalted is He, as a manifestation of miracles through the hands of the messengers.

* * *

As for the second, third and fourth kinds of the miracles:

﴿And I heal the blind and the leper, and I bring the dead to life by the permission of Allah﴾

This is His saying: ﴿And I heal the blind and the leper, and I bring the dead to life by the permission of Allah﴾.

[p. 51]

Most of the lexicographers held that al-akmah is the one born blind. Al-Khalil and others said it is the one who became blind after having been sighted. From Mujahid: it is the one who cannot see at night. It is said that there was no akmah in this community other than Qatadah ibn Di'amah al-Sadusi, the author of the tafsir. It is related that (peace be upon him) would sometimes have fifty thousand patients gathered around him; whoever was able came to him, and whoever was not able, 'Isa (peace be upon him) came to. His treatment was only by supplication alone. Al-Kalbi said: 'Isa (peace be upon him) used to bring the dead to life by saying: "O Living, O Self-Subsisting (ya Hayy ya Qayyum)."

He brought 'Azar to life, who had been his friend, and he called Sam ibn Nuh from his grave, and he came out alive. He passed by the dead son of an old woman, and he supplicated Allah, and the boy got down from his bier alive, returned to his family, and had children. His saying ﴿by the permission of Allah﴾ is a refutation of anyone who believed him to be divine.

* * *

As for the fifth kind:

﴿And I inform you of what you eat and what you store in your houses﴾

Among the miracles is his informing about unseen matters, and this is His saying, exalted is He, relating from him: ﴿And I inform you of what you eat and what you store in your houses﴾. Concerning it there are two issues:

The first issue: concerning this verse there are two views. One of them: that he (peace be upon him) informed about unseen matters from the very first time. Al-Suddi related: he used to play with the children, then he would tell them about the deeds of their fathers and mothers. He would tell a child: "Your mother has hidden such-and-such for you," and the child would return to his family and weep until he got that thing. Then they said to their children: "Do not play with this sorcerer." They gathered them into a house. 'Isa (peace be upon him) came seeking them, and they said to him: "They are not in the house." He said: "Who is in this house?" They said: "Pigs." 'Isa (peace be upon him) said: "Thus they shall be," and behold, they were pigs.

The second view: the informing about unseen matters appeared only at the time of the revelation of the table (al-Ma'idah), because the people had been forbidden to store up, and they used to hoard and store, and 'Isa (peace be upon him) would inform them of that.

The second issue: informing about unseen matters in this manner is a miracle, because soothsayers (munajjimun) who claim to extract news cannot do so except upon a prior question, and then they resort at that point to an instrument and arrive by it at knowledge of the states of the stars; then they admit that they err a great deal. As for informing about the unseen without the aid of an instrument, and without a prior question, it can only be by revelation from Allah, exalted is He.

* Then he (peace be upon him) concluded his speech with His saying: ﴿Indeed, in that is a sign for you, if you are believers﴾.

The meaning is: indeed, in these five there is a miracle that is overpowering and strong, indicating the truthfulness of the claimant for everyone who believes in the evidences of the miracle in leading to truthfulness. Rather, as for whoever denies that the miracle itself indicates the truthfulness of the claimant, namely the Barahimah (Brahmins), then the appearance of these signs is not sufficient for him. As for whoever believes in the indication of the miraculous act for truthfulness, there is no longer any objection left for him regarding these miracles at all.

[Page 53 marker in the source text omitted]

Commentary on the words of God Most High: ﴿And confirming what is before me of the Torah, and to make lawful for you some of what was forbidden to you. And I have come to you with a sign from your Lord, so fear God and obey me. Indeed, God is my Lord and your Lord, so worship Him. This is a straight path.﴾

Know that when he (peace be upon him) had demonstrated, through these dazzling miracles (al-mu'jizat), that he was a messenger from God Most High, he then explained what he had been sent with, and it consists of two matters. The first is His saying: ﴿And confirming what is before me of the Torah.﴾

On this there are two issues.

The first issue: We have mentioned, in His saying ﴿And a messenger to the Children of Israel: "Indeed I have come to you with a sign"﴾, that its implied meaning is: "And We send him as a messenger to the Children of Israel, saying: 'Indeed I have come to you with a sign.'" So His saying "and confirming" is coordinated with it, and the implied meaning is: "And We send him as a messenger to the Children of Israel, saying: 'I have come to you with a sign,' and that I have been sent confirming what is before me of the Torah." The omission of these words was good because the context indicates them.

The second issue: It is obligatory for every prophet to confirm all the prophets (peace be upon them), because the way to establishing their prophethood is the miracle. Thus, whoever is given a miracle, it becomes obligatory to acknowledge his prophethood. For this reason we say that Jesus (peace be upon him) must confirm Moses and the Torah. Perhaps among the purposes of Jesus' (peace be upon him) being sent to them is the affirmation of the Torah, the removal of the doubts of deniers, and the distortions of the ignorant.

As for the second purpose of Jesus' (peace be upon him) mission, it is His saying: ﴿and to make lawful for you some of what was forbidden to you.﴾

On this there is an objection: It is said that this last statement contradicts what precedes it, because this last statement clearly says that he came to make lawful some of what had been forbidden to them in the Torah, and this requires that his ruling be contrary to the ruling of the Torah, which contradicts His saying: ﴿And confirming what is before me of the Torah.﴾

The answer: There is no contradiction in the speech, because confirming the Torah has no meaning except believing that everything in it is true and correct. If the second matter (the abrogation) is not mentioned in the Torah, then Jesus' ruling to make lawful what had been forbidden in it does not contradict his being a confirmer of the Torah. Also, if the glad tidings of Jesus (peace be upon him) are present in the Torah, then the coming of Jesus (peace be upon him) and his law do not contradict the Torah.

[Page 53 marker omitted]

Then they differed. Some of them said that he (peace be upon him) did not change any of the rulings of the Torah. Wahb ibn Munabbih said: Jesus (peace be upon him) was upon the law of Moses (peace be upon him); he affirmed the Sabbath and faced Bayt al-Maqdis (Jerusalem). Then he interpreted His saying ﴿and to make lawful for you some of what was forbidden to you﴾ in two ways:

The first: The rabbis had invented false laws from their own selves and attributed them to Moses. So Jesus (peace be upon him) came, lifted them, nullified them, and returned the matter to what it was in the time of Moses (peace be upon him).

The second: God Most High had forbidden some things to the Jews as a punishment for some of the crimes that proceeded from them, as God Most High said: ﴿For the wrongdoing of those who became Jews, We forbade them good things that had been made lawful for them﴾ [al-Nisa: 160]. Then that prohibition remained in force upon the Jews, so Jesus (peace be upon him) came and lifted those severities from them.

Others said: Jesus (peace be upon him) abrogated many of the rulings of the Torah, and that did not undermine his being a confirmer of the Torah, as we have explained. He abolished the Sabbath and established Sunday in its place, and he was right in everything he did, because, as we have explained, the abrogating (al-nasikh) and the abrogated (al-mansukh) are both true and correct.

* * *

Then He said: ﴿And I have come to you with a sign from your Lord.﴾ He repeated it because removing a person from what is familiar and customary from ancient times is difficult, so he repeated the mention of the miracles so that his speech would be effective in their hearts and would influence their natures. Then he warned them, saying: ﴿so fear God and obey me.﴾ This is because obedience to the Messenger is a necessary consequence of the fear of God Most High. So he explained that if it is incumbent upon you to fear God, it is incumbent upon you to obey me in what I command you on behalf of my Lord.

Then he concluded his speech with His saying: ﴿Indeed, God is my Lord and your Lord,﴾ and his purpose is to show humility and to acknowledge servitude, so that they would not attribute falsehood to him by saying that he is a god or a son of God. This is because his acknowledgment of servitude to God prevents what the ignorant among the Christians claim about him. Then he said: "so worship Him." The meaning is that since God Most High is the Lord of all creation, it is obligatory upon all to worship Him. Then he emphasized this with His saying: ﴿This is a straight path.﴾

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 3, verses 52–54 (part 1 of 2):

﴿Then when Jesus sensed their disbelief, he said, "Who will be my helpers in God's cause?" The disciples said, "We are God's helpers. We believe in God, and bear witness that we are submitting."﴾ ﴿"Our Lord, we believe in what You have sent down and follow the Messenger, so record us among the witnesses."﴾ ﴿And they schemed, and God schemed, and God is the best of schemers.﴾

Know that when God, exalted is He, related the good news of Mary's child being like Jesus, and gave a full account of his attributes and explained his miracles, but left out here the story of his birth, which He had related fully in Surah Maryam, He began to explain that when Jesus had explained those miracles to them and displayed those proofs, they then treated him in a certain way. So God, exalted is He, said: ﴿Then when Jesus sensed their disbelief﴾. In this verse there are several issues:

The first issue: *al-iḥsās* (sensing) is an expression for perceiving something through a sense. Here there are two views. The first is that the wording is taken at face value: they spoke disbelief, and he perceived it with his ear. The second is that we take it as *ta'wīl* (figurative interpretation), meaning that he recognised from them their persistence in disbelief and their resolve to kill him. Since that knowledge was knowledge without any doubt, like knowledge obtained through the senses, he therefore expressed that knowledge by *iḥsās*.

The second issue: they differed about the cause by which their disbelief became apparent, in several views.

The first: al-Suddi said: When God sent him as a messenger to the Children of Israel, he came to them and called them to the religion of God, but they rebelled and disobeyed. So he feared them and hid from them. The affair of Jesus, peace be upon him, among his people was like the affair of Muhammad (ﷺ) while he was in Mecca, so he was oppressed and used to hide from the Children of Israel, just as the Prophet (ﷺ) hid in the cave, and in the homes of those who believed in him when they wanted to kill him. Then he, peace be upon him, went out with his mother wandering across the earth, and it happened that he stopped in a village at the house of a man who treated him with great hospitality. In that city there was a tyrannical king. One day that man came back grieved, and Jesus asked him about the reason. He said: "The king of this city is a tyrannical man, and his custom is that he assigns to each of us a day on which we must feed him and his soldiers and give them drink. Today is my turn, and the matter is impossible for me." When Mary, peace be upon her, heard this, she said: "My son, pray to God that He may suffice him in that." He said: "O mother, if I do that it would be an evil." She said: "He has been generous and honoured us, and we must honour him in return." Jesus, peace be upon him, said: "When the king's arrival draws near, fill your pots and jars with water, then inform me." When he did that, he called upon God, and what was in the pots turned into cooked food, and what was in the jars turned into wine. When the king came to him, he ate and drank and asked him: "Where did this wine come from?" The man gave evasive answers, and the king kept pressing him until he told him what had happened. The king said: "Whoever calls upon God so that He turns water into wine, if he calls for God to revive my son, it must be granted." His son had died a few days before that, so Jesus, peace be upon him, was asked and was requested to do this. Jesus said: "Do not do it, for if he lives, it will be an evil." The king said: "I do not care what it will be once I see him, and if you revive him I will leave you to do what you are doing." So Jesus called upon God, and the boy lived. When the people of his kingdom saw that he had come back to life, they rushed to arms and fought one another, and the affair of Jesus, peace be upon him, became famous among the people, and the Jews set out to kill him, openly attacking him, denying him and disbelieving in him.

The second view: The Jews knew that he was the Messiah promised in the Torah, and that he would abrogate their religion (*yansakh dīnahum*). So from the very beginning they were hostile to him and sought to kill him. When he made his call public, their anger intensified, and they began to harm him, to alienate him, and they sought to kill him.

The third view: Jesus, peace be upon him, thought that among his people whom he had called to faith, they would not believe in him and that his call would have no effect on them. So he wished to test them so that he could confirm what he suspected about them, and he said to them: ﴿Who will be my helpers in God's cause?﴾ Only the disciples answered him. At that point he sensed that all those other than the disciples were disbelievers, persisting in denying his religion and seeking to kill him.

* * *

As for His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Who will be my helpers in God's cause?﴾, there are two issues in it.

[Page 55]

The first issue: there are views on this verse.

The first: When Jesus, peace be upon him, called the Children of Israel to the religion and they rebelled against him, he fled from them and began to wander across the earth. He passed by a group of fishermen, among whom were Simon and James and John, the sons of Zebedee, who were among the twelve disciples. Jesus, peace be upon him, said: "Now you are catching fish; if you follow me you will become those who catch people for eternal life." They asked him for a miracle. Simon had cast his net into the water that night and caught nothing. So Jesus ordered him to cast his net into the water again, and so much fish gathered in that net that it nearly tore. They called on the people of another boat for help, and they filled both boats. At that point they believed in Jesus, peace be upon him.

The second view: His saying ﴿Who will be my helpers in God's cause?﴾ was said only at the end of his affair, when the Jews had united against him seeking to kill him. Here there are possibilities.

The first possibility: when the Jews sought him for killing and he was fleeing from them, he said to those twelve disciples: "Which of you would love to be my companion in Paradise, on condition that my likeness is cast upon him, and he is killed in my place?"

Some of them agreed to this. And in what the Christians mention in their Gospel (*Injīl*): when the Jews seized Jesus, Simon drew his sword and struck a servant of one of the great rabbis, and cut off his ear. Jesus said to him: "Enough." Then he took the servant's ear and returned it to its place, and it became as it had been. The point is that the purpose of seeking help was their readiness to ward off harm from him.

The second possibility: he called them to fight alongside the people, because of God's saying in another surah: ﴿So a group of the Children of Israel believed and a group disbelieved, then We strengthened those who believed against their enemy, and they became dominant﴾ [al-Saff: 14].

The second issue: His saying "in God's cause" (*ilā Allāh*) has several interpretations:

The first: the implied meaning is: "Who will be my helpers while going to God, or while seeking refuge in God?"

The second: the implied meaning is: "Who will be my helpers until I make known the command of God, and until I make His religion manifest?" Here *ilā* signifies a limit, as if he meant: "Whoever remains steadfast in supporting me until my call is completed and God's command becomes manifest."

The third: most of the linguists said that *ilā* here means *maʿa* (with). God said: ﴿And do not consume their property along with your own property﴾ [al-Nisa: 2], meaning "together with it." And the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "A few camels added to a few camels are (a herd of) camels," meaning "together with the few."

Al-Zajjaj said: The word *ilā* does not mean *maʿa*, for if you say "Zayd went to ʿAmr," you cannot say "Zayd went with ʿAmr," because *ilā* conveys the limit, while *maʿa* conveys the joining of one thing to another. Rather, what we mean when we say that *ilā* here means *maʿa* is that it conveys its function, in that the intended meaning is: "Whoever adds his support to God's support of me." Likewise the meaning of His saying ﴿And do not consume their property along with your own property﴾ is: "Do not consume their property joined to your property." Likewise the Prophet's saying, peace be upon him, "A few camels added to a few camels are (a herd of) camels," means: "A few added to a few make a herd."

The fourth: the meaning is: "Who will be my helpers in what is a means of drawing near to God and a way toward Him?" In a hadith, the Prophet (ﷺ) used to say when he sacrificed: "O God, from You and toward You" (*Allāhumma minka wa ilayka*), meaning: seeking nearness to You. And a man says to another when calling him: "Ilayya," meaning: "Join me." Thus here the meaning is: "Who will be my helpers in what brings nearness to God, exalted is He?"

The fifth: *ilā* has the meaning of *li* (for), as if he said: "Who will be my helpers for God?" A parallel to this is God's saying: ﴿Say: Is there any of your partners who guides to the truth? Say: God guides to the truth﴾ [Yunus: 35].

The sixth: the verse means: "Who will be my helpers in the way of God?" and the use of *ilā* in the sense of *fī* (in) is permissible. This is the view of al-Hasan.

* * *

[Page 56]

As for His saying, exalted is He: ﴿The disciples said, "We are God's helpers"﴾, there are several issues in it.

The first issue: they mentioned several views about the word *ḥawārī* (disciple):

The first: *al-ḥawārī* is a term applied to a man's special companion and his choice associate. From this, fine flour is called *ḥuwwārā*, because it is the pure essence of the grain. The Prophet (ﷺ) said to al-Zubayr: "He is the son of my paternal aunt and my *ḥawārī* from among my community." The *ḥawāriyyāt* among women are those with clear complexions and smooth skin. According to this view, the *ḥawāriyyūn* are the elite of the prophets who were pure and sincere in believing in them and in supporting them.

The second view: *al-ḥawārī* derives from *al-ḥawar*, which is intense whiteness. From this comes the word for fine flour, and from it *al-aḥwar* (one with white-of-eye prominence). *Al-ḥawar* is the purity of the whiteness of the eye, and *ḥawwartu al-thiyāb* means "I whitened the clothes." According to this view they differed about why those men were given this name. Saʿid ibn Jubayr said: because of the whiteness of their clothes. It was also said that they were launderers who whitened clothes. It was also said that because their hearts were pure and clean of all hypocrisy and doubt, they were named thus as a praise of them and as an indication of the purity of their hearts, like a white garment. This is like saying: "So-and-so is clean of collar, pure of hem," when he is far from blameworthy acts; and "So-and-so has soiled clothes" when he engages in what is not fitting.

The third view: al-Dahhak said: Jesus, peace be upon him, passed by a group of those who used to wash clothes, and he called them to faith, and they believed. In the Nabataean language, one who washes clothes is called *hawāriyy*, meaning a launderer. This word was arabised and became *ḥawārī*. Muqatil ibn Sulayman said: the *ḥawāriyyūn* are the launderers. Once you know the origin of this word, by customary usage it has become an indication of a man's special confidants and inner circle.

The second issue: they differed about who these disciples were.

The first view: he, peace be upon him, passed by them while they were catching fish, and said to them: "Come, let us catch people." They said: "Who are you?" He said: "I am Jesus son of Mary, the servant of God and His Messenger." They asked him for a miracle to confirm what he said. When he displayed the miracle, they believed in him, and these are the disciples.

The second view: They said: His mother entrusted him to a dyer. Whenever he wanted to teach him something, he already knew it better than the dyer. Once the dyer wanted to go away on some business, and said to him: "Here are clothes of various kinds, and I have marked each one with a specific sign. Dye them in those colours so that the desired result is achieved when I return." Then he left. Jesus, peace be upon him, boiled one vat, put all the garments into it, and said: "Become, by God's permission, as I wish." When the dyer returned and told him what he had done, the dyer said: "You have ruined the clothes for me!" He said: "Get up and look." So the dyer began to take out one garment red, one green, and one yellow, as he had wished, until he had taken out all of them in the colours he had intended. The onlookers marvelled at him and believed in him, and these are the disciples.

The third view: The disciples were twelve men who followed Jesus, peace be upon him. Whenever they said: "O Spirit of God, we are hungry," he would strike the ground with his hand, and out came for each of them two loaves. And when they were thirsty they would say: "O Spirit of God, we are thirsty," and he would strike the ground with his hand, and water would come forth and they would drink. They then said: "Who is greater than us? When we wish, you feed us, and when we wish, you give us drink, and we have believed in you." He said: "Greater than you is one who works with his hands and eats from his earnings." So they began to wash clothes for hire, and they were named *ḥawāriyyūn* for this.

The fourth view: They were kings. They said that one of the kings prepared a meal and gathered people to it, and there was

Jesus (peace be upon him) sat down with them at a dish from it, and the dish did not diminish. They mentioned this incident to that king, and he said, "Do you know him?" They said, "Yes." So they took Jesus (peace be upon him) to him. He said, "Who are you?" He said, "I am Jesus, son of Mary." He said, "Then I will leave my kingdom and follow you," and that king followed him together with his relatives. These are the *Hawariyyun* (the disciples, a term glossed as "those who were sincere and white-clothed" in some accounts, though here it denotes his close companions). Al-Qaffal said: It is possible that some of these twelve *Hawariyyun* were kings, some were fishermen, and some were fullers (*qassarin*). All of them were called *Hawariyyun* because they were the helpers (*ansar*) of Jesus (peace be upon him), his aides (*a'wan*), and those sincere in his love, obedience, and service.

**The third issue:** What is meant by His words ﴿We are the helpers of God﴾ is: we are the helpers of the religion of God and the helpers of His prophets, because the helping of God Most High is in reality impossible, so what is meant is what we have mentioned.

As for His words, "We believe in God," this operates as a mention of the cause (*'illah*). The meaning is: it is incumbent upon us to be among the helpers of God because we believe in God, for faith in God necessitates supporting the religion of God, defending His friends, and fighting alongside them against His enemies.

Then they said: ﴿And bear witness that we are Muslims﴾. This is because their calling Jesus (peace be upon him) to witness about themselves is also a calling upon God Most High to witness. Then there are two views on it:

The first: What is meant is, "Bear witness that we are submissive to what you desire from us in supporting you and defending you, surrendering to the command of God Most High regarding it."

The second: That this is an affirmation from them that their religion is Islam, and that it is the religion of all the prophets, may the blessings of God be upon them.

Know that when they called upon Jesus (peace be upon him) to witness their faith and their submission, they humbly turned to God Most High and said: ﴿Our Lord, we have believed in what You have sent down and followed the Messenger, so write us among the witnesses﴾. This is because the people believed in God when they said in the previous verse, "We believe in God," then they believed in the Books of God Most High when they said, "We believe in what You have sent down," and they believed in the Messenger of God when they said, "and we follow the Messenger." At that point they sought nearness and reward, so they said: ﴿so write us among the witnesses﴾. This implies that the witnesses have a merit that exceeds the merit of the *Hawariyyun* and surpasses their rank, because they are the ones specifically entrusted with bearing witness. God Most High said: ﴿And thus We have made you a middle nation, that you may be witnesses over the people, and the Messenger may be a witness over you﴾ [Al-Baqarah: 143].

The second view, which is also transmitted from Ibn 'Abbas: ﴿so write us among the witnesses﴾, meaning: write us in the group of the prophets, because every prophet is a witness over his people. God Most High said: ﴿So We will surely question those to whom messengers were sent, and We will surely question the messengers﴾ [Al-A'raf: 6].

God Most High answered their supplication and made them prophets and messengers, and they gave life to the dead and did everything that Jesus (peace be upon him) did.

The third view: ﴿so write us among the witnesses﴾, meaning: write us among those who bore witness to Your oneness and to the truthfulness of Your prophets. The purpose of this is that when they called Jesus (peace be upon him) to witness their own submission, saying, ﴿and bear witness that we are Muslims﴾, they had called God Most High to witness to that as well, to affirm and strengthen the matter. Also, they asked God for the reward equal to that of every believer who bore witness to God's oneness and to His prophets' prophethood.

The fourth view: His words ﴿so write us among the witnesses﴾ are an indication that the record of the righteous is kept in the heavens with the angels. God Most High said: ﴿Nay, indeed the record of the righteous is in 'Illiyyun﴾ [Al-Mutaffifin: 18]. So when God records their mention among the believing witnesses, their mention becomes famous in the highest assembly and among the near angels.

[Page 58]

The fifth view: God Most High said: ﴿God bears witness that there is no deity except Him, and the angels and those of knowledge [bear witness also]﴾ [Ali 'Imran: 18]. He made the people of knowledge among the witnesses and joined their mention with His own mention, and that is a great rank and a lofty station. So they said: ﴿so write us among the witnesses﴾, meaning: make us of that group whose mention You have joined with Your own mention.

The sixth view: "When Jibril (peace be upon him) asked Muhammad (ﷺ) about *ihsan* (excellence), he said: 'That you worship God as if you see Him.'" This is the utmost degree of the servant's engagement in servitude, which is that the servant be in the station of *shuhud* (witnessing), not in the station of *ghaybah* (absence). These people, when they became perfect in the degree of *istidlal* (inference and reasoning), desired to ascend from the station of *istidlal* to the station of *shuhud* and *mukashafah* (direct unveiling), so they said: ﴿so write us among the witnesses﴾.

The seventh view: Everyone who is in the station of witnessing the Truth does not care about the hardships and pains that reach him. So when they accepted from Jesus (peace be upon him) to be his helpers and defenders, they said: ﴿so write us among the witnesses﴾, meaning: make us of those who are in the witnessing of Your majesty, so that we become scornful of every hardship and toil that reaches us. Then it will be easy for us to fulfill what we have committed ourselves to, namely supporting Your Messenger and Your prophet.

* * *

Then God Most High said: ﴿And they schemed, and God schemed, and God is the best of schemers﴾. Concerning this there are issues:

**The first issue:** The root meaning of *makr* (scheming) in the language is striving toward corruption in secrecy and deceit. Al-Zajjaj said: One says *makr al-layl* (the scheming of the night), and *amkara* when it became dark. God Most High said: ﴿And when those who disbelieved schemed against you﴾ [Al-Anfal: 30], and He said: ﴿And you were not with them when they resolved their affair while they were scheming﴾ [Yusuf: 102]. It was also said that its origin is from the gathering of a matter and its firm arrangement. From this comes *imra'ah mamkurah*, meaning a woman whose physique is compact. The firm determination of an opinion is called *ijma'* (consensus, resolution) and *jam'*; God Most High said: ﴿So resolve upon your affair and your partners﴾ [Yunus: 71]. Since scheming is a firm, strong opinion protected from all aspects of deficiency and weakness, it was therefore called *makr*.

**The second issue:** As for their scheming against Jesus (peace be upon him), it was that they resolved to kill him. As for God's scheming against them, there are several aspects:

The first: God's scheming against them was that He raised Jesus (peace be upon him) to the heaven. This is because Yahuda, king of the Jews, wanted to kill Jesus (peace be upon him), and Jibril (peace be upon him) never left him for an hour. This is the meaning of His words: ﴿And We supported him with the Holy Spirit﴾ [Al-Baqarah: 87]. When they wanted to do that, Jibril (peace be upon him) commanded him to enter a house that had an opening (*rawzanah*). When they entered the house, Jibril (peace be upon him) brought him out through that opening, and he had cast his likeness upon another, who was seized and crucified. The attendees then split into three groups: one group said, "God was among us and has gone"; another said, "He was the son of God"; and the other said, "He was the servant and messenger of God." God honored him by raising him to the heaven, and each group had its own followers. The two disbelieving groups then prevailed over the believing group until God Most High sent Muhammad (ﷺ). In summary, the meaning of God's scheming against them is that He raised him to the heaven and did not enable them to bring harm to him.

The second aspect: The disciples were twelve and were gathered in a house. One man among them became a hypocrite and pointed the Jews to him. God cast his likeness upon that man and raised Jesus. They seized that hypocrite who was among them, killed him, and crucified him, thinking that he was Jesus (peace be upon him). That was God's scheming against them.

The third aspect: Muhammad ibn Ishaq mentioned that the Jews tortured the disciples after Jesus (peace be upon him) was raised. [Page 59] They burned them in the sun and tortured them, and they suffered great hardship. This reached the king of the Romans, and the king of the Jews was among his subjects. It was said to him: "A man from the Children of Israel, who is under your command, used to tell them that he was the Messenger of God, and he showed them the raising of the dead and the healing of the blind and the leper. He was killed." He said, "If I had known that, I would have stood between him and them." Then he sent for the disciples, took them from their hands, and asked them about Jesus (peace be upon him). They informed him, and he followed them in their religion. He took down the crucified one and buried him, and he took the wooden cross, honored it, and preserved it. Then he campaigned against the Children of Israel and killed a great multitude of them. From this the origin of Christianity among the Romans appeared. The name of this king was Tabaris, and he became a Christian, though he did not openly declare it. Then after him came another king called Matlis, who attacked Jerusalem about forty years after the raising of Jesus, killed and took captives, and left not a stone upon a stone in the city of Jerusalem. At that point Qurayza and al-Nadir went out to the Hijaz. All of this is among what God Most High requited them for denying the Messiah and for their intention to kill him.

The fourth view: God Most High gave power over them to the king of Persia until he killed them and took them captive. This is His saying: ﴿We sent against you servants of Ours of great might﴾ [Al-Isra': 5]. This is God's scheming against them.

The fifth view: It is possible that what is meant is that they schemed to hide His matter and nullify His religion, and God schemed against them by exalting His religion, manifesting His law, and subduing His enemies, the Jews, with humiliation and abasement. And God knows best.

**The third issue:** Scheming is an expression for devising means to bring about harm. Devising against God Most High is impossible, so the word *makr* regarding Him is among the ambiguous (*mutashabihat*) terms. They gave several interpretations of it:

The first: He Most High named the recompense for scheming "scheming," as in His saying: ﴿And the recompense for an evil is an evil like it﴾ [Al-Shura: 40]. He named the recompense for deceit "deceit," and the recompense for mockery "mockery."

The second: God's treatment of them resembled scheming, so it was called by that name.

The third: This word is not among the ambiguous terms, because it is an expression for a firm, complete plan, and then in common usage it became specific to planning the bringing of harm to others. That is not impossible with regard to God Most High. And God knows best.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 3, verses 52–54 (part 1 of 2):

﴿Then when Jesus sensed their disbelief, he said, "Who will be my helpers in God's cause?" The disciples said, "We are God's helpers. We believe in God, and bear witness that we are submitting."﴾ ﴿"Our Lord, we believe in what You have sent down and follow the Messenger, so record us among the witnesses."﴾ ﴿And they schemed, and God schemed, and God is the best of schemers.﴾

Know that when God, exalted is He, related the good news of Mary's child being like Jesus, and gave a full account of his attributes and explained his miracles, but left out here the story of his birth, which He had related fully in Surah Maryam, He began to explain that when Jesus had explained those miracles to them and displayed those proofs, they then treated him in a certain way. So God, exalted is He, said: ﴿Then when Jesus sensed their disbelief﴾. In this verse there are several issues:

The first issue: *al-iḥsās* (sensing) is an expression for perceiving something through a sense. Here there are two views. The first is that the wording is taken at face value: they spoke disbelief, and he perceived it with his ear. The second is that we take it as *ta'wīl* (figurative interpretation), meaning that he recognised from them their persistence in disbelief and their resolve to kill him. Since that knowledge was knowledge without any doubt, like knowledge obtained through the senses, he therefore expressed that knowledge by *iḥsās*.

The second issue: they differed about the cause by which their disbelief became apparent, in several views.

The first: al-Suddi said: When God sent him as a messenger to the Children of Israel, he came to them and called them to the religion of God, but they rebelled and disobeyed. So he feared them and hid from them. The affair of Jesus, peace be upon him, among his people was like the affair of Muhammad (ﷺ) while he was in Mecca, so he was oppressed and used to hide from the Children of Israel, just as the Prophet (ﷺ) hid in the cave, and in the homes of those who believed in him when they wanted to kill him. Then he, peace be upon him, went out with his mother wandering across the earth, and it happened that he stopped in a village at the house of a man who treated him with great hospitality. In that city there was a tyrannical king. One day that man came back grieved, and Jesus asked him about the reason. He said: "The king of this city is a tyrannical man, and his custom is that he assigns to each of us a day on which we must feed him and his soldiers and give them drink. Today is my turn, and the matter is impossible for me." When Mary, peace be upon her, heard this, she said: "My son, pray to God that He may suffice him in that." He said: "O mother, if I do that it would be an evil." She said: "He has been generous and honoured us, and we must honour him in return." Jesus, peace be upon him, said: "When the king's arrival draws near, fill your pots and jars with water, then inform me." When he did that, he called upon God, and what was in the pots turned into cooked food, and what was in the jars turned into wine. When the king came to him, he ate and drank and asked him: "Where did this wine come from?" The man gave evasive answers, and the king kept pressing him until he told him what had happened. The king said: "Whoever calls upon God so that He turns water into wine, if he calls for God to revive my son, it must be granted." His son had died a few days before that, so Jesus, peace be upon him, was asked and was requested to do this. Jesus said: "Do not do it, for if he lives, it will be an evil." The king said: "I do not care what it will be once I see him, and if you revive him I will leave you to do what you are doing." So Jesus called upon God, and the boy lived. When the people of his kingdom saw that he had come back to life, they rushed to arms and fought one another, and the affair of Jesus, peace be upon him, became famous among the people, and the Jews set out to kill him, openly attacking him, denying him and disbelieving in him.

The second view: The Jews knew that he was the Messiah promised in the Torah, and that he would abrogate their religion (*yansakh dīnahum*). So from the very beginning they were hostile to him and sought to kill him. When he made his call public, their anger intensified, and they began to harm him, to alienate him, and they sought to kill him.

The third view: Jesus, peace be upon him, thought that among his people whom he had called to faith, they would not believe in him and that his call would have no effect on them. So he wished to test them so that he could confirm what he suspected about them, and he said to them: ﴿Who will be my helpers in God's cause?﴾ Only the disciples answered him. At that point he sensed that all those other than the disciples were disbelievers, persisting in denying his religion and seeking to kill him.

As for His saying, exalted is He: ﴿The disciples said, "We are God's helpers"﴾, there are several issues in it.

The first issue: they mentioned several views about the word *ḥawārī* (disciple):

The first: *al-ḥawārī* is a term applied to a man's special companion and his choice associate. From this, fine flour is called *ḥuwwārā*, because it is the pure essence of the grain. The Prophet (ﷺ) said to al-Zubayr: "He is the son of my paternal aunt and my *ḥawārī* from among my community." The *ḥawāriyyāt* among women are those with clear complexions and smooth skin. According to this view, the *ḥawāriyyūn* are the elite of the prophets who were pure and sincere in believing in them and in supporting them.

The second view: *al-ḥawārī* derives from *al-ḥawar*, which is intense whiteness. From this comes the word for fine flour, and from it *al-aḥwar* (one with white-of-eye prominence). *Al-ḥawar* is the purity of the whiteness of the eye, and *ḥawwartu al-thiyāb* means "I whitened the clothes." According to this view they differed about why those men were given this name. Saʿid ibn Jubayr said: because of the whiteness of their clothes. It was also said that they were launderers who whitened clothes. It was also said that because their hearts were pure and clean of all hypocrisy and doubt, they were named thus as a praise of them and as an indication of the purity of their hearts, like a white garment. This is like saying: "So-and-so is clean of collar, pure of hem," when he is far from blameworthy acts; and "So-and-so has soiled clothes" when he engages in what is not fitting.

The third view: al-Dahhak said: Jesus, peace be upon him, passed by a group of those who used to wash clothes, and he called them to faith, and they believed. In the Nabataean language, one who washes clothes is called *hawāriyy*, meaning a launderer. This word was arabised and became *ḥawārī*. Muqatil ibn Sulayman said: the *ḥawāriyyūn* are the launderers. Once you know the origin of this word, by customary usage it has become an indication of a man's special confidants and inner circle.

The second issue: they differed about who these disciples were.

The first view: he, peace be upon him, passed by them while they were catching fish, and said to them: "Come, let us catch people." They said: "Who are you?" He said: "I am Jesus son of Mary, the servant of God and His Messenger." They asked him for a miracle to confirm what he said. When he displayed the miracle, they believed in him, and these are the disciples.

The second view: They said: His mother entrusted him to a dyer. Whenever he wanted to teach him something, he already knew it better than the dyer. Once the dyer wanted to go away on some business, and said to him: "Here are clothes of various kinds, and I have marked each one with a specific sign. Dye them in those colours so that the desired result is achieved when I return." Then he left. Jesus, peace be upon him, boiled one vat, put all the garments into it, and said: "Become, by God's permission, as I wish." When the dyer returned and told him what he had done, the dyer said: "You have ruined the clothes for me!" He said: "Get up and look." So the dyer began to take out one garment red, one green, and one yellow, as he had wished, until he had taken out all of them in the colours he had intended. The onlookers marvelled at him and believed in him, and these are the disciples.

The third view: The disciples were twelve men who followed Jesus, peace be upon him. Whenever they said: "O Spirit of God, we are hungry," he would strike the ground with his hand, and out came for each of them two loaves. And when they were thirsty they would say: "O Spirit of God, we are thirsty," and he would strike the ground with his hand, and water would come forth and they would drink. They then said: "Who is greater than us? When we wish, you feed us, and when we wish, you give us drink, and we have believed in you." He said: "Greater than you is one who works with his hands and eats from his earnings." So they began to wash clothes for hire, and they were named *ḥawāriyyūn* for this.

The fourth view: They were kings. They said that one of the kings prepared a meal and gathered people to it, and there was

Jesus (peace be upon him) sat down with them at a dish from it, and the dish did not diminish. They mentioned this incident to that king, and he said, "Do you know him?" They said, "Yes." So they took Jesus (peace be upon him) to him. He said, "Who are you?" He said, "I am Jesus, son of Mary." He said, "Then I will leave my kingdom and follow you," and that king followed him together with his relatives. These are the *Hawariyyun* (the disciples, a term glossed as "those who were sincere and white-clothed" in some accounts, though here it denotes his close companions). Al-Qaffal said: It is possible that some of these twelve *Hawariyyun* were kings, some were fishermen, and some were fullers (*qassarin*). All of them were called *Hawariyyun* because they were the helpers (*ansar*) of Jesus (peace be upon him), his aides (*a'wan*), and those sincere in his love, obedience, and service.

**The third issue:** What is meant by His words ﴿We are the helpers of God﴾ is: we are the helpers of the religion of God and the helpers of His prophets, because the helping of God Most High is in reality impossible, so what is meant is what we have mentioned.

As for His words, "We believe in God," this operates as a mention of the cause (*'illah*). The meaning is: it is incumbent upon us to be among the helpers of God because we believe in God, for faith in God necessitates supporting the religion of God, defending His friends, and fighting alongside them against His enemies.

Then they said: ﴿And bear witness that we are Muslims﴾. This is because their calling Jesus (peace be upon him) to witness about themselves is also a calling upon God Most High to witness. Then there are two views on it:

The first: What is meant is, "Bear witness that we are submissive to what you desire from us in supporting you and defending you, surrendering to the command of God Most High regarding it."

The second: That this is an affirmation from them that their religion is Islam, and that it is the religion of all the prophets, may the blessings of God be upon them.

Know that when they called upon Jesus (peace be upon him) to witness their faith and their submission, they humbly turned to God Most High and said: ﴿Our Lord, we have believed in what You have sent down and followed the Messenger, so write us among the witnesses﴾. This is because the people believed in God when they said in the previous verse, "We believe in God," then they believed in the Books of God Most High when they said, "We believe in what You have sent down," and they believed in the Messenger of God when they said, "and we follow the Messenger." At that point they sought nearness and reward, so they said: ﴿so write us among the witnesses﴾. This implies that the witnesses have a merit that exceeds the merit of the *Hawariyyun* and surpasses their rank, because they are the ones specifically entrusted with bearing witness. God Most High said: ﴿And thus We have made you a middle nation, that you may be witnesses over the people, and the Messenger may be a witness over you﴾ [Al-Baqarah: 143].

The second view, which is also transmitted from Ibn 'Abbas: ﴿so write us among the witnesses﴾, meaning: write us in the group of the prophets, because every prophet is a witness over his people. God Most High said: ﴿So We will surely question those to whom messengers were sent, and We will surely question the messengers﴾ [Al-A'raf: 6].

God Most High answered their supplication and made them prophets and messengers, and they gave life to the dead and did everything that Jesus (peace be upon him) did.

The third view: ﴿so write us among the witnesses﴾, meaning: write us among those who bore witness to Your oneness and to the truthfulness of Your prophets. The purpose of this is that when they called Jesus (peace be upon him) to witness their own submission, saying, ﴿and bear witness that we are Muslims﴾, they had called God Most High to witness to that as well, to affirm and strengthen the matter. Also, they asked God for the reward equal to that of every believer who bore witness to God's oneness and to His prophets' prophethood.

The fourth view: His words ﴿so write us among the witnesses﴾ are an indication that the record of the righteous is kept in the heavens with the angels. God Most High said: ﴿Nay, indeed the record of the righteous is in 'Illiyyun﴾ [Al-Mutaffifin: 18]. So when God records their mention among the believing witnesses, their mention becomes famous in the highest assembly and among the near angels.

[Page 58]

The fifth view: God Most High said: ﴿God bears witness that there is no deity except Him, and the angels and those of knowledge [bear witness also]﴾ [Ali 'Imran: 18]. He made the people of knowledge among the witnesses and joined their mention with His own mention, and that is a great rank and a lofty station. So they said: ﴿so write us among the witnesses﴾, meaning: make us of that group whose mention You have joined with Your own mention.

The sixth view: "When Jibril (peace be upon him) asked Muhammad (ﷺ) about *ihsan* (excellence), he said: 'That you worship God as if you see Him.'" This is the utmost degree of the servant's engagement in servitude, which is that the servant be in the station of *shuhud* (witnessing), not in the station of *ghaybah* (absence). These people, when they became perfect in the degree of *istidlal* (inference and reasoning), desired to ascend from the station of *istidlal* to the station of *shuhud* and *mukashafah* (direct unveiling), so they said: ﴿so write us among the witnesses﴾.

The seventh view: Everyone who is in the station of witnessing the Truth does not care about the hardships and pains that reach him. So when they accepted from Jesus (peace be upon him) to be his helpers and defenders, they said: ﴿so write us among the witnesses﴾, meaning: make us of those who are in the witnessing of Your majesty, so that we become scornful of every hardship and toil that reaches us. Then it will be easy for us to fulfill what we have committed ourselves to, namely supporting Your Messenger and Your prophet.

* * *

Then God Most High said: ﴿And they schemed, and God schemed, and God is the best of schemers﴾. Concerning this there are issues:

**The first issue:** The root meaning of *makr* (scheming) in the language is striving toward corruption in secrecy and deceit. Al-Zajjaj said: One says *makr al-layl* (the scheming of the night), and *amkara* when it became dark. God Most High said: ﴿And when those who disbelieved schemed against you﴾ [Al-Anfal: 30], and He said: ﴿And you were not with them when they resolved their affair while they were scheming﴾ [Yusuf: 102]. It was also said that its origin is from the gathering of a matter and its firm arrangement. From this comes *imra'ah mamkurah*, meaning a woman whose physique is compact. The firm determination of an opinion is called *ijma'* (consensus, resolution) and *jam'*; God Most High said: ﴿So resolve upon your affair and your partners﴾ [Yunus: 71]. Since scheming is a firm, strong opinion protected from all aspects of deficiency and weakness, it was therefore called *makr*.

**The second issue:** As for their scheming against Jesus (peace be upon him), it was that they resolved to kill him. As for God's scheming against them, there are several aspects:

The first: God's scheming against them was that He raised Jesus (peace be upon him) to the heaven. This is because Yahuda, king of the Jews, wanted to kill Jesus (peace be upon him), and Jibril (peace be upon him) never left him for an hour. This is the meaning of His words: ﴿And We supported him with the Holy Spirit﴾ [Al-Baqarah: 87]. When they wanted to do that, Jibril (peace be upon him) commanded him to enter a house that had an opening (*rawzanah*). When they entered the house, Jibril (peace be upon him) brought him out through that opening, and he had cast his likeness upon another, who was seized and crucified. The attendees then split into three groups: one group said, "God was among us and has gone"; another said, "He was the son of God"; and the other said, "He was the servant and messenger of God." God honored him by raising him to the heaven, and each group had its own followers. The two disbelieving groups then prevailed over the believing group until God Most High sent Muhammad (ﷺ). In summary, the meaning of God's scheming against them is that He raised him to the heaven and did not enable them to bring harm to him.

The second aspect: The disciples were twelve and were gathered in a house. One man among them became a hypocrite and pointed the Jews to him. God cast his likeness upon that man and raised Jesus. They seized that hypocrite who was among them, killed him, and crucified him, thinking that he was Jesus (peace be upon him). That was God's scheming against them.

The third aspect: Muhammad ibn Ishaq mentioned that the Jews tortured the disciples after Jesus (peace be upon him) was raised. [Page 59] They burned them in the sun and tortured them, and they suffered great hardship. This reached the king of the Romans, and the king of the Jews was among his subjects. It was said to him: "A man from the Children of Israel, who is under your command, used to tell them that he was the Messenger of God, and he showed them the raising of the dead and the healing of the blind and the leper. He was killed." He said, "If I had known that, I would have stood between him and them." Then he sent for the disciples, took them from their hands, and asked them about Jesus (peace be upon him). They informed him, and he followed them in their religion. He took down the crucified one and buried him, and he took the wooden cross, honored it, and preserved it. Then he campaigned against the Children of Israel and killed a great multitude of them. From this the origin of Christianity among the Romans appeared. The name of this king was Tabaris, and he became a Christian, though he did not openly declare it. Then after him came another king called Matlis, who attacked Jerusalem about forty years after the raising of Jesus, killed and took captives, and left not a stone upon a stone in the city of Jerusalem. At that point Qurayza and al-Nadir went out to the Hijaz. All of this is among what God Most High requited them for denying the Messiah and for their intention to kill him.

The fourth view: God Most High gave power over them to the king of Persia until he killed them and took them captive. This is His saying: ﴿We sent against you servants of Ours of great might﴾ [Al-Isra': 5]. This is God's scheming against them.

The fifth view: It is possible that what is meant is that they schemed to hide His matter and nullify His religion, and God schemed against them by exalting His religion, manifesting His law, and subduing His enemies, the Jews, with humiliation and abasement. And God knows best.

**The third issue:** Scheming is an expression for devising means to bring about harm. Devising against God Most High is impossible, so the word *makr* regarding Him is among the ambiguous (*mutashabihat*) terms. They gave several interpretations of it:

The first: He Most High named the recompense for scheming "scheming," as in His saying: ﴿And the recompense for an evil is an evil like it﴾ [Al-Shura: 40]. He named the recompense for deceit "deceit," and the recompense for mockery "mockery."

The second: God's treatment of them resembled scheming, so it was called by that name.

The third: This word is not among the ambiguous terms, because it is an expression for a firm, complete plan, and then in common usage it became specific to planning the bringing of harm to others. That is not impossible with regard to God Most High. And God knows best.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 3, verses 52–54 (part 1 of 2):

﴿Then when Jesus sensed their disbelief, he said, "Who will be my helpers in God's cause?" The disciples said, "We are God's helpers. We believe in God, and bear witness that we are submitting."﴾ ﴿"Our Lord, we believe in what You have sent down and follow the Messenger, so record us among the witnesses."﴾ ﴿And they schemed, and God schemed, and God is the best of schemers.﴾

Know that when God, exalted is He, related the good news of Mary's child being like Jesus, and gave a full account of his attributes and explained his miracles, but left out here the story of his birth, which He had related fully in Surah Maryam, He began to explain that when Jesus had explained those miracles to them and displayed those proofs, they then treated him in a certain way. So God, exalted is He, said: ﴿Then when Jesus sensed their disbelief﴾. In this verse there are several issues:

The first issue: *al-iḥsās* (sensing) is an expression for perceiving something through a sense. Here there are two views. The first is that the wording is taken at face value: they spoke disbelief, and he perceived it with his ear. The second is that we take it as *ta'wīl* (figurative interpretation), meaning that he recognised from them their persistence in disbelief and their resolve to kill him. Since that knowledge was knowledge without any doubt, like knowledge obtained through the senses, he therefore expressed that knowledge by *iḥsās*.

The second issue: they differed about the cause by which their disbelief became apparent, in several views.

The first: al-Suddi said: When God sent him as a messenger to the Children of Israel, he came to them and called them to the religion of God, but they rebelled and disobeyed. So he feared them and hid from them. The affair of Jesus, peace be upon him, among his people was like the affair of Muhammad (ﷺ) while he was in Mecca, so he was oppressed and used to hide from the Children of Israel, just as the Prophet (ﷺ) hid in the cave, and in the homes of those who believed in him when they wanted to kill him. Then he, peace be upon him, went out with his mother wandering across the earth, and it happened that he stopped in a village at the house of a man who treated him with great hospitality. In that city there was a tyrannical king. One day that man came back grieved, and Jesus asked him about the reason. He said: "The king of this city is a tyrannical man, and his custom is that he assigns to each of us a day on which we must feed him and his soldiers and give them drink. Today is my turn, and the matter is impossible for me." When Mary, peace be upon her, heard this, she said: "My son, pray to God that He may suffice him in that." He said: "O mother, if I do that it would be an evil." She said: "He has been generous and honoured us, and we must honour him in return." Jesus, peace be upon him, said: "When the king's arrival draws near, fill your pots and jars with water, then inform me." When he did that, he called upon God, and what was in the pots turned into cooked food, and what was in the jars turned into wine. When the king came to him, he ate and drank and asked him: "Where did this wine come from?" The man gave evasive answers, and the king kept pressing him until he told him what had happened. The king said: "Whoever calls upon God so that He turns water into wine, if he calls for God to revive my son, it must be granted." His son had died a few days before that, so Jesus, peace be upon him, was asked and was requested to do this. Jesus said: "Do not do it, for if he lives, it will be an evil." The king said: "I do not care what it will be once I see him, and if you revive him I will leave you to do what you are doing." So Jesus called upon God, and the boy lived. When the people of his kingdom saw that he had come back to life, they rushed to arms and fought one another, and the affair of Jesus, peace be upon him, became famous among the people, and the Jews set out to kill him, openly attacking him, denying him and disbelieving in him.

The second view: The Jews knew that he was the Messiah promised in the Torah, and that he would abrogate their religion (*yansakh dīnahum*). So from the very beginning they were hostile to him and sought to kill him. When he made his call public, their anger intensified, and they began to harm him, to alienate him, and they sought to kill him.

The third view: Jesus, peace be upon him, thought that among his people whom he had called to faith, they would not believe in him and that his call would have no effect on them. So he wished to test them so that he could confirm what he suspected about them, and he said to them: ﴿Who will be my helpers in God's cause?﴾ Only the disciples answered him. At that point he sensed that all those other than the disciples were disbelievers, persisting in denying his religion and seeking to kill him.

As for His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Who will be my helpers in God's cause?﴾, there are two issues in it.

[Page 55]

The first issue: there are views on this verse.

The first: When Jesus, peace be upon him, called the Children of Israel to the religion and they rebelled against him, he fled from them and began to wander across the earth. He passed by a group of fishermen, among whom were Simon and James and John, the sons of Zebedee, who were among the twelve disciples. Jesus, peace be upon him, said: "Now you are catching fish; if you follow me you will become those who catch people for eternal life." They asked him for a miracle. Simon had cast his net into the water that night and caught nothing. So Jesus ordered him to cast his net into the water again, and so much fish gathered in that net that it nearly tore. They called on the people of another boat for help, and they filled both boats. At that point they believed in Jesus, peace be upon him.

The second view: His saying ﴿Who will be my helpers in God's cause?﴾ was said only at the end of his affair, when the Jews had united against him seeking to kill him. Here there are possibilities.

The first possibility: when the Jews sought him for killing and he was fleeing from them, he said to those twelve disciples: "Which of you would love to be my companion in Paradise, on condition that my likeness is cast upon him, and he is killed in my place?"

Some of them agreed to this. And in what the Christians mention in their Gospel (*Injīl*): when the Jews seized Jesus, Simon drew his sword and struck a servant of one of the great rabbis, and cut off his ear. Jesus said to him: "Enough." Then he took the servant's ear and returned it to its place, and it became as it had been. The point is that the purpose of seeking help was their readiness to ward off harm from him.

The second possibility: he called them to fight alongside the people, because of God's saying in another surah: ﴿So a group of the Children of Israel believed and a group disbelieved, then We strengthened those who believed against their enemy, and they became dominant﴾ [al-Saff: 14].

The second issue: His saying "in God's cause" (*ilā Allāh*) has several interpretations:

The first: the implied meaning is: "Who will be my helpers while going to God, or while seeking refuge in God?"

The second: the implied meaning is: "Who will be my helpers until I make known the command of God, and until I make His religion manifest?" Here *ilā* signifies a limit, as if he meant: "Whoever remains steadfast in supporting me until my call is completed and God's command becomes manifest."

The third: most of the linguists said that *ilā* here means *maʿa* (with). God said: ﴿And do not consume their property along with your own property﴾ [al-Nisa: 2], meaning "together with it." And the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "A few camels added to a few camels are (a herd of) camels," meaning "together with the few."

Al-Zajjaj said: The word *ilā* does not mean *maʿa*, for if you say "Zayd went to ʿAmr," you cannot say "Zayd went with ʿAmr," because *ilā* conveys the limit, while *maʿa* conveys the joining of one thing to another. Rather, what we mean when we say that *ilā* here means *maʿa* is that it conveys its function, in that the intended meaning is: "Whoever adds his support to God's support of me." Likewise the meaning of His saying ﴿And do not consume their property along with your own property﴾ is: "Do not consume their property joined to your property." Likewise the Prophet's saying, peace be upon him, "A few camels added to a few camels are (a herd of) camels," means: "A few added to a few make a herd."

The fourth: the meaning is: "Who will be my helpers in what is a means of drawing near to God and a way toward Him?" In a hadith, the Prophet (ﷺ) used to say when he sacrificed: "O God, from You and toward You" (*Allāhumma minka wa ilayka*), meaning: seeking nearness to You. And a man says to another when calling him: "Ilayya," meaning: "Join me." Thus here the meaning is: "Who will be my helpers in what brings nearness to God, exalted is He?"

The fifth: *ilā* has the meaning of *li* (for), as if he said: "Who will be my helpers for God?" A parallel to this is God's saying: ﴿Say: Is there any of your partners who guides to the truth? Say: God guides to the truth﴾ [Yunus: 35].

The sixth: the verse means: "Who will be my helpers in the way of God?" and the use of *ilā* in the sense of *fī* (in) is permissible. This is the view of al-Hasan.
