Al-Qaffal said: It is possible that some of these twelve *Hawariyyun* were kings, some were fishermen, and some were fullers (*qassarin*). All of them were called *Hawariyyun* because they were the helpers (*ansar*) of Jesus (peace be upon him), his aides (*a'wan*), and those sincere in his love, obedience, and service.

**The third issue:** What is meant by His words ﴿We are the helpers of God﴾ is: we are the helpers of the religion of God and the helpers of His prophets, because the helping of God Most High is in reality impossible, so what is meant is what we have mentioned.

As for His words, "We believe in God," this operates as a mention of the cause (*'illah*). The meaning is: it is incumbent upon us to be among the helpers of God because we believe in God, for faith in God necessitates supporting the religion of God, defending His friends, and fighting alongside them against His enemies.

Then they said: ﴿And bear witness that we are Muslims﴾. This is because their calling Jesus (peace be upon him) to witness about themselves is also a calling upon God Most High to witness. Then there are two views on it:

The first: What is meant is, "Bear witness that we are submissive to what you desire from us in supporting you and defending you, surrendering to the command of God Most High regarding it."

The second: That this is an affirmation from them that their religion is Islam, and that it is the religion of all the prophets, may the blessings of God be upon them.

Know that when they called upon Jesus (peace be upon him) to witness their faith and their submission, they humbly turned to God Most High and said: ﴿Our Lord, we have believed in what You have sent down and followed the Messenger, so write us among the witnesses﴾. This is because the people believed in God when they said in the previous verse, "We believe in God," then they believed in the Books of God Most High when they said, "We believe in what You have sent down," and they believed in the Messenger of God when they said, "and we follow the Messenger." At that point they sought nearness and reward, so they said: ﴿so write us among the witnesses﴾. This implies that the witnesses have a merit that exceeds the merit of the *Hawariyyun* and surpasses their rank, because they are the ones specifically entrusted with bearing witness. God Most High said: ﴿And thus We have made you a middle nation, that you may be witnesses over the people, and the Messenger may be a witness over you﴾ [Al-Baqarah: 143].

The second view, which is also transmitted from Ibn 'Abbas: ﴿so write us among the witnesses﴾, meaning: write us in the group of the prophets, because every prophet is a witness over his people. God Most High said: ﴿So We will surely question those to whom messengers were sent, and We will surely question the messengers﴾ [Al-A'raf: 6].

God Most High answered their supplication and made them prophets and messengers, and they gave life to the dead and did everything that Jesus (peace be upon him) did.

The third view: ﴿so write us among the witnesses﴾, meaning: write us among those who bore witness to Your oneness and to the truthfulness of Your prophets. The purpose of this is that when they called Jesus (peace be upon him) to witness their own submission, saying, ﴿and bear witness that we are Muslims﴾, they had called God Most High to witness to that as well, to affirm and strengthen the matter. Also, they asked God for the reward equal to that of every believer who bore witness to God's oneness and to His prophets' prophethood.

The fourth view: His words ﴿so write us among the witnesses﴾ are an indication that the record of the righteous is kept in the heavens with the angels. God Most High said: ﴿Nay, indeed the record of the righteous is in 'Illiyyun﴾ [Al-Mutaffifin: 18]. So when God records their mention among the believing witnesses, their mention becomes famous in the highest assembly and among the near angels.

[Page 58]

The fifth view: God Most High said: ﴿God bears witness that there is no deity except Him, and the angels and those of knowledge [bear witness also]﴾ [Ali 'Imran: 18]. He made the people of knowledge among the witnesses and joined their mention with His own mention, and that is a great rank and a lofty station. So they said: ﴿so write us among the witnesses﴾, meaning: make us of that group whose mention You have joined with Your own mention.

The sixth view: "When Jibril (peace be upon him) asked Muhammad (ﷺ) about *ihsan* (excellence), he said: 'That you worship God as if you see Him.'" This is the utmost degree of the servant's engagement in servitude, which is that the servant be in the station of *shuhud* (witnessing), not in the station of *ghaybah* (absence). These people, when they became perfect in the degree of *istidlal* (inference and reasoning), desired to ascend from the station of *istidlal* to the station of *shuhud* and *mukashafah* (direct unveiling), so they said: ﴿so write us among the witnesses﴾.

The seventh view: Everyone who is in the station of witnessing the Truth does not care about the hardships and pains that reach him. So when they accepted from Jesus (peace be upon him) to be his helpers and defenders, they said: ﴿so write us among the witnesses﴾, meaning: make us of those who are in the witnessing of Your majesty, so that we become scornful of every hardship and toil that reaches us. Then it will be easy for us to fulfill what we have committed ourselves to, namely supporting Your Messenger and Your prophet.

* * *

Then God Most High said: ﴿And they schemed, and God schemed, and God is the best of schemers﴾. Concerning this there are issues:

**The first issue:** The root meaning of *makr* (scheming) in the language is striving toward corruption in secrecy and deceit. Al-Zajjaj said: One says *makr al-layl* (the scheming of the night), and *amkara* when it became dark. God Most High said: ﴿And when those who disbelieved schemed against you﴾ [Al-Anfal: 30], and He said: ﴿And you were not with them when they resolved their affair while they were scheming﴾ [Yusuf: 102]. It was also said that its origin is from the gathering of a matter and its firm arrangement. From this comes *imra'ah mamkurah*, meaning a woman whose physique is compact. The firm determination of an opinion is called *ijma'* (consensus, resolution) and *jam'*; God Most High said: ﴿So resolve upon your affair and your partners﴾ [Yunus: 71]. Since scheming is a firm, strong opinion protected from all aspects of deficiency and weakness, it was therefore called *makr*.

**The second issue:** As for their scheming against Jesus (peace be upon him), it was that they resolved to kill him. As for God's scheming against them, there are several aspects:

The first: God's scheming against them was that He raised Jesus (peace be upon him) to the heaven. This is because Yahuda, king of the Jews, wanted to kill Jesus (peace be upon him), and Jibril (peace be upon him) never left him for an hour. This is the meaning of His words: ﴿And We supported him with the Holy Spirit﴾ [Al-Baqarah: 87]. When they wanted to do that, Jibril (peace be upon him) commanded him to enter a house that had an opening (*rawzanah*). When they entered the house, Jibril (peace be upon him) brought him out through that opening, and he had cast his likeness upon another, who was seized and crucified. The attendees then split into three groups: one group said, "God was among us and has gone"; another said, "He was the son of God"; and the other said, "He was the servant and messenger of God." God honored him by raising him to the heaven, and each group had its own followers. The two disbelieving groups then prevailed over the believing group until God Most High sent Muhammad (ﷺ). In summary, the meaning of God's scheming against them is that He raised him to the heaven and did not enable them to bring harm to him.

The second aspect: The disciples were twelve and were gathered in a house. One man among them became a hypocrite and pointed the Jews to him. God cast his likeness upon that man and raised Jesus. They seized that hypocrite who was among them, killed him, and crucified him, thinking that he was Jesus (peace be upon him). That was God's scheming against them.

The third aspect: Muhammad ibn Ishaq mentioned that the Jews tortured the disciples after Jesus (peace be upon him) was raised. [Page 59] They burned them in the sun and tortured them, and they suffered great hardship. This reached the king of the Romans, and the king of the Jews was among his subjects. It was said to him: "A man from the Children of Israel, who is under your command, used to tell them that he was the Messenger of God, and he showed them the raising of the dead and the healing of the blind and the leper. He was killed." He said, "If I had known that, I would have stood between him and them." Then he sent for the disciples, took them from their hands, and asked them about Jesus (peace be upon him). They informed him, and he followed them in their religion. He took down the crucified one and buried him, and he took the wooden cross, honored it, and preserved it. Then he campaigned against the Children of Israel and killed a great multitude of them. From this the origin of Christianity among the Romans appeared. The name of this king was Tabaris, and he became a Christian, though he did not openly declare it. Then after him came another king called Matlis, who attacked Jerusalem about forty years after the raising of Jesus, killed and took captives, and left not a stone upon a stone in the city of Jerusalem. At that point Qurayza and al-Nadir went out to the Hijaz. All of this is among what God Most High requited them for denying the Messiah and for their intention to kill him.

The fourth view: God Most High gave power over them to the king of Persia until he killed them and took them captive. This is His saying: ﴿We sent against you servants of Ours of great might﴾ [Al-Isra': 5]. This is God's scheming against them.

The fifth view: It is possible that what is meant is that they schemed to hide His matter and nullify His religion, and God schemed against them by exalting His religion, manifesting His law, and subduing His enemies, the Jews, with humiliation and abasement. And God knows best.

**The third issue:** Scheming is an expression for devising means to bring about harm. Devising against God Most High is impossible, so the word *makr* regarding Him is among the ambiguous (*mutashabihat*) terms. They gave several interpretations of it:

The first: He Most High named the recompense for scheming "scheming," as in His saying: ﴿And the recompense for an evil is an evil like it﴾ [Al-Shura: 40]. He named the recompense for deceit "deceit," and the recompense for mockery "mockery."

The second: God's treatment of them resembled scheming, so it was called by that name.

The third: This word is not among the ambiguous terms, because it is an expression for a firm, complete plan, and then in common usage it became specific to planning the bringing of harm to others. That is not impossible with regard to God Most High. And God knows best.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 3, verse 55 (part 1 of 2):

God's words: ﴿When God said, "O Jesus, I will take you in death and raise you to Me and purify you from those who disbelieve, and I will make those who follow you superior to those who disbelieve until the Day of Resurrection. Then to Me is your return, and I will judge between you concerning that over which you used to differ."﴾

Regarding the verse, there are several issues:

The first issue: What governs "idh" (when)? It is His words, ﴿And they schemed, and God schemed, and God is the best of schemers﴾. That is, this scheming existed at the time God said this statement. It is also said that the implied meaning is: "That was when God said..."

[Page 60]

The second issue: They agree that God, exalted is He, honoured Jesus in this verse with attributes.

The first attribute: "I will take you in death" (innī mutawaffīka). A parallel to this is His statement, exalted is He, quoted from Jesus: ﴿So when You took me in death, You were the Watcher over them﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 117]. The people of ta'wil (interpretation) differed regarding these two verses in two ways:

One: to leave the verse on its apparent meaning without any advancement or delay within it.

The second: to posit advancement and delay within it.

As for the first way, its explanation comes in several aspects:

The first: The meaning of His words "I will take you in death" is: I will complete your lifespan. Then "I will take you" means: I will not leave them until they kill you; rather, I will raise you to My heaven, bring you near with My angels, and protect you from them being able to kill you. This is a good interpretation.

The second: "Taking you in death" means causing you to die (mumītuka). This is related from Ibn Abbas and Muhammad ibn Ishaq. They said: The purpose is that his enemies from among the Jews would not reach killing him. Then after that He honoured him by raising him to the heaven. Then they differed in three ways:

One of them: Wahb said: He was taken in death for three hours, then he was raised.

The second: Muhammad ibn Ishaq said: He was taken in death for seven hours, then God revived him and raised him.

The third: al-Rabi' ibn Anas said: God, exalted is He, took him in death when He raised him to the heaven. He, exalted is He, said: ﴿God takes the souls at the time of their death, and those that do not die during their sleep﴾ [al-Zumar: 42].

The fourth aspect in interpreting the verse: the "wa" (and) in His words ﴿mutawaffīka wa rāfi'uka ilayya (I will take you in death and raise you to Me)﴾ indicates sequence. So the verse indicates that God will do these actions to him. As for how He will do it and when He will do it, the matter is left open pending evidence. Evidence has established that he is alive, and a report has come from the Prophet (ﷺ) that "he will descend and kill the Antichrist (al-Dajjal)." Then, after that, God will take him in death.

The fifth aspect of interpretation: what Abu Bakr al-Wasiti said, namely that the meaning of "I will take you in death" is: (I will take you away) from your desires and the portions of your self. Then He said: "and raise you to Me." This is because whoever does not become annihilated from all other than God cannot attain the station of knowing God. Also, when Jesus was raised to the heaven, his state became like the state of the angels in the removal of desire, anger, and blameworthy character traits.

The sixth aspect: "tawaffi" means taking a thing in full. When God knew that some people would think that what God raised was his spirit and not his body, He mentioned this statement to indicate that he, peace be upon him, was raised in his entirety to the heaven, with his spirit and his body. A proof for the soundness of this interpretation is His words: ﴿And they cannot harm you in anything﴾ [al-Nisa': 113].

The seventh aspect: "I will take you in death" means: I will make you like one who has been taken in death. Because when he was raised to the heaven and his news and trace were cut off from the earth, he became like one taken in death. Applying the name of a thing to what resembles it in most of its properties and attributes is permissible and good.

The eighth aspect: "tawaffi" is "qabd" (seizing, taking possession). It is said: "Fulan paid me my dirhams in full (wafānī) and I took them from him in full (tawaffaytuhā minhu)," just as it is said: "Fulan handed over my dirhams to me and I received them from him." It may also be that "tuwuffiya" means "istawfā" (received in full). On both of these possibilities, bringing him out of the earth and ascending him to the heaven was a taking-in-full for him.

If it is said: On this aspect, the taking-in-full is the very raising to Him, so His words "and raise you to Me" become a repetition.

We say: His words "I will take you in full" indicate the occurrence of taking-in-full, which is a genus under which there are species, some by death and some by ascending to the heaven. So when He said after it "and raise you to Me," this was a specification of the species and not a repetition.

The ninth aspect: It may be considered that there is an elision of a modified term in it, and the meaning is: "one who completes your deed," meaning "one who completes your deed" (wa rāfi'uka) [and] (ilayya), i.e., "and the one who raises your deed to Me." This is like His words: ﴿To Him ascends the good word﴾ [Fatir: 10]. The purpose of this verse is that God gave him good news of the acceptance of his obedience and his deeds, and informed him that whatever hardships and difficulties reach him from his enemies in establishing his religion and manifesting his law, He will not waste his reward or destroy his recompense. This is the totality of the aspects mentioned according to the view of those who keep the verse on its apparent meaning.

The second way: the view of those who say that there must be advancement and delay in the verse, without needing to posit advancement or delay in it. They said: His words "and raise you to Me" require that He raised him alive, and "wa" does not require sequence. So nothing remains but to say: there is advancement and delay in it. The meaning is: "I will raise you to Me and purify you from those who disbelieve and take you in death after I have sent you down in this world." Advancement and delay of this kind are numerous in the Qur'an.

Know that the many aspects we have already presented make it unnecessary to commit to contradicting the apparent meaning, and God knows best.

The anthropomorphists (al-Mushabbihah) hold fast to this verse to establish a place for God, exalted is He, and that He is in the heaven. We have, in many places in this book, demonstrated with conclusive proofs that it is impossible for Him, exalted is He, to be in a place. Therefore it is obligatory to take the wording to an interpretation. This is in several aspects:

The first aspect: The meaning is "to the place of My honour." This raising to Him is for magnification and exalting. Similar to it is His words: ﴿I am going to my Lord﴾ [al-Saffat: 99]. Abraham, peace be upon him, went from Iraq to Syria. A ruler may say: "Refer this matter to the judge," and pilgrims are called "the visitors of God," and those who reside in sacred places are called "the neighbours of God." The purpose of all of that is magnification and exalting. So likewise here.

The second aspect of interpretation: His words "and raise you to Me" may mean that he is raised to a place where none other than God has authority to rule. This is because on earth various kinds of rulers may hold sway over creation, whereas in the heavens there is in reality and in appearance no ruler except God.

The third aspect: Given the assertion that God is in a place, the raising of Jesus to that place would not be a cause of his benefit and joy. Rather, he would benefit from it only if he found there what he sought: reward, rest, comfort and fragrance. So on both views it is necessary to take the wording to mean: "and raise you to the place of your reward and recompense." And since it is necessary to supply what we have mentioned, there remains in the verse no indication of establishing a place for God, exalted is He.

The third attribute of Jesus: God's words ﴿and purify you from those who disbelieve﴾. The meaning is: "bringing you out from among them and separating you from them." Just as He magnified his status by the expression of raising to Him, He expressed the meaning of deliverance by the expression of purification. All of this indicates exaggeration in elevating his status and magnifying his rank with God, exalted is He.

The fourth attribute: God's words ﴿and making those who followed you superior to those who disbelieve until the Day of Resurrection﴾ have two aspects:

The first: The meaning is: those who followed the religion of Jesus will be superior to those who disbelieved in him, namely the Jews, by force, authority and dominance until the Day of Resurrection. This would be a report about the humiliation of the Jews and that they will be subdued until the Day of Resurrection. As for those who followed the Messiah, peace be upon him, they are those who believed that he was the servant and messenger of God. And after Islam, they are the Muslims. As for the Christians, although they show agreement with him from themselves, they oppose him in the strongest opposition, in that clear reason testifies that he, peace be upon him, would not have approved of any of what these ignorant people say. Yet, despite this, we see that the power of the Christians in the world is greater and stronger than the affair of the Jews. We do not see in any corner of the world a Jewish kingdom, nor a town filled with Jews. Rather, wherever they are they live in humiliation. As for the Christians, their affair is the opposite of that.

The second: The purpose of this superiority is superiority by argument and proof.

Know that this verse indicates that his raising in His words "and raise you to Me" is elevation in rank and distinction, not in place and direction, just as superiority in this verse is not by place but by rank and elevation.

* * *

As for His words: ﴿Then to Me is your return, and I will judge between you concerning that over which you used to differ﴾, the meaning is that God, exalted is He, gave good news to Jesus, peace be upon him, that He will bestow upon him in this world those noble properties and those lofty high ranks. As for the Resurrection, He will judge between those who believe in him and those who deny his message. The manner of that judgment is what He mentions in the verse after this verse. There remains among the discussions of this verse a difficult point, namely that the text of the Qur'an indicates that when He raised him, He cast his likeness upon another, as He said: ﴿And they did not kill him, nor did they crucify him, but it was made to appear so to them﴾ [al-Nisa': 157]. The reports also come with this, although the narrations differ. Sometimes it is related that God cast his likeness upon one of the enemies who showed the Jews his location until they killed him and crucified him. And sometimes it is related that he, peace be upon him, encouraged one of his special companions to have his likeness cast upon him so that he would be killed in his place. In sum, however it was, there are difficulties in casting his likeness upon another:

The first difficulty: If we permit the casting of one person's likeness upon another person, it entails sophistry. For when I see my son and then see him a second time, I then allow that this one I saw the second time is not my son, but rather a person upon whom his likeness was cast. And then the security regarding sensible things is removed. Also, the Companions who saw Muhammad (ﷺ) commanding and forbidding them would have had to not know that he was Muhammad, because of the possibility that his likeness was cast upon another. And that leads to the collapse of the laws. Also, the basis of matters in the mass-transmitted reports rests upon the first informant having reported something sensed. So if the occurrence of error in perceived things is permissible, then the collapse of mass-transmitted report is more fitting. In sum, opening this door begins with sophistry and ends with the complete nullification of prophethoods.

The second difficulty: God, exalted is He, had commanded Gabriel, peace be upon him, to be with him for most of the time. This is what the commentators said in explaining His words: ﴿When I strengthened you with the Holy Spirit﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 110]. Then, the tip of one wing of Gabriel, peace be upon him, was sufficient for the world of men. So how was it not sufficient to prevent those Jews from him? Also, since he, peace be upon him, was able to revive the dead and heal the blind and the leper, how was he not able to cause the death of those Jews who intended evil against him, or to make them ill and inflict paralysis and palsy upon them until they became unable to approach him?

The third difficulty: God, exalted is He, was able to deliver him from those enemies by raising him to the heaven. So what is the benefit of casting his likeness upon another? Is there in it anything but throwing a poor man into death without any benefit to him?

The fourth difficulty: If his likeness was cast upon another, and then he was raised after that to the heaven, the people believed about that man that he was Jesus, though he was not Jesus. This would be a casting of them into ignorance and confusion, and this does not befit the wisdom of God, exalted is He.

The fifth objection: the Christians, despite their large numbers across the eastern and western parts of the earth, and their intense love for al-Masih (ʿIsa, peace be upon him) and their exaggeration regarding his matter, reported that they witnessed him killed and crucified. So if we deny that, it would be a rejection of what is established by tawatur (mass transmission). And rejecting tawatur necessitates rejecting the prophethood of Muhammad (ﷺ) and the prophethood of ʿIsa, and indeed their very existence, and the existence of all the prophets, may the blessings and peace of God be upon them. All of this is false.

The sixth objection: it is established by tawatur that the one crucified remained alive for a long time. So if that was not ʿIsa but someone else, he would have shown distress and said, "I am not ʿIsa, rather I am someone other than him," and he would have insisted on making this clear. Had that been said, this meaning would have become widely known among the people. Since nothing of this was found, we know that the matter is not as you have stated. This is the sum of the questions raised on this point.

As for the answer to the first: everyone who affirms a Capable, Choosing Agent concedes that God, exalted is He, is able to create another human being in the likeness of, for example, Zayd. Then this resemblance does not necessitate the doubt mentioned, and so the same holds for what you have mentioned.

As for the answer to the second: if Gabriel (peace be upon him) repelled the enemies from him, or if God, exalted is He, had enabled ʿIsa (peace be upon him) to repel the enemies from himself, his miracle would have reached the level of compulsion (ilja᾽), and that is not permissible.

This is the answer to the third objection, for if God, exalted is He, had raised him to the heavens and had not cast his likeness upon another, that miracle would have reached the level of compulsion.

As for the answer to the fourth: the disciples of ʿIsa were present, they knew the manner of the event, and they would have removed that confusion.

As for the answer to the fifth: those present at that time were few, and the entry of doubt upon a small group is possible, and tawatur, when it ultimately ends at a small group, is not productive of certain knowledge.

As for the answer to the sixth: on the assumption that the one upon whom the likeness of ʿIsa was cast was a Muslim, and that before that ʿIsa was silent, it is permissible for him to refrain from clarifying the reality of the situation in that event. In sum, the questions they raised are matters into which possibilities enter from certain aspects, and since the truthfulness of Muhammad (ﷺ) in everything he reported has been established by a decisive miracle, it is impossible for these merely possible questions to stand as a counter to a definitive text. And God is the Guardian of guidance.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 3, verse 56:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿As for those who disbelieve, I will punish them with a severe punishment in this world and the Hereafter, and they will have no helpers.﴾

Know that when He, exalted is He, mentioned ﴿To Me is your return; then I will judge between you concerning that wherein you used to differ﴾, He afterwards explained in detail what that difference was. As for the difference, it is that some people disbelieved and others believed. As for the ruling concerning those who disbelieved, it is that He will punish them with a severe punishment in this world and the Hereafter. As for the ruling concerning those who believed and did righteous deeds, it is that He will give them their rewards in full. In the verse there are several issues:

The first issue: As for the punishment of the disbeliever in this world, it is of two aspects:

One of them: killing, captivity, and what resembles them, so that even if he were to abandon disbelief, it would not be good to inflict it upon him; this falls within the punishment of this world.

The second: what befalls the disbeliever of illnesses and calamities. The scholars have differed as to whether that is a punishment or not. Some said: it is a punishment with respect to the disbeliever, and if the like of it befalls a believer, it is not a punishment for him but a trial and a test. Al-Hasan said: when the like of this befalls a disbeliever, it is not a punishment but also a trial and a test, and it runs in the manner of the legal punishments (hudud) that are carried out upon the repentant, for they are not a punishment but a test. The proof for this is that He promises everyone reward for patience in them, contentment with them, and submission to them, and what has this as its condition cannot be a punishment.

If it is said: You have already conceded in the first aspect that it is a punishment for the disbeliever for his disbelief, and this contradicts His saying: ﴿And if God were to take mankind to task for their wrongdoing, He would not leave upon it a single creature﴾ [al-Nahl: 61]; and the word "law" (lau) indicates the non-existence of one thing due to the non-existence of another, so it is necessary that the taking to account not occur in this world. Also He said: ﴿Today every soul will be recompensed for what it earned﴾ [Ghafir: 17], and that requires the occurrence of recompense on that day, not in this world. We say: the verse indicating the occurrence of punishment in this world is specific, and the verses you have cited are general, and the specific takes precedence over the general.

The second issue: One might say: describing the punishment as severe requires that the punishment of the disbeliever in this world be more severe, and we do not find the matter to be so, for the matter sometimes falls upon the disbelievers and sometimes upon the Muslims, and we do not find among people any disparity.

We say: rather, the disparity exists in this world; for the verse concerns the affair of the Jews who denied 'Isa (peace be upon him), and we see humiliation and wretchedness clinging to them. Thus the difficulty is resolved.

The third issue: He, exalted is He, described this punishment as being that they have no one who will help them or repel that punishment from them.

If it is said: Is it not the case that the killing of disbelievers is prohibited for the imams and believers because of a covenant and a contract of protection (dhimma)?

We say: The preventer is the covenant, and for that reason, when the covenant ends, killing him becomes lawful.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 3, verse 57:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿But as for those who believe and do righteous deeds, He will give them their rewards in full. And Allah does not love the wrongdoers.﴾

On this there are several issues:

The first issue: Hafs, on the authority of ʿAsim, read "fa-yuwaffīhim" (فَيُوَفِّيهِمْ) with the letter yāʾ, meaning "fa-yuwaffīhimu Allāh" (so Allah will give them their due in full). The rest read it with nūn, taking it as a continuation of what precedes it in His saying (fa-ahkumu) and (fa-uʿadhdhibuhum). The nūn reading is the preferred one, because it follows the sequence of the discourse (naskh al-kalām, meaning the continuity of the speech).

Page 65

The second issue: He mentioned those who believe, then described them as doing righteous deeds. This indicates that righteous deeds lie outside the designation of faith (ism al-īmān), and this indication has been mentioned many times before.

The third issue: Whoever holds that deeds are the cause (ʿilla, meaning the effective reason) of the reward argues from His saying: ﴿fa-yuwaffīhim ujūrahum﴾. He thus likens their worship, done for the sake of seeking reward, to the one who hires a worker (al-mustaʾjir). The discussion of this has also been mentioned before, and Allah knows best.

The fourth issue: The Muʿtazilah argued from His saying: ﴿And Allah does not love the wrongdoers﴾ that He, exalted is He, does not will disbelief and sins. They said: Because whoever wills a thing must love it, if that thing is an action. Love and will differ only when they are attached to persons: one may say "I love Zayd" but one does not say "I will him." When they are attached to actions, their meaning is one when used in their literal linguistic sense. Thus His saying ﴿And Allah does not love the wrongdoers﴾ is equivalent to His saying: (He does not will the wrongdoing of the wrongdoers). This is how al-Qadi established it. But according to our companions (the Ashʿarites), love is an expression for willing to bestow good upon the one loved. So He, exalted is He, although He wills the disbelief of the disbeliever, does not will to bestow reward upon him. This issue we have mentioned many times and in various ways.

Then God the Exalted said: ﴿That We recite to you, of the signs and the wise Reminder.﴾

Issues:

First issue: "dhalika" (ذَلِكَ) is a reference to what has preceded of the account of Jesus, Zakariyya and others. It is a subject (mubtada'), whose predicate is "natluhu" (نَتْلُوهُ, "We recite it"), and "min al-ayat" (مِنَ الآياتِ, "of the signs") is a predicate following a predicate, or the predicate of an omitted subject. It is also permissible that "dhalika" carries the meaning of "alladhi" (الَّذِي, "that which"), with "natluhu" as its relative clause (sila) and "min al-ayat" as the predicate.

Second issue: recitation (tilawa, التِّلاوَةُ, "reciting") and narration (qasas, القَصَصُ, "telling of stories") are one in meaning, since each of them refers to something whose parts are mentioned one after another. Then He, the Exalted, attributed recitation to Himself in this verse, and in His saying: ﴿We recite to you some of the news of Musa﴾ [al-Qasas: 3], and He attributed narration to Himself, saying: ﴿We relate to you the best of stories﴾ [Yusuf: 3]. All of this indicates that He, the Exalted, made the recitation of the angel take the place of His own recitation, glorified and exalted be He, and this is a great honour for the angel. This was fitting because the recitation of Jibril (ﷺ), since it was by His command without any discrepancy at all, was attributed to Him, glorified and exalted be He.

Third issue: His saying "min al-ayat" may mean that this is among the signs of the Qur'an, and it may mean that it is among the indications proving the truth of your prophethood; for these are reports that no one knows except one who reads from a book or one to whom revelation is made. It is evident that you neither write nor read, so it remains that this is from revelation.

Fourth issue: ﴿the wise Reminder﴾ has two views. The first: it refers to the Qur'an. Regarding the description of the Qur'an as a wise Reminder, there are several aspects:
The first: it means "the one who judges" (al-hakim), like "al-qadir" and "al-alim"; the Qur'an is judging in the sense that rulings are derived from it.
The second: its meaning is "possessing wisdom" in its composition, arrangement, and the abundance of its sciences.
The third: it means "the firmly established" (al-muhkam), with the form fa'il in the sense of maf'al. Al-Azhari said: this is common in the language, because "hakamtu" functions like "ahkamtu" in meaning, so it is returned to the original. The meaning of "muhkam" regarding the Qur'an is that it was made firm, free from the entry of any kinds of flaw into it. God, the Exalted, said: ﴿Its verses have been made firm﴾ [Hud: 1].
The fourth: it is said that because of the abundance of its wisdoms, it speaks with wisdom, so it is described as "wise" on this interpretation.
The second view: the wise Reminder here means other than the Qur'an, namely the Preserved Tablet (al-lawh al-mahfuz), from which all the books sent down upon the prophets, peace be upon them, were copied. He informed that God, the Exalted, sent down this account from what had been written there. And God knows best what is correct.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 3, verse 59:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, the likeness of Jesus to Allah is like the likeness of Adam. He created him from dust; then He said to him, "Be," and he was.﴾

The exegetes have unanimously agreed that this verse was revealed when the delegation of Najran came to the Messenger (ﷺ). Among their doubts was that they said: "O Muhammad, since you concede that he had no father among mankind, it is necessary that his father be Allah, exalted is He." So He said: "Adam had neither father nor mother, and it does not follow that he is a son of Allah, exalted is He. Likewise is the matter with Jesus, peace be upon him." This is the gist of the argument. Also, if it is permissible for Allah, exalted is He, to create Adam from dust, why is it not permissible for Him to create Jesus from the blood of Mary?

Rather, this is closer to reason, for the generation of a living being from the blood that gathers in the mother's womb is closer than its generation from dry dust. This is the summary of the argument.

Then here there are several issues:

The first issue: ﴿the likeness of Jesus to Allah is like the likeness of Adam﴾ means his state is like the state of Adam. A parallel to this is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿The likeness of Paradise which the righteous have been promised﴾ [al-Ra'd: 35], meaning the description of Paradise.

The second issue: His saying, exalted is He: ﴿He created him from dust﴾ is not a relative clause (silah) for Adam, nor a descriptive adjective (sifah), but rather a new statement by way of explaining Adam's condition. Al-Zajjaj said: This is like when you say in speech: "Your case is like the case of Zayd," intending to liken him to him in some matter, then you inform about the story of Zayd, saying: "He did such and such."

The third issue: Know that reason indicates that mankind must have a first parent, for otherwise it would follow that every child is preceded by a parent, without ending at a first, and that is impossible. The Qur'an indicates that this first parent is Adam, peace be upon him, as in this verse, and He said: ﴿O mankind, fear your Lord who created you from a single soul and created from it its mate﴾ [al-Nisa': 1], and He said: ﴿It is He who created you from a single soul and made from it its mate﴾ [al-A'raf: 189]. Then, exalted is He, mentioned several modes regarding the manner of the creation of Adam, peace be upon him:

The first: that he was created from dust, as in this verse.

The second: that he was created from water. Allah, exalted is He, said: ﴿And it is He who created from water a human being and made him [a relationship of] lineage and marriage﴾ [al-Furqan: 54].

The third: that he was created from clay. Allah, exalted is He, said: ﴿He who perfected everything He created and began the creation of man from clay, then made his descendants from an extract of worthless water﴾ [al-Sajdah: 7-8].

The fourth: that he was created from an extract of clay. He, exalted is He, said: ﴿And We did certainly create man from an extract of clay﴾ ﴿Then We placed him as a sperm-drop in a firm place﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 12-13].

The fifth: that he was created from sticky clay. He, exalted is He, said: ﴿Indeed, We created them from sticky clay﴾ [al-Saffat: 11].

The sixth: that he was created from ṣalṣāl. He, exalted is He, said: ﴿Indeed, I am going to create a human from clay from black mud altered [and dried]﴾ [al-Hijr: 28].

The seventh: that he was created from ʿajal. He, exalted is He, said: ﴿Man was created of haste﴾ [al-Anbiya': 37].

The eighth: He, exalted is He, said: ﴿We have certainly created man in hardship﴾ [al-Balad: 4].

As for the philosophers, they said: Adam, peace be upon him, was created from dust for several reasons:

The first: so that he would be humble.

The second: so that he would be concealing (sattar).

The third: so that he would be more firmly attached to the earth, because he was created for the succession (khilafah) of the people of the earth. He, exalted is He, said: ﴿Indeed, I will make upon the earth a successive authority (khalifah)﴾ [al-Baqarah: 30].

The fourth: He intended to manifest power. So He created the devils from fire, which is the brightest of bodies, and tested them with the darkness of misguidance; and He created the angels from air, which is the subtlest of bodies, and gave them perfect strength and power; and He created Adam, peace be upon him, from dust, which is the densest of bodies, then gave him love, knowledge, light and guidance; and He created the heavens from the waves of the seas' waters and kept them suspended in the air, so that His creating these bodies would be a manifest proof and a clear evidence that He, exalted is He, is the One who governs without need, and the Creator without contrivance or treatment.

The fifth: Man was created from dust so that he would extinguish the fires of desire, anger and greed, for these fires are not extinguished except by dust. And He created him from water so that he would be pure, in which the forms of things are reflected. Then, exalted is He, mixed the earth and water so that the dense would mix and become clay, and this is His saying: ﴿Indeed, I am going to create a human from clay﴾ [Sad: 71]. Then, in the fourth stage, He said: ﴿And We did certainly create man from an extract of clay﴾, and "sulalah" is in the sense of "maf'ulah" (that which is extracted), because it is what is extracted from the finest parts of the clay. Then, in the sixth stage, He established for him three types of attributes:

The first: that he is from ṣalṣāl, and ṣalṣāl is dry matter which, when shaken, rings like pottery, from whose inside a sound is heard.

The second: ḥama', which is that which has remained in water for a period and whose color has changed to blackness.

The third: the change of its smell. He, exalted is He, said: ﴿Look at your food and your drink; it has not changed﴾ [al-Baqarah: 259], meaning it has not changed.

This is the totality of the discussion regarding reconciling the verses that came concerning the creation of Adam, peace be upon him.

* * *
The fourth issue: In the verse there is a difficulty, namely that He, exalted is He, said: ﴿He created him from dust; then He said to him, "Be," and he was﴾. This requires that the creation of Adam preceded Allah's saying to him "Be," and that is not permissible.

He answered it in several ways:

The first: Abu Muslim said: We have explained that creation (khalq) is measuring and fashioning, and its meaning returns to Allah's knowledge of the manner of its occurrence and His will to bring it about in the specific way; all of that precedes the existence of Adam, peace be upon him, a precedence from eternity to eternity. As for His saying "Be" (kun), it is an expression for bringing him into existence. Thus it is established that the creation of Adam precedes His saying "Be."

The second answer, which al-Qadi relied upon: He, exalted is He, created him from clay, then said to him "Be," meaning He gave him life, as He said: ﴿Then We produced him as another creation﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 14]. If it is said: the pronoun in His saying "created him" refers to Adam, and when he was dust, Adam, peace be upon him, was not existent.

Al-Qadi answered and said: Rather he was existent, and he came into being only after his life, and life is not the self of Adam. This is weak, because Adam, peace be upon him, is not an expression for mere bodies shaped in a specific form, but rather an expression for another specific identity, which is either the balanced temperament or the soul. The discussion extends from this inquiry to what the soul is, and there is no doubt that it is among the most obscure of questions.

The answer: The correct view is to say: since that structure was such that it would soon become Adam, he named it Adam, peace be upon him, before that, as a naming of what will occur by way of actuality.

The third answer: His saying ﴿then He said to him "Be," and he was﴾ indicates the delay of this report from that report, as in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Then he was among those who believed﴾. And a speaker says: "I gave Zayd a thousand today, then I gave him two thousand yesterday," meaning: "I gave him a thousand today; then I inform you that I gave him two thousand yesterday." Likewise His saying: ﴿He created him from dust﴾, meaning He made him a complete creature; then He informs you that I created him by saying to him "Be."

The fifth issue: In the verse there is another difficulty, namely that it should have been said: "Then He said to him 'Be,' and he was," but He did not say it thus; rather He said: "Be, and he is" (kun fa-yakun).

The answer: it is the interpretation of the speech: "Then He said to him, 'Be, and he is,' and he was."

And know, O Muhammad, that whatever your Lord says to, "Be," it will certainly come to be.

The Words of Allah, ﴿The truth is from your Lord, so do not be among the doubters﴾. Concerning this there are several issues:

The first issue: al-Farra' and al-Zajjaj said: His words "al-haqq" (the truth) are the predicate of an omitted subject, and the meaning is: "The account I have informed you of concerning the story of ʿIsa, peace be upon him, or that report regarding the matter of ʿIsa, peace be upon him, is the truth," and the subject was omitted because it is known. Abu ʿUbayda said: it is a new sentence after the completion of the previous speech, and its predicate is His words "from your Lord." This is like your saying: "The truth is from Allah, and falsehood is from Satan." Others said: "al-haqq" is in the nominative case by the implied verb, meaning: "The truth has come to you."

It was also said that it is in the nominative case by virtue of being a modifier, and that there is inversion (taqdim wa-ta'khir) in it; its implied form is: "From your Lord is the truth, so do not be."

The second issue: al-imtira' (doubt, mira') is suspicion. Ibn al-Anbari said: it is derived from the saying of the Arabs: "maraytu al-naqata wa-al-shatta" (I milked the she-camel or the ewe) when you milk them, as the doubter draws out with his doubt a milk-like "mira'" that is drawn out at milking. It is said: "So-and-so disputed (mara) with so-and-so" when he argued with him, as if he were extracting his anger. From this it is said: "Gratitude draws on (yamtari) increase," meaning it brings it about.

The third issue: concerning "al-haqq" there are two interpretations. The first: Abu Muslim said: the meaning is that this which We have sent down to you is the truth regarding the report about ʿIsa, peace be upon him, not what the Christians and the Jews say. The Christians said that Mary bore a god, and the Jews accused Mary, peace be upon her, of slander and attributed her to Yusuf the carpenter. So Allah the Exalted explained that this which was revealed in the Qur'an is the truth, and then forbade doubt about it. The meaning of "mumtarin" is a form of "muftaʿil" derived from "al-miryah," which is doubt.

The second saying: the meaning is that the truth in the explanation of this matter is what We have mentioned of the parable, which is the story of Adam, peace be upon him, for there is no clearer explanation of this matter and no stronger proof than holding to this event. And Allah knows best.

The fourth issue: His words, ﴿so do not be among the doubters﴾, are apparently addressed to the Prophet (ﷺ). Outwardly this implies that he was doubtful about the soundness of what was revealed to him, and that is not permissible. People differed in answering this. Some said: although the address outwardly is to the Prophet, peace be upon him, in meaning it is addressed to the community (ummah), as He the Exalted said: ﴿O Prophet, when you divorce women﴾ [al-Talaq: 1].

The second: it is an address to the Prophet, peace be upon him, and the meaning is: "Remain steadfast in your certainty, and in what you are upon of abandoning doubt."

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 3, verse 61 (part 1 of 2):

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Then whoever argues with you about it after the knowledge has come to you, say: "Come, let us call our sons and your sons, our women and your women, ourselves and yourselves. Then let us earnestly pray [to Allah] and invoke the curse of Allah upon the liars."﴾

Know that in the beginning of this surah Allah, exalted is He, set forth aspects of decisive proofs against the falsehood of the Christians' claim of a wife and a son. He followed this with the answer to all their doubts, in a thoroughly complete manner, and concluded the discussion with this decisive point against their argument. It is this: since the lack of a human father and mother for Adam, peace be upon him, does not necessitate that he be a son of Allah, exalted is He, the lack of a human father for Isa, peace be upon him, does not necessitate that he be a son of Allah, exalted is He, far above that. And since the creation of Adam, peace be upon him, from dust was not far-fetched, the creation of Isa, peace be upon him, from the blood that gathered in the womb of Isa's mother, peace be upon her, is not far-fetched either. Whoever is fair and seeks the truth knows that the clarification has reached its utmost limit. At that point, Allah, exalted is He, said: "Whoever argues with you" after these clear proofs and manifest answers. So cut off the discussion with them and deal with them as one deals with an obstinate opponent, which is to invite them to mutual imprecation (mubahala, a mutual calling down of Allah's curse on the liar). Thus He said: ﴿Say: "Come, let us call...﴾ to the end of the verse. Then there are several issues here:

The first issue: It happened that when I was in Khwarazm, I was informed that a Christian had come, claiming to be well-versed and deeply knowledgeable in their creed. So I went to him and we began to converse. He said to me: "What is the proof of the prophethood of Muhammad ﷺ?" I said to him: "Just as the extraordinary events occurring at the hands of Musa, Isa and the other prophets, peace be upon them, have been transmitted to us, so too have extraordinary events occurring at the hands of Muhammad ﷺ been transmitted to us. If we reject mass transmission (tawatur, reports so numerous that they cannot be fabricated), or accept it but say that a miracle (mu'jizah) does not indicate truthfulness, then the prophethood of all the prophets, peace be upon them, is nullified. But if we acknowledge the validity of mass transmission and acknowledge that a miracle indicates truthfulness, and both are established in the case of Muhammad, then it is necessary to acknowledge with certainty the prophethood of Muhammad, peace be upon him, since when the evidence is equal, the thing proved must necessarily be equal." The Christian said: "I do not say that Isa, peace be upon him, was a prophet; rather I say that he was a god."

[Page 70]

I said to him: "Discussion of prophethood must necessarily be preceded by knowledge of God, and what you are saying is false. This is shown by the fact that God is defined as a being that necessarily exists in itself, and must not be a body, nor occupy space, nor be an accident. Isa is the name of this human, bodily person who came into existence after he was non-existent, and who was killed after he had been living, according to your own account. He was first an infant, then grew up, then became a young man, and he used to eat, drink, excrete, sleep and wake. It is established by the immediate judgment of reason that what is created cannot be eternal, what is needy cannot be self-sufficient, what is possible cannot be necessary, and what changes cannot be permanent."

The second argument against this doctrine: You acknowledge that the Jews seized him, crucified him and left him alive upon the wood, and they had torn his rib. He was trying to escape from them and hide from them, and when they treated him in those ways he showed intense distress. If he were a god, or if God indwelt him, or if a part of God indwelt him, then why did he not repel them from himself? Why did he not destroy them entirely? And what need had he to show distress at them and to scheme to flee from them? By Allah, I am greatly astonished! How can a rational person be fitting to say this and believe in its truth? The immediate judgment of reason almost testifies to its corruption.

The third argument: Either it is said that God is this bodily person who is observed, or it is said that God indwelt him in His entirety, or that some of God and a part of Him indwelt him. All three divisions are false. As for the first: if the Lord of the worlds were that body, then when the Jews killed him, that would amount to saying that the Jews killed the Lord of the worlds, so how did the world continue afterward without a god? Moreover, the most abject and base of people are the Jews, so the god whom the Jews can kill is a god of utmost helplessness. As for the second: that God in His entirety indwelt this body, that too is corrupt, for if God is not a body or an accident, indwelling in a body is impossible; and if He is a body, then His indwelling in another body would be the mixing of His parts with the parts of that body, and that would entail division occurring among the parts of that god. And if He were an accident, He would need a substrate, and God would be in need of something else, and all of that is nonsense. As for the third: that some of God's constituents and parts indwelt him, that too is impossible, for if that part is considered essential to divinity, then upon its separation from God, God would necessarily cease to be God; and if it is not considered essential to the realization of divinity, then it is not a part of God. Thus the falsity of these divisions is established, and the Christians' statement is false.

The fourth argument against the Christian doctrine: it is established by mass transmission that Isa, peace be upon him, had an enormous eagerness for worship and obedience to Allah, exalted is He. Had he been a god, this would have been impossible, for a god does not worship himself. These are arguments of utmost clarity and manifestness, indicating the corruption of their claim.

Then I said to the Christian: "What is it that indicates to you that he is a god?" He said: "What indicates it is the manifestation of wonders at his hand: the raising of the dead, and the healing of the blind and the leper. This is not possible except by the power of God, exalted is He." I said to him: "Do you accept that the absence of a proof does not necessitate the absence of what is proved, or not? If you do not accept it, it would follow for you that the negation of the knowing Creator in eternity entails the negation of the Creator. And if you accept that the absence of a proof does not necessitate the absence of what is proved, then I say: Why did you permit the indwelling of God in the body of Isa, peace be upon him? How did you know that God did not indwell my body, your body, the body of every animal, plant and inanimate thing?" He said: "The difference is clear, for I judged that indwelling because those wondrous acts appeared at his hand, and wondrous acts did not appear at my hand or at yours, so we know that this indwelling is absent here." I said to him:

[Page 71]

"Now it is clear that you did not understand the meaning of my statement that the absence of a proof does not necessitate the absence of what is proved. For the appearance of those extraordinary events indicates the indwelling of God in the body of Isa. So the non-appearance of those extraordinary events from me and from you only means that this proof is not found. Once it is established that the absence of a proof does not necessitate the absence of what is proved, it does not follow from the non-appearance of those extraordinary events from me and from you that there is no indwelling in my case, in your case, in the case of the dog, the cat or the mouse." Then I said: "A doctrine whose acceptance leads to permitting the indwelling of the essence of Allah in the body of a dog or a fly is in utmost baseness and feebleness."

The fifth argument: The turning of a staff into a serpent is further from reason than the restoration of the dead to life, for the resemblance between the body of the living and the body of the dead is greater than the resemblance between a piece of wood and the body of a serpent. So if the turning of the staff into a serpent did not necessitate that Musa be a god or a son of God, then the raising of the dead does not indicate divinity, and this is more fitting. At this point the Christian was silenced and had no further words. And Allah knows best.

The second issue: It is narrated that when he, peace be upon him, presented the proofs to the Christians of Najran, and they persisted in their ignorance, he, peace be upon him, said: "Indeed Allah has commanded me, if you do not accept the proof, to invoke the curse of mubahala upon you." They said: "O Abu al-Qasim, rather we shall return and consider our affair, then we will come to you." When they returned, they said to al-Aqib, who was their leader: "O Abd al-Masih, what is your view?" He said: "By Allah, O assembly of Christians, you know that Muhammad is a prophet sent by God, and he has brought you the true statement regarding the matter of your companion. By Allah, no people have ever invoked the curse upon a prophet and then their elder survived or their young ones grew up. If you do so, there will be utter destruction. But if you insist on your religion and persist in what you are upon, then make peace with the man and return to your lands." The Messenger of Allah ﷺ had gone out wearing a cloak of black wool, and he had embraced al-Husayn and taken the hand of al-Hasan, with Fatimah walking behind him and Ali, may Allah be pleased with him, behind her, and he was saying: "When I supplicate, say Amen." The bishop of Najran said: "O assembly of Christians, I see faces that, if they asked Allah to remove a mountain from its place, He would remove it by them. So do not invoke the curse, lest you perish and no Christian remains on the face of the earth until the Day of Resurrection." Then they said: "O Abu al-Qasim, we have decided not to invoke the curse upon you, and to leave you upon your religion." He, may the blessings of Allah be upon him, said: "If you refuse the mubahala, then embrace Islam, and you will have what the Muslims have, and you will bear what the Muslims bear." They refused. He said: "Then I will fight you." They said: "We have no power to fight the Arabs, but we will make peace with you on condition that you do not raid us and do not turn us away from our religion, on condition that we pay you two thousand garments every year: a thousand in Safar and a thousand in Rajab, and thirty coats of iron armour." So he made peace with them on that basis, and said: "By Him in whose hand is my soul, destruction had already hung over the people of Najran. Had they invoked the curse, they would have been transformed into monkeys and swine, and the valley would have been set ablaze with fire upon them, and Allah would have uprooted Najran and its people, even the birds upon the treetops, and within a year all the Christians would have perished."

And it is narrated that when he, peace be upon him, went out in the black cloak, al-Hasan, may Allah be pleased with him, came and he admitted him, then al-Husayn, may Allah be pleased with him, came and he admitted him, then Fatimah, then Ali, may Allah be pleased with them both. Then he said: ﴿Allah only desires to remove from you the impurity, O people of the household, and to purify you with a thorough purification﴾ [al-Ahzab: 33]. And know that this narration is considered as though it were agreed upon as sound among the scholars of exegesis and hadith.

* * *

The third issue: ﴿Whoever argues with you about it﴾ means about Isa, peace be upon him. It was also said that the pronoun refers to the truth, in His saying: ﴿the truth from your Lord﴾, ﴿after the knowledge has come to you﴾ that Isa is the servant of Allah and His messenger, peace be upon him. The knowledge here does not mean knowledge itself, because the knowledge that is in the heart does not affect this matter. Rather, what is meant by knowledge is what has been mentioned: the rational proofs and the proofs that reach him through revelation and the Revelation. (﴿say: "Come"﴾) Its original form is ta'alaw, because it is from the verb tafa'alu (form VI) derived from al-'uluw (height). So the damma was heavy upon the waw, and it was made sukun, then it was deleted because of the meeting of two sukuns. Its original meaning is elevation and rising, so the meaning of ta'ala is "he rose," except that it became so common in usage that it became used for every coming, and it took the place of halumma (come on).

The fourth issue: This verse indicates that al-Hasan and al-Husayn, peace be upon them, were the sons of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ. He promised to call his sons, and he called al-Hasan and al-Husayn, so it is necessary that they be his sons. Confirming this is His saying, exalted is He, in surah al-An'am: ﴿And from his offspring, Dawud and Sulayman﴾ [al-An'am: 84] up to His saying: ﴿and Zakariyya, Yahya and Isa﴾ [al-An'am: 85]. And it is well known that Isa, peace be upon him, was attributed to Ibrahim, peace be upon him, through his mother and not through a father. So it is established that the son of a daughter may be called a son. And Allah knows best.

* * *

**Fifth issue:** In al-Rayy there was a man called Mahmud ibn al-Hasan al-Himsi, who was a teacher of the Twelver Shi'a (al-Ithna 'Ashariyya). He claimed that ʿAli (may Allah be pleased with him) was superior to all the prophets except Muhammad (ﷺ). He said: What proves this is the words of Allah, Exalted: ﴿and our selves and your selves﴾. The phrase "our selves" does not refer to the self of Muhammad (ﷺ), because a person does not call upon his own self; rather, it refers to someone else. They agreed that this other person was ʿAli ibn Abi Talib (may Allah be pleased with him). The verse therefore shows that the self of ʿAli is the self of Muhammad. It is not possible that this means that this self is identical with that self, so the meaning is that this self is like that self, and this requires equality in all respects. This general equality was set aside with regard to prophethood and with regard to superiority, because there is proof that Muhammad (ﷺ) was a prophet and ʿAli was not, and because there is consensus (ijma', the agreement of the scholars) that Muhammad (ﷺ) was more excellent than ʿAli (may Allah be pleased with him). The equality remains operative in what lies beyond these. Then, consensus indicates that Muhammad (ﷺ) was more excellent than all the other prophets (peace be upon them), so it follows that ʿAli must be more excellent than the other prophets. This is the way of deriving the proof from the apparent meaning of this verse. He then said: The argument from this verse is strengthened by the hadith accepted by both those who agree and those who disagree, namely his saying (peace be upon him): "Whoever wishes to see Adam in his knowledge, Noah in his obedience, Abraham in his close friendship, Moses in his awe, and Jesus in his purity, let him look at ʿAli ibn Abi Talib (may Allah be pleased with him)." The hadith indicates that what was scattered among them was gathered in him. That indicates that ʿAli (may Allah be pleased with him) is more excellent than all the prophets except Muhammad (ﷺ).

As for the rest of the Shi'a, in both earlier and later times they have used this verse to argue that ʿAli (may Allah be pleased with him) is like the self of Muhammad (peace be upon him), except where specific evidence excludes him. The self of Muhammad was more excellent than that of the Companions (may Allah be pleased with them all), so the self of ʿAli must also be more excellent than the rest of the Companions. This is the outline of the Shi'a argument.

The answer is this: just as there is a consensus among the Muslims that Muhammad (peace be upon him) is more excellent than ʿAli, so too there was a consensus among them before this person appeared that a prophet is more excellent than one who is not a prophet. They agreed that ʿAli (may Allah be pleased with him) was not a prophet. Therefore it is necessarily certain that the apparent meaning of the verse is restricted with regard to Muhammad (ﷺ), and in the same way it is restricted with regard to the other prophets (peace be upon them).

* * *

**Sixth issue:** His words ﴿then let us invoke﴾ mean "let us engage in mutual imprecation" (tabahala), just as it is said "the people fought each other" (iqtatalu / taqatalu) and "they accompanied each other" (istahabu / tasahabu). The term ibtihal (invoking) has two meanings:

The first is that ibtihal is striving in supplication, even if it does not involve cursing. One does not say "he invoked (ibtahala) in supplication" unless there is effort involved.

The second is that it derives from the expression ʿalayhi bahlatu Allah, meaning "the curse of Allah be upon him," that is, his curse. Its root goes back to the meaning of cursing, because the meaning of cursing is distancing and expelling. Bahalahu Allah means "Allah cursed him and distanced him from His mercy," from your saying abhalahu when he left him neglected. A she-camel that is bahil is one without a tether; rather, she is released and left free, like a man expelled and banished. The precise sense of the word is this: since bahl means release and leaving free, the one whom Allah has bahalahu has been left free by Allah and entrusted to himself, and whoever is entrusted to himself is undoubtedly ruined. So whoever invokes a curse upon another person and says, "The curse of Allah be upon me if such-and-such is the case," means: "Allah has entrusted me to myself and has left me to my own strength and power," that is, deprived of His protection and safeguarding, like the bahil she-camel that has no guardian for her udder, so whoever wishes milks her and takes her milk, and she has no strength to defend herself. It is also said: "a man is bahil" if he has no staff with him; its meaning is that he has nothing with which to defend himself. The first meaning is preferable, because then his words ﴿then let us invoke﴾ mean "then let us strive in supplication and make the curse fall upon the liar." On the second meaning the sense would be: "then let us curse each other," that is, ﴿so We shall lay the curse of Allah upon the liars﴾, and this would be repetition.

* * *

Four questions remain concerning the verse:

**The first question:** If children are young, it is not permissible for punishment to descend upon them. Yet it is reported in a report that he (ﷺ) brought al-Hasan and al-Husayn (peace be upon them both) into the mubahala. What is the benefit of this?

The answer: the custom of Allah, Exalted, is that when the punishment of annihilation (isti'sal) descends upon a people, the children and women perish together with them. For the adults this is a punishment, but for the children it is not a punishment; rather, it is like causing them to die and inflicting pains and illnesses upon them. It is well known that a person's compassion for his children and family is very intense, so a person may make himself a ransom for them and a shield for them. Since this is so, he (peace be upon him) brought his children and women together with himself and commanded them to do the same, so that this would be more forceful in deterrence, stronger in frightening the opponent, and a clearer indication of his confidence (may the blessings of Allah be upon him and upon his household) that the truth was with him.

**The second question:** Does this incident prove the correctness of the prophethood of Muhammad (ﷺ)?

The answer: it proves the correctness of his prophethood (peace be upon him) in two ways:

The first: he (peace be upon him) warned them of the descent of punishment upon them. Had he not been confident of this, that would have been an effort on his part to expose the falsity of himself, because if they had agreed to his mubahala and the punishment had not descended, then his falsehood in what he had reported would have become evident. It is known that Muhammad (ﷺ) was among the most intelligent of people, so it would not befit him to do an act that leads to the exposure of his falsehood. When he insisted upon it, we know that he insisted only because he was confident that the punishment would descend upon them.

The second: when the people abandoned the mubahala with him, had they not recognized from the Torah and the Gospel what indicates his prophethood, they would not have refrained from confronting him.

If it is said: why can it not be said that they were in doubt, and so they abandoned the mubahala out of fear that he was truthful and the punishment he mentioned would befall them?

We reply: this is refuted in two ways:

The first: these people used to spend their lives and wealth in contending with the Messenger (peace be upon him), and had they been in doubt they would not have done that.

The second: it has been reported from those Christians that they said: "By Allah, he is the prophet foretold in the Torah and the Gospel, and if you were to invoke a curse upon him, annihilation would occur." This was an explicit statement from them that their refusal of the mubahala was because of their knowledge that he was a prophet sent from Allah, Exalted.

**The third question:** Did not some of the disbelievers engage in a form of mubahala with Muhammad (ﷺ), when they said: ﴿O Allah, if this is the truth from You, then rain down upon us stones from the sky﴾ [al-Anfal 8:32], and yet He never sent the punishment upon them at all? So likewise here. Moreover, if the punishment had descended, that would have contradicted His words: ﴿And Allah would not punish them while you are among them﴾ [al-Anfal 8:33].

The answer: the specific takes precedence over the general. Since he (peace be upon him) reported the descent of punishment in this sura specifically, it is necessary to believe that the matter is as he said.

**The fourth question:** His words ﴿Indeed, this is the true narrative﴾ — is it connected with what precedes it or not?

The answer: Abu Muslim said: it is connected with what precedes it, and it is not permissible to stop at His words "the liars." The sense of the verse is: ﴿so We shall lay the curse of Allah upon the liars﴾, [on the basis] that this is the true narrative. On this reading, the correct form of "inna" would have been with a fatha, but it was given a kasra because of the lam in His words "lahuwa," as in His words ﴿Indeed, their Lord, concerning them that Day, is surely All-Aware﴾ [al-ʿAdiyat 100:11]. The rest of the scholars said: the speech is complete at His words "upon the liars," and what follows is another independent sentence, not connected to what precedes it. And Allah knows best.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 3, verses 62–63:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, this is the true narrative. And there is no deity except Allah. And indeed, Allah – He is the Exalted in Might, the Wise.﴾ ﴿And if they turn away, then indeed Allah is Knowing of the corrupters.﴾ And in it are issues:

The first issue: His saying "Indeed, this" is a reference to what was mentioned before of the proofs and of the call to mubahala (mutual imprecation), ﴿is the true narrative﴾. Qasas (narrative) is the totality of speech that includes what guides to the religion, directs to the truth, and commands the seeking of salvation. Thus the Exalted explains that what He sent down to His Prophet is the true narrative, so that he may be certain of his matter. Although the address is directed to him, what is meant is all people.

The second issue: The "huwa" in His saying ﴿huwa al-qasas al-haqq (it is the true narrative)﴾ has two opinions. The first: it is a pronoun of separation (fasl) and a support (ʿimad), and the predicate of "inna" is His saying ﴿al-qasas al-haqq﴾.

If it is said: how is the lam permitted to enter upon the separating pronoun?

We say: if it is permitted for it to enter upon the predicate, then its entering upon the separating pronoun is better, because it is closer to the subject than the predicate is; and its original place is to enter upon the subject.

The second opinion: it is the subject (mubtada'), al-qasas is its predicate, and the whole sentence is the predicate of "inna."

The third issue: "lahu" was read with the vowelling of the ha' according to the original form, and with sukun, because the lam descends from "huwa" the status of a part of it, so it was lightened, just as ʿadud was lightened (from ʿadud, ʿudud-like reduction of the vowel).

صفحة ٧٥

The fourth issue: It is said: qassa fulan al-hadith yaqussuhu qassan and qasasan. Its origin is following a trace; it is said: fulan went out qasasan in the trace of fulan, and qassan, when he followed his trace. From it is His saying: ﴿And she said to his sister, "Follow him up (qussiyhi)"﴾ [al-Qasas: 11]. The storyteller (qassas) is called qass because he follows one report after another and drives speech along. So the meaning of qasas is a report comprising consecutive meanings.

* * *

Then He said: ﴿And there is no deity except Allah﴾. This serves to emphasize the negation, for if you say: "there is someone of the people with me," it conveys that some of the people are with you; but if you say: "there is not from the people anyone with me," it conveys that some of them are not with you; and if some of them are not with you, then all of them not being with you is more fitting. Thus it is established that His saying ﴿And there is no deity except Allah﴾ is an intensification in the statement that there is no deity except Allah, the One, the Real, glorified and exalted is He.

* * *

Then He said: ﴿And indeed, Allah – He is the Exalted in Might, the Wise﴾. In it is an indication of the answer to the doubts of the Christians, because their reliance was on two matters. The first: that he (Jesus) had power over raising the dead and healing the blind and the leper; so it is as if the Exalted said: this degree of power is not sufficient for divinity, rather it must be that He is Exalted, dominant, not overcome and not prevented; and you have acknowledged that ʿIsa was not like that, and how (could he be), when you say the Jews killed him? The second: they said that he used to inform of unseen matters and others, so he would be a god. So it is as if the Exalted said: this degree of knowledge is not sufficient for divinity, rather it must be that He is Wise, that is, knowing all knowable things and all the consequences of affairs. So the mention of "the Exalted in Might, the Wise" here is an indication of the answer to these two doubts. A parallel to this verse is what the Exalted mentioned at the beginning of the surah, His saying: ﴿He is the One who shapes you in the wombs however He wills. There is no deity except Him, the Exalted in Might, the Wise﴾ [Al 'Imran: 6].

* * *

Then He said: ﴿And if they turn away, then indeed Allah is Knowing of the corrupters﴾. The meaning: if they turn away from what I have described – that Allah is the One, and that He must be Exalted, dominant, capable of all that is capable, Wise, knowing of consequences and final ends – while ʿIsa, peace be upon him, was not dominant and was not wise, knowing of consequences and final ends.

Know that their turning away and their aversion is only out of stubbornness. So cut off your speech from them and entrust their affair to Allah, for Allah is Knowing of the corruption of the corrupters, aware of the corrupt aims in their hearts, and capable of recompensing them.
