Know that when the Prophet ﷺ presented to the Christians of Najran the various kinds of proofs and they were left without answer, he then invited them to *mubahala* (a mutual invocation of divine curse on the liar), but they feared it, did not proceed with it, and accepted humiliation by paying the *jizya* (poll tax). He, peace be upon him, had been eager for their faith. So God, exalted is He, said, as it were: "O Muhammad, leave that method of speech and turn to another method, one that every sound intellect and upright disposition will witness to be a discourse founded on fairness and the abandonment of contentious argument." The words ﴿Say, O People of the Scripture, come to a word that is equitable between us and you﴾ mean: come to a word in which there is fairness from each of us toward the other, with no inclination in it to favour one party over the other. The word is ﴿that we will not worship except Allah and not associate anything with Him﴾. This is the intended meaning of the discourse. Now let us mention the explanation of the individual words.

As for His words, ﴿O People of the Scripture﴾, there are three opinions concerning it. The first: what is meant is the Christians of Najran. The second: what is meant is the Jews of Medina. The third: it was revealed concerning both groups. This is indicated by two considerations. The first is that the apparent wording encompasses both. The second is that it has been narrated in the occasion of revelation that the Jews said to the Prophet, peace be upon him: "We want nothing except that we take you as a lord, just as the Christians took Jesus." And the Christians said: "O Muhammad, you want nothing except that we say about you what the Jews said about Uzayr!" So God, exalted is He, revealed this verse. In my view, the closer interpretation is to take it as referring to the Christians, for the reason we have explained: when He had first presented the proofs to them, then invited them to mutual imprecation a second time, He turned in this position to a discourse founded on the observance of fairness, the abandonment of disputation, and the seeking of silencing and binding argument. Among what indicates this is that He addressed them here with the words ﴿O People of the Scripture﴾. This title is among the finest names and most complete honorifics, as He made them people of God's Book. Its parallel is what is said to one who memorizes the Qur'an: "O bearer of God's Book," and to the exegete: "O interpreter of God's speech." This title indicates that the speaker intends to emphasise the honour of the addressee and to comfort his heart. This is said only when a person turns from the manner of obstinacy and contention with his opponent to the manner of seeking fairness.

As for His words, *ta'alaw* (تَعالَوْا), what is meant is determining what they are being called to and turning attention to consider it, even if this is not a movement from one place to another. This is because the root of the word is derived from *ta'ali*, which is rising from a low place to a high place. Then its usage became frequent until it came to signify the seeking of turning toward that to which one is invited.

As for His words, ﴿to a word that is equitable between us﴾, the meaning is: come to a word in which there is fairness from each of us toward the other, with no inclination in it to favour one party over the other. *Al-sawa'* (السَّواءُ) is justice and fairness. This is because the true reality of fairness is giving the half. For the intellects require abandoning injustice toward oneself and toward others, and this is not achieved except by giving the half. So when one is fair and abandons his injustice, he gives the other half, thereby equalising himself with others, and balance is achieved. But when one acts unjustly and takes more than he gives, balance is lost. Since equalisation is among the necessary consequences of justice and fairness, the word for equalisation was used as an expression for justice.

Then al-Zajjaj said: "*Sawa'* (سَواءٍ) is an attribute of *kalima* (the word), meaning: a word possessing equity." According to this, His words ﴿a word equitable﴾ mean: a word that is just, upright, and balanced. So if we and you believe in it, we shall be on equality and uprightness. Then He said: ﴿that we will not worship except Allah﴾, and in this there are two issues.

The first issue concerns the grammatical position of *an* (أنْ) in His words *an la na'bud* (أنْ لا نَعْبُدَ). There are two views concerning it. The first: it is in the nominative case by the implied *hiya* (هي, "it is"), as if someone had asked: "What is that word?" and it was said: "It is that we do not worship except Allah." The second: it is in the genitive case as an apposition (*badal*) to *kalima* (كَلِمَةٍ).

The second issue: He, exalted is He, mentioned three things. The first is ﴿that we will not worship except Allah﴾. The second is that ﴿we will not associate anything with Him﴾ [Page 77] (شَيْئًا). The third is that ﴿some of us will not take others as lords instead of Allah﴾. He mentioned these three because the Christians combined all three: they worship other than God, namely the Messiah, and they associate with Him other than Himself. This is because they say that He is "the third of three: Father, Son, and Holy Spirit." Thus they affirmed three eternal essences, equal in status. We say that they affirmed three eternal essences because they said that the hypostasis of the Word (*uqnum al-kalima*) clothed itself with the humanity (*nasut*) of the Messiah, and the hypostasis of the Holy Spirit clothed itself with the humanity of Mary. Had these two hypostases not been independent essences, it would not have been possible for them to be separated from the essence of the Father or to clothe themselves with the humanity of Jesus and Mary. And since they affirmed three independent essences, they associated partners with God. As for their taking their rabbis and monks as lords instead of God, this is indicated by several considerations:

The first: they used to obey them in permitting and forbidding.

The second: they used to prostrate to their rabbis.

The third: Abu Muslim said: "It is part of their doctrine that whoever becomes perfected in spiritual discipline and striving, the effect of the indwelling of divinity (*lahut*) becomes manifest in him, so that he is able to revive the dead and heal the blind and the leper." Although they did not apply the term "Lord" to him, they affirmed in his case the meaning of lordship.

The fourth: they used to obey their rabbis in sins, and there is no meaning of lordship except that. A parallel to this is His words: ﴿Have you seen him who has taken his own desire as his god?﴾ [al-Jathiya: 23]. Thus it is established that the Christians combined these three matters. The invalidity of these three matters is, for the majority of intelligent people, something agreed upon. For before the Messiah, the only one worshipped was God, so the matter must remain this way after the appearance of the Messiah. Also, the claim of partnership is invalid by the consensus of all. And also, if the Creator and the Bestower of all blessings is God, then it is necessary that in permitting and forbidding, and in submission and obedience, one should refer only to Him, not to the rabbis and monks. This is the explanation of these three matters.

* * *

Then God, exalted is He, said: ﴿But if they turn away, then say: Bear witness that we are Muslims﴾. The meaning is: if they refuse except to persist, then say: "We are Muslims," that is, make clear that you are upon this religion, and do not be in a position where you must compel others to it.

Verse 3:65: "O People of the Scripture, why do you argue about Abraham when the Torah and the Gospel were not revealed until after him? Will you not reason?"

Know that the Jews used to say: "Abraham was upon our religion," and the Christians used to say: "Abraham was upon our religion." So God refuted them by [pointing out] that the Torah and the Gospel were not revealed except after him. How, then, is it conceivable that he was a Jew or a Christian?

If it is said: "This also applies to you, because you say that Abraham was upon the religion of Islam, and Islam was revealed after him by a long time. If you say that what is meant is that Abraham was, in the fundamentals of religion, upon the creed that the Muslims hold now, we say: why is it not also permissible for the Jews to say that Abraham was a Jew in the sense that he was upon the religion that the Jews hold, and for the Christians to say that Abraham was a Christian in the sense that he was upon the religion that the Christians hold? Then the Torah and the Gospel being revealed after Abraham does not contradict his being a Jew or a Christian in this sense, just as the Qur'an being revealed after him does not contradict his being a Muslim."

The answer: The Qur'an reported that Abraham was a ḥanīf, a Muslim (muslim), whereas in the Torah and the Gospel there is no statement that Abraham was a Jew or a Christian. Thus the difference is evident. Then we say: as for the Christians not being upon the creed of Abraham, the matter in this is clear, because the Messiah did not exist in the time of Abraham, so worship of him was certainly not prescribed in Abraham's time, and therefore occupying oneself with the worship of the Messiah is necessarily contrary to the creed of Abraham. As for the Jews not being upon the creed of Abraham, that is because there is no doubt that God, glory be to Him and exalted, had obligations upon creation before the coming of Moses, peace be upon him. And there is no doubt that the conveyor of those obligations to creation was one of the human beings, and no doubt that this person was supported by miracles, for otherwise it would not be obligatory upon creation to accept those obligations from him. Therefore, before the coming of Moses there were prophets, and they had specific laws. When Moses came, either it is said that he came confirming those laws or with something other than them. If he came confirming them, Moses was not the bearer of that law, but was like a jurist confirming the law of one who preceded him, and the Jews would not accept that. And if he came with a law other than the law of those who preceded him, then he has spoken of abrogation (naskh). Thus it is established that the religion of all the prophets must permit the affirmation of abrogation, and the Jews deny that. It is therefore established that the Jews are not upon the creed of Abraham. The statement of the Jews and Christians that Abraham was a Jew or a Christian is thereby refuted. This is the meaning of the verse, and God knows best.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 3, verses 66–68:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Ha antum ha'ulaa' hajajtum fima lakum bihi 'ilm, falima tuhajjuna fima laysa lakum bihi 'ilm? Wallahu ya'lamu wa antum la ta'lamun﴾ ﴿Ma kana Ibrahimu yahudiyyan wa la nasraniyyan wa lakin kana hanifan musliman wa ma kana min al-mushrikin﴾ ﴿Inna awla al-nasi bi-Ibrahima lalladhina attaba'uhu wa hadha al-Nabiyyu wal-ladhina amanu, wallahu waliyyu al-mu'minin﴾

Concerning it, there are several issues:

The first issue: ʿĀṣim, Ḥamza and al-Kisāʾī read "Ha antum" with a long vowel (madd) and a hamza. Nāfiʿ and Abū ʿAmr read it without hamza or madd, except for the duration of the pronunciation of the unvowelled alif. Ibn Kathīr read it with a hamza and a short vowel (qaṣr), on the pattern of "ṣana'tum." Ibn ʿĀmir read it with madd without hamza. Whoever articulates it fully (taḥqīq) does so according to the original form, since they are two words: "ha" and "antum." Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 3, verse 69:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿A party of the People of the Book wish they could lead you astray, but they lead astray only themselves, and they perceive not.﴾

Know that when Allah, exalted is He, explained that among the way of the People of the Book is deviating from the truth and turning away from accepting the proof, He explained that they do not confine themselves to this degree, but strive to mislead those who believe in the Messenger, peace be upon him, by casting doubts, such as their saying: Muhammad, peace be upon him, acknowledges Moses and Jesus while claiming prophethood for himself; and also that Moses, peace be upon him, informed in the Torah that his law would not cease; and also that the claim of abrogation (naskh) leads to bada' (a change of divine intention, i.e., the notion that Allah came to know something new). The purpose of this is to warn the believers not to be deceived by the words of the Jews. A parallel to His saying, exalted is He, in Surat al-Baqarah: ﴿Many of the People of the Book wish they could turn you back into disbelievers after your belief, out of envy from themselves﴾ [al-Baqarah: 109], and His saying: ﴿They wish you would disbelieve as they disbelieved, so that you would be alike﴾ [al-Nisa': 89].

Know also that "min" (some of) here is for partitive meaning, and He mentioned "a party" (ba'd) and did not generalize them, because among them are those who believed, and Allah praised them with His saying: ﴿Among them is a moderate community﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 66], ﴿Among the People of the Book is a standing community﴾ [Al 'Imran: 113]. It is said that this verse was revealed concerning Mu'adh, 'Ammar ibn Yasir and Hudhayfah, whom the Jews invited to their religion. He said ﴿wish they could lead you astray﴾ and did not say "that they lead you astray," because "law" (law) here is for wishing; your saying "law kana kadha" conveys wishing, and a parallel to it is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Each one of them wishes he could be given a life of a thousand years﴾ [al-Baqarah: 96].

* * *
Then He, exalted is He, said: ﴿but they lead astray only themselves﴾, and this admits of several aspects: among them, their destruction of themselves by deserving punishment for their intention to lead others astray, as in His saying: ﴿They did not wrong Us, but they were wronging themselves﴾ [al-Baqarah: 57], and His saying: ﴿And they will surely bear their burdens and burdens along with their burdens﴾ [al-'Ankabut: 13], ﴿That they may bear their burdens in full on the Day of Resurrection and some of the burdens of those whom they mislead without knowledge. Unquestionably, evil is that which they bear﴾ [al-Nahl: 25]. Among them is their removing themselves from knowledge of guidance and truth, because one who departs from being guided is described as astray. Among them is that when they strove to mislead the believers, and the believers did not turn to them, they became failed and losers, since they believed in something and it became apparent to them that the matter was contrary to what they had imagined.

* * *
Then He said: ﴿and they perceive not﴾, i.e., they do not know that this harms them and does not harm the believers.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 3, verse 70:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿O People of the Scripture, why do you disbelieve in the signs of Allah while you witness [to them]?﴾

Know that when He, may He be exalted, explained the condition of the group who do not perceive from the Torah the indication of the prophethood of Muhammad (ﷺ), He also explained the condition of the group among their rabbis (aḥbār, scholars) who knew of this.

So He said: ﴿O People of the Scripture, why do you disbelieve in the signs of Allah﴾. And in this there are several issues:

The first issue: "limā" (why) is originally "li-mā," because it is "mā" (what), the interrogative, which had the lām prefixed to it, so the alif was deleted to seek lightness; and because the prepositional particle has become like a substitute for it; and because it occurs at the end of a clause, and the fatḥah indicates it. On this basis is His saying: ﴿About what do they question one another?﴾ [an-Naba' 1], and ﴿So by what [means] will you give me good tidings?﴾ [al-Ḥijr 54]. Stopping on these particles is done with the hā' (ha), as in: "fa-bimah" and "limah."

The second issue: concerning His saying ﴿the signs of Allah﴾ there are several views:

The first: that what is meant by them is the verses found in the Torah and the Gospel. On this view there are several aspects:

One of them: what is in these two Scriptures of the good tidings of Muhammad (peace be upon him). Another: what is in these two Scriptures that Abraham (peace be upon him) was a ḥanīf, a Muslim. Another: that in them is that the religion is Islam.

Know that according to this view, which admits of these aspects, we say: disbelief in the signs may carry two meanings:

One of them: that they were not disbelievers in the Torah itself, but were disbelievers in what the Torah indicates, so the name of the evidence was applied to the thing evidenced, by way of metaphor.

The second: that they were disbelievers in the Torah itself, because they used to distort it, and they used to deny the existence of those verses that indicate the prophethood of Muhammad (ﷺ).

As for His saying, may He be exalted, ﴿while you witness﴾, the meaning according to this view is that they, in the presence of the Muslims and in the presence of their common folk, would deny that the Torah and the Gospel contain the verses that indicate the prophethood of Muhammad (ﷺ); then, when some of them were alone with others, they would testify to their authenticity. A similar example is His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿You seek to make it crooked while you are witnesses﴾ [Al 'Imran 99].

Know that interpreting the verse according to this view indicates that this verse contains information about the unseen, because he (peace and blessings be upon him) informed them of what they concealed within themselves while displaying other than it, and there is no doubt that informing about the unseen is a miracle.

The second view: concerning the interpretation of "the signs of Allah": they are the Qur'an, and His saying ﴿while you witness﴾ means that you deny, before the common folk, that the Qur'an is a miracle, and then you witness with your hearts and intellects that it is a miracle.

The third view: that what is meant by the signs of Allah is the totality of the miracles that appeared at the hand of the Prophet (ﷺ). On this view, His saying, may He be exalted, ﴿while you witness﴾ means: you have only acknowledged the indication of the miracles that appeared at the hands of the other prophets (peace be upon them), which indicate their truthfulness, insofar as the miracle stands in the place of confirmation from Allah, may He be exalted. So when you testify that the miracle indicates the truthfulness of the other prophets (peace be upon them) in this respect, and you witness that this respect is present in the case of Muhammad (ﷺ), your insistence on denying his prophethood and messengerhood contradicts what you have testified to as true, namely the indication of the miracles of the other prophets (peace be upon them) of their truthfulness.

The Almighty's words: ﴿O People of the Book, why do you confuse the truth with falsehood and conceal the truth while you know?﴾

Know that the scholars of the Jews and the Christians had two stratagems. The first was that they disbelieved in Muhammad (ﷺ) even though they knew in their hearts that he was a true messenger from God. God forbade this stratagem in the first verse.

The second was that they strove to cast doubts and to conceal the proofs and clear signs. God forbade this stratagem in this second verse. So the first position is the position of deception and misguidance, and the second position is the position of misleading and leading astray. On this there are several issues.

**The first issue:** It is read as ﻿تُلَبِّسُونَ (tulabbisūna) with a shadda, and Yahya ibn Wathhab read it as تَلْبَسُونَ (talbasūna) with a fatha on the ba', meaning "you wear the truth together with falsehood," as in the Prophet's (peace be upon him) saying: "like one who wears two garments of falsehood" (ﷺ), and in the line of poetry:

"When he dresses himself in glory and wraps himself in it."

**The second issue:** Know that one who strives to conceal the truth has no way to do so except by one of two means: either by casting a doubt that points to falsehood, or by concealing the evidence that points to the truth. So His words ﴿why do you confuse the truth with falsehood﴾ refer to the first position, and His words ﴿and conceal the truth﴾ refer to the second position.

As for confusing the truth with falsehood, it may here have several meanings:

First: the distortion of the Torah, by mixing what was revealed with what was altered. This is related from al-Hasan and Ibn Zayd.

Second: they agreed to profess Islam at the beginning of the day and then to renounce it at the end of the day, in order to sow doubt among the people. This is related from Ibn Abbas and Qatadah.

Third: the Torah contains what indicates his prophethood (ﷺ) through glad tidings, description and attributes, and the Torah also contains what gives the appearance of the opposite. Thus it resembles the clear (muhkam) and the ambiguous (mutashabih) passages, and they would confuse the weak among the people, presenting one of the two matters in place of the other, as many of the anthropomorphists (al-mushabbihah) do. This is the view of al-Qadi.

Fourth: they used to say, "Muhammad acknowledges that Moses (peace be upon him) is true, and the Torah indicates that the law of Moses (peace be upon him) is not abrogated (naskh)." All of this is casting doubts.

As for His words ﴿and conceal the truth﴾, the meaning is that the verses in the Torah that indicate the prophethood of Muhammad (ﷺ) required reflection and contemplation to derive the argument from them, and the people strove to hide those words which, taken together, complete this argument. This is like the people of innovation (ahl al-bid'ah) in our time, who strive to ensure that the proofs of the researchers do not reach their common folk.

As for His words ﴿while you know﴾, there are several meanings:

First: that you know you are doing this out of obstinacy and envy.

Second: ﴿while you know﴾, that is, you are masters of knowledge and understanding, not masters of ignorance and superstition.

Third: ﴿while you know﴾ that the punishment for one who does such deeds is great.

**The third issue:** Al-Qadi said: His words ﴿why do you disbelieve﴾ and ﴿why do you confuse the truth with falsehood﴾ indicate that these acts are their own doing, because it is not permissible that He should create them in them and then say, "Why did you do it?"

Its answer is: an act depends on a motive. If that motive arises without a originator, it follows that the Creator is denied. If its originator is the servant, then it requires another will. If its originator is God the Exalted, then what you have imposed on us applies to you. And God knows best.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And a group of the People of the Book said: "Believe in what has been sent down to those who believe at the beginning of the day, and reject its end; perhaps they will turn back."﴾

Know that when God, exalted is He, related that they mix truth with falsehood, He followed this by relating one single type of their deceptions, which is the one mentioned in this verse. Here there are several issues:

**The first issue:** The saying of some of them to others, ﴿Believe in what has been sent down to those who believe at the beginning of the day﴾. It is possible that the intended meaning is all that was sent down, and it is possible that the intended meaning is some of what was sent down.

As for the first possibility, there are several aspects.

The first: The Jews and Christians devised a stratagem to cast doubt upon the weak among the Muslims concerning the soundness of Islam. It was to show affirmation of what was revealed to Muhammad (ﷺ) of laws at certain times, and then afterward to show denial of him. When people witness this denial, they say: this denial is not due to envy and obstinacy, for otherwise they would not have believed in him at first. And if this denial is not due to envy and obstinacy, it must be due to their being People of the Book, who have reflected on his affair and investigated thoroughly the proofs of his prophethood, and it became clear to them, after complete reflection and thorough inquiry, that he is a liar. So this course becomes a doubt for the weak Muslims regarding the soundness of his prophethood. It was said that twelve rabbis of the Jews of Khaybar agreed upon this course.

His saying ﴿perhaps they will turn back﴾ means: whenever we cast this doubt, perhaps his followers will turn back from his religion.

The second aspect: It is possible that the meaning of the verse is that the leaders of the Jews and Christians said to one another: "Feign and show agreement with the believers, but on condition that you remain upon your religion when you are alone with your brethren from the People of the Book. The affair of these believers is in turmoil, so pass the days with them in hypocrisy, for perhaps their affair will weaken and their religion will fade, and they will return to your religion." This is the view of Abu Muslim al-Isfahani, and two things indicate it.

The first: When He, exalted, said, ﴿Indeed those who believed, then disbelieved, then believed, then disbelieved﴾ [al-Nisa: 137], He followed it with His saying, ﴿Give tidings to the hypocrites﴾ [al-Nisa: 138]. This is equivalent to His saying, ﴿And when they meet those who believe, they say, "We believe"; but when they go alone to their devils, they say, "Indeed we are with you; we were only mocking."﴾ [al-Baqarah: 14].

The second: He, exalted, followed this verse with His saying, ﴿And do not believe except in one who follows your religion﴾. This indicates that they forbade (others) from any religion other than the one they were upon, so their saying ﴿Believe at the beginning of the day﴾ was a command to hypocrisy.

The third aspect: al-Asamm said: Some of them said to others, "If you deny him in all that he brought, your common people will know your lie, because much of what he brought is true. But affirm him in some and deny him in some, so that people take your denial of him as fairness, not obstinacy, and they accept your word."

**The second possibility:** That His saying ﴿Believe in what has been sent down to those who believe at the beginning of the day, and reject its end﴾ refers to some of what God sent down. Those who held this view understood it as relating to the matter of the qibla (the direction of prayer), and they mentioned two aspects.

The first: Ibn Abbas said: "The beginning of the day" is its first part, which is the Dawn prayer, and "reject its end" means the Noon prayer. Its explanation: when he (ﷺ) prayed toward Bayt al-Maqdis after he had arrived in Medina, the Jews rejoiced at that and hoped that he would be one of them. When God turned him to the Ka'bah, and that was at the time of the Noon prayer, Ka'b ibn al-Ashraf and others said: ﴿Believe in what has been sent down to those who believe at the beginning of the day﴾, meaning: believe in the qibla toward which he prayed the Dawn prayer, for it is the truth; and reject the qibla toward which he prayed the Noon prayer, which is the end of the day, for it is disbelief.

The second: When the qibla was turned to the Ka'bah, that was hard for them, so some of them said to others: "Pray toward the Ka'bah at the beginning of the day, then reject this qibla at the end of the day and pray toward the Rock. Perhaps they will say that the People of the Book are people of knowledge, and had they not known the falsity of this qibla they would not have abandoned it. Then they will turn back from this qibla."

**The second issue:** The benefit in God's informing about their agreement upon this stratagem is in several aspects.

The first: This stratagem was hidden among them, and they had not disclosed it to anyone outside. So when the Messenger reported it, that was reporting the unseen, and therefore it is a miracle.

The second: When He made the believers aware of their plotting over this stratagem, the stratagem had no effect on the hearts of the believers. Had this disclosure not occurred, this stratagem might have affected the heart of some whose faith was weak.

The third: When the people were exposed in this stratagem, that became a deterrent for them from undertaking similar stratagems and deceptions.

**The third issue:** Wajh al-nahar (the face of the day) is its beginning. In language, wajh is the front-facing part of everything, since it is the first thing one faces of it, as one says of the first part of a garment, "wajh al-thawb" (the face of the garment). Tha'lab related from Ibn al-A'rabi: "I came to him at wajh of the day, and sadr of the day, and shabab of the day," meaning the beginning of the day. And al-Rabi' ibn Ziyad recited and said:

"Whoever is pleased by the killing of Malik,
let him come to our women at the face of the day."

Then He, exalted is He, said: ﴿And do not believe except in one who follows your religion. Say: Indeed, the guidance is the guidance of God, that anyone be given the like of what you were given, or that they argue with you before your Lord. Say: Indeed, bounty is in the hand of God; He gives it to whom He wills, and God is All-Encompassing, All-Knowing.﴾ ﴿He specially favors with His mercy whom He wills, and God is the Possessor of great bounty.﴾

The exegetes (mufassirun) agree that this is the remainder of the speech of the Jews, and in it there are two interpretations.

The first: the meaning is, "Do not affirm the truth of anyone except a prophet who confirms the laws of the Torah. As for one who comes with a change to any of the rulings of the Torah, do not affirm him." This is the position of the Jews to this day. According to this interpretation, the "lām" in His saying ﴿except for one who follows﴾ is an extra (zā'idah) particle, since it is said "ṣaddaqtu fulānan" (I affirmed so-and-so) and not "ṣaddaqtu li-fulān" (I affirmed for so-and-so). The presence of this extra lām is permissible, as in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿radifa lakum﴾ [al-Naml: 72], where the intended meaning is radifakum (it followed you).

The second: He mentioned before this verse His saying: ﴿Believe at the beginning of the day, and disbelieve at its end﴾, then He said in this verse: ﴿do not believe except for one who follows your religion﴾, meaning: do not bring that faith except for the sake of one who follows your religion. It is as if they said: "The purpose of bringing that deception is only to keep your followers upon your religion." So the meaning is: "Do not bring that faith except for the sake of one who follows your religion, for the aim of each one is to preserve his followers and partisans upon his following."

* * *

Then He, exalted is He, said: ﴿Say: Indeed, the guidance is the guidance of God.﴾ Ibn 'Abbas, may God be pleased with him and his father, said, in substance: "The religion is the religion of God." A similar statement is in Surat al-Baqarah: ﴿Say: Indeed, the guidance of God is the guidance﴾ [al-Baqarah: 120].

Know that it is necessary to explain how this speech became an answer to what He related from them. We say: as for the first interpretation, which is their saying, "There is no religion except what they are upon," this speech is suitable as an answer to it insofar as what they are upon became a religion only from the side of God, because He commanded it, guided to it, and made obedience to it obligatory. And when this is so, then whenever He commands something else after that, and guides to something else, and makes obedience to something else obligatory, that one is a prophet who must be followed, even if he opposes what came before, because religion became a religion only by His ruling and guidance; wherever His ruling is, following it is obligatory. A parallel to this is His saying, exalted is He, as an answer to them concerning their saying: ﴿What has turned them from their qiblah which they used to face? Say: To God belong the east and the west﴾ [al-Baqarah: 142], meaning: all directions belong to God, so He may change the qiblah to whatever direction He wills. As for the second interpretation, the meaning is that the guidance is the guidance of God, and I have brought it to you, so this feeble scheme will not benefit you in repelling it.

* * *

Then He, exalted is He, said: ﴿that anyone be given the like of what you were given, or that they argue with you before your Lord.﴾

Know that this verse is among the difficult problems. We say: this either belongs to the speech of God, exalted is He, or it belongs to the speech of the Jews, as a completion of their saying, "do not believe except for one who follows your religion." Some of the exegetes have adopted each of these two possibilities.

As for the first possibility, there are several aspects:

The first: Ibn Kathir read ﴿an yu'ta﴾ with a lengthened alif as an interrogative, while the rest read it with an open alif without lengthening or interrogation. If we take the reading of Ibn Kathir, the meaning is clear, because this expression is established for reproach, as in His saying: ﴿Because he has wealth and sons﴾ and ﴿When Our verses are recited to him, he says: Tales of the ancients﴾ [al-Qalam: 14–15]. The meaning is: "Because someone is given laws like the laws you were given, do they deny following him?" Then the answer is omitted for brevity. This omission is common; a man, after long reproach to his companion and enumerating his sins against him after much kindness shown to him, says: "Is it because of my scant kindness to you? Is it because of my humiliating you?" The meaning is: "Because of this, did you do what you did?" A parallel to this is His saying: ﴿Is one who is devoutly obedient during the hours of the night, prostrating and standing, fearing the Hereafter and hoping for the mercy of his Lord?﴾ [al-Zumar: 9]. This aspect is transmitted from Mujahid and 'Isa ibn 'Umar. As for the reading of the one who reads with a short alif in "an", it is also possible to take it as carrying the sense of interrogation, as it was read: ﴿It is all the same for them whether you warn them or do not warn them﴾ [al-Baqarah: 6], with both lengthening and shortening; and likewise His saying: ﴿because he has wealth and sons﴾ [al-Qalam: 14], which is read with both lengthening and shortening. Imru' al-Qays said:

Do you depart from the tribe, or do you set out early? And what is upon you if you do not wait?

He meant: "Do you depart from the tribe?" and so he dropped the interrogative alif. When it is established that this reading admits the meaning of interrogation, the estimate is what we explained in the first reading.

The second aspect: when those people said to their followers, "Do not believe except for one who follows your religion," God, exalted is He, commanded His Prophet ﷺ to say to them: ﴿Indeed, the guidance is the guidance of God﴾, so do not deny ﴿that anyone be given﴾ from among others than you of guidance ﴿the like of what you were given﴾, and ﴿or that they argue with you﴾, meaning these Muslims by that, ﴿before your Lord﴾ if you do not accept that from them. The most that can be said is that this interpretation requires the implied phrase "so do not deny," because there is evidence for it, namely His saying: ﴿Indeed, the guidance is the guidance of God﴾, for since the guidance is the guidance of God, He has the right to give it to whomever He wills of His servants, and when that is so, it becomes obligatory not to deny.

The third aspect: the word "guidance" (al-huda) is a term for clarification, as in His saying: ﴿As for Thamud, We guided them, but they preferred blindness over guidance﴾ [Fussilat: 17]. So His saying ﴿Indeed, the guidance﴾ is the subject (mubtada'), His saying ﴿is the guidance of God﴾ is an apposition (badal) of it, and His saying ﴿that anyone be given the like of what you were given﴾ is the predicate (khabar) with the implied particle "lā" (not). The estimate is: "Say, O Muhammad: there is no doubt that the clarification of God is that no one be given the like of what you were given, and that is the religion of Islam, which is the best of religions; and that they (these Jews) not argue with you before your Lord in the Hereafter, because He will show them in the Hereafter that you are right and they are misguided." This interpretation has nothing except that the particle "lā" must be implied, and this is permissible, as in His saying: ﴿lest you go astray﴾ [al-Nisa': 176], meaning: lest you not go astray.

The fourth aspect: "al-huda" is a noun, and ﴿the guidance of God﴾ is an apposition of it, and ﴿that anyone be given﴾ is its predicate. The estimate is: "Indeed, the guidance of God is that anyone be given the like of what you were given." According to this interpretation, His saying ﴿or that they argue with you before your Lord﴾ requires an implied element, and the estimate is: "or that they argue with you before your Lord, so judgment is given in your favor against them." The meaning is: the guidance is that by which I guided you, the religion of Islam, that whoever argues with you by it before Me, I will decide in your favor against him. What is in His saying ﴿before your Lord﴾ indicates this implication, and because His ruling that He is their Lord indicates that He is pleased with them, and that suggests that He rules for them and not against them.

The second possibility: that His saying ﴿that anyone be given the like of what you were given﴾ is a completion of the speech of the Jews, and in it there is inversion (taqdim wa ta'khir). The estimate is: "Do not believe except for one who follows your religion that anyone be given the like of what you were given, or that they argue with you before your Lord. Say: Indeed, the guidance is the guidance of God, and indeed bounty is in the hand of God."

They said: the meaning is: "Do not reveal your faith by saying that anyone is given the like of what you were given except to the people of your religion. Keep secret your affirmation that the Muslims have been given from the books of God the like of what you were given, and do not disclose it except to your partisans alone, not to the Muslims, lest it increase them in firmness, and not to the polytheists, lest that call them to Islam."

As for His saying ﴿or that they argue with you before your Lord﴾, it is coordinated (ma'tuf) on "that anyone be given," and the pronoun in "yuhajjukum" (they argue with you) refers to "aḥad" (anyone), because it has the sense of the plural, in the sense of "do not believe except for your followers"; that the Muslims will argue with you on the Day of Resurrection with the truth and will overcome you before God with proof. In my view, this interpretation is weak, and its explanation is in several aspects:

The first: the earnestness of those people in preserving their followers from accepting the religion of Muhammad, peace be upon him, was greater than their earnestness in preserving others than their followers and partisans from it. How then is it fitting that some of them urge others to acknowledge what indicates the validity of the religion of Muhammad ﷺ before their followers and partisans, and to refrain from that before outsiders? This is in extreme remoteness.

The second: on this estimate the structure is disordered, and there is an inversion that does not befit the speech of eloquent people.

The third: on this estimate there must be omission, for the estimate would be: "Say: Indeed, the guidance is the guidance of God, and indeed bounty..." and "qul" (say) must be omitted in His saying: ﴿Say: Indeed, bounty is in the hand of God﴾.

The fourth: how did His saying ﴿Say: Indeed, the guidance is the guidance of God﴾ come between two parts of one speech? This is in extreme remoteness from upright speech. Al-Qaffal said: It is possible that His saying ﴿Say: Indeed, the guidance is the guidance of God﴾ is a statement that God commanded His Prophet to say at the end of the narration of the Jews at this point; because when He related from them at this point a false statement, He rightly taught His Messenger ﷺ to confront it with a true statement, and then returned to relating the completion of their speech, as when a Muslim relates from some disbelievers a statement containing disbelief, and when he reaches that word says: "I believe in God," or says: "There is no god but God," or says: "Exalted is God," then returns to completing the narration. So His saying, exalted is He, ﴿Say: Indeed, the guidance is the guidance of God﴾ is of this kind; then He mentioned after it the completion of the Jews' speech up to His saying ﴿or that they argue with you before your Lord﴾, then commanded the Prophet ﷺ to argue with them about this and to alert them to the falsehood of their saying, so it was said to him: ﴿Say: Indeed, bounty is in the hand of God﴾ to the end of the verse.

The fifth problem among these aspects: if faith (al-iman) means affirmation (al-tasdiq), it is not transitive to the one affirmed by the particle lām. One does not say "ṣaddaqtu li-Zayd" (I affirmed for Zayd); rather one says "ṣaddaqtu Zaydan" (I affirmed Zayd). So it should have been said: "Do not believe except one who follows your religion." And according to this estimate, one needs to omit the lām in His saying ﴿for one who follows your religion﴾ and to imply the preposition "bi" (with/that) or what takes its place in His saying ﴿that anyone be given﴾, because the estimate is: "Do not affirm except one who follows your religion, with the claim that anyone be given the like of what you were given." Thus in this exegesis there is combined omission, implication, poor structure, and corrupted meaning. Abu 'Ali al-Farisi said: It is not far-fetched to take faith as acknowledgment, so the meaning would be: "Do not acknowledge that anyone be given the like of what you were given except for one who follows your religion." On this estimate the lām is not extra, but there must in every case be an implied preposition "bi" or what takes its place. This is the summary of what has been said in the interpretation of this verse, and God knows best His intent.

Then He, exalted is He, said: ﴿Say: Indeed, bounty is in the hand of God; He gives it to whom He wills, and God is All-Encompassing, All-Knowing.﴾

Know that He, exalted is He, related from the Jews two matters: one of them: that they believe at the beginning of the day and disbelieve at its end, so that this would become a doubt for the Muslims regarding the validity of Islam. He answered it with His saying ﴿Say: Indeed, the guidance is the guidance of God﴾, and the meaning is: with the perfection of God's guidance and the strength of His clarification, this feeble doubt has no strength and no effect.

The second: He related from them that they denied that anyone be given the like of what they were given of the Book, the judgment, and prophethood.

Then He answered him with His saying: ﴿Say: Indeed, the bounty is in the hand of Allah; He gives it to whom He wills.﴾ By "the bounty" (al-fadl) is meant prophethood (al-risalah). Linguistically, al-fadl is an expression for an increase, and it is most often used for an increase in goodness; al-fadil is one who exceeds others in good qualities. Then the use of al-fadl became widespread for every benefit whose doer intends by it goodness toward another. His saying ﴿in the hand of Allah﴾ means that He is its Owner and is able over it. His saying ﴿He gives it to whom He wills﴾ means that it is a bounty (tafaddul) dependent on His will. This indicates that prophethood is attained by bounty, not by entitlement, because He, exalted is He, made it of the category of bounty, which its doer may do or may not do, and this cannot be applied to one who is entitled except in a figurative sense. His saying ﴿And Allah is All-Encompassing, All-Knowing﴾ confirms this meaning, because His being All-Encompassing (wasi') indicates perfection of power, and His being All-Knowing ('alim) indicates perfection of knowledge. Thus it is valid from Him, by virtue of power, that He bestow bounty upon whichever servant He wills with whatever bounty He wills, and it is valid from Him, by virtue of perfect knowledge, that none of His acts be except in accordance with wisdom and rightness.

Then He said: ﴿He singles out for His mercy whom He wills, and Allah is the Possessor of great bounty.﴾ This is like an emphasis of what came before. The difference between this verse and the one before it is that al-fadl is an expression for an increase, and an increase is of the same kind as that which it is added to. So by His saying ﴿Indeed, the bounty is in the hand of Allah﴾ He clarified that He is able to give some of His servants the like of what He gave them of high positions, and to increase upon them of the same kind. Then He said: ﴿He singles out for His mercy whom He wills.﴾ The mercy ascribed to Allah, glorified is He, is a matter higher than that bounty, for this mercy may reach such nobility and elevation of rank that it is not of the same kind as what He gave them, but is rather higher and more exalted than to be compared with what He gave them. It results from the two verses together that there is no limit to the degrees of Allah's honoring and ennobling of His servants, and that confining His bestowal and honoring to specific degrees and to specific persons is ignorance of Allah's perfection in power and wisdom.

As for His saying ﴿or that they argue with you before your Lord﴾, it is coordinated (ma'tuf) on "that anyone be given," and the pronoun in "yuhajjukum" (they argue with you) refers to "aḥad" (anyone), because it has the sense of the plural, in the sense of "do not believe except for your followers"; that the Muslims will argue with you on the Day of Resurrection with the truth and will overcome you before God with proof. In my view, this interpretation is weak, and its explanation is in several aspects:

The first: the earnestness of those people in preserving their followers from accepting the religion of Muhammad, peace be upon him, was greater than their earnestness in preserving others than their followers and partisans from it. How then is it fitting that some of them urge others to acknowledge what indicates the validity of the religion of Muhammad ﷺ before their followers and partisans, and to refrain from that before outsiders? This is in extreme remoteness.

The second: on this estimate the structure is disordered, and there is an inversion that does not befit the speech of eloquent people.

The third: on this estimate there must be omission, for the estimate would be: "Say: Indeed, the guidance is the guidance of God, and indeed bounty..." and "qul" (say) must be omitted in His saying: ﴿Say: Indeed, bounty is in the hand of God﴾.

The fourth: how did His saying ﴿Say: Indeed, the guidance is the guidance of God﴾ come between two parts of one speech? This is in extreme remoteness from upright speech. Al-Qaffal said: It is possible that His saying ﴿Say: Indeed, the guidance is the guidance of God﴾ is a statement that God commanded His Prophet to say at the end of the narration of the Jews at this point; because when He related from them at this point a false statement, He rightly taught His Messenger ﷺ to confront it with a true statement, and then returned to relating the completion of their speech, as when a Muslim relates from some disbelievers a statement containing disbelief, and when he reaches that word says: "I believe in God," or says: "There is no god but God," or says: "Exalted is God," then returns to completing the narration. So His saying, exalted is He, ﴿Say: Indeed, the guidance is the guidance of God﴾ is of this kind; then He mentioned after it the completion of the Jews' speech up to His saying ﴿or that they argue with you before your Lord﴾, then commanded the Prophet ﷺ to argue with them about this and to alert them to the falsehood of their saying, so it was said to him: ﴿Say: Indeed, bounty is in the hand of God﴾ to the end of the verse.

The fifth problem among these aspects: if faith (al-iman) means affirmation (al-tasdiq), it is not transitive to the one affirmed by the particle lām. One does not say "ṣaddaqtu li-Zayd" (I affirmed for Zayd); rather one says "ṣaddaqtu Zaydan" (I affirmed Zayd). So it should have been said: "Do not believe except one who follows your religion." And according to this estimate, one needs to omit the lām in His saying ﴿for one who follows your religion﴾ and to imply the preposition "bi" (with/that) or what takes its place in His saying ﴿that anyone be given﴾, because the estimate is: "Do not affirm except one who follows your religion, with the claim that anyone be given the like of what you were given." Thus in this exegesis there is combined omission, implication, poor structure, and corrupted meaning. Abu 'Ali al-Farisi said: It is not far-fetched to take faith as acknowledgment, so the meaning would be: "Do not acknowledge that anyone be given the like of what you were given except for one who follows your religion." On this estimate the lām is not extra, but there must in every case be an implied preposition "bi" or what takes its place. This is the summary of what has been said in the interpretation of this verse, and God knows best His intent.

* * *

Then He, exalted is He, said: ﴿Say: Indeed, bounty is in the hand of God; He gives it to whom He wills, and God is All-Encompassing, All-Knowing.﴾

Know that He, exalted is He, related from the Jews two matters: one of them: that they believe at the beginning of the day and disbelieve at its end, so that this would become a doubt for the Muslims regarding the validity of Islam. He answered it with His saying ﴿Say: Indeed, the guidance is the guidance of God﴾, and the meaning is: with the perfection of God's guidance and the strength of His clarification, this feeble doubt has no strength and no effect.

The second: He related from them that they denied that anyone be given the like of what they were given of the Book, the judgment, and prophethood.

Then He answered him with His saying: ﴿Say: Indeed, the bounty is in the hand of Allah; He gives it to whom He wills.﴾ By "the bounty" (al-fadl) is meant prophethood (al-risalah). Linguistically, al-fadl is an expression for an increase, and it is most often used for an increase in goodness; al-fadil is one who exceeds others in good qualities. Then the use of al-fadl became widespread for every benefit whose doer intends by it goodness toward another. His saying ﴿in the hand of Allah﴾ means that He is its Owner and is able over it. His saying ﴿He gives it to whom He wills﴾ means that it is a bounty (tafaddul) dependent on His will. This indicates that prophethood is attained by bounty, not by entitlement, because He, exalted is He, made it of the category of bounty, which its doer may do or may not do, and this cannot be applied to one who is entitled except in a figurative sense. His saying ﴿And Allah is All-Encompassing, All-Knowing﴾ confirms this meaning, because His being All-Encompassing (wasi') indicates perfection of power, and His being All-Knowing ('alim) indicates perfection of knowledge. Thus it is valid from Him, by virtue of power, that He bestow bounty upon whichever servant He wills with whatever bounty He wills, and it is valid from Him, by virtue of perfect knowledge, that none of His acts be except in accordance with wisdom and rightness.

Page 88

Then He said: ﴿He singles out for His mercy whom He wills, and Allah is the Possessor of great bounty.﴾ This is like an emphasis of what came before. The difference between this verse and the one before it is that al-fadl is an expression for an increase, and an increase is of the same kind as that which it is added to. So by His saying ﴿Indeed, the bounty is in the hand of Allah﴾ He clarified that He is able to give some of His servants the like of what He gave them of high positions, and to increase upon them of the same kind. Then He said: ﴿He singles out for His mercy whom He wills.﴾ The mercy ascribed to Allah, glorified is He, is a matter higher than that bounty, for this mercy may reach such nobility and elevation of rank that it is not of the same kind as what He gave them, but is rather higher and more exalted than to be compared with what He gave them. It results from the two verses together that there is no limit to the degrees of Allah's honoring and ennobling of His servants, and that confining His bestowal and honoring to specific degrees and to specific persons is ignorance of Allah's perfection in power and wisdom.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 3, verse 75–76:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And among the People of the Book is one who, if you entrust him with a qintar, will return it to you; and among them is one who, if you entrust him with a dinar, will not return it to you unless you keep standing over him. That is because they say, "There is no blame upon us regarding the unlettered." And they speak falsehood against Allah while they know.﴾ ﴿Yes, whoever fulfills his covenant and fears Allah – indeed, Allah loves the righteous.﴾

Know that the connection of this verse with what precedes it is in two respects:

The first: He, exalted is He, related about them in the previous verse that they claimed they had been given religious positions that no one else had been given the like of. Then He, exalted is He, made clear that treachery is considered abhorrent by all the adherents of religions, and yet they persist in it, and this indicates their lying.

The second: When He, exalted is He, related in the previous verse the ugly aspects of their conduct regarding religion, namely that they said: ﴿Do not believe except in one who follows your religion﴾, He related in this verse some of their ugly conduct regarding dealings with people, namely their persistence in treachery and injustice and taking people's wealth, in little and in much.

Here there are several issues:

The first issue: The verse indicates their division into two groups: some of them are people of trustworthiness, and some of them are people of treachery. And there are sayings on this:

The first: that the people of trustworthiness among them are those who embraced Islam, while those who remained on Judaism persist in treachery, because their doctrine is that it is lawful for them to kill anyone who opposes them in religion and to take their property. A parallel to this verse is His saying: ﴿They are not all alike. Among the People of the Book is an upright community who recite the verses of Allah during the night, prostrating﴾ [Al-Imran: 113], together with His saying: ﴿Among them are believers, but most of them are defiantly disobedient﴾ [Al-Imran: 110].

The second: that the people of trustworthiness are the Christians, and the people of treachery are the Jews. The evidence for this is what we mentioned, that the doctrine of the Jews is that it is lawful to kill the opponent and to take his property by any means.

The third: Ibn Abbas said: A man deposited with Abdullah ibn Salam a thousand and two hundred uqiyya of gold, and he returned it to him. Another deposited a dinar with Finhas ibn Azura, and he betrayed him, so the verse was revealed.

The second issue: It is said: "amintuhu bi kadha" and "ala kadha," just as one says "marartu bihi" and "alayhi." So the meaning of the ba' is the attachment of the trust, and the meaning of 'ala is the elevation of the trust. Whoever is entrusted with something, that thing becomes in the sense of being attached to him, because of his nearness to it and his connection with its safekeeping and preservation. Also, the depositary becomes like one who is elevated over that trust and who controls it. Therefore it is fine to express this meaning with either expression. It is also said: the meaning of your saying "amintuka bi dinar" is "I trusted you with it," and your saying "amintuka 'alayhi" means "I made you a trustee over it and a guardian of it."

The third issue: The purpose of mentioning the qintar and the dinar here is the large quantity and the small quantity; that is, among them is one who is at the extreme of trustworthiness, so that if he is entrusted with large amounts of wealth he fulfills the trust in them, and among them is one who is at the extreme of treachery, so that if he is entrusted with a small thing he permits treachery in it. A parallel is His saying: ﴿And if you desire to replace a wife with another and you have given one of them a qintar, do not take from it anything﴾ [An-Nisa: 20]. On this view there is no need for us to mention the measure of the qintar, but they mentioned several views about it:

The first: that the qintar is a thousand and two hundred uqiyya. They said: because the verse was revealed concerning Abdullah ibn Salam when a man of Quraysh deposited with him a thousand and two hundred uqiyya of gold, and he returned it and did not betray it; this indicates that the qintar is that amount.

The second: It has been narrated from Ibn Abbas that it is the filling of an ox-hide with wealth.

The third: It is said the qintar is a thousand thousand dinars or a thousand thousand dirhams, and the discussion of the interpretation of the qintar has already passed.

The fourth issue: Hamza and Asim, in the narration of Abu Bakr, read "yu'addihi" with a sukun on the ha'. This is also narrated from Abu Amr. Al-Zajjaj said: This is an error by the narrator from Abu Amr, just as he erred in "bari'kum" with a sukun on the hamza; rather, Abu Amr used to rapidly reduce the vowel (ikhtilas). Al-Zajjaj argued against the soundness of this reading by saying: the jazm (apocope) is not on the ha', but on what precedes the ha', and the ha' is a pronoun, and pronouns are not put in jazm in connected speech. Al-Farra' said: Some Arabs apocopate the ha' when the letter before it is vowelled, so they say "dharabtuhu darban shadidan," just as they make the mim of "antum" and "qumtum" quiescent, though its original is raf'. He recited:

When he saw that there was neither abundance nor satiety

It was also recited with the ikhtilas of the vowel of the ha', relying on the kasra from the ya', and it was recited with the full vowel (ishbaa') of the kasra on the ha', which is the original form.

* * *

Then He, exalted is He, said: ﴿And among them is one who, if you entrust him with a dinar, will not return it to you unless you keep standing over him﴾, and in this there are two issues:

The first issue: Regarding the word "qa'im" there are two views. Some took it in its literal sense. Al-Suddi said: it means "unless you remain standing over his head, in company with him and accompanying him." The meaning is that he acknowledges what you gave him only as long as you stand over his head; if you grant him respite and delay, he denies it. Others took the word "qa'im" in its figurative sense, and they mentioned several views about it:

The first: Ibn Abbas said: what is meant by this standing is insistence, dispute, demanding repayment, and claiming. Ibn Qutayba said: its origin is that the one who claims a thing "stands" in it, and the one who abandons it "sits" away from it. The evidence is His saying: ﴿an upright community﴾, that is, acting by the command of Allah without abandoning it. Then it was said of everyone who persists in demanding a matter that he "stood" with it, even if there was no actual standing.

The second: Abu Ali al-Farisi said: qiyam in the language means continuance and steadfastness, and we have discussed this in His saying: ﴿they establish the prayer﴾. From it is His saying: ﴿a upright religion (dinan qiyaman)﴾, that is, lasting, firm, not abrogated. So the meaning of His saying: ﴿unless you keep standing over him﴾ is: continuing firmly in your demand of that wealth from him.

The second issue: Included under His saying: ﴿whom if you entrust with a qintar﴾ and "with a dinar" are both specie and debt, because a person may entrust another with a deposit, or with a sale, or with a partnership on profit (muqaradah). There is nothing in the verse that specifies one of these. What is transmitted from Ibn Abbas is that he took it to mean a sale: he said, "Among them is one with whom you deal for a price of a qintar, and he pays it to you; and among them is one with whom you deal for a price of a dinar, and he does not pay it to you." We have also transmitted that the verse was revealed concerning a man who deposited a large amount of wealth with Abdullah ibn Salam and a small amount with Finhas ibn Azura, and this Jew betrayed in the small amount while Abdullah ibn Salam fulfilled the trust. Thus it is established that the wording is open to all these divisions.

* * *

Then He, exalted is He, said: ﴿That is because they say, "There is no blame upon us regarding the unlettered."﴾ The meaning is that this permitting and treachery is due to their saying: there is no blame on us for what we have taken of the wealth of the Arabs.

Here there are issues:

The first issue: They mentioned, regarding the cause for which the Jews believed in this permissibility, several views:

The first: they are exaggerated in their zeal for their religion, so they inevitably say: it is lawful to kill the opponent and to take his wealth by any means. It is narrated in a report that when this verse was revealed, the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "The enemies of Allah have lied. Nothing from the time of ignorance is not under my feet, except trust, for it is to be rendered to the pious and the wicked."

The second: The Jews said: ﴿We are the sons of Allah and His beloved﴾ [Al-Ma'idah: 18], and creation are our servants, so no one has a claim against us if we consume the wealth of our servants.

The third: The Jews only made this statement not absolutely toward everyone who opposed them, but toward the Arabs who believed in the Messenger (ﷺ). It is narrated that the Jews had dealt with men in the time of ignorance, and when they embraced Islam, the Jews demanded the wealth from them, and they said: "You have no right against us, because you have abandoned your religion." I say: it is probable that it was among the doctrine of the Jews that whoever moved from one false religion to another false religion was in the status of an apostate. So although they believed that the Arabs were unbelievers, when they considered Islam to be unbelief, they judged the Arabs who had embraced Islam to be apostates.

The second issue: Negation of "sabil" (way/claim) means negation of the capacity to demand and to compel.

He, exalted is He, said: ﴿There is no way (sabil) against the good-doers﴾ [At-Tawbah: 91], and He said: ﴿And Allah will not grant the disbelievers a way over the believers﴾ [An-Nisa: 141], and He said: ﴿And whoever defends himself after being wronged, those – there is no way against them. The way is only against those who wrong people﴾ [Ash-Shura: 41–42].

The third issue: "Ummi" is attributed to "umm" (mother). The Prophet (ﷺ) was called "ummi." It is said: because he did not write; and this is because the "umm" is the origin of a thing, so whoever does not write remains upon his original state of not writing. It is also said: he was attributed to Makkah, which is "Umm al-Qura" (the mother of the towns).

* * *

Then He, exalted is He, said: ﴿And they speak falsehood against Allah while they know﴾, and in this there are several views:

The first: that they said that the permissibility of treachery toward the opponent is mentioned in the Torah, and they were lying in that and knew that they were lying in it; and whoever is like that, his treachery is greater and his crime more shameful.

The second: that they know treachery is forbidden.

The third: that they know the sin that falls upon the traitor.

* * *

Then He, exalted is He, said: ﴿Yes, whoever fulfills his covenant and fears Allah – indeed, Allah loves the righteous.﴾

Know that "bala" has two aspects:

One of them: that it is merely a negation of what precedes it, namely His saying: ﴿There is no way upon us regarding the unlettered﴾; so Allah, exalted is He, replies to them, rejecting: "Yes (bala), there is a way upon them in that." This is the view chosen by al-Zajjaj, who said: "In my view, the pause of completion is on 'bala' and what follows is a new beginning."

The second: that the word "bala" is a word mentioned at the beginning of another speech that is mentioned after it, because their saying "there is no blame upon us in what we do" stands in place of their saying "we are the beloved of Allah, exalted is He." So Allah, exalted is He, mentioned that the people of fulfilling the covenant and piety are those whom Allah, exalted is He, loves, and no others. On this view, it is not good to pause on "bala." His saying: ﴿whoever fulfills his covenant﴾ — the discussion of the meaning of fulfilling the covenant has already passed. The pronoun in "bi'ahdihi" may refer to the name "Allah" in His saying: ﴿and they speak falsehood against Allah﴾, and it may refer to "man" (whoever), since "covenant" is a verbal noun which may be attributed to the object or to the subject. Here there are two questions:

The first question: On the assumption that the pronoun refers to the subject, which is "man," it is possible that if the People of the Book fulfilled their covenants and abandoned treachery, they would earn the love of Allah, exalted is He.

The answer: The matter is so, for if they fulfill covenants they fulfill first of all the greatest covenant, which is what Allah took from them in their Book concerning belief in Muhammad (ﷺ). And if they feared Allah in abandoning treachery, they would fear Him in abandoning lying against Allah and in abandoning distortion of the Torah.

The second question: Where is the pronoun returning from the consequent (jaza') to "man"?

The answer: The generality of "al-muttaqin" (the righteous) stands in place of the returning pronoun.

Know that this verse indicates the great importance of the matter of fulfilling covenants, because the acts of obedience are confined to two matters: magnifying the command of Allah, and compassion toward the creatures of Allah. Fulfilling a covenant includes both together, because it is a cause of benefit to creation, so it is compassion toward the creatures of Allah; and since Allah commanded it, fulfilling it is magnifying the command of Allah. Thus it is established that the expression includes all kinds of acts of obedience. And fulfilling a covenant, as it is possible with regard to others, is also possible with regard to oneself, because the one who fulfills the covenant with his own soul is the one who performs acts of obedience and abandons what is forbidden, for at that point the soul attains reward and is kept far from punishment.
