I say: it is probable that it was among the doctrine of the Jews that whoever moved from one false religion to another false religion was in the status of an apostate. So although they believed that the Arabs were unbelievers, when they considered Islam to be unbelief, they judged the Arabs who had embraced Islam to be apostates.

The second issue: Negation of "sabil" (way/claim) means negation of the capacity to demand and to compel.

He, exalted is He, said: ﴿There is no way (sabil) against the good-doers﴾ [At-Tawbah: 91], and He said: ﴿And Allah will not grant the disbelievers a way over the believers﴾ [An-Nisa: 141], and He said: ﴿And whoever defends himself after being wronged, those – there is no way against them. The way is only against those who wrong people﴾ [Ash-Shura: 41–42].

The third issue: "Ummi" is attributed to "umm" (mother). The Prophet (ﷺ) was called "ummi." It is said: because he did not write; and this is because the "umm" is the origin of a thing, so whoever does not write remains upon his original state of not writing. It is also said: he was attributed to Makkah, which is "Umm al-Qura" (the mother of the towns).

* * *

Then He, exalted is He, said: ﴿And they speak falsehood against Allah while they know﴾, and in this there are several views:

The first: that they said that the permissibility of treachery toward the opponent is mentioned in the Torah, and they were lying in that and knew that they were lying in it; and whoever is like that, his treachery is greater and his crime more shameful.

The second: that they know treachery is forbidden.

The third: that they know the sin that falls upon the traitor.

* * *

Then He, exalted is He, said: ﴿Yes, whoever fulfills his covenant and fears Allah – indeed, Allah loves the righteous.﴾

Know that "bala" has two aspects:

One of them: that it is merely a negation of what precedes it, namely His saying: ﴿There is no way upon us regarding the unlettered﴾; so Allah, exalted is He, replies to them, rejecting: "Yes (bala), there is a way upon them in that." This is the view chosen by al-Zajjaj, who said: "In my view, the pause of completion is on 'bala' and what follows is a new beginning."

The second: that the word "bala" is a word mentioned at the beginning of another speech that is mentioned after it, because their saying "there is no blame upon us in what we do" stands in place of their saying "we are the beloved of Allah, exalted is He." So Allah, exalted is He, mentioned that the people of fulfilling the covenant and piety are those whom Allah, exalted is He, loves, and no others. On this view, it is not good to pause on "bala." His saying: ﴿whoever fulfills his covenant﴾ — the discussion of the meaning of fulfilling the covenant has already passed. The pronoun in "bi'ahdihi" may refer to the name "Allah" in His saying: ﴿and they speak falsehood against Allah﴾, and it may refer to "man" (whoever), since "covenant" is a verbal noun which may be attributed to the object or to the subject. Here there are two questions:

The first question: On the assumption that the pronoun refers to the subject, which is "man," it is possible that if the People of the Book fulfilled their covenants and abandoned treachery, they would earn the love of Allah, exalted is He.

The answer: The matter is so, for if they fulfill covenants they fulfill first of all the greatest covenant, which is what Allah took from them in their Book concerning belief in Muhammad (ﷺ). And if they feared Allah in abandoning treachery, they would fear Him in abandoning lying against Allah and in abandoning distortion of the Torah.

The second question: Where is the pronoun returning from the consequent (jaza') to "man"?

The answer: The generality of "al-muttaqin" (the righteous) stands in place of the returning pronoun.

Know that this verse indicates the great importance of the matter of fulfilling covenants, because the acts of obedience are confined to two matters: magnifying the command of Allah, and compassion toward the creatures of Allah. Fulfilling a covenant includes both together, because it is a cause of benefit to creation, so it is compassion toward the creatures of Allah; and since Allah commanded it, fulfilling it is magnifying the command of Allah. Thus it is established that the expression includes all kinds of acts of obedience. And fulfilling a covenant, as it is possible with regard to others, is also possible with regard to oneself, because the one who fulfills the covenant with his own soul is the one who performs acts of obedience and abandons what is forbidden, for at that point the soul attains reward and is kept far from punishment.

[Page 92]

His statement, may He be exalted: ﴿Indeed, those who sell the covenant of God and their oaths for a small price — those will have no share in the Hereafter, and God will not speak to them, nor look at them on the Day of Resurrection, nor purify them, and for them is a painful punishment.﴾

Know that there are several aspects to how this verse relates to what precedes it:

The first: When He, exalted is He, described the Jews as treacherous with people's property, and it is well known that treachery with people's property is not carried out except through false oaths, He therefore mentioned, right after that verse, this verse which includes a warning against those who commit false oaths.

The second: When He, exalted is He, reported about them that they ﴿say about God what they know to be false﴾ (Al-Imran: 75), and there is no doubt that the covenant of God upon every accountable person is that he not lie about God and not betray His religion, He therefore mentioned this warning right after that.

The third: He, exalted is He, mentioned in the previous verse their treachery with people's property, then in this verse He mentioned their treachery regarding the covenant of God and their treachery in magnifying His names when they swear by them falsely. Some people said: this verse is the beginning of an independent statement prohibiting false oaths. This is because the wording is general, and many reports indicate that it was revealed concerning groups who committed false oaths. If that is so, it is necessary to hold that this warning is general with respect to everyone who does this act, and that it is not restricted to the Jews.

Regarding the verse, there are several issues:

The first issue: The reports differed concerning the occasion of revelation. Some restricted it to the Jews whose conditions God described in the preceding verses, and some restricted it to others.

As for the first view, there are two opinions:

The first: ʿIkrimah said: It was revealed concerning the rabbis of the Jews who concealed what God had covenanted with them in the Torah regarding the matter of Muhammad (ﷺ), wrote something else with their own hands, and swore that it was from God, so that the bribe would not escape them. Those who held this view cited His words in Surat al-Baqarah: ﴿And fulfill My covenant; I will fulfill your covenant﴾ (Al-Baqarah: 40).

The second: It was revealed concerning their claim that ﴿there is no blame upon us regarding the unlettered﴾ (Al-Imran: 75). They wrote a document about that with their own hands and swore that it was from God. This is the statement of al-Hasan.

As for the second possibility, there are several opinions:

The first: It was revealed concerning al-Ash'ath ibn Qays and an opponent of his regarding a piece of land. They brought their dispute before the Messenger of God (ﷺ), and he said to the man: "Bring your evidence." The man said: "I have no evidence." He said to al-Ash'ath: "Then the oath is upon you." Al-Ash'ath was about to swear, so God, exalted is He, revealed this verse. Al-Ash'ath then refrained from the oath, returned the land to the opponent, and acknowledged the truth. This is the statement of Ibn Jurayj.

The second: Mujahid said: It was revealed concerning a man who swore a false oath in order to sell his merchandise.

The third: It was revealed concerning ʿAbdan and Imru' al-Qays, who brought their dispute over a piece of land before the Messenger (ﷺ). The oath was directed at Imru' al-Qays, and he said: "Give me respite until tomorrow." Then he came the next day and acknowledged the land to him.

The closest view is to apply it to all of these.

So His statement ﴿Indeed, those who sell the covenant of God﴾ includes everything God has commanded, includes what evidence has established, includes the pledges taken on behalf of the Messenger, and includes what a person binds himself to, because all of that is part of the covenant of God which must be fulfilled.

He, exalted is He, said: ﴿And among them are those who made a covenant with God: "If He gives us of His bounty, we will surely give charity"﴾ (Al-Tawbah: 75), and so on. He said: ﴿And fulfill the covenant; indeed, the covenant will be questioned﴾ (Al-Isra': 34). He said: ﴿They fulfill vows﴾ (Al-Insan: 7). He said: ﴿Among the believers are men who were true to what they covenanted with God﴾ (Al-Ahzab: 23).

We have already discussed in Surat al-Baqarah the meaning of "purchase" (shira'). That is because the buyer takes something and gives something, so each of what is given and what is taken is a price for the other. As for oaths, their status is known: they are the swearing by which a person affirms his statement, whether it is a promise, a threat, a denial, or an affirmation.

* * *

Then He, exalted is He, said: ﴿Those will have no share in the Hereafter, and God will not speak to them, nor look at them on the Day of Resurrection, nor purify them, and for them is a painful punishment.﴾

Know that He, exalted is He, branched from that condition — which is buying with the covenant of God and oaths for a small price — five kinds of recompense. Four of them explain that they become deprived of reward, and the fifth explains that they fall into the most severe punishment. As for being barred from reward, know that reward (thawab) is an expression for pure benefit combined with honor.

The first, which is His statement ﴿those will have no share in the Hereafter﴾, indicates their deprivation of the benefits of the Hereafter.

The remaining three, which are His statement ﴿and God will not speak to them, nor look at them on the Day of Resurrection, nor purify them﴾, indicate their deprivation of honor and esteem.

The fifth, which is His statement ﴿and for them is a painful punishment﴾, indicates punishment. Now that I have pointed out this order, let us speak about the explanation of each of these five:

As for the first, His statement ﴿no share for them in the Hereafter﴾, the meaning is that they have no portion in the good of the Hereafter and its blessings. Know that this generality is conditioned, by the ijma' (scholarly consensus) of the community, on not repenting; for if he repents, the threat falls away by consensus. And according to our school it is also conditioned on not being pardoned, since He, exalted is He, said: ﴿Indeed, God does not forgive that He be associated with, but He forgives what is less than that for whom He wills﴾ (Al-Nisa': 48).

As for the second, His statement ﴿and God will not speak to them﴾, there is a question concerning it. He, exalted is He, said: ﴿So by your Lord, We will surely question them all, about what they used to do﴾ (Al-Hijr: 92–93), and He said: ﴿So We will surely question those to whom messengers were sent, and We will surely question the messengers﴾ (Al-A'raf: 6). So how can these two verses be reconciled with that verse? Al-Qaffal answered: The purpose of all these expressions is to show the intensity of God's wrath upon them. For whoever prevents another from speaking to him in this world does so out of the other's displeasure with him; and if a person is angry with another, he says to him, "I will not speak to you," and he may order that he be kept away from him, and say, "I do not want to see the face of so-and-so," and when his name is mentioned he does not mention him with good. So it is established that these expressions are metaphors (kinayat) for intense anger — we seek refuge in God from it — and this is the correct answer. Some people said: It is not far-fetched that God, majestic is His majesty, might make His friends hear His speech without an intermediary, as a special high honor reserved for His friends, and He will not speak to these disbelievers and wrongdoers, and the reckoning with them will be through the speech of the angels. Others said: The meaning of this verse is that He will not speak to them with speech that pleases them or benefits them. The one relied upon is the first answer.

As for the third, His statement ﴿nor look at them﴾, what is meant is that He will not look at them with kindness. It is said: "So-and-so does not look at so-and-so," and what is meant is the negation of regarding him as worthy of consideration and the withholding of kindness toward him. The reason for this figurative usage (majaz) is that whoever regards a person as worthy of consideration turns toward him and directs his gaze to him again and again. For this reason, God's looking came to be an expression for regarding someone as worthy and for kindness, even when there is no actual looking. It is not permissible that what is meant by this looking is seeing, because He sees them just as He sees others. Nor is it permissible that what is meant by looking is turning the pupil of the eye toward the object seen seeking to see it, because that is an attribute of bodies, and He, exalted is He, our God, is far above being a body. The opponent has used this verse to argue that looking when connected with the particle "ila" (toward) does not mean seeing; for otherwise it would follow in this verse that God would not be seeing them, and that is false.

As for the fourth, His statement ﴿nor purify them﴾, there are several views:

The first: That He will not cleanse them from the filth of their sins through forgiveness, but will punish them for them.

The second: He will not purify them, i.e., He will not praise them as He praises His righteous friends. Purification (tazkiyah) by the one who purifies a witness is praise from him toward him.

Know that God's purification of His servants may come through the tongues of the angels, as He said: ﴿And the angels will enter upon them from every gate: "Peace be upon you for what you patiently endured; how excellent is the final home"﴾ (Al-Ra'd: 23–24). He said: ﴿The angels will receive them: "This is your day which you were promised." ... "We are your allies in the life of this world and in the Hereafter"﴾ (Al-Anbiya': 103). And it may come without an intermediary: in this world, as in His statement ﴿the repentant, the worshippers﴾ (Al-Tawbah: 112), and in the Hereafter, as in His statement ﴿"Peace," a word from a Lord, Most Merciful﴾ (Ya-Sin: 58).

As for the fifth, His statement ﴿and for them is a painful punishment﴾: know that when He, exalted is He, explained their deprivation of reward, He explained that they are in severe, painful punishment.

﴿And among them is a group who twist their tongues with the Book, so that you may think it is from the Book, but it is not from the Book. And they say, "It is from Allah," but it is not from Allah. And they speak falsehood against Allah while they know.﴾

The meaning of this verse: It indicates that the preceding verse was revealed about the Jews without doubt, because this verse was revealed concerning the Jews and is joined (by ʿaṭf, conjunction) to what precedes it. This requires that the preceding verse was also revealed about the Jews. Know that *al-layy* (twisting) refers to bending a thing and turning it from straightness to crookedness. It is said: "I twisted his hand" (*layytu yadahu*); "the thing twisted" (*iltawā al-shayʾ*) when it deviated; "so-and-so twisted against me" (*iltawā fulān ʿalayya*) when he altered his character from uprightness to its opposite; "he twisted his tongue from such-and-such" when he changed it; and "he twisted so-and-so from his opinion" when he turned him away from it. In a hadith: "The procrastination of the wealthy is injustice." And Allah the Exalted says: ﴿and [they say], "Raʿina," twisting their tongues and attacking the religion﴾ [al-Nisāʾ: 46].

Having understood this principle, there are several interpretations of the verse:

The first: al-Qaffal, may Allah have mercy on him, said: His saying ﴿they twist their tongues﴾ means that they deliberately alter the word in its *iʿrab* (grammatical inflection, i.e., vowel endings), in a way that changes its meaning. This is common in the Arabic language, so it is not far-fetched in Hebrew. When they did such a thing with the verses indicating the prophethood of Muhammad (ﷺ) in the Torah, this is what was meant by His saying ﴿they twist their tongues﴾. This is an interpretation of great excellence.

The second: It is reported from Ibn ʿAbbas, may Allah be pleased with him and his father, that he said: The group whom Allah will not address on the Day of Resurrection, nor look at, wrote a book in which they confused the description of Muhammad (ﷺ) and mixed it with the book that contained the description of Muhammad (ﷺ). Then they said: ﴿This is from Allah﴾ [al-Baqarah: 79].

Having understood this, we say: The twisting of the tongue involves affectation, pretension, and artificiality, and this is blameworthy. So Allah the Exalted expressed their recitation of that false book by "twisting the tongue," as a censure and a reproach against them, and He did not express it by "recitation." The Arabs distinguish between words of praise and words of blame for the same thing: they say in praise "an eloquent orator" (*khaṭībun muṣqiʿun*), and in blame "a loud, verbose chatterer" (*mikthārun thartārun*).

So His saying ﴿And among them is a group who twist their tongues with the Book﴾ means the recitation of that false book, which is what Allah mentioned in His saying: ﴿So woe to those who write the Book with their own hands, then say, "This is from Allah"﴾ [al-Baqarah: 79]. Then He said: ﴿but it is not from the Book﴾, meaning it is not the true Book sent down from Allah. Two questions remain here:

The first question: To what does the pronoun in His saying "(*li-taḥsabūhu*) that you may think it" refer?

[p. 95]

Answer: To what is indicated by His saying ﴿they twist their tongues﴾, namely the altered text.

The second question: How is it possible for distortion to enter the Torah given its great fame among people?

Answer: Perhaps this act came from a small group, among whom collusion to distort was possible. Then they presented that altered text to some of the common people. On this assumption, the distortion is possible. But in my view, the more correct interpretation of the verse is another possibility: that the verses indicating the prophethood of Muhammad (ﷺ) required careful examination and reflection of the heart, while the people would raise confused questions and dark objections against them. Thus those proofs would become ambiguous to the listeners. The Jews would say: "God's intended meaning from these verses is what we have mentioned, not what you have mentioned." This is what was meant by the distortion and the twisting of tongues. This is similar to how, in our time, when a person of truth cites a verse of Allah's Book, the falsifier raises questions and doubts against him and says: "This is not what Allah intended, as you claim." So it is in this case as well.

\* \* \*

Then Allah the Exalted said: ﴿And they say, "It is from Allah."﴾ Know that some people said: There is no difference between His saying ﴿that you may think it is from the Book, but it is not from the Book﴾ and His saying ﴿they say, "It is from Allah," but it is not from Allah﴾; this statement was repeated in two different wordings for emphasis. But the verifiers (*al-muḥaqqiqūn*) said: There is a difference, because not everything that is not in the Book is not from Allah. The legal ruling is established sometimes by the Book, sometimes by the Sunnah, sometimes by consensus (*ijmāʿ*), and sometimes by analogy (*qiyās*), and all of it is from Allah.

So His saying ﴿that you may think it is from the Book, but it is not from the Book﴾ is a specific negation. Then the general negation is joined to it, when He said: ﴿they say, "It is from Allah," but it is not from Allah﴾. Also, it is possible that "the Book" means the Torah, and their saying "it is from Allah" means that it is found in the books of the other prophets, peace be upon them, such as Isaiah (Ashʿiyāʾ), Jeremiah (Armiyāʾ), and Habakkuk (Ḥaykūq). This is because the people, in attributing that distortion to Allah, were perplexed. If they found foolish and ignorant people who did not know the Torah, they attributed the altered text to the Torah. If they found intelligent people, they claimed that it is found in the books of the other prophets, peace be upon them, who came after Moses, peace be upon him.

Al-Jubbāʾī and al-Kaʿbī argued from this verse that the act of the servant is not created by Allah the Exalted. They said: If the twisting of the tongue through distortion and falsehood were a creation of Allah the Exalted, then the Jews would have spoken the truth in their saying "it is from Allah," and the statement of Allah the Exalted "it is not from Allah" would entail falsehood. That is because they attributed to Allah what is from Him, while Allah negates from Himself what is from Him. Then he said: "It is enough of a disgrace for a people who make the Jews more truthful than Allah!"

He said: No one may say that there is a difference between His saying ﴿that you may think it is from the Book, but it is not from the Book﴾ and His saying ﴿they say, "It is from Allah," but it is not from Allah﴾. If there is no difference, then the conjunction (*ʿaṭf*) is not fitting. Al-Kaʿbī also answered this question in two other ways:

The first: That a created thing being from the Creator is more emphatic than an ordered thing being from the one who orders it, and carrying the speech to the stronger meaning is more appropriate.

The second: That His saying ﴿and it is not from Allah﴾ is an absolute negation of its being from Allah, and this negates its being from Allah in any respect, so it must not be from Him either by creation or by command.

As for the objection of al-Jubbāʾī, that if we take His saying ﴿and they say, "It is from Allah"﴾ to be the speech of Allah, then repetition results: its answer is what we have mentioned, that His saying ﴿and it is not from the Book﴾ means that it is not found in the Book, and this does not prevent it from being a ruling of Allah the Exalted established by the saying of the Messenger or by another means. So when He said ﴿and it is not from Allah﴾, the negation of its being a ruling of Allah the Exalted was established, and on this interpretation the repetition disappears.

As for the first of the two answers given by al-Kaʿbī: its answer is that the reply must correspond to the question, and the people were not claiming that what they mentioned and did was a creation of Allah the Exalted; rather, they claimed that it is a ruling of Allah and descended in His Book.

Therefore His saying ﴿and it is not from Allah﴾ must refer to this meaning and not to anything else. And by this way the corruption of what he mentioned in the second answer becomes evident. And Allah knows best.

\* \* \*

Then Allah the Exalted said: ﴿And they speak falsehood against Allah while they know﴾. The meaning is that they deliberately commit that falsehood knowingly.

Know that if the intended meaning of the distortion is altering the words of the Torah and the grammatical inflection of its words, then those who undertake it must be a small group among whom collusion upon falsehood is possible. But if the intended meaning is confusing the indication of those verses regarding the prophethood of Muhammad (ﷺ) by casting doubts and objections into the lines of argument, then it is not far-fetched that a large number of people would agree upon it. And Allah knows best.

The Qur'anic commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 3, verses 79–80 (part 1 of 2):

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿It is not for a human being that Allah should give him the Scripture and wisdom and prophethood, and then he should say to the people, "Be servants of me rather than of Allah." Rather, [he would say], "Be people of the Lord (rabbaniyyin) by what you have been teaching of the Scripture and by what you have been studying."﴾ ﴿And He would not order you to take the angels and the prophets as lords. Would He order you to disbelief after you have submitted [to Allah]?﴾

Know that when He, may He be exalted, explained that the custom of the scholars of the People of the Book was distortion and alteration, He followed it with what indicates that among the things they distorted is what they claimed: that Jesus, peace be upon him, used to claim divinity and used to order his people to worship him. Therefore He said: ﴿It is not for a human being...﴾ and so on. Here there are several issues:

The first issue: concerning the occasion of revelation of this verse, there are several reports:

The first: Ibn 'Abbas said: When the Jews said, "Uzayr is the son of Allah," and the Christians said, "The Messiah is the son of Allah," this verse was revealed.

The second: It is said that Abu Rafi' al-Qurazi from among the Jews and the head of the delegation of Najran from among the Christians said to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ: "Do you want us to worship you and take you as a lord?" He, peace be upon him, said: "I seek refuge in Allah from worshipping other than Allah, or from ordering [anything] other than the worship of Allah. It is not for this that He sent me, nor for this that He commanded me." Then this verse was revealed.

The third:
Page 97
A man said: "O Messenger of Allah, we greet you as some of us greet one another. Should we not prostrate to you?" He, peace be upon him, said: "It is not befitting for anyone to prostrate to anyone other than Allah. But honour your Prophet and recognise the right of those who are entitled to it."

The fourth: When the Jews claimed that no one could attain the degrees of excellence and rank that they had attained, Allah, may He be exalted, said to them: If the matter is as you say, then it is necessary that you not occupy yourselves with enslaving and employing people. Rather, you must order people to obey Allah and submit to His commands. And then it would be incumbent upon you to urge people to acknowledge the prophethood of Muhammad ﷺ, because the manifestation of miracles through him necessitates that. This interpretation is admitted by the wording of the verse, for His saying ﴿then he should say to the people, "Be servants of me rather than of Allah"﴾ is like His saying: ﴿They have taken their rabbis and their monks as lords besides Allah﴾ [al-Tawbah: 31].

The second issue: They differed concerning the meaning of His saying ﴿It is not for a human being that Allah should give him the Scripture and wisdom and prophethood, and then he should say to the people, "Be servants of me rather than of Allah"﴾, in several ways:

The first: al-Asamm said: Its meaning is that if they had wanted to say that, He would have prevented them. The evidence for this is His saying: ﴿And if he had fabricated against Us some sayings, We would have seized him by the right hand﴾ [al-Haqqah: 44–45], and He said: ﴿And had We not strengthened you, you would have almost inclined toward them a little. Then We would have made you taste double [punishment] of life and double [punishment] of death﴾ [al-Isra': 74].

The second: The prophets, peace and blessings be upon them, are described with attributes such that, with those attributes, claiming divinity and lordship is not fitting. Among them: Allah, exalted is He, gave them the Scripture and revelation, and this occurs only in pure souls and good spirits, as Allah, exalted is He, said: ﴿Allah knows best where to place His message﴾ [al-An'am: 124], and He said: ﴿And We chose them with knowledge over the worlds﴾ [al-Dukhan: 32], and Allah, exalted is He, said: ﴿Allah chooses messengers from the angels and from mankind﴾ [al-Hajj: 75]. A pure soul is incapable of issuing this claim. Among them also: the bestowal of prophethood occurs only after the perfection of knowledge, and that does not allow this claim. In sum, a human being has two powers: theoretical and practical. As long as the theoretical power is not perfected with true sciences and knowledge, and the practical power is not purified of blameworthy character traits, the soul is not prepared to receive revelation and prophethood. The attainment of perfections in the theoretical and practical powers prevents such a saying and belief.

The third: Allah, exalted is He, does not honour His servant with prophethood and messengership unless He knows of him that he will not say such a statement.

The fourth: The Messenger claimed that he conveys the rulings from Allah, exalted is He, and he argued for the truth of this claim. So if he had commanded them to worship himself, then the proof of the miracle as evidence of his truthfulness would be invalidated, and that is impermissible. Know that what is meant by His saying ﴿It is not for a human being﴾ is not that this statement is forbidden to him, because that is forbidden to all creation. The apparent meaning of the verse indicates that it was not for him [to say that] only because Allah gave him the Scripture, wisdom and prophethood. Also, if the intended meaning were prohibition, it would not have been a refutation of the Christians in their claim about the Messiah, peace be upon him. For whoever claims that a man did an act, and it is said to him, "So-and-so is not permitted to do that," has not refuted him in what he claimed against him. Rather, their claim was that Jesus, peace be upon him, said to them, "Take me as a god besides Allah." So the meaning is then what we have mentioned. A parallel to this is His saying: ﴿It is not for Allah to take a son﴾ [Maryam: 35], in the sense of negating that for Himself, not in the sense of prohibition and forbidding. Likewise His saying: ﴿And it is not for a prophet to deceive﴾ [Al 'Imran: 161], where the meaning is negation, not prohibition. And Allah knows best.

The third issue: His saying ﴿that Allah should give him the Scripture and wisdom and prophethood﴾ refers to three things, which He mentioned in a sequence of great excellence. This is because the heavenly Scripture first descends, then its understanding comes into the intellect of the Prophet, and the reference to "wisdom" is to this. The people of language and tafsir agreed that this wisdom is knowledge, as He, exalted is He, said: ﴿And We gave him wisdom while he was a child﴾ [Maryam: 12], meaning knowledge and understanding. Then, when the understanding of the Scripture is attained, he conveys it to creation, and this is prophethood. How excellent is this sequence!

* * *

Then He, exalted is He, said: ﴿then he should say to the people, "Be servants of me rather than of Allah"﴾, and in it are two issues:

The first issue: The apparent reading is ثُمَّ يَقُولَ with the lām in the accusative (naṣb), and it is narrated from Abu 'Amr with the lām in the nominative (raf'). As for the naṣb, it is based on the presumption: "prophethood and this statement do not come together," and the governing element is "an" (that), which is coordinated with what precedes it, meaning: "then that he should say." As for the raf', it is on the basis of a new sentence (isti'naf).

The second issue: al-Wahidi related from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, that he said concerning His saying, exalted is He, ﴿Be servants of me﴾ that it is the dialect of Muzaynah, who say "ʿibādan" to mean slaves.

* * *

Then He said: ﴿But be people of the Lord (rabbaniyyin)﴾, and in it are two issues:

The first issue: In this verse there is an elision (idmar). The implied meaning is: "But rather he would say to them, 'Be rabbaniyyin'," so the saying was elided according to the Arab practice of permitting elision when the speech contains something that indicates it. A parallel to this is His saying: ﴿As for those whose faces will be blackened: "Did you disbelieve after your belief?"﴾ [Al 'Imran: 106], meaning: "it will be said to them that."

The second issue: They mentioned several views in explaining "rabbani" (rabbānī):

The first: Sibawayh said: The rabbānī is one attributed to the Lord (rabb), in the sense of being knowledgeable of Him and constant in His obedience, just as it is said: "a man is ilāhī" when he is devoted to knowing God and obeying Him. The addition of alif and nūn to it serves to indicate the perfection of this attribute, as they said: "sha'rānī" (hairy), "liḥyānī" (bearded), and "raqabānī" (thick-necked), when one is described as having abundant hair, long beard, or thick neck. When they attribute to hair they say sha'rī, to the neck raqabī, and to the beard liḥyī.

The second: al-Mubarrad said: "al-rabbāniyyūn" are masters of knowledge, singular rabbānī, who is one who nurtures knowledge and nurtures people, i.e., teaches them, reforms them, and takes charge of their affairs. The alif and nūn are for intensification, as they said: rayyān (quenched), 'aṭshān (thirsty), shab'ān (sated), 'uryān (naked). Then the nisbah yā' was added to it, as it is said liḥyānī and raqabānī. al-Wahidi said: According to Sibawayh's view, "rabbānī" is attributed to the Lord in the sense of being specialised in knowing the Lord and obeying Him, and according to al-Mubarrad's view, "rabbānī" is derived from upbringing (tarbiyah).

The third: Ibn Zayd said: The rabbānī is one who nurtures people, so the rabbāniyyūn are the rulers of the community and the scholars. He also mentioned this in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Why do the rabbaniyyun and the rabbis not forbid them?﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 63], meaning the rulers and the scholars, and these are the two groups who are obeyed. The meaning of the verse on this reading is: "I do not call you to be servants of me, but I call you to be kings and scholars by your enforcing the command of Allah, exalted is He, and your constancy in His obedience." al-Qaffal, may Allah have mercy on him, said: It is possible that the ruler was called rabbānī because he is obeyed as the Lord, exalted is He is obeyed, so he was attributed to Him.

The fourth: Abu 'Ubaydah said: I suppose this word is not Arabic; rather it is Hebrew or Syriac. Whether it is Arabic or Hebrew, it refers to a person who knows and acts on what he knows, and who busies himself with teaching the ways of goodness.

* * *

Then He, exalted is He, said: ﴿by what you have been teaching of the Scripture and by what you have been studying﴾, and in it are several issues:

The first issue: Regarding His saying ﴿by what you have been teaching of the Scripture﴾ there are two readings: one is (taʿlamūna), from knowledge ('ilm), and it is the reading of ʿAbd Allah ibn Kathir, Abu 'Amr and Nafi'. The second is (tuʿallimūna), from teaching (taʿlīm), and it is the reading of the rest of the Seven. Both are correct, because they used to know it within themselves and teach it to others. Abu 'Amr argued that his reading is preferable on two grounds:

The first: He said (tadrusūna) and did not say it with the doubling (tashdīd).

The second: Doubling requires two objects, and here the object is single. As for those who read with doubling, they claimed that the second object is omitted, its implied meaning being: "by what you have been teaching people the Scripture," or "others the Scripture," and it was omitted because the direct object is often omitted from speech. Then they argued that doubling is preferable on two grounds:

The first: Teaching includes knowledge but knowledge does not necessarily include teaching, so teaching is more appropriate.

The second: The rabbānīs do not suffice with knowledge until they add to it teaching for the sake of Allah, exalted is He. Do you not see that He, exalted is He, commanded Muhammad ﷺ with that, saying: ﴿Invite to the way of your Lord with wisdom and good instruction﴾ [al-Nahl: 125]? This is also indicated by the saying of Murrah ibn Sharahil: "ʿAlqamah was among the rabbānīs who taught people the Qur'an."

The second issue: Ibn Jinni related in al-Muhtasab, from Abu Haywah, that he read (tudrisūna) with a damma on the tā', a sukūn on the dāl, and a kasra on the rā'. Ibn Jinni said: This should be understood as transmitted from darasa (he studied) or darrasa (he taught others), just as he read "aqra'a" (he recited) in the sense of causing others to recite. Most Arabs use darasa and darrasa, and the verbal noun came in accordance with tadrīs.

The third question: "mā" in the two readings is the one that, together with the verb, has the meaning of a verbal noun (maṣdar). The implied sense is: "Be lordly (rabbaniyyin) because of your being knowledgeable and teachers, and because of your studying the Book." A similar case of "mā" with the verb meaning a verbal noun is His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿So today We forget them as they forgot the meeting of this their day﴾ [al-A'raf: 51]. The gist is that knowledge, teaching and study necessitate for their possessor that he be rabbani (lordly). The cause is necessarily other than the effect, so this requires that being rabbani is a matter different from being knowledgeable, being a teacher, and being constant in study. This can only be the case if his learning is for the sake of God, and his teaching and studying are for the sake of God. In summary, the one who motivates him toward all actions is the seeking of God's good pleasure, and what restrains him from all actions is fleeing from God's punishment. And if it is established that the Messenger commands all creation in this sense, it is established that it is impossible for him to command creation to worship him. The essence of the matter is one thing: the Messenger is the one whose utmost effort and striving is to turn spirits and hearts away from creation toward the Truth. How, then, could such a person possibly turn the minds of creation away from obedience to the Truth toward obedience to himself? At this point it becomes clear that it is impossible for any of the prophets — God's blessings be upon them — to command others to worship him.

The fourth question: The verse indicates that knowledge, teaching and study necessitate that a person become rabbani. Whoever engages in learning and teaching without this aim has wasted his effort and his work has failed, and he is like one who plants a beautiful tree, gracing the eye with its appearance, yet with no benefit in its fruit. For this reason the Prayer and Peace of God be upon him said: "We seek refuge in God from knowledge that does not benefit and a heart that does not humble itself."

* * *

Then He, may He be exalted, said: ﴿Nor would He command you to take the angels and the prophets as lords.﴾ On this there are several issues:

The first issue: ʿĀṣim, Ḥamzah and Ibn ʿĀmir read "wa-lā yamurakum" with a fatḥah on the rāʾ, while the rest read it with a ḍammah. As for the fatḥah reading, its basis is that it is coordinated (ʿaṭf) with "thumma yaqūla" (then he should say), and in this there are two possibilities:

One: that "lā" is taken as superfluous (mazīdah), and the meaning is: It is not for a human, to whom God has given the Book, the wisdom and prophethood, to say to people, "Be worshippers of me instead of God," and to command you to take the angels and the prophets as lords, just as you say, "It is not for Zayd that I should honor him, then he insults me and belittles me."

The second: that "lā" is not superfluous, and the meaning is that the Prophet ﷺ used to forbid the Quraysh from worshipping the angels, and the Jews and Christians from worshipping ʿUzayr and the Messiah. When they said, "Do you want us to take you as a lord?" it was said to them: It is not for a human whom God has made a prophet to then command people to worship himself and forbid them to worship the angels and the prophets. As for the reading with a ḍammah, as a new sentence (istiʾnāf), it is clear, since it comes after the verse has concluded and the speech is complete. Among what indicates the separation from the earlier part is what is narrated from Ibn Masʿūd, that he read: "wa-lan yamurakum" (and he will never command you).

The second issue: Al-Zajjāj said: "wa-lā yamurukumu Allāh" (God does not command you). Ibn Jurayj said: "lā yamurukum Muḥammad" (Muhammad does not command you). It was also said: "lā yamurukumu al-anbiyāʾ bi-an tattakhidhū al-malāʾikata arbāban kamā faʿalathu Quraysh" (the prophets do not command you to take the angels as lords, as Quraysh did).

The third issue: The angels and the prophets were specifically mentioned because those among the People of the Book who were described as worshipping other than God are not reported to have done anything but worship the angels and worship the Messiah and ʿUzayr. For this reason, He specified these two in mention.

* * *

Then He, may He be exalted, said: ﴿Would he command you to disbelieve after you have submitted?﴾ On this there are several issues:

The first issue: The interrogative hamzah in "a-yamurukum" carries the meaning of denunciation (inkār), that is, He does not do that.

The second issue: The author of al-Kashshāf said: His saying, ﴿after you have submitted﴾, is evidence that those addressed were Muslims, and they are the ones who asked the Messenger ﷺ for permission to prostrate to him.

The third issue: Al-Jubbāʾī said: The verse indicates the invalidity of the view of those who say that disbelief in God is ignorance of Him and belief in God is knowledge of Him. This is because God, exalted is He, judged these people to be disbelievers, as in His saying: ﴿Would he command you to disbelieve﴾. Yet these people were knowers of God, exalted is He, as evidenced by His saying: ﴿Then he should say to people, "Be worshippers of me instead of God"﴾, and the apparent sense of this indicates their knowledge of God. So when disbelief occurred here together with knowledge of God, this shows that belief in Him is not knowledge, and disbelief in Him is not ignorance of Him.

The response: Our saying that disbelief in God is ignorance of Him does not mean merely ignorance of His existence. Rather, we mean ignorance of His essence, His negative attributes, and His relational attributes, namely that He has no partner in being worshipped. So when one is ignorant of this, one has become ignorant of some of His attributes.

The Qur'anic commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 3, verses 79–80 (part 1 of 2):

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿It is not for a human being that Allah should give him the Scripture and wisdom and prophethood, and then he should say to the people, "Be servants of me rather than of Allah." Rather, [he would say], "Be people of the Lord (rabbaniyyin) by what you have been teaching of the Scripture and by what you have been studying."﴾ ﴿And He would not order you to take the angels and the prophets as lords. Would He order you to disbelief after you have submitted [to Allah]?﴾

Know that when He, may He be exalted, explained that the custom of the scholars of the People of the Book was distortion and alteration, He followed it with what indicates that among the things they distorted is what they claimed: that Jesus, peace be upon him, used to claim divinity and used to order his people to worship him. Therefore He said: ﴿It is not for a human being...﴾ and so on. Here there are several issues:

The first issue: concerning the occasion of revelation of this verse, there are several reports:

The first: Ibn 'Abbas said: When the Jews said, "Uzayr is the son of Allah," and the Christians said, "The Messiah is the son of Allah," this verse was revealed.

The second: It is said that Abu Rafi' al-Qurazi from among the Jews and the head of the delegation of Najran from among the Christians said to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ: "Do you want us to worship you and take you as a lord?" He, peace be upon him, said: "I seek refuge in Allah from worshipping other than Allah, or from ordering [anything] other than the worship of Allah. It is not for this that He sent me, nor for this that He commanded me." Then this verse was revealed.

The third:
Page 97
A man said: "O Messenger of Allah, we greet you as some of us greet one another. Should we not prostrate to you?" He, peace be upon him, said: "It is not befitting for anyone to prostrate to anyone other than Allah. But honour your Prophet and recognise the right of those who are entitled to it."

The fourth: When the Jews claimed that no one could attain the degrees of excellence and rank that they had attained, Allah, may He be exalted, said to them: If the matter is as you say, then it is necessary that you not occupy yourselves with enslaving and employing people. Rather, you must order people to obey Allah and submit to His commands. And then it would be incumbent upon you to urge people to acknowledge the prophethood of Muhammad ﷺ, because the manifestation of miracles through him necessitates that. This interpretation is admitted by the wording of the verse, for His saying ﴿then he should say to the people, "Be servants of me rather than of Allah"﴾ is like His saying: ﴿They have taken their rabbis and their monks as lords besides Allah﴾ [al-Tawbah: 31].

The second issue: They differed concerning the meaning of His saying ﴿It is not for a human being that Allah should give him the Scripture and wisdom and prophethood, and then he should say to the people, "Be servants of me rather than of Allah"﴾, in several ways:

The first: al-Asamm said: Its meaning is that if they had wanted to say that, He would have prevented them. The evidence for this is His saying: ﴿And if he had fabricated against Us some sayings, We would have seized him by the right hand﴾ [al-Haqqah: 44–45], and He said: ﴿And had We not strengthened you, you would have almost inclined toward them a little. Then We would have made you taste double [punishment] of life and double [punishment] of death﴾ [al-Isra': 74].

The second: The prophets, peace and blessings be upon them, are described with attributes such that, with those attributes, claiming divinity and lordship is not fitting. Among them: Allah, exalted is He, gave them the Scripture and revelation, and this occurs only in pure souls and good spirits, as Allah, exalted is He, said: ﴿Allah knows best where to place His message﴾ [al-An'am: 124], and He said: ﴿And We chose them with knowledge over the worlds﴾ [al-Dukhan: 32], and Allah, exalted is He, said: ﴿Allah chooses messengers from the angels and from mankind﴾ [al-Hajj: 75]. A pure soul is incapable of issuing this claim. Among them also: the bestowal of prophethood occurs only after the perfection of knowledge, and that does not allow this claim. In sum, a human being has two powers: theoretical and practical. As long as the theoretical power is not perfected with true sciences and knowledge, and the practical power is not purified of blameworthy character traits, the soul is not prepared to receive revelation and prophethood. The attainment of perfections in the theoretical and practical powers prevents such a saying and belief.

The third: Allah, exalted is He, does not honour His servant with prophethood and messengership unless He knows of him that he will not say such a statement.

The fourth: The Messenger claimed that he conveys the rulings from Allah, exalted is He, and he argued for the truth of this claim. So if he had commanded them to worship himself, then the proof of the miracle as evidence of his truthfulness would be invalidated, and that is impermissible. Know that what is meant by His saying ﴿It is not for a human being﴾ is not that this statement is forbidden to him, because that is forbidden to all creation. The apparent meaning of the verse indicates that it was not for him [to say that] only because Allah gave him the Scripture, wisdom and prophethood. Also, if the intended meaning were prohibition, it would not have been a refutation of the Christians in their claim about the Messiah, peace be upon him. For whoever claims that a man did an act, and it is said to him, "So-and-so is not permitted to do that," has not refuted him in what he claimed against him. Rather, their claim was that Jesus, peace be upon him, said to them, "Take me as a god besides Allah." So the meaning is then what we have mentioned. A parallel to this is His saying: ﴿It is not for Allah to take a son﴾ [Maryam: 35], in the sense of negating that for Himself, not in the sense of prohibition and forbidding. Likewise His saying: ﴿And it is not for a prophet to deceive﴾ [Al 'Imran: 161], where the meaning is negation, not prohibition. And Allah knows best.

The third issue: His saying ﴿that Allah should give him the Scripture and wisdom and prophethood﴾ refers to three things, which He mentioned in a sequence of great excellence. This is because the heavenly Scripture first descends, then its understanding comes into the intellect of the Prophet, and the reference to "wisdom" is to this. The people of language and tafsir agreed that this wisdom is knowledge, as He, exalted is He, said: ﴿And We gave him wisdom while he was a child﴾ [Maryam: 12], meaning knowledge and understanding. Then, when the understanding of the Scripture is attained, he conveys it to creation, and this is prophethood. How excellent is this sequence!

The third issue: Al-Jubbāʾī said: The verse indicates the invalidity of the view of those who say that disbelief in God is ignorance of Him and belief in God is knowledge of Him. This is because God, exalted is He, judged these people to be disbelievers, as in His saying: ﴿Would he command you to disbelieve﴾. Yet these people were knowers of God, exalted is He, as evidenced by His saying: ﴿Then he should say to people, "Be worshippers of me instead of God"﴾, and the apparent sense of this indicates their knowledge of God. So when disbelief occurred here together with knowledge of God, this shows that belief in Him is not knowledge, and disbelief in Him is not ignorance of Him.

The response: Our saying that disbelief in God is ignorance of Him does not mean merely ignorance of His existence. Rather, we mean ignorance of His essence, His negative attributes, and His relational attributes, namely that He has no partner in being worshipped. So when one is ignorant of this, one has become ignorant of some of His attributes.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 3, verses 81–82 (part 1 of 2):

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And when Allah took the covenant of the Prophets: "Whatever I have given you of Scripture and wisdom, and then there comes to you a Messenger confirming what is with you, you must believe in him and you must support him." He said: "Do you affirm, and accept on that My burden?" They said: "We affirm." He said: "Then bear witness, and I am with you among the witnesses."﴾ ﴿Then whoever turns away after that, they are the defiantly disobedient.﴾

Know that the purpose of these verses is to enumerate matters established and known among the People of the Book, which indicate the prophethood of Muhammad (ﷺ), in order to cut off their excuse and to manifest their obstinacy. Among these matters is what Allah, exalted is He, mentions in this verse: that He, exalted is He, took the covenant from the Prophets to whom He gave the Scripture and wisdom, that whenever a Messenger came to them confirming what was with them, they would believe in him and support him. He informed that they accepted this, and He, exalted is He, judged that whoever turned back from this would be among the defiantly disobedient. This is the purpose of the verse. The upshot of the discourse is that He, exalted is He, made it obligatory upon all the Prophets to believe in every Messenger who came confirming what was with them. However, this one premise alone is not sufficient to establish the prophethood of Muhammad (ﷺ) unless another premise is joined to it, namely that Muhammad is the Messenger of Allah who came confirming what was with them.

At this point someone may say: this is establishing a thing by itself, since it establishes his being a Messenger by his being a Messenger.

The answer: what is meant by his being a Messenger is the manifestation of a miracle at his hands, and at that point this objection falls away, and Allah knows best. Let us return to the explanation of the words.

As for his saying, ﴿And when Allah took﴾, Ibn Jarir al-Tabari said: its meaning is: remember, O People of the Book, when Allah took the covenant of the Prophets. al-Zajjaj said: remember, O Muhammad, in the Qur'an, ﴿and when Allah took the covenant of the Prophets﴾.

As for his saying ﴿covenant of the Prophets﴾, know that the verbal noun (masdar) may be annexed to the agent or to the object. Thus it is possible that the covenant was taken from them, and it is possible that it was taken for them from others. For this reason they differed in the interpretation of this verse on these two readings.

As for the first possibility, that He, exalted is He, took the covenant from them that some of them would confirm others, this is the view of Sa'id ibn Jubayr, al-Hasan and Tawus, may Allah have mercy on them. It was also said that this covenant is specific to Muhammad (ﷺ), and this is narrated from Ali, Ibn Abbas, Qatada and al-Suddi, may Allah be pleased with them. The proponents of this view argued for its soundness in several ways:

The first: His saying, exalted is He, ﴿And when Allah took the covenant of the Prophets﴾ indicates that the one taking the covenant is Allah, exalted is He, and those from whom it is taken are the Prophets. There is no mention of the community in the verse, so it is not appropriate to turn the covenant to the community. It may be answered in several ways:

The first: according to the way you have stated, the covenant would be annexed to the one who is bound by it, and according to the way we have stated, its annexation to them is the annexation of the act to the agent, who is the one who binds (the one for whom the covenant is made). There is no doubt that the annexation of the act to the agent is stronger than its annexation to the object; and if not stronger, then at least equal. It is like saying "the covenant of Allah and His pledge," so the meaning is: "And when Allah took the covenant which Allah established for the Prophets over their nations."

The second: that what is meant is the covenant of the children of the Prophets, namely the Children of Israel, with the omission of the annexed noun, as one says: "Bakr ibn Wa'il did such and such, and Ma'add ibn Adnan did such and such," and what is meant is their descendants and their people; so likewise here.

The third: that what is meant by the word "the Prophets" is the People of the Book, and this term was applied to them in mockery of their claim, because they used to say: "We have more right to prophethood than Muhammad, upon him be prayers and peace, because we are the People of the Book, and the Prophets were from among us."

The fourth: that the word "Prophet" frequently occurs in the Qur'an with its intended meaning being his community, as Allah, exalted is He, says: ﴿O Prophet, when you divorce women﴾ [al-Talaq: 1].

The second argument of the proponents of this view: what is narrated that he, upon him be prayers and peace, said: "I have brought it to you white and pure; by God, if Musa ibn Imran were alive, he would have no choice but to follow me."

The third argument: what is narrated from Ali, may Allah be pleased with him, that he said: Allah, exalted is He, did not send Adam, peace be upon him, nor any of the Prophets after him, peace and blessings be upon them, except that He took from them the covenant that if Muhammad, peace and blessings be upon him, were sent while they were alive, they would surely believe in him and surely support him. This provides support for this view, and Allah knows best.

The second possibility: that the meaning of the verse is that the Prophets, peace and blessings be upon them, used to take the covenant from their nations that when Muhammad (ﷺ) is sent, they must believe in him and support him. This is the view of many scholars, and we have explained that the wording admits of it. They argued for its soundness with several arguments:

The first: what Abu Muslim al-Isfahani mentioned, saying: the apparent meaning of the verse indicates that those from whom Allah took the covenant are obliged to believe in Muhammad (ﷺ) at his sending, and all the Prophets, peace and blessings be upon them, would at the time of Muhammad's sending be among the dead, and the dead are not under obligation. So since those upon whom the covenant was taken are obliged to believe in Muhammad, peace be upon him, at his sending, and it is not possible to impose belief upon the Prophets at the sending of Muhammad, peace be upon him, we know that those upon whom the covenant was taken are not the Prophets themselves, but rather the nations of the Prophets. He said: what confirms this is that He, exalted is He, judged that those upon whom the covenant was taken would be defiantly disobedient if they turned away, and this description does not befit the Prophets, peace be upon them, but befits the nations.

al-Qaffal, may Allah have mercy on him, answered, saying: why should it not be possible that the meaning of the verse is that if the Prophets were alive, it would be obligatory upon them to believe in Muhammad, peace and blessings be upon him? A parallel to this is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿If you associate partners, your deeds will surely be voided﴾ [al-Zumar: 65], though Allah knew that he would never associate partners at all; but this statement came in the manner of supposition and hypothesis. So likewise here. And He said: ﴿And if he had fabricated against Us some sayings, We would have seized him by the right hand, then We would have cut from him the aorta﴾ [al-Haqqah: 44–46]; and He said concerning the angels: ﴿And whoever among them should say, "Indeed, I am a deity besides Him," We would recompense him with Hell. Thus do We recompense the wrongdoers﴾ [al-Anbiya: 29], although He informed about them that they do not precede Him in speech and that they fear their Lord above them; all of that came in the manner of supposition, and the reckoning is likewise here. We say: He named them defiantly disobedient on the supposition of turning away, for the name of disobedience (fisq) is no more grave than the name of associating partners (shirk), and He mentioned that in the manner of supposition, as in His saying: ﴿If you associate partners, your deeds will surely be voided﴾; so likewise here.

The second argument: that the purpose of this verse is that those who were in the time of the Messenger (ﷺ) should believe; and if the covenant was taken from them, that would be more effective in achieving this purpose than if it were taken from the Prophets, peace be upon them. It has been answered that the ranks of the Prophets, peace be upon them, are higher and more noble than the ranks of the nations; so when this verse indicates that Allah, exalted is He, made it obligatory upon all the Prophets to believe in Muhammad, peace be upon him, had they been alive, and that if they abandoned that they would become among the defiantly disobedient, then it is all the more fitting that belief in Muhammad (ﷺ) be obligatory upon their nations; so turning this covenant to the Prophets is stronger in achieving the aim by this way.

The third argument: what is narrated from Ibn Abbas that it was said to him: the companions of Abdullah recite: ﴿And when Allah took the covenant of those given the Scripture﴾ [Al 'Imran: 187], while we recite ﴿And when Allah took the covenant of the Prophets﴾. Ibn Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, said: Allah only took the covenant of the Prophets concerning their peoples.

The fourth argument: that this possibility is reinforced by His saying, exalted is He: ﴿O Children of Israel, remember My favor which I bestowed upon you, and fulfill My covenant, I will fulfill your covenant﴾ [al-Baqarah: 40], and by His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And when Allah took the covenant of those given the Scripture, "You must make it clear to the people and not conceal it"﴾ [Al 'Imran: 187]. This is the sum of what has been said on this subject, and Allah knows best what He intends.

* * *

As for His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Whatever I have given you of Scripture and wisdom﴾, there are several issues concerning it:

The first issue: the majority read "lamā" with a fatha on the lam; Hamza read it with a kasra on the lam; and Sa'id ibn Jubayr read "lammā" with a shadda. As for the reading with a fatha, it has two aspects:

The first: that "mā" is a relative pronoun, the clause following it is its relative clause, and its predicate is His saying: ﴿you must believe in him﴾. The implied sense is: "for that which I have given you of Scripture and wisdom, then there comes to you a Messenger confirming what is with you, you must believe in him." On this reading, "mā" is in the nominative as the subject, and the returning pronoun to the word "mā," which is its relative clause, is omitted; the sense is: "for what I have given you (it)," so the returning pronoun was omitted, as it is omitted in His saying: ﴿Is this the one whom Allah has sent as a Messenger?﴾ [al-Furqan: 41]. And there are two questions on this:

The first question: if "mā" is a relative pronoun, it is necessary that a reference back from the conjoined clause to the relative pronoun be present, otherwise it is not permissible. Do you not see that if you said: "the one whose father stood up, then Zayd set out," it would not be permissible?

And His saying ﴿then there comes to you a Messenger confirming what is with you﴾ contains no reference back to the relative pronoun. We reply: it is permissible, according to al-Akhfash, to place the apparent noun in the place of the pronoun, and the evidence for this is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, whoever fears Allah and is patient, then indeed Allah does not waste the reward of the doers of good﴾ [Yusuf: 90], and He did not say "then indeed Allah does not waste his reward"; and He said: ﴿Indeed, those who believe and do righteous deeds—indeed, We do not waste the reward of one who does good work﴾ [al-Kahf: 30], and He did not say "indeed We do not waste their reward." That is because the apparent noun mentioned stands in the place of the pronoun; so likewise here.

The second question: what is the function of the lam in His saying "lamā"? We reply: this lam is the lam of the beginning (lam al-ibtida'), like your saying "Zayd is surely better than Amr," and it is well placed before what functions as the object of an oath (al-muqsam 'alayhi), because His saying ﴿And when Allah took the covenant of the Prophets﴾ functions as an oath, and the meaning is: "He made them swear." This lam is the one that precedes the oath. This is the explanation of this statement.

The second aspect, which is the choice of Sibawayh, al-Mazini and al-Zajjaj: that "mā" here is the one that implies the meaning of a condition, and the sense is: "whatever I have given you of Scripture and wisdom, then there comes to you a Messenger confirming what is with you, you must believe in him." So the lam in His saying ﴿you must believe in him﴾ is the one that precedes the oath. As for the lam in "lamā," it is a lam that is sometimes omitted and sometimes mentioned, without any difference in meaning. Its parallel is your saying: "By God, if you do, I will do," where the particle "an" does not change the situation whether it is mentioned or omitted; so likewise here. On this reading, "mā" is in the accusative position governed by "ātaytukum," and "wa-jā'akum" is conjoined to "ātaytukum" and put in the jussive by the conjunction; and "la-tu'minunna bihi" is the answer of the condition. Sibawayh did not accept the first view because he does not allow placing the apparent noun in the place of the pronoun.

As for the reading "limā" with a kasra on the lam, its basis is that this is the lam of causation, as if it were said: He took their covenant for this reason, because whoever is given the Scripture and wisdom, his being singled out with this virtue obliges him to confirm all the other Prophets and Messengers. And "mā" on this reading is a relative pronoun. The full discussion of it is what we have already presented in the first aspect.

As for the reading "lammā" with a shadda, al-Zamakhshari, the author of the "Kashshaf," mentioned two aspects concerning it:

[Page 104]

The first: the meaning is: "When I gave you some of the Scripture and wisdom, and then a messenger came to you confirming what is with you, it became obligatory upon you to believe in him and support him." The second: the original form of *lamā* was *lamin mā*. They found the combination of three *mīms* burdensome: the two *mīms* and the *nūn* that changes into a *mīm* by assimilation into the *mīm*. So they dropped one of them, and it became *lamā*. Its meaning is: "Because of what I have given you, you shall most certainly believe in it." This is close in meaning to the reading of Hamzah.

The second issue: Nāfiʿ read *ātaynākum* with a *nūn*, for magnification (*al-tafkhīm*), while the rest read it with a *tāʾ*, for singularity (*al-tawḥīd*). Nāfiʿ's evidence is His saying: ﴿And We gave David the Psalms﴾ [al-Nisāʾ: 163], ﴿And We gave him judgment while a child﴾ [Maryam: 12], and ﴿And We gave them both the clear Book﴾ [al-Ṣāffāt: 117]. Also, this reading indicates greatness more clearly, so it carries more awe in the heart of the listener, and this context suits this meaning. The majority's evidence is His saying: ﴿He it is who sends down upon His servant clear signs﴾ [al-Ḥadīd: 9], and ﴿Praise be to God, who sent down upon His servant the Book﴾ [al-Kahf: 1]. Also, this reading is more consistent with what comes before this verse and what comes after it, because He, exalted is He, said before this verse: ﴿And when God took [the covenant]﴾, and said after it: ﴿My burden (iṣrī)﴾. Nāfiʿ answered this by saying that one of the doors of eloquence is changing the expression from the singular to the plural, and from the plural to the singular. He, exalted is He, said: ﴿And We made it a guidance for the Children of Israel: that you shall not take other than Me as Guardian﴾ [al-Isrāʾ: 2]. He did not say "other than Us," as He said "And We made it." And God knows best.

The third issue: He, exalted is He, mentioned the prophets in the third person, then said *ātaytukum* ("I gave you"), which is direct address after an implied (*iḍmār*) shift. The estimate is: "And when God took the covenant of the prophets, He said, addressing them, 'Whatever I have given you of a Book and wisdom...'" The use of implied words (*iḍmār*) is a wide matter in the Qurʾan. Some scholars adopted another implied word in this verse and relieved themselves of those strained explanations that we have related from the grammarians. They said: the estimate of the verse is: "And when God took the covenant of the prophets: you shall certainly convey to the people what I have given you of a Book and wisdom." He said: but He omitted *latuballigunna* ("you shall certainly convey") because the meaning indicates it, since the *lām* of the oath only falls upon a verb. So when this *lām* indicated this verb, he omitted it for brevity. Then He, exalted is He, said after it: ﴿Then there came to you a messenger confirming what is with you﴾, and that is Muḥammad (ﷺ), ﴿you shall certainly believe in him and certainly support him﴾. With this estimate the structure is coherent and does not need those forced explanations. And if it is necessary to adopt an implied word, then this implied word through which the speech is arranged in a clear and evident order is better than those strained explanations.

The fourth issue: in His saying ﴿what I have given you of a Book﴾ there is a difficulty, namely that this address is either to the prophets or to the nations. If it is to the prophets, then not all prophets were given a Book; only some of them were. If it is to the nations, the difficulty is more apparent. The answer to it is from two aspects:

The first: all the prophets, peace be upon them, were given the Book in the sense that he was guided by it and called to act upon it, even if it was not revealed to him.

The second: the most noble of the prophets, peace be upon them, are those who were given the Book, so He described all by the description of the most noble category.

The fifth issue: the Book is what is revealed and recited, and wisdom is the revelation that brings detailed obligations which the Book did not include.

The sixth issue: the word *min* in His saying (*min kitāb*, "of a Book") entered as an explanation of *mā* (what), like your saying: "What I have of paper is two *dānaqs*."

* * *

As for His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Then there came to you a messenger confirming what is with you﴾, there are questions about it.

The first question: what is the meaning of His saying ﴿Then there came to you﴾, since a messenger does not come to the prophets, but comes to the nations?

The answer: if we take His saying ﴿And when God took the covenant of the prophets﴾ to mean taking the covenant of their nations, the question disappears. If we take it to mean taking the covenant of the prophets themselves, then His saying ﴿Then there came to you﴾ means: came in your time.

The second question: how can Muḥammad (ﷺ) be confirming what is with them when his law differs from their law?

[Page 105]

We say: what is intended is agreement in monotheism, prophethood, and the foundations of the laws. As for their details, even if disagreement occurs concerning them, that in reality is not disagreement, because all the prophets, peace be upon them, agree that the truth in the time of Mūsā, peace be upon him, was nothing but his law, and that the truth in the time of Muḥammad (ﷺ) is nothing but his law. So this, although it appears to be disagreement, is in reality agreement. Also, what is meant by His saying ﴿Then there came to you a messenger confirming what is with you﴾ is Muḥammad (ﷺ), and what is meant by his confirming what is with them is that his description and the manner of his circumstances are mentioned in the Torah and the Gospel. So when he appeared with circumstances matching what was mentioned in those books, his very coming was a confirmation of what was with them. This is what is meant by his confirming what is with them.

The third question: the sum of the speech is that God took the covenant from all the prophets to believe in every messenger who comes confirming what is with them. So what is the meaning of that covenant?

The answer: it may be that this covenant is what was established in their intellects of the proofs indicating that submission to God's command is obligatory. So when the messenger comes, he is only a messenger upon the appearance of the miracles that indicate his truthfulness. Then, when he informs them afterward that God commanded creation to believe in him, they then recognize its obligation. So the establishing of this proof in their intellects is what is meant by taking the covenant. It may also be that what is meant by taking the covenant is that He, exalted is He, explained His attributes in the books of the earlier prophets. So when his circumstances match what came in the earlier divine books, obedience to him becomes obligatory. Thus His saying, exalted is He, ﴿Then there came to you a messenger confirming what is with you﴾ indicates these two aspects. As for the first aspect, it is His saying "messenger" (*rasūl*). As for the second aspect, it is His saying ﴿confirming what is with you﴾.

* * *

As for His saying: ﴿you shall certainly believe in him and certainly support him﴾, the meaning is clear, because He, exalted is He, first made believing in him obligatory, then engaging in supporting him second. The *lām* in *latu'minunna bihi* ("you shall certainly believe in him") is the *lām* of the oath, as if it were said: "By God, you shall certainly believe in him."

* * *

Then He, exalted is He, said: ﴿He said: "Do you affirm and accept My burden (iṣrī) on that?"﴾ There are issues concerning this:

The first issue: if we interpret His saying, exalted is He, ﴿And when God took the covenant of the prophets﴾ as meaning that He, exalted is He, took the covenants from the prophets, then His saying ﴿Do you affirm?﴾ means: God, exalted is He, said to the prophets: "Do you affirm belief in Him and support for Him?" If we interpret the taking of the covenant as meaning that the prophets, peace be upon them, took the covenants from the nations, then the meaning of His saying ﴿He said: "Do you affirm?"﴾ is: every prophet said to his nation, "Do you affirm?" This is because He, exalted is He, attributed the taking of the covenant to Himself, though the prophets took it from the nations. Likewise, the request for this affirmation He attributed to Himself, though it was made by the prophets, peace be upon them. The purpose is that the prophets exaggerated in establishing and emphasizing this meaning. They did not limit themselves to taking the covenant from the nations, but demanded from them an affirmation in words, and confirmed that with testimony.

The second issue: *al-iqrār* ("affirmation") in the language is transferred with an *alif* (in causative form) from *qarra al-shayʾ yaqirru*, when a thing is established and remains in its place, and *aqarrahu* is when someone else causes it to remain. And one who affirms (*al-muqirr*) something acknowledges it against himself, that is, he establishes it.

As for His saying, exalted is He, ﴿Do you affirm and accept My burden (iṣrī) on that?﴾, that means: "Have you accepted My covenant?" Taking in the sense of accepting is common in speech. He, exalted is He, said: ﴿nor shall ransom be accepted from it﴾ [al-Baqarah: 48], meaning ransom will not be accepted from it. And He said: ﴿and He takes the charities﴾ [al-Tawbah: 104], meaning He accepts them. The *iṣr* is what befalls a person because of the work that is binding on him. He, exalted is He, said: ﴿and do not lay upon us a burden (iṣran)﴾ [al-Baqarah: 286]. So He named the covenant *iṣr* for this meaning. The author of *al-Kashshāf* said: the covenant was named *iṣr* because it is something that is bound (*yuʾṣar*), that is, tied and knotted, and from it comes *al-iṣār* with which something is tied. It is recited as *iṣrī*. It is also permissible that it is a dialectal form of *iṣr*.

* * *

Then He, exalted is He, said: ﴿They said: "We affirm." He said: "Then bear witness, and I am with you among the witnesses."﴾ There are several interpretations of His saying ﴿Then bear witness﴾:

The first: let some of you bear witness against others concerning the affirmation, and I am, with your affirmation and the witnessing of some of you for others, ﴿among the witnesses﴾. This is an emphasis upon them and a warning against retraction, since they know the testimony of God and the testimony of some of them against others.

The second: His saying ﴿Then bear witness﴾ is addressed to the angels.

The third: His saying ﴿Then bear witness﴾ means: let each person make himself a witness against himself. Its parallel is His saying: ﴿And He made them testify concerning themselves: "Am I not your Lord?" They said: "Yes, we testify"﴾ [al-Aʿrāf: 172], that is, against ourselves. This is of the category of hyperbole.

The fourth: ﴿Then bear witness﴾ means: make this covenant clear to the elite and the common people, so that no one has an excuse for ignorance of it. Its root meaning is that the witness is the one who makes clear the truth of a claim.

The fifth: ﴿Then bear witness﴾ means: be certain of what I have established upon you of this covenant, and be in it like one who sees the thing directly.

The sixth: if we say that the taking of the covenant was from the nations, then His saying ﴿Then bear witness﴾ is addressed to the prophets, peace be upon them, that they should be witnesses over them.

* * *

As for His saying, exalted is He: ﴿and I am with you among the witnesses﴾, it is for emphasis and for strengthening the obligation. There is another benefit in it, namely that He, exalted is He, although He made another witness, does not need that witnessing, because nothing is hidden from Him, but for a kind of benefit. He, glory be to Him and exalted is He, knows the secret and what is more hidden. Then He, exalted is He, added to it another emphasis, saying: ﴿Then whoever turns away after that, those are the defiantly disobedient (al-fāsiqūn)﴾, meaning: whoever turns away from believing in this Messenger and supporting him after these proofs have preceded is among the defiantly disobedient. The threat against the defiantly disobedient is known. His saying ﴿Then whoever turns away after that﴾ is a condition (*sharṭ*), and the past verb turns into the future in the condition and its response. And God knows best.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 3, verses 81–82 (part 1 of 2):

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And when Allah took the covenant of the Prophets: "Whatever I have given you of Scripture and wisdom, and then there comes to you a Messenger confirming what is with you, you must believe in him and you must support him." He said: "Do you affirm, and accept on that My burden?" They said: "We affirm." He said: "Then bear witness, and I am with you among the witnesses."﴾ ﴿Then whoever turns away after that, they are the defiantly disobedient.﴾

Know that the purpose of these verses is to enumerate matters established and known among the People of the Book, which indicate the prophethood of Muhammad (ﷺ), in order to cut off their excuse and to manifest their obstinacy. Among these matters is what Allah, exalted is He, mentions in this verse: that He, exalted is He, took the covenant from the Prophets to whom He gave the Scripture and wisdom, that whenever a Messenger came to them confirming what was with them, they would believe in him and support him. He informed that they accepted this, and He, exalted is He, judged that whoever turned back from this would be among the defiantly disobedient. This is the purpose of the verse. The upshot of the discourse is that He, exalted is He, made it obligatory upon all the Prophets to believe in every Messenger who came confirming what was with them. However, this one premise alone is not sufficient to establish the prophethood of Muhammad (ﷺ) unless another premise is joined to it, namely that Muhammad is the Messenger of Allah who came confirming what was with them.

At this point someone may say: this is establishing a thing by itself, since it establishes his being a Messenger by his being a Messenger.

The answer: what is meant by his being a Messenger is the manifestation of a miracle at his hands, and at that point this objection falls away, and Allah knows best. Let us return to the explanation of the words.

As for his saying, ﴿And when Allah took﴾, Ibn Jarir al-Tabari said: its meaning is: remember, O People of the Book, when Allah took the covenant of the Prophets. al-Zajjaj said: remember, O Muhammad, in the Qur'an, ﴿and when Allah took the covenant of the Prophets﴾.

As for his saying ﴿covenant of the Prophets﴾, know that the verbal noun (masdar) may be annexed to the agent or to the object.
