Thus it is possible that the covenant was taken from them, and it is possible that it was taken for them from others. For this reason they differed in the interpretation of this verse on these two readings.

As for the first possibility, that He, exalted is He, took the covenant from them that some of them would confirm others, this is the view of Sa'id ibn Jubayr, al-Hasan and Tawus, may Allah have mercy on them. It was also said that this covenant is specific to Muhammad (ﷺ), and this is narrated from Ali, Ibn Abbas, Qatada and al-Suddi, may Allah be pleased with them. The proponents of this view argued for its soundness in several ways:

The first: His saying, exalted is He, ﴿And when Allah took the covenant of the Prophets﴾ indicates that the one taking the covenant is Allah, exalted is He, and those from whom it is taken are the Prophets. There is no mention of the community in the verse, so it is not appropriate to turn the covenant to the community. It may be answered in several ways:

The first: according to the way you have stated, the covenant would be annexed to the one who is bound by it, and according to the way we have stated, its annexation to them is the annexation of the act to the agent, who is the one who binds (the one for whom the covenant is made). There is no doubt that the annexation of the act to the agent is stronger than its annexation to the object; and if not stronger, then at least equal. It is like saying "the covenant of Allah and His pledge," so the meaning is: "And when Allah took the covenant which Allah established for the Prophets over their nations."

The second: that what is meant is the covenant of the children of the Prophets, namely the Children of Israel, with the omission of the annexed noun, as one says: "Bakr ibn Wa'il did such and such, and Ma'add ibn Adnan did such and such," and what is meant is their descendants and their people; so likewise here.

The third: that what is meant by the word "the Prophets" is the People of the Book, and this term was applied to them in mockery of their claim, because they used to say: "We have more right to prophethood than Muhammad, upon him be prayers and peace, because we are the People of the Book, and the Prophets were from among us."

The fourth: that the word "Prophet" frequently occurs in the Qur'an with its intended meaning being his community, as Allah, exalted is He, says: ﴿O Prophet, when you divorce women﴾ [al-Talaq: 1].

The second argument of the proponents of this view: what is narrated that he, upon him be prayers and peace, said: "I have brought it to you white and pure; by God, if Musa ibn Imran were alive, he would have no choice but to follow me."

The third argument: what is narrated from Ali, may Allah be pleased with him, that he said: Allah, exalted is He, did not send Adam, peace be upon him, nor any of the Prophets after him, peace and blessings be upon them, except that He took from them the covenant that if Muhammad, peace and blessings be upon him, were sent while they were alive, they would surely believe in him and surely support him. This provides support for this view, and Allah knows best.

The second possibility: that the meaning of the verse is that the Prophets, peace and blessings be upon them, used to take the covenant from their nations that when Muhammad (ﷺ) is sent, they must believe in him and support him. This is the view of many scholars, and we have explained that the wording admits of it. They argued for its soundness with several arguments:

The first: what Abu Muslim al-Isfahani mentioned, saying: the apparent meaning of the verse indicates that those from whom Allah took the covenant are obliged to believe in Muhammad (ﷺ) at his sending, and all the Prophets, peace and blessings be upon them, would at the time of Muhammad's sending be among the dead, and the dead are not under obligation. So since those upon whom the covenant was taken are obliged to believe in Muhammad, peace be upon him, at his sending, and it is not possible to impose belief upon the Prophets at the sending of Muhammad, peace be upon him, we know that those upon whom the covenant was taken are not the Prophets themselves, but rather the nations of the Prophets. He said: what confirms this is that He, exalted is He, judged that those upon whom the covenant was taken would be defiantly disobedient if they turned away, and this description does not befit the Prophets, peace be upon them, but befits the nations.

al-Qaffal, may Allah have mercy on him, answered, saying: why should it not be possible that the meaning of the verse is that if the Prophets were alive, it would be obligatory upon them to believe in Muhammad, peace and blessings be upon him? A parallel to this is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿If you associate partners, your deeds will surely be voided﴾ [al-Zumar: 65], though Allah knew that he would never associate partners at all; but this statement came in the manner of supposition and hypothesis. So likewise here. And He said: ﴿And if he had fabricated against Us some sayings, We would have seized him by the right hand, then We would have cut from him the aorta﴾ [al-Haqqah: 44–46]; and He said concerning the angels: ﴿And whoever among them should say, "Indeed, I am a deity besides Him," We would recompense him with Hell. Thus do We recompense the wrongdoers﴾ [al-Anbiya: 29], although He informed about them that they do not precede Him in speech and that they fear their Lord above them; all of that came in the manner of supposition, and the reckoning is likewise here. We say: He named them defiantly disobedient on the supposition of turning away, for the name of disobedience (fisq) is no more grave than the name of associating partners (shirk), and He mentioned that in the manner of supposition, as in His saying: ﴿If you associate partners, your deeds will surely be voided﴾; so likewise here.

The second argument: that the purpose of this verse is that those who were in the time of the Messenger (ﷺ) should believe; and if the covenant was taken from them, that would be more effective in achieving this purpose than if it were taken from the Prophets, peace be upon them. It has been answered that the ranks of the Prophets, peace be upon them, are higher and more noble than the ranks of the nations; so when this verse indicates that Allah, exalted is He, made it obligatory upon all the Prophets to believe in Muhammad, peace be upon him, had they been alive, and that if they abandoned that they would become among the defiantly disobedient, then it is all the more fitting that belief in Muhammad (ﷺ) be obligatory upon their nations; so turning this covenant to the Prophets is stronger in achieving the aim by this way.

The third argument: what is narrated from Ibn Abbas that it was said to him: the companions of Abdullah recite: ﴿And when Allah took the covenant of those given the Scripture﴾ [Al 'Imran: 187], while we recite ﴿And when Allah took the covenant of the Prophets﴾. Ibn Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, said: Allah only took the covenant of the Prophets concerning their peoples.

The fourth argument: that this possibility is reinforced by His saying, exalted is He: ﴿O Children of Israel, remember My favor which I bestowed upon you, and fulfill My covenant, I will fulfill your covenant﴾ [al-Baqarah: 40], and by His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And when Allah took the covenant of those given the Scripture, "You must make it clear to the people and not conceal it"﴾ [Al 'Imran: 187]. This is the sum of what has been said on this subject, and Allah knows best what He intends.

* * *

As for His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Whatever I have given you of Scripture and wisdom﴾, there are several issues concerning it:

The first issue: the majority read "lamā" with a fatha on the lam; Hamza read it with a kasra on the lam; and Sa'id ibn Jubayr read "lammā" with a shadda. As for the reading with a fatha, it has two aspects:

The first: that "mā" is a relative pronoun, the clause following it is its relative clause, and its predicate is His saying: ﴿you must believe in him﴾. The implied sense is: "for that which I have given you of Scripture and wisdom, then there comes to you a Messenger confirming what is with you, you must believe in him." On this reading, "mā" is in the nominative as the subject, and the returning pronoun to the word "mā," which is its relative clause, is omitted; the sense is: "for what I have given you (it)," so the returning pronoun was omitted, as it is omitted in His saying: ﴿Is this the one whom Allah has sent as a Messenger?﴾ [al-Furqan: 41]. And there are two questions on this:

The first question: if "mā" is a relative pronoun, it is necessary that a reference back from the conjoined clause to the relative pronoun be present, otherwise it is not permissible. Do you not see that if you said: "the one whose father stood up, then Zayd set out," it would not be permissible?

And His saying ﴿then there comes to you a Messenger confirming what is with you﴾ contains no reference back to the relative pronoun. We reply: it is permissible, according to al-Akhfash, to place the apparent noun in the place of the pronoun, and the evidence for this is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, whoever fears Allah and is patient, then indeed Allah does not waste the reward of the doers of good﴾ [Yusuf: 90], and He did not say "then indeed Allah does not waste his reward"; and He said: ﴿Indeed, those who believe and do righteous deeds—indeed, We do not waste the reward of one who does good work﴾ [al-Kahf: 30], and He did not say "indeed We do not waste their reward." That is because the apparent noun mentioned stands in the place of the pronoun; so likewise here.

The second question: what is the function of the lam in His saying "lamā"? We reply: this lam is the lam of the beginning (lam al-ibtida'), like your saying "Zayd is surely better than Amr," and it is well placed before what functions as the object of an oath (al-muqsam 'alayhi), because His saying ﴿And when Allah took the covenant of the Prophets﴾ functions as an oath, and the meaning is: "He made them swear." This lam is the one that precedes the oath. This is the explanation of this statement.

The second aspect, which is the choice of Sibawayh, al-Mazini and al-Zajjaj: that "mā" here is the one that implies the meaning of a condition, and the sense is: "whatever I have given you of Scripture and wisdom, then there comes to you a Messenger confirming what is with you, you must believe in him." So the lam in His saying ﴿you must believe in him﴾ is the one that precedes the oath. As for the lam in "lamā," it is a lam that is sometimes omitted and sometimes mentioned, without any difference in meaning. Its parallel is your saying: "By God, if you do, I will do," where the particle "an" does not change the situation whether it is mentioned or omitted; so likewise here. On this reading, "mā" is in the accusative position governed by "ātaytukum," and "wa-jā'akum" is conjoined to "ātaytukum" and put in the jussive by the conjunction; and "la-tu'minunna bihi" is the answer of the condition. Sibawayh did not accept the first view because he does not allow placing the apparent noun in the place of the pronoun.

As for the reading "limā" with a kasra on the lam, its basis is that this is the lam of causation, as if it were said: He took their covenant for this reason, because whoever is given the Scripture and wisdom, his being singled out with this virtue obliges him to confirm all the other Prophets and Messengers. And "mā" on this reading is a relative pronoun. The full discussion of it is what we have already presented in the first aspect.

As for the reading "lammā" with a shadda, al-Zamakhshari, the author of the "Kashshaf," mentioned two aspects concerning it:

[Page 104]

The first: the meaning is: "When I gave you some of the Scripture and wisdom, and then a messenger came to you confirming what is with you, it became obligatory upon you to believe in him and support him." The second: the original form of *lamā* was *lamin mā*. They found the combination of three *mīms* burdensome: the two *mīms* and the *nūn* that changes into a *mīm* by assimilation into the *mīm*. So they dropped one of them, and it became *lamā*. Its meaning is: "Because of what I have given you, you shall most certainly believe in it." This is close in meaning to the reading of Hamzah.

The second issue: Nāfiʿ read *ātaynākum* with a *nūn*, for magnification (*al-tafkhīm*), while the rest read it with a *tāʾ*, for singularity (*al-tawḥīd*). Nāfiʿ's evidence is His saying: ﴿And We gave David the Psalms﴾ [al-Nisāʾ: 163], ﴿And We gave him judgment while a child﴾ [Maryam: 12], and ﴿And We gave them both the clear Book﴾ [al-Ṣāffāt: 117]. Also, this reading indicates greatness more clearly, so it carries more awe in the heart of the listener, and this context suits this meaning. The majority's evidence is His saying: ﴿He it is who sends down upon His servant clear signs﴾ [al-Ḥadīd: 9], and ﴿Praise be to God, who sent down upon His servant the Book﴾ [al-Kahf: 1]. Also, this reading is more consistent with what comes before this verse and what comes after it, because He, exalted is He, said before this verse: ﴿And when God took [the covenant]﴾, and said after it: ﴿My burden (iṣrī)﴾. Nāfiʿ answered this by saying that one of the doors of eloquence is changing the expression from the singular to the plural, and from the plural to the singular. He, exalted is He, said: ﴿And We made it a guidance for the Children of Israel: that you shall not take other than Me as Guardian﴾ [al-Isrāʾ: 2]. He did not say "other than Us," as He said "And We made it." And God knows best.

The third issue: He, exalted is He, mentioned the prophets in the third person, then said *ātaytukum* ("I gave you"), which is direct address after an implied (*iḍmār*) shift. The estimate is: "And when God took the covenant of the prophets, He said, addressing them, 'Whatever I have given you of a Book and wisdom...'" The use of implied words (*iḍmār*) is a wide matter in the Qurʾan. Some scholars adopted another implied word in this verse and relieved themselves of those strained explanations that we have related from the grammarians. They said: the estimate of the verse is: "And when God took the covenant of the prophets: you shall certainly convey to the people what I have given you of a Book and wisdom." He said: but He omitted *latuballigunna* ("you shall certainly convey") because the meaning indicates it, since the *lām* of the oath only falls upon a verb. So when this *lām* indicated this verb, he omitted it for brevity. Then He, exalted is He, said after it: ﴿Then there came to you a messenger confirming what is with you﴾, and that is Muḥammad (ﷺ), ﴿you shall certainly believe in him and certainly support him﴾. With this estimate the structure is coherent and does not need those forced explanations. And if it is necessary to adopt an implied word, then this implied word through which the speech is arranged in a clear and evident order is better than those strained explanations.

The fourth issue: in His saying ﴿what I have given you of a Book﴾ there is a difficulty, namely that this address is either to the prophets or to the nations. If it is to the prophets, then not all prophets were given a Book; only some of them were. If it is to the nations, the difficulty is more apparent. The answer to it is from two aspects:

The first: all the prophets, peace be upon them, were given the Book in the sense that he was guided by it and called to act upon it, even if it was not revealed to him.

The second: the most noble of the prophets, peace be upon them, are those who were given the Book, so He described all by the description of the most noble category.

The fifth issue: the Book is what is revealed and recited, and wisdom is the revelation that brings detailed obligations which the Book did not include.

The sixth issue: the word *min* in His saying (*min kitāb*, "of a Book") entered as an explanation of *mā* (what), like your saying: "What I have of paper is two *dānaqs*."

* * *

As for His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Then there came to you a messenger confirming what is with you﴾, there are questions about it.

The first question: what is the meaning of His saying ﴿Then there came to you﴾, since a messenger does not come to the prophets, but comes to the nations?

The answer: if we take His saying ﴿And when God took the covenant of the prophets﴾ to mean taking the covenant of their nations, the question disappears. If we take it to mean taking the covenant of the prophets themselves, then His saying ﴿Then there came to you﴾ means: came in your time.

The second question: how can Muḥammad (ﷺ) be confirming what is with them when his law differs from their law?

[Page 105]

We say: what is intended is agreement in monotheism, prophethood, and the foundations of the laws. As for their details, even if disagreement occurs concerning them, that in reality is not disagreement, because all the prophets, peace be upon them, agree that the truth in the time of Mūsā, peace be upon him, was nothing but his law, and that the truth in the time of Muḥammad (ﷺ) is nothing but his law. So this, although it appears to be disagreement, is in reality agreement. Also, what is meant by His saying ﴿Then there came to you a messenger confirming what is with you﴾ is Muḥammad (ﷺ), and what is meant by his confirming what is with them is that his description and the manner of his circumstances are mentioned in the Torah and the Gospel. So when he appeared with circumstances matching what was mentioned in those books, his very coming was a confirmation of what was with them. This is what is meant by his confirming what is with them.

The third question: the sum of the speech is that God took the covenant from all the prophets to believe in every messenger who comes confirming what is with them. So what is the meaning of that covenant?

The answer: it may be that this covenant is what was established in their intellects of the proofs indicating that submission to God's command is obligatory. So when the messenger comes, he is only a messenger upon the appearance of the miracles that indicate his truthfulness. Then, when he informs them afterward that God commanded creation to believe in him, they then recognize its obligation. So the establishing of this proof in their intellects is what is meant by taking the covenant. It may also be that what is meant by taking the covenant is that He, exalted is He, explained His attributes in the books of the earlier prophets. So when his circumstances match what came in the earlier divine books, obedience to him becomes obligatory. Thus His saying, exalted is He, ﴿Then there came to you a messenger confirming what is with you﴾ indicates these two aspects. As for the first aspect, it is His saying "messenger" (*rasūl*). As for the second aspect, it is His saying ﴿confirming what is with you﴾.

* * *

As for His saying: ﴿you shall certainly believe in him and certainly support him﴾, the meaning is clear, because He, exalted is He, first made believing in him obligatory, then engaging in supporting him second. The *lām* in *latu'minunna bihi* ("you shall certainly believe in him") is the *lām* of the oath, as if it were said: "By God, you shall certainly believe in him."

* * *

Then He, exalted is He, said: ﴿He said: "Do you affirm and accept My burden (iṣrī) on that?"﴾ There are issues concerning this:

The first issue: if we interpret His saying, exalted is He, ﴿And when God took the covenant of the prophets﴾ as meaning that He, exalted is He, took the covenants from the prophets, then His saying ﴿Do you affirm?﴾ means: God, exalted is He, said to the prophets: "Do you affirm belief in Him and support for Him?" If we interpret the taking of the covenant as meaning that the prophets, peace be upon them, took the covenants from the nations, then the meaning of His saying ﴿He said: "Do you affirm?"﴾ is: every prophet said to his nation, "Do you affirm?" This is because He, exalted is He, attributed the taking of the covenant to Himself, though the prophets took it from the nations. Likewise, the request for this affirmation He attributed to Himself, though it was made by the prophets, peace be upon them. The purpose is that the prophets exaggerated in establishing and emphasizing this meaning. They did not limit themselves to taking the covenant from the nations, but demanded from them an affirmation in words, and confirmed that with testimony.

The second issue: *al-iqrār* ("affirmation") in the language is transferred with an *alif* (in causative form) from *qarra al-shayʾ yaqirru*, when a thing is established and remains in its place, and *aqarrahu* is when someone else causes it to remain. And one who affirms (*al-muqirr*) something acknowledges it against himself, that is, he establishes it.

As for His saying, exalted is He, ﴿Do you affirm and accept My burden (iṣrī) on that?﴾, that means: "Have you accepted My covenant?" Taking in the sense of accepting is common in speech. He, exalted is He, said: ﴿nor shall ransom be accepted from it﴾ [al-Baqarah: 48], meaning ransom will not be accepted from it. And He said: ﴿and He takes the charities﴾ [al-Tawbah: 104], meaning He accepts them. The *iṣr* is what befalls a person because of the work that is binding on him. He, exalted is He, said: ﴿and do not lay upon us a burden (iṣran)﴾ [al-Baqarah: 286]. So He named the covenant *iṣr* for this meaning. The author of *al-Kashshāf* said: the covenant was named *iṣr* because it is something that is bound (*yuʾṣar*), that is, tied and knotted, and from it comes *al-iṣār* with which something is tied. It is recited as *iṣrī*. It is also permissible that it is a dialectal form of *iṣr*.

* * *

Then He, exalted is He, said: ﴿They said: "We affirm." He said: "Then bear witness, and I am with you among the witnesses."﴾ There are several interpretations of His saying ﴿Then bear witness﴾:

The first: let some of you bear witness against others concerning the affirmation, and I am, with your affirmation and the witnessing of some of you for others, ﴿among the witnesses﴾. This is an emphasis upon them and a warning against retraction, since they know the testimony of God and the testimony of some of them against others.

The second: His saying ﴿Then bear witness﴾ is addressed to the angels.

The third: His saying ﴿Then bear witness﴾ means: let each person make himself a witness against himself. Its parallel is His saying: ﴿And He made them testify concerning themselves: "Am I not your Lord?" They said: "Yes, we testify"﴾ [al-Aʿrāf: 172], that is, against ourselves. This is of the category of hyperbole.

The fourth: ﴿Then bear witness﴾ means: make this covenant clear to the elite and the common people, so that no one has an excuse for ignorance of it. Its root meaning is that the witness is the one who makes clear the truth of a claim.

The fifth: ﴿Then bear witness﴾ means: be certain of what I have established upon you of this covenant, and be in it like one who sees the thing directly.

The sixth: if we say that the taking of the covenant was from the nations, then His saying ﴿Then bear witness﴾ is addressed to the prophets, peace be upon them, that they should be witnesses over them.

* * *

As for His saying, exalted is He: ﴿and I am with you among the witnesses﴾, it is for emphasis and for strengthening the obligation. There is another benefit in it, namely that He, exalted is He, although He made another witness, does not need that witnessing, because nothing is hidden from Him, but for a kind of benefit. He, glory be to Him and exalted is He, knows the secret and what is more hidden. Then He, exalted is He, added to it another emphasis, saying: ﴿Then whoever turns away after that, those are the defiantly disobedient (al-fāsiqūn)﴾, meaning: whoever turns away from believing in this Messenger and supporting him after these proofs have preceded is among the defiantly disobedient. The threat against the defiantly disobedient is known. His saying ﴿Then whoever turns away after that﴾ is a condition (*sharṭ*), and the past verb turns into the future in the condition and its response. And God knows best.

[Page 107]

The Most High said: ﴿Do they seek other than the religion of God, while to Him submits whoever is in the heavens and the earth, willingly or unwillingly, and to Him they will be returned?﴾

Know that when the Most High explained in the previous verse that belief in Muhammad (peace be upon him) is a law that God established and made obligatory upon all the prophets and nations who came before, it follows that whoever dislikes this is seeking a religion other than the religion of God. Therefore He said after it: ﴿Do they seek other than the religion of God?﴾ There are several issues concerning the verse:

The first issue: Hafs, on the authority of ʿAsim, read "yabghūna" and "yurjaʿūna" with a yāʾ dotted from below (i.e., in the third person), for two reasons:

One: to make them refer back to His saying: ﴿And those are the defiantly disobedient﴾ [Āl ʿImrān: 82].

The second: The Most High only mentioned the account of the taking of the covenant in order to make clear that the Jews and Christians are obligated to believe in Muhammad ﷺ. When they persisted in their disbelief, He said, in a tone of disapproval: ﴿Do they seek other than the religion of God?﴾ Abu ʿAmr read "tabghūna" with a tāʾ, addressing the Jews and other disbelievers, and "yurjaʿūna" with a yāʾ, so that it refers back to all the responsible persons mentioned in His saying: ﴿And to Him submits whoever is in the heavens and the earth.﴾ The rest read both with a tāʾ, as address, because what precedes it is address, like His saying: ﴿Do you affirm and accept?﴾ Moreover, it is not far-fetched to say to the Muslim, the disbeliever, and everyone: "Do you seek other than the religion of God, while you know that whoever is in the heavens and the earth has submitted to Him, and that your return is to Him?" This is like His saying: ﴿How can you disbelieve while the verses of God are recited to you and His Messenger is among you?﴾ [Āl ʿImrān: 101].

The second issue: The hamza (ʾalif-hamza, the interrogative particle) is for asking a question, and the purpose is either to express disapproval that they would do this, or to affirm that they are doing it. The place of the hamza is the word "yabghūna" (they seek); its implied form is: "Do they seek other than the religion of God?" because a question is only asked about actions and events. However, the Most High placed the object, which is (other than the religion of God), before its verb, because it is more important, since the denial that the hamza expresses is directed at the false object of worship. As for the fāʾ (the particle "fa"), it is for conjoining one sentence to another, and there are two views about it:

One: the implied sense is: "Then those are the defiantly disobedient; so do they seek other than the religion of God?"

Know that if it were said "awa-ghayra dīn Allāh yabghūn" it would be permissible, but the fāʾ carries an additional benefit, as if it were said: "So after taking this covenant, confirmed by these emphatic affirmations, do you seek [another]?"

The third issue: It is reported that two groups of the People of the Book disputed before the Messenger ﷺ regarding what they differed about in the religion of Abraham (peace be upon him), and each of the two groups claimed that it was more entitled to it. The Prophet ﷺ said: "Both groups are free of the religion of Abraham (peace be upon him)." They said: "We will not accept your judgment, nor will we follow your religion," and so this verse was revealed. However, it seems unlikely to me to link this verse to this cause, because on this reading the verse would be disconnected from what precedes it, whereas a question in the form of disapproval requires that it be connected to what came before. Rather, the correct understanding of the verse is this: since this covenant was mentioned in their books, and they knew it, they were aware of the truth of Muhammad ﷺ in prophethood. Thus, there remained no cause for their disbelief except mere enmity and envy, and they became like Iblis, whom envy drove to disbelief. So the Most High informed them that they, whenever they seek a religion other than the religion of God, and a deity other than God, the Glorified, [they are like him].

* * *

Then He explained that rebellion against God the Most High and turning away from His judgment is not befitting of people of intellect, so He said: ﴿And to Him submits whoever is in the heavens and the earth, willingly or unwillingly, and to Him you will be returned.﴾ Concerning this there are two issues:

The first issue: Islam (al-islām) is submission, surrender, and humility.

Having understood this, there are several aspects of the humility of everyone in the heavens and the earth to God:

The first, which in my view is the most correct: every existent other than God, the Glorified, is contingent in its essence (mumkin li-dhātihi), and everything contingent in its essence does not come into existence except by His bringing it into being, and does not cease to exist except by His causing it to cease. Therefore everything other than God is subject and humbled before the majesty of God in both its states of existence and non-existence, and this is the utmost degree of submission and humility. Moreover, in this aspect there is another subtle point: His saying "﴿to Him submits﴾" implies restriction (ḥaṣr), meaning: "to Him alone submits whoever is in the heavens and the earth, and not to other than Him." Thus this verse indicates that the Necessary Existent is one, and that everything other than Him does not come into being except by His creating it, and does not perish except by His annihilating it, whether it is an intellect, a soul, a spirit, a body, a substance, an accident, an agent, or an action. A verse with a similar indication of this meaning is His saying: ﴿And to God prostrate whoever is in the heavens and the earth﴾ [al-Raʿd: 15], and His saying: ﴿And there is nothing that does not glorify Him with His praise﴾ [al-Isrāʾ: 44].

The second aspect in interpreting this verse: there is no way for anyone to resist Him in what He wills, and they must either submit to Him willingly or unwillingly. The righteous Muslims submit to God willingly in matters related to religion, and submit to Him unwillingly in what opposes their natures, such as illness, poverty, death, and the like. As for the disbelievers, they submit to God, the Most High, in every state unwillingly, because they do not submit in matters related to religion, and in other matters they submit to Him, the Glorified, unwillingly, since they cannot repel His decree and destiny.

The third: the Muslims submitted willingly, and the disbelievers submitted unwillingly at the moment of their death, based on His saying: ﴿So their faith did not benefit them when they saw Our might﴾ [Ghāfir: 85].

The fourth: all creation submits willingly to His divinity, based on His saying: ﴿And if you asked them, "Who created the heavens and the earth?" they would surely say, "God"﴾ [Luqmān: 25], and they submit unwillingly to His obligations and His causing them to suffer pains.

The fifth: the submission of all took place at the time of the taking of the covenant, which is His saying: ﴿And when your Lord took from the Children of Adam, from their loins, their descendants, and made them testify concerning themselves: "Am I not your Lord?" They said: "Yes"﴾ [al-Aʿrāf: 172].

The sixth: al-Ḥasan [al-Baṣrī] said: willingness is specific to the people of the heavens; as for the people of the earth, some submit willingly and some unwillingly. I say: He, the Glorified, mentioned this in the creation of the heavens and the earth, which is His saying: ﴿Then He said to it and to the earth: "Come, willingly or unwillingly." They said: "We come willingly"﴾ [Fuṣṣilat: 11], and in it there are wondrous secrets.

As for His saying: ﴿and to Him you will be returned﴾, the meaning is that whoever opposes Him in this world, his return will be to Him, to a place where no one other than Him possesses harm or benefit. This is a great threat for whoever opposes the true religion.

The second issue: Al-Wāḥidī, may God have mercy on him, said: ṭawʿ means submission. It is said: "ṭāʿahu yaṭūʿuhu ṭawʿan" when he submitted to him and humbled himself; and when one carries out his command, he has obeyed him (aṭāʿahu); and when one agrees with him, he has complied with him (ṭāwaʿahu). Ibn al-Sikkīt said: it is said "ṭāʿa lahu" and "aṭāʿa," so ṭawʿan and karhan are in the accusative as a verbal noun standing in the place of a circumstantial clause (ḥāl), and its implied sense is "obedient" and "unwilling," like your saying "atānī rākiḍan" (he came to me running). It is not permissible to say "atānī kalāman" (he came to me speaking) in the sense of "speaking," because speech is not a manner of coming. And God knows best.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 3, verse 84:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Say: "We believe in God, and in what has been sent down to us, and what was sent down to Abraham, Ishmael, Isaac, Jacob and the Tribes, and what was given to Moses and Jesus and the prophets from their Lord. We make no distinction between any of them, and to Him we are submitting."﴾

Know that when He, exalted is He, mentioned in the previous verse that He had taken the covenant from the prophets to confirm the Messenger who would come confirming what was with them, He made clear in this verse that among the attributes of Muhammad (ﷺ) is that he confirms what was with them. So He said: ﴿Say: "We believe in God"﴾ to the end of the verse. And here there are issues:

The first issue: the pronoun in "Say" (qul) is singular, while in "We believe" (amanna) it is plural, and in this there are several aspects:

The first: when He addressed him, He addressed him only in the singular, and taught him that when he addresses the people he should address them in the plural form, out of reverence and dignity, just as kings and great men speak.

The second: He first addressed him in the singular so that this speech would indicate that there is no one who conveys this obligation from God to creation except him. Then He said "We believe" as an alert that when he says this statement, his companions agree with him in it.

The third: He specified him in this obligation by the word "Say," so as to show by it that he is confirming what was with them. Then He said "We believe" as an alert that this obligation is not exclusive to him, but is binding on all believers, as He said: ﴿The believers, each one believes in God, His angels, His books and His messengers. We make no distinction between any of His messengers﴾ [al-Baqarah: 285].

The second issue: He placed belief in God before belief in the prophets, because belief in God is the root of belief in prophethood. In the second rank He mentioned belief in what was sent down to him, because the books of the other prophets have been distorted and altered, so there is no way to know their condition except through what God sent down to Muhammad (ﷺ). Thus what was sent down to Muhammad is like the foundation for what was sent down to the other prophets, and for this reason He placed it before them. In the third rank He mentioned some of the prophets, namely those prophets whose existence the People of the Book acknowledge, while they differ regarding their prophethood. "The Tribes" (al-asbat) are the sons of Jacob, peace be upon him, whose twelve nations God mentioned in Surah al-A'raf. God made it obligatory to affirm the prophethood of all the prophets, peace be upon them, for several reasons:

The first: establishing that he, peace be upon him, confirms all the prophets, because this condition was considered in taking the covenant.

The second: an alert that the positions of the People of the Book are contradictory. This is because they only confirm the prophet whom they confirm on account of the manifestation of a miracle upon him, and this requires that everyone upon whom a miracle manifested was a prophet. In this case, singling out some for confirmation and others for denial is contradictory. Rather, the truth is to confirm all and to acknowledge the prophethood of all.

The third: He said before this verse: ﴿Do they seek other than the religion of God, while to Him submits whoever is in the heavens and the earth?﴾ This is an alert that their insistence on denying some of the prophets is turning away from the religion of God and contending with God. Here he manifested belief in the prophethood of all the prophets, so that what He described the People of the Book with, of contending with God in judgment and obligation, would be removed from him and from his community.

The fourth: that in the first verse He mentioned that He took the covenant from all the prophets that they would believe in every messenger who came after them, and here He took the covenant from Muhammad (ﷺ) that he would believe in every messenger who came before him, and did not take the covenant from him for those messengers who would come after him. So this verse indicates in this respect that there is absolutely no prophet after him. If it is asked: why was "was sent down" (unzila) in this verse followed by the preposition of elevation (ʿalā), while in similar previous instances it was followed by the preposition of termination (ilā)? We say: because both meanings exist together, since revelation descends from above and ends at the messengers, so it came sometimes with one of the two meanings and sometimes with the other. It has also been said that "upon us" (ʿalaynā) is used with respect to the Messenger, because revelation descends upon him, and "to us" (ilaynā) with respect to the community, because revelation reaches them from the Messenger in terms of termination. But this is forced. Do you not see His saying: (what was sent down to you) and (He sent down to you the Book), and His saying: ﴿Believe in what has been sent down to those who believed﴾?

* * *

The second issue: The scholars differed concerning how belief in these prophets who came before, whose laws were abrogated, should be. The real point of disagreement is this: when their law became abrogated, does their prophethood become abrogated as well? Whoever says that it becomes abrogated says: We believe that they were prophets and messengers, but we do not believe that they are now prophets and messengers. Whoever says that abrogation of the law does not entail abrogation of prophethood says: We believe that they are prophets and messengers at present. So be attentive to this point.

The fourth issue: His saying: ﴿We make no distinction between any of them﴾ has several aspects:

The first: al-Asamm said: division may occur by preferring some over others, and it may occur on the basis of claiming that they were not on a single path in obedience to God. The meaning in this respect is: we acknowledge that they were all upon one religion in calling to God and in submission to the commands of God.

The second: some have said the meaning is: ﴿We make no distinction between any of them﴾ by believing in some and not others, as the Jews and Christians divided.

The third: Abu Muslim said: "﴿We make no distinction between any of them﴾" means we do not separate what they agreed upon, like His saying: ﴿And hold fast to the rope of God all together and do not be divided﴾ [Al 'Imran: 103], and He censured a people described as divided, saying: ﴿Certainly your bonds have been cut, and what you used to claim has gone astray from you﴾ [al-An'am: 94].

As for His saying: ﴿and to Him we are submitting﴾, there are several aspects:

The first: our acknowledgment of the prophethood of these prophets was only because we are subservient to God, exalted is He, submitting to His judgment and command. In this there is an alert that his condition is contrary to those whom God addressed with His saying: ﴿Do they seek other than the religion of God, while to Him submits whoever is in the heavens and the earth?﴾

The second: Abu Muslim said: "﴿and to Him we are submitting﴾" means submitting to the command of God with contentment and abandoning opposition, and that is the attribute of believers in God, who are people of peace, while disbelievers are described as waging war against God, as He said: ﴿The recompense of those who wage war against God and His Messenger is only...﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 33].

The third: His saying: ﴿and to Him we are submitting﴾ conveys restriction, and the implied meaning is: to Him alone we submit, not for another purpose of showing off, ostentation, or seeking wealth. This is an alert that their condition is the opposite of that, for they do not act or speak except for show, ostentation and seeking wealth. And God knows best.

Know that when He, exalted is He, said at the end of the preceding verse, ﴿and we are Muslims to Him﴾, He followed it by explaining in this verse that religion is nothing but Islam, and that every religion other than Islam is not accepted by God. This is because acceptance of a deed means that God is pleased with that deed, is pleased with its doer, and rewards him for it. Hence He said, ﴿Indeed God accepts only from the God-fearing﴾ (al-Ma'idah: 27). Then He, exalted is He, explained that whoever has a religion other than Islam, just as it is not accepted by God, so he is among the losers. Loss in the Hereafter is by being deprived of reward and incurring punishment. It includes what befalls him of regret and remorse over the righteous deeds he missed in this world, and over the toil and hardship he bore in this world in establishing that false religion.

Know that the apparent meaning of this verse indicates that faith (al-iman) is Islam, since if faith were other than Islam, faith would necessarily not be accepted, by His saying, ﴿and whoever seeks other than Islam as religion, it will not be accepted from him﴾. However, the apparent meaning of His saying, ﴿The Bedouins say, "We believe." Say, "You have not believed; rather say, 'We have submitted'"﴾ (al-Hujurat: 14), requires that Islam be distinct from faith. The way to reconcile the two is to take the first verse in the sense of the sharia usage (al-'urf al-shar'i, the technical usage of the religious law), and the second verse in the sense of the linguistic usage (al-wad' al-lughawi, the lexical meaning of the word).

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 3, verses 86–89:

"How will Allah guide a people who disbelieved after their belief and had testified that the Messenger is true and clear proofs had come to them? And Allah does not guide the wrongdoing people." "Those – their recompense is that upon them is the curse of Allah and of the angels and of mankind, all together," "abiding therein; the punishment will not be lightened for them, nor will they be reprieved," "except for those who repent after that and make amends. Indeed, Allah is Forgiving and Merciful."

Know that when Allah magnified the matter of Islam and faith with His saying, "And whoever seeks other than Islam as a religion – never will it be accepted from him, and he, in the Hereafter, will be among the losers" (3:85), He confirmed that magnification by explaining the threat against one who abandons Islam, so He said: "How will Allah guide a people who disbelieved after their belief." In the verse there are several issues:

The first issue: concerning the occasion of revelation (sabab al-nuzul), there are several reports. The first: Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him, said: This verse was revealed concerning ten men who had believed, then apostatized and joined Mecca, and began to wait for the Prophet's misfortune (rayb al-manun). So Allah revealed this verse concerning them, and among them were some who repented, so He excepted the repentant among them with His saying: "except for those who repent." The second: also transmitted from Ibn 'Abbas that he said: It was revealed concerning the Jews of Qurayzah and al-Nadir and whoever followed their religion, who disbelieved in the Prophet ﷺ after having been believers before his mission, and used to testify on his behalf to prophethood. When he was sent and came to them with the clear proofs and miracles, they disbelieved out of rebellion and envy. 

The third: It was revealed concerning al-Harith ibn Suwayd, a man of the Ansar, when he regretted his apostasy and sent to his people, "Ask for me whether there is repentance for me?" His brother sent to him with the verse, and he came to Medina and repented at the hand of the Messenger ﷺ, and the Messenger ﷺ accepted his repentance. 

Al-Qaffal, may Allah have mercy on him, said: People have two opinions regarding this verse. Some say that His saying, "And whoever seeks other than Islam as a religion," and what follows it, from His saying, "How will Allah guide a people who disbelieved after their belief," up to His saying, "And those are the astray," all of it was revealed in one single story. Others took the beginning of the story from His saying: "Indeed, those who disbelieved and died while they were disbelievers" (2:161). Then, according to both views, there are also two opinions: one, that it is concerning the People of the Book; the other, that it is concerning a people who apostatized from Islam, who believed and then apostatized, as we have explained.

The second issue: The scholars differed in interpreting His saying, "How will Allah guide a people who disbelieved after their belief." As for the Mu'tazilah, they said: Our principles testify that He, exalted is He, guided all creation to the religion in the sense of making it known, setting out the proofs, and doing favours (al-alutaf); for if it were to encompass all in these things, the disbeliever and the astray would be excused. Then He, exalted is He, judged that He did not guide these disbelievers, so it is necessary to interpret this guidance as something other than the setting up of proofs. Then they mentioned several aspects regarding it:

The first: What is meant by this verse is the withholding of the favours (alutaf) which He bestows upon the believers as a reward for their faith, as He, exalted is He, said: "And those who strive for Us – We will surely guide them to Our paths" (29:69), and He, exalted is He, said: "And Allah increases those who are guided in guidance" (19:76), and He, exalted is He, said: "And those who are guided – He increases them in guidance" (47:17), and He said: "By which Allah guides whoever follows His pleasure to the ways of peace" (5:16). These verses indicate that the one who is guided may be increased in guidance by Allah.

The second: that what is meant is that Allah, exalted is He, does not guide them to Paradise. He, exalted is He, said: "Indeed, those who disbelieved and wronged – Allah would never forgive them, nor would He guide them to a path, except the path of Hell" (4:168–169), and He said: "Their Lord guides them by their faith; beneath them rivers flow" (10:9).

The third: It is not possible that the meaning of guidance is the creation of knowledge in him, because on this supposition it would necessarily follow that it is also from Allah, exalted is He; for when He creates knowledge he is a believer and guided, and when He does not create it he is a disbeliever and astray. And if disbelief were from Allah, exalted is He, it would not be valid for Allah to blame them for disbelief, nor would it be valid to attribute disbelief to them. But the verse speaks clearly of them being blamed on account of disbelief and of their being the doers of disbelief, for He, exalted is He, said: "How will Allah guide a people who disbelieved after their belief," so He attributed disbelief to them and blamed them for that disbelief. This is the sum of their statements on this verse.

As for the People of the Sunnah, they said: What is meant by guidance is the creation of knowledge. They said: The practice of Allah in the abode of obligation is that every act which the servant intends to bring about, Allah, exalted is He, creates it immediately after the servant's intention. So it is as if He, exalted is He, said: How would Allah create knowledge in them when they intended or willed the acquisition of disbelief? And Allah knows best.
* * *
The third issue: His saying "and testified" (wa-shahidu) has two views:
The first: that it is a conjunction (ʿatf), and the meaning is "after they believed and after they testified that the Messenger is true," because conjoining a verb to a noun is not permissible; so it is, outwardly, although it implies conjoining a verb to a noun, in meaning it conjoins a verb to a verb.

The second: that the waw is for the circumstantial (hal) with "qad" implied, and the meaning is: "How will Allah guide a people who disbelieved after their belief, while they had testified that the Messenger is true."

The fourth issue: The construction of the verse: "How will Allah guide a people who disbelieved after their belief, and after the testimony that the Messenger is true, and the clear proofs had come to them." So He conjoined the testimony that the Messenger is true to the belief. The conjoined is different from the thing conjoined to, so it follows that the testimony that the Messenger is true is different from the belief. The answer: our doctrine is that faith is assent in the heart, and testimony is affirmation by the tongue, and these two are distinct; so this verse, from this aspect, indicates that faith is distinct from verbal affirmation and that it is a meaning subsisting in the heart.

The fifth issue: Know that He, exalted is He, magnified the disbelief of these people in that it occurred after three qualities: first, after belief; second, after testifying that the Messenger is true; third, after the coming of the clear proofs. Since this is so, that disbelief is a corruption after insight and after manifesting testimony, so disbelief after these things is more vile, because such disbelief is like obstinacy and denial. This indicates that the slip of the learned is more grievous than the slip of the ignorant.

* * *
As for His saying, "And Allah does not guide the wrongdoing people," there are two questions:
The first question: He said at the beginning of the verse, "How will Allah guide a people," and He said at its end, "And Allah does not guide the wrongdoing people," and this is repetition.

The answer: His saying "How will Allah guide" is specific to apostates; then He generalized that ruling to the apostate and to the original disbeliever, saying: "And Allah does not guide the wrongdoing people."

The second question: Why was the disbeliever called a wrongdoer?

The answer: He, exalted is He, said: "Indeed, association is a great wrong" (31:13). The reason is that the disbeliever brought himself into places of trial and punishment because of that disbelief, so he was a wrongdoer to himself.
* * *
Then He, exalted is He, said: "Those – their recompense is that upon them is the curse of Allah and of the angels and of mankind, all together," "abiding therein." The meaning is that He, exalted is He, ruled that those who disbelieved after their belief, Allah prevents them from His guidance; then He explained that the matter is not confined to that, but just as He does not guide them in this world, He curses them with a great curse and punishes them in the Hereafter, in the manner of perpetuity and eternity.

Know that the curse of Allah differs from the curse of the angels, because His curse is by distance from Paradise and sending down punishment and torment, whereas the curse from the angels is by speech; and likewise from mankind. All of this is merited for them because of their wrongdoing and disbelief, so it is valid that it be a recompense for that. Here there are two questions:

The first question: Why did He encompass all of mankind, while those who agree with him do not curse him?

We say: There are several answers:

The first: Abu Muslim said: He has the right to curse him, even if he does not curse him.

The second: that in the Hereafter some of them will curse one another, as He said: "Every time a nation enters, it curses its sister" (7:38), and He said: "Then on the Day of Resurrection, some of you will disavow others and some of you will curse others" (29:25). On this supposition, the cursing of the disbelievers by the disbelievers has occurred.

The third: as if "mankind" refers to the believers, and the disbelievers are not of mankind; then when He mentioned the cursing of the three, He said "all together" (ajma'in).

The fourth, and it is the most correct in my view: all creation curses the falsifier and the disbeliever, but he believes of himself that he is neither a falsifier nor a disbeliever. So when he curses the disbeliever, and he in Allah's knowledge is a disbeliever, he has cursed himself, even if he does not know it.

The second question: His saying "abiding therein" – i.e., abiding in the curse – so what is the eternity of the curse?

We say: There are two aspects:

The first: that the perpetuity in the curse means that on the Day of Resurrection the angels, the believers, and those with them will not cease to curse them in the Fire, so no state of theirs is free from being cursed by one of these.
The second: that what is meant by the eternity of the curse is the eternity of the effect of the curse, because the curse necessitates punishment, so the eternity of the effect of the curse was expressed as the eternity of the curse. A parallel is His saying: "Whoever turns away from it, he will bear on the Day of Resurrection a burden, abiding therein" (20:100–101).

The third: Ibn 'Abbas said that His saying "abiding therein" means in Hell; on this view, it is a kinaya for something not mentioned. Know that His saying "abiding therein" is in the accusative as a circumstantial clause (hal) from what precedes it, namely His saying: "upon them is the curse of Allah."

* * *
Then He said: "The punishment will not be lightened for them, nor will they be reprieved." The meaning of reprieve (inzar) is postponement, as He said: "then a respite until a time of ease" (2:280). So the meaning is that He does not make their punishment lighter, nor does He postpone the punishment from one time to another. This is the confirmation of the words of the theologians: that the punishment inflicted on the disbeliever is a pure harm, free of any admixture of benefit, lasting and never ending; we seek refuge in Allah from it.
* * *
Then He said: "except for those who repent after that." The meaning is: except those who repent of it. Then He explained that repentance alone is not sufficient until good action is added to it, so He said: "and make amends" (wa-aslahu), i.e., they set right their inner state with the Truth through vigilance, and their outward state with creation through worship, and that is by declaring that "we were upon falsehood," so that if anyone is deceived by their corrupt way, he turns back from it.
* * *
Then He said: "Indeed, Allah is Forgiving and Merciful." Regarding this there are two aspects:
The first: Forgiving of their ugly deeds in this world by covering, and Merciful in the Hereafter by pardon.

The second: Forgiving by removing punishment, Merciful by bestowing reward. A parallel is His saying: "Say to those who disbelieve: If they desist, what has already passed will be forgiven them" (8:38). The fa' entered into His saying "Indeed, Allah is Forgiving and Merciful" because it is the consequent (jaza'), and the construction of the speech is: "If they repent, then indeed Allah will forgive them."
