Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 3, verse 90:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Indeed, those who disbelieve after their belief and then increase in disbelief - their repentance will never be accepted. And those are the ones who are astray.﴾ In the verse there are two issues:

The first issue: The scholars differed concerning what it is by which disbelief increases. The governing principle is that the apostate may be the doer of the increase by persisting and remaining steadfast in it, so that persistence is like an increase. He may also be the doer of the increase by adding to that disbelief another disbelief. On this second assumption, they have mentioned several opinions:

The first: The People of the Book were believers in Muhammad (peace be upon him) before his mission, then they disbelieved in him at the time of his mission, then they increased in disbelief through their slandering of him at all times, their breaking of his covenant, their tempting of the believers, and their denial of every miracle that appeared.

The second: The Jews were believers in Moses (peace be upon him), then they disbelieved through their denial of Jesus and the Gospel, then they increased in disbelief through their denial of Muhammad (peace be upon him) and the Qur'an.

The third: The verse was revealed concerning those who apostatized and went to Mecca, and their increase in disbelief was that they said: "We shall remain in Mecca and await for Muhammad ﷺ the vicissitudes of fate (rayb al-manun)."

The fourth: The intended meaning is a group who apostatized, then resolved to return to Islam in the manner of hypocrisy, so God, may He be exalted, named that hypocrisy disbelief.

The second issue: In the first verse He, may He be exalted, ruled that the repentance of apostates is accepted, and in this verse He ruled that it is not accepted, which gives the appearance of contradiction. Also, it has been established by evidence that whenever repentance exists with its conditions, it is necessarily accepted. Therefore the exegetes differed in interpreting His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿their repentance will never be accepted﴾ in several ways:

The first: Al-Hasan, Qatadah and Ata said: the reason is that they do not repent except at the presence of death, and God, may He be exalted, says: ﴿And repentance is not for those who do evil deeds until, when death approaches one of them, he says, "Indeed, I have repented now"﴾ [al-Nisa: 18].

The second: This may be understood as referring to the case where they repent with the tongue but sincerity does not arise in their hearts.

The third: Al-Qadi, al-Qaffal and Ibn al-Anbari said: when He, may He be exalted, mentioned first those who disbelieve after belief and made clear that they are among those deserving the curse unless they repent, He mentioned in this verse that if they disbelieve a second time after that repentance, the first repentance becomes unaccepted and becomes as though it had never been. He said: this opinion fits the verse better than all the other opinions, because the sense is: "Except those who repent and amend, for indeed God is Forgiving and Merciful." So if they are like that and then increase in disbelief, their repentance will never be accepted.

The fourth: The author of al-Kashshaf said: His saying ﴿their repentance will never be accepted﴾ is made a metonymy for dying in disbelief, because the one whose repentance is not accepted from among the disbelievers is the one who dies in disbelief. It is as if it were said: the Jews and the apostates who did what they did are destined to die in disbelief and are included among those whose repentance is not accepted.

The fifth: Perhaps the intended meaning is only the case where they repent of that increase alone, for repentance from that increase does not become accepted unless repentance from the original disbelief occurs.

Comment: All of these answers hold only if we take His saying ﴿Indeed, those who disbelieve after their belief and then increase in disbelief﴾ as referring to the previously known group, not as a general statement. Otherwise, how many an apostate has repented of his apostasy with a sound repentance joined with sincerity during the period of accountability! As for the answer we have reported from al-Qaffal and al-Qadi, it is a consistent answer whether we take the wording as referring to the previously known group or as a general statement.

As for His saying ﴿And those are the ones who are astray﴾, there are two questions: The first: ﴿And those are the ones who are astray﴾ denies that others are astray, and that is not the case, for every disbeliever is astray, whether he disbelieved after belief or was a disbeliever originally. The answer: this is to be understood as meaning that they are the ones who are astray in the complete sense.

The second question: He first described them with persistence in disbelief and excess in it, and disbelief is the worst kind of error, and description is intended for emphasis, and emphasis is only achieved by describing a thing with what is stronger in state than it, not with what is weaker in state than it. The answer: we have already mentioned that the intended meaning is that they are the ones who are astray in the complete sense, and on this assumption emphasis is achieved.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 3, verse 91:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, those who disbelieve and die while they are disbelievers – never will be accepted from any of them the earth filled with gold even if he would ransom himself therewith. Those will have a painful punishment, and they will not have any helpers.﴾

Know that the disbeliever is of three categories. The first: one who repents from disbelief with a sound, accepted repentance, and this is the one whom Allah, exalted is He, mentioned in His saying: ﴿Except those who repent after that and reform, for indeed, Allah is Forgiving and Merciful.﴾

The second: one who repents from that disbelief with a corrupt repentance, and this is the one whom Allah mentioned in the previous verse, and He said that his repentance will never be accepted. The third: one who dies upon disbelief without any repentance at all, and this is the one mentioned in this verse. Then Allah, exalted is He, informed about these with three kinds:

The first kind: His saying, ﴿never will be accepted from any of them the earth filled with gold even if he would ransom himself therewith.﴾ Al-Wahidi said: "Mil' al-shay' (the filling of a thing) is the quantity that fills it. And dhahaban (gold) is put in the accusative as a tamyiz (specification). The meaning of tamyiz is that the statement is complete but ambiguous, like your saying: 'I have twenty.' The number is known, but the counted item is ambiguous. When you say 'dirhaman' (a dirham), you specify the number. Likewise, when you say: 'He is the best of people,' you have informed about his goodness but not specified in what respect. When you say 'wajhan' (in face) or 'fi'lan' (in deed), you have specified it and put it in the accusative as tamyiz. You put it in the accusative only because it has nothing that would make it genitive or nominative, and when it was free of these two, it was put in the accusative because the accusative is the lightest of the vowels, so it is treated as though there were no governing word affecting it."

The author of al-Kashshaf said: "al-A'mash read dhahabun (gold) in the nominative, as a substitution for mil' (the filling), just as one says: 'I have twenty persons, men.'"

Here there are three questions:

The first question: Why was it said in the previous verse "lan tuqbila" (will never be accepted) without fa', and in this verse "fa-lan yuqbila" with fa'?

Answer: The entry of the fa' indicates that the statement is built upon the conditional and its response. Without the fa', it is not understood from the statement that it is a condition and response. You say: "The one who came to me has a dirham," and this does not indicate that the dirham was obtained for him because of the coming. But when you say: "The one who came to me, then for him is a dirham," this indicates that the dirham was obtained for him because of the coming. Thus the mention of the fa' in this verse indicates that the non-acceptance of the ransom is causally linked to dying in disbelief.

The second question: What is the benefit of the waw in His saying: ﴿even if he would ransom himself therewith﴾?

Answer: They mentioned several aspects regarding it:

The first: Al-Zajjaj said: it is for conjunction (ʿatf), and the implied meaning is: even if he drew near to Allah with the earth filled with gold, that would not benefit him with his disbelief; and even if he ransomed himself from the punishment with the earth filled with gold, it would not be accepted from him. This is the choice of Ibn al-Anbari, who said: "This is more emphatic in severity, since it is an explicit denial of acceptance from all aspects."

The second: The waw entered to explain the detail after the general, because His saying: ﴿never will be accepted from any of them the earth filled with gold﴾ admits of many aspects, so He specified the denial of acceptance by way of ransom.

The third: This is an aspect that occurred to my mind: that whoever is angry with one of his slaves, if that slave presents him with a gift or present, he will never accept it at all, except that he may accept a ransom from him. But if he does not accept a ransom from him either, that is the utmost anger, and the emphasis is only achieved at that level which is the ultimate. So Allah, exalted is He, judged that He will not accept from them the earth filled with gold even if it were offered as a ransom, as a warning that since it is not accepted by this way, it is even more so that it will not be accepted from him by any other way.

The third question: It is known that the disbeliever does not own on the Day of Resurrection even a speck (naqir) or a thin membrane (qitmir). And it is known that even if he owned gold, gold would not benefit at all in the Hereafter. So what is the benefit of His saying: ﴿never will be accepted from any of them the earth filled with gold﴾?

Answer: There are two aspects to it:

One of them: that when they die upon disbelief, even if they had spent in the world the earth filled with gold, Allah, exalted is He, would never accept that from them, because obedience alongside disbelief is not accepted. The second: that the statement is in the form of a supposition, so gold is a metaphor for the most precious things, and the meaning is: even if the disbeliever on the Day of Resurrection were able to obtain the most precious things and then were able to expend them in the utmost abundance, he would be unable to use that to deliver himself from the punishment of Allah. In sum, the purpose is that they are in despair of saving themselves from the punishment.

The second kind of threat mentioned in this verse: His saying, ﴿Those will have a painful punishment﴾. Know that when Allah, exalted is He, made clear that the disbeliever cannot deliver himself from the punishment, He followed it with a description of that punishment, saying: ﴿Those will have a painful punishment﴾, i.e., painful (mu'lim).

The third kind of threat: His saying, ﴿and they will not have any helpers﴾. The meaning is that when Allah, exalted is He, made clear that there is no deliverance for them from this painful punishment by means of ransom, He also made clear that there is no deliverance for them from it by means of help, aid, or intercession. Our companions may argue from this verse for the establishment of intercession, because He concluded the enumeration of the threat against the disbelievers with the absence of help and intercession. If this meaning were realized with respect to a non-disbeliever, then the restriction of this threat to disbelief would be void. And Allah knows best.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 3, verse 92:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿You will never attain righteousness until you spend of that which you love﴾

Know that when Exalted God had explained that spending does not benefit the disbeliever in the slightest, He taught the believers the manner of spending by which they benefit in the Hereafter, so He said: ﴿You will never attain righteousness until you spend of that which you love﴾. In this verse He made clear that whoever spends of what he loves is among the righteous (al-abrar). Then He said in another verse: ﴿Indeed, the righteous will be in bliss﴾ [al-Infitar: 13]. He also said: ﴿Indeed, the righteous will drink from a cup whose mixture is of camphor﴾ [al-Insan: 5]. And He said: ﴿Indeed, the righteous will be in bliss, upon couches, observing. You will recognize in their faces the radiance of bliss. They will be given to drink of a sealed nectar, its seal is musk, and for this let the competitors compete﴾ [al-Mutaffifin: 22-26]. And He said: ﴿It is not righteousness that you turn your faces toward the east or the west﴾ [al-Baqarah: 177]. So when Exalted God had detailed the reward of the righteous in the rest of the verses, He here sufficed with mentioning that whoever spends what he loves attains righteousness. And in this there is another subtle point:

It is that He, exalted is He, said: ﴿It is not righteousness that you turn your faces toward the east or the west, but righteousness is [in] one who believes in Allah, the Last Day, the angels﴾ [al-Baqarah: 177], to the end of the verse. In this verse He mentioned most of the acts of good and called them righteousness. Then He said in this verse: ﴿You will never attain righteousness until you spend of that which you love﴾. The meaning is that even if you perform all those good deeds mentioned in that verse, you will not attain the excellence of righteousness until you spend of what you love. This indicates that when a person spends what he loves, that is the best of acts of obedience. Here there is a question: one may say that the word "until" (hatta) indicates the endpoint, so His saying: ﴿You will never attain righteousness until you spend of that which you love﴾ implies that whoever spends of what he loves has attained righteousness, and whoever attains righteousness enters under the verses indicating the great reward for the righteous. Thus this implies that whoever spends what he loves reaches the great reward, even if he does not perform the rest of the acts of obedience, and this is false.

The answer to this difficulty: a person cannot spend what he loves except when he uses the spending of that beloved thing as a means to finding a beloved that is nobler than the first. Accordingly, a person cannot spend the world in the world unless he is certain of the happiness of the Hereafter, and he cannot acknowledge the happiness of the Hereafter unless he affirms the existence of the Creator, the Knowing, the Powerful, and affirms that it is obligatory upon him to submit to His obligations, commands, and prohibitions. So when you reflect, you will know that a person cannot spend the world in the world unless he possesses all the praiseworthy qualities of the world. Let us return to the exegesis and say concerning the verse several issues:

The first issue: the predecessors (al-salaf), when they loved something, dedicated it to Allah. It is related that when this verse was revealed, Abu Talha said: "O Messenger of Allah, I have an orchard in Medina, and it is the dearest of my wealth to me. Shall I give it in charity?" He, peace be upon him, said: "Bakh, bakh, that is profitable wealth, and I see that you should place it among the nearest relatives." Abu Talha said: "I will do so, O Messenger of Allah," and he divided it among his relatives. It is also narrated that he gave it between Hassan ibn Thabit and Ubayy ibn Ka'b, may Allah be pleased with them both. It is related that Zayd ibn Harithah, may Allah be pleased with him, came at the revelation of this verse with a horse of his that he loved, and made it for the cause of Allah, and the Messenger of Allah ﷺ mounted Usama upon it, and Zayd felt something in himself, so he (peace be upon him) said: "Indeed Allah has accepted it." Ibn Umar bought a slave-girl who pleased him and freed her; it was said to him: "Why did you free her when you had not had intercourse with her?" He said: ﴿You will never attain righteousness until you spend of that which you love﴾.

The second issue: the exegetes have two views concerning the meaning of righteousness (al-birr). One: that by which they become righteous, so that they enter under His saying: ﴿Indeed, the righteous will be in bliss﴾ [al-Infitar: 13]; so the intended meaning of righteousness is the acceptable deeds that come from them. The second: the reward and Paradise, as if He said: you will not attain this station except by spending in this manner.

As for those who held the first view, some said: "al-birr" is piety (taqwa), and they argued with His saying: ﴿But righteousness is [in] one who believes in Allah﴾ up to His saying: ﴿Those are the ones who have been truthful, and those are the righteous (al-muttaqun)﴾ [al-Baqarah: 177]. Abu Dharr said: righteousness is goodness, and this is close to what preceded.

As for those who said: righteousness is Paradise, some said: ﴿You will never attain righteousness﴾ means you will never attain the reward of righteousness. Others said: the intended meaning is the righteousness of Allah toward His friends, His honoring them, and His bounty upon them; it is from the saying of people: "So-and-so was righteous (barrani) to me with such-and-such," and "So-and-so's righteousness does not cease toward me." Exalted is He said: ﴿Allah does not forbid you from those who do not fight you over religion... that you be righteous to them﴾ [al-Mumtahanah: 8].

The third issue: the exegetes differed regarding His saying: ﴿of that which you love﴾. Some said: it refers to wealth itself; He, exalted, said: ﴿And indeed he is intensely loving of wealth﴾ [al-'Adiyat: 8]. Others said: that the gift be excellent and good; He, exalted, said: ﴿And do not aim at the bad from it to spend﴾ [al-Baqarah: 267]. Others said: what one is in need of; He, exalted, said: ﴿And they give food, in spite of love for it, to the needy﴾ [al-Insan: 8], one of the interpretations of "love" in this verse being their need for it. And He said: ﴿And they prefer [others] over themselves, even though they are in privation﴾ [al-Hashr: 9]. And he, peace be upon him, said: "The best charity is what you give while you are healthy and miserly, hoping for wealth and fearing poverty." The better view is to say that all of this is taken into account in the category of excellence and abundance of reward.

* * *

The fourth issue: the exegetes differed as to whether this spending is zakat or something else. Ibn Abbas said: he meant by it zakat, i.e., until you give out the zakat of your wealth. Al-Hasan said: whatever a Muslim spends from his wealth seeking the face of Allah, he is among those whom Allah, glorified is He, meant by His saying: ﴿You will never attain righteousness until you spend of that which you love﴾, even a date. The judge (al-Qadi) preferred the first view and argued for it that this spending is that upon which Allah made dependent the servant's being among the righteous and his attaining Paradise, such that if this spending were not present, the servant would not attain this station, and that is none other than obligatory spending. I say: if we restricted the verse to other than zakat, it would be better, because the verse is specific to giving what is most beloved, and obligatory zakat does not involve giving what is most beloved, for it is not obligatory upon the one paying zakat to give out his most noble and precious wealth. Rather, the correct view is that this verse is specific to giving wealth by way of recommendation (nadb).

The fifth issue: al-Wahidi transmitted from Mujahid and al-Kalbi that this verse is abrogated (mansukh) by the verse of zakat. This is extremely far-fetched, because how could the obligation of zakat contradict the encouragement to give up what is loved for the sake of Allah, glorified and exalted is He?

The sixth issue: some said that the particle "min" in His saying ﴿of that which you love﴾ is partitive (li-l-tab'id), and 'Abdullah read: "until you spend some of what you love," and in this there is an indication that spending all of it is not permissible. Then He said: ﴿And those who, when they spend, are neither extravagant nor stingy, but are ever, between that, a moderate way﴾ [al-Furqan: 67]. Others said: it is explanatory (li-l-tabyin).

* *
* * *

As for His saying: ﴿And whatever you spend of anything, indeed Allah is Knowing of it﴾, there is a question concerning it:

It is that one may say: it is said: "indeed Allah is Knowing of it" as the response to the conditional, although Allah, exalted is He, knows it in every state.

The answer is in two respects:

The first: that it carries the meaning of recompense (jaza'). Its implied sense is: "And whatever you spend of anything, indeed Allah will recompense you for it, whether little or much, since He is Knowing of it, nothing of it being hidden from Him." So He made His being knowing of that spending a metaphor for giving the reward, and allusion (ta'rid) in such a place is more eloquent than explicit statement.

The second: that He, exalted is He, knows the aspect for which they do it, and knows whether the motive for it is sincerity or showing off, and knows whether you spend what is beloved and best, or what is base and worst.

Know that a parallel to this verse is His saying: ﴿And whatever good you do, Allah knows it﴾ [al-Baqarah: 197], and His saying: ﴿And whatever expenditure you spend or vow you vow, indeed Allah knows it﴾ [al-Baqarah: 270]. The author of al-Kashshaf said: "min" in His saying "min shay'" (of anything) is explanatory of what they spend, i.e., of anything that was good which you love, or bad which you dislike, indeed Allah is Knowing of it, recompensing you according to its measure.

**Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 3, verse 93 (part 1 of 2):**

**[Translation of the verses]**

﴿All food was lawful for the Children of Israel, except what Israel (Jacob) made unlawful for himself before the Torah was revealed. Say: "Bring the Torah and recite it, if you are truthful."﴾ ﴿Whoever fabricates a lie against Allah after this, those are the wrongdoers.﴾ ﴿Say: "Allah has spoken the truth. So follow the religion of Abraham, a man of pure faith, and he was not one of the polytheists."﴾

Know that the verses preceding this verse were concerned with establishing the proofs that point to the prophethood of Muhammad (ﷺ), and with directing the obligations addressed to the People of the Book in this regard.

As for this verse, it is concerned with answering the doubts of the people. The apparent meaning of the verse indicates that he (ﷺ) claimed that all food had been lawful, and then some of it became unlawful after having been lawful. The people disputed this with him and claimed that what is now unlawful had always been unlawful.

Having understood this, we say: the verse admits of several interpretations.

**The first:** The Jews relied in denying the law of Muhammad (ﷺ) on the denial of *naskh* (abrogation, the replacement of one ruling by a later one). So Allah refuted them with His words: ﴿All food was lawful for the Children of Israel, except what Israel made unlawful for himself﴾. That which he made unlawful for himself had been lawful, and then became unlawful for him and his descendants. Thus abrogation has occurred, and your claim that abrogation is impermissible is refuted. Then, when this question was put to the Jews, they denied that the prohibition of that food, which Allah had made unlawful, was because Israel had made it unlawful for himself. Rather, they claimed that it had been unlawful from the time of Adam (peace be upon him) until this time. At this point, the Messenger (peace be upon him) asked them to bring the Torah, for the Torah states that some kinds of food were made unlawful only because Israel had made them unlawful for himself. They feared disgrace and refused to bring the Torah. Thereupon many matters occurred which strengthen the proofs of the prophethood of Muhammad (ﷺ). Among them: first, this question was directed at them in denying abrogation, and it is an inescapable obligation from which there is no escape. Second, their lies became apparent to people, for they sometimes attribute to the Torah what is not in it, and at other times refuse to acknowledge what is in it. Third, the Messenger (ﷺ) was an unlettered man who could neither read nor write, so it was impossible for him to know this obscure matter from the sciences of the Torah except through news from heaven. This is a sound and well-founded interpretation of the verse and an explanation of its composition.

**The second:** The Jews said to him: "You claim that you follow the religion of Abraham. If that were so, how could you eat the flesh and milk of camels, when that was unlawful in the religion of Abraham?" They made this statement a doubt that undermined the validity of his claim. The Prophet (ﷺ) answered this doubt by saying: "That was lawful for Abraham, Ishmael, Isaac and Jacob (peace be upon them all), except that Jacob made it unlawful for himself for some reason, and that prohibition remained among his descendants." The Jews denied this, so the Messenger (peace be upon him) commanded them to bring the Torah and challenged them to extract from it a verse indicating that the flesh and milk of camels had been unlawful for Abraham (peace be upon him). They were unable to do so and were disgraced. It thus became clear that they were lying in claiming that these things were unlawful for Abraham (peace be upon him).

**The third:** When Allah revealed His words: ﴿And to those who were Jews We made unlawful every animal with claws, and from cattle and sheep We made unlawful to them their fat, except what their backs carry or the entrails, or what is mixed with bone. That We repaid them for their rebellion, and indeed We are truthful﴾ [al-An'am: 146], and He also said: ﴿For the wrongdoing of those who were Jews, We made unlawful to them good things that had been made lawful for them﴾ [al-Nisa': 160], these verses indicate that Allah made these things unlawful to the Jews only as a recompense for their rebellion, their wrongdoing and their evil deeds, and that no food had been unlawful except the one food which Israel had made unlawful for himself. This troubled the Jews in two respects:

One of them: that this indicates that those things were made unlawful after having been lawful, and this requires the occurrence of abrogation, which they deny.

The second: that this indicates that they were characterized by evil deeds. When these two matters were established against them, they denied that the prohibition of these things was newly introduced. Rather, they claimed that they had always been unlawful. The Prophet (ﷺ) challenged them to produce a verse from the Torah that supports their claim, but they were unable to do so and were disgraced. This is the sense of the explanation of this verse, and all of it is sound and correct. Let us now return to the explanation of the words.

As for His words: ﴿All food was lawful for the Children of Israel﴾, there are several issues concerning it:

**The first issue:** The author of *al-Kashshaf* said: ﴿All food﴾ means "all edible things" or "all kinds of food." I say: People have differed on whether a singular noun preceded by the definite article *al-* (alif-lam) indicates generality or not.

Some jurists and scholars of language held that it does indicate generality, and they argued for this with several points:

First: Allah placed the word *kull* ("all") before the word *ta'am* ("food") in this verse. Had the word *ta'am* not been equivalent to the word *ma'kulat* ("edible things"), this would not have been permissible.

Second: He made an exception from it, saying "except what Israel made unlawful for himself." An exception removes from the statement what would otherwise have been included. Therefore, unless all the categories were included under the word *ta'am*, this exception would not be valid. They reinforced this with the words of Allah: ﴿Indeed, mankind is in loss, except those who believe﴾ [al-'Asr: 2–3].

Third: Allah described this singular word with what is used to describe a plural word, saying: ﴿And the palm trees with their tall spathes, having layered clusters, as provision for the servants﴾ [Qaf: 10–11]. Accordingly, whoever holds this view does not need the implied supposition mentioned by the author of *al-Kashshaf*. As for those who say that a singular noun preceded by *al-* does not indicate generality, which is the view we examined in the principles of jurisprudence (usul al-fiqh), they need the implied supposition that the author of *al-Kashshaf* mentioned.

**The second issue:** *Al-ta'am* is a term for everything that is eaten and consumed. Some followers of Abu Hanifa (may Allah have mercy on him) claimed that it refers only to wheat (*al-burr*). This verse indicates the weakness of this view, because it made an exception from the word *ta'am* of what Israel made unlawful for himself, and the exegetes agreed that what Israel made unlawful for himself was something other than wheat and what is made from it. Something that confirms this is the words of Allah concerning water: ﴿And whoever does not taste it, he is indeed of me﴾ [al-Baqarah: 249]. And He said: ﴿The food of those who were given the Book is lawful for you, and your food is lawful for them﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 5], meaning slaughtered animals. And 'A'isha (may Allah be pleased with her) said: "We had no food except the two blacks," meaning dates and water.

Having understood this, we say: the apparent meaning of this verse indicates that all edible things were lawful for the Children of Israel. Then al-Qaffal said: "It has not reached us that carrion was permitted to them, although it is food; and likewise with pork." Then he said: "It is possible that this refers to the foods which the Jews claimed at the time of the Messenger (ﷺ) had been unlawful for Abraham. On this interpretation, the *alif-lam* in the word *ta'am* is not for generality but for a previously known reference, and on this interpretation the difficulty disappears." A similar case is the words of Allah: ﴿Say: "I do not find in what has been revealed to me anything forbidden to one who eats, except that it be carrion, or flowing blood, or the flesh of swine"﴾ [al-An'am: 145]. This statement was made concerning things about which they had asked, and they learned that the unlawful ones among them were such-and-such and not others. The same applies to this verse.

**The third issue:** *Al-hill* ("lawfulness") is a verbal noun (masdar). One says: *halla al-shay'u hillan*, like your saying: *dhallat al-dabbah dhillan* ("the animal became tame") and *'azza al-rajul 'izzan* ("the man became powerful"). For this reason, the masculine and feminine, singular and plural are alike when described by it. Allah said: ﴿They are not lawful for them﴾ [al-Mumtahanah: 10]. Describing something with a verbal noun conveys emphasis. Here, *al-hill* and *al-muhallal* ("that which is made lawful") are the same. Ibn 'Abbas (may Allah be pleased with both of them) said concerning Zamzam: "It is *hill* and *bill*" (lawful and sufficient), narrated by Sufyan ibn 'Uyayna. Sufyan was asked: "What is *hill*?" He said: "*Muhallal*" (that which is made lawful).

* * *

As for His words: ﴿except what Israel made unlawful for himself﴾, there are several issues concerning it:

**The first issue:** The scholars differed about the thing which Israel made unlawful for himself, in several views:

**The first:** Ibn 'Abbas narrated that the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Jacob became seriously ill, and he vowed that if Allah restored him to health, he would make unlawful for himself the food and drink he loved most. The food he loved most was the flesh of camels, and the drink he loved most was their milk." This is the view of Abu al-'Aliya, 'Ata' and Muqatil.

**The second:** It was said that he had sciatica, and he vowed that if Allah cured him, he would not eat any sinews.

**The third:** It is reported in some narrations that what he made unlawful for himself was the extra parts of the liver and the fat, except what is on the back. Al-Qaffal (may Allah have mercy on him) related from the translation of the Torah that when Jacob left Haran for Canaan, he sent a messenger to his brother Esau in the land of Seir. The messenger returned to him and said: "Esau is coming to meet you, and with him are four hundred men." Jacob was terrified and deeply grieved, and he prayed, supplicated, and sent gifts to his brother. He related the story until he mentioned the king who met him in the form of a man. That man drew near and placed his finger on the place of the sciatic nerve, so that nerve became numb and dried up. For this reason, the Children of Israel do not eat sinews.

**The second issue:** The apparent meaning of the verse indicates that Israel made that unlawful for himself. Here there is a question: prohibition and permission are established only by the address of Allah, so how did Jacob's prohibition (peace be upon him) become the cause of the prohibition arising?

The exegetes answered this in several ways:

**The first:** It is not far-fetched that when a person makes something unlawful for himself, Allah makes it unlawful for him. Do you not see that a person makes his wife unlawful for himself by divorce, and makes his slave-girl unlawful by manumission? Likewise, it is permissible that Allah says: If you make something unlawful for yourself, I also make it unlawful for you.

**The second:** The Prophet (upon him be blessings and peace) may have exercised *ijtihad* (independent legal reasoning), and his reasoning led him to prohibition, so he declared it unlawful. We say that *ijtihad* is permissible for the prophets for several reasons:

The first: the words of Allah: ﴿So take warning, O you who have sight﴾ [al-Hashr: 2]. There is no doubt that the prophets (peace be upon them) are the foremost of those who have sight.

The second: He said: ﴿Those among them who draw conclusions would know it﴾ [al-Nisa': 83]. He praised those who draw conclusions, and the prophets are more deserving of this praise.

The third: Allah said to Muhammad (peace be upon him): ﴿May Allah pardon you. Why did you grant them permission?﴾ [al-Tawbah: 43]. Had that permission been by explicit text, He would not have said "Why did you grant them permission?" This indicates that it was by *ijtihad*.

Fourthly: There is no obedience except to God and to the prophets, peace be upon them, and they have the greatest share in it. There is no doubt that deriving the rulings of God, Exalted, through *ijtihad* (independent legal reasoning) is a great and arduous act of obedience. Therefore it is necessary that the prophets, peace be upon them, have a share in it, especially since their knowledge is greater, their intellects are brighter, their minds are purer, and God's guidance and support are greater with them. Moreover, if they issue a ruling on the basis of *ijtihad*, it becomes unlawful for the community to oppose them in that ruling, just as when a *ijma'* (scholarly consensus) is reached on an *ijtihad*, opposing it is unlawful. The more evident and stronger view is that Israel, may God's blessings be upon him, prohibited that only for himself, on the basis of *ijtihad*. For if it had been by explicit text, he would have said: "except what God prohibited for Israel." Since the prohibition was attributed to Israel, this indicates that it was by *ijtihad*. It is like saying: al-Shafi'i permits eating horse meat, while Abu Hanifa prohibits it, meaning that his *ijtihad* led him to that. So likewise here.

Thirdly: It is possible that the prohibition in his law was like the *nadhr* (vow) in our law. Just as fulfilling a vow is obligatory on us, so fulfilling the prohibition was obligatory in his law.

Know that even if this were so, it would have been specific to his law. In our law, it is not established. God, Exalted, said: ﴿O Prophet, why do you prohibit what God has made lawful for you?﴾ [al-Tahrim: 1]

Fourthly: al-Asamm said: Perhaps his soul inclined toward eating those kinds, so he refrained from eating them, subduing his soul and seeking the pleasure of God, Exalted, as many ascetics do. He expressed that abstention as prohibition.

Fifthly: Some of the theologians said that it is permissible for God, Exalted, to say to His servant: "Judge, for you will only judge correctly." Perhaps this incident was of this type. The theologians have many disputes on this question, which we have mentioned in *usul al-fiqh* (the principles of jurisprudence).

* * *

The third issue: The apparent meaning of this verse indicates that what Israel prohibited for himself, God prohibited for the Children of Israel. This is because He, Exalted, said: ﴿All food was lawful for the Children of Israel﴾. So He ruled that all kinds of food were lawful for the Children of Israel, and then made an exception of what Israel had prohibited for himself. Therefore, by the force of the exception, it is necessary that this be forbidden to the Children of Israel. And God knows best.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 3, verses 94–95:

As for His saying, ﴿Before the Torah was revealed﴾, the meaning is that before the revelation of the Torah, all kinds of foods were lawful for the Children of Israel, except what Israel (Ya'qub) had forbidden upon himself. After the Torah, however, this was no longer the case; rather, Allah Most High forbade them many kinds [of food]. It is narrated that when the Children of Israel committed a great sin, Allah forbade them a type of food, or sent upon them something to destroy or harm them. The evidence for this is His saying: ﴿For the wrongdoing of those who were Jews, We forbade them good things which had been made lawful for them﴾ [al-Nisa': 160].

* * *

Then He said: ﴿Say, "Bring the Torah and recite it, if you are truthful."﴾ This indicates that the people disputed with the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, either because they claimed that the prohibition of these things had existed from the time of Adam (peace be upon him) until this era, so the Messenger of Allah ﷺ refuted them in that, or because the Messenger ﷺ claimed that these foods were permissible in ancient times, and that they were only forbidden because Israel had forbidden them upon himself, so they disputed with him on that. The Messenger (peace be upon him) then requested that the Torah be brought so that the Muslims could extract from the scholars of the People of the Book a verse agreeing with the words of the Messenger. In either case, the interpretation is clear. And those who deny analogy (qiyas) may use this verse as evidence, because the Messenger (peace be upon him) challenged them, regarding what they claimed, to produce the Book of Allah. Had analogy been a proof, they would have been able to say: "The absence of this ruling from the Torah does not necessitate its absence, because we establish it by analogy." It may be answered that the dispute did not concern a legal ruling; rather, it concerned whether this ruling existed in the time of Abraham and the rest of the prophets (peace be upon them) or not. Such a matter cannot be established except by explicit text, and for this reason the Messenger (may Allah's blessings and peace be upon him) challenged them with the explicit text of the Torah.

* * *

Then He said, Most High: ﴿Whoever then fabricates a lie against Allah﴾. Al-iftira' is the invention of falsehood. Al-firya is falsehood and slander, and its root is from the tearing of hide (fari al-adim), meaning cutting it. Falsehood is called iftira' because the liar cuts (his speech) without verifying it in reality.

* * *

Then He said: ﴿after that﴾, meaning after the proof has become manifest that the prohibition originated from Ya'qub and was not forbidden before him. ﴿Then those are the wrongdoers﴾, deserving the punishment of Allah, because their disbelief is a wrong against themselves and against those whom they led astray from the religion.

* * *

Then He said, Most High: ﴿Say, "Allah has spoken the truth."﴾ It may bear several meanings:

First: ﴿Say, "He has spoken the truth"﴾ regarding the fact that this kind of food became forbidden to Israel and his descendants after having been lawful to them. Thus the notion of abrogation (naskh) is valid, and the doubt of the Jews is refuted.

Second: ﴿Allah has spoken the truth﴾ in His saying that the flesh and milk of camels were lawful for Abraham (peace be upon him), and that they were forbidden to the Children of Israel only because Israel had forbidden them upon himself. Thus it is established that when Muhammad ﷺ gave the ruling of the permissibility of camel flesh and milk, he was ruling according to the religion of Abraham.

Third: ﴿Allah has spoken the truth﴾ in that all foods were lawful for the Children of Israel, and that they were forbidden to the Jews only as a punishment for their vile deeds.

* * *

Then He said, Most High: ﴿So follow the religion of Abraham, a ḥanīf﴾, i.e., follow what Muhammad (may Allah's blessings be upon him) calls you to of the religion of Abraham. Whether he said "the religion of Abraham, a ḥanīf" or "the religion of Abraham, the ḥanīf," is the same in meaning, because the circumstantial qualifier (al-ḥāl) and the attribute (al-ṣifa) are equivalent in meaning.

Page 124

Then He said: ﴿And he was not of the polytheists﴾, i.e., he did not invoke any other god alongside Allah, nor worship other than Him, as some did in worshipping the sun and the moon, or as the Arabs did in worshipping idols, or as the Jews did in claiming that Uzair is the son of Allah, and as the Christians did in claiming that the Messiah is the son of Allah. The purpose of this is to show that Muhammad (may Allah's blessings be upon him) follows the religion of Abraham (peace be upon him) in both the branches and the foundations.

As for the branches: since it is established that whatever he ruled to be lawful, Abraham had also ruled to be lawful. As for the foundations: since Muhammad (may Allah's blessings and peace be upon him) calls only to monotheism and to disavowal of every object of worship other than Allah Most High, and Abraham (may Allah's blessings and peace be upon him) was only upon this religion.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 3, verse 96 (part 1 of 3):

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, the first House established for mankind is that at Bakkah, blessed and a guidance for the worlds﴾ ﴿In it are clear signs, the Station of Ibrahim; and whoever enters it is safe﴾. Regarding the connection of this verse with what precedes it, there are several aspects:

The first: its purpose is to answer another doubt from the doubts of the Jews concerning the denial of the prophethood of Muhammad, peace be upon him. This is because when he, peace be upon him, changed the qiblah to the Ka'bah, the Jews attacked his prophethood and said: "Bayt al-Maqdis is superior to the Ka'bah and more deserving of facing towards it, because it was established before the Ka'bah, it is the land of the gathering, and it is the qiblah of all the prophets. If that is so, then changing the qiblah from it to the Ka'bah is false." So God, exalted is He, answered them with His saying: ﴿Indeed, the first House established for mankind﴾, thereby making clear that the Ka'bah is more excellent and more honourable than Bayt al-Maqdis, so making it the qiblah was more fitting.

The second: the intended purpose of the preceding verse is to show whether abrogation (naskh) is permissible or not. The Prophet (ﷺ) argued for its permissibility by pointing out that foods had been permitted to the Children of Israel, then God forbade some of them, and the people disputed this with the Messenger of God (ﷺ). Among the greatest matters whose abrogation the Messenger of God made manifest is the qiblah. Therefore God, exalted is He, mentioned in this verse the explanation of why the Ka'bah was made the qiblah, namely that the Ka'bah is more excellent than others.

The third: when God, exalted is He, said in the preceding verse: ﴿Follow the religion of Ibrahim, a hanif, and he was not of the polytheists﴾ [Al 'Imran: 95], and since among the greatest symbols of the religion of Ibrahim is the Hajj, He mentioned in this verse the virtue of the House, so as to derive from it the obligation of the Hajj.

The fourth: the Jews and Christians each claimed that they were upon the religion of Ibrahim, and this debate has already passed in the preceding verses. God, exalted is He, showed their falsehood, in that the pilgrimage to the Ka'bah was the religion of Ibrahim, while the Jews and Christians do not make pilgrimage; this indicates their falsehood in that claim.

In the verse there are issues:

The first issue: The scholars who investigate said: "The first" (al-awwal) is the single, preceding item. If someone says, "The first slave I buy is free," and then he buys two slaves at the first time, neither of them is freed, because the "first" is the single one. Then if he buys one slave the second time, it is not freed either, because the condition of "first" is that it be preceding. Thus it is established that "the first" is the single preceding item.

Having understood this, we say: God's saying, ﴿Indeed, the first House established for mankind﴾, does not indicate that it is the first house God created, nor the first house to appear on the earth. Rather, the apparent meaning of the verse indicates that it is the first house established for mankind. Its being established for mankind requires that it be shared among all people, whereas each of the other houses is specific to one person, so none of the houses is established for mankind. A house being shared among all people is achieved only if it is established for acts of obedience and worship and as a qiblah for creation. Thus God's saying, ﴿Indeed, the first House established for mankind﴾, indicates that God established this House as a place for obedience, good works and worship; and this includes that this House is a qiblah for prayers, a place for the Hajj, and a place where the reward of worship and obedience is increased.

If it is said: its being first in this description requires that it have a second, and this requires that Bayt al-Maqdis share with it these qualities, among which is the obligation of its pilgrimage; and it is known that this is not so.

The answer is in two respects: The first: the word "first" in the language is a name for the thing that exists at the beginning, whether or not something else occurs after it. One says: "This is my first arrival at Makkah," and "This is the first wealth I obtained." If someone says, "The first slave I own is free," and he owns a slave, he is freed, even if he does not own another slave after him; so it is the same here. The second: the meaning of God's saying, ﴿Indeed, the first House established for mankind﴾, is the first house established for the obedience and worship of people; and Bayt al-Maqdis shares with it in being a house established for acts of obedience and worship, by the evidence of the saying of the Prophet, peace be upon him: "Travel is not undertaken except to three mosques: the Sacred Mosque, al-Masjid al-Aqsa, and this mosque of mine." This degree is sufficient for the truth that the Ka'bah is the first house established for mankind. As for Bayt al-Maqdis sharing with it in all matters, even in the obligation of the Hajj, this does not follow. And God knows best.

* * *

The second issue: Know that God's saying, ﴿Indeed, the first House established for mankind at Bakkah, blessed﴾, may mean that it was first in its establishment and construction, or that it was first in being blessed and a guidance. Therefore the exegetes have two views on the interpretation of this verse.

The first: that it is first in construction and establishment. Those who hold this view have several sayings. One of them: what al-Wahidi, may God have mercy on him, transmitted in "al-Basit" with his chain from Mujahid that he said: God created this House before He created any of the earths; and in another narration: God created the place of this House two thousand years before He created any part of the earth, and its foundations are in the lowest seventh earth. It is also narrated from Muhammad ibn 'Ali ibn al-Husayn ibn 'Ali ibn Abi Talib, may God be pleased with them all, from his father, from the Prophet (ﷺ) who said: "God, exalted is He, sent His angels and said: Build for Me on the earth a house in the likeness of the Bayt al-Ma'mur, and God commanded whoever is on the earth to circumambulate it as the people of heaven circumambulate the Bayt al-Ma'mur. This was before the creation of Adam."

Also it is found in the other books of tafsir, from 'Abd Allah ibn 'Umar, Mujahid and al-Suddi, that it was the first house placed upon the surface of the water at the creation of the earth and the heaven, and God created it two thousand years before the earth, and it was a white foam upon the water; then the earth was spread out beneath it. Al-Qaffal said in his tafsir: Habib ibn Thabit transmitted from Ibn 'Abbas that he said: It was found in a book at the Maqam, or beneath the Maqam: "I am God, Lord of Bakkah. I placed it on the day I placed the sun and the moon, and I made it sacred on the day I placed these two stones, and I secured it with seven angels, hanifs."

The second: when Adam, may the blessings and peace of God be upon him, was sent down to the earth, he complained of loneliness, so God commanded him to build the Ka'bah, and he circumambulated it. This remained until the time of Noah, peace be upon him. When God sent the flood, He raised the House to the seventh heaven opposite the Ka'bah, where the angels worship; seventy thousand angels enter it every day, apart from those who had entered it before. Then after the flood, the site of the Ka'bah was obliterated and remained hidden until God, exalted is He, sent Jibril, peace be upon him, to Ibrahim, peace be upon him, and he guided him to the place of the House and commanded him to rebuild it. So Jibril was the engineer, Ibrahim the builder, and Isma'il the helper, peace be upon them.

Know that these two views agree that the Ka'bah existed in the time of Adam, peace be upon him. This is the more correct view, and several things indicate it. The first: the obligation of prayer was binding in the religion of all the prophets, peace be upon them, by the evidence of God's saying in Surah Maryam: ﴿Those are the ones upon whom God bestowed favour from among the prophets, of the descendants of Adam, and of those We carried with Noah, and of the descendants of Ibrahim and Israel, and of those whom We guided and chose. When the verses of the Most Merciful are recited to them, they fell down prostrating and weeping﴾ [Maryam: 58]. The verse indicates that all the prophets, peace be upon them, used to prostrate to God, and prostration must have a qiblah. If the qiblah of Shith, Idris and Noah, peace be upon them, had been a place other than this qiblah, then His saying, ﴿Indeed, the first House established for mankind at Bakkah﴾, would be false. Therefore it must be said that the qiblah of those earlier prophets was the Ka'bah, and this shows that this direction was always honoured and exalted. The second: God, exalted is He, named Makkah "the Mother of Villages," and the apparent meaning of this requires that it was preeminent over all other regions in excellence and honour since it existed. The third: it is narrated that the Prophet (ﷺ) said in his sermon on the day of the conquest of Makkah: "Indeed God made Makkah sacred on the day He created the heavens and the earth, the sun and the moon," and the sanctification of Makkah is not possible unless Makkah existed. The fourth: the reports we have related from the Companions and the Successors indicate that it existed before the time of Ibrahim, peace be upon him.

Know that whoever denies this has arguments. The first: what is narrated that the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "O God, I have made Madinah sacred as Ibrahim made Makkah sacred." The apparent meaning of this requires that Makkah is the building of Ibrahim, peace be upon him. The opponent may say: it is not unlikely that the House existed before Ibrahim and was not sacred, then Ibrahim made it sacred, peace be upon him. The second: they held to God's saying: ﴿And when Ibrahim was raising the foundations of the House, and Isma'il﴾ [al-Baqarah: 127]. The opponent may say: perhaps the House existed before that, then it collapsed, then God commanded Ibrahim to raise its foundations, and this is what appears in most reports. The third: al-Qadi said: What is said, that it was raised to the heaven at the time of the flood, is far-fetched, because the noble place is that specific direction, and a direction cannot be raised to the heaven. Do you not see that if the Ka'bah, God forbid, were demolished and its stones, wood and dust were transported to another place, that place would have no honour at all, and the honour of that direction would remain after the demolition, and every Muslim must face that very direction in prayer. If so, there is no benefit in transporting those walls to the heaven. The opponent may say: when those bodies reached such a level of honour that God commanded their transfer to the heaven, and they attained this honour only because they were situated in that direction, then their transfer to the heaven becomes one of the greatest proofs of the utmost glorification and honouring of that direction. This is the sum of what is in this view.

The second view: that the intended meaning of this priority is that this House was first in being blessed and a guidance for creation. It is narrated that the Prophet, peace be upon him, was asked about the first mosque established for mankind, and he said, peace be upon him: "The Sacred Mosque, then Bayt al-Maqdis." It was asked: "How long between them?" He said: "Forty years." And from 'Ali, may God be pleased with him, that a man said to him: "Is it the first house?" He said: "No, there were houses before it, but it is the first house established for mankind, blessed, in which there is guidance, mercy and blessing. The first to build it was Ibrahim, then a people of the Arabs from Jurhum built it, then it was demolished and the Amalekites built it, who were kings from the descendants of 'Imliq ibn Sam ibn Noah, then it was demolished and Quraysh built it."

Know that the indication of the verse for priority in excellence and honour is something necessary, because the primary purpose of mentioning this priority is to show its excellence, since the aim is to prefer it over Bayt al-Maqdis. This is accomplished only through priority in excellence and honour, and priority in construction has no effect on this aim. Yet the establishment of priority by virtue of excellence does not negate the establishment of priority in construction, and we have already demonstrated the establishment of this meaning as well.

* * *

The third issue: Since it has been established that the intended meaning of this priority is the increase of excellence and distinction, we shall now mention here the aspects of the House's excellence:

The First Virtue: The nations agree that the builder of this House was Abraham (peace be upon him), and the builder of Bayt al-Maqdis was Solomon (peace be upon him). Without doubt, Abraham is greater in rank and more excellent in merit than Solomon (peace be upon him). From this aspect, the Ka'bah must be nobler than Bayt al-Maqdis.

Know that God Most High commanded Abraham (peace be upon him) to rebuild this House, saying: ﴿And when We settled for Abraham the place of the House, [saying], "Do not associate anything with Me, and purify My House for those who circumambulate and stand [in prayer] and bow and prostrate."﴾ [al-Hajj: 26]. The one who conveyed this command was Gabriel (peace be upon him). Hence it was said: there is no building in the world nobler than the Ka'bah. The commander is the Majestic King, the engineer is Gabriel, the builder is the Friend (Abraham), and the student is Isma'il (peace be upon them all).

The Second Virtue: ﴿The station of Abraham﴾, which is the stone upon which Abraham placed his foot. God made the part of that stone beneath Abraham's foot, alone among its other parts, soft like clay, until Abraham's foot sank into it. This is something none can do except God, and He manifests it only to the prophets. Then, when Abraham lifted his foot from it, God again created in it the hardness of stone. Then God Most High preserved that stone in a continuous and enduring state. These are kinds of wondrous signs and striking miracles that God, glorified be He, manifested in that stone.

The Third Virtue: the scarcity of the pebbles of the jamarat that gather there. For since a thousand years ago, the number of those who stone [the pillars] each year has reached six hundred thousand people, each of them throwing seventy pebbles, yet there is seen there only what, if it were gathered in a single year, would not be much. The place to which the pebbles are cast is neither a watercourse nor a place of strong winds. It has been related in reports that whoever's pilgrimage is accepted, the pebbles of his stoning are lifted up to heaven.

The Fourth Virtue: birds avoid passing over the Ka'bah when flying in the air; rather, they veer away from it when they reach its vicinity.

The Fifth Virtue: wild animals gather there without harming one another, such as dogs and gazelles, and dogs and wild beasts are not hunted within it. This is a wondrous property. Also, whoever dwells in Makkah is safe from plunder and raids, and this is the blessing of Abraham's prayer when he said: ﴿My Lord, make this a secure city﴾ [al-Baqarah: 126]. And God Most High said describing its security: ﴿Have they not seen that We made a sanctuary secure while people are being snatched away from around them?﴾ [al-'Ankabut: 67]. And He said: ﴿So let them worship the Lord of this House, who has fed them against hunger and secured them against fear﴾ [Quraysh: 3-4].

It has never been reported at all that a tyrant demolished the Ka'bah and utterly ruined Makkah. As for Bayt al-Maqdis, Bukhtansar (Nebuchadnezzar) utterly demolished it.

The Sixth Virtue: the Companion of the Elephant, who is Abrahah al-Ashram, when he led the armies and the elephant to Makkah to destroy the Ka'bah, and the Quraysh were unable to resist those armies and departed from Makkah, leaving the Ka'bah to him. God sent against them birds in flocks (ababil). The ababil are groups of birds following one another; they were small, carrying stones which they hurled at them. The king perished and the army perished by those stones, although they were extremely small. This is a striking sign indicating the nobility of the Ka'bah and a prelude (irhas) to the prophethood of Muhammad (peace be upon him).

If someone says: why is it not possible to say that all of that was due to a talisman (tilsam) placed there in such a way that no one knows it, for the matter of composing talismans is well known?

We say: if this were from the category of talismans, it would be a talisman unlike all other talismans, for nothing other than the Ka'bah has attained such lengthy endurance over this great period. Something like this is among the miracles, and so none can achieve it except the prophets.

The Seventh Virtue: God Most High placed it in a valley without cultivation. The wisdom behind this is in several respects. First: by this He cut off the hopes of the people of His sanctuary and the custodians of His House from others, so that they would rely on none but God. Second: no tyrant or emperor would settle there, for they seek the delights of this world; if they do not find them there, they abandon that place. So the purpose is to purify that place from the defilement of the presence of worldly people. Third: He did this so that no one would come to it for trade; rather, it would be solely for pure worship and visitation. Fourth: through this God manifested the nobility of poverty, for He placed the noblest houses in the places least endowed with worldly portion. It is as if He said: I made the poor in this world the people of the secure city, and likewise I will make them in the Hereafter the people of the secure station; for them in this world is the House of Security, and in the Hereafter the Abode of Security. Fifth: it is as if He said: since I did not place the Ka'bah except in a place empty of all the blessings of this world, so likewise I will not place the Ka'bah of knowledge except in every heart empty of love of this world. This is what pertains to the virtues of the Ka'bah. At this point it becomes clear that this House is the first House established for people in all kinds of virtues and merits. And when this is clear, the claim of the Jews that Bayt al-Maqdis is nobler than the Ka'bah is refuted. And God knows best.

* * *

Then God Most High said: ﴿That which is at Bakkah﴾, and concerning it there are issues:

First issue: There is no doubt that by "Bakkah" is meant Makkah. Then they differed. Some said: Bakkah and Makkah are two names for one referent, for the letters ba' and mim are close in their point of articulation, so each may stand in place of the other. It is said: "darbat lazim" and "darbat lazib"; it is said: "da'im" and "da'ib"; it is said: "rati b" and "rati m"; and it is said: "samada ra'sahu" and "sabada-hu." Regarding the derivation of Bakkah there are two views. The first: that it is from al-bakk, which means pushing some of a thing against another, one says: "bakkahu yabukkuhu bakkan" if he pushed and crowded him, and "tabakka al-qawm" if the people crowded together. For this reason Sa'id ibn Jubayr said: Makkah was called Bakkah because they crowd there, that is, they press upon one another in circumambulation. This is also the view of Muhammad ibn 'Ali al-Baqir, Mujahid, and Qatadah. Some said: I saw Muhammad ibn 'Ali al-Baqir praying, and a woman passed in front of him, so I went to push her away, and he said: "Leave her, for it is called Bakkah because they press one another there: a woman passes before a man while he prays, and a man passes before a woman while she prays; there is no harm in that in this place."

Page 129

The second view: it was named Bakkah because it crushes the necks of tyrants; no tyrant intends it with evil except that his neck is broken. Qutrub said: the Arabs say "bakaktu 'unuqahu abukkuhu bakkan" when you lower a man and curb his pride.

As for Makkah, there are several views on its derivation. The first: that its derivation is from its "tamukku al-dhunub," that is, it removes sins entirely, from your saying: "imtakka al-fasil dar' ummihi," when the young camel sucks out what is in the udder. The second: it was so named because it draws people from every side of the earth; one says: "imtakka al-fasil" when it has exhausted what is in the udder, and "tamakkaktu al-'azm" when you have exhausted what is in the bone. The third: Makkah was named for the scarcity of its water, as if its land had sucked up its water. The fourth: it is said that Makkah is the center of the earth, and springs and waters gush out from beneath Makkah, so the whole earth drinks (tamukku) from the water of Makkah. Some people distinguished between Makkah and Bakkah. Some of them said: Bakkah is a name for the mosque specifically, while Makkah is a name for the entire town. They said: the evidence for this is that the derivation of Bakkah is from crowding and pushing, and this occurs only in the mosque during circumambulation, not in other places. Most scholars said: Makkah is the name for the mosque and the place of circumambulation, and Bakkah is the name of the town. The evidence for this is that God's saying ﴿for people, that which is at Bakkah﴾ indicates that the House is situated in Bakkah and contained within Bakkah. If Bakkah were a name for the House, then Bakkah could not be the container of the House; but if we make Bakkah a name for the town, the statement holds together.

Second issue: Makkah has many names. Al-Qaffal, may God have mercy on him, said in his Tafsir: Makkah, Bakkah, Umm Rahm, Kuwaysa', al-Bashasha, and al-Hatimah, which crushes whoever treats it lightly; and Umm al-Qura. God Most High said: ﴿That you may warn the mother of cities and those around it﴾ [al-Shura: 7]. It was named Umm al-Qura because it is the origin of every town, and from it the earth was spread out; and for this meaning that place is visited from all regions of the earth.

Third issue: The Ka'bah has names. One of them: al-Ka'bah. God said: ﴿God made the Ka'bah, the Sacred House﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 97]. The reason is that this name indicates elevation and height; the ankle (ka'b) was named ka'b because of its prominence and height above the wrist; and a woman with high breasts is called ka'ib because her breasts are raised. Since this House is the noblest of the houses of the earth, the oldest in time, and the most excellent, it was named by this name. Second: al-Bayt al-'Atiq. God said: ﴿Then its place of sacrifice is at the Ancient House﴾ [al-Hajj: 33], and He said: ﴿And let them circumambulate the Ancient House﴾ [al-Hajj: 29]. Regarding its derivation there are several views. The first: al-'Atiq is the ancient, and we have shown that it is the oldest house on earth; indeed, according to some, God created it before the earth and the heavens. The second: God freed it (a'taqahu) from drowning when He raised it up to heaven. The third: from 'atiqa al-tair, when a bird grows strong in its nest; when it reached such strength that whoever intended its destruction was destroyed by God, it was called ancient (atiq). The fourth: God freed it from being the property of any created being. The fifth: it is ancient in the sense that whoever visits it is freed by God Most High from the Fire. Sixth: al-Masjid al-Haram. God, glorified be He, said: ﴿Glory be to He who took His servant by night from al-Masjid al-Haram to al-Masjid al-Aqsa﴾ [al-Isra': 1]. The meaning of its being sacred will come, God willing, in the commentary on this verse.

If someone says: how is one to reconcile His saying ﴿Indeed, the first House established for people﴾ with His saying ﴿and purify My House for those who circumambulate﴾ [al-Hajj: 26], attributing it once to Himself and once to the people?

Page 130

The answer: it is as if it was said: the House is Mine, but I established it not for My benefit, for I am exalted above need; rather I established it for you, so that it would be a qibla for your supplication. And God knows best.
