Then God Most High said: ﴿Blessed and a guidance for the worlds﴾.

Know that God Most High described this House with kinds of virtues. The first of them: it is the first House established for people, and we have mentioned the meaning of its being first in virtue, and we add here other aspects. First: 'Ali, may God be pleased with him, said: it is the first house singled out for blessing, and whoever enters it is safe. al-Hasan said: it is the first mosque in which God was worshipped on earth. Mutarrif said: it is the first house made a qibla. Second: God described it as blessed, and on this there are two issues:

First issue: "Mubarakan" is in the accusative as a circumstantial (hal), and the implied sense is: the one which is established at Bakkah, blessed.

**Second issue:** Barakah (blessing) has two meanings. The first is growth and increase. The second is permanence and continuity. It is said "tabaraka Allah" (blessed is God) because He is established and has never ceased. A birkah (pool) is so named because water remains settled in it. And "baraka al-ba'ir" means the camel lowered its chest to the ground, settled and stayed in place. If we interpret blessing as increase and growth, then this House is blessed in several respects.

The first respect is that acts of worship performed in it have their reward multiplied. The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "The virtue of the Sacred Mosque over my mosque is like the virtue of my mosque over the other mosques." Then he (ﷺ) said: "A prayer in this mosque of mine is better than a thousand prayers elsewhere." This concerns prayer. As for pilgrimage, the Prophet (ﷺ) said, peace and blessings be upon him: "Whoever performs the Hajj without indecency or sin returns free of his sins as on the day his mother bore him." In another hadith: "The accepted Hajj has no reward but Paradise." It is known that nothing brings more blessing than that which brings forgiveness and mercy.

The second respect: al-Qaffal, may God have mercy on him, said: It is possible that its blessing is what is mentioned in God's words: ﴿To which are brought the fruits of every thing﴾ (28:57), and this would be like His words: ﴿To the farthest mosque, whose surroundings We have blessed﴾ (17:1).

The third respect: The intelligent person must bring to mind that the Ka'bah is like a point, and he should imagine that the rows of those facing it in prayer are like circles surrounding the center. Let him consider how many rows surround this circle while they are occupied in prayer. There is no doubt that among these worshippers there are persons whose spirits are lofty, whose hearts are holy, whose secrets are luminous and whose inner consciences are divine. Then, when those pure spirits turn toward the Ka'bah of knowledge while their bodies turn toward this physical Ka'bah, the lights of the spirits of those who face it connect with the light of the spirit of whoever is in the Ka'bah. Thus the divine lights increase in his heart, and the radiance of the spiritual lights grows in his secret. This is a great sea and a noble station, and it points you to the meaning of its being blessed.

If we interpret blessing as permanence, it is also so, because the Ka'bah is never without those who circumambulate, those who remain in devotion, and those who bow and prostrate. Moreover, the earth is a sphere. Given this, every time that can be imagined is morning for one people, noon for a second, afternoon for a third, sunset for a fourth and night for a fifth. When this is the case, the Ka'bah is never free at any moment from a people turning toward it from some side of the world to perform the obligatory prayer. Thus permanence is achieved in this respect. Also, the Ka'bah's remaining in this state for thousands of years is a permanence as well. So it is established that it is blessed in both respects.

**The third attribute:** Among the attributes of this House is that it is ﴿a guidance for the worlds﴾. On this there are two issues.

**The first issue:** It was said: the meaning is that it is a qiblah (direction of prayer) for the worlds, by which they are guided to the direction of their prayers. It was also said: it is guidance for the worlds, that is, a proof of the existence of the Creator who chooses, and of the truthfulness of Muhammad (ﷺ) in prophethood, through the signs it contains that we have mentioned and the wonders we have related. For everything that points to prophethood also points first to the existence of the Creator and all His attributes: knowledge, power, wisdom and self-sufficiency. It was also said: it is guidance for the worlds to Paradise, because whoever performs the obligatory prayers facing it deserves Paradise.

**The second issue:** Al-Zajjaj said: the meaning is "and it is guidance for the worlds." He said: it is possible that (wa-hudan) is in the nominative position, meaning "and it is guidance."

As for His words ﴿In it are clear signs﴾, there are two views. The first is that what is meant is the signs we mentioned that are in it: the safety of the fearful; the pebbles of the stoning place wearing away despite the frequent throwing; birds being unable to fly over it; the sick seeking healing by it; the swift punishment of whoever violates its sanctity; and the destruction of the People of the Elephant when they intended to destroy it. According to this view, the explanation and clarification of the signs is not mentioned.

[Page 132]

As for His saying, ﴿the station of Abraham﴾, it has no connection to His saying, ﴿in it are clear signs﴾. It is as if He, exalted is He, said: ﴿in it are clear signs﴾, and among them is that it is the station of Abraham, his place of residence, and the place he chose and where he worshipped Allah. All of these are among the attributes by which a place is honored and esteemed.

The second opinion: the explanation of the signs is mentioned, which is His saying, ﴿the station of Abraham﴾, meaning: they are the station of Abraham.

If it is said: the signs are plural, and it is not valid to explain them by one thing. The scholars answered this in several ways. The first: the station of Abraham is equivalent to many signs, because whatever is a miracle of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ is a proof of the existence of the Creator, His knowledge, His power, His will, His life, and His being self-sufficient, transcendent, and holy, far removed from resemblance to created things. So the station of Abraham, although it is one thing, when these many aspects are present in it, it is equivalent to proofs, as in His saying: ﴿Indeed, Abraham was a nation, devoutly obedient﴾ [an-Nahl: 120]. The second: the station of Abraham includes signs, because the mark of the foot on the hard rock is a sign, his sinking into it up to the ankles is a sign, the softening of part of the rock and not the rest is a sign, since only the rock beneath his two feet became soft, and its preservation, unlike the other signs of the prophets, peace be upon them, is a special sign for Abraham, peace be upon him, and its being kept safe for thousands of years despite the great number of his enemies among the Jews, Christians, polytheists, and atheists. Thus it is established that the station of Abraham, peace be upon him, comprises many signs. The third: al-Zajjaj said: His saying, ﴿and whoever enters it is safe﴾, is part of the explanation of the signs, as if it were said: in it are clear signs: the station of Abraham and the safety of whoever enters it. The plural form may be used for two, as He, exalted is He, said: ﴿If you two repent to Allah, your hearts have indeed inclined﴾ [at-Tahrim: 4], and the Prophet ﷺ said: "Two and whatever is above them is a congregation." Some of them completed the three, saying: the station of Abraham, that whoever enters it is safe, and that for Allah, upon the people, is the pilgrimage to the House, and then the particle "an" (that) was omitted for brevity, as in His saying: ﴿Say: My Lord has commanded justice﴾ [al-A'raf: 29], meaning: my Lord has commanded that you act justly. The fourth: it is permissible that these two verses be mentioned and the mention of others be omitted, as an indication of the multiplicity of signs, as if it were said: in it are clear signs: the station of Abraham, the safety of whoever enters it, and many others besides them. The fifth: Ibn Abbas, Mujahid, and Abu Ja'far al-Madani in the transmission of Qutaybah recited: (آيَةٌ بَيِّنَةٌ) in the singular. The sixth: al-Mubarrad said: "maqam" (station) is a verbal noun, so it was not made plural, as in His saying: ﴿and over their hearing﴾ [al-Baqarah: 7]. The intended meaning is the stations of Abraham, which are what Abraham, peace be upon him, established of the matters of the Hajj and the acts of the rites, and there is no doubt that they are many. In this case, the intended meaning of "signs" is the symbols of the Hajj, as in His saying: ﴿and whoever honors the symbols of Allah﴾ [al-Hajj: 32].

[Page 133]

Then He, exalted is He, said: ﴿the station of Abraham﴾, and concerning it there are opinions. One of them: when the building of the Ka'bah rose high and Abraham became too weak to lift the stones, he stood on this stone, and his two feet sank into it. The second: he came as a visitor from Syria to Makkah, and he had sworn to his wife that he would not dismount in Makkah until he returned. When he reached Makkah, Umm Isma'il said to him: "Dismount until we wash your head." He did not dismount, so she brought him this stone and placed it on the right side, and he placed his foot on it until she had washed one side of his head. Then she moved it to the left side until she had washed the other side, and the mark of his two feet remained on it. The third: it is the stone on which Abraham stood when he proclaimed the call to the Hajj. Al-Qaffal, may Allah have mercy on him, said: It is possible that Abraham stood on that stone in all of these places.

* * *

Then He, exalted is He, said: ﴿and whoever enters it is safe﴾. Similar to this verse are other verses, among them His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And when We made the House a place of return for the people and a sanctuary﴾ [al-Baqarah: 125], and His saying: ﴿Have they not seen that We made a secure sanctuary?﴾ [al-'Ankabut: 67], and Abraham said: ﴿My Lord, make this a secure city﴾ [al-Baqarah: 126], and He, exalted is He, said: ﴿Who fed them against hunger and secured them against fear﴾ [Quraysh: 4]. Abu Bakr al-Razi said: Since the aforementioned signs follow His saying: ﴿Indeed, the first House established for the people﴾, and they exist within the Haram, and then He said: ﴿and whoever enters it is safe﴾, it is necessary that His intended meaning is the entire Haram. The scholars agreed that if someone commits murder within the Haram, retribution (qisas, legal retaliation) is carried out against him within the Haram. They also agreed that the Haram does not grant safety in matters other than the soul. The disagreement concerns the case where retribution became obligatory for a person outside the Haram, and then he sought refuge in the Haram: is retribution carried out against him within the Haram? Al-Shafi'i said: it is carried out. Abu Hanifa said: it is not carried out, rather he is prevented from food, drink, buying, selling, and speech until he leaves, and then retribution is carried out against him. The discussion of this issue has already passed in the commentary on His saying: ﴿And when We made the House a place of return for the people and a sanctuary﴾. Abu Hanifa, may Allah be pleased with him, used this verse as evidence, saying: The apparent meaning of the verse is a report about its being a place of safety, but it cannot be taken literally, since it may not become safe, and then the report would be false. Therefore it must be taken as a command. It is left unapplied in offenses short of killing, because the harm in them is lighter than the harm of killing, and in the case where retribution became obligatory on him for a crime he committed within the Haram, because it is he who violated the sanctity of the Haram. So it remains in the area of disagreement according to the apparent meaning of the verse.

The response: His saying ﴿was safe﴾ is an affirmation of the essence of safety, and to act upon it, it is sufficient to establish safety in some respect, and we say this. Its explanation is in several ways. The first: whoever enters it for the rites, seeking nearness to Allah, will be safe from the Fire on the Day of Resurrection. The Prophet ﷺ said: "Whoever dies in one of the two Harams will be raised on the Day of Resurrection safe." He also said: "Whoever endures the heat of Makkah for an hour of the day, Hell will be removed from him a distance of two hundred years' journey." And he said: "Whoever performs Hajj and does not commit obscenity or sin will return from his sins as on the day his mother bore him." The second: it may be that what is intended is what Allah placed in the hearts of creatures of compassion toward everyone who seeks refuge with them and repels harm from him. Since the matter in most cases occurs in this way, He informed of its occurrence in this manner absolutely. This is better than what they have said, for two reasons. The first: on this assumption, we do not make the report stand in place of the command, whereas they make it stand in place of the command. The second: He, exalted is He, mentioned this only to explain the virtue of the House, and that virtue is established only by something known to the people, so that it becomes proof of the House's excellence. As for a ruling that Allah has explained in the law of Muhammad ﷺ, it does not become proof against the Jews and Christians in establishing the excellence of the Ka'bah.

The third aspect in interpreting the verse: the meaning is that whoever entered it in the year of the Qada' 'Umrah (the make-up 'Umrah) with the Prophet ﷺ was safe, because He, exalted is He, said: ﴿You will surely enter the Sacred Mosque, if Allah wills, in security﴾ [al-Fath: 27]. The fourth: al-Dahhak said: Whoever performs one Hajj will be safe from the sins he had committed before that.

Know that the methods of argument in all of these answers are one thing: His saying ﴿was safe﴾ is a ruling establishing safety, and to act upon it, it is sufficient to establish safety in one respect and in one case. When we interpret it according to one of these aspects, we have acted upon the requirement of this text, so the text no longer indicates what they have said. Furthermore, this is reinforced by the fact that interpreting the text this way does not lead to restricting the texts that indicate the obligation of retribution, whereas interpreting it as they have said leads to that. So our view is more preferable, and Allah knows best.

* *

His, exalted is He, saying: ﴿And it is a duty upon the people toward Allah to make pilgrimage to the House, for whoever is able to find a way to it﴾.

Know that when He, exalted is He, mentioned the virtues and merits of the House, He followed it with mention of the obligation of the Hajj. In the verse there are several issues:

The first issue: Hamzah, al-Kisa'i, and Hafs from 'Asim recited ﴿ḥijju l-bayt﴾ with a kasrah on the ḥa' (ḥijj), while the rest recited it with a fatha (ḥajj). It is said: the fatha is the dialect of the Hijaz, and the kasrah is the dialect of Najd, and both are the same in meaning. It is also said that both are permissible in the language without restriction, like raṭl and riṭl, and bazr and bizr. It is also said that the kasrah form denotes the act, and the fatha form is the verbal noun. Sibawayh said: it is permissible that the kasrah form also be a verbal noun, like dhikr (remembrance) and 'ilm (knowledge).

The second issue: concerning His saying ﴿for whoever is able to find a way to it﴾ there are several aspects. The first: al-Zajjaj said: the position of "man" (whoever) is in the genitive case, as an apposition to "an-nas" (the people), and the meaning is: it is a duty upon those among the people who are able, toward Allah, to make pilgrimage to the House. The second: al-Farra' said: if you intend "man" to begin a new clause, it is a conditional, and the response is omitted because the preceding words indicate it, and the implied meaning is: whoever is able to find a way to the Hajj, then it is a duty upon him toward Allah to make pilgrimage to the House. The third: Ibn al-Anbari said: it is permissible for "man" to be in the nominative case, in the sense of explaining "an-nas," as if it were said: Who are the people upon whom it is a duty toward Allah to make pilgrimage to the House? Then it is answered: they are those who are able to find a way to it.

* * *

The third issue: most scholars agree that provision and a mount are conditions for the existence of ability. Several of the Companions narrated from the Prophet ﷺ that he explained the ability to find a way to the Hajj as the existence of provision and a mount. Al-Qaffal narrated from Juwaybir, from al-Dahhak, that he said: If he is a young, healthy man with no wealth, he must hire himself out until he can pay for his Hajj. Someone said to him: Did Allah impose upon people that they walk to the House? He said: If some of them had an inheritance in Makkah, would he leave it? He said: No, rather he would set out toward it even if crawling. He said: Likewise, the pilgrimage to the House is obligatory upon him. Also from 'Ikrimah, he said: Ability is physical health and the possibility of walking if he does not find a mount.

Know that everyone who is physically healthy and able to walk if he does not find a mount, it is correct to say of him that he is able to perform that act. Therefore, restricting this ability to provision and a mount is a departure from the apparent wording, and it requires a separate proof. It is not possible to rely on the reports transmitted on this topic, because they are solitary reports (akhbar ahad), and the apparent meaning of the Book is not abandoned on their account, especially since Muhammad ibn Jarir al-Tabari criticized the transmitters of those reports, and also criticized them on another ground: that possessing provision and a mount is not sufficient for ability, since bodily health and the absence of fear on the road are also required for ability, and the apparent meaning of these reports implies that none of these are required. Thus these reports are open to criticism on this ground as well. Rather, reliance in this matter must be placed on the apparent meaning of His, exalted is He, saying: ﴿He has not placed upon you any hardship in the religion﴾ [al-Hajj: 78], and His saying: ﴿Allah intends for you ease and does not intend for you hardship﴾ [al-Baqarah: 185].

* * *

The fourth issue: some have used this verse as evidence that disbelievers are addressed with the subsidiary rulings of the law (furu' ash-shara'i). They said: because the apparent meaning of His, exalted is He, saying ﴿And it is a duty upon the people toward Allah to make pilgrimage to the House﴾ is general, encompassing believer and disbeliever, and the absence of faith is not fit to be a counter-argument or a restriction on this generality. For the dahri (one who denies a Creator and holds that time alone causes events) is obligated to believe in Muhammad ﷺ, even though faith in Allah, which is the condition for the validity of faith in Muhammad, peace be upon him, is not present. And the one in a state of ritual impurity (muhdith) is obligated to pray, even though the ablution (wudu'), which is the condition for the validity of prayer, is not present. So the absence of a condition does not prevent one from being obligated to the conditioned act. The same applies here, and Allah knows best.

* * *

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 3, verse 97 (part 2 of 2):

**The fifth issue:** The majority of the Mu'tazilah (the Mu'tazilites, a theological school that emphasized human free will and divine justice) used this verse as evidence that capacity (istita'ah) exists before the act. They said: If capacity were concurrent with the act, then whoever did not perform the Hajj would not be capable of the Hajj. Whoever is not capable of the Hajj is not covered by the obligation mentioned in this verse. It would follow that everyone who does not perform the Hajj would not become commanded to perform it through this verse, and that is false by consensus.

The Ash'arites (al-Ashab, the followers of Abu al-Hasan al-Ash'ari) answered: This also applies to them. The capable person either becomes commanded to perform the act before the motive for the act arises, or after it arises. As for before the motive arises, it is impossible, because before the motive arises the act cannot occur, so the obligation to it would be an obligation to what cannot be done. As for after the motive arises, the act becomes necessary to occur, so there is no benefit in obligating it. Since capacity is absent in both states, the obligation mentioned in this verse must not be directed at anyone.

* * *

**The sixth issue:** It is reported that when this verse was revealed, it was said: "O Messenger of God, is the Hajj prescribed for us every year?" They repeated this three times. The Messenger of God ﷺ remained silent. Then in the fourth time he said: "If I had said yes, it would have become obligatory, and if it had become obligatory you would not have been able to fulfill it, and if you did not fulfill it you would have disbelieved. Leave me alone as long as I leave you alone. When I command you with something, do from it what you are able, and when I forbid you from something, abstain from it. For those before you were destroyed by their great disputing with their prophets."

Then the scholars used this report as evidence that a command does not imply repetition, from two aspects. The first: the command to the Hajj came and did not imply repetition. The second: the Companions asked whether the form implies repetition or not, and if this form implied repetition they would not have needed to ask, given that they knew the language.

* * *

**The seventh issue:** The expression "a way to something" (istita'at al-sabil ila al-shay') means the possibility of reaching it. God Most High said: ﴿Is there any way out?﴾ [Ghafir: 11] and He said: ﴿Is there any way to return?﴾ [al-Shura: 44] and He said: ﴿There is no cause against the good-doers.﴾ [al-Tawbah: 91]. So for this possibility to be realized, the following are required: soundness of the body; the absence of fear of perishing from a predator or an enemy; the absence of lack of food and drink; the ability to have wealth with which to buy provisions and a mount; and that one settles all debts and returns all deposits. If one is obligated to support someone, the Hajj is not obligatory on him unless he leaves behind enough wealth to suffice them for the going and the returning. The details of this topic are mentioned in the books of the jurists, and God knows best.

* * *

Then God Most High said: ﴿And whoever disbelieves, then God is Free of need from the worlds.﴾ On this there are issues:

**The first issue:** On this verse there are two opinions.

The first opinion: It is a self-standing statement and a general warning concerning everyone who disbelieves in God, and it has no connection to what came before it.

The second opinion: It is connected to what came before it. Among those who hold this view, some interpreted it as referring to the one who abandons the Hajj, and some interpreted it as referring to the one who does not believe the Hajj is obligatory. As for those who interpreted it as referring to the one who abandons the Hajj, they relied on the apparent meaning of the verse. Since the command to the Hajj had been mentioned earlier and then He followed it with ﴿And whoever disbelieves﴾, it is understood from this that this disbelief is nothing but abandoning what had been commanded. Furthermore, they reinforced this aspect with reports. It is related from the Prophet ﷺ that he said: "Whoever dies without performing the Hajj, let him die either as a Jew or as a Christian." And from Abu Umamah, who said: The Prophet ﷺ said: "Whoever dies without performing the Hajj of Islam, and no apparent need prevented him, nor an illness that restrained him, nor an oppressive ruler, let him die in any state he wishes, as a Jew or as a Christian." And from Sa'id ibn Jubayr: "If my neighbor died and he had means, and did not perform the Hajj, I would not pray over him."

If it is said: How is it permissible to rule that he is a disbeliever because of abandoning the Hajj?

Al-Qaffal, may God have mercy on him, answered this: It is possible that what is meant is intensification, i.e., he has come close to disbelief and has done what the disbeliever does by abandoning the Hajj. The parallel to this is God Most High's saying: ﴿And the hearts reached the throats﴾ [al-Ahzab: 10], meaning they nearly reached them. A parallel to this is the saying of the Prophet, peace be upon him: "Whoever abandons the prayer deliberately has disbelieved," and his saying, peace be upon him: "Whoever has intercourse with a menstruating woman or in her anus has disbelieved."

As for the majority, they are those who interpreted this warning as referring to the one who abandons belief in the obligation of the Hajj. Al-Dahhak said: "When the verse of the Hajj was revealed, the Messenger of God ﷺ gathered the people of the six religions: the Muslims, the Christians, the Jews, the Sabians, the Magians, and the polytheists, and he addressed them and said: 'God Most High has prescribed the Hajj upon you, so perform the Hajj.' The Muslims believed in it, but the five communities disbelieved in it and said: 'We do not believe in it, we do not pray toward it, and we will not perform it.' So God Most High revealed His saying: ﴿And whoever disbelieves, then God is Free of need from the worlds.﴾" And this opinion is the strongest.

* * *

**The second issue:** Know that the legal obligations in acts of worship are of two kinds. Among them is that whose root is rationally understood, but whose details are not rationally understood, such as the prayer: its root is understandable, which is the glorification of God, but the manner of the prayer is not understandable. Likewise, zakat: its root is relieving the need of the poor, and its manner is not understandable. Fasting: its root is understandable, which is subduing the self, and its manner is not understandable. As for the Hajj, it is a journey to a specific place in specific manners. So the wisdom in the manners of these acts of worship is not understandable, and their roots are not known.

Having understood this, we say: The verifying scholars (al-Muhaqqiqun) said that performing this kind of worship is a stronger indication of perfect servitude, submission, and obedience than performing the first kind. This is because the one who performs the first kind may perform it because he knows by his intellect of its various benefits. But the one who performs the second kind does not perform it except for the mere sake of submission, obedience, and servitude. For this reason, the command to the Hajj in this verse includes many kinds of emphasis.

The first: His saying ﴿And for God is the right over the people, the pilgrimage to the House﴾. The meaning is that He, being God, has obligated His servants to this obedience, so submission is obligatory whether they know the wisdom behind it or not.

The second: He mentioned "the people" and then substituted for it ﴿whoever is able to make his way to it﴾. In this there are two kinds of emphasis. First, because substitution is a repetition and restatement of the intended meaning, which indicates intense care. Second, because He stated it generally first and then specified it, which indicates intense concern.

The third: He, glorified be He, expressed this obligation with two expressions. One: the particle of ownership (lam al-milk) in His saying "for God" (wa lillah). The second: the word "upon" (ʿala), which indicates obligation, in His saying ﴿for God upon the people﴾.

The fourth: The apparent meaning of the words requires its obligation upon every person who is able to do it, and generalizing the obligation indicates intense concern.

The fifth: He said ﴿And whoever disbelieves﴾ instead of "and whoever does not perform the Hajj," and this is a severe intensification concerning the one who abandons the Hajj.

The sixth: The mention of independence (from need), and this is among what indicates displeasure, anger, and abandonment.

The seventh: His saying ﴿from the worlds﴾ rather than "from Him." Since the one who is independent of all the worlds is more deserving of being independent of that single person and of his obedience, this is a stronger indication of wrath.

The eighth: At the beginning of the verse He said ﴿for God upon the people﴾, thereby clarifying that this obligation was merely for the sake of the majesty of divinity and the greatness of lordship, not for bringing benefit or repelling harm. Then He emphasized this at the end of the verse with His saying ﴿then God is Free of need from the worlds﴾.

Among the reports that indicate the emphasis of the command to the Hajj is the saying of the Prophet, peace be upon him: "Perform the Hajj before you are prevented from performing it, for the House has been destroyed twice and it will be raised a third time." And it is related: "Perform the Hajj before you are prevented from performing it. Perform the Hajj before the land prevents its surroundings." It was said: The meaning is that travel by land to Makkah will become impossible for you because of insecurity or other reasons. And from Ibn Mas'ud: "Perform the Hajj to this House before a tree grows in the desert from which no animal eats without perishing."

[p. 137]

Allah the Exalted says: ﴿Say: O People of the Scripture, why do you disbelieve in the signs of Allah while Allah is Witness over what you do?﴾ ﴿Say: O People of the Scripture, why do you bar from the way of Allah those who believe, seeking to make it crooked, while you are witnesses? And Allah is not unaware of what you do.﴾

Know that there are two ways of understanding the arrangement (nazm) of the verses. The first, which is the more suitable: when Allah the Exalted had presented the proofs for the prophethood of Muhammad, peace be upon him, from what was reported in the Torah and the Gospel concerning the good tidings of his coming, He then mentioned, following that, the doubts (shubuhat) of the people.

The first doubt concerns the denial of abrogation (naskh, the replacement of one ruling by a later one).

He answered it with His saying: ﴿All food was lawful to the Children of Israel, except what Israel had forbidden to himself﴾ [Al 'Imran: 93].

The second doubt concerns the Ka'bah, the obligation of facing it in prayer, and the obligation of pilgrimage to it.

He answered it with His saying: ﴿Indeed, the first House established for mankind...﴾ to its end. At this point the task of argument was completed and the answer to the doubts of the people of misguidance was perfected. Then He addressed them with gentle speech and said: ﴿Why do you disbelieve in the signs of Allah?﴾ after the clear proofs had become manifest and the doubts had been removed. This is the ultimate in the ordering of speech and the excellence of its arrangement.

The second way: when Allah the Exalted had explained the virtues of the Ka'bah and the obligation of the pilgrimage, and the people knew that this is the true religion and the correct creed, He said to them: ﴿Why do you disbelieve in the signs of Allah?﴾ after you have known that they are true and correct.

Know that the one who upholds falsehood is either merely astray, or, being astray, also leads others astray. The people were characterized by both of these qualities together. So Allah began by rebuking them for the first quality in a manner of gentleness and kindness.

* * *

In the verse there are several issues.

The first issue: His saying: ﴿O People of the Scripture, why do you disbelieve in the signs of Allah?﴾ Scholars differed about who is meant by the People of the Scripture. Al-Hasan said: they are the scholars of the People of the Scripture who knew the truth of his prophethood, and he based this on His saying: ﴿while you are witnesses﴾. Others said: rather, the intended meaning is all the People of the Scripture, because even if they did not know, the proof is established against them; so, by abandoning reasoning and turning to imitation (taqlid), they are like one who knew and then denied.

If it is asked: why were the People of the Scripture singled out for mention, rather than the rest of the disbelievers?

We answer: for two reasons. The first: we have explained that He presented the proof against them from the Torah and the Gospel for the truth of the prophethood of Muhammad, peace be upon him, then answered their doubts concerning that. When that was complete, He addressed them, saying: ﴿O People of the Scripture﴾. This is the correct order. The second: their knowledge of the signs of Allah is stronger, because they had previously acknowledged the oneness of God and the principle of prophethood, and because of their knowledge of what is in their books of testimony to the truthfulness of the Messenger and the good tidings of his prophethood.

The second issue: The Mu'tazilah said that His saying: ﴿why do you disbelieve in the signs of Allah?﴾ indicates that disbelief originates from them, so that this rebuke is valid; and likewise it would not be valid to rebuke them for their height, health, or sickness.

The answer to this: it is countered by knowledge and motive (da'i).

The third issue: What is meant by ﴿the signs of Allah﴾ is the signs which Allah set up as evidence for the prophethood of Muhammad, peace be upon him, and what is meant by their disbelief in them is their disbelief in their indication of the prophethood of Muhammad, peace be upon him.

* * *

Then He said: ﴿And Allah is Witness over what you do.﴾ The waw here is for the circumstantial clause (hal), and the meaning is: why do you disbelieve in the signs of Allah which have shown you the truthfulness of Muhammad, peace be upon him, while the state is that Allah is Witness over your deeds and will recompense you for them? This state requires that you not dare to disbelieve in His signs.

Then, when He had denounced them for their misguidance, He afterwards denounced them for their leading astray of the weak among the Muslims, and said: ﴿O People of the Scripture, why do you bar from the way of Allah those who believe﴾. Al-Farra' said: it is said "ṣaddadtuhu aṣudduhu ṣaddan" and "aṣdadtuhu iṣdādan". Al-Hasan read "tuṣiddūna" with a ḍammah on the tā', from "aṣadda". The commentators said: their barring from the way of Allah was by casting doubts and suspicions into the hearts of the weak among the Muslims, and they used to deny that his description was in their Scripture.

* * *

Then He said: ﴿seeking to make it crooked (tabghūnahā 'iwajan)﴾. ʿIwaj, with a kasrah on the ʿayn, means deviation from straightness in everything that is not seen, such as religion and speech; but for something that is seen one says ʿawaj with a fatḥah on the ʿayn, such as a wall, a spear, or a tree. Ibn al-Anbari said: the verb baghā is used with a single object when it is not accompanied by the preposition lām, as in your saying: "baghaytu al-māla, wal-ajra, wath-thawāb" (I sought the wealth, the reward, the recompense). Here the meaning intended is: "tabghūna lahā ʿiwajan" (you seek for it crookedness), and then the lām was dropped, as they said: "wahabtuka dirhaman" meaning "wahabtu laka dirhaman" (I gave you a dirham), and similarly "ṣidtu laka ẓabyan" (I hunted a gazelle for you). And he recited:

"So their servant turned and called out: 'Shall I hunt for you a gazelle, or a donkey?'"

He meant: "uṣīdu lakum" (I hunt for you). The pronoun in "tabghūnahā" refers to "al-sabīl" (the way), because sabīl may be feminine or masculine. And ʿiwaj here means deviation and distortion; that is, you seek for His way deviation and distortion through the doubts which you cast upon the weak, such as your saying: "abrogation indicates a change of mind (badāʾ)", and your saying: "it occurred in the Torah that the law of Moses, peace be upon him, remains forever." There is another possibility in the verse: that ʿiwajan is in the position of a circumstantial clause, and the meaning is: you seek it while you are astray. This is because they were, as it were, claiming that they were upon the religion and way of Allah; so Allah the Exalted said: "You seek the way of Allah while you are astray." According to this view there is no need to posit an implied lām in "tabghūnahā".

* * *

Then He said: ﴿while you are witnesses﴾. Concerning this there are several views. First: Ibn ʿAbbas, may Allah be pleased with both of them, said: the meaning is that you are witnesses that in the Torah the religion of Allah which is not accepted other than it is Islam. Second: and you are witnesses to the manifestation of the miracles which testify to his prophethood, peace be upon him. Third: and you are witnesses that it is not permissible to bar from the way of Allah. Fourth: and you are witnesses among the people of your religion, being upright, whom they trust in your words and rely upon your testimony in great matters, and they are the rabbis. The meaning is that whoever is like this, how is it fitting for him to persist in falsehood, lying, misguidance, and leading astray?

* * *

Then He said: ﴿And Allah is not unaware of what you do.﴾ The intended meaning is a threat, and it is like the saying of a man to his slave, when he has denied his way: "What you are upon is not hidden from me, and I am not unaware of your matter." He ended the first verse with His saying: ﴿Allah is Witness﴾, and this verse with His saying: ﴿And Allah is not unaware of what you do﴾. This is because they used to openly display disbelief in the prophethood of Muhammad, peace be upon him, but they did not openly display casting doubts into the hearts of the Muslims; rather they used to scheme in that matter by various stratagems. Therefore He said, concerning what they openly displayed: ﴿Allah is Witness﴾, and concerning what they concealed: ﴿And Allah is not unaware of what you do﴾. He repeated the phrase ﴿O People of the Scripture﴾ in the two verses because the aim is rebuke in the gentlest manner, and the repetition of this gentle address is closer to kindness in turning them away from their way of misguidance and leading astray, and more indicative of sincere advice to them in religion and of compassion for them.

**Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 3, verses 100–101:**

The Exalted said: ﴿O you who have believed, if you obey a faction of those who were given the Scripture, they will return you, after your belief, to disbelief.﴾ ﴿And how could you disbelieve while the verses of Allah are recited to you and His Messenger is among you? And whoever holds firmly to Allah has certainly been guided to a straight path.﴾

Know that when the Exalted warned, in the first verse, the group of the People of the Book against misleading and misguiding, He warned the believers in this verse against their misleading and misguiding them, and against their preventing them from paying heed to their words. It is related that Shas ibn Qays, a Jew, was greatly disbelieving, intensely hostile toward the Muslims, and extremely envious. It happened that he passed by a group of the Ansar from the Aws and the Khazraj, and he saw them in a gathering of theirs, talking. The enmity that had existed between them in the Jahiliyyah (the Age of Ignorance) had been removed by the blessing of Islam, and this grieved the Jew. So he sat with them, reminded them of the wars that had taken place between them before that, and recited to them some of the poetry that had been composed about those wars. The people quarrelled and grew angry, and they said: "The weapons! The weapons!" The news reached the Prophet (ﷺ), so he went out to them with those of the Muhajirun and the Ansar who were with him, and said: "Will you return to the ways of the Jahiliyyah while I am among you, after Allah has honoured you with Islam and joined your hearts together?" The people then realised that this had been the work of Satan and a plot of that Jew. So they cast down their weapons, embraced one another, and then departed with the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). There was never a day worse at its beginning and better at its end than that day. Then Allah revealed this verse.

His saying: ﴿If you obey a faction of those who were given the Scripture﴾ may refer to this incident, and it may refer to everything they attempt of the kinds of misguidance. The Exalted explained that if the believers yield and accept their words, this will lead them, state after state, until they become disbelievers. Disbelief brings ruin in this world and in the religion. In this world, it brings about enmity and hatred, the stirring up of strife, and the eruption of warfare that leads to the shedding of blood. As for the religion, that is obvious.

* * *

Then the Exalted said: ﴿And how could you disbelieve while the verses of Allah are recited to you and His Messenger is among you?﴾ The word (kayfa) ("how") expresses amazement, and amazement is fitting only for one who does not know the cause, and that is impossible for Allah. What is meant is prohibition and severe reproach. This is because the recitation of the verses of Allah to them, state after state, together with the presence of the Messenger among them, who removes every doubt and establishes every proof, acts as a preventive against their falling into disbelief. Therefore, disbelief occurring among those who were in the presence of the Messenger is even more remote in this respect. His saying: ﴿If you obey a faction of those who were given the Scripture, they will return you, after your belief, to disbelief﴾ is an alert that the ultimate aim of these Jews and hypocrites is to turn the Muslims back from Islam. Then He guided the Muslims that they must not pay heed to their words, but rather that they must return, whenever they hear any doubt from these Jews, to the Messenger (ﷺ), until he clarifies it and removes the face of the doubt in it.

* * *

Then He said: ﴿And whoever holds firmly to Allah has certainly been guided to a straight path.﴾ The purpose is: since He mentioned the threat, He followed it with this promise. The meaning is: whoever holds fast to the religion of Allah. It is also possible that this is an exhortation to them to seek refuge in Him in repelling the evils of the disbelievers.

(al-I'tisam) in the language means holding fast to a thing, and its root is from (al-ismah) (protection). (al-ismah) in the speech of the Arabs means prevention, and (al-'asim) means the preventer. (I'tasama fulan bi al-shay') means that a person grasped a thing in order to protect himself from falling into some calamity. From this is His saying: ﴿And she certainly sought to seduce him, but he refused (fa-sta'sama)﴾ [Yusuf: 32]. Qatadah said: "He mentioned in the verse two matters that prevent one from falling into disbelief. The first: the recitation of the Book of Allah. The second: the presence of the Messenger among them. As for the Messenger (ﷺ), he has passed on to the mercy of Allah. As for the Book, it remains upon the face of time."

* * *

As for His saying: ﴿has certainly been guided to a straight path﴾, our companions (the Ash'ari scholars) have used it as evidence that the act of the servant is created by Allah, the Exalted. They said: because He made their holding fast a guidance from Allah, and since that holding fast was made an act of theirs and a guidance from Allah, what we have said is established. As for the Mu'tazilah (the Mu'tazila, a rationalist school), they have offered several interpretations of it.

The first: the intended meaning of this guidance is the increase of divine favours (al-altaf) that are bestowed upon the performance of acts of obedience, as the Exalted said: ﴿By it Allah guides whoever follows His pleasure to the ways of peace﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 16]. This is the view chosen by al-Qaffal, may Allah have mercy on him.

The second: the implied meaning is: "whoever holds fast to Allah, then how excellent is what he has done, for he has only been guided to the straight path so that he may do that."

The third: whoever holds fast to Allah has been guided to the way of Paradise.

The fourth: the author of al-Kashshaf said: ﴿has been guided﴾ means that guidance has certainly been attained for him, just as you say: "If you come to so-and-so, you have succeeded," as if the guidance has already been attained, and so he reports it as already achieved. This is because the one who holds fast to Allah is awaiting guidance, just as one who seeks a generous person is awaiting success from him.

**Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 3, verses 100–101:**

The Exalted said: ﴿O you who have believed, if you obey a faction of those who were given the Scripture, they will return you, after your belief, to disbelief.﴾ ﴿And how could you disbelieve while the verses of Allah are recited to you and His Messenger is among you? And whoever holds firmly to Allah has certainly been guided to a straight path.﴾

Know that when the Exalted warned, in the first verse, the group of the People of the Book against misleading and misguiding, He warned the believers in this verse against their misleading and misguiding them, and against their preventing them from paying heed to their words. It is related that Shas ibn Qays, a Jew, was greatly disbelieving, intensely hostile toward the Muslims, and extremely envious. It happened that he passed by a group of the Ansar from the Aws and the Khazraj, and he saw them in a gathering of theirs, talking. The enmity that had existed between them in the Jahiliyyah (the Age of Ignorance) had been removed by the blessing of Islam, and this grieved the Jew. So he sat with them, reminded them of the wars that had taken place between them before that, and recited to them some of the poetry that had been composed about those wars. The people quarrelled and grew angry, and they said: "The weapons! The weapons!" The news reached the Prophet (ﷺ), so he went out to them with those of the Muhajirun and the Ansar who were with him, and said: "Will you return to the ways of the Jahiliyyah while I am among you, after Allah has honoured you with Islam and joined your hearts together?" The people then realised that this had been the work of Satan and a plot of that Jew. So they cast down their weapons, embraced one another, and then departed with the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). There was never a day worse at its beginning and better at its end than that day. Then Allah revealed this verse.

His saying: ﴿If you obey a faction of those who were given the Scripture﴾ may refer to this incident, and it may refer to everything they attempt of the kinds of misguidance. The Exalted explained that if the believers yield and accept their words, this will lead them, state after state, until they become disbelievers. Disbelief brings ruin in this world and in the religion. In this world, it brings about enmity and hatred, the stirring up of strife, and the eruption of warfare that leads to the shedding of blood. As for the religion, that is obvious.

* * *

Then the Exalted said: ﴿And how could you disbelieve while the verses of Allah are recited to you and His Messenger is among you?﴾ The word (kayfa) ("how") expresses amazement, and amazement is fitting only for one who does not know the cause, and that is impossible for Allah. What is meant is prohibition and severe reproach. This is because the recitation of the verses of Allah to them, state after state, together with the presence of the Messenger among them, who removes every doubt and establishes every proof, acts as a preventive against their falling into disbelief. Therefore, disbelief occurring among those who were in the presence of the Messenger is even more remote in this respect. His saying: ﴿If you obey a faction of those who were given the Scripture, they will return you, after your belief, to disbelief﴾ is an alert that the ultimate aim of these Jews and hypocrites is to turn the Muslims back from Islam. Then He guided the Muslims that they must not pay heed to their words, but rather that they must return, whenever they hear any doubt from these Jews, to the Messenger (ﷺ), until he clarifies it and removes the face of the doubt in it.

* * *

Then He said: ﴿And whoever holds firmly to Allah has certainly been guided to a straight path.﴾ The purpose is: since He mentioned the threat, He followed it with this promise. The meaning is: whoever holds fast to the religion of Allah. It is also possible that this is an exhortation to them to seek refuge in Him in repelling the evils of the disbelievers.

(al-I'tisam) in the language means holding fast to a thing, and its root is from (al-ismah) (protection). (al-ismah) in the speech of the Arabs means prevention, and (al-'asim) means the preventer. (I'tasama fulan bi al-shay') means that a person grasped a thing in order to protect himself from falling into some calamity. From this is His saying: ﴿And she certainly sought to seduce him, but he refused (fa-sta'sama)﴾ [Yusuf: 32]. Qatadah said: "He mentioned in the verse two matters that prevent one from falling into disbelief. The first: the recitation of the Book of Allah. The second: the presence of the Messenger among them. As for the Messenger (ﷺ), he has passed on to the mercy of Allah. As for the Book, it remains upon the face of time."

* * *

As for His saying: ﴿has certainly been guided to a straight path﴾, our companions (the Ash'ari scholars) have used it as evidence that the act of the servant is created by Allah, the Exalted. They said: because He made their holding fast a guidance from Allah, and since that holding fast was made an act of theirs and a guidance from Allah, what we have said is established. As for the Mu'tazilah (the Mu'tazila, a rationalist school), they have offered several interpretations of it.

The first: the intended meaning of this guidance is the increase of divine favours (al-altaf) that are bestowed upon the performance of acts of obedience, as the Exalted said: ﴿By it Allah guides whoever follows His pleasure to the ways of peace﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 16]. This is the view chosen by al-Qaffal, may Allah have mercy on him.

The second: the implied meaning is: "whoever holds fast to Allah, then how excellent is what he has done, for he has only been guided to the straight path so that he may do that."

The third: whoever holds fast to Allah has been guided to the way of Paradise.

The fourth: the author of al-Kashshaf said: ﴿has been guided﴾ means that guidance has certainly been attained for him, just as you say: "If you come to so-and-so, you have succeeded," as if the guidance has already been attained, and so he reports it as already achieved. This is because the one who holds fast to Allah is awaiting guidance, just as one who seeks a generous person is awaiting success from him.

**Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on Surah 3, verses 102–109 (part 1 of 2)**

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿O you who believe, fear Allah with the fear due to Him, and do not die except as Muslims.﴾ ﴿And hold fast, all together, to the rope of Allah, and do not be divided. And remember the favor of Allah upon you when you were enemies and He brought your hearts together, so you became, by His favor, brothers. And you were on the brink of a pit of the Fire, and He saved you from it. Thus does Allah make clear to you His verses that you may be guided.﴾

Know that when He, exalted is He, warned the believers against the misguidance of the disbelievers and their deceptions in the first verse, He commanded the believers in these verses with the most comprehensive of acts of obedience and the foundations of all good. He commanded them, first, with the fear of Allah, which is His saying: ﴿Fear Allah﴾. Second, with holding fast to the rope of Allah, which is His saying: ﴿And hold fast to the rope of Allah﴾. Third, with remembering the blessings of Allah, which is His saying: ﴿And remember the favor of Allah upon you﴾. The reason for this order is that a person's action must have a motive, either fear or desire, and fear takes precedence over desire, because averting harm takes precedence over acquiring benefit. So His saying ﴿Fear Allah with the fear due to Him﴾ indicates warning of the punishment of Allah, exalted is He. Then He made it a cause for the command to adhere to the religion of Allah and to hold fast to the rope of Allah. Then He followed it with desire, which is His saying: ﴿And remember the favor of Allah upon you﴾. It is as if He said: the fear of the punishment of Allah necessitates this, and the abundance of the favors of Allah necessitates this. Thus no aspect of the aspects that necessitate the act remains except that it is present in making it obligatory for you to submit to the command of Allah and obligatory for you to obey the judgment of Allah. From what we have mentioned it becomes clear that the three matters mentioned in this verse are arranged in the best manner. Let us now return to the exegesis.

As for His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Fear Allah with the fear due to Him﴾, there are several issues concerning it.

**The first issue:** Some said: this verse is abrogated (*mansukh*). This is because of what is narrated from Ibn ʿAbbas, may Allah be pleased with him and his father, that he said: When this verse was revealed it was difficult for the Muslims, because the fear due to Allah means that He is obeyed and not disobeyed for the blink of an eye, that He is thanked and not ungrateful, and that He is remembered and not forgotten, and the servants have no capacity for that. So Allah, exalted is He, revealed after this: ﴿So fear Allah as much as you are able﴾ (At-Taghabun 64:16), and this verse abrogated its first part, while its last part was not abrogated, which is His saying: ﴿And do not die except as Muslims﴾. However, the majority of the verifiers (*muhaqqiqun*) held that the claim of this abrogation is false, and they argued against it in several ways.

The first: what is narrated from Muʿadh that the Prophet (ﷺ) said to him: "Do you know what the right of Allah upon the servants is?" He said: "Allah and His Messenger know best." He said: "It is that they worship Him and do not associate anything with Him." And this cannot be abrogated.

The second: the meaning of His saying ﴿Fear Allah with the fear due to Him﴾ is: as it is due that He be feared. This is achieved by avoiding all of His acts of disobedience. Something like this cannot be abrogated, because it would permit some acts of disobedience. If that is the case, the meaning of this and the meaning of His saying ﴿So fear Allah as much as you are able﴾ become one, because whoever fears Allah as much as he is able has feared Him with the fear due to Him. It is not permissible that what is meant by His saying ﴿with the fear due to Him﴾ is what cannot be achieved of fear, because Allah, glorified is He, informed that He does not burden a soul beyond its capacity (*wusʿ*), and *wusʿ* is less than *ṭaqa* (what one can bear). A parallel to this verse is His saying: ﴿And strive for Allah with the striving due to Him﴾ (Al-Hajj 22:78).

If it is said: Did He not say: ﴿They did not measure Allah with His true measure﴾ (Al-Anʿam 6:91)?

We say: We will explain in the exegesis of that verse that it occurs in the Qur'an in three places, and all of them describe the disbelievers, not the Muslims. As for those who said that what is meant is that He is obeyed and not disobeyed, this is correct. What proceeds from a person by way of forgetfulness and heedlessness is not detrimental to it, because the obligation is lifted at such times. Likewise His saying: that He is thanked and not ungrateful, because this is obligatory upon him when the favors of Allah come to mind, but at the time of heedlessness it is not obligatory. Likewise His saying: that He is remembered and not forgotten, because this is only obligatory at the time of supplication and worship, and all of that is what cannot be borne constantly. So there is no basis for what they assumed, that it is abrogated.

The author, may Allah be pleased with him, said: I say: the first group may establish their claim in two ways. The first: the essence of divinity (*kunh al-ilahiyya*) is not known to creation, so the full extent of His dominance, power, and might is not known to creation. When knowledge of that is not attained, the fear appropriate to it is not attained, and so the fear of Him appropriate to it is not attained. The second: they were commanded with a stringent fear and a lenient fear together, so the stringent was abrogated and the lenient remained. It has been said: this is false, because what is obligatory upon him is that he fear as much as he is able, and abrogation applies to obligations, not to negation, because it would necessitate lifting a restriction concerning what would require that a person be restricted from it, and that is not permissible.

**The second issue:** His saying, exalted is He: ﴿with the fear due to Him﴾, meaning: as it is due that He be feared. This is indicated by His saying, exalted is He: ﴿the certainty of truth (*ḥaqq al-yaqin*)﴾ (Al-Waqiʿah 56:95). It is said: "He is a man in truth (*ḥaqqan*)." From this is the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ): "I am the Prophet, there is no falsehood, I am the son of ʿAbd al-Muttalib." And it is narrated from ʿAli, may Allah be pleased with him, that he said:
"I am ʿAli, there is no lie,
I am the son of ʿAbd al-Muttalib."
And *al-tuqa* (fear/piety) is the verbal noun (*ism al-fiʿl*) of your saying "I feared (*ittaqaytu*)," just as *al-huda* (guidance) is the verbal noun of your saying "I was guided (*ihtadaytu*)."

[p. 142]

As for His saying, exalted is He: ﴿and do not die except as Muslims﴾, the wording of the prohibition falls upon death, but the intended meaning is the command to remain upon Islam. This is because, since it was possible for them to remain steadfast upon Islam until death came to them while they were upon Islam, death upon Islam became like something that has already entered within their capacity. The discussion of this has already passed at His saying: ﴿Indeed, Allah has chosen for you this religion, so do not die except as Muslims﴾ (Al-Baqarah 2:132).

* * *

Then He, exalted is He, said: ﴿And hold fast, all together, to the rope of Allah﴾.

Know that when He commanded them to guard against the prohibited matters, He commanded them to hold fast to that which is like the root of all good deeds and acts of obedience, which is holding fast to the rope of Allah.

Know that everyone who walks along a narrow path, fearing that his foot might slip, if he holds onto a rope fixed at both ends on the two sides of that path, he is safe from fear. There is no doubt that the path of truth is a narrow path, and the feet of many people have slipped from it. So whoever holds fast to the proof of Allah and His clear signs, he is safe from that fear. Therefore what is meant by the "rope" here is everything through which one can reach the truth on the path of religion, and it has many types. Each of the exegetes mentioned one of those things. Ibn ʿAbbas, may Allah be pleased with him and his father, said: What is meant by the rope here is the covenant mentioned in His saying: ﴿And fulfill My covenant, I will fulfill your covenant﴾ (Al-Baqarah 2:40), and He said: ﴿except by a rope from Allah and a rope from the people﴾ (Aal ʿImran 3:112), meaning, by a covenant. The covenant was called a rope because it removes from a person the fear of going to any place he wishes, and it was like a rope which, whoever holds to it, the fear leaves him.

It has been said: it is the Qur'an. It is narrated from ʿAli, may Allah be pleased with him, from the Prophet (ﷺ) that he said: "Indeed, there will be a trial." It was said: "What is the way out of it?" He said: "The Book of Allah, in which is the news of those before you, the report of those after you, and the judgment of what is among you; and it is the firm rope of Allah." And it is narrated from Ibn Masʿud, from the Prophet (ﷺ), that he said: "This Qur'an is the rope of Allah." And it is narrated from Abu Saʿid al-Khudri, from the Prophet (ﷺ), that he said: "Indeed, I leave among you the two weighty things: the Book of Allah, the Exalted, a rope extended from the heaven to the earth, and my progeny (*ʿitrati*), the people of my household." It has been said: it is the religion of Allah. It has been said: it is obedience to Allah. It has been said: it is sincere repentance. It has been said: it is the community (*jamaʿa*), because after that He mentioned His saying: ﴿and do not be divided﴾. All of these statements are close in meaning. The verified view is what we have mentioned: that since the one who descends into a well holds onto a rope as a safeguard against falling into it, and the Book of Allah, His covenant, His religion, His obedience, and His agreement with the community of believers are a safeguard for their possessor from falling into the depths of Hell, He made that a "rope of Allah," and they were commanded to hold fast to it.

* * *

Then He, exalted is He, said: ﴿and do not be divided﴾. Concerning this there are two issues.

**The first issue:** Regarding its interpretation there are several views.

The first: He forbade disagreement in religion, because the truth is only one, and what is other than it is ignorance and misguidance. Since this is the case, the prohibition must be against disagreement in religion, and this is what is alluded to by His saying, exalted is He: ﴿So what is there after the truth except error?﴾ (Yunus 10:32).

The second: He forbade enmity and hostility, because they used to be persistently engaged in warfare and strife in the time of ignorance, so Allah forbade them from that.

The third: He forbade what causes division and removes affection and love.

Know that it has been narrated from the Prophet (ﷺ) that he said: "My community will split into over seventy sects, of which only one will be saved, and the rest will be in the Fire." It was asked: "And who are they, O Messenger of Allah?" He said: "The community (*al-jamaʿa*)." And it was narrated: "the great majority (*al-sawad al-aʿzam*)." And it was narrated: "What I and my companions are upon."

[p. 143]

The rational explanation of this is that the prohibition against disagreement and the command to unity indicate that the truth is only one, and if that is so, the one who is saved is one.

**The second issue:** The opponents of analogical reasoning (*nufat al-qiyas*), meaning those who reject qiyas (analogical reasoning), used this verse as evidence. They said: The legal rulings (*al-ahkam al-shar'iyya*) — either it is said that He, glorified is He, established definitive (*yaqiniyya*) proofs for them, or He established speculative (*zanniyya*) proofs for them. If it is the first, then it is impossible to rely on analogy (qiyas), which yields only probable opinion, because a speculative proof is not sufficient in a place of certainty. If it is the second, then the command to return to those speculative proofs would entail the occurrence of disagreement and the occurrence of dispute, so division and disputing should not be forbidden. But it is forbidden by His saying: ﴿and do not be divided﴾ and His saying: ﴿and do not dispute﴾ (Al-Anfal 8:46). One may say: The proofs indicating the validity of acting upon analogy (qiyas) are specifying what is general in His saying: ﴿and do not be divided﴾ and in the general sense of His saying: ﴿and do not dispute﴾ (Al-Anfal 8:46). And Allah knows best.

* * *

Then He, exalted is He, said: ﴿And remember the favor of Allah upon you﴾. Know that the blessings of Allah upon creation are either worldly or otherworldly, and He, exalted is He, mentioned both in this verse. As for the worldly blessing, it is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿when you were enemies and He brought your hearts together, so you became, by His favor, brothers﴾. There are several issues concerning it:

**The first issue:** It was said that when that Jew cast strife between the Aws and the Khazraj, and each of them intended to fight the other, the Messenger (ﷺ) went out and continued to be gentle with them until the strife subsided. The Aws and the Khazraj were brothers of one father and one mother, but enmity arose between them, and wars extended for one hundred and twenty years until Allah extinguished that with Islam. So the verse is an allusion to them and their circumstances, for before Islam one of them used to fight the other and hate the other. When Allah, exalted is He, honored them with Islam, they became brothers, showing mercy to one another and giving sincere counsel to one another, and became brothers in Allah. A parallel to this verse is His saying: ﴿If you had spent whatever is on the earth entirely, you could not have brought their hearts together, but Allah brought them together﴾ (Al-Anfal 8:63).

Know that whoever has his face turned toward the world becomes hostile to most of creation, and whoever has his face turned toward serving Allah, exalted is He, does not become hostile to anyone. The reason for this is that he looks at creation from the perspective of the Truth, and sees everyone as a captive in the grip of destiny and divine decree, so he does not become hostile to anyone. For this reason it has been said: when the knower (*ʿarif*) commands, he commands with gentleness, and is a sincere advisor; he does not rebuke harshly or reproach, for he is one who perceives with insight the secret of Allah in destiny.

**Second Issue:** Al-Zajjaj said: The root of *akh* (brother) in the language is from *tawakhkhi*, which means seeking. So a brother's aim is the aim of his brother. *Sadiq* (friend) derives from each of the two friends being truthful (*yasduqa*) to the other about what is in his heart, and not concealing anything from him. Abu Hatim said: The people of Basra said: *ikhwa* (brothers) is used for kinship, and *ikhwan* (brothers) for friendship. He said: This is an error. Allah the Exalted says: ﴿The believers are but brothers﴾ [al-Hujurat: 10], and He did not mean kinship. And He says: ﴿or the houses of your brothers﴾ [al-Nur: 61], and that refers to kinship.

**Third Issue:** His saying: ﴿So you became, by His favour, brothers﴾ indicates that the good dealings among them after Islam came about only from Allah, because He created that inclination in their hearts. That inclination was a favour from Allah, necessarily producing the act. This refutes the position of the Mu'tazila (the rationalist school) regarding the creation of acts. Al-Ka'bi said: That is by guidance, clarification, warning, knowledge, and *lutf* (divine grace, favour that facilitates obedience).

*Page 144*

We say: All of this was present at the time of the wars and fights. Therefore, the singling out of one of the two periods for the arising of affection and love must be due to some additional factor beyond what you have mentioned.

* * *

Then He the Exalted said: ﴿And you were on the brink of a pit of the Fire, and He saved you from it.﴾

Know that when He the Exalted had explained the worldly blessing, He mentioned after it the blessing of the Hereafter, which is what He mentions at the end of this verse. There are issues concerning the verse:

**First Issue:** The meaning is that you were, by your disbelief, standing at the edge of Hell. This is because Hell is likened to the pit in which there is fire. So their deserving of the Fire through their disbelief is treated as their standing over the Fire and their going toward its pit. Thus He the Exalted made clear that He rescued them from this pit, when they had come close to falling into it.

The Mu'tazila said: The meaning of that is that He showed them kindness through the Messenger, peace be upon him, and His other graces, until they believed. Our companions (the Ash'arites) said: All graces are shared between the believer and the unbeliever. If the doer and originator of faith were the servant himself, then the servant would be the one who saved himself from the Fire. But Allah the Exalted has judged that He is the one who saved them from the Fire. This indicates that the Creator of the acts of the servants is Allah, glorified and exalted.

**Second Issue:** *Shafa* (edge) of a thing is its border, and it is a defective noun (with final *alif*), like *shafa al-bi'r* (the edge of the well). Its plural is *al-ashfa'*. From it one says *ashfa 'ala al-shay'* when one overlooks something, as if he has reached its edge, meaning its limit and border. As for His saying ﴿and He saved you from it﴾, al-Azhari said: One says *naqadhtuhu*, *anqadhtuhu*, and *istanqadhtuhu*, meaning I freed him and delivered him.

There is a question regarding His saying ﴿and He saved you from it﴾: He only rescues them from the place in which they were, and they were on the edge of a pit, and the edge of the pit is masculine. So how does He say *minha* (from it, feminine)?

They answered this in several ways. The first: the pronoun refers to the pit, and since He rescued them from the pit, He has rescued them from the edge of the pit, because its edge is part of it. The second: it refers to the Fire, because the aim is rescue from the Fire, not from the edge of the pit; this is the view of al-Zajjaj. The third: the edge of the pit (*shafa*) and its lip (*shafatuha*) mean its rim, so it is permissible to speak of it with either masculine or feminine gender.

**Third Issue:** If they had died in disbelief, they would have fallen into the Fire. Their life, after which falling into the Fire is expected, is thus depicted as sitting on its edge. This contains an admonition to belittle the duration of life, for there is nothing between life and death, which necessitates falling into the pit, except what lies between the edge of a thing and the thing itself.

Then He said: ﴿Thus Allah makes clear﴾. The *kaf* (thus) is in the accusative position: that is, like the clarification mentioned, Allah makes clear to you all the other signs, so that you may be guided by them. Al-Jubba'i said: The verse indicates that He desires guidance from them. Al-Wahidi answered this in *al-Basit*, saying: Rather, the meaning is *li-takunu 'ala raja' hidayah* (so that you may be in hope of guidance).

I say: This answer is weak, because on this interpretation it follows that Allah desires from them that hope, and it is known that according to our position He may not desire that hope. The correct answer is to say that the word *la'alla* (so that) expresses hope, and the meaning is that We have done an act resembling the act of one who hopes for that. And Allah knows best.

A parallel to this verse is His saying: ﴿And strive for Allah with the striving due to Him﴾ (Al-Hajj 22:78).

As for those who said that what is meant is that He is obeyed and not disobeyed, this is correct. What proceeds from a person by way of forgetfulness and heedlessness is not detrimental to it, because the obligation is lifted at such times. Likewise His saying: that He is thanked and not ungrateful, because this is obligatory upon him when the favors of Allah come to mind, but at the time of heedlessness it is not obligatory. "I am ʿAli, there is no lie,
I am the son of ʿAbd al-Muttalib."
And *al-tuqa* (fear/piety) is the verbal noun (*ism al-fiʿl*) of your saying "I feared (*ittaqaytu*)," just as *al-huda* (guidance) is the verbal noun of your saying "I was guided (*ihtadaytu*)."

[p. 142]

This is because, since it was possible for them to remain steadfast upon Islam until death came to them while they were upon Islam, death upon Islam became like something that has already entered within their capacity. The discussion of this has already passed at His saying: ﴿Indeed, Allah has chosen for you this religion, so do not die except as Muslims﴾ (Al-Baqarah 2:132).

* * *

Then He, exalted is He, said: ﴿And hold fast, all together, to the rope of Allah﴾.

Know that everyone who walks along a narrow path, fearing that his foot might slip, if he holds onto a rope fixed at both ends on the two sides of that path, he is safe from fear. There is no doubt that the path of truth is a narrow path, and the feet of many people have slipped from it. So whoever holds fast to the proof of Allah and His clear signs, he is safe from that fear. Therefore what is meant by the "rope" here is everything through which one can reach the truth on the path of religion, and it has many types. Each of the exegetes mentioned one of those things. * * *

Then He, exalted is He, said: ﴿and do not be divided﴾. Concerning this there are two issues.

**The first issue:** Regarding its interpretation there are several views.

The first: He forbade disagreement in religion, because the truth is only one, and what is other than it is ignorance and misguidance. Since this is the case, the prohibition must be against disagreement in religion, and this is what is alluded to by His saying, exalted is He: ﴿So what is there after the truth except error?﴾ (Yunus 10:32).

The second: He forbade enmity and hostility, because they used to be persistently engaged in warfare and strife in the time of ignorance, so Allah forbade them from that.

The third: He forbade what causes division and removes affection and love.

Know that it has been narrated from the Prophet (ﷺ) that he said: "My community will split into over seventy sects, of which only one will be saved, and the rest will be in the Fire." It was asked: "And who are they, O Messenger of Allah?" He said: "The community (*al-jamaʿa*)." And it was narrated: "the great majority (*al-sawad al-aʿzam*)." And it was narrated: "What I and my companions are upon."

[p. 143]

The rational explanation of this is that the prohibition against disagreement and the command to unity indicate that the truth is only one, and if that is so, the one who is saved is one.

They said: The legal rulings (*al-ahkam al-shar'iyya*) — either it is said that He, glorified is He, established definitive (*yaqiniyya*) proofs for them, or He established speculative (*zanniyya*) proofs for them. If it is the first, then it is impossible to rely on analogy (qiyas), which yields only probable opinion, because a speculative proof is not sufficient in a place of certainty. If it is the second, then the command to return to those speculative proofs would entail the occurrence of disagreement and the occurrence of dispute, so division and disputing should not be forbidden. * * *

Then He, exalted is He, said: ﴿And remember the favor of Allah upon you﴾. As for the worldly blessing, it is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿when you were enemies and He brought your hearts together, so you became, by His favor, brothers﴾. There are several issues concerning it:

**The first issue:** It was said that when that Jew cast strife between the Aws and the Khazraj, and each of them intended to fight the other, the Messenger (ﷺ) went out and continued to be gentle with them until the strife subsided. The Aws and the Khazraj were brothers of one father and one mother, but enmity arose between them, and wars extended for one hundred and twenty years until Allah extinguished that with Islam. So the verse is an allusion to them and their circumstances, for before Islam one of them used to fight the other and hate the other. When Allah, exalted is He, honored them with Islam, they became brothers, showing mercy to one another and giving sincere counsel to one another, and became brothers in Allah. A parallel to this verse is His saying: ﴿If you had spent whatever is on the earth entirely, you could not have brought their hearts together, but Allah brought them together﴾ (Al-Anfal 8:63).

The reason for this is that he looks at creation from the perspective of the Truth, and sees everyone as a captive in the grip of destiny and divine decree, so he does not become hostile to anyone. For this reason it has been said: when the knower (*ʿarif*) commands, he commands with gentleness, and is a sincere advisor; he does not rebuke harshly or reproach, for he is one who perceives with insight the secret of Allah in destiny.

So a brother's aim is the aim of his brother. *Sadiq* (friend) derives from each of the two friends being truthful (*yasduqa*) to the other about what is in his heart, and not concealing anything from him.
