Al-Ka'bi said: That is by guidance, clarification, warning, knowledge, and *lutf* (divine grace, favour that facilitates obedience).

*Page 144*

We say: All of this was present at the time of the wars and fights. Therefore, the singling out of one of the two periods for the arising of affection and love must be due to some additional factor beyond what you have mentioned.

* * *

Then He the Exalted said: ﴿And you were on the brink of a pit of the Fire, and He saved you from it.﴾

Know that when He the Exalted had explained the worldly blessing, He mentioned after it the blessing of the Hereafter, which is what He mentions at the end of this verse. There are issues concerning the verse:

**First Issue:** The meaning is that you were, by your disbelief, standing at the edge of Hell. This is because Hell is likened to the pit in which there is fire. So their deserving of the Fire through their disbelief is treated as their standing over the Fire and their going toward its pit. Thus He the Exalted made clear that He rescued them from this pit, when they had come close to falling into it.

The Mu'tazila said: The meaning of that is that He showed them kindness through the Messenger, peace be upon him, and His other graces, until they believed. Our companions (the Ash'arites) said: All graces are shared between the believer and the unbeliever. If the doer and originator of faith were the servant himself, then the servant would be the one who saved himself from the Fire. But Allah the Exalted has judged that He is the one who saved them from the Fire. This indicates that the Creator of the acts of the servants is Allah, glorified and exalted.

**Second Issue:** *Shafa* (edge) of a thing is its border, and it is a defective noun (with final *alif*), like *shafa al-bi'r* (the edge of the well). Its plural is *al-ashfa'*. From it one says *ashfa 'ala al-shay'* when one overlooks something, as if he has reached its edge, meaning its limit and border. As for His saying ﴿and He saved you from it﴾, al-Azhari said: One says *naqadhtuhu*, *anqadhtuhu*, and *istanqadhtuhu*, meaning I freed him and delivered him.

There is a question regarding His saying ﴿and He saved you from it﴾: He only rescues them from the place in which they were, and they were on the edge of a pit, and the edge of the pit is masculine. So how does He say *minha* (from it, feminine)?

They answered this in several ways. The first: the pronoun refers to the pit, and since He rescued them from the pit, He has rescued them from the edge of the pit, because its edge is part of it. The second: it refers to the Fire, because the aim is rescue from the Fire, not from the edge of the pit; this is the view of al-Zajjaj. The third: the edge of the pit (*shafa*) and its lip (*shafatuha*) mean its rim, so it is permissible to speak of it with either masculine or feminine gender.

**Third Issue:** If they had died in disbelief, they would have fallen into the Fire. Their life, after which falling into the Fire is expected, is thus depicted as sitting on its edge. This contains an admonition to belittle the duration of life, for there is nothing between life and death, which necessitates falling into the pit, except what lies between the edge of a thing and the thing itself.

Then He said: ﴿Thus Allah makes clear﴾. The *kaf* (thus) is in the accusative position: that is, like the clarification mentioned, Allah makes clear to you all the other signs, so that you may be guided by them. Al-Jubba'i said: The verse indicates that He desires guidance from them. Al-Wahidi answered this in *al-Basit*, saying: Rather, the meaning is *li-takunu 'ala raja' hidayah* (so that you may be in hope of guidance).

I say: This answer is weak, because on this interpretation it follows that Allah desires from them that hope, and it is known that according to our position He may not desire that hope. The correct answer is to say that the word *la'alla* (so that) expresses hope, and the meaning is that We have done an act resembling the act of one who hopes for that. And Allah knows best.

**Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on Surah 3, verses 102–109 (part 1 of 2)**

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿O you who believe, fear Allah with the fear due to Him, and do not die except as Muslims.﴾ ﴿And hold fast, all together, to the rope of Allah, and do not be divided. And remember the favor of Allah upon you when you were enemies and He brought your hearts together, so you became, by His favor, brothers. And you were on the brink of a pit of the Fire, and He saved you from it. Thus does Allah make clear to you His verses that you may be guided.﴾

Know that when He, exalted is He, warned the believers against the misguidance of the disbelievers and their deceptions in the first verse, He commanded the believers in these verses with the most comprehensive of acts of obedience and the foundations of all good. He commanded them, first, with the fear of Allah, which is His saying: ﴿Fear Allah﴾. Second, with holding fast to the rope of Allah, which is His saying: ﴿And hold fast to the rope of Allah﴾. Third, with remembering the blessings of Allah, which is His saying: ﴿And remember the favor of Allah upon you﴾. The reason for this order is that a person's action must have a motive, either fear or desire, and fear takes precedence over desire, because averting harm takes precedence over acquiring benefit. So His saying ﴿Fear Allah with the fear due to Him﴾ indicates warning of the punishment of Allah, exalted is He. Then He made it a cause for the command to adhere to the religion of Allah and to hold fast to the rope of Allah. Then He followed it with desire, which is His saying: ﴿And remember the favor of Allah upon you﴾. It is as if He said: the fear of the punishment of Allah necessitates this, and the abundance of the favors of Allah necessitates this. Thus no aspect of the aspects that necessitate the act remains except that it is present in making it obligatory for you to submit to the command of Allah and obligatory for you to obey the judgment of Allah. From what we have mentioned it becomes clear that the three matters mentioned in this verse are arranged in the best manner. Let us now return to the exegesis.

**The first issue:** Some said: this verse is abrogated (*mansukh*). For this reason it has been said: when the knower (*ʿarif*) commands, he commands with gentleness, and is a sincere advisor; he does not rebuke harshly or reproach, for he is one who perceives with insight the secret of Allah in destiny.

**Second Issue:** Al-Zajjaj said: The root of *akh* (brother) in the language is from *tawakhkhi*, which means seeking. So a brother's aim is the aim of his brother. *Sadiq* (friend) derives from each of the two friends being truthful (*yasduqa*) to the other about what is in his heart, and not concealing anything from him. That inclination was a favour from Allah, necessarily producing the act. This refutes the position of the Mu'tazila (the rationalist school) regarding the creation of acts. Al-Ka'bi said: That is by guidance, clarification, warning, knowledge, and *lutf* (divine grace, favour that facilitates obedience).

*Page 144*

We say: All of this was present at the time of the wars and fights. Therefore, the singling out of one of the two periods for the arising of affection and love must be due to some additional factor beyond what you have mentioned.

* * *

Then He the Exalted said: ﴿And you were on the brink of a pit of the Fire, and He saved you from it.﴾

Know that when He the Exalted had explained the worldly blessing, He mentioned after it the blessing of the Hereafter, which is what He mentions at the end of this verse. There are issues concerning the verse:

**First Issue:** The meaning is that you were, by your disbelief, standing at the edge of Hell. This is because Hell is likened to the pit in which there is fire. So their deserving of the Fire through their disbelief is treated as their standing over the Fire and their going toward its pit. Thus He the Exalted made clear that He rescued them from this pit, when they had come close to falling into it.

The Mu'tazila said: The meaning of that is that He showed them kindness through the Messenger, peace be upon him, and His other graces, until they believed. Our companions (the Ash'arites) said: All graces are shared between the believer and the unbeliever. If the doer and originator of faith were the servant himself, then the servant would be the one who saved himself from the Fire. But Allah the Exalted has judged that He is the one who saved them from the Fire. This indicates that the Creator of the acts of the servants is Allah, glorified and exalted.

**Second Issue:** *Shafa* (edge) of a thing is its border, and it is a defective noun (with final *alif*), like *shafa al-bi'r* (the edge of the well). Its plural is *al-ashfa'*. They answered this in several ways. The first: the pronoun refers to the pit, and since He rescued them from the pit, He has rescued them from the edge of the pit, because its edge is part of it. The second: it refers to the Fire, because the aim is rescue from the Fire, not from the edge of the pit; this is the view of al-Zajjaj. The third: the edge of the pit (*shafa*) and its lip (*shafatuha*) mean its rim, so it is permissible to speak of it with either masculine or feminine gender.

This contains an admonition to belittle the duration of life, for there is nothing between life and death, which necessitates falling into the pit, except what lies between the edge of a thing and the thing itself.

Then He said: ﴿Thus Allah makes clear﴾. The *kaf* (thus) is in the accusative position: that is, like the clarification mentioned, Allah makes clear to you all the other signs, so that you may be guided by them. Al-Wahidi answered this in *al-Basit*, saying: Rather, the meaning is *li-takunu 'ala raja' hidayah* (so that you may be in hope of guidance).

**Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on Surah 3, verses 102–109 (part 1 of 2)**

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿O you who believe, fear Allah with the fear due to Him, and do not die except as Muslims.﴾ ﴿And hold fast, all together, to the rope of Allah, and do not be divided. And remember the favor of Allah upon you when you were enemies and He brought your hearts together, so you became, by His favor, brothers. And you were on the brink of a pit of the Fire, and He saved you from it. Thus does Allah make clear to you His verses that you may be guided.﴾

Know that when He, exalted is He, warned the believers against the misguidance of the disbelievers and their deceptions in the first verse, He commanded the believers in these verses with the most comprehensive of acts of obedience and the foundations of all good. He commanded them, first, with the fear of Allah, which is His saying: ﴿Fear Allah﴾. Second, with holding fast to the rope of Allah, which is His saying: ﴿And hold fast to the rope of Allah﴾. Third, with remembering the blessings of Allah, which is His saying: ﴿And remember the favor of Allah upon you﴾. The reason for this order is that a person's action must have a motive, either fear or desire, and fear takes precedence over desire, because averting harm takes precedence over acquiring benefit. So His saying ﴿Fear Allah with the fear due to Him﴾ indicates warning of the punishment of Allah, exalted is He. Then He made it a cause for the command to adhere to the religion of Allah and to hold fast to the rope of Allah. Then He followed it with desire, which is His saying: ﴿And remember the favor of Allah upon you﴾. It is as if He said: the fear of the punishment of Allah necessitates this, and the abundance of the favors of Allah necessitates this. Thus no aspect of the aspects that necessitate the act remains except that it is present in making it obligatory for you to submit to the command of Allah and obligatory for you to obey the judgment of Allah. From what we have mentioned it becomes clear that the three matters mentioned in this verse are arranged in the best manner. Let us now return to the exegesis.

As for His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Fear Allah with the fear due to Him﴾, there are several issues concerning it.

**The first issue:** Some said: this verse is abrogated (*mansukh*). This is because of what is narrated from Ibn ʿAbbas, may Allah be pleased with him and his father, that he said: When this verse was revealed it was difficult for the Muslims, because the fear due to Allah means that He is obeyed and not disobeyed for the blink of an eye, that He is thanked and not ungrateful, and that He is remembered and not forgotten, and the servants have no capacity for that. So Allah, exalted is He, revealed after this: ﴿So fear Allah as much as you are able﴾ (At-Taghabun 64:16), and this verse abrogated its first part, while its last part was not abrogated, which is His saying: ﴿And do not die except as Muslims﴾. However, the majority of the verifiers (*muhaqqiqun*) held that the claim of this abrogation is false, and they argued against it in several ways.

The first: what is narrated from Muʿadh that the Prophet (ﷺ) said to him: "Do you know what the right of Allah upon the servants is?" He said: "Allah and His Messenger know best." He said: "It is that they worship Him and do not associate anything with Him." And this cannot be abrogated.

The second: the meaning of His saying ﴿Fear Allah with the fear due to Him﴾ is: as it is due that He be feared. This is achieved by avoiding all of His acts of disobedience. Something like this cannot be abrogated, because it would permit some acts of disobedience. If that is the case, the meaning of this and the meaning of His saying ﴿So fear Allah as much as you are able﴾ become one, because whoever fears Allah as much as he is able has feared Him with the fear due to Him. It is not permissible that what is meant by His saying ﴿with the fear due to Him﴾ is what cannot be achieved of fear, because Allah, glorified is He, informed that He does not burden a soul beyond its capacity (*wusʿ*), and *wusʿ* is less than *ṭaqa* (what one can bear). A parallel to this verse is His saying: ﴿And strive for Allah with the striving due to Him﴾ (Al-Hajj 22:78).

If it is said: Did He not say: ﴿They did not measure Allah with His true measure﴾ (Al-Anʿam 6:91)?

We say: We will explain in the exegesis of that verse that it occurs in the Qur'an in three places, and all of them describe the disbelievers, not the Muslims. As for those who said that what is meant is that He is obeyed and not disobeyed, this is correct. What proceeds from a person by way of forgetfulness and heedlessness is not detrimental to it, because the obligation is lifted at such times. Likewise His saying: that He is thanked and not ungrateful, because this is obligatory upon him when the favors of Allah come to mind, but at the time of heedlessness it is not obligatory. Likewise His saying: that He is remembered and not forgotten, because this is only obligatory at the time of supplication and worship, and all of that is what cannot be borne constantly. So there is no basis for what they assumed, that it is abrogated.

The author, may Allah be pleased with him, said: I say: the first group may establish their claim in two ways. The first: the essence of divinity (*kunh al-ilahiyya*) is not known to creation, so the full extent of His dominance, power, and might is not known to creation. When knowledge of that is not attained, the fear appropriate to it is not attained, and so the fear of Him appropriate to it is not attained. The second: they were commanded with a stringent fear and a lenient fear together, so the stringent was abrogated and the lenient remained. It has been said: this is false, because what is obligatory upon him is that he fear as much as he is able, and abrogation applies to obligations, not to negation, because it would necessitate lifting a restriction concerning what would require that a person be restricted from it, and that is not permissible.

**The second issue:** His saying, exalted is He: ﴿with the fear due to Him﴾, meaning: as it is due that He be feared. This is indicated by His saying, exalted is He: ﴿the certainty of truth (*ḥaqq al-yaqin*)﴾ (Al-Waqiʿah 56:95). It is said: "He is a man in truth (*ḥaqqan*)." From this is the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ): "I am the Prophet, there is no falsehood, I am the son of ʿAbd al-Muttalib." And it is narrated from ʿAli, may Allah be pleased with him, that he said:
"I am ʿAli, there is no lie,
I am the son of ʿAbd al-Muttalib."
And *al-tuqa* (fear/piety) is the verbal noun (*ism al-fiʿl*) of your saying "I feared (*ittaqaytu*)," just as *al-huda* (guidance) is the verbal noun of your saying "I was guided (*ihtadaytu*)."

[p. 142]

As for His saying, exalted is He: ﴿and do not die except as Muslims﴾, the wording of the prohibition falls upon death, but the intended meaning is the command to remain upon Islam. This is because, since it was possible for them to remain steadfast upon Islam until death came to them while they were upon Islam, death upon Islam became like something that has already entered within their capacity. The discussion of this has already passed at His saying: ﴿Indeed, Allah has chosen for you this religion, so do not die except as Muslims﴾ (Al-Baqarah 2:132).

It has been said: it is the Qur'an. It is narrated from ʿAli, may Allah be pleased with him, from the Prophet (ﷺ) that he said: "Indeed, there will be a trial." The rational explanation of this is that the prohibition against disagreement and the command to unity indicate that the truth is only one, and if that is so, the one who is saved is one.

As for those who said that what is meant is that He is obeyed and not disobeyed, this is correct. What proceeds from a person by way of forgetfulness and heedlessness is not detrimental to it, because the obligation is lifted at such times. Likewise His saying: that He is thanked and not ungrateful, because this is obligatory upon him when the favors of Allah come to mind, but at the time of heedlessness it is not obligatory. Likewise His saying: that He is remembered and not forgotten, because this is only obligatory at the time of supplication and worship, and all of that is what cannot be borne constantly. **The second issue:** His saying, exalted is He: ﴿with the fear due to Him﴾, meaning: as it is due that He be feared. "I am ʿAli, there is no lie,
I am the son of ʿAbd al-Muttalib."
And *al-tuqa* (fear/piety) is the verbal noun (*ism al-fiʿl*) of your saying "I feared (*ittaqaytu*)," just as *al-huda* (guidance) is the verbal noun of your saying "I was guided (*ihtadaytu*)."

[p. 142]

This is because, since it was possible for them to remain steadfast upon Islam until death came to them while they were upon Islam, death upon Islam became like something that has already entered within their capacity. The discussion of this has already passed at His saying: ﴿Indeed, Allah has chosen for you this religion, so do not die except as Muslims﴾ (Al-Baqarah 2:132).

* * *

Know that everyone who walks along a narrow path, fearing that his foot might slip, if he holds onto a rope fixed at both ends on the two sides of that path, he is safe from fear. There is no doubt that the path of truth is a narrow path, and the feet of many people have slipped from it. So whoever holds fast to the proof of Allah and His clear signs, he is safe from that fear. Therefore what is meant by the "rope" here is everything through which one can reach the truth on the path of religion, and it has many types. Each of the exegetes mentioned one of those things. It has been said: it is the religion of Allah. It has been said: it is obedience to Allah. It has been said: it is sincere repentance. It has been said: it is the community (*jamaʿa*), because after that He mentioned His saying: ﴿and do not be divided﴾. All of these statements are close in meaning. * * *

Then He, exalted is He, said: ﴿and do not be divided﴾. Concerning this there are two issues.

**The first issue:** Regarding its interpretation there are several views.

The first: He forbade disagreement in religion, because the truth is only one, and what is other than it is ignorance and misguidance. Since this is the case, the prohibition must be against disagreement in religion, and this is what is alluded to by His saying, exalted is He: ﴿So what is there after the truth except error?﴾ (Yunus 10:32).

The second: He forbade enmity and hostility, because they used to be persistently engaged in warfare and strife in the time of ignorance, so Allah forbade them from that.

The third: He forbade what causes division and removes affection and love.

Know that it has been narrated from the Prophet (ﷺ) that he said: "My community will split into over seventy sects, of which only one will be saved, and the rest will be in the Fire." It was asked: "And who are they, O Messenger of Allah?" He said: "The community (*al-jamaʿa*)." And it was narrated: "the great majority (*al-sawad al-aʿzam*)." And it was narrated: "What I and my companions are upon."

[p. 143]

The rational explanation of this is that the prohibition against disagreement and the command to unity indicate that the truth is only one, and if that is so, the one who is saved is one.

They said: The legal rulings (*al-ahkam al-shar'iyya*) — either it is said that He, glorified is He, established definitive (*yaqiniyya*) proofs for them, or He established speculative (*zanniyya*) proofs for them. If it is the first, then it is impossible to rely on analogy (qiyas), which yields only probable opinion, because a speculative proof is not sufficient in a place of certainty. If it is the second, then the command to return to those speculative proofs would entail the occurrence of disagreement and the occurrence of dispute, so division and disputing should not be forbidden. * * *

As for the worldly blessing, it is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿when you were enemies and He brought your hearts together, so you became, by His favor, brothers﴾. There are several issues concerning it:

**The first issue:** It was said that when that Jew cast strife between the Aws and the Khazraj, and each of them intended to fight the other, the Messenger (ﷺ) went out and continued to be gentle with them until the strife subsided. The Aws and the Khazraj were brothers of one father and one mother, but enmity arose between them, and wars extended for one hundred and twenty years until Allah extinguished that with Islam. So the verse is an allusion to them and their circumstances, for before Islam one of them used to fight the other and hate the other. When Allah, exalted is He, honored them with Islam, they became brothers, showing mercy to one another and giving sincere counsel to one another, and became brothers in Allah. A parallel to this verse is His saying: ﴿If you had spent whatever is on the earth entirely, you could not have brought their hearts together, but Allah brought them together﴾ (Al-Anfal 8:63).

The reason for this is that he looks at creation from the perspective of the Truth, and sees everyone as a captive in the grip of destiny and divine decree, so he does not become hostile to anyone. For this reason it has been said: when the knower (*ʿarif*) commands, he commands with gentleness, and is a sincere advisor; he does not rebuke harshly or reproach, for he is one who perceives with insight the secret of Allah in destiny.

**Second Issue:** Al-Zajjaj said: The root of *akh* (brother) in the language is from *tawakhkhi*, which means seeking. So a brother's aim is the aim of his brother. *Sadiq* (friend) derives from each of the two friends being truthful (*yasduqa*) to the other about what is in his heart, and not concealing anything from him. Al-Ka'bi said: That is by guidance, clarification, warning, knowledge, and *lutf* (divine grace, favour that facilitates obedience).

*Page 144*

We say: All of this was present at the time of the wars and fights. Therefore, the singling out of one of the two periods for the arising of affection and love must be due to some additional factor beyond what you have mentioned.

* * *

Then He the Exalted said: ﴿And you were on the brink of a pit of the Fire, and He saved you from it.﴾

Know that when He the Exalted had explained the worldly blessing, He mentioned after it the blessing of the Hereafter, which is what He mentions at the end of this verse. There are issues concerning the verse:

**First Issue:** The meaning is that you were, by your disbelief, standing at the edge of Hell. This is because Hell is likened to the pit in which there is fire. So their deserving of the Fire through their disbelief is treated as their standing over the Fire and their going toward its pit. Thus He the Exalted made clear that He rescued them from this pit, when they had come close to falling into it.

The Mu'tazila said: The meaning of that is that He showed them kindness through the Messenger, peace be upon him, and His other graces, until they believed. Our companions (the Ash'arites) said: All graces are shared between the believer and the unbeliever. If the doer and originator of faith were the servant himself, then the servant would be the one who saved himself from the Fire. But Allah the Exalted has judged that He is the one who saved them from the Fire. This indicates that the Creator of the acts of the servants is Allah, glorified and exalted.

**Second Issue:** *Shafa* (edge) of a thing is its border, and it is a defective noun (with final *alif*), like *shafa al-bi'r* (the edge of the well). Its plural is *al-ashfa'*. From it one says *ashfa 'ala al-shay'* when one overlooks something, as if he has reached its edge, meaning its limit and border. As for His saying ﴿and He saved you from it﴾, al-Azhari said: One says *naqadhtuhu*, *anqadhtuhu*, and *istanqadhtuhu*, meaning I freed him and delivered him.

There is a question regarding His saying ﴿and He saved you from it﴾: He only rescues them from the place in which they were, and they were on the edge of a pit, and the edge of the pit is masculine. So how does He say *minha* (from it, feminine)?

They answered this in several ways. The first: the pronoun refers to the pit, and since He rescued them from the pit, He has rescued them from the edge of the pit, because its edge is part of it. The second: it refers to the Fire, because the aim is rescue from the Fire, not from the edge of the pit; this is the view of al-Zajjaj. The third: the edge of the pit (*shafa*) and its lip (*shafatuha*) mean its rim, so it is permissible to speak of it with either masculine or feminine gender.

**Third Issue:** If they had died in disbelief, they would have fallen into the Fire. Their life, after which falling into the Fire is expected, is thus depicted as sitting on its edge. This contains an admonition to belittle the duration of life, for there is nothing between life and death, which necessitates falling into the pit, except what lies between the edge of a thing and the thing itself.

Then He said: ﴿Thus Allah makes clear﴾. The *kaf* (thus) is in the accusative position: that is, like the clarification mentioned, Allah makes clear to you all the other signs, so that you may be guided by them. Al-Jubba'i said: The verse indicates that He desires guidance from them. Al-Wahidi answered this in *al-Basit*, saying: Rather, the meaning is *li-takunu 'ala raja' hidayah* (so that you may be in hope of guidance).

I say: This answer is weak, because on this interpretation it follows that Allah desires from them that hope, and it is known that according to our position He may not desire that hope. The correct answer is to say that the word *la'alla* (so that) expresses hope, and the meaning is that We have done an act resembling the act of one who hopes for that. And Allah knows best.

**Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on Surah 3, verses 102–109 (part 1 of 2)**

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿O you who believe, fear Allah with the fear due to Him, and do not die except as Muslims.﴾ ﴿And hold fast, all together, to the rope of Allah, and do not be divided. And remember the favor of Allah upon you when you were enemies and He brought your hearts together, so you became, by His favor, brothers. And you were on the brink of a pit of the Fire, and He saved you from it. Thus does Allah make clear to you His verses that you may be guided.﴾

Know that when He, exalted is He, warned the believers against the misguidance of the disbelievers and their deceptions in the first verse, He commanded the believers in these verses with the most comprehensive of acts of obedience and the foundations of all good. He commanded them, first, with the fear of Allah, which is His saying: ﴿Fear Allah﴾. Second, with holding fast to the rope of Allah, which is His saying: ﴿And hold fast to the rope of Allah﴾. Third, with remembering the blessings of Allah, which is His saying: ﴿And remember the favor of Allah upon you﴾. The reason for this order is that a person's action must have a motive, either fear or desire, and fear takes precedence over desire, because averting harm takes precedence over acquiring benefit. So His saying ﴿Fear Allah with the fear due to Him﴾ indicates warning of the punishment of Allah, exalted is He. Then He made it a cause for the command to adhere to the religion of Allah and to hold fast to the rope of Allah. Then He followed it with desire, which is His saying: ﴿And remember the favor of Allah upon you﴾. It is as if He said: the fear of the punishment of Allah necessitates this, and the abundance of the favors of Allah necessitates this. Thus no aspect of the aspects that necessitate the act remains except that it is present in making it obligatory for you to submit to the command of Allah and obligatory for you to obey the judgment of Allah. From what we have mentioned it becomes clear that the three matters mentioned in this verse are arranged in the best manner. Let us now return to the exegesis.

As for His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Fear Allah with the fear due to Him﴾, there are several issues concerning it.

**The first issue:** Some said: this verse is abrogated (*mansukh*). This is because of what is narrated from Ibn ʿAbbas, may Allah be pleased with him and his father, that he said: When this verse was revealed it was difficult for the Muslims, because the fear due to Allah means that He is obeyed and not disobeyed for the blink of an eye, that He is thanked and not ungrateful, and that He is remembered and not forgotten, and the servants have no capacity for that. So Allah, exalted is He, revealed after this: ﴿So fear Allah as much as you are able﴾ (At-Taghabun 64:16), and this verse abrogated its first part, while its last part was not abrogated, which is His saying: ﴿And do not die except as Muslims﴾. However, the majority of the verifiers (*muhaqqiqun*) held that the claim of this abrogation is false, and they argued against it in several ways.

The first: what is narrated from Muʿadh that the Prophet (ﷺ) said to him: "Do you know what the right of Allah upon the servants is?" He said: "Allah and His Messenger know best." He said: "It is that they worship Him and do not associate anything with Him." And this cannot be abrogated.

That inclination was a favour from Allah, necessarily producing the act. This refutes the position of the Mu'tazila (the rationalist school) regarding the creation of acts. Al-Ka'bi said: That is by guidance, clarification, warning, knowledge, and *lutf* (divine grace, favour that facilitates obedience).

*Page 144*

We say: All of this was present at the time of the wars and fights. Therefore, the singling out of one of the two periods for the arising of affection and love must be due to some additional factor beyond what you have mentioned.

* * *

Then He the Exalted said: ﴿And you were on the brink of a pit of the Fire, and He saved you from it.﴾

Know that when He the Exalted had explained the worldly blessing, He mentioned after it the blessing of the Hereafter, which is what He mentions at the end of this verse. There are issues concerning the verse:

**First Issue:** The meaning is that you were, by your disbelief, standing at the edge of Hell. This is because Hell is likened to the pit in which there is fire. So their deserving of the Fire through their disbelief is treated as their standing over the Fire and their going toward its pit. Thus He the Exalted made clear that He rescued them from this pit, when they had come close to falling into it.

The Mu'tazila said: The meaning of that is that He showed them kindness through the Messenger, peace be upon him, and His other graces, until they believed. Our companions (the Ash'arites) said: All graces are shared between the believer and the unbeliever. If the doer and originator of faith were the servant himself, then the servant would be the one who saved himself from the Fire. But Allah the Exalted has judged that He is the one who saved them from the Fire. This indicates that the Creator of the acts of the servants is Allah, glorified and exalted.

**Second Issue:** *Shafa* (edge) of a thing is its border, and it is a defective noun (with final *alif*), like *shafa al-bi'r* (the edge of the well). Its plural is *al-ashfa'*. There is a question regarding His saying ﴿and He saved you from it﴾: He only rescues them from the place in which they were, and they were on the edge of a pit, and the edge of the pit is masculine. So how does He say *minha* (from it, feminine)?

They answered this in several ways. The first: the pronoun refers to the pit, and since He rescued them from the pit, He has rescued them from the edge of the pit, because its edge is part of it. The second: it refers to the Fire, because the aim is rescue from the Fire, not from the edge of the pit; this is the view of al-Zajjaj. The third: the edge of the pit (*shafa*) and its lip (*shafatuha*) mean its rim, so it is permissible to speak of it with either masculine or feminine gender.

This contains an admonition to belittle the duration of life, for there is nothing between life and death, which necessitates falling into the pit, except what lies between the edge of a thing and the thing itself.

Then He said: ﴿Thus Allah makes clear﴾. The *kaf* (thus) is in the accusative position: that is, like the clarification mentioned, Allah makes clear to you all the other signs, so that you may be guided by them. Al-Jubba'i said: The verse indicates that He desires guidance from them. Al-Wahidi answered this in *al-Basit*, saying: Rather, the meaning is *li-takunu 'ala raja' hidayah* (so that you may be in hope of guidance).

I say: This answer is weak, because on this interpretation it follows that Allah desires from them that hope, and it is known that according to our position He may not desire that hope. The correct answer is to say that the word *la'alla* (so that) expresses hope, and the meaning is that We have done an act resembling the act of one who hopes for that. And Allah knows best.

**Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on Surah 3, verses 102–109 (part 1 of 2)**

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿O you who believe, fear Allah with the fear due to Him, and do not die except as Muslims.﴾ ﴿And hold fast, all together, to the rope of Allah, and do not be divided. And remember the favor of Allah upon you when you were enemies and He brought your hearts together, so you became, by His favor, brothers. And you were on the brink of a pit of the Fire, and He saved you from it. Thus does Allah make clear to you His verses that you may be guided.﴾

Know that when He, exalted is He, warned the believers against the misguidance of the disbelievers and their deceptions in the first verse, He commanded the believers in these verses with the most comprehensive of acts of obedience and the foundations of all good. He commanded them, first, with the fear of Allah, which is His saying: ﴿Fear Allah﴾. Second, with holding fast to the rope of Allah, which is His saying: ﴿And hold fast to the rope of Allah﴾. Third, with remembering the blessings of Allah, which is His saying: ﴿And remember the favor of Allah upon you﴾. The reason for this order is that a person's action must have a motive, either fear or desire, and fear takes precedence over desire, because averting harm takes precedence over acquiring benefit. So His saying ﴿Fear Allah with the fear due to Him﴾ indicates warning of the punishment of Allah, exalted is He. Then He made it a cause for the command to adhere to the religion of Allah and to hold fast to the rope of Allah. Then He followed it with desire, which is His saying: ﴿And remember the favor of Allah upon you﴾. It is as if He said: the fear of the punishment of Allah necessitates this, and the abundance of the favors of Allah necessitates this. Thus no aspect of the aspects that necessitate the act remains except that it is present in making it obligatory for you to submit to the command of Allah and obligatory for you to obey the judgment of Allah. From what we have mentioned it becomes clear that the three matters mentioned in this verse are arranged in the best manner. Let us now return to the exegesis.

As for His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Fear Allah with the fear due to Him﴾, there are several issues concerning it.

**The first issue:** Some said: this verse is abrogated (*mansukh*). This is because of what is narrated from Ibn ʿAbbas, may Allah be pleased with him and his father, that he said: When this verse was revealed it was difficult for the Muslims, because the fear due to Allah means that He is obeyed and not disobeyed for the blink of an eye, that He is thanked and not ungrateful, and that He is remembered and not forgotten, and the servants have no capacity for that. So Allah, exalted is He, revealed after this: ﴿So fear Allah as much as you are able﴾ (At-Taghabun 64:16), and this verse abrogated its first part, while its last part was not abrogated, which is His saying: ﴿And do not die except as Muslims﴾. However, the majority of the verifiers (*muhaqqiqun*) held that the claim of this abrogation is false, and they argued against it in several ways.

The first: what is narrated from Muʿadh that the Prophet (ﷺ) said to him: "Do you know what the right of Allah upon the servants is?" He said: "Allah and His Messenger know best." He said: "It is that they worship Him and do not associate anything with Him." And this cannot be abrogated.

The second: the meaning of His saying ﴿Fear Allah with the fear due to Him﴾ is: as it is due that He be feared. This is achieved by avoiding all of His acts of disobedience. Something like this cannot be abrogated, because it would permit some acts of disobedience. If that is the case, the meaning of this and the meaning of His saying ﴿So fear Allah as much as you are able﴾ become one, because whoever fears Allah as much as he is able has feared Him with the fear due to Him. It is not permissible that what is meant by His saying ﴿with the fear due to Him﴾ is what cannot be achieved of fear, because Allah, glorified is He, informed that He does not burden a soul beyond its capacity (*wusʿ*), and *wusʿ* is less than *ṭaqa* (what one can bear). A parallel to this verse is His saying: ﴿And strive for Allah with the striving due to Him﴾ (Al-Hajj 22:78).

If it is said: Did He not say: ﴿They did not measure Allah with His true measure﴾ (Al-Anʿam 6:91)?

We say: We will explain in the exegesis of that verse that it occurs in the Qur'an in three places, and all of them describe the disbelievers, not the Muslims. As for those who said that what is meant is that He is obeyed and not disobeyed, this is correct. What proceeds from a person by way of forgetfulness and heedlessness is not detrimental to it, because the obligation is lifted at such times. Likewise His saying: that He is thanked and not ungrateful, because this is obligatory upon him when the favors of Allah come to mind, but at the time of heedlessness it is not obligatory. Likewise His saying: that He is remembered and not forgotten, because this is only obligatory at the time of supplication and worship, and all of that is what cannot be borne constantly. So there is no basis for what they assumed, that it is abrogated.

The author, may Allah be pleased with him, said: I say: the first group may establish their claim in two ways. The first: the essence of divinity (*kunh al-ilahiyya*) is not known to creation, so the full extent of His dominance, power, and might is not known to creation. When knowledge of that is not attained, the fear appropriate to it is not attained, and so the fear of Him appropriate to it is not attained. The second: they were commanded with a stringent fear and a lenient fear together, so the stringent was abrogated and the lenient remained. It has been said: this is false, because what is obligatory upon him is that he fear as much as he is able, and abrogation applies to obligations, not to negation, because it would necessitate lifting a restriction concerning what would require that a person be restricted from it, and that is not permissible.

**The second issue:** His saying, exalted is He: ﴿with the fear due to Him﴾, meaning: as it is due that He be feared. This is indicated by His saying, exalted is He: ﴿the certainty of truth (*ḥaqq al-yaqin*)﴾ (Al-Waqiʿah 56:95). It is said: "He is a man in truth (*ḥaqqan*)." From this is the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ): "I am the Prophet, there is no falsehood, I am the son of ʿAbd al-Muttalib." And it is narrated from ʿAli, may Allah be pleased with him, that he said:
"I am ʿAli, there is no lie,
I am the son of ʿAbd al-Muttalib."
And *al-tuqa* (fear/piety) is the verbal noun (*ism al-fiʿl*) of your saying "I feared (*ittaqaytu*)," just as *al-huda* (guidance) is the verbal noun of your saying "I was guided (*ihtadaytu*)."

[p. 142]

As for His saying, exalted is He: ﴿and do not die except as Muslims﴾, the wording of the prohibition falls upon death, but the intended meaning is the command to remain upon Islam. This is because, since it was possible for them to remain steadfast upon Islam until death came to them while they were upon Islam, death upon Islam became like something that has already entered within their capacity. The discussion of this has already passed at His saying: ﴿Indeed, Allah has chosen for you this religion, so do not die except as Muslims﴾ (Al-Baqarah 2:132).

Then He, exalted is He, said: ﴿And hold fast, all together, to the rope of Allah﴾.

Know that everyone who walks along a narrow path, fearing that his foot might slip, if he holds onto a rope fixed at both ends on the two sides of that path, he is safe from fear. There is no doubt that the path of truth is a narrow path, and the feet of many people have slipped from it. So whoever holds fast to the proof of Allah and His clear signs, he is safe from that fear. The covenant was called a rope because it removes from a person the fear of going to any place he wishes, and it was like a rope which, whoever holds to it, the fear leaves him.

It has been said: it is the Qur'an. It is narrated from ʿAli, may Allah be pleased with him, from the Prophet (ﷺ) that he said: "Indeed, there will be a trial." It was said: "What is the way out of it?" He said: "The Book of Allah, in which is the news of those before you, the report of those after you, and the judgment of what is among you; and it is the firm rope of Allah." The verified view is what we have mentioned: that since the one who descends into a well holds onto a rope as a safeguard against falling into it, and the Book of Allah, His covenant, His religion, His obedience, and His agreement with the community of believers are a safeguard for their possessor from falling into the depths of Hell, He made that a "rope of Allah," and they were commanded to hold fast to it.

**The first issue:** Regarding its interpretation there are several views.

The first: He forbade disagreement in religion, because the truth is only one, and what is other than it is ignorance and misguidance. Since this is the case, the prohibition must be against disagreement in religion, and this is what is alluded to by His saying, exalted is He: ﴿So what is there after the truth except error?﴾ (Yunus 10:32).

The second: He forbade enmity and hostility, because they used to be persistently engaged in warfare and strife in the time of ignorance, so Allah forbade them from that.

The rational explanation of this is that the prohibition against disagreement and the command to unity indicate that the truth is only one, and if that is so, the one who is saved is one.

If it is the second, then the command to return to those speculative proofs would entail the occurrence of disagreement and the occurrence of dispute, so division and disputing should not be forbidden. One may say: The proofs indicating the validity of acting upon analogy (qiyas) are specifying what is general in His saying: ﴿and do not be divided﴾ and in the general sense of His saying: ﴿and do not dispute﴾ (Al-Anfal 8:46). So there is no basis for what they assumed, that it is abrogated.

The author, may Allah be pleased with him, said: I say: the first group may establish their claim in two ways. The first: the essence of divinity (*kunh al-ilahiyya*) is not known to creation, so the full extent of His dominance, power, and might is not known to creation. When knowledge of that is not attained, the fear appropriate to it is not attained, and so the fear of Him appropriate to it is not attained. The second: they were commanded with a stringent fear and a lenient fear together, so the stringent was abrogated and the lenient remained. It has been said: this is false, because what is obligatory upon him is that he fear as much as he is able, and abrogation applies to obligations, not to negation, because it would necessitate lifting a restriction concerning what would require that a person be restricted from it, and that is not permissible.

**The second issue:** His saying, exalted is He: ﴿with the fear due to Him﴾, meaning: as it is due that He be feared. This is indicated by His saying, exalted is He: ﴿the certainty of truth (*ḥaqq al-yaqin*)﴾ (Al-Waqiʿah 56:95). It is said: "He is a man in truth (*ḥaqqan*)." From this is the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ): "I am the Prophet, there is no falsehood, I am the son of ʿAbd al-Muttalib." And it is narrated from ʿAli, may Allah be pleased with him, that he said:
"I am ʿAli, there is no lie,
I am the son of ʿAbd al-Muttalib."
And *al-tuqa* (fear/piety) is the verbal noun (*ism al-fiʿl*) of your saying "I feared (*ittaqaytu*)," just as *al-huda* (guidance) is the verbal noun of your saying "I was guided (*ihtadaytu*)."

[p. 142]

As for His saying, exalted is He: ﴿and do not die except as Muslims﴾, the wording of the prohibition falls upon death, but the intended meaning is the command to remain upon Islam. This is because, since it was possible for them to remain steadfast upon Islam until death came to them while they were upon Islam, death upon Islam became like something that has already entered within their capacity. The discussion of this has already passed at His saying: ﴿Indeed, Allah has chosen for you this religion, so do not die except as Muslims﴾ (Al-Baqarah 2:132).

* * *

Then He, exalted is He, said: ﴿And hold fast, all together, to the rope of Allah﴾.

Know that when He commanded them to guard against the prohibited matters, He commanded them to hold fast to that which is like the root of all good deeds and acts of obedience, which is holding fast to the rope of Allah.

Know that everyone who walks along a narrow path, fearing that his foot might slip, if he holds onto a rope fixed at both ends on the two sides of that path, he is safe from fear. There is no doubt that the path of truth is a narrow path, and the feet of many people have slipped from it. So whoever holds fast to the proof of Allah and His clear signs, he is safe from that fear. Therefore what is meant by the "rope" here is everything through which one can reach the truth on the path of religion, and it has many types. Each of the exegetes mentioned one of those things. Ibn ʿAbbas, may Allah be pleased with him and his father, said: What is meant by the rope here is the covenant mentioned in His saying: ﴿And fulfill My covenant, I will fulfill your covenant﴾ (Al-Baqarah 2:40), and He said: ﴿except by a rope from Allah and a rope from the people﴾ (Aal ʿImran 3:112), meaning, by a covenant. The covenant was called a rope because it removes from a person the fear of going to any place he wishes, and it was like a rope which, whoever holds to it, the fear leaves him.

It has been said: it is the Qur'an. It is narrated from ʿAli, may Allah be pleased with him, from the Prophet (ﷺ) that he said: "Indeed, there will be a trial." It was said: "What is the way out of it?" He said: "The Book of Allah, in which is the news of those before you, the report of those after you, and the judgment of what is among you; and it is the firm rope of Allah." And it is narrated from Ibn Masʿud, from the Prophet (ﷺ), that he said: "This Qur'an is the rope of Allah." And it is narrated from Abu Saʿid al-Khudri, from the Prophet (ﷺ), that he said: "Indeed, I leave among you the two weighty things: the Book of Allah, the Exalted, a rope extended from the heaven to the earth, and my progeny (*ʿitrati*), the people of my household." It has been said: it is the religion of Allah. It has been said: it is obedience to Allah. It has been said: it is sincere repentance. It has been said: it is the community (*jamaʿa*), because after that He mentioned His saying: ﴿and do not be divided﴾. All of these statements are close in meaning. The verified view is what we have mentioned: that since the one who descends into a well holds onto a rope as a safeguard against falling into it, and the Book of Allah, His covenant, His religion, His obedience, and His agreement with the community of believers are a safeguard for their possessor from falling into the depths of Hell, He made that a "rope of Allah," and they were commanded to hold fast to it.

* * *

Then He, exalted is He, said: ﴿and do not be divided﴾. Concerning this there are two issues.

**The first issue:** Regarding its interpretation there are several views.

The first: He forbade disagreement in religion, because the truth is only one, and what is other than it is ignorance and misguidance. Since this is the case, the prohibition must be against disagreement in religion, and this is what is alluded to by His saying, exalted is He: ﴿So what is there after the truth except error?﴾ (Yunus 10:32).

The second: He forbade enmity and hostility, because they used to be persistently engaged in warfare and strife in the time of ignorance, so Allah forbade them from that.

The third: He forbade what causes division and removes affection and love.

Know that it has been narrated from the Prophet (ﷺ) that he said: "My community will split into over seventy sects, of which only one will be saved, and the rest will be in the Fire." It was asked: "And who are they, O Messenger of Allah?" He said: "The community (*al-jamaʿa*)." And it was narrated: "the great majority (*al-sawad al-aʿzam*)." And it was narrated: "What I and my companions are upon."

[p. 143]

The rational explanation of this is that the prohibition against disagreement and the command to unity indicate that the truth is only one, and if that is so, the one who is saved is one.

**The second issue:** The opponents of analogical reasoning (*nufat al-qiyas*), meaning those who reject qiyas (analogical reasoning), used this verse as evidence. They said: The legal rulings (*al-ahkam al-shar'iyya*) — either it is said that He, glorified is He, established definitive (*yaqiniyya*) proofs for them, or He established speculative (*zanniyya*) proofs for them. If it is the first, then it is impossible to rely on analogy (qiyas), which yields only probable opinion, because a speculative proof is not sufficient in a place of certainty. If it is the second, then the command to return to those speculative proofs would entail the occurrence of disagreement and the occurrence of dispute, so division and disputing should not be forbidden. But it is forbidden by His saying: ﴿and do not be divided﴾ and His saying: ﴿and do not dispute﴾ (Al-Anfal 8:46). One may say: The proofs indicating the validity of acting upon analogy (qiyas) are specifying what is general in His saying: ﴿and do not be divided﴾ and in the general sense of His saying: ﴿and do not dispute﴾ (Al-Anfal 8:46). And Allah knows best.

* * *

Then He, exalted is He, said: ﴿And remember the favor of Allah upon you﴾. Know that the blessings of Allah upon creation are either worldly or otherworldly, and He, exalted is He, mentioned both in this verse. As for the worldly blessing, it is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿when you were enemies and He brought your hearts together, so you became, by His favor, brothers﴾. There are several issues concerning it:

**The first issue:** It was said that when that Jew cast strife between the Aws and the Khazraj, and each of them intended to fight the other, the Messenger (ﷺ) went out and continued to be gentle with them until the strife subsided. The Aws and the Khazraj were brothers of one father and one mother, but enmity arose between them, and wars extended for one hundred and twenty years until Allah extinguished that with Islam. So the verse is an allusion to them and their circumstances, for before Islam one of them used to fight the other and hate the other. When Allah, exalted is He, honored them with Islam, they became brothers, showing mercy to one another and giving sincere counsel to one another, and became brothers in Allah. A parallel to this verse is His saying: ﴿If you had spent whatever is on the earth entirely, you could not have brought their hearts together, but Allah brought them together﴾ (Al-Anfal 8:63).

Know that whoever has his face turned toward the world becomes hostile to most of creation, and whoever has his face turned toward serving Allah, exalted is He, does not become hostile to anyone. The reason for this is that he looks at creation from the perspective of the Truth, and sees everyone as a captive in the grip of destiny and divine decree, so he does not become hostile to anyone. For this reason it has been said: when the knower (*ʿarif*) commands, he commands with gentleness, and is a sincere advisor; he does not rebuke harshly or reproach, for he is one who perceives with insight the secret of Allah in destiny.

**Second Issue:** Al-Zajjaj said: The root of *akh* (brother) in the language is from *tawakhkhi*, which means seeking. So a brother's aim is the aim of his brother. *Sadiq* (friend) derives from each of the two friends being truthful (*yasduqa*) to the other about what is in his heart, and not concealing anything from him. Abu Hatim said: The people of Basra said: *ikhwa* (brothers) is used for kinship, and *ikhwan* (brothers) for friendship. He said: This is an error. Allah the Exalted says: ﴿The believers are but brothers﴾ [al-Hujurat: 10], and He did not mean kinship. And He says: ﴿or the houses of your brothers﴾ [al-Nur: 61], and that refers to kinship.

**Third Issue:** His saying: ﴿So you became, by His favour, brothers﴾ indicates that the good dealings among them after Islam came about only from Allah, because He created that inclination in their hearts. That inclination was a favour from Allah, necessarily producing the act. This refutes the position of the Mu'tazila (the rationalist school) regarding the creation of acts. Al-Ka'bi said: That is by guidance, clarification, warning, knowledge, and *lutf* (divine grace, favour that facilitates obedience).

*Page 144*

We say: All of this was present at the time of the wars and fights. Therefore, the singling out of one of the two periods for the arising of affection and love must be due to some additional factor beyond what you have mentioned.

* * *

Then He the Exalted said: ﴿And you were on the brink of a pit of the Fire, and He saved you from it.﴾

Know that when He the Exalted had explained the worldly blessing, He mentioned after it the blessing of the Hereafter, which is what He mentions at the end of this verse. There are issues concerning the verse:

**First Issue:** The meaning is that you were, by your disbelief, standing at the edge of Hell. This is because Hell is likened to the pit in which there is fire. So their deserving of the Fire through their disbelief is treated as their standing over the Fire and their going toward its pit. Thus He the Exalted made clear that He rescued them from this pit, when they had come close to falling into it.

The Mu'tazila said: The meaning of that is that He showed them kindness through the Messenger, peace be upon him, and His other graces, until they believed. Our companions (the Ash'arites) said: All graces are shared between the believer and the unbeliever. If the doer and originator of faith were the servant himself, then the servant would be the one who saved himself from the Fire. But Allah the Exalted has judged that He is the one who saved them from the Fire. This indicates that the Creator of the acts of the servants is Allah, glorified and exalted.

**Second Issue:** *Shafa* (edge) of a thing is its border, and it is a defective noun (with final *alif*), like *shafa al-bi'r* (the edge of the well). Its plural is *al-ashfa'*. From it one says *ashfa 'ala al-shay'* when one overlooks something, as if he has reached its edge, meaning its limit and border. As for His saying ﴿and He saved you from it﴾, al-Azhari said: One says *naqadhtuhu*, *anqadhtuhu*, and *istanqadhtuhu*, meaning I freed him and delivered him.

There is a question regarding His saying ﴿and He saved you from it﴾: He only rescues them from the place in which they were, and they were on the edge of a pit, and the edge of the pit is masculine. So how does He say *minha* (from it, feminine)?

They answered this in several ways. The first: the pronoun refers to the pit, and since He rescued them from the pit, He has rescued them from the edge of the pit, because its edge is part of it. The second: it refers to the Fire, because the aim is rescue from the Fire, not from the edge of the pit; this is the view of al-Zajjaj. The third: the edge of the pit (*shafa*) and its lip (*shafatuha*) mean its rim, so it is permissible to speak of it with either masculine or feminine gender.

**Third Issue:** If they had died in disbelief, they would have fallen into the Fire. Their life, after which falling into the Fire is expected, is thus depicted as sitting on its edge. This contains an admonition to belittle the duration of life, for there is nothing between life and death, which necessitates falling into the pit, except what lies between the edge of a thing and the thing itself.

Then He said: ﴿Thus Allah makes clear﴾. The *kaf* (thus) is in the accusative position: that is, like the clarification mentioned, Allah makes clear to you all the other signs, so that you may be guided by them. Al-Jubba'i said: The verse indicates that He desires guidance from them. Al-Wahidi answered this in *al-Basit*, saying: Rather, the meaning is *li-takunu 'ala raja' hidayah* (so that you may be in hope of guidance).

I say: This answer is weak, because on this interpretation it follows that Allah desires from them that hope, and it is known that according to our position He may not desire that hope. The correct answer is to say that the word *la'alla* (so that) expresses hope, and the meaning is that We have done an act resembling the act of one who hopes for that. And Allah knows best.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 3, verse 110 (part 1 of 5):

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And let there be among you a community who invite to good, enjoin what is right, and forbid what is wrong. And those are the successful.﴾ ﴿And do not be like those who became divided and differed after the clear proofs had come to them. And those will have a great punishment.﴾ ﴿On the Day when faces will turn white and faces will turn black. As for those whose faces turn black: "Did you disbelieve after your belief? So taste the punishment for what you used to disbelieve."﴾ ﴿And as for those whose faces turn white, they will be in the mercy of Allah, wherein they will abide eternally.﴾ ﴿These are the verses of Allah; We recite them to you in truth. And Allah does not desire injustice for the worlds.﴾ ﴿And to Allah belongs whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth, and to Allah all matters are returned.﴾

Know that He, exalted is He, in the preceding verses, reproached the People of the Book for two things. The first: He reproached them for disbelief, saying: ﴿Say, "O People of the Scripture, why do you disbelieve in the signs of Allah?"﴾ [Al 'Imran: 70]. Then after that He reproached them for their effort in turning others away into disbelief, saying: ﴿Say, "O People of the Scripture, why do you avert from the way of Allah those who believe?"﴾ [Al 'Imran: 99]. When He moved from that to addressing the believers, He first commanded them to piety and faith, saying: ﴿O you who have believed, fear Allah as He should be feared and do not die except as Muslims﴾ ﴿And hold firmly to the rope of Allah all together﴾. Then He commanded them to strive to turn others toward faith and obedience, saying: ﴿And let there be among you a community who invite to good﴾. This is the good order, agreeable to reason. In the verse there are two issues:

The first issue: concerning His saying "from among you" (min-kum), there are two views. One is that "min" here is not partitive (li-l-tab'id), for two reasons. The first: Allah, exalted is He, made the enjoining of what is right and the forbidding of what is wrong obligatory upon the entire community in His saying: ﴿You are the best community produced for mankind; you enjoin what is right and forbid what is wrong﴾ [Al 'Imran: 110]. The second: there is no mukallaf (accountable person) who is not obligated to enjoin what is right and forbid what is wrong, either with his hand, or with his tongue, or with his heart; and it is obligatory upon everyone to repel harm from himself. Given this established, we say: the meaning of this verse is, "Be a community calling to good, enjoining what is right and forbidding what is wrong." As for the word "min," it is here for explanation (li-l-tabyin), not partition, like His saying: ﴿So avoid the abomination of the idols﴾ [al-Hajj: 30]. It is also said: "For so-and-so there is an army of his children (min awladihi jund)," and "For the commander there is a military force of his servants (min ghilmanihi 'uskar)," meaning all his children and servants, not some of them; so also here. Then they said: although that is obligatory upon all, once a group performs it, the obligation falls from the rest. Its parallel is His saying: ﴿Go forth, light and heavy﴾ [al-Tawbah: 41] and His saying: ﴿If you do not go forth, He will punish you with a painful punishment﴾ [al-Tawbah: 39]. So the command is general; then when a group undertakes it, sufficiency is achieved and the obligation is removed from the rest.

The second view: that "min" here is partitive. Those who hold this view also differ on two views. One is that the purpose of the word "min" is that among the people are those who cannot call to good or enjoin what is right and forbid what is wrong, such as women, the sick, and the infirm. The second: that this obligation is specific to the scholars, and this is indicated by two considerations. The first: this verse includes a command concerning three things: calling to good, enjoining what is right, and forbidding what is wrong. It is known that calling to good is conditional upon knowledge of the good, of what is right, and of what is wrong, for the ignorant person may often return to falsehood, command what is wrong, and forbid what is right; and he may know the ruling in his own school but be ignorant of it in the school of another, so he forbids what is not wrong; and he may be harsh where gentleness is required and gentle where firmness is required, and he may rebuke someone whose rebuke only increases him in obstinacy. Thus it is established that this obligation is directed at the scholars, and there is no doubt that they are part of the community. A parallel to this verse is His saying: ﴿Why should not a group from every division among them go forth to gain understanding in the religion﴾ [al-Tawbah: 122]. The second: we have agreed that this is obligatory by way of sufficiency (fard kifayah), meaning that when some of them undertake it, it is dropped from the rest. If that is so, the meaning is "let some of you undertake this," so in reality this is an obligation upon a part, not upon all. And Allah knows best.

There is also a fourth view, which is the view of al-Dahhak: that the intended people of this verse are the Companions of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, because they used to learn from the Messenger, peace be upon him, and teach the people. The interpretation according to this view is: "Be a community united in preserving the Sunnah of the Messenger ﷺ and learning the religion."

The second issue: this verse includes the obligation of three things, the first of which is calling to good, then enjoining what is right, then forbidding what is wrong. Because of the conjunction, these three must be distinct. We say: as for calling to good, the best of it is calling to the affirmation of the essence of Allah, His attributes, and His sanctification above resemblance to contingent things. We said that calling to good includes what we mentioned because of His saying: ﴿Invite to the way of your Lord with wisdom﴾ [al-Nahl: 125] and His saying: ﴿Say, "This is my way; I invite to Allah with insight, I and those who follow me"﴾ [Yusuf: 108].

Having known this, we say: calling to good is a genus under which are two species. One is encouragement to doing what is fitting, which is "what is right" (al-ma'ruf). The other is encouragement to abandoning what is not fitting, which is forbidding what is wrong (al-munkar). He mentioned the genus first, then followed it with its two species, for the sake of emphasis in clarification. As for the conditions of enjoining what is right and forbidding what is wrong, they are mentioned in the books of kalam.

* * *

Then He, exalted is He, said: ﴿And those are the successful﴾, and its explanation has already passed. In it are issues:

The first issue: some have held on to this verse for the view that the sinner (al-fasiq) does not have the right to enjoin what is right and forbid what is wrong. They said: this verse indicates that the one who enjoins what is right and forbids what is wrong is among the successful, and the sinner is not among the successful; therefore the one who enjoins what is right must not be a sinner. It has been answered that this came in the manner of what is generally the case, for the apparent situation is that whoever enjoins what is right and forbids what is wrong does not begin it except after the affairs of his own self are in good order, because the sensible person gives precedence to his own important matters over the important matters of others. Then they reinforced this with His saying: ﴿Do you order the people to righteousness and forget yourselves?﴾ [al-Baqarah: 44], and His saying: ﴿Why do you say what you do not do?﴾ ﴿Greatly hateful in the sight of Allah is that you say what you do not do﴾ [al-Saff: 2, 3]. Also, if that were permitted, it would be permitted for one who commits adultery with a woman to command her, "Why did you uncover your face?" And it is known that this is in the extreme of ugliness. The scholars said: the sinner has the right to enjoin what is right, because it is obligatory upon him to abandon that wrong and obligatory upon him to forbid that wrong; so abandoning one of two obligations does not necessitate abandoning the other obligation. And from the early generations (al-salaf): "Command the good even if you do not do it." And it is related from al-Hasan that he heard Mutarrif ibn 'Abd Allah saying: "I do not say what I do not do." So he said: "Which of us does what he says? Satan would love to snatch this word from you, so that no one would enjoin what is right or forbid what is wrong."

The second issue: from the Prophet ﷺ: "Whoever enjoins what is right and forbids what is wrong is the successor (khalifah) of Allah on His earth, and the successor of His Messenger, and the successor of His Book." And from 'Ali, may Allah be pleased with him: "The best jihad is enjoining what is right and forbidding what is wrong." He also said: "Whoever does not recognize with his heart what is right and does not denounce what is wrong, will be turned upside down, and his highest will be made his lowest." And al-Hasan related from Abu Bakr al-Siddiq, may Allah be pleased with him, that he said: "O people, enjoin one another to what is right and refrain from what is wrong, and you will live in goodness." And from al-Thawri: "If a man is beloved among his neighbors and praised among his brethren, know that he is a flatterer (mudahin)."

The third issue: Allah, glorified and exalted is He, said: ﴿And if two groups among the believers fight, then make reconciliation between them. But if one of them oppresses the other, then fight against the one that oppresses until it returns to the command of Allah﴾ [al-Hujurat: 9]. Reconciliation was given precedence over fighting. This indicates that in enjoining what is right and forbidding what is wrong one should begin with the gentlest means, progressing to the harsher and the harsher. Likewise His saying: ﴿And forsake them in the beds and strike them﴾ [al-Nisa': 34] indicates what we have mentioned. Then if the matter is not accomplished by harshness and severity, it becomes obligatory to change it by hand; if he is unable, then by tongue; if he is unable, then by heart. And people's circumstances differ in this matter.

* * *

Then He, exalted is He, said: ﴿And do not be like those who became divided and differed after the clear proofs had come to them.﴾

In the verse there are issues:

The first issue: concerning the arrangement (al-nazm), there are two views. The first: He, exalted is He, mentioned in the preceding verses that He had made clear in the Torah and the Gospel what indicates the validity of the religion of Islam and the validity of the prophethood of Muhammad ﷺ. Then He mentioned that the People of the Book envied Muhammad ﷺ and schemed to cast doubts and suspicions upon those clear texts. Then He commanded the believers to have faith in Allah and to call to Allah. Then He concluded that by warning the believers against the like of the deed of the People of the Book, which is casting doubts upon these texts and extracting corrupt interpretations that nullify the indication of these texts. So He said: ﴿And do not be,﴾ O believers, upon hearing these clear proofs, ﴿like those who became divided and differed﴾ from among the People of the Book ﴿after there had come to them﴾ in the Torah and the Gospel those clear texts. On this view the verse is part of the completion of the preceding group of verses. The second: that when He commanded enjoining what is right and forbidding what is wrong, which cannot be completed unless the one who enjoins what is right is able to enforce this obligation upon the oppressors and the excessive, and this ability is not attained unless affection and love are present among the people of truth and religion, therefore He warned them against division and disagreement, lest that become a cause of their inability to undertake this obligation. On this view this verse is part of completing only the preceding verse.

The second issue: His saying: ﴿became divided and differed﴾, there are several views. The first: they became divided and differed because of following desire, obeying the self, and envy, just as Iblis abandoned the command of Allah, exalted is He, because of his envy of Adam. The second: they became divided, to the extent that each group among them believed in some of the prophets and not others, and so they came to enmity and division. The third: they became like the innovators of this community, such as the Mushabbihah, the Qadariyyah, and the Hashwiyyah.

The third issue: some said: ﴿became divided and differed﴾, their meaning is one and the same, and He mentioned both for emphasis. It was also said: rather, their meanings differ. Then they differed: it was said, they became divided by enmity and differed in religion; it was said, they became divided by means of extracting corrupt interpretations from those texts, then they differed in that each one of them tried to support his own saying and school. And a third: they became divided in their bodies, in that each one of those rabbis became a leader in a land, then they differed in that each one of them claimed that he was upon the truth and that his companion was upon falsehood. And I say: if you are fair, you will know that most of the scholars of this era have become described by this attribute; so we ask Allah for pardon and mercy.

The fourth issue: He said: ﴿after there had come to them the clear proofs﴾ and did not say "after there had come to them" (jaat-hum) because it is permissible to omit the feminine marker of the verb when the feminine verb is placed before its subject.

* * *

Then He, exalted is He, said: ﴿And those will have a great punishment﴾, meaning: those who became divided will have a great punishment in the Hereafter because of their division. This was a deterrent for the believers against division.

* * *

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 3, verse 110 (part 2 of 5):

Then He, exalted is He, said: ﴿On the Day when some faces will turn white and some faces will turn black﴾. Know that when Allah, exalted is He, commanded the Jews regarding some matters and forbade them from others, and then commanded the Muslims regarding some matters and forbade them from others, He followed that with mention of the conditions of the Hereafter, as an emphasis on the command. There are several issues in the verse:

The first issue: regarding the accusative of "yawma" (on the Day), there are two views. The first: it is in the accusative as an adverb of time (ẓarf), and the implied meaning is: "and for them is a great punishment on this Day." On this reading there are two benefits. One: that punishment is on this Day. The other: that it is part of the judgment of this Day that some faces will turn white and some faces will turn black. The second: it is in the accusative by the implied verb "udhkur" (remember).

The second issue: this verse has parallels, among them His saying: ﴿And on the Day of Resurrection you will see those who lied against Allah, their faces blackened﴾ [al-Zumar: 60]. Among them His saying: ﴿Neither darkness nor humiliation will cover their faces﴾ [Yunus: 26]. Among them His saying: ﴿Faces that Day will be bright, laughing, joyful. And faces that Day will have dust upon them, covered by darkness﴾ [Abasa: 38–41]. Among them His saying: ﴿Faces that Day will be radiant, looking at their Lord﴾ ﴿And faces that Day will be frowning, expecting that a calamity will be inflicted upon them﴾ [al-Qiyamah: 22–25]. Among them His saying: ﴿You will recognize in their faces the radiance of bliss﴾ [al-Mutaffifin: 24]. Among them His saying: ﴿The criminals will be known by their marks﴾ [al-Rahman: 41].

Having understood this, we say: regarding this whiteness, blackness, dust, darkness and radiance, there are two views among the exegetes. One: whiteness is a metaphor for joy and happiness, and blackness for grief, and this is a familiar usage. Allah, exalted is He, said: ﴿When one of them is given news of a female, his face becomes dark, and he suppresses grief﴾ [al-Nahl: 58]. It is said: "So-and-so has a white hand with me," meaning a clear and pleasing favour. When al-Hasan ibn 'Ali (may Allah be pleased with him) handed over the matter to Mu'awiyah, some of them said to him: "O you who blackened the faces of the believers!" And one of them said regarding white hair:

O whiteness of the temples, you have blackened my face before the white-faced ones with black temples.
By my life, I will certainly hide you with all my effort, from the sight of eyes and from the sight of onlookers,
With a blackness in which there is whiteness for my face, and blackness for your cursed face.

The Arabs say of one who attains his desire and succeeds in his aim: "his face has turned white," meaning delight and gladness. And when congratulating someone on joy, they say: "Praise be to Allah who has whitened your face." And of one who meets with something disliked, it is said: "his face has become dusty, his colour has darkened, and his form has changed." According to this, the meaning of the verse is that the believer comes on the Day of Resurrection to what his hands have sent forward; if it is among the good deeds, his face turns white, meaning he rejoices in the blessings and bounty of Allah. And on the opposite, when the disbeliever sees his evil deeds recorded, his face turns black, meaning intense sorrow and grief. This is the view of Abu Muslim al-Isfahani.

The second view: this whiteness and blackness occur on the faces of both believers and disbelievers, because the word is literal in both senses, and there is no evidence requiring abandonment of the literal meaning, so it is necessary to adopt it. I say: Abu Muslim may reply that the evidence supports what we have said, because He, exalted is He, said: ﴿Faces that Day will be bright, laughing, joyful. And faces that Day will have dust upon them, covered by darkness﴾ [Abasa: 38–41]. He placed dust and darkness in opposition to laughter and joy. Had the intended meaning of "dust" and "darkness" not been the figurative sense we mentioned, the opposition would not be valid. So we know that what is meant by this dust and darkness is grief and sorrow, so that this opposition holds. Then those who hold this view say: the wisdom in this is that when the people of the place of standing see whiteness on a person's face, they know he is among the people of reward, so they increase in honouring him, and joy is thereby attained by him in two ways. One: the blessed one rejoices in informing his people that he is among the people of felicity, as He, exalted is He, said, reporting of them: ﴿He said: "Would that my people knew what my Lord has forgiven me and made me among the honoured"﴾ [Ya-Sin: 26–27]. Two: when they know that, they single him out with greater honour. Thus it is established that the appearance of whiteness on the face of the responsible person is a cause of increased happiness for him in the Hereafter, and by the same reasoning the appearance of blackness on the faces of the disbelievers is a cause of increased grief for them in the Hereafter. This is the wisdom in the Hereafter. As for this world: the responsible person in this world, when he knows that this state will occur in the Hereafter, that becomes an incentive for him toward acts of obedience and abandonment of what is forbidden, so that in the Hereafter he will be among those whose faces are whitened, not among those whose faces are blackened. This is the explanation of these two views.

* * *

The third issue: our scholars (the Ash'arites) have argued from this verse that the responsible person is either a believer or a disbeliever, and that there is no intermediate position between the two positions, as the Mu'tazilites maintain.
