They said: Allah, exalted is He, divided the people of the Resurrection into two groups: some whose faces turn white, who are the believers, and some whose faces turn black, who are the disbelievers, and He did not mention a third. Had there been a third group, Allah, exalted is He, would have mentioned it. They said: this is further confirmed by His saying: ﴿Faces that Day will be bright, laughing, joyful. And faces that Day will have dust upon them, covered by darkness. Those are the disbelievers, the wicked﴾ [Abasa: 38–42].

Al-Qadi answered this by saying: the non-mention of a third group does not indicate its non-existence. This is shown by the fact that He, exalted is He, said: ﴿On the Day when some faces will turn white and some faces will turn black﴾, mentioning both in indefinite form, and indefinite form does not signify generality. Also, what is mentioned in the verse are the believers and those who disbelieved after faith, and there is no doubt that the original disbeliever is among the people of the Fire, even though he is not included in these two groups; likewise the case of the sinners.

Know that the basis of the argument from the verse is this: we say that the preceding verses were nothing but an encouragement to faith in the Oneness of God and the prophethood, and a warning against disbelief in both. Then He, exalted is He, followed that with this verse, so its apparent meaning requires that whiteness of the face be the portion of those who believed in the Oneness and prophethood, and blackness of the face be the portion of those who denied that. Then what follows this verse indicates that the owner of whiteness is among the people of Paradise and the owner of blackness among the people of the Fire. At that point it necessarily follows that there is no intermediate position between the two positions. As for the objection that this is problematic in the case of the original disbeliever, our answer to it is on two grounds. The first: why could it not be that what is meant is that every person submitted at the time the offspring were brought forth from the loins of Adam? If that is so, then all are included in it. The second: He, exalted is He, said at the end of the verse: ﴿So taste the punishment for what you used to disbelieve﴾. He made the cause of the punishment disbelief as such, not disbelief in so far as it is after faith. When the reason given is disbelief in general, all disbelievers are included in it, whether one disbelieved after faith or was an original disbeliever. And Allah knows best.

* * *

Then He said: ﴿As for those whose faces turned black: "Did you disbelieve after your faith?"﴾ And there are questions regarding the verse:

The first question: He, exalted is He, mentioned the two groups first, saying: ﴿On the Day when some faces will turn white and some faces will turn black﴾, placing whiteness before blackness in wording; then, when He began on the ruling for these two groups, He placed the ruling for blackness first, whereas the proper order would have been to place the ruling for whiteness first.

The answer to this is in several respects. First: the particle "wa" (and) denotes general conjunction, not sequence. Second: the purpose of creation is the conveying of mercy, not the conveying of punishment. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said, relating from the Lord of Might, glorified is He: "I created them so that they might profit from Me, not so that I might profit from them." Given this, He, exalted is He, began with mention of the people of reward, who are the people of whiteness, because placing the more noble before the less noble in mention is better; then He concluded with mention of them as well, to indicate that the will for mercy is greater than the will for wrath, as He said: "My mercy has preceded My wrath." Third: the eloquent and poets have said that the opening and closing of speech should be something that delights the nature and expands the breast, and there is no doubt that the mention of Allah's mercy is what is like that; therefore the beginning with mention of the people of reward and the ending with mention of them occurred.

The second question: where is the answer to "amma" (as for)?

The answer: it is omitted, and the implied meaning is: "it will be said to them: Did you disbelieve after your faith?" The omission is acceptable because the sense of the speech indicates it, and there are many similar instances in the revelation. He, exalted is He, said: ﴿And the angels will enter upon them from every gate﴾ ﴿Peace be upon you﴾ [al-Ra'd: 23–24]. And He said: ﴿And when Abraham and Ishmael were raising the foundations of the House, [they said:] "Our Lord, accept from us"﴾ [al-Baqarah: 127]. And He said: ﴿If you could see when the criminals hang their heads before their Lord, [saying:] "Our Lord"﴾ [al-Sajdah: 12].

The third question: who is meant by those who disbelieved after their faith?

The answer: the exegetes have several views on this. First: Ubayy ibn Ka'b said: all believed at the time He drew them forth from the loins of Adam, peace be upon him; so whoever disbelieved in this world has disbelieved after faith. Al-Wahidi related this in al-Basit with its chain from the Prophet (ﷺ). Second: the meaning is "Did you disbelieve after there became manifest to you what requires faith, namely the proofs which Allah, exalted is He, established regarding the Oneness and the prophethood?" The evidence for the soundness of this interpretation is His saying before this verse: ﴿O People of the Book, why do you disbelieve in the signs of Allah while you are witnesses?﴾ [Al 'Imran: 70], where He reproached them for disbelief after the signs had become clear, and He said to the believers: ﴿And do not be like those who separated and differed after clear proofs had come to them﴾. Then He said here: ﴿Did you disbelieve after your faith?﴾, so this is to be understood in the light of what we have mentioned, so that this verse confirms what precedes it. On these two interpretations the verse is general with respect to all disbelievers. As for those who restricted this verse to some disbelievers, they have several views. First: 'Ikrimah, al-Asamm and al-Zajjaj said: the meaning is the People of the Book, for before the mission of the Prophet (ﷺ) they were believers in him, and when he was sent they disbelieved in him. Second: Qatadah said: the meaning is those who disbelieved after faith by apostasy. Third: al-Hasan said: those who disbelieved after faith by hypocrisy. Fourth: it is said they are the people of innovations and desires from this community. Fifth: it is said they are the Kharijites, for the Prophet (ﷺ) said about them: "They pass out of the religion as an arrow passes out of its target." These last two views are very far-fetched, because they do not suit what precedes this verse, because they are a specification without evidence, and because rebellion against the imam does not necessarily entail disbelief at all.

The fourth question: what is the purpose of the interrogative hamzah in His saying: ﴿Did you disbelieve?﴾

The answer: this is an interrogation meaning denunciation, and it emphasizes what was mentioned before this verse, namely His saying: ﴿Say: "O People of the Book, why do you disbelieve in the signs of Allah, while Allah is witness to what you do?"﴾ ﴿Say: "O People of the Book, why do you bar from the way of Allah?"﴾ [Al 'Imran: 98–99].

* * *

Then He, exalted is He, said: ﴿So taste the punishment for what you used to disbelieve﴾.

In this there are several benefits. The first: had this not been mentioned, the threat would have been restricted to those who disbelieved after their faith; since this is mentioned, the threat is established both for those who disbelieved after their faith and for the original disbelievers. The second: al-Qadi said: His saying "Did you disbelieve after your faith" indicates that the disbelief is from them and not from Allah, and likewise His saying "So taste the punishment for what you used to disbelieve." The third: the Murji'ah said: the verse indicates that every kind of punishment was caused by disbelief, and this negates the occurrence of punishment for other than the disbeliever.

* * *

Then He, exalted is He, said: ﴿As for those whose faces turned white, they will be in the mercy of Allah, wherein they will abide forever﴾. And there are questions regarding it:

The first question: what is meant by the mercy of Allah?

Answer: The Answer: Ibn ʿAbbas said: what is meant is Paradise. The verifying scholars of our school said: this is an indication that the servant, however much his obedience increases, does not enter Paradise except by the mercy of God. And how could we not say this, since as long as the servant's motive toward doing and toward abandoning is equal, the act is prevented from him? Therefore, unless the motive toward obedience predominates, it is impossible that obedience should arise from him; and that predominance can only come about by the creation of God, Exalted. Thus the issuing of that obedience from the servant is a blessing from God toward the servant, so how could that make anything binding upon God? It is established, then, that entry into Paradise is only by the grace of God, His mercy and His generosity, not by our merit.

The Second Question: What is the position of His saying ﴿They therein abide forever﴾ after His saying ﴿then in the mercy of God﴾?
The Answer: It is as if it were said: How will they be therein? So it is said: ﴿They therein abide forever﴾, not departing from it, and not dying.

The Third Question: The disbelievers abide forever in the Fire just as the believers abide forever in Paradise. Then He, Exalted, did not specify the abiding of the people of the Fire in this verse, although He specified the abiding of the people of Paradise therein. What is the benefit?
Page 152
The Answer: All of that is an indication that the side of mercy is predominant. This is because He began the mention with the people of mercy and ended with the people of mercy. When He mentioned the punishment, He did not attribute it to Himself; rather He said: ﴿So taste the punishment﴾, although He mentioned mercy attributed to Himself when He said: ﴿then in the mercy of God﴾. And when He mentioned the punishment, He did not specify the abiding, although He specified the abiding on the side of reward. And when He mentioned the punishment, He gave its cause as their own deeds, saying: ﴿So taste the punishment because you used to disbelieve﴾; and when He mentioned the reward, He gave its cause as His mercy, saying: ﴿then in the mercy of God﴾. Then He said at the end of the verse: ﴿And God does not desire injustice to the worlds﴾, and this runs in the manner of an apology for the threat of punishment. All of this is among what indicates that the side of mercy is dominant. O Most Merciful of the merciful, do not deprive us of the cool of Your mercy, and of the honour of Your forgiveness and Your kindness.

* * *

Then the Exalted said: ﴿These are the signs of God, which We recite to you in truth﴾. Regarding His saying "these" (tilka), there are two aspects. The first: what is meant is that these verses which we have mentioned are the proofs of God; and the use of "tilka" in place of "hadhihi" is permissible because these verses mentioned have passed away after being mentioned, so it is as if they have become distant, and therefore "tilka" is said regarding them. The second: that God, Exalted, promised him that He would send down to him a Book comprising everything that is necessary in the religion; so when He sent down these verses, He said: these promised verses are those which We recite to you in truth. The full discussion of this matter has already been given in Surat al-Baqarah in the commentary on His saying: ﴿That is the Book﴾. Regarding His saying "in truth" (bil-haqq) there are two aspects. The first: that is, connected with truth and justice, from the recompense of the good-doer and the evildoer with what they deserve. The second: "in truth," that is, in the true sense, because the meaning of recitation is truth.

* * *

Then the Exalted said: ﴿And God does not desire injustice to the worlds﴾, and regarding it there are issues:

The First Issue: The mention of injustice is good here because the mention of severe punishment preceded it, and He, Glorified and Exalted, is the Most Generous of the generous. So it is as if He, Exalted, is offering an apology for that and said: They fell into it only because of their objectionable deeds, for the interests of the world cannot be upheld except by threatening wrongdoers; and when this threat occurs, there must be verification in order to repel falsehood. Thus this apology is among the strongest proofs that the side of mercy prevails. Its parallel is His saying, Exalted, in Surat ʿAmma after mentioning the threat to the disbelievers: ﴿Indeed they did not expect a reckoning﴾ ﴿and denied Our signs with complete denial﴾ [An-Naba: 27-28], meaning: this severe threat occurred only because of these objectionable deeds.

* * *

The Second Issue: Al-Jubba'i said: this verse indicates that He, Glorified, does not desire any of the abominations, neither from His own acts nor from the acts of His servants, and does not do any of that. Its explanation: injustice is either supposed to issue from God, Exalted, or from the servant; and supposing it issues from the servant, either he wrongs himself, by his persisting in sins, or wrongs others. So the divisions of injustice are these three. And His saying, Exalted: ﴿And God does not desire injustice to the worlds﴾ is an indefinite noun in the context of negation, so it is necessary that He does not desire anything that is injustice, whether it issues from Him or from another. Thus it is established that this verse indicates that He does not desire any of these three divisions; and when that is established, it is necessary that He is not the doer of any of these divisions, and it follows that He is not the doer of injustice at all, and it follows that He is not the doer of the actions of the servants, because among their actions is their wronging themselves and some of them wronging others. And we say that the verse indicates that He, Exalted, is not at all a doer of injustice, because it indicates that He does not desire any of it; and if He were a doer of any division of injustice, He would be desiring it, and that has been refuted. They said: Thus it is established by this verse that He, Exalted, is not a doer of injustice, and not a doer of the actions of the servants, and not a desirer of the abominations of the servants' actions. Then they said: He, Exalted, praised Himself by saying that He does not desire that; and praise is valid only if it is valid for Him to do that thing and valid for Him to be desiring it; so this verse indicates that He, Exalted, is capable of injustice. At this point they boasted and said: this one verse suffices to establish all the principles of the Mu'tazila in the matters of justice. Then they said: When He, Exalted, mentioned that He does not desire injustice nor does He do injustice, He said after it: ﴿And to God belongs whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth, and to God all matters are returned﴾. He mentioned this verse after what preceded for two reasons. The first: when He, Exalted, mentioned that He does not desire injustice and abominations, He argued for it by saying that the doer of an abomination does it either out of ignorance, or incapacity, or need; and all of that is impossible for God, because He is the owner of everything in the heavens and on the earth, and this ownership negates ignorance, incapacity, and need; and when these attributes are impossible to ascribe to Him, Exalted, it is impossible that He be a doer of abomination. The second: when He, Exalted, mentioned that He does not desire injustice in any way, one might say: we witness the existence of injustice in the world; so if its occurrence is not by His will, it would be against His will, and it would follow that He is weak, incapable, overpowered; and that is impossible.

God, Exalted, answered this by His saying: ﴿And to God belongs whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth﴾, meaning: He, Exalted, is able to prevent the wrongdoers from wrongdoing by way of compulsion and subjugation; and since He is able to do that, He is outside being incapable and weak. It is not that He, Exalted, wanted from them the abandoning of disobedience by choice and willingly, so that by that they would become deserving of reward; for if He subdued them to abandon disobedience, this benefit would be void. This is the summary of the words of the Mu'tazila on this verse. And perhaps they raised this discussion from another aspect, saying: the meaning of His saying: ﴿And God does not desire injustice to the worlds﴾ is either that He does not desire to wrong them, or that He does not desire from them that some of them wrong others. If it is the first, this does not hold according to your view, because your doctrine is that if He, Exalted, punished the innocent of sin with the most severe punishment, it would not be injustice but justice; because injustice is a disposal of another's property, and He, Exalted, disposes only of His own property; so it is impossible that He be a wrongdoer. And if that is so, it is not possible to take the verse to mean that He does not desire to wrong creation. And if you take the verse to mean that He does not desire that some servants wrong others, this too does not hold according to your view, because all of that is by the will of God and His decree according to your view. Thus it is established that according to your doctrine it is not possible to take the verse in a valid sense. The answer: Why is it not permissible that what is meant is that He, Exalted, does not desire to wrong any of His servants? Your statement that injustice from Him is impossible according to your doctrine makes the praise of it impossible. We say: the discussion on this has two aspects. The first: He, Exalted, praised Himself by saying: ﴿Neither drowsiness nor sleep overtakes Him﴾ [Al-Baqarah: 255], and by saying: ﴿And He feeds but is not fed﴾ [Al-An'am: 14]; and it does not follow from that that sleep and eating are valid for Him; so likewise here. The second: that if He punished one who did not deserve punishment, then although it would not be injustice in itself, it would be in the form of injustice; and the name of one of two similar things is sometimes applied to the other, as in His saying: ﴿And the recompense of an evil is an evil like it﴾ [Ash-Shura: 40], and its parallels are numerous in the Qur'an. This is the complete discussion in this debate.

* * *

The Third Issue: Our companions argued by His saying: ﴿And to God belongs whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth﴾ that He is the creator of the actions of the servants. They said: there is no doubt that the actions of the servants are among what is in the heavens and the earth; so it is necessary that they belong to Him by His saying: ﴿And to God belongs whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth﴾; and our saying that they belong to Him is valid only if they are created by Him; so this verse indicates that He is the creator of the actions of the servants.

Al-Jubba'i answered this by saying that His saying "to God" (lillah) is an idafa of ownership, not an idafa of action. Do you not see that it is said: "this house is for so-and-so," and they mean that it is his possession, not that it is his product? Also, the purpose of the verse is that God magnifies Himself and praises His own divinity, and it is not permissible for Him to praise Himself by attributing to Himself indecencies and abominations. Also, His saying "whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth" applies only to what is contained within the heavens and the earth, and that belongs to the attributes of bodies, not to the attributes of actions, which are accidents.

Our companions answered him: this idafa is an idafa of action, as is evident from the fact that the one who is capable of the evil and the good does not prefer the good over the evil except when there arises in his heart a motive that calls him to doing the good; and that motive arises by the creation of God, Exalted, to prevent an infinite regress. And when the effective cause in the occurrence of the servant's act is the combination of power and motive, and it is established that the combination of power and motive is by the creation of God, Exalted, it is established that the servant's act is ascribed to God, Exalted, as creation and bringing into being, through the intermediary of the act of the means. This is the complete statement in this debate.

The Fourth Issue: His saying, Exalted: ﴿And to God belongs whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth﴾. The philosophers claimed that the mention of what is in the heavens was placed before the mention of what is on the earth only because the heavenly conditions are causes of the earthly conditions; so the cause was placed before the effect. This indicates that all earthly conditions are ascribed to heavenly conditions. There is no doubt that heavenly conditions are ascribed to God's creation and bringing into being; so compulsion (jabr) also becomes necessary from this aspect.

The Fifth Issue: He, Exalted, said: ﴿And to God belongs whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth, and to God all matters are returned﴾. He repeated the mention of God at the beginning of the two verses, and the purpose of it is to emphasize the magnification. The intended meaning is that from Him is the origin of the created beings and to Him is their return. So His saying: ﴿And to God belongs whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth﴾ is an indication that He, Glorified, is the First; and His saying: ﴿And to God all matters are returned﴾ is an indication that He is the Last. This indicates the encompassing of His rule, His disposal and His governance over their first and last, and that the causes are attributed to Him, and that needs end with Him.

The Sixth Issue: The word "to" (ila) in His saying: ﴿And to God all matters are returned﴾ does not indicate that He, Exalted, is in a place or direction. Rather, what is meant is that the return of creation is to a place in which no one's judgment is executed except His judgment, and in which no one's decree operates except His decree.

[Page 155]

The composition (nazm) of the verse has two aspects.

The first: When Allah commanded the believers to do certain things and forbade them from others, and warned them against becoming like the People of the Book in rebellion and disobedience, and then mentioned after that the reward of the obedient and the punishment of the disbelievers, the purpose of all these verses was to move the responsible believers to submission and obedience, and to restrain them from rebellion and disobedience. Then Allah followed this with another method that calls the believers to submission and obedience, saying: ﴿You are the best community brought forth for mankind﴾. The meaning is that you were, in the Preserved Tablet (al-Lawh al-Mahfuz), the best and most excellent of nations. It is therefore fitting that you should not nullify this excellence for yourselves, should not remove this praiseworthy quality from yourselves, and should be submissive and obedient in everything that the obligations require of you.

The second: When Allah mentioned the complete state of the wretched, which is His saying: ﴿As for those whose faces turn black﴾, and the complete state of the blessed, which is His saying: ﴿As for those whose faces turn white﴾, He pointed out the cause of the threat against the wretched by His saying: ﴿And Allah does not intend any injustice to the worlds﴾, meaning that they deserved that only because of their ugly deeds. Then in this verse He pointed out the cause of the promise to the blessed by His saying: ﴿You are the best community brought forth for mankind﴾, meaning that those felicities, perfections and honours they attained in the Hereafter were because they were in this world ﴿the best community brought forth for mankind﴾.

There are several issues concerning the verse.

First issue: The word (kana) may be complete, incomplete (a copula), or redundant, as explained in grammar. The exegetes differed concerning the word (kuntum) in several ways.

The first: (kana) here is complete, meaning "to occur" or "to come into being," and it needs no predicate. The meaning is: you came into being as the best community, you were found and created as the best community. The phrase ﴿best community﴾ would then function as a circumstantial state (hal). This is the view of a group of exegetes.

The second: (kana) here is incomplete (a copula). This raises an objection: that this implies they were described with this quality in the past and that they no longer remain so now.

The answer to this: the word (kana) is an expression of the existence of a thing in past time in an undefined manner, and this does not indicate a sudden cessation, as is evident from His saying: ﴿Seek forgiveness from your Lord; indeed He is ever Forgiving﴾ [Nuh: 10], and His saying: ﴿And Allah is ever Forgiving and Merciful﴾ [an-Nisa: 100]. Having established this, we say: the exegetes, on this assumption, have several views. One: You were, in the knowledge of Allah, the best community. Two: You were, among the nations that came before you, described as the best community, and this is like His saying: ﴿Harsh against the disbelievers, merciful among themselves﴾ [al-Fath: 29], up to His saying: ﴿That is their example in the Torah﴾ [al-Fath: 29]. Their harshness toward the disbelievers is their enjoining what is right and forbidding what is wrong. Three: You were, in the Preserved Tablet, described as the best community. Four: You have been, since you believed, the best community brought forth for mankind. Five: Abu Muslim said: His saying ﴿You were the best community﴾ is connected to His saying: ﴿As for those whose faces turn white﴾, and the meaning is that it will be said to them when they abide in Paradise: "You were, in your worldly life, the best community, so you deserved what you are in of mercy and the whiteness of your faces because of it," and what has intervened between the beginning and the end of the narrative is like what keeps occurring in the Qur'an of its kind. Six: Some said: Had Allah willed, He would have said (antum) ("you," plural pronoun), and this honour would have been attained by all of us. But His saying (kuntum) is specific to particular people among the Companions of the Messenger (ﷺ), namely the foremost early ones, and those who did as they did. Seven: You have been, since you believed, the best community, as an indication that they were described with this quality since they existed.

The third possibility: It may be said that (kana) here is redundant. Some said that His saying ﴿You were the best community﴾ is like His saying: ﴿And remember when you were few and He multiplied you﴾ [al-A'raf: 86], and He said in another place: ﴿And remember when you were few and oppressed﴾ [al-Anfal: 26]. The omission and the mention of (kana) are equivalent, except that it is mentioned for emphasis and to affirm that the matter will certainly occur. Ibn al-Anbari said: This view is clearly flawed, because (kana) is elided when it is in the middle or at the end of a sentence, but it is not elided when it comes first. The Arabs say: "Abdullah was standing" (kana qa'iman), and "Abdullah was standing" (qa'imun kana) with (kana) being elided, but they do not say "Kana Abdullah standing" with its elision, because their way is to begin with what the attention is directed to, and the elided element is not in the place of attention. Also, it is not permissible to elide the verb "to be" in the verse because its predicate is in the accusative case, and when the verb "to be" governs the predicate and puts it in the accusative, it is not elided.

The fourth possibility: (kana) means (sara), "to become." Thus His saying ﴿You were the best community﴾ means: you became the best community brought forth for mankind, enjoining what is right, forbidding what is wrong, meaning you became the best community because of your being those who enjoin what is right, forbid what is wrong, and believe in Allah.

* * *

Then He said: ﴿And if the People of the Book had believed, it would have been better for them﴾. He means: just as you attained this excellence because of these qualities, so too the People of the Book, had they believed, would also have attained the quality of excellence. And Allah knows best.

* * *

Second issue: Our companions (the Ash'arite scholars) cited this verse as evidence that the consensus (ijma') of the community is a proof (hujjah). Its argument is from two aspects.

The first: His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And among the people of Moses is a community that guides by the truth﴾ [al-A'raf: 159]. Then He said in this verse: ﴿You are the best community﴾. Therefore, by the ruling of this verse, this community must be more excellent than those who guide by the truth among the people of Moses. And if these are more excellent than them, it follows that this community does not rule except by the truth, for if it were permissible in this community to rule by what is not true, it would be impossible for this community to be more excellent than the community that guides by the truth, because the one who follows falsehood cannot be better than the one who follows truth. Thus it is established that this community does not rule except by the truth, and if this is so, their consensus is a proof.

The second aspect: The definite article in the words (al-ma'ruf, "what is right") and (al-munkar, "what is wrong") indicates comprehensiveness (istighraq), and this requires that they enjoin every right and forbid every wrong. And whenever they are like this, their consensus is necessarily true and correct, and so it is a proof. The extensive discussions on this we have mentioned in the principles of jurisprudence (usul al-fiqh).

Third issue: Al-Zajjaj said: His saying ﴿You were the best community﴾: the apparent address in it is with the Companions of the Prophet (ﷺ), but it is general to the whole community. Its parallel is His saying: ﴿Fasting is prescribed for you﴾ [al-Baqarah: 183], and ﴿Retribution is prescribed for you﴾ [al-Baqarah: 178]. All of these are addressed to those present according to the wording, but they are general in application to all. Likewise here.

Fourth issue: Al-Qaffal, may Allah have mercy on him, said: The root meaning of "ummah" is a group gathered upon one thing. So the ummah of our Prophet (ﷺ) are the group characterized by belief in him and acknowledgment of his prophethood. It may also be said that everyone whom his call has gathered is his ummah, but when the word "ummah" is used alone, it applies to the first group. Do you not see that when it is said "the ummah agreed upon such and such," the first group is understood from it? The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "My ummah will not agree upon misguidance." And it is narrated that on the Day of Resurrection he (ﷺ) will say: "My ummah, my ummah!" So the word "ummah" in these contexts and similar ones is understood to refer to those who acknowledge his prophethood. As for those whom his call reached, it is said of them only that they are "the ummah of the call," and the word "ummah" is applied to them only with this qualification.

As for His saying ﴿brought forth for mankind﴾, there are two views. The first: The meaning is "You were the best of the nations brought forth for mankind in all eras." So His saying ﴿brought forth for mankind﴾ means "made manifest to mankind, until they were distinguished, recognized, and separated from others." The second: His saying (lil-nas, "for mankind") completes His saying (kuntum, "you were"), and the meaning is: "You were, for mankind, the best community." Some said: ﴿brought forth﴾ is a relative clause (silah), and the meaning is: "You were the best community for mankind."

* * *

Then He said: ﴿enjoining what is right, forbidding what is wrong, and believing in Allah﴾.

Know that this is a new independent statement, and its purpose is to explain the cause of that excellence, as when you say: "Zayd is generous; he feeds people, clothes them, and attends to what benefits them." The clarification of the matter is that it is established in the principles of jurisprudence that mentioning a ruling together with a descriptive attribute appropriate to it indicates that the ruling is caused by that attribute. Here, Allah ruled that the quality of excellence belongs to this community, then mentioned after this ruling these acts of obedience, namely enjoining what is right, forbidding what is wrong, and faith. Therefore that excellence must be caused by these acts of worship.

Here there are questions.

First question: In what respect do enjoining what is right, forbidding what is wrong, and belief in Allah require that this community be the best of nations, given that these three qualities were present among the other nations as well?

The answer: Al-Qaffal said: Their being preferred over the nations before them occurred because they enjoined what is right and forbade what is wrong in the most emphatic manner, which is fighting (qital). For enjoining what is right may be done by the heart, by the tongue, or by the hand, and the strongest of these is that which is done by fighting, since it involves exposing oneself to the danger of being killed. The most known of rights is the true religion and faith in the Oneness of Allah and in prophethood, and the most reprehensible of wrongs is disbelief in Allah. So struggle (jihad) in religion became the bearer of the greatest harms, for the purpose of bringing others to the greatest benefits and rescuing them from the greatest harms. Therefore jihad must be the greatest of acts of worship. And since the command of jihad in our law is stronger than in all other laws, this necessarily became the cause of this community's superiority over all other nations. This is the meaning of what is narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, that he said in explaining this verse: His saying ﴿You were the best community brought forth for mankind﴾: "You command them to bear witness that there is no god but Allah, and to acknowledge what Allah has sent down, and you fight them over it." And "There is no god but Allah" is the greatest of what is right, and denial is the most reprehensible of what is wrong.

Al-Qaffal then said: The benefit of fighting over religion is not denied by any fair-minded person, because most people love their religions through habit and custom, and do not reflect on the proofs presented to them. When they are compelled to enter the religion through the threat of killing, they enter it, and then the love of the false religion in their hearts continues to weaken, and the love of the true religion continues to grow in their hearts, until they move from falsehood to truth, and from deserving everlasting punishment to deserving everlasting reward.

Second question: Why is enjoining what is right and forbidding what is wrong mentioned before belief in Allah, given that belief in Allah must necessarily precede all acts of obedience?

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 3, verse 110 (part 5 of 5):

The answer is that belief in Allah is something shared by all the righteous nations. Then Allah, exalted is He, preferred this nation over the other righteous nations. It is therefore impossible that the cause of this excellence should be faith, which is the common element shared by all. Rather, the cause of this added excellence is that this nation is stronger in its state of enjoining what is good (al-amr bil-ma'ruf) and forbidding what is evil (al-nahy 'an al-munkar) than the other nations. So the cause of this excellence is enjoining what is good and forbidding what is evil. As for belief in Allah, it is a condition (shart) for this cause to have its effect in this ruling, because as long as faith does not exist, no act of obedience becomes effective in producing the attribute of excellence. Thus it is established that what necessitates this excellence is that they enjoin what is good and forbid what is evil, while their faith is the condition for that effect. The cause is closer to the effect than the condition for the effect is. For this reason, Allah, exalted is He, mentioned enjoining good and forbidding evil before mentioning faith.

The third question: Why did He mention only belief in Allah and not belief in prophethood, although it is necessary?

The answer: Belief in Allah necessarily entails belief in prophethood, because belief in Allah is not attained unless belief in His truthfulness is attained, and belief in His truthfulness is not attained unless the one who displayed the miracle in accordance with his claim is truthful. This is because the miracle stands in the place of verbal confirmation. So when we witnessed the appearance of a miracle in accordance with the claim of Muhammad (ﷺ), belief in the prophethood of Muhammad (ﷺ) became a necessary part of belief in Allah. Therefore, mentioning only belief in Allah was an alert to this subtle point.

* * *

Then He, exalted is He, said: ﴿And if the People of the Scripture had believed, it would have been better for them.﴾ There are two interpretations of this. The first: If the People of the Scripture had believed in this religion, for the sake of which the attribute of excellence was obtained by the followers of Muhammad (upon him be peace and blessings), this excellence would have been obtained by them too. So the purpose of this statement is to encourage the People of the Scripture toward this religion. The second: The People of the Scripture only preferred their religion over the religion of Islam out of love for leadership and for having followers of knowledge. If they had believed, this leadership would have been theirs in this world, together with the great reward in the Hereafter. That would have been better for them than what they were content with.

Know that He, exalted is He, followed this statement with two sentences, without a conjunction, as a fresh beginning. One of them is His saying: ﴿Among them are believers, but most of them are defiant transgressors.﴾ The second is His saying: ﴿They will not harm you except for a little annoyance. And if they fight you, they will turn their backs to you; then they will not be helped.﴾ The author of al-Kashshaf (al-Zamakhshari) said: These are two statements that come as a digression (istitrad) when mention of the People of the Scripture is brought up, as a speaker says: "And regarding so-and-so, his matter is such-and-such." For this reason, the word (آمَنَ) came without a conjunction.

As for His saying: ﴿Among them are believers, but most of them are defiant transgressors﴾, there are two questions about it:

The first question: Is the definite article in His saying (المُؤْمِنُونَ, "the believers") for comprehensive scope (istighraq) or for a previously known group (al-ma'hud al-sabiq)?

The answer: Rather, it is for a previously known group. What is meant is Abdullah ibn Salam and his group from the Jews, and al-Najashi and his group from the Christians.

The second question: An attribute is mentioned only for emphasis, so what emphasis is achieved by describing the disbeliever as a defiant transgressor?

The answer: A disbeliever may be upright in his own religion, or he may be a defiant transgressor in his own religion. In the latter case, he is rejected by all groups, because the Muslims do not accept him due to his disbelief, and the disbelievers do not accept him because he is a transgressor among them. So it is as if it were said: The People of the Scripture are of two kinds. Among them are those who believed. As for those who did not believe, they are defiant transgressors in their religions, so they are by no means among those whom anyone of sound mind would ever follow.

As for His saying, exalted is He: ﴿They will not harm you except for a little annoyance.﴾ Know that when He encouraged the believers to be steadfast in their faith and to disregard the sayings and deeds of the disbelievers, through His saying ﴿You are the best nation﴾, He encouraged them in this regard from another angle. That is, the People of the Scripture have no power to harm the Muslims except by a small amount of speech that has no significance. And if they fought the Muslims, they would be defeated and abandoned. Since this is the case, it is not necessary to pay attention to their sayings and deeds. All of this confirms what preceded in His saying: ﴿If you obey a party of those who were given the Scripture﴾ [Al 'Imran: 100]. This is the connection of the verses (wajh al-nazm).

As for His saying: ﴿They will not harm you except for a little annoyance﴾, its meaning is that the disbelievers among the People of the Scripture cannot inflict real harm on the Muslims. The most they can do is annoy you with the tongue, either by slandering Muhammad and Jesus (upon them both be peace and blessings), or by openly expressing blasphemous words, such as their saying ﴿Uzayr is the son of Allah﴾ [al-Tawbah: 30], and ﴿The Messiah is the son of Allah﴾ [al-Tawbah: 30], and ﴿Allah is the third of three﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 73]. Or by distorting the texts of the Torah and the Gospel, or by casting doubts into people's ears, or by frightening the weak among the Muslims. Some people have said that His saying ﴿except for a little annoyance﴾ is a disjunctive exception (istithna' munqati'), but this is far-fetched, because all the aspects mentioned cause distress to the hearts of the Muslims, and distress is a form of harm. So the sense is: They will not harm you except with the harm that is annoyance. This is therefore a valid exception, and the meaning is: They will not harm you except with a slight harm. The word "annoyance" (adha) takes the place of harm, and adha is the verbal noun of "adhaytu al-shay'" (I caused a thing harm).

Then Allah, exalted is He, said: ﴿And if they fight you, they will turn their backs to you; then they will not be helped﴾. This is a report that if they fought the Muslims, they would become defeated and forsaken. ﴿Then they will not be helped﴾ means that after they have become defeated, they will never obtain any strength or power. A similar statement is His saying: ﴿And if they are fought, they will not help them; and if they should help them, they would surely turn their backs; then they would not be helped﴾ [al-Hashr: 12], and His saying: ﴿Say to those who disbelieve: "You will be overcome and gathered to Hell"﴾ [Al 'Imran: 12], and His saying: ﴿Are we a host that is victorious?﴾ ﴿The multitude will be routed and they will turn their backs﴾ [al-Qamar: 44-45]. All of this is a promise of conquest, support and victory.

Know that this verse includes reports of many unseen matters. Among them: the believers are safe from their harm; among them: if they fought the believers, they would be routed; and among them: after the rout, they will obtain no strength or power. All these reports came to pass just as Allah had reported about them, for the Jews did not fight except that they were routed, and they never undertook a war or sought leadership except that they were forsaken. All of this is a report of the unseen, and so it is a miracle. Here there are some questions:

The first question: Suppose the Jews are as described, but the Christians are not; this would cast doubt on the soundness of these verses. We say: these verses are specific to the Jews, and the occasions of revelation confirm this, so this difficulty is removed.

The second question: Why is His saying ﴿then they will not be helped﴾ not in the jussive mood?

We say: It was turned away from the rule of the conditional response to the rule of a fresh independent statement, as if it were said: "I inform you that they will not be helped." The benefit of this is that if it had been jussive, the negation of help would have been restricted to their fighting, like the turning of backs; but when it was in the nominative, the negation of help became an unrestricted promise, as if He said: "Then their state and their story, which I inform you of and give you good tidings of, after the turning of backs, is that they will find no help after that ever, but will remain in humiliation and abasement forever and always."

The third question: What is the phrase ﴿then they will not be helped﴾ coordinated with?

The answer: It is the conditional clause and its response, as if it were said: "I inform you that if they fight you, they will be routed; then I inform you that they will not be helped." The word (ثم, then) is used to convey the sense of a gap in rank, because the report of Allah imposing abandonment upon them is greater than the report of their turning their backs.

**Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on Surah 3, verse 112:**

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Humiliation has been decreed upon them wherever they are found, except under a covenant from Allah and a covenant from the people. They have incurred wrath from Allah, and destitution has been decreed upon them. That is because they used to disbelieve in the signs of Allah and kill the prophets without right. That is because they disobeyed and were transgressors.﴾

Know that when He, may He be exalted, explained that if they fought, they would return defeated and unsupported, He mentioned that, in addition to this, humiliation has been decreed upon them. There are several issues in the verse.

**First issue:** We have already explained the meaning of this word in Surah al-Baqarah. The meaning is that humiliation was made to cling to them like something struck onto a thing that then adheres to it. From this comes their saying: "This is not a *darbat lazib* (a stroke that sticks) upon me," and from it comes the naming of the kharaj (land tax) as *dariba*.

**Second issue:** *al-dhilla* is *al-dhull* (abasement). Regarding what is meant by this abasement, there are opinions:

The first, and the strongest, is that what is meant is that they will be fought, killed, have their wealth seized, their offspring taken captive, and their lands taken as property. This is like His saying: ﴿And kill them wherever you find them﴾ [al-Baqarah: 191].

* * *

Then He said: ﴿except under a covenant from Allah﴾. What is meant is: except under a covenant from Allah, a protection and a guarantee from Allah and from the believers, because at that point the rulings cease to apply, so there is no killing, no seizure of booty, and no taking of captives.

The second opinion: this humiliation is the *jizya* (poll tax levied on non-Muslim subjects), because the imposition of the *jizya* upon them entails abasement and disgrace.

The third: what is meant by this humiliation is that you will not see among them a dominant king or a respected leader; rather, they are despised in all lands, abased and humiliated.

Know that it is not possible to say that the meaning of *dhilla* is only the *jizya*, or only this degradation, because His saying ﴿except under a covenant from Allah﴾ requires that this abasement be removed upon obtaining this covenant, whereas the *jizya*, disgrace and baseness are not removed by obtaining this covenant at all. Therefore it is impossible to restrict the abasement to the *jizya* alone. Some who supported this opinion answered this objection by saying that this exception is *munqati'* (disconnected, i.e., not of the same category as what precedes), and this is the view of Muhammad ibn Jarir al-Tabari. He said: The Jews have had abasement decreed upon them, whether or not they are under a covenant from Allah, so by this exception they do not move from abasement to honour. Thus His saying ﴿except under a covenant from Allah﴾ means: "But they may cling to a covenant from Allah and a covenant from the people."

Know that this is weak, because taking the particle *illa* ("except") to mean *lakin* ("but") is contrary to the apparent sense. Also, if we take the sentence to mean "But they may cling to a covenant from Allah and a covenant from the people," this sense is not complete, so it is necessary to supply something to which they cling by these things, for the sake of avoiding it. Supplying is contrary to the original principle, so one does not resort to it except out of necessity. Since there is no necessity here for that, resorting to it is impermissible. Rather, there is another view, which is that the abasement is taken to include all of these things, namely killing, captivity, the taking of offspring as captives, the seizure of wealth, the infliction of disgrace and degradation. The benefit of the exception is that the totality of these rulings does not remain, and that does not contradict the continuation of some of these rulings, namely the taking of a small portion of their wealth, which is called the *jizya*, and the continuation of degradation, baseness and disgrace among them. This is the view on this point.

His saying ﴿wherever they are found﴾ means: wherever they are found and encountered. It is said: "I *thaqaftu* so-and-so in battle," meaning I overtook him. The discussion of this has already passed at His saying ﴿wherever you find them﴾ [al-Baqarah: 191].

**Third issue:** His saying ﴿except under a covenant from Allah﴾ has several aspects:

The first: al-Farra' said: The construction is "except that they cling to a covenant from Allah," and he cited as evidence:

*"She saw me with her rope and withdrew in fear, while in the rope there was a frightened, trembling heart."*

They objected to this, saying: It is not permissible to delete the relative pronoun (*al-mawsul*) and keep its relative clause (*al-silah*), because the *mawsul* is the principal element and the *silah* is the subordinate; so it is permissible to delete the subordinate because the principal indicates it, but deleting the principal while keeping the subordinate is not permissible.

The second: this exception occurs in terms of meaning, because the meaning of the imposition of abasement is its adherence to them in the strongest way, such that it does not leave them and is not separated from them. It is as if it were said: abasement does not depart from them, and they will not be freed except by a covenant from Allah and a covenant from the people.

The third: the *ba'* (in *bi-habl*) may be in the sense of *ma'a* ("with"), as in their saying: "Come out with us and we will do such-and-such," meaning "with us." The construction would then be: "except with a covenant from Allah."

* * *

**Fourth issue:** What is meant by the rope of Allah is His covenant. We have mentioned earlier that the covenant was called a "rope" because a person, before the covenant, is fearful, and that fear prevents him from reaching his goal. When the covenant is obtained, he reaches his goal through that covenant. So it resembles a rope: whoever grips it is freed from fear of harm.

If it is said: He joined to "the rope of Allah" a "rope from the people," and that requires a difference, so how is this difference?

We say: Some said: The rope of Allah is Islam, and the rope of the people is the covenant and the protection (*dhimma*). This is far-fetched, because if this were what was meant, He would have said "or a rope from the people." Others said: What is meant by both ropes is the covenant, the protection and the safe-conduct, and He mentioned the two ropes because the safe-conduct taken from the believers is the safe-conduct taken by the permission of Allah. In my view this is also weak. What I hold regarding this is that the safe-conduct granted to the *dhimmi* (protected non-Muslim) is of two kinds:

One: that which Allah has specified explicitly, which is the taking of the *jizya*.

Two: that which has been left to the judgment of the Imam, so he may add to it at times and reduce it at others according to his independent reasoning (*ijtihad*).

The first is what is called the rope of Allah, and the second is what is called the rope of the believers. And Allah knows best.

* * *

Then He said: ﴿They have incurred wrath from Allah﴾. We have mentioned that its meaning is that they remained, stayed and persisted in the wrath of Allah. The root of this is taken from *ba'* (a return or abode), which means a place; from it comes "so-and-so *tabawwa'a* the house of such-and-such," and "I *bawwa'tuhu* it," meaning I settled him in it. The meaning is that they remained in the wrath of Allah and dwelt in it. Your saying "the wrath befell them" and "they dwelt in it" are the same in meaning.

* * *

Then He said: ﴿And destitution has been decreed upon them﴾. Most of the commentators understood *al-maskana* (destitution) to mean the *jizya*, and this is the view of al-Hasan. He said: This is because He excluded destitution from the exception, and that indicates that it remains upon them and does not leave them. What remains upon them is nothing but the *jizya*. Others said: What is meant by *maskana* is that the Jew shows himself to be poor even if he is wealthy and affluent. Some said: This is a report from Allah, glorified is He, that He made the Jews a provision for the Muslims, so they become needy. Then, when He, may He be exalted, mentioned these kinds of threat, He said:

*﴿That is because they used to disbelieve in the signs of Allah and kill the prophets without right﴾*. The meaning is that He, may He be exalted, attached to the Jews three kinds of disliked things:

The first: He made abasement binding upon them.

The second: He made the wrath of Allah binding upon them.

The third: He made destitution binding upon them.

Then in this verse He explained that the cause for attaching these disliked things to them is that they used to disbelieve in the signs of Allah and kill the prophets without right. Here there are questions:

**First question:** This abasement and destitution became attached to the Jews only after the rise of the state of Islam, whereas those who killed the prophets without right were those who lived before Muhammad (ﷺ) by ages and eras. So in this case, the place where the cause occurred, namely the killing of the prophets, did not see the effect, which is abasement and destitution; and the place where this effect occurred did not see the cause. Therefore the problem remains.

The answer to this: Although those later ones did not themselves kill the prophets, peace be upon them, nevertheless they were content with that, since their forefathers were those who killed the prophets, and these later ones were content with the deeds of their forefathers. So that deed was attributed to them, insofar as that repugnant deed was the deed of their fathers and forefathers, while they were approving of their forefathers in those deeds.

**Second question:** Why was the saying ﴿That is because they disobeyed﴾ repeated, and what is the wisdom in it? It cannot be said that the repetition is for emphasis, because emphasis must be with something stronger than the emphasized item, and disobedience is of lesser standing than disbelief, so it is not permissible to emphasize disbelief with disobedience.

The answer is in two respects:

The first: The cause of the abasement, the wrath and the destitution is disbelief and the killing of the prophets; and the cause of disbelief and the killing of the prophets is disobedience. This is because, when they went deep into sins and transgressions, the darkness of sins increased state after state, and the light of faith weakened state after state, and this continued until the light of faith was extinguished and the darkness of disbelief arose. To this the indication is His saying: ﴿Nay, rather, what they used to earn has rusted upon their hearts﴾ [al-Mutaffifin: 14]. So His saying ﴿That is because they disobeyed﴾ points to the cause of the cause. For this reason the masters of conduct (*arbab al-mu'amalat*) said: Whoever is tested with neglecting the courtesies falls into neglecting the sunnas; whoever is tested with neglecting the sunnas falls into neglecting the obligations; whoever is tested with neglecting the obligations falls into belittling the Shari'a; and whoever is tested with that falls into disbelief.

The second: It is possible that by His saying ﴿That is because they used to disbelieve﴾ He means those who came before them, and by His saying ﴿That is because they disobeyed﴾ He means those who were present among them in the time of the Messenger (ﷺ). On this view there is no repetition. So it is as if He, may He be exalted, explained the cause of the punishment of those who came before, and then explained that those who came after, when they followed those who came before, were deserving of a punishment like theirs because of their disobedience and enmity, so that it would become clear to creation that what Allah sent upon both groups of affliction and trial is nothing but a matter of justice and wisdom.

[p. 163]

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿They are not all alike. Among the People of the Book (ahl al-kitab) is an upright community who recite the verses of Allah in the hours of the night while they prostrate.﴾ ﴿They believe in Allah and the Last Day, enjoin what is right, forbid what is wrong, and hasten to good deeds. And those are among the righteous.﴾ ﴿Whatever good they do, it will not be denied them. And Allah is Knowing of the God-conscious.﴾

In the verse there are several issues:

The first issue: Know that regarding His saying, ﴿They are not all alike﴾, there are two opinions.

One of them: His saying, ﴿They are not all alike﴾, is a complete statement, and His saying, ﴿Among the People of the Book is an upright community﴾, is a new statement that explains ﴿They are not all alike﴾, just as His saying, ﴿you enjoin what is right﴾, came as an explanation of His saying, ﴿you are the best community﴾. The meaning is that the People of the Book who have been mentioned are not all alike. This is an affirmation of what came before in His saying, ﴿Among them are believers, but most of them are defiantly disobedient﴾. Then He began, saying, ﴿Among the People of the Book is an upright community﴾. According to this opinion there are two possibilities.

The first: when He said, ﴿Among the People of the Book is an upright community﴾, the complete statement would have been: "And among them is a blameworthy community." However, He omitted mention of the blameworthy community, according to the way of the Arabs, in which mentioning one of two opposites makes mention of the other opposite unnecessary. The verification of this is that two opposites are known together, so mentioning one of them is sufficient to convey knowledge of both, and therefore it is fitting to omit the other opposite.

Abu Dhu'ayb said:

*"The heart called me to her, for I am a man who obeys it, so I do not know whether its pursuit is right guidance."*

He meant (am ghayy), "or error," and so he suffices with mentioning the right guidance (rushd) rather than mentioning error (ghayy). This is the view of al-Farra' and Ibn al-Anbari. Al-Zajjaj said: there is no need to supply the blameworthy community, because mention of the blameworthy community has already occurred before these verses, so there is no need to supply it again. For we have stated that since knowledge of the two opposites is together, mention of one of them suffices instead of mention of the other. This is like when one says: "Zayd and 'Abd Allah are not equal: Zayd is intelligent, pious, and pure," and so it suffices, instead of this, to say: "And 'Abd Allah is not like that." Likewise here, since His saying ﴿They are not all alike﴾ came before, that suffices instead of supplying the omitted part.

The second opinion: His saying ﴿They are not all alike﴾ is an incomplete statement, and it is not permissible to pause at it according to this view. Rather, it is connected to what follows, and the sense is: "They are not all alike: among the People of the Book is an upright community and a blameworthy community." Thus ﴿ummah﴾ (community) is in the nominative case because of laysa (the negative verb "is not"). The phrase "they are not" (laysu) is said according to the usage of those who say, "The fleas bit me" (akaluni al-baraghith). According to this interpretation it is necessary to supply the blameworthy community. This is the choice of Abu 'Ubayda, but most grammarians rejected this view, since there is agreement among most of them that the saying "The fleas bit me" and similar expressions are a weak dialect. And Allah knows best.

The fifth attribute: His saying: ﴿and they enjoin what is right﴾.

The sixth attribute: His saying, ﴿and they enjoin what is right and forbid what is wrong﴾. Know that the supreme goal of perfection is that a person be complete and beyond completeness. A person's being complete lies only in the perfection of his practical and theoretical faculties, which has already been mentioned. We say: promptness is specific to bringing forward what ought to be brought forward, while haste is specific to bringing forward what ought not to be brought forward. Thus, when everything that occurs is of the category of what ought to be, righteousness has been attained, and so righteousness indicates the highest of ranks.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿They are not all alike. Among the People of the Book (ahl al-kitab) is an upright community who recite the verses of Allah in the hours of the night while they prostrate.﴾ ﴿They believe in Allah and the Last Day, enjoin what is right, forbid what is wrong, and hasten to good deeds. And those are among the righteous.﴾ ﴿Whatever good they do, it will not be denied them. And Allah is Knowing of the God-conscious.﴾

In the verse there are several issues:

The first issue: Know that regarding His saying, ﴿They are not all alike﴾, there are two opinions.

One of them: His saying, ﴿They are not all alike﴾, is a complete statement, and His saying, ﴿Among the People of the Book is an upright community﴾, is a new statement that explains ﴿They are not all alike﴾, just as His saying, ﴿you enjoin what is right﴾, came as an explanation of His saying, ﴿you are the best community﴾. The meaning is that the People of the Book who have been mentioned are not all alike. This is an affirmation of what came before in His saying, ﴿Among them are believers, but most of them are defiantly disobedient﴾. Then He began, saying, ﴿Among the People of the Book is an upright community﴾. According to this opinion there are two possibilities.

The first: when He said, ﴿Among the People of the Book is an upright community﴾, the complete statement would have been: "And among them is a blameworthy community." However, He omitted mention of the blameworthy community, according to the way of the Arabs, in which mentioning one of two opposites makes mention of the other opposite unnecessary. The verification of this is that two opposites are known together, so mentioning one of them is sufficient to convey knowledge of both, and therefore it is fitting to omit the other opposite.

Abu Dhu'ayb said:

*"The heart called me to her, for I am a man who obeys it, so I do not know whether its pursuit is right guidance."*

He meant (am ghayy), "or error," and so he suffices with mentioning the right guidance (rushd) rather than mentioning error (ghayy). This is the view of al-Farra' and Ibn al-Anbari. Al-Zajjaj said: there is no need to supply the blameworthy community, because mention of the blameworthy community has already occurred before these verses, so there is no need to supply it again. For we have stated that since knowledge of the two opposites is together, mention of one of them suffices instead of mention of the other. This is like when one says: "Zayd and 'Abd Allah are not equal: Zayd is intelligent, pious, and pure," and so it suffices, instead of this, to say: "And 'Abd Allah is not like that." Likewise here, since His saying ﴿They are not all alike﴾ came before, that suffices instead of supplying the omitted part.

The second opinion: His saying ﴿They are not all alike﴾ is an incomplete statement, and it is not permissible to pause at it according to this view. Rather, it is connected to what follows, and the sense is: "They are not all alike: among the People of the Book is an upright community and a blameworthy community." Thus ﴿ummah﴾ (community) is in the nominative case because of laysa (the negative verb "is not"). The phrase "they are not" (laysu) is said according to the usage of those who say, "The fleas bit me" (akaluni al-baraghith). According to this interpretation it is necessary to supply the blameworthy community. This is the choice of Abu 'Ubayda, but most grammarians rejected this view, since there is agreement among most of them that the saying "The fleas bit me" and similar expressions are a weak dialect. Know that the terms al-ma'ruf (what is right) and al-munkar (what is wrong) are unrestricted, so it is not permitted to specify them without evidence; they therefore encompass every right thing and every wrong thing.

The seventh attribute: His saying, ﴿and they hasten in good works﴾. In this there are two views. The first is that they rush toward them for fear of being overtaken by death; the second is that they perform them without being sluggish. If it is said: Is not haste blameworthy? He (ﷺ) said, peace be upon him: "Haste is from Satan and deliberation is from the Most Merciful." What, then, is the difference between promptness (al-sur'ah) and haste (al-'ajalah)? We say: promptness is specific to bringing forward what ought to be brought forward, while haste is specific to bringing forward what ought not to be brought forward. So hastening (al-musara'ah) is specific to intense desire for what pertains to the religion, because whoever desires a matter prefers doing it immediately rather than delaying. Allah, exalted is He, says: ﴿And hasten to forgiveness from your Lord﴾ [Al 'Imran: 133]. Also, haste is not blameworthy absolutely, as shown by His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And I hastened to You, my Lord, that You might be pleased﴾ [Ta-Ha: 84].

The eighth attribute: His saying, ﴿and they are among the righteous﴾. The meaning is: they, being described by what they have been described with, are among the righteous whose states are sound before Allah, exalted is He, and whom He is pleased with. Know that being described thus is the utmost praise, and this is indicated by both the Qur'an and reason. As for the Qur'an: Allah, exalted is He, praised the greatest of the prophets, peace be upon them, with this description. After mentioning Isma'il, Idris, Dhu al-Kifl and others, He said: ﴿And We admitted them into Our mercy; indeed they were among the righteous﴾ [al-Anbiya': 86]. And He related of Sulayman, peace be upon him, that he said: ﴿And admit me by Your mercy among Your righteous servants﴾ [al-Naml: 19]. And He said: ﴿Indeed, Allah is his Protector, and Jibril and the righteous among the believers﴾ [al-Tahrim: 4]. As for reason: righteousness (al-salah) is the opposite of corruption (al-fasad), and everything that should not be is corruption, whether in beliefs or in actions. Thus, when everything that occurs is of the category of what ought to be, righteousness has been attained, and so righteousness indicates the highest of ranks.

ص ١٦٧

Then, after He, exalted is He, had mentioned these eight attributes, He said: ﴿And whatever good they do, it will not be denied them; and Allah is Knowing of the righteous.﴾ And concerning this there are several issues:

The first issue: Hamzah, al-Kisa'i and Hafs from ʿAsim recited ﴿wa-ma yafʿalū min khayrin fa-lan yukfarūhu﴾ with the yā' (third person, "they do"), because the discourse is connected to what precedes it concerning the believers among the People of the Book, who recite (the Qur'an), prostrate, believe, enjoin good, forbid evil, and hasten to good deeds, and their deeds will not go unrewarded. The intended meaning is that when the ignorant Jews said to ʿAbdullah ibn Salam, "You have lost by this faith," He, exalted is He, said: "Rather, they have attained the highest ranks." The purpose was to exalt them so that the effect of the words of those ignorant people might be removed from his heart. Then, although this is, in terms of the wording, returning to everything previously mentioned of the believers among the People of the Book, all of creation enters into it by way of the underlying reason (ʿillah).

As for the rest, they recited with the tā' (second person, "you do"), in the manner of direct address. So it is the beginning of an address to all the believers, meaning that the deeds of the believers among the People of the Book were mentioned, then He said: "And whatever good you do, O assembly of believers, those among you who are of their kind, it will not be denied you." The benefit is that the ruling of this verse is general in wording with respect to all who are responsible (mukallafun). What confirms this is that similar verses came addressing all creatures without restriction to one people over another, such as His saying: ﴿And whatever good you do, Allah knows it﴾ [al-Baqarah: 197], ﴿And whatever you spend of good, it will be repaid to you﴾ [al-Baqarah: 272], ﴿And whatever good you send forth for yourselves, you will find it with Allah﴾ [al-Baqarah: 110]. As for Abu ʿAmr, it is reported from him that he would recite this verse in both readings.

The second issue: ﴿fa-lan yukfarūhu﴾ means: you will not be deprived of its reward and its recompense. The denial of recompense is called kufr (ingratitude/denial) for two reasons. The first: He, exalted is He, named the granting of reward "gratitude (shukr)," as He said: ﴿Indeed, Allah is Appreciative (shākir), Knowing﴾ [al-Baqarah: 158], and He said: ﴿And those, their effort is appreciated (mashkūr)﴾ [al-Isra': 19]. Since He named the granting of recompense "gratitude," He named withholding it "ingratitude." The second: kufr in the language means covering, so the withholding of recompense was called kufr because it is in the position of denial and concealment.

If it is said: Why did He say ﴿fa-lan yukfarūhu﴾ and make it transitive to two objects, when shakara and kafara are only transitive to one object? One says shakara al-niʿmah and kafarahā.

We say: Because we have explained that the meaning of kufr here is withholding and deprivation, so it is as if He said: "you will not be deprived of it, and you will not be prevented from its recompense."

* * *

The third issue: Those who argue for the balancing (muwāzanah) among those who hold the doctrine of nullification (iḥbāṭ) cite this verse, saying: The plain meaning of this verse indicates that the effect of the servant's deed must reach him. So if it is nullified, and nothing of the nullified deed's measure remains, the implication of this verse would be void. A parallel to this verse is His saying: ﴿So whoever does an atom's weight of good will see it﴾ ﴿and whoever does an atom's weight of evil will see it﴾ [al-Zalzalah: 7–8].

Then He said: ﴿and Allah is Knowing of the righteous.﴾ The meaning is that when He, exalted is He, informed of the non-deprivation and the recompense, He established what serves as evidence for it: that the non-granting of reward and recompense is either due to forgetfulness and oblivion, which is impossible with respect to Him, since He is Knowing of all knowable things; or due to incapacity, stinginess and need, which is impossible since He is the God of all created things. So the name Allah indicates the absence of incapacity, stinginess and need, and His saying "Knowing" indicates the absence of ignorance. When these attributes are negated, withholding recompense becomes impossible, since withholding what is due must be for one of these reasons. And Allah knows best.

He said "Knowing of the righteous" although He knows everything, as a glad tiding to the righteous of abundant reward, and as an indication that none attains success with Him except the people of taqwa.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 3, verse 116:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Indeed, those who disbelieve, neither their wealth nor their children will avail them anything against Allah. And those are the companions of the Fire; they will abide therein forever.﴾

Know that He, exalted is He, mentioned in these verses at one time the states of the disbelievers regarding the manner of punishment, and at another time the states of the believers regarding reward, combining warning and encouragement, promise and threat. So when He described those among the disbelievers who believed with the good attributes that preceded, He followed it with the threat against the disbelievers, saying: ﴿Indeed, those who disbelieve, neither their wealth nor their children will avail them anything﴾. And in the verse there are issues:

The first issue: regarding His saying ﴿Indeed, those who disbelieve﴾ there are two opinions. The first: what is meant is some of the disbelievers. Those who hold this view have mentioned several aspects. One of them: Ibn 'Abbas said: it refers to Qurayzah and al-Nadir, because the aim of the Jewish leaders in opposing the Messenger was nothing but wealth, and the evidence for this is the saying of Allah, exalted, in Surat al-Baqarah: ﴿And do not exchange My verses for a small price﴾ [al-Baqarah: 41]. Second: it was revealed concerning the polytheists of Quraysh, for Abu Jahl was much given to boasting of his wealth, and for this reason His saying was revealed concerning him: ﴿And how many generations We destroyed before them, who were better in goods and appearance﴾ [Maryam: 74], and His saying: ﴿Then let him call his assembly. We will call the guards of Hell﴾ [al-'Alaq: 17, 18]. Third: it was revealed concerning Abu Sufyan, for he spent much wealth on the polytheists on the day of Badr and Uhud in hostility toward the Prophet (ﷺ).

The second opinion: the verse is general concerning all the disbelievers, because they all used to take pride in abundance of wealth, and they used to reproach the Messenger (ﷺ) and his followers for poverty. Among their doubts was their saying: "If Muhammad were upon the truth, his Lord would not have left him in this poverty and hardship." Also, the wording is general, and there is no evidence requiring specification, so it is obligatory to keep it on its generality. As for the first group, they may say: He, exalted, said after this verse ﴿The likeness of what they spend﴾, so the pronoun in His saying "yunfiquna" (they spend) refers to this place, which is His saying ﴿Indeed, those who disbelieve﴾. Then His saying "yunfiquna" is specified to some of the disbelievers, so this too must be specified.

The second issue: Allah specifically mentioned wealth and children because the most beneficial of inanimate things is wealth, and the most beneficial of living things is the child. Then Allah, exalted, made clear that the disbeliever derives no benefit from either of them whatsoever in the Hereafter, and this indicates that he derives no benefit from all other things a fortiori. A parallel to this is His saying: ﴿The day when neither wealth nor children will benefit, except one who comes to Allah with a sound heart﴾ [al-Shu'ara': 88, 89], and His saying: ﴿And fear a day when no soul will avail another at all﴾ [al-Baqarah: 48], and His saying: ﴿So never will be accepted from one of them the earth full of gold even if he should ransom himself with it﴾ [Al 'Imran: 91], and His saying: ﴿And it is not your wealth or your children that bring you near to Us in position﴾ [Saba': 37]. When He, exalted, made clear that they derive no benefit from their wealth or their children, He said: ﴿And those are the companions of the Fire; they will abide therein forever.﴾

Our companions (the Ash'aris) have used this verse as evidence that the sinful people of the prayer (fussaq ahl al-salat) will not remain in the Fire forever. They said: His saying ﴿And those are the companions of the Fire﴾ is a phrase that conveys restriction (hasr), for it is said: "Those are the companions of Zayd, and no others," and they are the ones who benefit from him and no others. Since this phrase conveys the meaning of restriction, it is established that eternal abiding in the Fire belongs only to the disbeliever.

He, exalted is He, said: when He explained that the wealth of the disbelievers does not avail them anything, it might occur to someone that they sometimes spend their wealth on good works, and so one might think they benefit from it. God, exalted is He, dispelled this doubt with this verse, and made clear that they gain nothing from those expenditures, even though they intended thereby the Face of God.

In the verse there are several issues.

**First issue:** *al-mathal* (the likeness, parable) is a resemblance that becomes like a known term through its frequent use for what it is compared to. The essential meaning is that their disbelief nullifies the reward of their spending, just as a cold wind destroys crops.

If it is said: on this reading, the likeness of their spending is the crop that was destroyed, so how is their spending compared to a destructive cold wind?

We reply: a likeness is of two kinds. In one, the resemblance occurs between the principal matters of the two clauses, even if no resemblance occurs between the parts of the two clauses. This is what is called *al-tashbih al-murakkab* (the composite comparison). In the other, the resemblance occurs between the principal matters of the two clauses and between the parts of each of them. If we take this likeness as belonging to the first kind, the question is dissolved. If we take it as belonging to the second kind, there are several possibilities. The first: the sense is, "The likeness of disbelief in destroying what they spend is like the likeness of a wind that destroys the crop." The second: "The likeness of what they spend is like the destroyed object of the wind, which is the crop." The third: perhaps the reference in His words, *"the likeness of what they spend,"* is to what they spent in harming the Messenger of God (ﷺ) by assembling armies against him, and this expenditure was destructive for all the acts of goodness and piety they had performed. In that case the comparison is correct without any need for supposing an ellipsis or transposition. The sense is: "The likeness of what they spend, in its being nullifying of the acts of piety they performed before that, is like the likeness of a wind containing *ṣirr* (bitter cold), in its being destructive of the crop." This possibility occurred to me when I was writing on this passage, for their spending in harming the Messenger (ﷺ) is among the greatest kinds of disbelief and among the most effective in cancelling the effects of works of piety.

**Second issue:** They differed about the interpretation of this spending, on two views. The first: the intended meaning of "spending" here is all their deeds through which they hope to benefit in the Hereafter. God called it "spending," just as He called it "sale and purchase" in His words: *"Indeed, God has purchased from the believers their selves..."* (9:111) up to *"so rejoice in your transaction which you have made"* (9:111).
