Among what proves the soundness of this interpretation is His words: *"You will not attain righteousness until you spend from what you love"* (3:92), where what is meant is all acts of goodness; and His words: *"And do not consume your wealth among yourselves in falsehood"* (2:188), where what is meant is all kinds of benefit.

The second view, which is the more likely, is that what is meant is the spending of wealth. The evidence for this is what precedes this verse, namely His words: *"Neither their wealth nor their children will avail them at all"* (3:116).

**Third issue:** As for His words, *"the likeness of what they spend,"* what is meant by it is either all the disbelievers or some of them. There are two views. The first: the report concerns all the disbelievers. This is because their spending is either for the benefits of this world or for the benefits of the Hereafter. If it is for the benefits of this world, no trace of it at all remains in the Hereafter, with regard to a Muslim, let alone a disbeliever. If it is for the benefits of the Hereafter, they do not benefit from it in the Hereafter, because disbelief prevents benefit from it. Thus it is established that none of the expenditures of the disbelievers has any benefit in the Hereafter. Perhaps they spent their wealth on good works, such as building hostels and bridges, and kindness to the weak, orphans and widows, and that spender hoped for much good from that expenditure. Then when he arrives in the Hereafter, he sees that his disbelief has nullified the effects of the good works. He is like one who planted a crop and expected from it much benefit, but a wind struck it and burned it, so that nothing remains with him except grief and sorrow. This is the case if they spent wealth on the paths of good works. But if they spent it on what they supposed to be good works, while it was in fact of the sins, such as spending wealth in harming the Messenger (ﷺ), in killing Muslims and ruining their homes, then what we have said about it is more fitting and more forceful. A parallel to this verse is His words: *"And We will regard what they did of deeds and make it scattered dust"* (25:23). And He said: *"Indeed, those who disbelieve spend their wealth to avert [people] from the way of God. They will spend it; then it will be for them a source of regret"* (8:36). And His words: *"And those who disbelieve, their deeds are like a mirage in a desert"* (24:39). All of this indicates that the good deeds of disbelievers do not result in reward. All of this is gathered in His words: *"Indeed, God accepts only from the righteous"* (5:27). And this view is the stronger and more correct.

Know that we have explained the verse as referring to the failure of these disbelievers in the Hereafter, but it is not far-fetched to explain it as referring to their failure in this world. For they spent large amounts of wealth in assembling armies and endured hardships, then the matter turned against them. God made Islam manifest and strengthened it, and nothing remained for the disbelievers from that expenditure except disappointment and regret.

The second view: what is meant is the report concerning some of the disbelievers. On this view, there are several possibilities in the verse. The first: the hypocrites used to spend their wealth in God's way, but out of dissimulation (*taqiyyah*) and fear of the Muslims, and as a form of conciliation toward them. So the verse is about them. The second: this verse was revealed concerning Abu Sufyan and his companions on the day of Badr, when they gathered against the Messenger, peace be upon him. The third: it was revealed concerning the spending of the base Jews upon their rabbis in order to distort [the scripture]. The fourth: what is meant is what they spend while thinking that it brings them nearer to God, even though it is not so.

**Fourth issue:** They differed about *al-ṣirr* (the bitter cold) on several points. The first: most exegetes and lexicographers said *al-ṣirr* is severe cold. This is the view of Ibn ʿAbbas, Qatadah, al-Suddi and Ibn Zayd. The second: *al-ṣirr* is scorching hot winds and fire that boils. This is the choice of Abu Bakr al-Asamm and Abu Bakr ibn al-Anbari. Ibn al-Anbari said: fire is described as *ṣirr* only because of its sound when it blazes, as in the creaking (*ṣarīr*) of a door. The *ṣarṣar* (violent wind) is well known, and *al-ṣarrah* is a cry. From this is His words: *"Then his wife came forward with a cry"* (51:29). Ibn al-Anbari also transmitted with his chain of narration from Ibn ʿAbbas, may God be pleased with them both, regarding *"in which is ṣirr"* that he said: "In it is fire." On both views, the purpose of the comparison is achieved, because whether it is destructive cold or burning heat, it renders the crop and the sown field nullified, so the comparison with it is correct.

**Fifth issue:** The Muʿtazilah (the Rationalist theological school) argued from this verse for the soundness of the doctrine of *al-iḥbāṭ* (the nullification of good deeds by subsequent sin). Their argument is that just as this wind destroys the crop, so disbelief destroys the spending. This is valid only if we say that, were it not for disbelief, that spending would necessitate benefits in the Hereafter, and then the doctrine of nullification would be sound. Our scholars replied that a deed does not necessitate reward except by virtue of a promise, and God's promise is conditional on the attainment of faith. When disbelief occurs, the conditioned thing is lost because its condition is lost, since disbelief removed it after it had been established. The proofs of the falsity of the doctrine of nullification have already been mentioned in the commentary on Surat al-Baqarah.

\* \* \*

Then He, exalted is He, said: *"it struck the crop of a people who had wronged themselves."* Here there is a question: why did He not limit Himself to saying, *"it struck the crop of a people,"* and what is the benefit of His words, *"who had wronged themselves"*?

We reply: concerning the explanation of His words, *"who had wronged themselves,"* there are two views. The first: they disobeyed God, and so they deserved the destruction of their crop as a punishment for them. The benefit of mentioning it is that the aim is to liken what they spend to something that perishes entirely, so that nothing remains of it. The crop of the disbelieving wrongdoers is what perishes entirely, and no benefit comes from it either in this world or in the Hereafter. As for the crop of a believing Muslim, it does not perish entirely, for although it perishes in appearance, it does not perish in meaning, because God, exalted is He, increases his reward on account of those griefs reaching him. The second: what is meant by His words, *"who had wronged themselves,"* is that they sowed in a place other than the place of sowing, or at a time other than its time, for wronging (*ẓulm*) is placing a thing in other than its proper place. On this interpretation the aspect of the comparison is strengthened, for whoever sows not in its place and not at its time is lost, and then if the cold wind strikes it, it is all the more likely to become lost. Likewise here: when the disbelievers brought their spending not in its place and not at its time, and then the ill omen of their disbelief struck it, it was impossible that it should not become lost. And God knows best.

\* \* \*

Then He, exalted is He, said: *"And God did not wrong them, but they were wronging themselves."* The meaning is that God, exalted is He, did not wrong them in not accepting their expenditures, but they wronged themselves in bringing them accompanied by the impediments that prevent them from being accepted by God, exalted is He. The author of *al-Kashshaf* (the commentary of al-Zamakhshari) said: it has been read as *wa-lākinna* with a shadda (doubling of the nun), in the sense of "but indeed they wronged themselves," and it is not permissible to read it as *wa-lākinnahu* ("but indeed it [is that] they wrong themselves") with the omission of the pronoun of the matter (*ḍamīr al-shaʾn*), because that is not permitted except in poetry.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 3, verse 118:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿O you who believe, do not take as intimate friends (biṭāna) others than your own; they will spare no effort to ruin you; they love that you suffer hardship. Hatred has already appeared from their mouths, and what their breasts conceal is greater. We have indeed made the signs clear to you, if you use your reason.﴾

Know that when Exalted is He had explained the conditions of the believers and the disbelievers, He began in this verse to warn the believers against associating closely with the disbelievers. Here there are several issues:

The first issue: They differ over who the people from whom God forbade the believers to take intimacy are. There are several views. The first: they are the Jews, because the Muslims used to consult them in their affairs and be familiar with them, due to the foster-relations and alliances between them, thinking that although they differed in religion, they would advise them in matters of livelihood. So God, exalted is He, forbade this by this verse. The argument of the proponents of this view is that these verses, from beginning to end, are addressed to the Jews, so this verse too is likewise. The second: they are the hypocrites, because the believers used to be deceived by the outward statements of the hypocrites and think they were truthful, so they would disclose secrets to them and inform them of hidden matters. God, exalted is He, forbade them from that. The argument of the proponents of this view is that what follows this verse indicates it, namely His saying: ﴿When they meet you they say, "We believe"; but when they are alone they bite the tips of their fingers at you in rage﴾ [Al 'Imran: 119]. It is known that this does not befit the Jews but is the attribute of the hypocrites. A parallel is His saying in Surat al-Baqarah: ﴿When they meet those who believe they say, "We believe"; but when they are alone with their devils they say, "We are truly with you; we were only mocking"﴾ [al-Baqarah: 14]. The third: what is meant is all kinds of disbelievers, and the evidence for this is His saying: ﴿biṭāna min dūnikum﴾, so He prohibited the believers from taking an intimate friend from among non-believers, and this is a prohibition against all disbelievers. He also said: ﴿O you who believe, do not take My enemy and your enemy as allies﴾ [al-Mumtahanah: 1]. What further confirms this is what is related: it was said to 'Umar ibn al-Khattab, may Allah be pleased with him: "There is a man from the people of al-Hirah, a Christian, whose memory and handwriting are unmatched, so if you see fit, take him as a scribe." 'Umar refused and said: "If so, I would have taken an intimate friend from among non-believers." So 'Umar, may Allah be pleased with him, made this verse a proof for the prohibition against taking an intimate friend. As for what they cite, that what follows the verse is specific to the hypocrites, this does not prevent the generality of the beginning of the verse, for it is established in the principles of jurisprudence that when the beginning of a verse is general and its end is specific, the specificity of the end does not prevent the generality of its beginning.

The second issue: Abu Hatim related from al-Asma'i: "Fulan became intimate with Fulan (baṭana bihi), yabṭinu bihi, buṭūnan and biṭānatan, when he was special to him and entered into his affair." So biṭānah is a verbal noun used for both the singular and the plural. The biṭānah of a man is his inner circle, those who are privy to his affairs, and its origin is from the belly (baṭn), the opposite of the back (ẓahr); from it comes biṭānat al-thawb, the lining of a garment, the opposite of its outer face. The summary is that the one whom a person singles out for special closeness is called a biṭānah, because he is like what is adjacent to the belly in extreme nearness to it.

The third issue: His saying: ﴿lā tattakhidhū biṭānatan﴾ is an indefinite noun in a negative context, which conveys generality.

* * *

As for His saying: ﴿min dūnikum﴾, there are issues:

The first issue: min dūnikum means: other than the Muslims, and from outside the people of your religion. The expression ﴿min dūnikum﴾ may reasonably be taken in this sense, as a man says: "You have done good to us and bestowed favours upon us," meaning: "You have done good to our brothers." And He said: ﴿and they kill the prophets without right﴾ [Al 'Imran: 21], meaning: their forefathers did that.

The second issue: In His saying ﴿min dūnikum﴾ there are two possibilities. One is that it is connected to His saying ﴿lā tattakhidhū﴾, meaning: do not take, from other than you, an intimate friend. The second is that it is made a qualifier of biṭānah, and the sense is: an intimate friend who is from other than you.

If it is said: What is the difference between His saying "Do not take from other than you an intimate friend" and His saying "Do not take an intimate friend from other than you"?

We say: Sibawayh said that they put first what is most important and what they are most concerned with. Here the intended object is not the taking of an intimate friend as such; rather the intention is that one should take from them an intimate friend. So the saying "do not take from other than you an intimate friend" is stronger in conveying the intended meaning.

The third issue: It is said that (min) is superfluous. It is also said that it is addressed to the prophets: "Do not take an intimate friend from other than the people of your religion." If it is said: this verse requires the prohibition of associating with disbelievers absolutely, yet He said: ﴿God does not forbid you from those who do not fight you over religion and do not expel you from your homes, from being kind to them﴾ [al-Mumtahanah: 8], and ﴿God forbids you only from those who fight you﴾ [al-Mumtahanah: 9]. How then is the combining of these? We say: there is no doubt that the specific takes precedence over the general.

* * *

Know that when Exalted is He had forbidden the believers from taking an intimate friend from among the disbelievers, He mentioned the cause of this prohibition, which consists of several matters. The first of them is His saying: ﴿they will spare no effort to ruin you﴾. Here there are issues:

The first issue: The author of al-Kashshaf said: it is said (alā) in a matter, yaʾlū, when one falls short in it; then it is used transitively to two objects in the expressions "lā ālūka nuṣḥan" and "lā ālūka jahdan," by way of implication (taḍmīn), and the meaning is: I do not withhold from you sincere advice nor do I diminish my effort for you.

The second issue: khabāl is corruption and deficiency. They cited the verse:

"You are not a hand except a hand forever, / with a crippled arm (makhbūlat al-ʿaḍud)"

That is: corrupted of arm, its strength diminished. From this comes the saying: a man is makhbūl, mukhbal and mukhtabal, for one whose intellect is deficient. And He said: ﴿Had they gone forth among you, they would have increased you only in khabāl﴾ [al-Tawbah: 47], meaning corruption and harm.

The third issue: His saying ﴿lā yaʾlūnakum khabālan﴾ means: they do not leave off their utmost effort in harming you and corrupting you. It is said: "mā ālaytuhu nuṣḥan," meaning: I did not fall short in advising him, and "mā ālaytuhu sharran mithlahu," meaning: I did not fall short in doing him evil of the same kind.

The fourth issue: khabāl is in the accusative because it is governed by lā yaʾlūnakum, since it transitively takes two objects as we have mentioned. If you wish, you may put it in the accusative as a verbal noun, since the meaning of His saying ﴿lā yaʾlūnakum khabālan﴾ is: they do not cause you corruption as corruption. The second of them is His saying: ﴿they love that you suffer hardship (mā ʿanitum)﴾. Here there are issues:

(Page 174)

The first issue: It is said: wadadtu kadhā, meaning I loved it. And al-ʿanat is severity of harm and hardship. He said: ﴿Had God willed, He would have made you suffer hardship﴾ [al-Baqarah: 220].

The second issue: mā is verbal (maṣdariyyah), as in His saying: ﴿That is because you used to exult in the land without right and because you used to be insolent﴾ [Ghafir: 75], meaning: for your exulting and your insolence; and as in His saying: ﴿By the sky and He who built it, by the earth and He who spread it﴾ [al-Shams: 5–6], meaning: by His building it and His spreading it.

The third issue: The sense of the verse is: they wish that they would harm you in your religion and your worldly life with the utmost harm.

The fourth issue: al-Wahidi, may Allah have mercy on him, said: there is no place in grammatical terms for His saying ﴿wadadu mā ʿanitum﴾, because it is a resumed independent clause. It is also said that it is a qualifier of biṭānah, but this is not correct, because biṭānah has already been qualified by His saying ﴿lā yaʾlūnakum khabālan﴾; so if this were also a qualifier, a conjunction would have to be inserted between them.

The fifth issue: The difference in meaning between His saying ﴿lā yaʾlūnakum khabālan﴾ and His saying ﴿wadadu mā ʿanitum﴾ lies in several respects. The first: they do not fall short in corrupting your religion; if they are unable to do so, they wish to cast you into the worst kinds of harm. The second: they do not fall short in corrupting your worldly affairs; if they are unable to do so, the love of causing you hardship does not leave their hearts. The third: they do not fall short in corrupting your affairs; if they fail to do so because of some external obstacle, the love of that does not leave their hearts.

* * *

The third of them is His saying: ﴿Hatred has already appeared from their mouths﴾. Here there are issues:

The first issue: al-baghḍāʾ is the most intense hatred, so bughḍ together with baghḍāʾ is like ḍurr together with ḍarrāʾ.

The second issue: al-afwāh is the plural of al-fam (mouth), and fam originally is fawh, as evidenced by its plural being afwāh. It is said: fawh and afwāh, like sawt and aswāt, and ṭawq and aṭwāq. It is said: rajul mufawwah if he speaks eloquently, and afwah if he is of wide understanding. Thus it is established that the origin of fam is fawh on the pattern of sawt; then the h was dropped for lightness, and then the mīm was put in place of the wāw, because both are labial letters.

The third issue: His saying ﴿Hatred has already appeared from their mouths﴾: if we take it to refer to the hypocrites, then there are two explanations regarding it. The first: that a hypocrite must in his speech let slip what indicates his hypocrisy and his departure from the path of sincerity in love and counsel. A parallel is His saying: ﴿and you will surely recognise them by the tone of their speech﴾ [Muhammad: 30]. The second: Qatadah said: "Hatred has appeared to their allies among the hypocrites and disbelievers, because some of them became aware of it." As for if we take it to refer to the Jews, the explanation of His saying ﴿Hatred has already appeared from their mouths﴾ is that they openly display the denial of your Prophet and your Book and attribute ignorance and folly to you; and whoever believes that another persists in ignorance and folly is unable to love him, rather he must hate him. This is what is meant by His saying: ﴿Hatred has already appeared from their mouths﴾.

* * *

Then He, exalted is He, said: ﴿and what their breasts conceal is greater﴾, meaning: what appears on the tongue of the hypocrite of the signs of hatred is less than what is in his heart of aversion, and what appears on his tongue of the signs of rancour is less than what is in his heart of rancour. Then Exalted is He explained that the disclosure of these secrets to the believers is one of His blessings upon them, so He said: ﴿We have indeed made the signs clear to you, if you use your reason﴾, meaning: if you are among the people of intellect, understanding and discernment. It is also said: ﴿if you use your reason﴾ means: distinguishing between what the enemy deserves and what the friend deserves. The purpose is to urge them to employ their reason in contemplating this verse and reflecting upon these clear signs. And God knows best.

The commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 3, verse 119:

The words of the Most High: ﴿Here you are, loving them, yet they do not love you, though you believe in the whole Book. When they meet you they say, "We believe," but when they are alone they bite their fingertips at you out of rage. Say: "Die in your rage. Indeed, God knows what is in the breasts."﴾

Know that this is another kind of warning to the believers against associating closely with the hypocrites (munafiqun). On this there are several issues:

The first issue: Al-Sayyid al-Sarakhsi (may God preserve him) said: (ها) (ha) is for calling attention, (أنتم) (antum) is a subject (mubtada'), and ﴿أولاء﴾ (ula') is its predicate (khabar). ﴿تحبونهم﴾ (tuhibbunahum) is in the accusative position as a circumstantial clause (hal) from the demonstrative noun. It is also permissible for ﴿أولاء﴾ to mean "those who" (alladhina), with ﴿تحبونهم﴾ as its relative clause (sila), so that the relative pronoun with its clause is the predicate of (أنتم). Al-Farra' said: ﴿أولاء﴾ is the predicate, and ﴿تحبونهم﴾ is a predicate following a predicate.

The second issue: God Most High mentioned in this verse three things, each of which shows that the believer may not take a non-believer as an intimate confidant (bitana) for himself. The first is His saying: ﴿you love them, yet they do not love you﴾, and on this there are several explanations.

One: Al-Mufaddal said: ﴿you love them﴾ means you want Islam for them, which is the best of things; ﴿yet they do not love you﴾ because they want you to remain in disbelief, and there is no doubt that this brings ruin.

Two: ﴿you love them﴾ because of the bond of fosterage and marriage between you and them; ﴿yet they do not love you﴾ because of your being Muslims.

Three: ﴿you love them﴾ because they have shown you faith; ﴿yet they do not love you﴾ because disbelief is firmly settled in their inner selves.

Four: Abu Bakr al-Asamm said: ﴿you love them﴾ means that you do not want to cast them into calamities and trials; ﴿yet they do not love you﴾ means that they want to cast you into calamities and trials, and they lie in wait for you for misfortunes.

Five: ﴿you love them﴾ because they show you love for the Messenger, and the lover of one who is loved is himself loved; ﴿yet they do not love you﴾ because they know that you love the Messenger while they hate the Messenger, and the lover of one who is hated is himself hated.

Six: ﴿you love them﴾ means you mix with them and disclose to them your secrets concerning the affairs of your religion; ﴿yet they do not love you﴾ means they do not do the same toward you.

Know that these aspects that we have mentioned point to the causes that make the believers love them and make them hate the believers. All of them fall under the verse. When God Most High made known to them that they hate the believers, and made known to them that they are in the wrong in that hatred, this became a motive, both by nature and by the sacred law, for the believers to come to hate these hypocrites.

* * *

The second cause for this is His saying: ﴿yet you believe in the whole Book﴾, and on this there are several issues:

The first issue: There is an ellipsis in the verse, and the implied meaning is: "and you believe in the whole Book, while they do not believe in it." The omission is good because we have explained that opposites are known together, so mentioning one of them suffices in place of mentioning the other.

The second issue: He mentioned (al-Kitab) (the Book) in the singular for several reasons. One: he used it in the sense of a genus, as in the saying: "the dirham has become abundant in people's hands." Two: a verbal noun (masdar) is not pluralized except by interpretation, which is why he did not say al-Kutub (the Books) in place of al-Kitab, though if he had said it, it would have been permissible as a broadening of usage.

The third issue: The meaning of the sentence is: "you believe in all their books, and yet they hate you. So what is the matter with you that you love them, when they do not believe in any part of your Book?" This contains severe rebuke, namely that they are more firmly set in their falsehood than you are in your truth. A parallel to this is His saying: ﴿They suffer as you suffer, but you hope from God for what they do not hope for﴾ [al-Nisa: 104].

* * *

The third cause of the ugliness of this association is His saying: ﴿When they meet you they say, "We believe," but when they are alone they bite their fingertips at you out of rage.﴾ The meaning is that when some of them are alone with others, they display intense enmity and intense rage against the believers, to the point that this intensity reaches the biting of fingertips, just as one of us does when his anger is intense and his grief is great over the loss of what he desires. Since this action was frequently performed by the angry, it became a metonymy (kinaya) for anger, so that it is said of an angry man, "he bites his hand in rage," even if no biting actually occurs. The exegetes said: this intense rage arose in them only because of what they saw of the believers' unity, the gathering of their word, and the harmony of their mutual relations.

* * *

Then He Most High said: ﴿Say: "Die in your rage."﴾ This is a supplication against them, that their rage should increase until they perish from it. What is meant by the increase of rage is the increase of what causes them that rage, namely the strength of Islam, the might of its people, and the humiliation and disgrace that they suffer because of it.

If it is said: the words ﴿Say: "Die in your rage"﴾ are a command to them to persist in rage, and that rage is disbelief, so this would be a command to persist in disbelief, which is not permissible.

We say: We have already explained that it is a supplication for the increase of what causes this rage, which is the strength of Islam, so the objection falls away.

Also, it is a supplication against them for death before they attain what they wish for.

* * *

Then He said: ﴿Indeed, God knows what is in the breasts.﴾ On this there are several issues:

The first issue: (ذات) (dhat) is a word established to denote the feminine, just as (ذو) (dhu) is a word established to denote the masculine. What is meant by "what is in the breasts" is the thoughts that arise in the heart, and the motives and deterrents present in it. Because they inhere in the heart and are attributed to it, they are called "what is in the breasts." The meaning is that God Most High knows everything that occurs in your hearts of thoughts, impulses, and deterrents.

The second issue: The author of al-Kashshaf (al-Zamakhshari) said: this verse may or may not be included within the content of what is spoken. As for the first possibility: the implied meaning is: "Inform them of what they conceal of their biting of fingertips in rage when they are alone, and say to them: Indeed God knows what is more hidden than what you conceal among yourselves, namely the things hidden in the breasts, so do not suppose that any of your secrets is hidden from Him." As for the second possibility, that it is not part of the speech, its meaning is: "Say this to them, O Muhammad, and do not be surprised at My informing you of what they conceal, for I know what is more hidden than that, namely what they have hidden in their breasts and not revealed with their tongues." It is also possible that it is not so. Then, as for His saying: ﴿Say: "Die in your rage"﴾, it is a command to the Messenger (ﷺ) to have good cheer, strong hope, and to rejoice in God's promise to him that they will perish in rage at the honoring of Islam and their humiliation by it. It is as if it were said: "Speak to yourself about this." And God knows best.

[Page 176]

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 3, verse 120:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿If good touches you, it distresses them; but if an evil befalls you, they rejoice at it. But if you are steadfast and mindful of God, their scheming will not harm you in the least. Indeed, God encompasses what they do.﴾

Know that this verse is part of the completion of the description of the hypocrites. God, exalted is He, explains that, together with the blameworthy qualities and ugly deeds they possess, they await the arrival of some kind of trial and affliction upon the believers. In the verse there are several issues:

The first issue: the root of mass (al-mass, "touching") is with the hand, and then everything that reaches a thing is called "touching" (māssan) by way of metaphor. So it is said: "Fulan was touched by fatigue and weariness." God, exalted is He, said: ﴿And no weariness touched Us﴾ [Qaf: 38], and He said: ﴿And when harm touches you at sea﴾ [al-Isra: 67]. The author of al-Kashshaf said: mass here means iṣābah (reaching, befalling). God, exalted is He, said: ﴿If good befalls you, it distresses them; but if a calamity befalls you﴾ [al-Tawbah: 50], and His saying: ﴿Whatever good befalls you is from God, and whatever evil befalls you is from yourself﴾ [al-Nisa: 79]. And He said: ﴿When evil touches him, he is distressed; and when good touches him, he withholds﴾ [al-Ma'arij: 20–21].

The second issue: what is meant by good (ḥasanah) here is the benefit of this world in its various states. Among them are bodily health, abundance, gaining booty, victory over enemies, and the arising of love and affection among loved ones. What is meant by evil (sayyi'ah) is their opposites: sickness, poverty, defeat and fleeing from the enemy, the separation of relatives, killing, plunder, and raids. So God, exalted is He, explains that they grieve and are distressed when some kind of good comes to the Muslims, and they rejoice when some kind of evil befalls them.

The third issue: it is said sā'a al-shay'u yasū'u fahuwa sayyi', and the feminine is sayyi'ah, meaning it became ugly. From this is His saying: ﴿Evil is what they do﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 66]. And al-sawʾā is the opposite of al-ḥusnā.

* * *

Then He said: ﴿But if you are steadfast﴾, meaning in obedience to God and in the hardship and grief that befalls you therein, and (are mindful of God) regarding everything He has forbidden you, and rely upon God in your affairs. ﴿Their scheming will not harm you in the least.﴾ There are issues concerning this:

The first issue: Ibn Kathir, Nafi' and Abu 'Amr recited (lā yiḍrkum) with a fatḥah on the yā', a kasrah on the ḍād and a sukūn on the rā', from ḍārahu yaḍīruhu, and ḍāra yaḍūruhu ḍawran, meaning he harmed him. The rest recited ﴿lā yaḍurrukum﴾ with a ḍammah on the ḍād and a shaddah on the rā', from al-ḍurr (harm). Its original form is yaḍrurukum in the jussive; the rā' was assimilated into the rā', the ḍammah of the first rā' was transferred to the ḍād, and the final rā' was given a ḍammah to conform to the nearest vowel, which is the ḍammah of the ḍād. Some have said that it is by inversion of order, its sense being: "Their scheming will not harm you in the least if you are steadfast and mindful of God." The author of al-Kashshaf said: al-Mufaḍḍal narrated from 'Asim (lā yaḍarrakum) with a fatḥah on the rā'.

The second issue: al-kayd is that a person devises a plan to bring another into something disliked. Ibn 'Abbas interpreted al-kayd here as enmity.

[Page 178]

The third issue: (shay'an) is in the accusative as a verbal noun (maṣdar), meaning "any harm whatsoever."

The fourth issue: the meaning of the verse is that whoever endures in performing God's commands and is mindful of all that God has forbidden, is under God's protection, so the scheming of the disbelievers and the stratagems of the schemers will not harm him.

The reality of this matter is that He, glorified is He, created creation only for worship, as He said: ﴿I did not create the jinn and humankind except that they should worship Me﴾ [al-Dhariyat: 56]. Whoever fulfils the covenant of worship in this, God, glorified is He, is too generous to fail to fulfil the covenant of lordship by protecting him from calamities and fears. To this points His saying: ﴿Whoever is mindful of God, He will make for him a way out, and provide for him from where he does not expect﴾ [al-Talaq: 2–3], indicating that He brings to him everything that gladdens him. Some of the wise have said: If you wish to vex the one who envies you, strive to acquire virtues.

* * *

Then God, exalted is He, said: ﴿Indeed, God encompasses what they do.﴾ There are issues concerning this:

The first issue: it was recited (bimā ya'malūn) with the yā', in the third person, meaning: He knows what they do in opposing you, so He will punish them for it. Whoever recites with the tā', in the second person, the meaning is: He knows and encompasses what you do of patience and piety, so He will deal with you as you deserve.

The second issue: applying the word muḥīṭ (encompassing) to God is a metaphor, because the one who encompasses a thing is one who surrounds it on all sides, and that is a property of bodies. But since He, exalted is He, knows all things and is capable of all possibilities, it is permissible in the figurative usage of the language to say that He encompasses them. From this is His saying: ﴿And God encompasses them from behind﴾ [al-Buruj: 20], and He said: ﴿And God encompasses the disbelievers﴾ [al-Baqarah: 19], and He said: ﴿They cannot encompass Him in knowledge﴾ [Taha: 110], and He said: ﴿He has encompassed what is with them and has numbered all things in number﴾ [al-Jinn: 28].

The third issue: He said, "Indeed, God encompasses what they do," and did not say "Indeed God encompasses what they do" in the other order, because they give priority to what is more important and what they are most concerned with. The purpose here is not to show that He is All-Knowing, because we have explained that all their deeds are known to God, exalted is He, and that He will recompense them for them; therefore He mentioned the deed. And God knows best.

**[p. 179]**

Al-Razi's commentary (*Mafatih al-Ghayb*) on Surah 3, verse 121:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And [remember] when you set out early from your family to station the believers at their positions for battle; and Allah is Hearing and Knowing.﴾ ﴿When two parties among you were about to lose heart, while Allah was their ally. And upon Allah let the believers rely.﴾

Know that when Allah, exalted is He, said, ﴿But if you are patient and mindful of Allah, their plotting will not harm you at all﴾, He followed it with what indicates Allah's custom (*sunnah*) regarding them, concerning victory, support, and repelling the harm of the enemy, when they are patient and mindful, and the opposite of that when they are not patient. So He said: ﴿And when you set out early from your family﴾. This means that on the day of Uhud they were many and ready for battle, but when they disobeyed the Messenger's command, they were routed. On the day of Badr they were few and not prepared for battle, but when they obeyed the Messenger's command, they prevailed and overcame their adversaries. This confirms what we have said. There is also another interpretation: the defeat at Uhud came about only because of the withdrawal of Abdullah ibn Ubayy ibn Salul, the hypocrite, and this indicates that it is not permissible to take these hypocrites as intimate confidants (*bitanah*). There are several issues here:

**The first issue:** His saying, ﴿And when you set out early from your family﴾. Concerning it there are three interpretations. The first: its implied meaning is "and remember when you set out early." The second: Abu Muslim said, this is a sentence joined by the conjunction *wa* (and) to His saying: ﴿There has already been a sign for you in the two armies that met: one fighting in the cause of Allah, and another disbelieving﴾ [Ali Imran: 13]. It means: there has already been for you, in Allah's support of that small group of believers over the large group of disbelievers, a matter worthy of reflection, so that you would know that Allah is the supporter of the believers. And for them there was a similar sign in the event when the Messenger ﷺ set out early to station the believers at their positions for battle. The third: the word governing this (*al-'amil*) is "encompassing": its implied meaning is "and Allah is encompassing of what they do, when you set out early."

**The second issue:** They differed about which day this was. Most scholars say it was the day of Uhud. This is the view of Ibn Abbas, al-Suddi, Ibn Ishaq, al-Rabi, al-Asamm, and Abu Muslim. It was also said that it was the day of Badr, which is the view of al-Hasan. It was also said that it was the day of the Confederates (al-Ahzab), which is the view of Mujahid and Muqatil. The arguments of those who say this day is the day of Uhud are several. The first: most scholars of the military expeditions (*al-maghazi*, the accounts of the Prophet's campaigns) claimed that this verse was revealed concerning the battle of Uhud. The second: after this verse He, exalted is He, says: ﴿And Allah had already given you victory at Badr﴾ [Ali Imran: 123]. The apparent meaning is that this is joined to what came before, and the joined element must be different from the element it is joined to. As for the day of the Confederates, the people disobeyed the Messenger's command at Uhud, not at the Confederates. So the story of Uhud is more fitting to this discourse, because the purpose of mentioning this story is to affirm His saying: ﴿But if you are patient and mindful of Allah, their plotting will not harm you at all﴾. Thus it is established that this day is the day of Uhud. The third: the defeat and the enemy's domination were greater at the day of Uhud than at the day of the Confederates, because at the day of Uhud they killed a large number of the senior Companions, and that did not happen on the day of the Confederates. So applying the verse to the day of Uhud is more appropriate.

**The third issue:** It is narrated that "the polytheists camped at Uhud on the day of Wednesday, and the Messenger of Allah ﷺ consulted his Companions. He summoned Abdullah ibn Ubayy ibn Salul, whom he had never summoned before, and consulted him. Abdullah and most of the Ansar said: 'O Messenger of Allah, remain in Medina and do not go out to them. By Allah, we have never gone out from it against an enemy except that the enemy inflicted harm upon us, and no enemy has entered upon us except that we inflicted harm upon them. So how much more so when you are among us! Leave them. If they stay, they will remain in the worst of places; if they enter, the men will kill them face to face, and the women and children will pelt them with stones; and if they return, they will return disappointed.' Others said: 'Take us out to these dogs, so that they do not think we are afraid of them.' So the Prophet, peace be upon him, said: 'I have seen in my dream cows being slaughtered around me, and I interpreted that as good. I saw a notch in the edge of my sword, and I interpreted that as a defeat. And I saw as if I had put my hand into a strong coat of mail, and I interpreted that as Medina. So if you see fit to remain in Medina and leave them [be]...'" Some Muslims, from among those who had missed Badr and whom Allah had honored with martyrdom at Uhud, said: "Take us out to our enemies." They kept at him until he went in, put on his armour (*la'mah*), and when he had put it on, the people regretted and said: "Evil is what we have done; we advised the Messenger of Allah while revelation comes to him." They said to him: "Do as you see fit, O Messenger of Allah." He said: "It is not fitting for a prophet to put on his armour and then take it off until he has fought." So he went out on Friday after the Friday prayer, and he arrived at the ravine of Uhud on the morning of Saturday, in the middle of Shawwal. He walked on foot and began arranging his Companions for battle as if he were straightening arrows with them. If he saw a man protruding from the line, he would say to him: "Step back." His camp was on the side of the valley, and he placed his back and his army toward Uhud. He appointed Abdullah ibn Jubayr over the archers and said: "Repel them from us with arrows, so that they cannot come at us from behind." The Prophet, peace be upon him, said to his Companions: "Stand firm in this position. If they face you, they will turn their backs; do not pursue the fleeing, and do not leave this position." Then when the Messenger, peace be upon him, opposed the opinion of Abdullah ibn Ubayy, it grieved him, and he said: "He obeyed the youths and disobeyed me." Then he said to his companions: "Muhammad only triumphs over his enemy through you, and he has promised his Companions that when their enemies see them, they will be routed. So when you see their enemies, flee, and they will follow you, and the matter will turn contrary to what Muhammad, peace be upon him, said." When the two parties met, Abdullah withdrew with the hypocrites, and the total strength of the Muslim army was a thousand. Abdullah ibn Ubayy withdrew with three hundred, so seven hundred remained. Then Allah strengthened them despite that, until they routed the polytheists. When the believers saw the enemy's rout, and Allah had given them good news of it, they hoped that this event would be like the event of Badr. So they pursued the fleeing and abandoned that position, and they disobeyed the Messenger's command after he had shown them what they loved. Allah, exalted is He, wanted to wean them from this act, so that they would not dare to oppose the Messenger, peace be upon him, and so that they would know that their victory at Badr had come about only through the blessing of their obedience to Allah and His Messenger. Had Allah left them alone with their enemy, they would not have stood against them. So Allah removed terror from the hearts of the polytheists, and the polytheists multiplied against them, and the army scattered away from the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, as Allah, exalted is He, said: ﴿When you were climbing away and not turning back for anyone, while the Messenger was calling you from behind you﴾ [Ali Imran: 153]. The face of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ was wounded, his lower front tooth was broken, and the hand of Talhah was paralyzed while shielding him. Only Abu Bakr, Ali, al-Abbas, and Sa'd remained with him. A cry spread through the army that Muhammad had been killed. A man of the Ansar known by the kunya Abu Sufyan called out to the Ansar, saying: "This is the Messenger of Allah!" So the Muhattirun and the Ansar returned to him. Seventy of them had been killed, and many were wounded. He ﷺ said: "May Allah have mercy on a man who defends his brothers," and he charged against the polytheists with those who were with him until he drove them away from the dead and the wounded." And Allah knows best.

The point of the story is that the disbelievers were three thousand, and the Muslims were a thousand or fewer. Then Abdullah ibn Ubayy withdrew with three hundred of his companions, so the Messenger ﷺ remained with seven hundred. Allah helped them until they routed the disbelievers. Then, when they opposed the Messenger's command and busied themselves with seeking spoils, the matter turned against them, they were routed, and what happened, happened. All of this confirms His saying: ﴿But if you are patient and mindful of Allah, their plotting will not harm you at all﴾, and that the one who advances is the one whom Allah helps, and the one who turns back is the one whom Allah forsakes.

**The fourth issue:** It is said: "I made him settle in a dwelling" (*bawwa'tuhu manzilan*) and "I made him settle for him in a dwelling" (*bawwa'tu lahu manzilan*), meaning I lodged him in it. *Al-mabaah* and *al-baah* mean a dwelling. His saying: ﴿positions for battle (*maqa'ida lil-qital*)﴾ means places and locations. People have extended the use of *al-maq'ad* and *al-maqam* to mean a place. From this is His saying: ﴿in a seat of truth﴾ [al-Qamar: 55], and His saying: ﴿before you rise from your place﴾ [al-Naml: 39], meaning from your assembly and the place of your judgment. He expressed the places here as *maqa'id* (seats) for two reasons. The first: he, peace be upon him, commanded them to remain at their positions and not move from them, and one who sits in a place does not move from it, so he called those places *maqa'id* to signal that they were commanded to remain in them and never move from them. The second: fighters may sit in designated places until the enemy meets them, and then they stand up when there is need to fight, so those places were called *maqa'id* for this reason.

**The fifth issue:** His saying: ﴿And when you set out early from your family to station the believers at their positions for battle﴾. It is narrated that "he, peace be upon him, set out early from the house of Aisha, may Allah be pleased with her, and walked on foot to Uhud." This is the view of Mujahid and al-Waqidi. This report indicates that Aisha, may Allah be pleased with her, was the Prophet's ﷺ "family" (*ahl*). And He, exalted is He, said: ﴿Good women are for good men, and good men are for good women﴾ [al-Nur: 26]. This text indicates that she was pure and free from every defect. Do you not see that when Noah's son was a disbeliever, He said: ﴿Indeed, he is not of your family﴾ [Hud: 46], and likewise the wife of Lot.

* * *

Then He, exalted is He, said: ﴿And Allah is Hearing and Knowing﴾, meaning: He hears your words and knows your hearts and intentions. As we have mentioned, he, peace be upon him, consulted his Companions in that battle. Some of them said to him: "Remain in Medina," and some said: "Go out to them." Each one had a different aim in what he said. Some agreed and some disagreed. So He, exalted is He, said: I am Hearing of what they say and Knowing of what they conceal.

Then God, exalted is He, said: ﴿When two parties among you were about to lose heart﴾. And concerning this there are several issues:

First issue: Regarding the element governing His saying ﴿when two parties among you were about to﴾, there are several views. The first: al-Zajjaj said: the governing element is "al-tabwi'a" (the settling of the believers in their positions), and the meaning is that the settling occurred at that time. The second: the governing element is His saying ﴿All-Hearing, All-Knowing﴾. The third: it is permissible for it to be a substitute (badal) for ﴿when you set out early﴾.

Second issue: The two parties were two clans of the Ansar: Banu Salamah of the Khazraj and Banu Harithah of the Aws. When 'Abd Allah ibn Ubayy was defeated, the two parties were about to follow him, but God protected them, and they remained steadfast with the Messenger (ﷺ). Some scholars said: God, exalted is He, left their names unspecified and concealed them, so it is not permissible for us to expose that concealment.

Third issue: Al-fashal (failure) is cowardice and weakness. If it is said: al-hamm (intention) regarding a matter is resolve, then the apparent meaning of the verse indicates that the two parties resolved upon failure and abandonment, and that is disobedience. How then can it be said of them, "and God is their guardian"?

The answer: al-hamm may mean resolve, may mean thought, may mean the inner self's whispering, and may mean what appears of speech indicating the enemy's strength, the multitude of its numbers and the abundance of its equipment. For any such thing that appears, it is correct to describe the one from whom it appears as having intended to lose heart, insofar as there appeared from him what necessitates weakness of heart. Thus His saying ﴿when two parties among you were about to lose heart﴾ does not indicate that an act of disobedience occurred from them. Furthermore, granting that it is said to be disobedience, it is among the minor sins and not among the major sins, by the evidence of His saying, exalted is He, ﴿and God is their guardian﴾, for if that intention had been among the major sins, God's guardianship over them would not have remained.

* * *

Then God, exalted is He, said: ﴿and God is their guardian﴾. And concerning this there are several issues:

First issue: 'Abd Allah (ibn Mas'ud) read (wa-Allahu waliyyuhum), like His saying: ﴿And if two groups of the believers fight﴾ [al-Hujurat: 9].

Second issue: As to the meaning, there are several views. The first: its purpose is to explain that that intention did not remove them from God's guardianship. The second: it is as if it were said: God is their helper and the one who manages their affairs, so how does this failure and abandonment of reliance upon God, exalted is He, befit them? The third: in it is an indication that that failure did not come into existence because God, exalted is He, is their guardian, so He supported them with success and protection. Its purpose is to make clear that, were it not for His, glorified is He, granting of success and His guidance, no one would be delivered from the darknesses of sins. The soundness of this interpretation is shown by His saying, exalted is He, after this verse: ﴿and upon God let the believers rely﴾.

If it is said: what is the meaning of what was narrated from some of them, upon the revelation of this verse, that he said: "By God, it does not gladden us that we did not intend what the two parties intended," and God, exalted is He, has informed us that He is their guardian?

We say: the meaning of that is the excess of joy at the honor they gained through God's praise and His sending down of a verse explicitly affirming the validity of guardianship for them, and that this resolve did not remove them from God's guardianship, exalted is He.

* * *

Then He said: ﴿and upon God let the believers rely﴾. Al-tawakkul is a form of tafa''ul, from "wakala amrahu ila fulan" when one relies upon another for his sufficiency in a matter without taking charge of it himself. And in the verse there is an indication that a person should repel what befalls him of hardship or calamity by relying upon God, and should turn away distress from himself by that reliance.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 3, verse 123:

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And Allah had already given you victory at Badr when you were weak. So fear Allah that you may be grateful.﴾

Regarding the manner of the arrangement (naẓm) of the verses, there are two views. The first: when Exalted is He mentioned the story of Uhud, He followed it with the mention of the story of Badr. This is because the Muslims on the day of Badr were in the utmost state of poverty and helplessness, while the disbelievers were in the utmost state of strength and power. Then Exalted is He empowered the Muslims over the polytheists, and this became one of the strongest proofs that the rational person must not seek to attain his aim and objective except through reliance upon Allah and seeking His help. The purpose of mentioning this story is to confirm His saying: ﴿But if you are patient and mindful of Allah, their plotting will not harm you at all﴾, and to confirm His saying: ﴿And upon Allah let the believers rely.﴾ The second: Exalted is He related about the two groups that they had both intended to lose heart.

* * *
Then He said: ﴿And Allah is the protector of both of them, and upon Allah let the believers rely.﴾ That is: whoever Allah is a helper and supporter for, how does weakness, cowardice and feebleness befit him? Then He confirmed this with the story of Badr, for the Muslims were in the utmost weakness, but since Allah was their helper, they attained their objective and overpowered their opponents. So it is here as well. This is the explanation of the aspect of the arrangement. In the verse there are several issues:

The first issue: regarding Badr there are several views. The first: Badr is the name of a well belonging to a man called Badr, so the well was named after its owner; this is the view of al-Sha'bi. The second: it is the name of the well itself, just as a town is named after something without the name of its owner being transferred to it; this is the view of al-Waqidi and his teachers, and they denied the view of al-Sha'bi. It is water between Makkah and Madinah.

The second issue: (adhillah) is the plural of dhalil. Al-Wahidi said: The original form for fa'il when it is a descriptive adjective is to be pluralized as fu'ala', like ẓarif and ẓurafa', and kathir and kuthara', and sharik and shuraka'. However, they avoided the pattern fu'ala' in doubled forms, because if they had said qalil and qulala', and khalil and khulala', two letters of the same kind would have come together; so they turned to af'ila, since among the plurals of fa'il is af'ila, like jarib and ajriba, and qafiz and aqfiza. So they made the plural of dhalil as adhillah. The author of al-Kashshaf said: adhillah is a plural of paucity (jam' qillah), and he mentioned the plural of paucity only to indicate that they, together with their humiliation, were few in number.

The third issue: His saying ﴿and you were weak﴾ is in the position of a circumstantial clause (hal). They were weak for several reasons. The first: Exalted is He said: ﴿And to Allah belongs honour, and to His Messenger and to the believers﴾ [al-Munafiqun: 8]. Therefore this humiliation must be explained by a meaning that does not contradict the implication of this verse, and that is to explain it as the smallness of their number, the weakness of their condition, the scarcity of weapons and wealth, and the lack of ability to resist the enemy. The meaning of humiliation (dhull) is weakness in resisting, and its opposite is honour (izz), which is strength and dominance. It is narrated that the Muslims were three hundred and some odd (bid'a 'ashara), and among them there was not more than one horse, and most of them were on foot, and perhaps a group of them would ride one camel, while the disbelievers were nearly a thousand fighters, with a hundred horses, together with abundant weapons and complete equipment. The second: perhaps what is meant is that they were weak in the assumption and belief of the polytheists, because of the smallness of their number and weapons; this is like what Allah related of the disbelievers, that they said: ﴿The mightier will surely expel the weaker from it﴾ [al-Munafiqun: 8]. The third: the Companions had witnessed the disbelievers in Makkah in strength and wealth, and up to that time no conquest over those disbelievers had happened for them, so their awe remained in their hearts and their magnification of them was established in their souls; for this reason they feared them and were apprehensive of them.

* * *
Then Exalted is He said: ﴿So fear Allah﴾, that is, in steadfastness alongside His Messenger, ﴿that you may be grateful﴾, by your piety, for what He has bestowed upon you of His help; or perhaps Allah will bestow upon you another blessing which you will be grateful for. Thus He placed gratitude in the position of bestowal, because it is its cause.

**Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 3, verse 124 (part 1 of 2):**

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿When you said to the believers, "Is it not enough for you that your Lord reinforce you with three thousand angels sent down?"﴾

There are several issues here.

**The first issue:** The exegetes disagree about whether this promise was fulfilled on the day of Badr or the day of Uhud. This disagreement leads to the question of what governs *idh* ("when"). If we say the promise was fulfilled on the day of Badr, then the governing element of *idh* is His saying, ﴿Allah had already given you victory﴾. The meaning is: "when Allah gave you victory at Badr, while you were humble, you were saying to the believers..." If we say it was fulfilled on the day of Uhud, then this clause is a second substitute (*badal*) for His saying, ﴿and when you set out early from your family﴾.

Having understood this, we say:

**The first opinion:** That it was the day of Uhud. This is narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, al-Kalbi, al-Waqidi, Muqatil and Muhammad ibn Ishaq. The argument for it runs in several ways:

**The first argument:** On the day of Badr the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) was reinforced only with one thousand angels. He said in Surat al-Anfal: ﴿When you sought help from your Lord and He answered you, "I will reinforce you with a thousand angels"﴾ [al-Anfal 8:9]. So how can what is mentioned here, three thousand and five thousand, fit the day of Badr?

**The second argument:** On the day of Badr the disbelievers were about a thousand or close to it, and the Muslims were about a third of them, since they were three hundred and some odd. So Allah sent down a thousand angels on the day of Badr, and the number of disbelievers became matched by the number of angels, with the number of Muslims added. Therefore the defeat fell upon the disbelievers. Likewise on the day of Uhud the number of Muslims was a thousand and the number of disbelievers was three thousand. So the number of Muslims was a third of the number of disbelievers on this day, as on the day of Badr. Allah therefore promised them on this day that He would send down three thousand angels, so that the number of disbelievers would be matched by the number of angels together with the number of Muslims. This would be a sign that the Muslims would defeat them on this day as they had defeated them on the day of Badr. Then He made the three thousand five thousand, so that the courage of the Muslims' hearts would increase on this day and fear would be removed from their hearts. It is well known that this meaning is achieved only if we say that this promise was fulfilled on the day of Uhud.

**The third argument:** He, exalted is He, said in this verse: ﴿And if they come upon you immediately, your Lord will reinforce you with five thousand angels, marked﴾ [Al 'Imran 3:125]. The meaning is: "if your enemies come upon you immediately." The day of Uhud is the day when the enemies were coming upon them. As for the day of Badr, the enemies did not come upon them; rather, they went out toward the enemies.

If it is said: If His saying, ﴿Is it not enough for you that your Lord reinforce you with three thousand angels?﴾ was about the day of Uhud, and then this reinforcement did not occur, then a lie is implied.

The answer to this is in two parts. **The first:** His sending down five thousand angels was conditional on their being patient and being mindful of Allah concerning the spoils. Then they were not patient and were not mindful concerning the spoils, but opposed the command of the Messenger (ﷺ). So when the condition was lost, the conditioned thing was lost as well. As for the sending down of three thousand angels, the Messenger promised this to the believers whom he had stationed in positions for fighting and commanded to remain still and steadfast in those positions. This shows that he (ﷺ) promised them this only on the condition that they remain steadfast in those positions. When they neglected this condition, the conditioned thing did not occur.

**The second part of the answer:** We do not grant that the angels were not sent down. Al-Waqidi narrated from Mujahid that he said: "The angels were present on the day of Uhud, but they did not fight." It is also narrated that "the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) gave the banner to Mus'ab ibn 'Umayr, and Mus'ab was killed. Then an angel in the form of Mus'ab took it. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said, 'Advance, O Mus'ab!' The angel said, 'I am not Mus'ab.' So the Messenger (ﷺ) knew that he was an angel who had been sent as reinforcement." And from Sa'd ibn Abi Waqqas, may Allah be pleased with him, that he said: "I was shooting arrows that day, and a man with a white, handsome face returned them to me, and I did not know him. So I thought he was an angel." This is what we say in establishing this argument.

Having understood this, we say: The arrangement of the verse according to this interpretation is that He, exalted is He, mentioned the story of Uhud, then said: ﴿And upon Allah let the believers rely﴾. That is, their reliance must be upon Allah and not upon the abundance of their numbers and equipment. ﴿Allah had already given you victory at Badr, while you were humble.﴾ So likewise He is capable of such victory in all other situations. After this He returned the speech to the story of Uhud and said: ﴿When you said to the believers, "Is it not enough for you that your Lord reinforce you with three thousand angels sent down?"﴾

**The second opinion:** That this promise was on the day of Badr. This is the view of most exegetes, and they argued for its soundness with several arguments.

**The first argument:** Allah, exalted is He, said: ﴿And Allah had already given you victory at Badr, while you were humble﴾ and ﴿When you said to the believers, "Is it not enough for you ..."﴾ and so on. The apparent meaning of this speech requires that Allah gave them victory at Badr at the very time the Messenger said this speech to the believers. This requires that he (peace be upon him) said this speech on the day of Badr.

**The second argument:** The scarcity of numbers and equipment was greater on the day of Badr, and the need to strengthen the heart was greater on that day. So it is better to direct this speech to that day.

**The third argument:** The promise of sending down three thousand angels was unconditional, not tied to any condition, so it had to occur. And it did occur on the day of Badr, not on the day of Uhud. Nobody can say that the angels descended but did not fight, because the promise was of reinforcement with three thousand angels, and mere descent does not achieve reinforcement; assistance is necessary. And the assistance was achieved on the day of Badr but was not achieved on the day of Uhud.

[p. 185]

Then the proponents of this view answered the arguments of the first group. They said:

As for the first argument, which is your saying that the Messenger (ﷺ) was reinforced on the day of Badr only with a thousand angels:

The answer to it is in two parts. **The first:** Allah reinforced the Companions of the Messenger (ﷺ) with a thousand, then increased them by two thousand more, so they became three thousand. Then He added two other thousand, so they became five thousand. So it is as if he (peace be upon him) said to them: "Is it not enough for you that your Lord reinforce you with a thousand angels?" They said: "Yes." Then he said: "Is it not enough for you that your Lord reinforce you with three thousand?" They said: "Yes." Then he said to them: "If you are patient and mindful of Allah, your Lord will reinforce you with five thousand." This is like what is narrated: that he (ﷺ) said to his Companions: "Would it please you to be a quarter of the people of Paradise?" They said: "Yes." He said: "Would it please you to be a third of the people of Paradise?" They said: "Yes." He said: "Indeed I hope that you will be half of the people of Paradise."

**The second part of the answer:** The people of Badr were reinforced only with a thousand, as is mentioned in Surat al-Anfal. Then it reached them that some of the polytheists intended to reinforce the Quraysh with a large number. So they feared, and it was hard for them because of their small number. Allah therefore promised them that if reinforcement came to the disbelievers, He would reinforce them with five thousand angels. But that reinforcement never reached the Quraysh; rather, they withdrew when news reached them of the defeat of the Quraysh. So He dispensed with reinforcing the Muslims beyond the thousand.

As for the second argument, which is your saying: The disbelievers were a thousand on the day of Badr, so Allah sent down a thousand angels, and on the day of Uhud they were three thousand, so Allah sent down three thousand.

The answer is that this is a good approximation, but it does not necessitate that the matter is not so. Rather, Allah, exalted is He, may increase and may decrease in number according to what He wills.

As for the third argument, which is the clinging to His saying: ﴿And if they come upon you immediately﴾.

The answer to it is that when the polytheists heard that the Messenger (ﷺ) and his Companions had intercepted the caravan, anger stirred in their hearts, and they gathered and went toward the Prophet (ﷺ). Then, when the Companions heard that, they feared. So Allah, exalted is He, informed them that if they came upon them immediately, He would reinforce them with five thousand angels. This is the summary of what has been said in establishing these two opinions, and Allah knows best what He intends.

\* \* \*

**The second issue:** They differed about the number of the angels. The summary of the positions is that some people added the smaller number to the larger number. They said: since the promise of reinforcement with three thousand has no condition attached to it, and the promise of reinforcement with five thousand is conditioned on patience, piety and the enemy's coming immediately, there must be a difference. But this is weak, because it does not follow from the five being conditioned that the three, which is part of them, must be conditioned by that same condition. Others included the smaller number within the larger number. As for the first approach: if we take the verse as referring to the story of Badr, the number of angels would be nine thousand, because He mentioned the thousand, He mentioned three thousand, and He mentioned five thousand, and the total is nine thousand. If we take it as referring to the story of Uhud, there is no mention of the thousand in it, but only three thousand and five thousand, and the total is eight thousand. As for the second approach, which is including the smaller in the larger: they said the number of angels is five thousand, then two more thousand were added to it, so they were promised a thousand, then two thousand more were added to it, so they were promised three thousand, then two other thousand were added to it, so they were promised five thousand. We have reported from some of them that he said: "The people of Badr were reinforced with a thousand." It was said that Kurz ibn Jabir al-Muharibi intended to reinforce the polytheists, and this was hard on the Muslims. So the Prophet (ﷺ) said to them: "Is it not enough for you"—meaning, on the assumption that reinforcement might come to the polytheists, Allah will also reinforce you with three thousand and five thousand. Then reinforcement did not come to the polytheists, so likewise here, the increase beyond the thousand did not come to the Muslims. These are all possible views, and Allah knows best what He intends.

\* \* \*

**The third issue:** The people of tafsir and of the biographies (*siyar*) agree that Allah sent down the angels on the day of Badr and that they fought the disbelievers. Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him and his father, said: "The angels did not fight except on the day of Badr. On other occasions they were a number and a reinforcement; they neither fought nor struck." This is the view of the majority. As for Abu Bakr al-Asamm, he denied this most strongly and argued against it with several arguments.

**The first argument:** A single angel is enough to destroy the earth. It is well known that Gabriel (peace be upon him) placed his wing beneath the four cities of the people of Lot and his wing reached the seventh earth. Then he lifted them to the sky and turned their uppermost part to their lowest. So if he was present on the day of Badr, what need was there for people to fight the disbelievers? And even granting his presence, what benefit was there in sending the rest of the angels?

**The second argument:** The prominent disbelievers were well known, and each of them had a known counterpart among the Companions. When this is so, it is impossible to attribute his killing to the angels.

**The third argument:** If the angels had fought, they would either have become visible to people or not visible to them. If people saw them, then either they saw them in human form or in a form other than human. If it was the first, then on this assumption the visible army of the Messenger would have become three thousand or more, and no one has said so. Moreover, this contradicts His saying: ﴿and He makes you appear few in their eyes﴾ [al-Anfal 8:44]. And if they saw them in a form other than human forms, then it would necessarily follow that terror struck the hearts of creation intensely, for whoever sees jinn undoubtedly becomes greatly frightened, and this is not transmitted at all.

The second part of the argument: as for the second case, namely that people did not see the angels, then on this supposition: when they fought and cut off heads, tore open bellies, and unhorsed the disbelievers, then the people would have been witnessing the occurrence of these acts while they had not seen anyone of the doers. Such a thing would be among the greatest miracles, and whoever denies such a situation would necessarily become an unbelieving rebel. Since nothing of this kind was found, the corruption of this case is also known.

The fourth argument: these angels who descended, it may be said that they were either dense bodies or subtle bodies. If the first, then everyone would have to see them and their seeing would be like the seeing of other things, and it is known that the matter was not so. And if they were subtle, fine bodies like air, then there would be no hardness or strength in them, and it would be impossible for them to be riding horses, and all of that is something you see.

Know that this doubt befits only one who denies the Qur'an and prophethood. As for one who affirms both, nothing of these statements befits him. It was not fitting for Abu Bakr al-Asamm to deny these things, although the text of the Qur'an speaks of them clearly and their transmission in the reports is close to mass-transmitted (mutawatir). 'Abdullah ibn 'Umar narrated: When the Quraysh returned from Uhud, they began to speak in their assemblies about what they had gained, saying: "We did not see the piebald horses nor the white men whom we used to see on the day of Badr." The aforementioned doubt, when we set it against the perfect power of God Most High, vanishes and collapses, for He does what He wills, since He is able over all possibilities, and He decrees what He desires, since He is exalted above needs.

* * *

The fifth issue: they differed concerning the manner of the angels' support. Some said: by fighting alongside the believers. Others said: rather by strengthening their souls and making them aware that victory belongs to them, and by casting terror into the hearts of the disbelievers. The apparent meaning of "reinforcement" is that they join the army in fighting if the need for them arises, and it is possible that the need for them does not arise during the actual fighting, and that their mere presence suffices to strengthen the heart. Many exegetes claimed that they fought on the day of Badr and did not fight on the other days.

* * *

The sixth issue: God Most High says: ﴿Will it not suffice you﴾. The meaning of sufficiency (kifaya) is filling the need and taking charge of the matter; it is said "kafāhu amr kadhā" when he fills his need. The meaning of imdad (reinforcement) is giving a thing repeatedly, one after another. Al-Mufaddal said: what is in the manner of strength and aid is said of it "amadda yumiddu," and what is in the manner of increase is said of it "madda yamudduhu," and from it is His saying: ﴿And the sea, after it, extends it﴾ [Luqman: 27].

The seventh issue: Ibn 'Amir read (munazzalin) with the zay doubled and fatha, for intensification, while the rest read with the zay light and fatha. Both are two dialects.

The eighth issue: the author of al-Kashshaf said: He only mentioned to them the promise of the descent of the angels in order that their hearts might be strengthened, and that they might resolve on steadfastness and trust in God's victory. The meaning of ﴿Will it not suffice you﴾ is a denial that the reinforcement with three thousand angels would not suffice you. The particle lan, which is for emphasizing negation, was used to indicate that they, because of their fewness, weakness and the large number of their enemies, were like those who despair of victory.

Then Allah the Exalted said: ﴿Yes, if you are patient and god-fearing, and they come upon you suddenly this very moment, your Lord will reinforce you with five thousand angels, marked out.﴾

Concerning the verse there are several issues:

The first issue: "Bala" (yes/indeed) is an affirmation of what follows "lan" (never), meaning: "Rather, the reinforcement will suffice for you," so it affirmed sufficiency. Then He said: ﴿If you are patient and god-fearing, and they come upon you suddenly this very moment﴾, meaning: "and the polytheists come upon you suddenly this very moment, your Lord will reinforce you with more than that number, which is five thousand." Thus He made the coming of five thousand angels conditional upon three things: patience (al-sabr), god-fearing (al-taqwa), and the disbelievers coming upon them at once (al-fawr). Since these conditions did not occur, the conditioned matter did not occur either.

The second issue: "Al-fawr" is a verbal noun from "fara al-qidr" (the pot boiled over) when it boiled. He said: ﴿until when Our command came and the oven gushed forth﴾ [Hud: 40]. It was said: it is the first rising of the water from it. Then they used this word metaphorically for speed. One says: "So-and-so came and returned at once (min fawrihi)." From this is the statement of the usulis (jurists of legal theory): "The command is for immediacy (al-fawr) or delay (al-tarakhi)." The meaning is the intensity, heat, and swiftness of the enemy's coming.

The third issue: Ibn Kathir, Abu 'Amr, and 'Asim read ﴿musawwimin﴾ with a kasra on the waw, meaning "marking themselves," i.e., they marked themselves with specific signs. Most reports say they marked their horses with signs placed upon them. The rest read it with a fatha on the waw, meaning Allah marked them, or in the sense that they marked themselves. Regarding the meaning of "tasweem" in His words ﴿musawwimin﴾ there are two views.

The first: "al-sawma" is the sign by which a thing is distinguished from others, and the explanation of this has passed in His words ﴿and the marked horses﴾ [Ali 'Imran: 14]. This sign is placed by the rider on the day of encounter so that he may be recognized by it. In a report, the Prophet (ﷺ) said on the day of Badr: "Mark yourselves, for the angels have marked themselves." Ibn 'Abbas said: the angels had marked themselves with yellow turbans and their horses, and they were on piebald horses, having hung white wool on their forelocks and tails. It is narrated that Hamza ibn 'Abd al-Muttalib was marked with an ostrich feather, that 'Ali was marked with a white woolen tuft, that al-Zubayr wore a yellow headband, and that Abu Dujana was marked with a red headband.

The second view: regarding the meaning of "musawwimin," it means "sent forth," derived from grazing camels (al-ibil al-sa'ima) that are sent out to pasture. You say: "asamtu al-ibil" when you send them out. It is also said in the intensive form "sawwamtu," just as you say "akramtu" and "karramtu." So whoever reads ﴿musawwimin﴾ with a kasra on the waw, the meaning is that the angels sent their horses against the disbelievers to kill and capture them. Whoever reads with a fatha on the waw, the meaning is that Allah the Exalted sent them against the polytheists to destroy them, just as livestock destroys plants and grass.

The commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 3, verses 126–127:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And Allah did not make it except as glad tidings for you, and that your hearts may be assured thereby. And victory is not except from Allah, the Almighty, the Wise.﴾ ﴿That He may cut off a portion of those who disbelieve or subdue them so they return defeated.﴾

The pronoun in His saying ﴿And Allah did not make it﴾ refers to the verbal noun (al-masdar), as if He had said: "And Allah did not make the supplying and the reinforcement except as glad tidings for you, that you would be helped." So ﴿He will reinforce you﴾ indicates the reinforcement, and the pronoun refers back to it, as in His saying: ﴿And do not eat of that over which the name of Allah has not been mentioned, for indeed it is defiance (fisq)﴾ [al-An'am: 121], meaning: "Indeed, eating it is defiance." So ﴿you eat﴾ indicates the eating, and the pronoun refers back to it.

Al-Zajjaj said: ﴿And Allah did not make it﴾ means the mention of the reinforcement, ﴿except as glad tidings (bushra)﴾. Bushra is a noun derived from ibshar (giving good news). The discussion of the meaning of tabshir (giving glad tidings) has already passed in surah al-Baqarah, in His saying: ﴿And give glad tidings to those who believe﴾ [al-Baqarah: 25].

* * *

Then He said: ﴿and that your hearts may be assured thereby﴾, and here there is a question:

It is that His saying ﴿and that your hearts may be assured﴾ is a verb, while His saying ﴿except as glad tidings﴾ is a noun, and coordinating a verb with a noun is objectionable. It would have been proper to say "except as glad tidings for you and assurance," or to say "except that He might give you glad tidings and that your hearts be assured thereby." Why, then, did He leave that and turn away from it to coordinate a verb with a noun?

The answer to this is in two respects. The first: in the mention of the reinforcement there are two aims, and one of them is stronger in being intended than the other. The first is bringing joy into their hearts, which is what is meant by His saying ﴿except as glad tidings﴾. The second is the attainment of tranquility, by establishing that Allah's help and support are with them, so that they do not shrink back from fighting; and this is the primary aim. So He distinguished between these two expressions, as an alert to the difference in intendedness between these two matters. Thus being glad tidings is intended, but the stronger intended aim is the attainment of assurance. For this reason He introduced the particle of causation (lam al-ta'lil) before the verb of assurance, saying ﴿and that your hearts may be assured﴾. A parallel to this is His saying: ﴿and horses, mules and donkeys, that you may ride them, and as adornment﴾ [al-Nahl: 8]. Since the primary aim was riding, He introduced the particle of causation before it. Likewise here, the second. Some have said in answer: the waw is superfluous, and the meaning is: "And Allah did not make it except as glad tidings for you, so that your hearts may be assured thereby."

* * *

Then He said: ﴿And victory is not except from Allah﴾. The purpose of this is that their trust should be in Allah and not in the angels. This is an alert that the faith of a servant is not perfected except by turning away from means (al-asbab) and turning wholly toward the Causer of causes. His saying ﴿the Almighty, the Wise﴾: "the Almighty" points to the perfection of His power, and "the Wise" points to the perfection of His knowledge. So the needs of the servants are not hidden from Him, and He is not incapable of answering supplications. Whoever is like this, victory is not expected except from His mercy, nor help except from His grace and generosity.

* * *
