As for the hidden verb before it, the sense is: "And those days We alternate among the people for several reasons, among them so that Allah may know those who believe, among them that He may take martyrs from among you, among them that Allah may purify those who believe, among them that He may destroy the disbelievers." All of these are like the cause and reason for that alternation.

The second issue: the waw in His saying ﴿and so that Allah may know those who believe﴾ has many parallels in the Qur'an. Allah says: ﴿and so that he may be among the certain﴾ [al-An'am: 75], and He says: ﴿and so that the hearts of those who do not believe may incline to it﴾ [al-An'am: 113]. The sense is: "And those days We alternate among the people so that such-and-such may be, and so that Allah may know." The thing coordinated with is omitted to signal that the wisdom in this alternation is not one thing, in order to console them for what happened, and to make them aware that in that event and their situation in it there are aspects of wisdom which, if they knew them, would gladden them.

The third issue: the apparent meaning of His saying ﴿and so that Allah may know those who believe﴾ indicates that He did that alternation in order to acquire this knowledge, and it is known that this is impossible for Allah the Exalted. A similar difficulty in this verse is found in His saying: ﴿Or did you think that you would enter Paradise while Allah has not yet known those of you who strove and known the steadfast?﴾ [Al ʿImran: 142], and His saying: ﴿And We had certainly tested those before them, and Allah will surely know those who are truthful and will surely know the liars﴾ [al-ʿAnkabut: 3], and His saying: ﴿That We may know which of the two parties is more precise in computing what they remained in terms of time﴾ [al-Kahf: 12], and His saying: ﴿And We will surely test you until We know those who strive among you and the steadfast﴾, and His saying: ﴿except that We might know who follows the Messenger﴾ [al-Baqarah: 143], and His saying: ﴿to test you as to which of you is best in deed﴾ [Hud: 7]. Hisham ibn al-Hakam argued from the apparent meanings of these verses that Allah the Exalted does not know the occurrence of events except at the time they occur. He said: all these verses indicate that He became knowing of these things only when they occurred.

The Mutakallimun answered him: rational proofs have established that He the Exalted knows events before they occur, so it is established that change in knowledge is impossible. However, applying the word "knowledge" to the known and "power" to the powered is a well-known metaphor. It is said: "This is the knowledge of so-and-so," meaning what is known by him, and "This is the power of so-and-so," meaning what is within his power. So every verse whose apparent meaning suggests a renewal of knowledge, what is meant is a renewal of the known.

[Page 15]
Having understood this, we say: in this verse there are several aspects:

One of them: that the sincere be made distinct from the hypocrite, and the believer from the disbeliever.

The second: that He may know the friends of Allah, and He attributed them to Himself as an honour.

The third: that He may judge distinction; He placed "knowledge" in the place of "judgment of distinction," because judgment of distinction only takes place after knowledge.

The fourth: that He may know it as having occurred from them, just as He knew that it would occur; for reward falls upon what has happened, not upon what is known but has not come into existence.

The fourth issue: knowledge may be such that it requires only one object, as one says: "I know Zayd," meaning I know his essence and recognise him. It may also require two objects, as one says: "I know Zayd generous." The meaning here is this second kind, except that the second object is omitted. The sense is: "And so that Allah may know those who believe as distinguished by faith from others," i.e., the wisdom in this alternation is that those who believe become distinguished from those who claim faith, by means of their patience and their steadfastness in Islam. It is also possible that knowledge here is of the first kind, meaning acquaintance with the essence, and the sense is: "and so that Allah may know those who believe, by what appears of their patience in striving against their enemy," i.e., that He may recognise them by their very persons; but the cause of the occurrence of this knowledge, which is the manifestation of patience, is omitted here.

* * *

As for His saying: ﴿and take martyrs from among you﴾, what is meant is mention of the second wisdom in that alternation, and there are issues in it:

The first issue: there are two opinions regarding this verse:
The first: "takes martyrs from among you" means witnesses over people for what has proceeded from them of sins and disobediences, for their being witnesses over people is a lofty station and an exalted rank.
The second: what is meant is "and that He may honour a people with martyrdom." This is because a group of Muslims had missed the day of Badr and used to wish to meet the enemy and that there might be for them a day like the day of Badr in which they would fight the enemy and seek martyrdom. Also, the Qur'an is filled with the exaltation of the state of martyrs. Allah says: ﴿And do not think of those who were killed in the way of Allah as dead; rather, they are alive with their Lord, being provided for﴾ [Al ʿImran: 169]; He says: ﴿And the prophets and the martyrs will be brought forward﴾ [al-Zumar: 69]; and He says: ﴿Those will be with those upon whom Allah has bestowed favour of the prophets, the truthful, the martyrs, and the righteous﴾ [al-Nisa': 69]. Thus this station is the third station after prophethood, and if that is so, then among the desired benefits of that alternation is the attainment of this great rank by some of the believers.

The second issue: our companions (the Ash'arites) argued from this verse that all events occur by the will of Allah the Exalted. They said: the station of martyrdom is as you have mentioned; if it were possible to attain it without the disbelievers being empowered over the believers, there would be no sense in the causal explanation; and if it is not possible, then the killing of the believers by the disbelievers is a necessary consequence of that martyrdom. So if attaining that martyrdom for the servant is willed by Allah the Exalted, then that killing must also be willed by Allah the Exalted. Moreover, His saying ﴿and take martyrs from among you﴾ explicitly states that that by which that martyrdom was obtained is from Allah the Exalted, and this indicates that the act of the servant is the creation of Allah the Exalted.

The third issue: "shuhada'" is the plural of "shahid," like "kuramaʾ" and "ẓurafaʾ." The Muslim killed by the sword of the disbelievers is a shahid. Regarding the explanation of this name there are several views:
The first: al-Nadr ibn Shumayl said: the martyrs are alive, based on His saying: ﴿but they are alive with their Lord, being provided for﴾ [Al ʿImran: 169]. So their spirits are living and have attended the Abode of Peace, whereas the spirits of others do not witness it.
The second: [Page 16 continues]

Ibn al-Anbari: Because God Most High and His angels testified to him (the martyr) of Paradise, so "shahid" is a fa'il in the sense of maf'ul (mafa'il, one who is witnessed to).

The third view: They were called "shuhada'" (witnesses) because on the Day of Resurrection they will bear witness together with the prophets and the truthful (siddiqin), as God Most High said: ﴿That you may be witnesses over mankind﴾ [al-Baqarah: 143].

The fourth view: They were called "shuhada'" because just as they were killed, they were admitted into Paradise. The evidence is that the disbelievers, just as they died, were admitted into the Fire, as shown by His saying: ﴿They were drowned and then admitted into Fire﴾ [Nuh: 25]. Likewise here, it must be said: those who were killed in the way of God, just as they died, entered Paradise.

* * *

Then God Most High said: ﴿And God does not love the wrongdoers﴾. Ibn 'Abbas, may God be pleased with him and his father, said: that is, the polytheists (mushrikin), due to His saying: ﴿Indeed, association [with God] is a great injustice﴾ [Luqman: 13]. It is an interjection (i'tiraD) between one part of the reasoning and another. There are several aspects to it:

The first: God does not love whoever is not steadfast in faith and patient in jihad.

The second: It contains an indication that God Most High only grants the disbelievers victory over the believers for the benefits He mentioned, not because He loves them.

* * *

Then He said: ﴿And that God may purify those who believe﴾, that is, to cleanse them of their sins and remove them from them. Al-mahs in the language means purification (tanqiyah), and al-mahq in the language means diminution (nuqsan). Al-Mufaddal said: it is for a thing to go away entirely until nothing of it is seen. From this is His saying: ﴿God destroys interest﴾ [al-Baqarah: 276], that is, uproots it. Al-Zajjaj said: the meaning of the verse is that God Most High made the days alternate between the Muslims and the disbelievers. If victory goes to the disbelievers over the believers, the intended meaning is the purification of the believers' sins; and if victory goes to the believers over those disbelievers, the intended meaning is the obliteration and erasure of the disbelievers' traces. Thus He contrasted the purification of the believers with the annihilation of the disbelievers, because the purification of the former through the destruction of their sins is like the annihilation of the latter through the destruction of themselves. This is a subtle contrast in meaning. The closer view is that the intended "disbelievers" here is a specific group of them, namely those who fought the Messenger ﷺ on the day of Uhud. We say this because we know that God did not annihilate all the disbelievers, but many of them remained in their disbelief. And God knows best.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 3, verse 142–143:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Or did you think that you would enter Paradise while Allah has not yet made evident those of you who strive [in His cause] and made evident those who are patient?﴾ ﴿And you had certainly wished for death before you encountered it; and now you have seen it while you were looking on.﴾

Know that when He, exalted is He, had explained in the first verse the aspects which are the causes and influences in the alternation of days, He mentioned in this verse what is the fundamental cause of that. So He said: ﴿Or did you think that you would enter Paradise﴾ without bearing hardships? And in the verse there are several issues:

The first issue: "Am" (or) is disjunctive (munqati'ah), and the explanation of its being disjunctive has already been mentioned in Surat al-Baqarah. Abu Muslim said: In ﴿Am hasibtum﴾ there is a prohibition expressed with the interrogative particle that comes for rebuke, and its summary is: Do not think that you will enter Paradise when jihad has not occurred from you. It is like His saying: ﴿Alif, Lam, Mim. Do the people think that they will be left to say, "We have believed," and they will not be tested?﴾ [al-'Ankabut: 1-2]. He opened the speech with the mention of "am," which in their speech most often occurs between two options, one of which is doubtful without being specified. They say: "Did you strike Zayd or 'Amr?", while the occurrence of striking with one of them is certain. He said: It is the custom of the Arabs to use this kind of interrogation for emphasis.

Page 17
So when He said: ﴿And do not weaken and do not grieve﴾ [Al 'Imran: 139], it was as if He said: Do you know that this is as you are commanded, or do you think that you will enter Paradise without striving and patience? This is considered unlikely because Allah, exalted is He, made jihad obligatory before this event, and made patience in bearing its hardships obligatory, and explained the aspects of its benefits in religion and in worldly life. Since this is the case, it is far-fetched that a person should attain happiness and Paradise while neglecting this obedience.

The second issue: al-Zajjaj said: If it is said "fa'ala fulan" (Fulan did), its answer is "lam yaf'al" (he did not do); and if it is said "qad fa'ala fulan" (Fulan has indeed done), its answer is "lamma yaf'al" (he has not yet done). Because it was emphasized on the affirmative side with "qad," it was therefore emphasized on the negative side with the word "lamma."

The third issue: The apparent meaning of the verse indicates that negation falls upon knowledge, while the intended meaning is that it falls upon the negation of the known. The estimate is: Or did you think that you would enter Paradise while jihad has not issued from you? Its explanation is that knowledge is related to the known as it is; so when this correspondence was achieved, it was fitting for each of the two to take the place of the other. The complete discussion of this has already been mentioned.

As for His saying: ﴿and [that] He may make evident those who are patient﴾, know that al-Hasan read (wa-ya'lami) with the jussive, coordinated with ﴿wa-lamma ya'lami Allah﴾. As for the accusative, it is by the implicit "an." This waw is called waw al-sarf, as in your saying: "Do not eat the fish and drink the milk," meaning: do not combine the two. Likewise here, the intended meaning is that entering Paradise and abandoning steadfastness in jihad are things that cannot be combined. Abu 'Amr read (wa-ya'lamu) with the nominative, on the assumption that the waw is for the circumstantial (hal), as if it were said: "while you have not struggled and you are patient."

Know that the summary of the speech is that love of this world does not combine with the happiness of the Hereafter; the more one of them increases, the more the other decreases. This is because the happiness of this world is not attained except by the heart being occupied with seeking the world, while happiness in the Hereafter is not attained except by the heart being emptied of everything other than Allah and filled with love of Allah. These two matters cannot combine, and for this secret, the strong improbability of their combination is stated in this verse. Also, love of Allah and love of the Hereafter are not perfected by mere claim; not everyone who professes the religion of Allah is truthful. Rather, the distinction in this is the imposition of disliked and beloved things, for love is that which is not diminished by harshness and not increased by fidelity. If love remains when the causes of trial are imposed, it becomes clear that this love was genuine. For this wisdom He said: ﴿Or did you think that you would enter Paradise﴾ merely by your affirming the Messenger before Allah tests you with jihad and the tightening of trial. And Allah knows best.

**Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 3, verse 144:**

His statement, exalted is He: ﴿Muhammad is only a messenger; messengers have passed away before him. So if he dies or is killed, will you turn back on your heels? And whoever turns back on his heels will not harm Allah at all, and Allah will reward the grateful.﴾

Concerning it there are several issues:

**The first issue:** Ibn ʿAbbas, Mujahid and al-Dahhak said: "When the Prophet (ﷺ) arrived at Uhud, he ordered the archers to hold fast to the foot of the mountain and not to move from that position, whether the outcome was in their favour or against them. When they stood firm and charged the unbelievers, they defeated them. ʿAli killed Talhah ibn Abi Talhah, the bearer of their standard, and al-Zubayr and al-Miqdad attacked the polytheists. Then the Messenger (ﷺ), together with his companions, charged and defeated Abu Sufyan. Then, when some of the people saw the unbelievers in flight, a group of the archers rushed to the spoils. Khalid ibn al-Walid, who was commander of the right wing of the unbelievers, saw the archers scattered, so he charged against the Muslims, defeated them, broke their ranks, and many Muslims were killed. ʿAbd Allah ibn Qamiʾah al-Harithi struck the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) with a stone, which broke his incisor and wounded his face, and he came seeking to kill him. Musʿab ibn ʿUmayr, who was the bearer of the banner on the day of Badr and on the day of Uhud, defended him until Ibn Qamiʾah killed him. Ibn Qamiʾah thought he had killed the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), so he said: 'I have killed Muhammad.' A crier cried out: 'Truly Muhammad has been killed,' and the crier was Satan. The news of his death spread among the people. At that point some of the Muslims said: 'Would that ʿAbd Allah ibn Ubayy might obtain safe-conduct for us from Abu Sufyan.' A group of the hypocrites said: 'If he were a prophet, he would not have been killed. Return to your brethren and to your religion.' Anas ibn al-Nadr, the paternal uncle of Anas ibn Malik, said: 'O people, if Muhammad has been killed, the Lord of Muhammad is living and does not die. What good is life after the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ)? Fight for what he fought for, and die for what he died for.' Then he said: 'O Allah, I apologise to You for what these people say,' then he drew his sword and fought until he was killed, may Allah have mercy on him. A man of the Muhajirun passed by an Ansari who was writhing in his blood, and said: 'O so-and-so, do you know that Muhammad has been killed?' The Ansari said: 'If he has been killed, then he has delivered the message. Fight for your religion.' When that unbeliever wounded the face of the Messenger (ﷺ) and broke his incisor, Talhah ibn ʿUbayd Allah carried him, and Abu Bakr, ʿAli and a few others defended him, may Allah be pleased with them all. Then the Messenger (ﷺ) began calling out: 'Come to me, servants of Allah!' until a group of his companions gathered around him, and he reproached them for their flight. They said: 'O Messenger of Allah, we ransom you with our fathers and mothers. The news of your death reached us, and terror filled our hearts, so we turned and fled.'"

The meaning of the verse ﴿Muhammad is only a messenger; messengers have passed away before him﴾ is: he will pass away as they passed away. Just as their followers remained holding to their religion after they had passed away, so you must hold to his religion after he has passed away, because the purpose of sending messengers is to convey the message and establish the proof, not for their presence among their peoples forever.

**The second issue:** Abu ʿAli said: The word *rasul* (messenger) comes in two senses. One is the sender (*al-mursal*), and the other is the message (*al-risalah*). Here it is meant in the sense of the sender, as evidenced by His statement: ﴿Indeed you are among the messengers﴾ [al-Baqarah: 252] and His statement: ﴿O Messenger, convey﴾ [al-Maʾidah: 67]. The form *faʿul* may mean *mafʿul* (the object), like *rakub* (what is ridden) and *halub* (what is milked). The word *rasul* may also mean *risalah*, as in the verse of the poet:

*"The slanderers have lied; I did not disclose a secret to them before them, nor did I send them with a message."*

That is, with a message. He said: From this is His statement: ﴿Indeed we are the messengers of your Lord﴾, which we will mention in its proper place, if Allah wills. Then He said: ﴿So if he dies or is killed, will you turn back on your heels?﴾ Concerning it there are several issues:

**The first issue:** The interrogative particle entered upon the condition, while in reality it enters upon the consequence. The meaning is: Will you turn back on your heels if Muhammad dies or is killed? Its parallel is when you say: "Is Zayd standing?" You are actually asking about his standing, except that you have placed the interrogative *hal* before the noun. And Allah knows best.

**The second issue:** He, exalted is He, has clarified in many verses that he (peace be upon him) will not be killed. He said: ﴿Indeed you will die, and indeed they will die﴾ [al-Zumar: 30], and He said: ﴿And Allah will protect you from the people﴾ [al-Maʾidah: 67]. So no one may say: Since He knew he would not be killed, why did He say "or is killed"? The answer to this has several aspects:

**First:** The truth of a conditional proposition does not require the truth of its two parts. For you may say: "If the number five is even, then it is divisible into two equal parts." The conditional is true while both its parts are false. And He, exalted is He, said: ﴿Had there been in them gods other than Allah, they would both have been corrupted﴾ [al-Anbiyaʾ: 22]. This is true, though there are no other gods in them, and no corruption in them. So it is likewise here.

**Second:** This was revealed by way of argument against the opponents. Moses (peace be upon him) died, and his community did not turn back from his religion, and the Christians claimed that Jesus (peace be upon him) was killed, yet they do not turn back from his religion. So it is likewise here.

**Third:** Death does not necessitate the community's turning back from its religion; likewise, being killed should not necessitate turning back from his religion, since He has distinguished between the two matters. When the matter returns to this meaning, the purpose of it is to refute those who doubted the validity of the religion and were inclined to apostasy.

**The third issue:** His statement ﴿you turned back on your heels﴾ means: you became unbelievers after your faith. It is said of everyone who returns to what he was previously upon: "He went back behind him," "he turned back on his heel," and "he retreated on his heels." This is because the hypocrites said to the weaker Muslims: "If Muhammad has been killed, then return to your religion." Some of the Ansar said: "If Muhammad has been killed, the Lord of Muhammad has not been killed, so fight for what Muhammad fought for." The gist of the matter is that He, exalted is He, clarified that his being killed does not necessitate weakness in his religion, by two proofs:

**The first:** By analogy with the death and killing of the other prophets.

**The second:** That the need for the Messenger is for conveying the religion, and after that there is no need for him. Therefore, from his being killed there does not follow the corruption of the religion. And Allah knows best.

**The fourth issue:** No one may say: His statement ﴿So if he dies or is killed﴾ expresses doubt, and doubt concerning Allah, exalted is He, is impermissible. We say: The meaning is that whether this or that occurs, it has no effect upon the weakening of the religion or the obligation of apostasy.

\* \* \*

Then He, exalted is He, said: ﴿And whoever turns back on his heels will not harm Allah at all﴾. The purpose of it is to emphasise the threat, because every rational person knows that Allah, exalted is He, is not harmed by the unbelief of unbelievers. Rather, the meaning is that he harms no one but himself. This is like when a man says to his child during reproach: "What you are doing of these deeds does not harm the heavens and the earth," meaning that its harm returns upon him. It is likewise here. Then He followed the threat with the promise, saying: ﴿And Allah will reward the grateful﴾. The meaning is that when doubt entered the hearts of some of them because of that defeat, and doubt did not enter the hearts of the strong scholars among the believers, those latter ones gave thanks to Allah for their steadfastness in faith and the firmness of their adherence to it. Therefore Allah praised them by His statement: ﴿And Allah will reward the grateful﴾. Muhammad ibn Jarir al-Tabari narrated from ʿAli, may Allah be pleased with him, that he said: "The intended meaning of His statement ﴿And Allah will reward the grateful﴾ is Abu Bakr and his companions." It is also narrated from him that he said: "Abu Bakr is among the grateful, and he is among the beloved of Allah." And Allah knows best what is correct.

[Page 18] [Page 19]

[Page 20]

**His saying, exalted is He: ﴿No soul could die except by Allah's permission, a decree with a fixed term. Whoever desires the reward of this world, We will give him of it; and whoever desires the reward of the Hereafter, We will give him of it; and We will reward the grateful.﴾**

Concerning this there are several questions.

**First question:** On how this verse is connected to what comes before it, there are several views.

The first: The hypocrites spread the rumor that Muhammad (ﷺ) had been killed. So Allah, exalted is He, says: No soul dies except by Allah's permission, His decree, and His destiny. His being killed is therefore like his dying, in that it does not occur except at the appointed, specified time. Just as, had he died in his house, that would not have indicated the corruption of his religion, so too, if he was killed, that should not affect the corruption of his religion. The purpose of this is to refute the saying of the hypocrites to the weak among the Muslims: "Since Muhammad has been killed, return to the religions you were upon."

The second: The intent is to urge the Muslims to jihad by informing them that caution does not avert destiny, that no one dies before his term, and that when the term comes, death cannot be averted by anything. So there is no benefit in cowardice and fear.

The third: The intent is Allah's preservation of the Messenger (ﷺ) and His delivering him from that frightening battle. For in that event, no cause of destruction remained except that it occurred in it. But since Allah, exalted is He, is the Guardian and the Helper, nothing of that harmed him. In this there is also a reminder that his companions fell short in defending him.

The fourth: "No soul could die except by Allah's permission." So the rumor of those who spread the news of the Prophet's (ﷺ) death does not bring about that death or help strengthen disbelief. Rather, Allah keeps him until he makes the religion prevail over all others.

The fifth: The purpose of it is an answer to what the hypocrites said. When the Companions returned, some of them having been killed, they said: "If they had been with us, they would not have died or been killed." So Allah, exalted is He, informed them that both death and killing happen only by Allah's permission and the arrival of the term. And Allah knows best what is correct.

**Second question:** They differed about the interpretation of *al-idhn* (permission) in several views:

The first: *al-idhn* means the command. This is the view of Abu Muslim. The meaning is that Allah, exalted is He, commands the Angel of Death to seize the souls, so no one dies except by this command.

The second: What is meant by this permission is what is meant by His saying: ﴿Our word to a thing, when We intend it, is only that We say to it, "Be," and it is﴾ [an-Nahl: 40]. What is meant by this command is only creation, bringing into being, and origination. For no one has power over life and death except Allah, exalted is He. So the meaning is: no soul will die except by what Allah has caused it to die.

The third: *al-idhn* means allowing, releasing, and not preventing by force or compulsion. It was interpreted this way in His saying: ﴿They could not harm anyone thereby except by Allah's permission﴾ [al-Baqarah: 102], meaning by His allowing it. For He, exalted is He, is capable of preventing that by force. So the meaning is: no soul could die except by Allah's permission, through Allah's leaving the killer and the killed to one another. But He, exalted is He, protects His Prophet and places watchers before him and behind him, so that he may complete the delivery of what he was sent with. And He does not leave anyone free to kill him until he reaches the term that Allah decreed for him. So do not be broken after this in your military expeditions by someone spreading the rumor that Muhammad has been killed.

The fourth: *al-idhn* means knowledge. Its meaning is that no soul will die except at the time in which Allah knows its death. When that time comes, death is inevitable, as He said: ﴿So when their term comes, they cannot delay it an hour, nor can they advance it﴾ [an-Nahl: 61].

The fifth: Ibn ʿAbbas said: *al-idhn* is Allah's decree and destiny. For nothing occurs except by His will and purpose. This is expressed in a figurative way, as if it were an act that no one should undertake except by Allah's permission.

**Third question:** Al-Akhfash and al-Zajjaj said: The lam in ﴿for a soul﴾ has the sense of negation, and the implied meaning is: "No soul would ever die except by Allah's permission."

**Fourth question:** The verse indicates that the one who is killed dies at his appointed term, and that changing the terms is impossible.

On His saying, exalted is He, ﴿a decree with a fixed term﴾, there are several questions:

**First question:** His saying ﴿a decree with a fixed term﴾ is in the accusative, governed by a verb implied by what precedes it. For His saying ﴿No soul could die except by Allah's permission﴾ stands in the place of saying: "Allah has decreed." So the implied meaning is: "Allah has decreed a decree with a fixed term." A parallel to this is His saying: ﴿the decree of Allah upon you﴾ [an-Nisa': 24], because in His saying ﴿Forbidden to you are your mothers﴾ [an-Nisa': 23] there is an indication that He has prescribed this prohibition upon you. Similar to it are: *sunʿa Allah* (the work of Allah), *waʿda Allah* (the promise of Allah), *fitrata Allah* (the nature of Allah), and *sibghata Allah* (the dye of Allah).

**Second question:** By "the book with a fixed term" is meant the book that contains the terms. It is said that it is the Preserved Tablet (al-lawh al-mahfuz), as is reported in the hadiths: that He, exalted is He, said to the Pen (al-qalam): "Write," and it wrote what will be until the Day of Resurrection.

Know that all events must be known to Allah, exalted is He. All events of this world, including creation, provision, terms, happiness, and misery, must be written in the Preserved Tablet. For if things occurred contrary to Allah's knowledge, His knowledge would turn into ignorance, and that Book would turn into falsehood. All of that is impossible. And if the matter is so, it is established that everything is by Allah's decree and destiny. Some scholars have mentioned this meaning in interpreting this verse and have confirmed it with the hadith of the truthful and believed one (ﷺ), and with the well-known hadith of his saying, peace be upon him: "Then Adam argued with Moses." The Qadi said: As for the term and provision, they are attributed to Allah. As for disbelief, wickedness, faith, and obedience, all of these are attributed to the servant. So when Allah writes that, He writes it with His knowledge of the servant's choice, and that does not remove the servant from being the one blamed or praised.

Know that it was not right for the Qadi to overlook the point of difficulty. For we say: If Allah knows from the servant disbelief and writes disbelief for him in the Preserved Tablet, then if he were to come with faith, that would be combining two contradictories. For knowledge of disbelief and a true report of disbelief together with the absence of disbelief is a combination of two contradictories, which is impossible. And if the point of the objection is this, how could fleeing from it to extraneous words that are unrelated to this objection benefit him?

* * *

As for His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Whoever desires the reward of this world, We will give him of it; and whoever desires the reward of the Hereafter, We will give him of it; and We will reward the grateful.﴾

Know that those who were present on the Day of Uhud were of two groups: some desired this world, and some desired the Hereafter, as Allah, exalted is He, mentioned later in this surah. Those who came to fight for the sake of this world were those who came seeking spoils, mention, and praise. These were bound to be defeated. Those who came for the religion were bound not to be defeated. Then Allah, exalted is He, informed in this verse that whoever seeks this world will certainly reach some of his aim, and whoever seeks the Hereafter likewise. Its confirmation is His, peace be upon him, saying: "Indeed, the deeds are by intentions," up to the end of the hadith.

Know that although this verse came concerning jihad in particular, it is general in regard to all deeds. This is because what influences the bringing about of reward and punishment is the intention and motives, not the outward appearances of deeds. For whoever places his forehead on the ground in the noon prayer while the sun is in front of him: if he intends by that prostration the worship of Allah, exalted is He, it is one of the greatest pillars of Islam; and if he intends by it the worship of the sun, it is one of the greatest pillars of disbelief. Abu Hurayrah reported from him, peace be upon him, that Allah, exalted is He, says on the Day of Resurrection to a man who fought in the way of Allah: "For what were you killed?" He says: "I was commanded to fight in Your way, so I fought until I was killed." He, exalted is He, says: "You lie. Rather, you wanted it to be said, 'So-and-so is a warrior,' and that has been said." Then Allah, exalted is He, commands that he be taken to the Fire.

[Page 22]

His saying, may He be exalted and glorified: ﴿And how many a prophet fought, along with him many devoted followers; they did not falter for what befell them in the way of God, nor did they weaken, nor did they submit. And God loves the steadfast.﴾

Know that, as part of His discipline (ta'dib) of the believers, He said to those who fled on the day of Uhud: ﴿Indeed, you have in the earlier prophets and their followers a good example.﴾ Since the way of the followers of the earlier prophets was patience in jihad and not turning away in flight, how then is this flight and defeat fitting for you? There are several issues concerning the verse:

The first issue: Ibn Kathir read "wa-ka'in" (وكائِنْ) on the pattern of "ka'in," with a long vowel, a hamza and no doubling. The others read "ka'ayyin" (كَأيِّنْ) with a doubled yod, on the pattern of "ka'ayyin," and this is the dialect of Quraysh. From the first dialect is the verse of Jarir:

"And many a friend in the valleys, who sees me, would be struck if I were struck."

Al-Mufaddal recited:

"And many a one you see in the tribe, of close kinship..."

The second issue: Ibn Kathir, Nafi' and Abu 'Amr read "qutila ma'ahu" (قُتِلَ مَعَهُ, "was killed alongside him"), and the rest read ﴿qatala ma'ahu﴾ (قاتَلَ مَعَهُ, "fought alongside him"). On the first reading, the meaning is that many of the prophets were killed, and those who remained after them did not weaken in their religion, but continued in jihad against their enemy and in supporting their religion. So it was fitting that your condition, O community of Muhammad, should be like this. Al-Qaffal, may God have mercy on him, said: the pause on this interpretation is at His saying "qutila" (قُتِلَ), and His saying ﴿ma'ahu ribbiyyun﴾ (مَعَهُ رِبِّيُّونَ) is a circumstantial clause meaning "he was killed while there were with him the ribbiyyun." Or it may be understood with inversion of order, meaning: "And how many a prophet, with him many ribbiyyun, was killed; the ribbiyyun did not weaken despite their number." There is another possibility: the meaning is "And how many a prophet was killed from among their brothers, yet they went on in jihad against their enemy. So it was fitting that your condition be likewise." The argument for this reading is that the purpose of this verse is to narrate what happened to all the prophets so that this community may follow their example, and He, may He be exalted, has said: ﴿Is it, if he dies or is killed, that you will turn back on your heels?﴾ Therefore the thing mentioned must be the killing of all the prophets, not their fighting.

As for the one who reads ﴿qatala ma'ahu﴾, the meaning is: "And how many a prophet fought alongside him a great number of his companions, and there befell them from their enemy a wound, yet they did not weaken. For what befell them was in the way of God, in His obedience, in establishing His religion and supporting His Messenger. Likewise, it was fitting that you should do the same, O community of Muhammad."

The argument for this reading is that the aim of this verse is to encourage those who were with the Prophet ﷺ in fighting, so the thing mentioned must be fighting.

Also, it is narrated from Sa'id ibn Jubayr that he said: "We have not heard of any prophet killed in battle."

The third issue: Al-Wahidi, may God have mercy on him, said: They are agreed that the meaning of "ka'ayyin" is "how many," and its interpretation is the multiplication of the number of prophets who have this description. Its parallel is His saying: ﴿So how many a town We destroyed﴾ [al-Hajj: 45] and ﴿And how many a town I gave respite to﴾ [al-Hajj: 48]. The kaf in "ka'ayyin" is the kaf of comparison, which entered upon "ayy" (أيّ), which is interrogative, just as it entered upon "dha" in "kadha" and "anna" in "ka'anna." There is no meaning of comparison in it, just as there is no meaning of comparison in "kadha." You say: "I have such-and-such (kadha wa-kadha) against him," meaning: "I have a certain number against him." So there is no meaning of comparison, except that it is an obligatory addition that may not be omitted. Know that the form of the nunation (tanwin) in writing occurs only in this letter alone. Likewise the use of this word, so it became one word established for multiplication.

The fourth issue: The author of al-Kashshaf said: "The ribbiyyun are the rabbaniyyun (the godly ones)." It was read with the three vowels, and with fatha according to analogy (al-qiyas), while the damma and kasra are alterations of the forms of the relative adjective (al-nisab). Al-Wahidi related from al-Farra' that he said: "The ribbiyyun are the first ones (al-awwaluna)." Al-Zajjaj said: "They are the large groups; the singular is ribbiyy." Ibn Qutayba said: "Its origin is from ribba, which means a group. It is said: ribbiyy, as if it were attributed to ribba." Al-Akhfash said: "The ribbiyyun are those who worship the Lord (rabb)." Tha'lab criticized this and said: "It should have been said rabbiyy, so that it would be attributed to the Lord (rabb)." Those who supported al-Akhfash replied: "When the Arabs attribute one thing to another, they change its vowel, as when they say basriyy in attribution to Basra, and dahriyy in attribution to dahr (time)." Ibn Zayd said: "The rabbaniyyun are the imams and rulers, and the ribbiyyun are the subjects, and they are those who are attributed to the Lord."

Know that He, may He be exalted, praised these ribbiyyun with two kinds: first, with attributes of negation, and second, with attributes of affirmation. As for praise by attributes of negation, it is His saying: ﴿They did not weaken for what befell them in the way of God, nor did they become feeble, nor did they submit.﴾ There is a necessity to distinguish between these three matters. The author of al-Kashshaf said: "'They did not weaken' means at the killing of the Prophet; 'nor did they become feeble' means in jihad after him; 'nor did they submit' means to the enemy. This is an allusion to what befell them of weakness and breaking at the rumor of the killing of their Messenger, and to their weakness at that time in striving against the polytheists, and their submission to the disbelievers, until they wanted to strengthen themselves with the hypocrite Abdullah ibn Ubayy, and to ask for safety from Abu Sufyan."

It is also possible to interpret "weakness" (wahn) as the seizing of fear over them, to interpret "feebleness" (du'f) as their faith becoming weak and doubts and suspicions entering their hearts, and "submission" (istikana) as the transition from their religion to the religion of their enemy. There is a third possibility, that wahn is a weakness that reaches the heart, while absolute du'f is the disruption of strength and capacity in the body, and istikana is the manifestation of that incapacity and that weakness. All these interpretations are good and possible. Al-Wahidi said: "Istikana is humility (al-khudu'), which is that one becomes quiet before his companion so that he may do what he wishes to him."

* * *

Then He, may He be exalted, said: ﴿And God loves the steadfast.﴾ The meaning is that whoever endures patiently the hardships on the path of God, and does not show anguish, incapacity, or distress, God loves him. God's love for the servant is an expression of His will to honor him, to strengthen him, and to exalt him, and to decree for him reward and Paradise, and that is the ultimate goal.

Then, Exalted is He, He followed that by praising them with attributes of steadfastness, so He said:

﴿And their saying was only that they said, "Our Lord, forgive us our sins and our excesses in our affairs, and make firm our feet, and help us against the disbelieving people."﴾

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And their saying was only that they said, "Our Lord, forgive us our sins and our excesses in our affairs, and make firm our feet, and help us against the disbelieving people."﴾ In it are two issues:

The first issue: His saying ﴿and make firm our feet﴾ indicates that the act of the servant is the creation of God, Exalted is He, whereas the Mu'tazilah interpret it as referring to the bestowal of favours (al-alṭaf, i.e., acts of divine kindness that facilitate obedience).

The second issue: God, Exalted is He, explained that they were prepared, at that time of patient endurance and steadfastness, through supplication and humble entreaty, seeking aid and assistance from God. The purpose of this is that the community of Muhammad (ﷺ) should follow them in this way, for whoever relies on himself in achieving his affairs is humbled, and whoever holds fast to God attains the sought goal. The judge (al-Qadi) said: They placed their saying ﴿Our Lord, forgive us our sins and our excesses in our affairs﴾ first because God, Exalted is He, had guaranteed victory to the believers. So when victory does not come and the signs of the enemy's domination appear, this clearly indicates that a sin and a shortcoming have proceeded from the believers. For this reason, it is obligatory upon them to give precedence to repentance and seeking forgiveness over seeking victory. God, Exalted is He, explained that they began with repentance from all sins, and this is what is meant by His saying ﴿Our Lord, forgive us our sins﴾, so that all sins are included in it, whether minor or major. Then they singled out the great and grave sins for mention after that, due to their magnitude and the magnitude of their punishment, and this is what is meant by His saying ﴿and our excesses in our affairs﴾, because excess (isrāf) in anything is going to the extreme in it. God, Exalted is He, said: ﴿Say, "O My servants who have transgressed against themselves..."﴾ [az-Zumar: 53], and He said: ﴿so let him not commit excess in killing﴾ [al-Isra': 33], and He said: ﴿Eat and drink, but do not commit excess﴾ [al-A'raf: 31]. It is said: "So-and-so is musrif" when he is extravagant in spending and otherwise. Then, when they had finished with that, they asked their Lord to make their feet firm, and that means by removing fear from their hearts and removing corrupt thoughts from their breasts. After that they asked that He help them against the disbelieving people, because this victory necessarily requires matters beyond the firmness of their feet, such as the terror He casts into their hearts and the creation of heavenly or earthly conditions that cause their defeat, like winds that stir dust into their faces, or a flood flowing through the place where they stand. Then al-Qadi said: This is a lesson from God, Exalted is He, in the manner of seeking by supplications at times of calamity and trials, whether in jihad or otherwise.

Then Allah, exalted is He, said: ﴿So Allah gave them the reward of this world and the excellent reward of the Hereafter. And Allah loves the good-doers﴾.

Know that when He, exalted is He, described the way of the Rabbiyyun (the devoted scholars) in patience and their way in supplication, He also mentioned what He guaranteed them in return, in this world and the Hereafter, saying: ﴿So Allah gave them the reward of this world and the excellent reward of the Hereafter﴾. On this there are several issues:

The first issue: His saying ﴿So Allah gave them﴾ indicates that He gave them both. As for the reward of this world, it is victory, booty, the subjugation of the enemy, good repute, the expansion of the breast with the light of faith, the removal of the darkness of doubts, and the expiation of sins and misdeeds. As for the reward of the Hereafter, there is no doubt that it is Paradise and what is in it of benefits and pleasures, all kinds of joy and honour, and that is not attained at present. So the meaning is that He, exalted is He, decreed for them that these would be attained in the Hereafter, and He placed the decree of Allah in this regard in the position of the attainment itself, just as lying in the promise of Allah and injustice in His justice are impossible. Or his saying ﴿So He gave them﴾ may be understood as meaning that He will give them, on the analogy of His saying ﴿The command of Allah has come﴾ [al-Nahl: 1], i.e. the command of Allah will come. The judge (al-Qadi) said: It is not impossible that this verse is specific to the martyrs, and Allah, exalted is He, has informed us concerning some of them that they are alive with their Lord, being provided for. So the condition of these Rabbiyyun is likewise, for at the time this verse was revealed He, exalted is He, had already given them the excellent reward of the Hereafter in the gardens of heaven.

The second issue: He, exalted is He, specified the reward of the Hereafter with the adjective "excellent" to draw attention to the greatness of their reward, because the entire reward of the Hereafter is of the utmost excellence. So when Allah specifies it as excellent within this category, consider how excellent it must be. He did not describe the reward of this world with that, because of its scarcity, its mixture with harms, and its being cut off and transient. Al-Qaffal, may Allah have mercy on him, said: It is possible that "husn" (excellence) here is in the sense of "hasan" (good), as in His saying ﴿And speak to people good (husnan)﴾ [al-Baqarah: 83], meaning "good", and the purpose of it is emphasis, as if those good things, because of their great excellence, became excellence itself, just as one says: "So-and-so is generosity and bounty" when he is at the utmost of generosity and bounty. And Allah knows best.

The third issue: He had said earlier: ﴿And whoever desires the reward of this world, We will give him of it, and whoever desires the reward of the Hereafter, We will give him of it﴾ [Al 'Imran: 145], mentioning the particle "min" (of), which indicates partiality, but in this verse He said ﴿So Allah gave them the reward of this world and the excellent reward of the Hereafter﴾ without the word "min". The difference is that those who desire the reward of the Hereafter only engage in worship seeking reward, so their rank in worship is lower. As for those mentioned in this verse, they mentioned in themselves nothing but sin and deficiency, which is the meaning of His saying ﴿Our Lord, forgive us our sins and our excesses in our affair﴾ [Al 'Imran: 147], and they saw management, victory and help only from their Lord, which is the meaning of His saying ﴿And make firm our feet and help us against the disbelieving people﴾ [Al 'Imran: 147]. So the station of these people in servitude was at the utmost perfection, and therefore those people attained some of the reward, while these attained all of it. Also, those people desired the reward, whereas these did not desire the reward; they desired only to serve their Master. Therefore those were deprived and these were given, so that it may be known that whoever turns to serving Allah, everything other than Allah turns to serving him.

* * *

Then He said: ﴿And Allah loves the good-doers﴾. In this there is a subtle point: these people acknowledged that they were wrongdoers when they said ﴿Our Lord, forgive us our sins and our excesses in our affair﴾. When they acknowledged that, Allah named them good-doers, as if Allah, exalted is He, were saying to them: When you acknowledge your wrongdoing and your helplessness, I describe you with excellence and make you a beloved to Myself, so that you know there is no way for the servant to reach the presence of Allah except by displaying humility, need and helplessness. Also: when they wished to advance into jihad, they asked from Allah, exalted is He, to make their feet firm in His religion and to grant them victory over the enemy, and at that point He named them "the good-doers". This indicates that the servant cannot perform a good act unless Allah gives him that good act and helps him to it. Then He, exalted is He, said: ﴿Is the reward of good other than good?﴾ [al-Rahman: 60], and said: ﴿For those who did good is the best (reward) and more﴾ [Yunus: 26]. All of this indicates that it is He, glorified is He, who gives the servant the good act, and then rewards him for it, so that the servant knows that all of it is from Allah and by the help of Allah.

O you who have believed, if you obey those who disbelieve, they will turn you back on your heels, and you will become losers. Rather, Allah is your Protector, and He is the best of helpers.

Know that this verse is a continuation of the previous discourse, because when the disbelievers spread the rumour that the Prophet ﷺ had been killed, and the hypocrites called some of the weak among the Muslims to disbelief, Allah prevented the Muslims through this verse from paying attention to the words of those hypocrites. So He said: ﴿O you who have believed, if you obey those who disbelieve﴾. There are several issues concerning the verse:

The first issue: It has been said that by ﴿those who disbelieve﴾ is meant Abu Sufyan, for he was the leader of the people on that day. al-Suddi said: What is meant is Abu Sufyan, because he was the tree of strife (shajarat al-fitan). Others said: What is meant is Abdullah ibn Ubayy and his followers from among the hypocrites, who cast doubts into the hearts of the weak and said: "If Muhammad were a messenger of Allah, this calamity would not have befallen him. He is only a man like other men: a day for him and a day against him. So return to your religion in which you were." Others said: What is meant is the Jews, because there was in Medina a group of Jews who used to cast doubt into the hearts of the Muslims, especially when this calamity occurred. The closer view is that it encompasses all disbelievers, because the wording is general, and the specific occasion of revelation does not prevent the generality of the wording.

The second issue: The statement ﴿if you obey those who disbelieve﴾ cannot be taken to mean obeying them in everything they say; rather, it must be restricted. It has been said: if you obey them in what they command you on the day of Uhud of abandoning Islam. It has been said: if you obey them in everything they command you of misguidance. It has been said: in consultation. It has been said: in abandoning fighting, which is their saying: [﴿If they had been with us, they would not have died or been killed﴾].

* * *

Then He said: ﴿they will turn you back on your heels﴾, meaning they will return you to disbelief after belief, because accepting their words in calling to disbelief is disbelief.

* * *

Then He said: ﴿and you will become losers﴾.
Know that since the wording is general, it must include the loss of this world and the Hereafter. As for the loss of this world, it is because the hardest thing for the intelligent in this world is submitting to the enemy, humbling oneself before him, and showing need of him. As for the loss of the Hereafter, it is deprivation of everlasting reward and falling into everlasting punishment.

* * *

Then the Exalted said: ﴿Rather, Allah is your Protector, and He is the best of helpers﴾. The meaning is that you obey the disbelievers so that they may help you and assist you in your aims, and this is ignorance, because they are powerless and bewildered, whereas the intelligent person seeks help from Allah, the Exalted, for He is the One who gives you victory over the enemy and repels his plotting from you. Then He clarified that He is the best of helpers. Had the intended meaning of His saying ﴿your Protector, and He is the best of helpers﴾ not been help, it would not have been correct to follow it with this statement. The Exalted is the best of helpers for several reasons:
The first: He, the Exalted, is the One capable of helping you in everything you desire, the Knower to whom your supplication and humbling are not hidden, and the Generous who does not withhold in His bounty; the help of servants for one another differs from this in all these respects.

The second: He helps you in this world and the Hereafter, whereas others are not like that.

The third: He helps you before you ask and before you know your need, as He said: ﴿Say, who protects you by night and day?﴾ [al-Anbiya': 42], whereas others are not like that.

Know that His saying ﴿and He is the best of helpers﴾ outwardly implies that He is of the same kind as the other helpers, and He is far exalted above that; but the speech came according to their customary usage, as in His saying: ﴿And it is easier for Him﴾ [al-Rum: 27].

The first: He, the Exalted, is the One capable of helping you in everything you desire, the Knower to whom your supplication and humbling are not hidden, and the Generous who does not withhold in His bounty; the help of servants for one another differs from this in all these respects.

The second: He helps you in this world and the Hereafter, whereas others are not like that.

The third: He helps you before you ask and before you know your need, as He said: ﴿Say, who protects you by night and day?﴾ [al-Anbiya': 42], whereas others are not like that.

Know that His saying ﴿and He is the best of helpers﴾ outwardly implies that He is of the same kind as the other helpers, and He is far exalted above that; but the speech came according to their customary usage, as in His saying: ﴿And it is easier for Him﴾ [al-Rum: 27].

**[p. 27]**

The statement of the Exalted: ﴿We shall cast terror into the hearts of those who disbelieved, because they associated with God that for which He had sent down no authority; their refuge is the Fire, and wretched is the abode of the wrongdoers.﴾

Know that this verse is part of what preceded it, for the Exalted mentioned many aspects of encouragement to jihad and of not caring about the disbelievers. Among them is what He mentions in this verse: that He, the Exalted, casts fear into the hearts of the disbelievers. There is no doubt that this necessitates the Muslims' gaining mastery over them. There are several issues in the verse:

**The first issue:** The scholars differed over whether this promise is specific to the Day of Uhud or general for all times. Many of the exegetes (mufassirun) said that it is specific to this day, because all the preceding verses were revealed concerning this event. Then those who held this view mentioned two explanations of how terror was cast into the hearts of the polytheists on this day:

The first: When the disbelievers gained control over the Muslims and defeated them, God cast terror into their hearts, so they abandoned them and fled from them without any cause. It is related that Abu Sufyan climbed the mountain and said: "Where is the son of Abu Kabsha? Where is the son of Abu Quhafa? Where is the son of al-Khattab?" 'Umar answered him, and words passed between them, but Abu Sufyan did not dare to come down from the mountain and go to them.

The second: When the disbelievers went back to Mecca, and when they were part of the way, they said: "We have done nothing. We killed most of them, then we left them while we were dominant. Return so that we may utterly eradicate them." When they resolved upon this, God cast terror into their hearts.

The second view: This promise is not specific to the Day of Uhud, but is general. al-Qaffal, may God have mercy on him, said: "It is as if it were said: although this event happened to you on the Day of Uhud, God, the Exalted, will cast terror of you into the hearts of the unbelievers after that, until He overcomes the disbelievers and makes your religion prevail over all other religions. God has done that, until the religion of Islam became dominant over all religions and creeds. A parallel to this verse is his saying, peace be upon him: 'I have been supported with terror over a distance of a month's journey.'"

**The second issue:** Ibn 'Amir and al-Kisa'i read (al-ru'ub) with a dammah on the ʿayn, while the rest read it with a sukun in all of the Qur'an. al-Wahidi said: "They are two dialects. It is said: ra'abtuhu ru'ban and ru'uban, and he is marg'ub (terrified). It is permissible that ar-ru'b be a maṣdar (verbal noun), and ar-ru'ub be a noun derived from it."

**The third issue:** ar-ru'b is the fear that arises in the heart. The root meaning of ar-ru'b is filling. It is said: "sayl ra'ib" when it fills the valleys and rivers. Fear is called ru'b only because it fills the heart with dread.

**The fourth issue:** The apparent meaning of His saying ﴿We shall cast terror into the hearts of those who disbelieved﴾ requires that terror befall all the disbelievers. Some scholars took this generality in its apparent sense, because no one opposes the religion of Islam without having within his heart some kind of terror of the Muslims, either in war or at the time of argument.

However, His saying ﴿We shall cast terror into the hearts of those who disbelieved﴾ does not require that all kinds of terror fall into the hearts of the disbelievers; it only requires that this reality occur in their hearts in some respects. A group of the exegetes held that it is restricted to those disbelievers.

As for His saying ﴿because they associated with God﴾: know that the ma here is maṣdariyya (verbal-noun forming), and the meaning is: "because of their associating partners with God."

Know that the rational explanation of this is that supplication only becomes answerable at the time of distress, as He said: ﴿Who responds to the distressed one when he calls upon Him?﴾ [al-Naml: 62]. Whoever believes that God has a partner does not reach a state of distress, because he says: "If this worshipped one does not help me, then that other one helps me." And if distress does not arise in his heart, then answer and help do not come. When that does not happen, terror and fear must arise in his heart. Thus it is established that associating partners with God necessitates terror.

As for His saying ﴿for which He had sent down no authority﴾, there are several issues in it:

**The first issue:** Sultan (authority) here means proof and evidence. Concerning its derivation there are several views:

The first: al-Zajjaj said: it is from as-saliṭ, which is that by which a lamp is lit. Rulers are called salatin (sultans) because they are those through whom people reach the attainment of their rights.

The second: Sultan in the language means proof, and a ruler is called sultan only because its meaning is that he possesses proof.

The third: al-Layth said: sultan means power, because the origin of its formation is from tasliṭ (empowerment). Accordingly, the sultan of a king is his strength and power, and evidence is called sultan because of its strength in repelling falsehood.

The fourth: Ibn Duraid said: the sultan of everything is its sharpness, and it is taken from the sharp tongue (lisan salit), and salaṭa means sharpness.

**The second issue:** His saying ﴿for which He had sent down no authority﴾ suggests that there is an authority in it, except that God did not send it down or make it manifest. The answer to this is that if it existed, God would have sent down authority concerning it. Since He did not send down authority concerning it, its non-existence is necessary. The essence of the matter, as the theologians (mutakallimun) say, is that this is something for which there is no evidence, so it is not permissible to affirm it. Some of them go to an extreme and say: there is no evidence for it, so it must be negated. Among them are those who used this phrase as an argument for the oneness of the Creator, saying: there is no way to establish the Creator except through the need of created things for Him, and the establishment of one Creator suffices to remove this need; whatever exceeds that, there is no way to establish it, so it is not permissible to affirm it.

**The third issue:** This verse indicates the invalidity of blind imitation (taqlid), because the verse indicates that associating partners with God has no evidence for it, so it must be that the claim of it is false. This is only valid if the claim of affirming what has no evidence for its establishment is false, and it follows that the position of blind imitation is invalid.

* * *

Then He, the Exalted, said: ﴿And their refuge is the Fire﴾.

Know that He, the Exalted, has explained that the condition of these polytheists in this world is the occurrence of fear in their hearts, and He has explained their condition in the Hereafter, which is that their refuge and dwelling is the Fire.

* * *

Then He said: ﴿and wretched is the abode of the wrongdoers﴾. Al-mathwa (abode) is the place which is a person's residence and refuge, from their saying: thawa yathwi thawiyyan. The plural of al-mathwa is mathawin.

**[p. 28]**

[Page 29]

**The Exalted One said:** ﴿Allah had certainly fulfilled His promise to you when you were killing them by His permission, until when you lost courage and disputed about the matter and disobeyed after He had shown you what you love. Among you are those who desire this world, and among you are those who desire the Hereafter. Then He turned you away from them to test you. And He has certainly pardoned you; and Allah is bounteous to the believers.﴾

Know that the connection of this verse with what precedes it is in several respects:

The first: "When the Messenger of Allah ﷺ and his Companions returned to Madinah, after what had befallen them at Uhud, some of his Companions said: 'How has this befallen us when Allah promised us victory?!' So Allah the Exalted revealed this verse."

The second: Some of them said: "The Prophet ﷺ had seen in a dream that he was slaughtering a ram, and Allah made his dream come true by the killing of Talhah ibn ʿUthman, the standard-bearer of the polytheists, on the day of Uhud. After him, nine men were killed around the banner. This is what is meant by His saying: ﴿Allah had certainly fulfilled His promise to you﴾, meaning the fulfilment of the Messenger's ﷺ dream."

The third: It is possible that this promise is what He mentioned in His saying: ﴿Yes! If you are patient and fear Allah, and they come upon you suddenly, your Lord will reinforce you﴾ (Āl ʿImrān: 125), except that this was conditional upon the condition of patience and piety.

The fourth: It is possible that this promise is His saying: ﴿Allah will surely help those who help Him﴾, except that this too is conditional upon a condition.

The fifth: It is possible that this promise is His saying: ﴿We shall cast terror into the hearts of those who disbelieve﴾ (Āl ʿImrān: 151).

The sixth: It has been said: the promise is that the Prophet ﷺ said to the archers: "Do not leave this place, for we will not cease to be victorious as long as you remain in this place."

The seventh: Abu Muslim said: When Allah promised them in the preceding verse the casting of terror into their hearts, He confirmed that by reminding them of what He had fulfilled of the promise of victory in the event of Uhud. For when He promised them victory on the condition that they fear Allah and be patient, then when they fulfilled that condition, Allah the Exalted, without doubt, fulfilled the conditioned promise and gave them victory. But when they abandoned the condition, without doubt the conditioned promise was lost to them.

Now that you know the connection of the arrangement, there are several issues concerning the verse.

**Issue one:** al-Wahidi, may Allah have mercy on him, said: *al-ṣidq* (to be truthful/fulfil) takes two objects; you say: "I fulfilled him the promise and the threat" (ṣadaqtuhu al-waʿda wal-waʿīd).

**Issue two:** We have mentioned in the story of Uhud that the Prophet ﷺ placed Uhud behind his back, faced Madinah, and stationed the archers at the mountain, and ordered them to hold their position there and not leave, whether the victory was for the Muslims or against them. When the polytheists advanced, the archers began shooting their arrows, and the rest struck them with swords until they were routed, and the Muslims were on their heels, *yaḥussūnahum* (cutting them down). Al-Layth said: *al-ḥass* is the devastating killing. *Taḥussūnahum* means: you kill them in great numbers. Abu ʿUbayd, al-Zajjaj and Ibn Qutaybah said: *al-ḥass* is the complete eradication by killing; one says: "locust that has been *maḥsūs*" when the cold has destroyed it, and "a *ḥasūs* year" when it has affected everything. The meaning of *taḥussūnahum* is: you eradicate them by killing. The scholars of etymology said: *ḥassahu* means he killed him, because he nullified his sense (*ḥiss*) by killing, just as one says: *baṭanahu* (he struck his belly) if he hit his belly, and *raʾsahu* (he struck his head) if he hit his head. His saying *bi-idhnihi* means "by His knowledge." The sense of the speech is that when He promised you victory on the condition of piety and patience in obedience, then as long as you fulfilled this condition He fulfilled His promise and gave you victory over your enemies. But when you abandoned the condition and disobeyed the command of your Lord, without doubt that victory ceased.

\* \* \*

As for His saying: ﴿until when you lost courage and disputed about the matter and disobeyed after He had shown you what you love﴾, there are several issues:

**Issue one:** One may say: the apparent meaning of His saying ﴿until when you lost courage﴾ functions like a conditional clause, and it needs an answer. Where is its answer?

Know that the scholars have two approaches here:

The first: This is not a conditional clause. Rather the meaning is: ﴿Allah had certainly fulfilled His promise to you﴾ *until* (*ḥattā*, meaning "up to") *when you lost courage*; that is, He gave you victory up to the point at which there was among you cowardice and dispute. For He promised them victory only on the condition of piety and patience in obedience; so when they lost courage and disobeyed, the victory ended. According to this view, the word *ḥattā* is a limit meaning "up to," so that the phrase *ḥattā idhā* means "until" or "up to the time that."

The second approach: One may hold that ﴿until when you lost courage﴾ is a conditional clause. On this view, the scholars differ regarding the answer, in several ways:

The first, which is the view of the Basrans, is that its answer is omitted, and the estimated sense is: "until when you lost courage and disputed about the matter and disobeyed after He had shown you what you love, Allah withheld His victory from you." The omission of this answer is good because of the indication of His saying ﴿Allah had certainly fulfilled His promise to you﴾ upon it. Its parallels in the Qur'an are many. He the Exalted said: ﴿So if you are able to seek a tunnel in the earth or a ladder into the sky to bring them a sign…﴾ (al-Anʿām: 35), and the estimated sense is: then do it. The answer was dropped because the speech indicates it. And He said: ﴿Is one who is devoutly obedient during the hours of the night…﴾ (al-Zumar: 9), and the estimated sense is: is he [the same] as one who is not like that?

The second answer, which is the view of the Kufans and the choice of al-Farrāʾ, is that its answer is His saying *wa-ʿaṣaytum* ("and you disobeyed"), and the *wāw* is superfluous, as He said: ﴿So when they had both submitted and he put him down upon his forehead﴾ and ﴿We called out to him﴾ (al-Ṣāffāt: 103–104). The meaning is "We called out to him." Likewise here: the loss of courage and the dispute became a cause for disobedience, so the estimated sense is: "until when you lost courage and disputed about the matter, you disobeyed," and the *wāw* is superfluous. Some of those who supported this view claimed that it is the practice of the Arabs to place the *wāw* in the answer of *ḥattā idhā*, based on His saying: ﴿until when they came to it, its gates were opened and its keepers said to them…﴾ (al-Zumar: 73), and the estimated sense is: "until when they came to it, its gates were opened for them."

If it is said: "Losing courage and disputing" is itself disobedience, so if we make the loss of courage and the dispute a cause of disobedience, it would follow that a thing is a cause of itself, and that is invalid.

We reply: What is meant by disobedience here is their departure from that place. Without doubt, it was the loss of courage and the dispute that made them leave that place, so it does not follow that a thing is explained by itself.

Know that the Basrans did not accept this answer only because their doctrine is that it is not permissible to treat the *wāw* as superfluous.

The third answer: It may be said that the estimated sense of the verse is: "until when you lost courage and disputed about the matter and disobeyed after He had shown you what you love, you became two groups: among you are those who desire this world, and among you are those who desire the Hereafter."

So the answer is His saying "you became two groups," but it was dropped because His saying ﴿Among you are those who desire this world, and among you are those who desire the Hereafter﴾ conveys its meaning and fulfils its sense, since the word *man* ("those who") is for partition, so it indicates this division. This is a possibility that occurred to my mind.

The fourth answer: Abu Muslim said: the answer to His saying ﴿until when you lost courage﴾ is His saying ﴿then He turned you away from them﴾, and the estimated sense is: "until when you lost courage and so on and so forth, He turned you away from them to test you." The word *thumma* ("then") here is as though it were superfluous. This view is extremely far-fetched. And Allah knows best.

**Issue two:** He the Exalted mentioned three matters:

The first is *al-fashal*, which is weakness. It has also been said that *al-fashal* is cowardice, but this is invalid, by the evidence of His saying: ﴿and do not dispute, lest you lose courage﴾ (al-Anfāl: 46), meaning: lest you become weak; for it is not fitting that the meaning should be: lest you become cowardly.

The second is the dispute about the matter, and concerning it there are two discussions:

The first discussion: What is meant by the dispute is that the Prophet ﷺ, peace be upon him, ordered the archers not to leave their place at all, and appointed as their commander ʿAbdullah ibn Jubayr. When the polytheists were defeated, the archers turned upon them with a great volley of arrows until the polytheists were routed. Then the archers saw the women of the polytheists climbing the mountain and uncovering their thighs, so that their anklets were visible. They said: "The booty! The booty!" ʿAbdullah said: "The Messenger ﷺ charged us that we must not leave this place." But they refused him and went off to seek the booty, and ʿAbdullah remained with a small group, fewer than ten, until the polytheists killed them. This is the dispute.

The second discussion: His saying *fī al-amr* ("about the matter") has two possible meanings:

The first: *al-amr* here means "the situation" or "the affair," that is, you disputed about what you were in of the situation.

The second: It is the command, which is opposed by the prohibition. The meaning is: you disputed about what the Messenger had commanded you regarding remaining in that place.

The third is: "and you disobeyed after He had shown you what you love." The meaning is that you disobeyed by abandoning remaining in that place.

Questions remain concerning this verse:

**First question:** Why did He mention the loss of courage before the dispute and the disobedience?

The answer: When the people saw the defeat of the unbelievers and became eager for the booty, they lost courage within themselves about holding firm, out of desire for the booty. Then they disputed among themselves by way of speech, saying: "Shall we go to seek the booty or not?" Then they occupied themselves with seeking the booty.

**Second question:** Since the disobedience through leaving those positions was specific to some of them, why did this rebuke come in general terms?

The answer: Although this wording is general, what follows it specifies it, namely His saying ﴿Among you are those who desire this world, and among you are those who desire the Hereafter﴾.

**Third question:** What is the benefit of His saying ﴿after He had shown you what you love﴾?

The answer to this: its purpose is to draw attention to the gravity of the disobedience. For when they witnessed that Allah the Exalted had honoured them by fulfilling the promise, it was their duty to refrain from disobedience; but when they went ahead with it, without doubt Allah deprived them of that honour and made them taste the evil consequence of their affair.

\* \* \*

Then He the Exalted said: ﴿Then He turned you away from them to test you﴾. The opinions of our companions (the Ashʿarite theologians) and of the Muʿtazila (the rationalist school) differ regarding the interpretation of this verse, because turning away from the unbelievers is a disobedience, so how did He attribute it to Himself? As for our companions, this problem does not arise for them, because their doctrine is that good and evil are by the will of Allah and His creation. On this basis they said: the meaning of this turning away is that Allah the Exalted turned the Muslims back from the unbelievers, cast defeat upon them, and gave the unbelievers power over them. This is the view of the majority of the exegetes. The Muʿtazila said: this interpretation is not permissible, and the Qur'an and reason indicate this. As for the Qur'an, it is His saying: ﴿Indeed, those of you who turned away on the day the two hosts met, it was only Satan who caused them to slip because of some of what they had earned﴾ (Āl ʿImrān: 155). So He attributed what came from them to the action of Satan. How then would He attribute it to Himself after this? As for reason, He the Exalted rebuked them for that withdrawal, and if it were by the action of Allah, it would not be permissible to rebuke the people for it, just as it is not permissible to rebuke them for their tallness or shortness, their health or sickness. Then, at this point, they mentioned several interpretations:

The first: al-Jubba'i said: The archers were two groups. Some of them left the place first in pursuit of the spoils, and some of them remained there. Then those who remained were surrounded by the enemy; if they had persisted in staying there, the enemy would have killed them with no benefit at all. For this reason it was permissible for them to withdraw from that place to a place where they could protect themselves from the enemy. Do you not see that the Prophet ﷺ went up the mountain with a group of his Companions and they took refuge in it, and they were not disobedient by doing so? So since that withdrawal was permissible, He attributed it to Himself in the sense that it was by His command and permission. Then He said: ﴿to test you﴾, and the meaning is that when He turned them to that place and they took refuge in it, He commanded them there to fight and to defend the rest of the Muslims. Without doubt, undertaking the fight after the rout, and after they had witnessed in that battle the killing of their relatives and loved ones, is among the greatest kinds of trial.

If it is said: "On this interpretation, those whom Allah turned away from the disbelievers were not sinners, so why did He say: ﴿And certainly He pardoned you﴾?"

We say: The verse includes mention of those who were excused in turning away and those who were not. Those who began the rout, fled, and disobeyed are the ones concerned. So His saying ﴿Then He turned you away from them﴾ refers to those who were excused, because the verse, when it contains two groups and two rulings, has each ruling returned to the group it befits. A parallel to this is His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿The second of two, when they were both in the cave, when he said to his companion, "Do not grieve; indeed Allah is with us." So Allah sent down His tranquility upon him﴾ [At-Tawbah: 40]. The one addressed with "Do not grieve" is Abu Bakr, because he had been fearful before this statement, and when he heard it he calmed down. Then He said: ﴿And supported him with soldiers you did not see﴾ [At-Tawbah: 40], and by that He meant the Messenger, not Abu Bakr, since both had been mentioned together. This is the sum of what al-Jubba'i mentioned on this point.

The second opinion is what Abu Muslim al-Isfahani mentioned: that the meaning of His saying ﴿Then He turned you away from them﴾ is that He removed from the hearts of the disbelievers the terror of the Muslims, as a punishment from Him for their disobedience and cowardice. Then He said: ﴿so that He might test you﴾, meaning, that He made that turning away a trial for you, so that you would repent to Allah, return to Him, and seek His forgiveness for what you opposed of His command and inclined toward in pursuit of booty. Then He informed them that He had pardoned them.

The third opinion: al-Ka'bi said: ﴿Then He turned you away from them﴾ means that He did not command you to return to them immediately, ﴿so that He might test you﴾ with an abundance of favor upon you and lightening of burdens for you. This is what has been said on this point, and Allah knows best.

* * *

Then He said: ﴿And certainly He pardoned you﴾. Its apparent meaning requires that a sin had preceded from them. The judge (al-Qadi) said: If that sin was among the minor sins, it is valid for Him to describe Himself as having pardoned them without repentance; but if it was among the major sins, then their repentance must be implied, because of the evidence that the person who commits a major sin and does not repent is not among those deserving pardon and forgiveness.

Know that there is no doubt the sin was a major sin, because they opposed the clear text of the Messenger, that opposition became a cause of the Muslims' defeat and the killing of a great number of their elders, and it is known that all of this is of the category of major sins. Also, the apparent meaning of His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And whoever turns his back to them on that day﴾ [Al-Anfal: 16] indicates that it is a major sin. The statement of whoever says that it was specific to Badr is weak, because the wording is general and there is no difference in the intended meaning, so specification is impermissible. Furthermore, the apparent meaning of this verse indicates that He pardoned them without repentance, since repentance is not mentioned.
