This becomes evidence that He may pardon the people of major sins. As for the Mu'tazilah's proof against that, the answer to it has already been given in Surat al-Baqarah.

* * *

Then He said: ﴿And Allah is full of bounty toward the believers﴾. This refers back to what preceded of the mention of His favors, Glorified and Exalted is He, first by granting victory, then by pardoning the sinners second. This verse indicates that the person who commits a major sin is a believer, because we have shown that this sin was among the major sins, and then He named them "the believers." This requires that the person who commits a major sin is a believer, unlike what the Mu'tazilah say. And Allah knows best.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 3, verse 153:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿When you were climbing and not turning aside for anyone, while the Messenger was calling you from behind you, so He rewarded you with grief upon grief, so that you would not grieve over what had escaped you nor over what had befallen you. And Allah is Aware of what you do.﴾

In this there are two opinions.

The first: it is connected to what precedes it. On this reading there are several possibilities:

The first: it is as if He said, "And He pardoned you when you were climbing," because His pardon must relate to some deed they committed, and that deed is what He explained by His saying "when you were climbing." What is meant is their departure from that place and their taking to the valley like fleeing people who do not turn aside for anyone.

The second: the implied sense is, "Then He turned you away from them when you were climbing."

The third: the implied sense is, "In order to test you when you were climbing."

The second opinion: it is the beginning of a new statement with no connection to what precedes it, the implied sense being, "Remember when you were climbing."

There are issues concerning the verse:

The first issue: The author of al-Kashshaf said: al-Hasan recited (when you were climbing into the mountain), Ubayy recited (when you were climbing into the valley), and Abu Haywa recited (when you were tasa"ʻadūn), with a fatha on the ta' and a shadda on the ʻayn, from taṣaʻʻada (to climb) on a ladder.

The second issue: al-ith'ād (ascending) is going off into the land and moving far away in it. One says ṣaʻida fi al-jabal (he climbed the mountain) and aṣʻada fi al-ard (he went far into the land), and one says aṣʻadnā min Makkah ilā al-Madīnah (we went up from Makkah to Madinah). Abu Mu'adh al-Nahwi said: every thing that has a bottom and a top, such as a valley, a river, or an alley, one says ṣaʻʻada fulān yuṣaʻʻidu fi al-wādī when he goes from its bottom up to its top. As for what rises, like a ladder, one says ṣaʻidtu.

The third issue: wa-lā talwūna ʻalā aḥad: that is, you do not turn your attention to anyone out of intense flight. Its origin is that one who pauses over something turns his neck or the rein of his mount toward it; when he passes on without pausing, it is said, "he did not turn to it" (lam yalwihi). Then laww (turning) was used for abandoning a pause over something and abandoning attention to something. One says: fulān lā yalwī ʻalā shay', meaning he does not incline toward it nor care for it.

* * *

Then He, exalted is He, said: ﴿while the Messenger was calling you﴾. He used to say: "To me, servants of Allah! I am the Messenger of Allah; whoever turns back, for him is Paradise." It is possible that what is meant is that he, peace be upon him, was calling them to himself so that they would gather around him and not scatter; and it is possible that what is meant is that he was calling them to fight the enemy.

* * *

Then He said: ﴿from behind you﴾, meaning from the back of you. One says: I came at the end of the people and their last part (akhrāhum), just as one says at their beginning and their first part (ūlāhum). And one says: so-and-so came among the last of the people (ukhrayāt al-nās), meaning their last. The meaning is that he, peace be upon him, was calling them while standing at the rear of them, because the people, by reason of the defeat, had gone ahead of him.

* * *

Then He said: ﴿so He rewarded you with grief upon grief﴾. On this there are issues:

The first issue: the word thawāb (reward) is in most usage not employed except for good, but it is also permissible to use it for evil, because it is derived from their saying thāba ilayhi ʻaqluhu, meaning his reason returned to him. He, exalted is He, said: ﴿And when We made the House a place of return (mathābah) for the people﴾ [al-Baqarah: 125]. A woman is called thayyib because the one who has intercourse with her returns to her. The origin of thawāb is whatever returns to the doer as the recompense of his action, whether good or bad; however, by convention the word thawāb has become restricted to good. If we take the word thawāb here in its original linguistic sense, the statement is sound; if we take it according to conventional usage, it comes as sarcasm, as one says: your greeting is a blow, and your rebuke is the sword, meaning He placed grief in the place of the reward they hoped for. He, exalted is He, said: ﴿So give them the tidings of a painful punishment﴾ [Al 'Imran: 21].

The second issue: the bāʼ in His saying (grief upon grief) may mean exchange, as one says: this for that, meaning this is a substitute for that. It may also mean "with" (maʻa), so the sense is: He rewarded them with grief together with grief. As for the first reading, there are several possibilities:

The first, which is the saying of al-Zajjaj: when you caused the Messenger grief by disobeying his command, Allah, exalted is He, made you taste this grief, namely the grief that befell them because of the flight and the killing of their beloved ones. The meaning is that He repaid them for that grief with this grief.

The second: al-Hasan said: He means the grief of the day of Uhud for the Muslims in exchange for the grief of the day of Badr for the polytheists. The purpose of this is that no attachment to the world should remain in your hearts, so you do not rejoice at its coming nor grieve at its departure; this is what is meant by His saying: ﴿so that you do not despair over what has escaped you﴾ [al-Hadid: 23] concerning the event of Uhud, and ﴿nor exult in what He has given you﴾ [al-Hadid: 23] concerning the event of Badr. The judge (al-Qadi) criticized this view and said: their grief on the day of Uhud came from the domination of the disbelievers, and that is disbelief and disobedience, so how does Allah attribute it to Himself? It may be answered that it is not far-fetched that Allah, exalted is He, knows that in the empowerment of the disbelievers over the Muslims there is a kind of benefit, namely that they do not rejoice at the coming of the world nor grieve at its departure, so no preoccupation with other than Allah remains in their hearts.

The third: it is permissible that the pronoun in His saying (so He rewarded you) refers to the Messenger. The meaning is that when the Companions saw that the Prophet ﷺ had his face wounded, his incisor broken, and his uncle killed, they grieved for his sake; and when the Messenger, peace be upon him, saw that they had disobeyed their Lord in pursuit of booty, and then remained deprived of the booty, and their relatives were killed, he grieved for their sake. So the meaning of His saying ﴿so He rewarded you with grief upon grief﴾ is this. As for the second reading, that the bāʼ in His saying (grief upon grief) means "with" (maʻa), i.e., grief together with grief, or grief upon grief, this is permissible, because prepositions may stand in place of one another. You say: ma ziltu bihi ḥattā faʻala (I did not cease with him until he did), and ma ziltu maʻahu ḥattā faʻala; and you say: nazaltu bi-Banī Fulān and ʻalā Banī Fulān.

Know that the griefs there were many:

The first: their grief over what they suffered from the enemy in their persons and property.

The second: their grief over what befell the rest of the believers of that.

The third: their grief over what reached the Messenger of the wound and the breaking of the incisor.

The fourth: what was rumored about the killing of the Messenger ﷺ.

The fifth: what they had committed of disobedience and what they feared of its punishment.

The sixth: their grief because of the repentance that became obligatory upon them, for when they repented of that disobedience, their repentance would not be complete except by abandoning the flight and returning to fighting after the defeat, and that is among the most difficult things, because a person after becoming defeated becomes weak of heart and cowardly; when he is commanded to return, if he does so he fears death, and if he does not, he fears disbelief or the punishment of the Hereafter. This grief is undoubtedly the greatest of griefs and sorrows. Having understood this whole matter, each of the exegetes explained this verse by one of these aspects, and we shall enumerate them:

The first aspect: the first grief is what befell them at the time of cowardice and dispute, and the second grief is what occurred at the defeat.

The second aspect: the first grief was caused by the loss of the spoils, and the second grief was caused by Abu Sufyan and Khalid ibn al-Walid coming upon the Muslims, so they attacked them and killed a great number of them.

The third aspect: the first grief was at the approach of Abu Sufyan and Khalid ibn al-Walid against them to kill them, and the second grief was that when the polytheists returned, the rest of the Muslims feared that if they returned they would kill them all, so this grief became such that it distracted them from the first grief.

The fourth aspect: the first grief reached them because of their persons and property, and the second grief reached them because of the rumor of the killing of the Prophet ﷺ.

In the verse there is a third opinion, chosen by al-Qaffal, may Allah have mercy on him, who said: In our view, Allah, exalted is He, did not intend by His saying "grief upon grief" two griefs; rather He intended the continuation of griefs and their length, meaning that Allah punished you with many griefs, such as the killing of your brothers and relatives, the descent of the polytheists upon you from above the mountain, such that you did not feel safe that most of you would perish, and such as your undertaking disobedience. So it is as if He, exalted is He, said: He rewarded you with these successive griefs so that this would be a deterrent for you from undertaking disobedience and occupying yourselves with what opposes the command of Allah, exalted is He.

The third issue: the meaning of Allah rewarding them with grief upon grief is that He created grief in them. As for the Mu'tazilah, this does not befit their principles, so they mentioned several reasons for this attribution:

The first: al-Ka'bi said: when the hypocrites spread the rumor that Muhammad, peace be upon him, had been killed, and Allah did not make clear the falsity of that speaker, it became as if He Himself had done that grief. This is like a man who receives news that grieves him while someone with him knows that this news is false; if he does not quickly reveal it to him, and leaves him to ponder it before informing him, he says to him: "You have grieved me and prolonged my sorrow," though he did nothing of that, but rather kept silent and refrained from informing him. So it is here too.

The second: even though the grief is from the act of the servant, its cause is the act of Allah, exalted is He, because Allah created the servants with a nature that they grieve at the calamities that befall them, and they are neither praised nor blamed for that.

The third: it is not far-fetched that Allah, exalted is He, creates grief in the heart of some of the responsible persons for the sake of preserving some interests.

* * *

Then He, exalted is He, said: ﴿so that you would not grieve﴾. In this there are two views:

The first: it is connected to His saying: ﴿And He had certainly pardoned you﴾, as if He said: "And He had certainly pardoned you so that you would not grieve," because in His pardon, exalted is He, there is what removes every grief and sorrow.

The second: the lam is connected to His saying "so He rewarded you." On this view they mentioned several aspects:

The first: al-Zajjaj said: the meaning is: He rewarded you with the grief of the defeat in exchange for your grief over the Prophet ﷺ because of your opposition to him, so that your grief would be only over having opposed him, not over the loss of the spoils and the befalling of the defeat. This is because the grief arising from committing disobedience makes one forget the grief arising from the calamities of this world.

The second: al-Hasan said: He made you grieved on the day of Uhud in return for your having made them grieved on the day of Badr, so that the matter of this world would become easy in your eyes, so you would not grieve over its loss nor rejoice over its coming. These two aspects are based on our saying that the bāʼ in His saying "grief upon grief" is for recompense. As for when we say that it means "with" (maʻa), the meaning is that you said: "If we had remained in this place and obeyed the command of the Messenger, we would have fallen into the grief of losing the spoils." So know that when you disobeyed the command of the Messenger and sought the spoils, you fell into these great griefs, each one of which is many times greater than that grief. When a sensible person faces two harms, he must give priority in repelling the greater of them. Thus the reward of grief upon grief became a barrier for you from grieving over the loss of the spoils, and a deterrent for you from that. Then, just as He deterred them from that disobedience through this deterrence which occurs in this world, He deterred them from it through the deterrents present in the spoils, saying: ﴿And Allah is Aware of what you do﴾, meaning He is knowing of all your deeds, intentions, and motives, and capable of recompensing them: if good, then good, and if evil, then evil. This is among the greatest deterrents for the servant from undertaking disobedience. And Allah knows best.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 3, verse 154 (part 1 of 2):

Regarding the manner of the arrangement (naẓm, the coherence linking this verse to what precedes it), there are two views:

The first: When Allah promised the believers victory over the disbelievers, and this victory must be preceded by the removal of fear from the believers, He explained in this verse that He removed fear from them, so that this would serve as a sign that Allah fulfills His promise of supporting the believers.

The second: Allah explained that He had granted the believers victory at first. When some of them disobeyed, He imposed fear upon them. Then He mentioned that He removed that fear from the heart of those who were sincere in their faith and firm in their religion, to the extent that drowsiness overcame them.

Know that those who were with the Messenger ﷺ on the Day of Uhud were of two groups:

One of them: those who were certain that Muhammad, peace be upon him, was a true prophet from Allah, and that "he does not speak from desire; it is nothing but a revelation that is revealed" (53:3-4). They had heard from the Prophet ﷺ that Allah would support this religion and make it prevail over all other religions. So they were certain that this event would not lead to their annihilation. Therefore they were secure, and this security reached the point that drowsiness overcame them, for sleep does not come with fear. The arrival of sleep indicates the complete removal of fear. Thus, here, concerning the events of Uhud and these people, He said: ﴿Then He sent down upon you, after distress, security, drowsiness﴾. And concerning the events of Badr He said: ﴿when He caused drowsiness to overcome you as security from Him﴾ (8:11). So in the account of Uhud He placed "security" before "drowsiness," and in the account of Badr He placed "drowsiness" before "security."

As for the second group, namely the hypocrites (munafiqun) who were doubtful about his prophethood, peace be upon him, and who had come only to seek booty, their distress was intense and their fear was great. Then Allah described the state of each of these two groups. Concerning the attribute of the believers He said: ﴿Then He sent down upon you, after distress, security, drowsiness﴾. And on this there are several issues:

Issue one: al-Wahidi said: "al-amana" (security) is a verbal noun like "al-amn," and similar to it among verbal nouns are "al-azama" (greatness) and "al-ghalaba" (dominance). al-Jubba'i said: it is said "amina fulan, ya'manu, amnan wa amanan" (Fulan became secure).

Issue two: The author of al-Kashshaf (al-Zamakhshari) said: it has been read as "amnatan" with the mim sukun, because it signifies a single instance of security.

Issue three: Concerning His saying "nu'asan" (drowsiness) there are two possibilities:
One: that it is a substitute (badal) for "amana."
The second: that it is an object (maf'ul). On this reading, concerning "amanatan" there are several possibilities:
The first: that it is a circumstantial qualifier (ḥal) of it, placed before it, like your saying: "I saw a rider, a man."
The second: that it is an object of purpose (maf'ul lahu), meaning "you became drowsy out of security."
The third: that it is a circumstantial qualifier of the addressees, meaning "possessors of security."

* * *

Then He said: ﴿it overcomes a group of you﴾. On this there are two issues:

Issue one: We have mentioned that this group is the believers who had insight into their faith. Abu Talha said: "Drowsiness overcame us while we were in our battle lines, and a sword would fall from one of us, and he would take it, then it would fall and he would take it again." And from al-Zubayr, who said: "I was with the Prophet ﷺ when fear grew intense, and Allah sent sleep upon us. I could hear the words of Mu'attib ibn Qushayr while drowsiness was overcoming me, saying: 'If we had any share in the matter, we would not have been killed here.'" And 'Abd al-Rahman ibn 'Awf said: "Sleep was cast upon us on the Day of Uhud." And from Ibn Mas'ud: "Drowsiness in battle is security, and drowsiness in prayer is from Satan." That is because in battle it arises only from complete trust in Allah and detachment from this world, and in prayer it arises only from being far from Allah.

Know that this drowsiness contained several benefits:

The first: it fell upon all the believers, not in the usual manner. Therefore it was a clear miracle for the Prophet ﷺ. There is no doubt that when believers witness that new miracle, their faith increases over their existing faith, and when they become so, their earnestness in fighting the enemy and their trust that Allah will fulfill His promise increase.

The second: sleeplessness and wakefulness cause weakness and exhaustion, while sleep restores strength and vigor and reinforces power and ability.

The third: when the disbelievers were occupied with killing the Muslims, Allah cast sleep over the eyes of those among them who remained, so that they would not witness the killing of their dear ones, which would intensify fear and cowardice in their hearts.

The fourth: the enemies were eager to the utmost to kill them, so their remaining asleep, safe, in such a battle is among the clearest proofs that Allah's protection and preservation were with them. This removes fear from their hearts and gives them greater trust in Allah's promise. Some people said: mentioning drowsiness in this context is a metaphor (kināya) for complete security. This is weak, because turning the word from its literal sense (ḥaqiqa) to a figurative sense (majaz) is not permissible except when there is a counter-evidence. How then could the literal meaning of the word be abandoned when it includes these benefits and wisdoms?

Issue two: Ḥamzah and al-Kisa'i read "taghsha" with a ta', referring it back to "amana." The rest read it with a ya', referring it back to "nu'as." This is the choice of Abu Hatim, Khalaf and Abu 'Ubayd.

Know that each of "amana" and "nu'as" indicates the other, so it is appropriate to refer the pronoun back to whichever you wish, as in His saying: ﴿Indeed, the tree of zaqqum﴾ ﴿is the food of the sinful﴾ ﴿like molten brass, boiling in the bellies﴾ (44:43-45), where "taghli" (boils) is used. Once you know that both are permissible, we say: among the things that strengthen the reading with ta' is that the original is "amana," and "nu'as" is a substitute, and referring the pronoun back to the original is better. Also, "amana" is the intended goal, and when security is attained, drowsiness is attained, because security is its cause, for the fearful hardly ever becomes drowsy. As for the one who reads with ya', his argument is that drowsiness is what overcomes, for the Arabs say: "drowsiness overcame us" (ghashiyana al-nu'as), and they rarely say "security from drowsiness overcame me." Also, drowsiness is mentioned with overcoming in His saying: ﴿when He caused drowsiness to overcome you as security from Him﴾ (8:11). Also: drowsiness comes immediately after the verb, and it is closer in wording to the mention of overcoming than "amana," so the masculine form is preferable.

* * *

Then He said: ﴿and another group, concerned only for themselves﴾. On this there are two issues:

Issue one: These are the hypocrites, 'Abd Allah ibn Ubayy, Mu'attib ibn Qushayr, and their companions. Their concern was the salvation of themselves. It is said: "hammani al-shay'" means the matter was of my concern and aim. Abu Muslim said: it is a habit of the Arabs to say to one who fears: "his own self has concerned him." These hypocrites, because of their intense fear of being killed, lost their sleep. It is also said: the believers, their concern was the Prophet ﷺ and their fellow believers, while the hypocrites' concern was themselves. The truth of the matter is this: when a person's preoccupation with something becomes intense and he is absorbed in it, he becomes unaware of everything else. Since the thing most beloved to a person is himself, when he fears for his self he becomes oblivious to everything besides it. This is what is meant by His saying: ﴿concerned only for themselves﴾. That is because the causes of fear, namely the enemy's intent, were present, while the impelling factor, namely trust in the promise of Allah and the promise of His Messenger, carried no weight with them, because they were disbelievers in the Messenger in their hearts. Therefore fear grew great in their hearts.

Issue two: ﴿and another group﴾ is in the nominative case as the subject (mubtada'), and its predicate is ﴿thinking﴾ (yaẓunnun). It is also said its predicate is ﴿concerned only for themselves﴾. Then He described this group with several kinds of attributes.

The first attribute: among their attributes is His saying: ﴿thinking about Allah other than the truth, the thought of the Age of Ignorance﴾. On this there are issues:

Issue one: Regarding this thought there are two possibilities:
One, and it is the more apparent: that this thought was that they were saying to themselves: "If Muhammad were right in his claim, the disbelievers would not have been given power over him." This is a corrupt thought. As for the view of Ahl al-Sunnah wa al-Jama'ah, it is because He, glorified is He, does what He wills and decrees what He desires, and no one can object to Him. Prophethood is a robe of honor from Allah, glorified is He, with which He honors His servant. Reason does not require that when a master honors his servant with a robe, he must honor him with another robe. Rather, He has the command and the prohibition however He wills, by the judgment of divinity. As for the view of those who consider interests (maṣāliḥ) in the acts and rulings of Allah, it is not far-fetched that in Allah, exalted is He, allowing the disbeliever and the Muslim to be left to one another, to the point that the disbeliever overpowers the Muslim, there are hidden wisdoms and observed kindnesses, since this world is the abode of trial and testing, and the aspects of benefit are hidden from the intellects. Thus perhaps the benefit lies in allowing the disbeliever and the believer to be left to one another until the disbeliever overpowers the believer, and perhaps the benefit lies in imposing poverty and affliction upon the believers. al-Qaffal said: if the believer being in the right required the removal of these meanings, it would be necessary for people to be compelled to know the one who is in the right by coercion, and that would contradict moral obligation (taklif) and the deserving of reward and punishment. Rather, a person is known to be in the right only through the proofs and clear evidences he has. As for coercion, it may come from the wrongdoer against the one in the right, and from the one in the right against the wrongdoer. This is a sufficient statement to show that it is not permissible to infer from dynastic power, might, and abundance of strength that its possessor is upon the truth.

The second: that this thought was that they used to deny the God of the worlds, who knows all things and is capable of all things, and they used to deny prophethood [p. 39] and resurrection. Therefore they did not trust the words of the Prophet ﷺ that Allah would strengthen and support them.

Issue two: ﴿other than the truth﴾ is in the position of a verbal noun (maṣdar). Its meaning: they think about Allah other than the true thought that ought to be held about Him. [And the thought of the Age of Ignorance] is an apposition (badal) of it. The benefit of this order is that "other than the truth" comprises many religions, and the most repugnant of them are the doctrines of the people of the Age of Ignorance. So He mentioned first that they think about Allah other than the true thought, then He explained that they chose from among the kinds of religions that are not true the most corrupt and the most false, namely the thought of the people of the Age of Ignorance, as one says: "So-and-so's religion is not true; his religion is the religion of the atheists."

Issue three: Regarding His saying: ﴿the thought of the Age of Ignorance﴾ there are two views:
One: that it is like your saying: "Hatim of generosity" and "Umar of justice," meaning the thought specific to the ignorant religion.
The second: the intended meaning is: the thought of the people of the Age of Ignorance.

The second attribute: among the attributes which Allah mentioned for these hypocrites is His saying: ﴿They say, "Do we have any share in the matter?" Say, "Indeed the matter belongs entirely to Allah."﴾

Know that His saying: ﴿Do we have any share in the matter?﴾ is a report of the doubt to which the hypocrites clung, and it may bear several meanings.

[End of part 1]

The first aspect: when the Prophet (ﷺ) consulted ʿAbd Allah ibn Ubayy about this incident, he advised him not to leave Medina. Then the Companions insisted that the Prophet (ﷺ) go out to them, and ʿAbd Allah ibn Ubayy became angry about that and said: "He disobeyed me and obeyed the youths." Then, when many of the Banu al-Khazraj were killed and ʿAbd Allah ibn Ubayy returned, he was told: "The Banu al-Khazraj have been killed." He said: "Do we have any say in the matter?" meaning: Muhammad did not accept my opinion when I ordered him to stay in Medina and not leave it. A parallel to this is what Allah related about them, that they said: ﴿Had they obeyed us, they would not have been killed﴾ [Al ʿImran: 168]. The meaning is: "Do we have any matter that is obeyed?" This is an interrogative expressing denial.

The second interpretation: it is a habit of the Arabs that when victory belongs to their enemy, they say: "The matter is his." So his saying ﴿Do we have any say in the matter at all?﴾ means: "Do we have any share in that thing which Muhammad promised us, namely support and strength?" This is also an interrogative expressing denial. Their purpose in it was to use it as evidence that Muhammad (ﷺ) was lying in claiming support and protection from Allah for his community. This too is an interrogative expressing denial.

The third: the implied meaning is: "Do we hope that we will gain the upper hand over these people?" Its purpose was to strengthen the Muslims in persevering in jihad and fighting against the disbelievers. Then Allah, glorified is He, answered this doubt with His saying: ﴿Say: Indeed, the matter is entirely for Allah﴾. In this regard there are several issues:

The first issue: Abu ʿAmr read (kulluhu) with a raised lam (ruffing), while the rest read it in the accusative (naṣb). As for the reading with raising, it is that ﴿kulluhu﴾ is the subject (mubtada'), and ﴿lillah﴾ is its predicate (khabar). Then this sentence became the predicate of ﴿inna﴾ (indeed). As for the accusative, it is because the word "kull" serves as an emphasis, so it was like the word "ajmaʿ" (entirely). If one said "inna al-amra ajmaʿa" (indeed the matter entirely), it would only be in the accusative, so likewise when one says "kullahu".

The second issue: The way to establish this answer is what we have explained: if we hold the doctrine of Ahl al-Sunnah (the people of the Sunnah), there is no objection against Allah in any of His acts concerning causing death and giving life, poverty and enrichment, happiness and hardship. If we hold the doctrine of those who maintain that Allah observes what is in the interest of creatures (riʿayat al-maṣalih), then the aspects of the interests are hidden and known only to Allah, the Exalted. Perhaps the interest lies in bringing joy and pleasure, and perhaps it lies in imposing sorrows and pains. Thus the doubt of the hypocrites is dispelled from this perspective.

The third issue: Our companions (the Ashʿarites) used this verse as evidence that all originated things occur by the decree and predestination of Allah. That is because the hypocrites said: "If Muhammad had accepted our opinion and our advice, he would not have fallen into this trial." So Allah answered them that the matter is entirely for Allah. This answer only holds if the acts of servants are by the decree, predestination and will of Allah. For if they were outside His will, this answer would not repel the doubt of the hypocrites. Thus it is established that this verse indicates what we have mentioned. Moreover, the apparent meaning of this verse agrees with rational proof: the existent is either necessary in its essence (wajib li-dhatihi) or possible in its essence (mumkin li-dhatihi). A possible-in-essence thing does not have its existence preferred over its non-existence except upon reaching that which is necessary in essence. Thus it is established that everything other than Allah, the Exalted, depends on His bringing into being and His creating. This principle is not specific to one originated thing over another, or one possible thing over another, so the acts of servants, their movements and their stillnesses are included in it. That is what is meant by His saying: ﴿Say: Indeed, the matter is entirely for Allah﴾. This is a statement most clear to whoever Allah has granted fairness.

* * *

Then He, the Exalted, said: ﴿They conceal within themselves what they do not reveal to you﴾.

Know that He, the Exalted, related about them that they said: "Do we have any say in the matter?" This statement is open to interpretation. Perhaps its speaker was among the sincere believers, and his purpose was to show compassion, and to ask when relief would come and from where support would arrive. Perhaps he was one of the hypocrites, and he said it to cast doubt on the prophethood of Muhammad (ﷺ) and on Islam. So Allah, the Exalted, made clear in this verse that the purpose of these people in this statement was the second category. The benefit of this warning is that the Prophet (ﷺ) would be cautious against their deceit and their plotting.

The third type of what Allah related about the hypocrites is their saying: "If we had any say in the matter, we would not have been killed here." There is a difficulty in this, which is that someone may say: What is the difference between this statement and what came before, his saying ﴿Do we have any say in the matter?﴾ It can be answered in two ways:

The first: when He, the Exalted, related their statement ﴿Do we have any say in the matter?﴾ and answered it with His saying ﴿the matter is entirely for Allah﴾, the hypocrites argued, to criticize this answer, by saying: "If we had any say in the matter, we would not have gone out from Medina, and we would not have been killed here." This indicates that the matter is not as you say, that the matter is entirely for Allah. This is exactly the debate that takes place between Ahl al-Sunnah and the Mu'tazilah (the Mu'tazila). The Sunni says: the matter, in obedience and disobedience, faith and disbelief, is entirely in the hand of Allah. The Mu'tazili says: the matter is not so, for the human being is free and independent in his act: if he wills, he believes, and if he wills, he disbelieves. According to this aspect, this statement is not a doubt standing on its own; rather its purpose is to criticize what Allah made the answer to the first doubt.

The second: that the meaning of His saying ﴿Do we have any say in the matter?﴾ is: "Do we have any share of the victory that Muhammad promised us?" And the meaning of His saying ﴿If we had any say in the matter, we would not have been killed here﴾ is what ʿAbd Allah ibn Ubayy used to say: that if Muhammad had obeyed me and not gone out from Medina, we would not have been killed here.

Know that He, the Exalted, answered this doubt in three ways:

The first aspect of the answer is His saying: ﴿Say: Even if you had been in your houses, those for whom killing had been decreed would have come forth to their places of death﴾. The meaning is that caution does not repel decree, and planning cannot withstand predestination. Those for whom Allah decreed killing must be killed under all assumptions; for when Allah, the Exalted, informed that they would be killed, if they were not killed His knowledge would turn into ignorance. We have also explained that [the possible] must end in the bringing into being by Allah, the Exalted; if it did not find [an existence from Him], His power would turn into incapacity, and all of this is impossible. Among what confirms the establishment of necessity, as we have set out, is His saying: ﴿for whom killing had been decreed﴾. This expression conveys obligation, for this word in His saying ﴿Fasting has been prescribed for you﴾ and ﴿retaliation has been prescribed for you﴾ [al-Baqarah: 178] conveys the obligation of the act. Here it cannot be taken to mean the obligation of the act, so it must be taken to mean the necessity of existence. This is a statement most clear to whom Allah has strengthened with success. Then we say: the exegetes have two opinions on it:

The first: "Even if you had sat in your houses, there would have come out from among you those whom Allah decreed killing for, to their places of death and their falling, until what Allah knew would exist comes into existence."

The second: it is as if it were said to the hypocrites: "Even if you had sat in your houses and stayed back from jihad, the believers for whom fighting the disbelievers had been prescribed would have come forth to their places of death, and they would not have held back from this obedience because of your holding back."

The second aspect of the answer to that doubt is His saying: ﴿and that Allah may test what is in your breasts﴾. That is because the people claimed that going out to that fighting was a corruption, and if the matter had been up to them they would not have gone out to it. So He, the Exalted, said: Rather, this fighting includes two kinds of interest: that the sincere be distinguished from the hypocrite. In the well-known proverb: "Do not dislike trials, for they are the harvest of the hypocrites." The meaning of testing with respect to Allah, the Exalted, has been explained many times before.

If it is asked: Why did He mention testing when it had already been mentioned in His saying ﴿Then He turned you away from them in order to test you﴾?

We answer: When the discourse was long, He repeated its mention. It was also said: the first testing is the defeat of the believers, and the second is all the other circumstances.

The third aspect of the answer is His saying: ﴿and that He may purify what is in your hearts﴾. There are two views on it:

One: that this event purifies your hearts of whisperings and doubts.

The second: that it becomes an expiation for your sins, so it purifies you from the consequences of sins and misdeeds. He mentioned "breasts" in regard to testing, and "hearts" in regard to purification, and there is a discussion on this. Then He said: ﴿And Allah is Knowing of what is within the breasts﴾.

Know that "the essence of the breasts" (dhat al-sudur) refers to the things present in the breasts, which are secrets and inner thoughts. It is called "the essence of the breasts" because it is a state within them, accompanying them; the companion of a thing is its possessor, and its accompanying companion is its essence. He mentioned this to indicate that His testing was not because something concealed from Him in the breasts, or otherwise; for He knows all that is known. He tested them either purely by virtue of His divinity, or for the sake of improvement.

[Page 42]

Know that the meaning is: the people who turned away on the Day of Uhud, when the two hosts met, and left their position and fled, Allah has pardoned them. There are several issues (masa'il) concerning the verse.

**First issue:** The reports differ about who stood firm on that day and who turned away. Muhammad ibn Ishaq reported that a third of the people were wounded, a third fled, and a third stood firm. They differed about the fleeing ones. It was said that some of them reached Medina and reported that the Prophet ﷺ had been killed; this was Sa'd ibn Uthman. After him, men came and entered upon their wives, and the women began saying, "Are you fleeing from the Messenger of Allah ﷺ?" They threw dust in their faces and said, "Take the spindle and spin with it." Others said that the Muslims did not go beyond the mountain. Al-Qaffal said: What the reports indicate in general is that a group of them turned away and went far off. Some of them entered Medina, and some went off in other directions. As for the majority, they came down near the mountain and gathered there. Among those who fled was Umar, though he was not among the first to flee and did not go far; rather, he remained on the mountain until the Prophet ﷺ went up. Among them also was Uthman, who fled together with two men from the Ansar called Sa'd and Uqbah. They fled until they reached a distant place, then returned after three days. The Prophet ﷺ said to them, "You have gone far away in it (in your flight)." Fatimah said to Ali, "What did Uthman do?" and belittled him. The Prophet ﷺ said, "O Ali, the husbands of the sisters have worn me out in trying to make them love one another." As for those who stood firm with the Messenger ﷺ, they were fourteen men: seven of the Muhajirun and seven of the Ansar. Of the Muhajirun were Abu Bakr, Ali, Abd al-Rahman ibn Awf, Sa'd ibn Abi Waqqas, Talhah ibn Ubayd Allah, Abu Ubaydah ibn al-Jarrah, and al-Zubayr ibn al-'Awwam. Of the Ansar were al-Habbab ibn al-Mundhir, Abu Dujanah, Asim ibn Thabit, al-Harith ibn al-Simmah, Sahl ibn Hunayf, Usayd ibn Hudayr, and Sa'd ibn Mu'adh. It is also reported that eight of these had pledged to him that day to die (fight to the death): three of the Muhajirun, namely Ali, Talhah, and al-Zubayr, and five of the Ansar, namely Abu Dujanah, al-Harith ibn al-Simmah, Habbab ibn al-Mundhir, Asim ibn Thabit, and Sahl ibn Hunayf. Then none of them was killed. Ibn 'Uyaynah reported that about thirty men were struck alongside the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, each of them coming and kneeling before him, saying, "My face is a ransom for your face, my soul is a ransom for your soul, and peace be upon you, not as one bidding farewell."

**Second issue:** His saying, ﴿Indeed, those of you who turned away on the day the two hosts met﴾: this is an address specifically to the believers, meaning those who fled on the Day of Uhud. ﴿It was only Satan who caused them to slip﴾, i.e., drove them to a slip (lapse). "Azalla" and "istazalla" have the same meaning. Allah the Exalted said: ﴿So Satan caused them both to slip from it﴾ (2:36). Ibn Qutaybah said: "istazallahum" means he sought their slip, as one says "I hastened him" meaning I sought his haste, and "I employed him" meaning I sought his work.

**Third issue:** Al-Ka'bi said: The verse indicates that sins are not attributed to Allah, for He attributed it in this verse to Satan. This is like the saying of Allah the Exalted about Moses: ﴿This is of the work of Satan﴾ (28:15), and like the saying of Joseph: ﴿after Satan had sown discord between me and my brothers﴾ (12:100), and like the saying of the companion of Moses: ﴿And none made me forget it except Satan﴾ (18:63).

**Fourth issue:** Allah the Exalted did not specify in what matter Satan caused them to slip. That is because, with pardon, there is no need to specify the disobedience. However, the scholars allowed that what is meant is their leaving that position, that their desire was for booty, that their cowardice in jihad and their departure from sincerity was the cause. Whichever of these it was, it is established that Allah the Exalted pardoned them. It is reported that Uthman was reproached for his flight on the Day of Uhud, and he said: "Although that was an error, Allah has pardoned him," and he recited this verse.

As for the words of Allah the Exalted, ﴿because of some of what they had earned﴾, there are two possible meanings:

The first is that the particle "bi" (ba') denotes attachment, like your saying: "I wrote with the pen" and "I cut with the knife." The meaning is that offenses had proceeded from them, and through those offenses Satan was enabled to cause them to slip. On this interpretation there are several views:

The first: Al-Zajjaj said: They did not turn away out of defiance, nor out of fleeing from the battle, desiring the world. Rather, Satan reminded them of sins they had committed, so they disliked meeting Allah except in a state they would be content with, and except after sincere repentance. This was a thought that passed through their minds, and in it they were mistaken.

The second: When they sinned by leaving that place, Satan made them slip through the ill omen of this disobedience and brought them to defeat, because one sin draws another sin, just as obedience draws obedience, and it is a means of grace (lutf) in that.

The third: When they sinned through cowardice and disputing among themselves, they fell into that sin.

The second possibility is that the meaning be: Satan caused them to slip in some of what they had earned, not in all of what they had earned. What is intended by this is to show that they did not disbelieve and did not abandon their religion; rather, this was a lapse that befell them in some of their deeds.

* * *

Then Allah the Exalted said: ﴿And Allah has certainly pardoned them﴾.

Know that this verse indicates that that lapse was not caused by disbelief, for pardon of disbelief is not permitted, due to the saying of Allah the Exalted: ﴿Indeed, Allah does not forgive association with Him, but He forgives what is less than that for whom He wills﴾ (4:48). Then the Mu'tazilah said: If that sin was among the minor sins, pardon for it is permissible without repentance; if it was among the major sins, it is not permissible except with repentance. So here repentance must have preceded on their part, even though that is not mentioned in the verse. The Qadi (Abd al-Jabbar) said: The more likely view is that this sin was among the minor sins, and two things indicate this:

The first: It is hardly said of major sins that they are a "lapse"; that term is used only for minor sins.

The second: The people thought that since the defeat had fallen upon the polytheists, there was no further need for their staying in that place, so they moved away from it and departed seeking booty. Such a matter is not unlikely to be among the minor sins, because ijtihad (independent reasoning) has a place in such matters. As for our companions' view, pardon for both minor and major sins is permissible, so there is no need for these strained interpretations.

* * *

Then Allah the Exalted said: ﴿Indeed, Allah is Forgiving and Forbearing﴾, i.e., Forgiving toward whoever repents and turns back, Forbearing, who does not hasten punishment. Our companions have argued from this verse that that sin was among the major sins, because if it had been among the minor sins it would have been obligatory, according to the Mu'tazilah, for Allah to pardon it. And if pardoning it had been obligatory, praising oneself for it would not be fitting, since one who wrongs a person does not fittingly boast that he pardoned and forgave him. Since He mentioned this praise, we know that the sin was among the major sins, and since He pardoned it, we know that pardon of major sins does occur. And Allah knows best.

[Page 44]

His saying, Exalted is He:

﴿O you who believe, do not be like those who disbelieved and said of their brothers, when they journeyed in the land or were out on a raid, "Had they stayed with us they would not have died or been killed," so that God may make that a regret in their hearts. God gives life and causes death, and God sees what you do.﴾ ﴿And if you are killed in the way of God or die, surely forgiveness from God and mercy are better than what they amass.﴾ ﴿And if you die or are killed, surely to God you will be gathered.﴾

Know that the hypocrites used to reproach the believers for fighting alongside the disbelievers, saying: "Had they stayed with us they would not have died or been killed." Then, when some of the believers showed slackness and weakness in jihad, to the extent that what happened at the Battle of Uhud happened, and God pardoned them by His grace, He mentioned in this verse what indicates the prohibition against any of the believers saying something like their saying. So He said: "O you who believe, do not say to one who wishes to go out to jihad: 'Had you not gone out, you would not have died or been killed.'" For God is the One who gives life and causes death. Whoever is destined to remain alive will not be killed in jihad, and whoever is destined to die will not remain alive even if he does not fight. This is what is meant by His saying: ﴿God gives life and causes death﴾. Also, the one who was killed in jihad, had he not gone out to jihad, would have died inevitably. So if death is unavoidable, then being killed in jihad, so that he earns the great reward, is better for him than dying without benefit. This is what is meant by His saying: ﴿And if you are killed in the way of God or die, surely forgiveness from God and mercy are better than what they amass.﴾ This is the purpose of the speech. There are the following issues in the verse.

The first issue: They differed regarding the intended meaning of His saying ﴿those who disbelieved﴾. Some said it is general, so it includes every disbeliever who says this kind of statement, whether he is a hypocrite or not. Others said it is specific to the hypocrites, because these verses, from beginning to end, are specifically about explaining their conditions. Others said it is specific to Abd Allah ibn Ubayy ibn Salul, Mu'attib ibn Qushayr, and the rest of their companions. According to these two opinions, the verse indicates that faith is not merely the affirmation of the tongue, as the Karramiyya (a sect that held this view) say. For if it were so, the hypocrite would be a believer, and if he were a believer, God would not have called him a disbeliever.

The second issue: The author of al-Kashshaf said: His saying ﴿and said to their brothers﴾ means "on account of their brothers' going out," like His saying: ﴿And those who disbelieved said to those who believed, "Had it been good, they would not have preceded us to it."﴾ [al-Ahqaf 46:11]. I say: The explanation of this view is that when they said, "Had they stayed with us they would not have died or been killed," this indicates that those brothers were dead or killed at the time of this statement. Therefore, His saying ﴿and said to their brothers﴾ must mean that they said that on account of their brothers, and the meaning cannot be that they mentioned this statement while with their brothers.

The third issue: His saying ﴿to their brothers﴾ may mean brotherhood by lineage, even if they were Muslims, as in His saying: ﴿And to ʿAd their brother Hud﴾ [al-A'raf 7:65] and ﴿And to Thamud their brother Salih﴾ [al-A'raf 7:73]. For the brotherhood in these verses is brotherhood of lineage, not brotherhood of religion. So perhaps those slain Muslims were relatives of the hypocrites, and so the hypocrites made this statement. It may also mean brotherhood of similarity in religion, and it happened that some of the hypocrites were killed in some of the expeditions, and so those of the hypocrites who remained said that.

The fourth issue: The hypocrites thought that the one who went out of them was going on a distant journey, and this is what is meant by His saying ﴿when they journeyed in the land﴾, and the one who went out to a raid, and this is what is meant by His saying ﴿or were out on a raid﴾. If death or killing befell them, that happened only because of the journey and the raid. They made this a cause for turning people away from jihad. This is because human nature loves life and dislikes death and killing. So when it is said to a man: "If you avoid travel and jihad, you are safe and your life is pleasant; but if you plunge into one of them, you reach death or killing," then most likely his nature recoils from that and he prefers to stay at home. This was among the schemes of the hypocrites for turning the believers away from jihad.

If it is asked: Why did He mention raiding after journeying in the land, when raiding is included in it?

We say: Because journeying in the land refers to going far away on a journey, not what is near to it. As for raiding, there is no difference between its far and near, since one who goes out of Medina to Mount Uhud is not described as one who journeys in the land, despite the nearness of the distance, even though he is a raider. This is the benefit of mentioning raiding separately from journeying in the land.

The fifth issue: There is a problem in the verse, namely that His saying ﴿and said﴾ indicates the past, while His saying ﴿when they journeyed﴾ indicates the future. How then can the two be combined? Rather, if He had said, "and said to their brothers when they journeyed in the land" (i.e., at the time they journeyed), there would have been no problem.

The answer to this is from several aspects:

The first: His saying ﴿and said﴾ is in the sense of "they say," as if it were said: "Do not be like those who disbelieve, saying to their brothers such and such." He expressed the future with the past form for two benefits:

One of them: What is certain to occur in the future is sometimes expressed as though it has already happened or is happening, as He, Exalted, said: ﴿The command of God has come﴾ [al-Nahl 16:1], and He said: ﴿Indeed, you will die﴾ [al-Zumar 39:30]. Here, if it had been expressed with the active participle form, there would be no exaggeration in it. But since it was expressed with the past form, this indicates that their zeal and effort in establishing this doubt had reached its utmost limit, and because of that zeal this future became as if it were an existing event.

The second benefit: Since He, Exalted, expressed the future with the past form, this indicates that the purpose is not to report that this statement was uttered, but rather to report their zeal and effort in establishing this doubt. This is the answer I rely upon, and God knows best.

The second answer: The speech came in the manner of narrating a past situation, and the meaning is that their brothers, when they journeyed in the land, the disbelievers would say, "Had they stayed with us they would not have died or been killed." So whoever reports about them after that must say "they said." This is what we mean by saying that the speech came in the manner of narrating a past situation.

The third answer: Qutrub said: The words ʾidh (إذ) and ʾidhā (إذا) may each be used in place of the other. I say: What Qutrub said is a good statement, because if we allow establishing the language by an unknown poem transmitted from an unknown poet, then it is more fitting to allow establishing it by the Mighty Qur'an. At most, one might say that ʾidhā (إذا) is literally for the future, but why not allow its use for the past figuratively, given the strong resemblance between it and ʾidh (إذ)? I often see the grammarians perplexed in establishing the words found in the Qur'an, and when they cite an unknown verse to establish it, they rejoice in it. I am extremely astonished at them, for if they take the occurrence of that unknown verse in agreement with it as evidence of its correctness, then it is even more fitting that they take the occurrence of the Qur'an with it as evidence of its correctness.

The sixth issue: ﴿ghuzzā(n)﴾ [غُزًّى] is the plural of ghāzin (غازٍ), like al-qawwal, al-ruka', and al-sujjad, the plurals of qā'il, rāki', and sājid. A similar one from the defective (weak-final) roots is ʿafā (عَفا). It is also permissible to say ghuzāh (غُزاةٌ), like qudāh and rumāh, the plurals of qāḍī and rāmī. The meaning of ghazw (الغَزْو) in the speech of the Arabs

[Page 45]

is the intention of the enemy, and al-maghzā (المَغْزى) is the destination.

The seventh issue: Al-Wahidi said: In the verse there is an omitted element that the context indicates, and the implied meaning is: "When they journeyed in the land and died, or were raiders and were killed, had they stayed with us they would not have died or been killed." So His saying ﴿they would not have died or been killed﴾ indicates their death and their killing.

* * *

Then He, Exalted, said: ﴿so that God may make that a regret in their hearts﴾, and in it there are two views:

The first: The implied meaning is that they said that statement so that God would make that statement a regret in their hearts, like what is said: "I raised him so that he would hurt me," "I supported him so that he would overpower me." Similar to this is His saying, Exalted: ﴿Then the family of Pharaoh picked him up so that he would become for them an enemy and a grief﴾ [al-Qasas 28:8]. Having understood this, we say: They mentioned, in explaining how that statement resulted in the arising of regret in their hearts, several aspects:

The first: When the relatives of the one who was killed heard this statement, their regret increased in their hearts. For one of them believes that if he had insisted more in preventing him from that journey and that raid, he would have remained alive. So that person died or was killed only because this man fell short in preventing him. The listener to this statement thus believes that he is the one who caused the death of that dear person or killed him. When he believes this about himself, there is no doubt that his regret and grief increase. As for the Muslim who believes that life and death occur only by God's decree and decision, nothing of this kind of regret arises in his heart at all. So it is established that the doubt the hypocrites raised yields them nothing but increased regret.

The second aspect: When the hypocrites cast this doubt upon their brothers, they were discouraged from raiding and jihad and stayed behind from it. Then when the Muslims were occupied with jihad and raiding, and through it reached great spoils, the conquest of the enemies, and the attainment of hopes, that one who stayed behind remained in disappointment and regret.

The third aspect: This regret will occur on the Day of Resurrection in the hearts of the hypocrites when they see God singling out the mujahidun with greater honors and elevated ranks, and singling out these hypocrites with greater disgrace, curse, and punishment.

The fourth aspect: When the hypocrites put forward this doubt to the weak among the Muslims and found acceptance of it among them, they rejoiced in that, since their scheme and deceit succeeded upon those weak ones. God, Exalted, says that it will become a regret in their hearts when they learn that they were upon falsehood in establishing this doubt.

The fifth aspect: Their zeal and effort in multiplying doubts and casting misguidance blinds their hearts, so they fall at that point into bewilderment, disappointment, and constriction of the breast. This is what is meant by "regret," like His saying: ﴿And whoever God wills to lead astray, He makes his breast tight and constricted﴾ [al-An'am 6:125].

The sixth aspect: When they cast this doubt upon the strong among the Muslims, they were not heeded, so their effort is wasted and their scheme is nullified, and thus regret arises in their hearts.

The second view concerning the interpretation of the verse: The lam (اللام) in His saying ﴿so that God may make﴾ is connected to what the prohibition indicates, and the implied meaning is: "Do not be like them, so that God makes your not being like them a regret in their hearts, because your opposing them in what they say and believe, and your contrariness to them, is what enrages them."

[Page 46]

Then He, Exalted, said: ﴿God gives life and causes death﴾, and in it there are two views:

The first: The purpose of it is to explain the answer to this doubt. Its statement is that the Giver of life and the Causer of death is God, and nothing else has any influence on life and death; that God's knowledge does not change, His judgment does not reverse, and His decree does not alter. So how does sitting at home benefit against death?

[Page 47]

"If it is said: If the doctrine that God's decree does not change prevents striving and effort from being useful in guarding against killing and death, then likewise the doctrine that God's decree does not change should prevent action from being useful in avoiding the punishment of the Hereafter. This would negate the imposition of obligation (al-taklif), and the purpose of these verses is to establish the command to jihad and obligation. And if the answer leads, in the Hereafter, to the cancellation of obligation, then this statement, whose affirmation leads to its negation, is false.

The answer: For us, the goodness of imposing obligation is not contingent upon any cause or the preservation of any benefit (maslahah). Rather, according to us, He does what He wills and decrees what He desires.

The second aspect concerning the interpretation of the verse: The purpose of this statement is not to answer that doubt. Rather, the intent is that when He, exalted is He, forbade the believers from saying the like of what the hypocrites said, He said: ﴿And God gives life and causes death﴾, meaning: He gives life to the hearts of His friends and the people of His obedience through light and discernment (al-furqan), and He causes the hearts of His enemies among the hypocrites to die."

Commentary of al-Razi (*Mafatih al-Ghayb*) on surah 3, verse 157:

Then He, exalted is He, said: ﴿And God is Seeing of what you do.﴾ On this there are two issues.

The first issue: its purpose is to encourage and to warn regarding what was mentioned earlier concerning the way of the believers and the way of the hypocrites.

The second issue: Ibn Kathir, Hamzah and al-Kisa'i (a recitation, *qira'ah*) read (يَعْمَلُونَ, *ya'maluna*, "they do") with the *ya'* (third person), as a reference to the absent people. The sense is: ﴿That God may make that a regret in their hearts. God gives life and causes death, and God is Seeing of what you do.﴾ The rest read it with the *ta'* (second person), as direct address, so that it matches what precedes it in His words: ﴿Do not be like those who disbelieved﴾, and what follows it in His words: ﴿And if you are killed in the way of God, or die﴾.

* * *

Then He, exalted is He, said: ﴿And if you are killed in the way of God or die, forgiveness from God and mercy are better than what they amass.﴾

Know that this is the second answer to the doubt of the hypocrites. Its explanation is that this death is certain to occur, and there is no escape for a person from being killed or dying. So if this death or killing happens in the way of God and in seeking His good pleasure, it is better than spending that effort in seeking the world and its pleasures, from which a person gains nothing at all after death. This is an answer of the utmost excellence and strength. The reason is that when a person turns to jihad, his heart turns away from the world and turns toward the Hereafter. So if he dies, it is as if he has escaped from the enemy and reached the Beloved. But if he sits in his house, fearful of death and greedy for gathering worldly wealth, and then dies, it is as if he has been veiled from the Beloved and cast into the house of exile. There is no doubt about the complete happiness of the first, and the complete misery of the second.

There are issues concerning the verse:

The first issue: Nafi', Hamzah and al-Kisa'i read (مِتُّمْ, *mittum*, "you died") with a *kasrah* on the *mim*, while the rest read it with a *dammah* on the *mim*. The first group derived it from *mata yamatu*, *mittu*, like *haba yahabu*, *hibtu*, and *khafa yakhafu*, *khiftu*. Al-Mubarrad transmitted this dialect, and if it is authentic, then this recitation is also sound. As for the recitation of the majority, it is derived from *mata yamutu*, *mutu*, like *qala yaqulu*, *qultu*.

The second issue: Al-Wahidi, may God have mercy on him, said: The *lam* in His words (﴿And if you are killed﴾, *la'in qutiltum*) is the *lam* of oath (*lam al-qasam*), with the implied meaning: "By God, if you are killed in the way of God." The *lam* in His words (﴿surely forgiveness from God and mercy﴾, *la-maghfiratun min Allah wa rahmah*) is the answer to the oath, and it indicates that what enters upon it is a condition. But in my view, the more correct position is to say that this *lam* is for emphasis (*lam al-ta'kid*). The meaning then is: if it is necessary that you die and be killed in your journey and your military campaign, then likewise it is necessary that you attain forgiveness as well. So why do you shun it? It is as if it were said: death and killing are not necessarily unavoidable, but even if they were necessary, they entail the necessity of forgiveness. How then is it fitting for an intelligent person to shun it?

The third issue: Hafs, from Asim, read (يَجْمَعُونَ, *yajma'un*, "they gather") with the *ya'*, as the third person. The rest read it with the *ta'*, as the second person. As for the third-person reading, the meaning is that God's forgiveness is better than what these hypocrites gather of perishable worldly goods. As for the second-person reading, the meaning is that He, exalted is He, is addressing the believers as if saying to them: God's forgiveness is better for you than the wealth you gather in this world.

The fourth issue: We have said that the mercy and forgiveness of God are better than the delights of this world, for several reasons:

The first: whoever seeks wealth is in hardship from that seeking right now, and perhaps he will not benefit from it tomorrow, because he may die before tomorrow. But seeking mercy and forgiveness, he will certainly benefit from it, because God does not break His promise, and He has said: ﴿So whoever does an atom's weight of good will see it﴾ [al-Zalzalah: 7].

The second: suppose he remains until tomorrow, yet perhaps that wealth will not remain until tomorrow. How many a person has become a ruler in the morning and a prisoner by evening! The good things of the Hereafter do not pass away, because of His words: ﴿But the enduring good deeds are better with your Lord﴾ [al-Kahf: 46], and His words: ﴿What you have will run out, but what is with God is lasting﴾ [al-Nahl: 96].

The third: suppose he remains until tomorrow and the wealth remains until tomorrow, yet perhaps some event will occur that prevents you from benefiting from it, such as illness, pain, or other things. The benefits of the Hereafter are not like that.

The fourth: suppose that tomorrow it is possible for you to benefit from that wealth, but the pleasures of this world are mixed with pains, and its benefits are blended with harms, and this is not hidden. As for the benefits of the Hereafter, they are not like that.

The fifth: suppose those benefits occur tomorrow, pure and free from impurities, but they do not last or endure. Rather, they end and perish. And the stronger and more perfect the pleasure, the greater and more intense the regret and grief at its loss. The benefits of the Hereafter are protected from cutting off and from ending.

The sixth: the benefits of this world are sensory, and the benefits of the Hereafter are intellectual. The sensory is base, and the intellectual is noble. Do you think that the enjoyment of a donkey in the pleasure of its belly and its private parts equals the joy of the closest angels when they are illuminated by the divine lights? These six foundations alert you to endless aspects that indicate the soundness of His words, glorified and exalted is He: ﴿Surely forgiveness from God and mercy are better than what they amass.﴾

If it is said: How can forgiveness be described as better than what you amass, when there is no good at all in what you amass?

We say: What you amass in this world may at times be of what is lawful, which is considered good. Also, this is stated in accordance with their own opinion and belief that those possessions are goods. So it is said: forgiveness is better than these things which you suppose to be goods.

* * *

Then He said: ﴿And if you die or are killed, surely to God you will be gathered.﴾

Know that He, glorified and exalted is He, encouraged the fighters in the first verse by the gathering to God's forgiveness. In this verse He increased the elevation of ranks, and so He encouraged them here by the gathering to God. It is related that Isa ibn Maryam, may God's blessings and peace be upon him, passed by people whose bodies were emaciated and whose faces had turned pale, and he saw upon them the marks of worship. He said: "What are you seeking?" They said: "We fear the punishment of God." He said: "He is too noble to not deliver you from His punishment." Then he passed by other people and saw upon them the same marks, and he asked them. They said: "We seek Paradise and mercy." He said: "He is too noble to not grant you His mercy." Then he passed by a third group and saw upon them the marks of servitude even more,

[Page 49]

and he asked them. They said: "We worship Him because He is our God, and we are His servants, not out of desire or fear." He said: "You are the sincere servants and the truly devoted worshippers." So consider the arrangement of these verses. In the first verse He said: ﴿Surely forgiveness from God﴾, which refers to one who worships Him out of fear of His punishment. Then He said: ﴿and mercy﴾, which refers to one who worships Him seeking His reward. Then He said at the end of the verse: ﴿surely to God you will be gathered﴾, which refers to one who worships God purely for His lordship and servitude. This is the highest station and the furthest goal in servitude, in the loftiness of rank. Do you not see that when He honored the angels He said: ﴿And those who are with Him do not disdain His worship﴾ [al-Anbiya': 19], and He said to those near to Him among the people of reward: ﴿In the presence of a Sovereign, Omnipotent﴾ [al-Qamar: 55]? So He made clear that those who expended their souls and bodies in His obedience and in striving against His enemy, their gathering will be to Him, their companionship will be with His generosity, and their enjoyment will be in the radiance of the light of His lordship. This is a station that calls for elaboration, and the discerning person is guided by the measure we have presented.

Let us return to the exegesis (*tafsir*, explanation of the Qur'an). It is as if it were said: if you abandon jihad and shun killing and death, you will remain a few days in this world with those base pleasures, and then you will inevitably leave them, so their pleasures will belong to others and their consequences will fall upon you. But if you turn away from the pleasures of this world and its goods, and offer your souls and wealth to the Master, your gathering will be to God, your standing at the threshold of God's mercy, and your delight in the remembrance of God. How far apart are these two ranks and these two positions!

And know that in His words ﴿Indeed, to Allah you will be gathered﴾ there are subtleties:

First: He did not say "you will be gathered to Allah." Instead He said, "To Allah you will be gathered" (*ilā Allāhi tuḥsharūn*), which conveys restriction (*ḥaṣr*). Its meaning is that the worlds are gathered only to Allah and to no other. This indicates that on that Day there is no judge, no one who harms, and no one who benefits except Him. He, exalted is He, says: ﴿Whose is the dominion today? It is for Allah, the One, the Subduer﴾ [Ghafir: 16], and He says: ﴿And the affair, that Day, belongs entirely to Allah﴾ [al-Infitar: 19].

Second: He mentioned among His names this name (Allah), and this name is the greatest of the names. It indicates both perfection of mercy and perfection of dominance. Because it indicates perfection of mercy, it is the greatest kind of promise, and because it indicates perfection of dominance, it is the most severe kind of threat.

Third: the introduction of the emphatic lam (*lām al-ta'kīd*) before the name of Allah, in His words ﴿Indeed, to Allah﴾. This alerts you that divinity (*al-ilāhiyya*) requires this gathering and resurrection, as He says: ﴿Indeed, the Hour is coming; I almost conceal it, so that every soul may be recompensed for what it strives﴾ [Ta-Ha: 15].

Fourth: His words ﴿you will be gathered﴾ are in the passive form (*fi'l mā lam yusamma fā'iluh*), although the one who performs that gathering is Allah. The reason it is not stated explicitly is that He, exalted and great, is the one whom the intellects testify to be Allah, who originates and repeats creation, and from Him comes both the origination and the return. Therefore, omitting explicit mention in such a context is more indicative of greatness. A parallel to this is His saying: ﴿And it was said, "O earth, swallow your water"﴾ [Hud: 44].

Fifth: He attributed their gathering to something other than themselves. This alerts the intellect to the fact that all creation is compelled within the grip of power and the penetration of will. Whether they are living or dead, they cannot escape the domination of lordship and the majesty of divinity.

Sixth: His words ﴿you will be gathered﴾ are addressed to everyone. This indicates that all the worlds will be gathered and made to stand on the plain of resurrection and the carpet of justice. Thus the oppressed will be brought together with the oppressor, and the one slain with the slayer. The Truth, glorified and exalted is He, judges among His servants with justice, free from injustice, as He says: ﴿And We will set up the scales of justice for the Day of Resurrection﴾ [al-Anbiya': 47]. Whoever reflects upon His words ﴿Indeed, to Allah you will be gathered﴾, and is aided by success, will know that these benefits we have mentioned are like a drop from the oceans of secrets deposited in this verse.

The al-Qadi relied on this verse to argue that the one who is killed is not dead. He said: because His words ﴿And if you die or are killed﴾ require conjoining the one killed with the one who dies, and conjoining a thing with itself is impermissible.

**Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 3, verse 159 (part 1 of 3)**

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿So by a mercy from Allah, you were lenient with them. And if you had been harsh and hard-hearted, they would have dispersed from around you. So pardon them, ask forgiveness for them, and consult them in the matter. And when you have decided, then rely upon Allah. Indeed, Allah loves those who rely upon Him.﴾

Know that when the people fled from the Prophet ﷺ on the Day of Uhud and then returned, the Messenger ﷺ did not address them with harshness and severity, but spoke to them with gentle words. Then, when He, glorified and exalted is He, had guided them in the preceding verses to what benefits them in this life and the next, and among that was that He pardoned them, He increased His bounty and kindness by praising the Messenger ﷺ for pardoning them and for not being harsh with them. So He said: ﴿So by a mercy from Allah, you were lenient with them.﴾ Whoever is fair will know that this is a fine arrangement in speech.

There are several issues concerning the verse.

**The first issue:** Know that his ﷺ gentleness with the people is an expression of the goodness of his character with them. Allah, exalted is He, says: ﴿And lower your wing to those who follow you of the believers﴾ [al-Shu'ara: 215], and He says: ﴿Take what is given freely, enjoin what is good, and turn away from the ignorant﴾, and He says: ﴿And indeed, you are of a great moral character﴾ [al-Qalam: 4], and He says: ﴿There has certainly come to you a Messenger from among yourselves; grievous to him is what you suffer; he is concerned over you and to the believers is kind and merciful﴾ [al-Tawbah: 128]. The Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, said: "No forbearance is more beloved to Allah, exalted is He, than the forbearance of a leader and his gentleness, and no ignorance is more hateful to Allah than the ignorance and harshness of a leader." Since he, peace and blessings be upon him, was the leader of all the worlds, it was necessary that he be the most forbearing of them and the best of them in character.

It is narrated that the wife of Uthman entered upon him ﷺ while the Prophet and Ali were washing weapons. She said: "What has Ibn Affan done? By Allah, you will not find him in front of the people." Ali said to her: "Indeed Uthman has disgraced the age today." Then the Prophet, peace be upon him, said: "Mah (enough)." It is also narrated that he said at that time: "The husbands of the sisters have wearied me; let them love one another." When Uthman entered upon him along with his two companions, he did not say more than: "Indeed you have gone too far in this matter." It is also narrated from some of the Companions that he said: "Allah has done us the greatest kindness. We were polytheists, and if the Messenger of Allah had brought us this religion all at once, and the Qur'an all at once, these obligations would have been too heavy upon us, and we would not have entered Islam. But he called us to one word. When we accepted it and knew the sweetness of faith, we accepted what came after it, word after word, by way of gentleness, until the religion was complete and the Shari'ah was perfected." It is also narrated that he, peace be upon him, said: "I am to you like a father. When one of you goes to relieve himself, let him not face the qiblah nor turn his back to it."

Know that the secret of the matter regarding good character consists of two things: considering the state of the speaker, and considering the state of the doer. As for considering the state of the speaker, the souls differ in their essence, as the Prophet, peace be upon him, said: "Souls are armies gathered together." And he said: "People are mines like the mines of gold and silver." Just as souls in the direction of deficiency reach the extreme of baseness, humiliation, and vileness, with desire and anger dominating them and love of wealth and pleasures taking hold of them, so too in the direction of perfection they may reach the extreme of strength and majesty. As for the theoretical faculty, it is as Allah described it with His saying: ﴿Light upon light﴾ [al-Nur: 35], and His saying: ﴿And He taught you what you did not know, and the bounty of Allah upon you has been great﴾ [al-Nisa: 113]. As for the practical faculty, it is as Allah described it with His saying: ﴿And indeed, you are of a great moral character﴾, as if it were of the same kind as the spirits of the angels. It does not submit to desire, nor incline to the calls of anger, nor is it affected by love of wealth or status. For whoever is affected by something is weaker than that which affects him. So when the soul inclines toward these sensible things, its spiritual faculties are weaker than its bodily faculties; and when it does not incline to them nor turn to them, its spiritual faculties are exalted above the bodily ones. These are theoretical qualities, and his blessed soul was at the utmost of majesty and perfection in these traits.

As for considering the state of the doer, it is his, peace and blessings be upon him, saying: "Whoever knows the secret of Allah in the decree, calamities become easy for him." For he knows that earthly events are based on divine causes, so he knows that caution does not avert the decree. Therefore, if he fails to attain something he seeks, he does not become angry; and if something he loves comes to him, he does not become attached to it, because he is aware of the spiritual realities which are nobler than these bodily things. So he does not contend with anyone in this world over seeking any of its pleasures and delights, nor does he become angry with anyone because of the loss of any of its aims. Whenever a person is like this, he is of good character, pleasant in companionship with creation. Since the blessings and peace of Allah be upon him were the most perfect of humanity in these qualities that necessitate good character, he was necessarily the most perfect of creation in good character.

**The second issue:** Our companions (the Ash'arites) argued concerning the question of qada' and qadar (divine decree and predestination) with His saying: ﴿So by a mercy from Allah, you were lenient with them.﴾ The basis of the argument is that He, exalted is He, made clear that the goodness of his character with creation was only due to the mercy of Allah, exalted is He. We say: the mercy of Allah, according to the Mu'tazilah, is general with respect to the responsible persons. So everything He did with Muhammad, peace be upon him, of guidance, calling, clarification, and direction, He also did similarly with Iblis, Pharaoh, Haman, Abu Jahl, and Abu Lahab. If this is so, then everything Allah, exalted is He, did with the responsible persons in this regard is shared between the purest of the pure and the most wretched of the wretched. Then the special goodness of some of them in character and perfection of path would not be derived from the mercy of Allah. So on this view, explaining the goodness of the Messenger's character by the mercy of Allah would be false. And since this is false, we know that all the actions of servants are by the decree and predestination of Allah. The Mu'tazilah interpret this as an increase of favors (al-luṭf), but this is extremely far-fetched. For everything possible of favors, He has already done for the responsible persons.
