What the responsible person deserves, on the basis of his obedience, of additional favor, is in reality something he has earned from himself, not from Allah. For whenever he performs obedience he deserves that additional favor, and it becomes obligatory to deliver it to him; and whenever he does not perform it, its delivery is withheld. So that is for the servant from himself, not from Allah.

**The third issue:** Most scholars held that the *ma* in His saying ﴿So by a mercy from Allah﴾ is a superfluous particle (ṣilah zā'idah), and there are many like it in the Qur'an, such as His saying: ﴿After a little while﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 40], and ﴿A host of them is defeated there﴾ [Sad: 11], ﴿So for their breaking of their covenant﴾ [al-Nisa: 155], ﴿For their sins﴾ [al-'Ankabut: 12]. They said: the Arabs may add to speech for emphasis what is not needed, as He, exalted is He, says: ﴿So when the bringer of good news came﴾ [Yusuf: 96], meaning "so when he came," and emphasized it with *an*. But the verifying scholars said: the entry of a meaningless, wasted word into the speech of the Wisest of the wise is not permissible. Here it is possible that *ma* is an interrogative for amazement, its implied meaning being: "By what kind of mercy from Allah were you lenient with them?" This is because their offense was great, and yet he did not display at all any harshness in speech or roughness in word. They knew that this could not come about except by a Lordly support and a Divine guidance. So that became an occasion for amazement at the perfection of that support and guidance, and it was said: "By what kind of mercy from Allah were you lenient with them?" And this is the most correct in my view.

**The fourth issue:** Know that this verse indicates that the mercy of Allah is what makes Muhammad, peace and blessings be upon him, merciful toward the Ummah. If you reflect on the reality of this verse, you will know its indication that there is no mercy except for Allah, glorified is He. What establishes this are several points:

The first: Had Allah not placed in the heart of His servant the motive of goodness, mercy, and kindness, he would not have done any of these things. And when He places this motive in his heart, he will certainly perform these acts. On this basis, there is no mercy except from Allah. Every merciful person other than Allah, exalted is He, gains a return from his mercy, either to flee punishment, or to seek reward, or to seek a good reputation. If we suppose a situation free of these matters, the cause would be natural tenderness of heart, for whoever sees an animal in pain has his heart softened and is pained by seeing it in pain, so he relieves it of that pain to remove that tenderness from his heart. If none of these incidental causes existed, he would not show mercy at all. As for the Truth, glorified and exalted is He, He is the One who shows mercy without any purpose of any kind. So there is no mercy except from Allah.

The third: Every person who shows mercy to another does so by giving him wealth, or by removing from him some cause of harm and calamity. However, the one shown mercy does not benefit from that wealth except with the soundness of his limbs, and these are only from Allah, exalted is He. So in reality there is no mercy except from Allah. As for outwardly, whoever Allah helps to be merciful is called merciful. He, peace be upon him, said: "The merciful are shown mercy by the Most Merciful." And He said, describing Muhammad, peace be upon him: ﴿To the believers he is kind and merciful﴾ [al-Tawbah: 128].

* * *

Then He, exalted is He, said: ﴿And if you had been harsh and hard-hearted, they would have dispersed from around you.﴾

Know that the perfection of Allah's mercy toward Muhammad ﷺ is that He informed him of the corruptions of harshness and severity. On this there are issues.

**The first issue:** Al-Wahidi, may Allah have mercy on him, said: *al-fazz* is one who is harsh in manner, bad in character. It is said: "fazizta, tafuzzu, fazaatan, fa-anta fazz." Its origin is *fazi*, like *hadhira* from *hadhirtu*, and *faraqa* from *fariqtu*, except that what is doubled in this pattern is assimilated, as in *rajulun sabbun*, whose origin is *sababun*. As for *al-fadd* with the *dad*, it means separating a thing, and "*infadda al-qawm*" means the people dispersed. He, exalted is He, says: ﴿And when they see a trade or amusement, they disperse toward it﴾ [al-Jumu'ah: 11]. From it: "fadadtu al-kitab" (I broke open the book), and from it it is said: "May Allah not break your mouth (lā yafdud Allahu fāka)."

If it is asked: what is the difference between *al-fazz* and *ghaliz al-qalb* (hard-hearted)?

We say: *al-fazz* is one who is bad in character, while *ghaliz al-qalb* is one whose heart is not affected by anything. A person may not be bad in character and may not harm anyone, but he does not soften toward them nor show mercy to them. So the difference is clear from this aspect.

**The second issue:** The purpose of the mission is that the Messenger convey the obligations of Allah to creation, and this purpose is not accomplished unless their hearts incline to him and their souls are at rest with him. This purpose is not accomplished unless he is merciful and generous, forgiving their wrongdoing, pardoning their offenses, and favoring them with the qualities of goodness, nobility, and compassion. For these reasons, it was necessary for the Messenger to be free from bad character, and just as he is so, it was necessary that he not be hard-hearted, but rather that he be much inclined to help the weak, much engaged in aiding the poor, much forgiving of their wrongs, and much pardoning their slips. For this meaning He said: ﴿And if you had been harsh and hard-hearted, they would have dispersed from around you.﴾ And if they had dispersed from around you, the purpose of the mission and the message would have been defeated.

Al-Qaffal, may Allah have mercy on him, understood this verse as referring to the event of Uhud. He said: ﴿So by a mercy from Allah, you were lenient with them﴾ on the Day of Uhud, when they returned to you after the rout. ﴿And if you had been harsh and hard-hearted﴾ and had confronted them with blame for that rout, they would have dispersed from around you out of awe of you and shame because of what had come from them of the rout. So that would have been something that would have made the enemy covet you and them.

**Third issue:** Gentleness and leniency are permissible only so long as they do not lead to neglecting one of God's rights. If they do, they are not permissible. God says: ﴿O Prophet, strive against the disbelievers and the hypocrites, and be harsh with them﴾ [al-Tawbah: 73]. He also said to the believers concerning the punishment for fornication: ﴿And let not pity for them take hold of you in the religion of God﴾ [al-Nur: 2].

Here is another subtle point. In this verse God forbade him (ﷺ) from harshness, while in the other verse He commanded him to be harsh. Here He forbade harshness toward the believers, and there He commanded harshness toward the disbelievers. This is like His saying: ﴿humble toward the believers, mighty against the disbelievers﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 54], and His saying: ﴿harsh against the disbelievers, merciful among themselves﴾ [al-Fath: 29]. The essence of the matter is that both extremes, excess (ifrat) and deficiency (tafrit), are blameworthy, and virtue lies in the middle. The command to be harsh at one time and the prohibition of it at another exist so that he would keep away from excess and deficiency and remain on the middle path, which is the straight path. For this very reason God praised the middle course, saying: ﴿And thus We have made you a middle nation﴾ [al-Baqarah: 143].

* * *

Then God said: ﴿So pardon them, ask forgiveness for them, and consult them in the matter﴾. Know that in this verse God commanded him with three things:

The first: to pardon them. On this there are several points.

The first point: The perfection of a servant's state lies only in his adopting the character of God, the Exalted. He (peace be upon him) said: "Adopt the character of God." Then, since God had pardoned them in the previous verse, He also commanded the Messenger to pardon them, so that the Messenger, peace be upon him, would attain the virtue of adopting the character of God.

The second point: The author of al-Kashshaf (al-Zamakhshari) said: ﴿So pardon them﴾ regarding what concerns your own right, ﴿and ask forgiveness for them﴾ regarding what concerns the right of God, the Exalted.

The third point: The apparent meaning of a command is obligation. The "fa" (so) in His saying ﴿So pardon them﴾ indicates immediate sequence. This indicates that God made it obligatory upon him to pardon them immediately. It also indicates the perfection of divine mercy, in that He pardoned them Himself and then made it obligatory upon His Messenger to pardon them immediately.

Know that His saying ﴿So pardon them﴾ is an obligation of pardon upon the Messenger, peace be upon him. When the matter reached the community, He did not make it obligatory upon them but encouraged them toward it, saying: ﴿and those who pardon people﴾, so that it would be known that the good deeds of the righteous are the sins of those brought near (to God).

The second: His saying: ﴿and ask forgiveness for them﴾. On this verse there are several points.

The first point: In this verse there is a strong indication that God pardons the perpetrators of major sins. This is because fleeing during battle is a major sin, as He says: ﴿And whoever turns his back to them on that day… [then] he has returned with anger from God﴾ [al-Anfal: 16]. Thus it is established that the flight of the people of Uhud was a major sin. Then God explicitly stated in the previous verse that He had pardoned them, and in this verse He commanded His Messenger (ﷺ) to pardon them, and then commanded him to ask forgiveness for them. This is among the strongest proofs for what we have mentioned.

The second point: His saying ﴿and ask forgiveness for them﴾ is a command to him to ask forgiveness for the perpetrators of major sins. When He commands him to seek forgiveness, it is not permissible that He would not grant it, since that would not befit the Generous. Thus this verse indicates that God grants intercession to Muhammad (ﷺ) in this world on behalf of the perpetrators of major sins; and so it is more fitting that He would grant him intercession on their behalf on the Day of Resurrection.

[Page 54]

The third point: He, glorified and exalted, pardoned them first by His saying: ﴿And God has certainly pardoned them﴾ [Al 'Imran: 155]. Then He commanded Muhammad (ﷺ) in this verse to ask forgiveness for them and on their behalf, as if it were said to him: "O Muhammad, ask forgiveness for them, for I have already forgiven them before you ask forgiveness for them; and pardon them, for I have already pardoned them before your pardon of them." This indicates the perfection of God's mercy toward this community.

The third: His saying: ﴿and consult them in the matter﴾. On this there are several points.

The first point: It is said: he consulted them (shawarahum), consultation (mushawarah), shiwar, and mashurah. "Al-qawm shura" (the people are a consultation) is a verbal noun by which the people are named, like His saying: ﴿when they are in private consultation (najwa)﴾ [al-Isra': 47]. It has been said: consultation (mushawarah) is derived from their saying: "I extracted the honey (shurtu al-'asal), I extract it (ashuruhu)," when you take it from its place and extract it. It has also been said that it is derived from their saying: "I displayed the animal (shurtu al-dabbah) shawran," when you show it off; and the place where animals are displayed is called "mishwar." It is as if by display its good and bad are known; likewise, through consultation the best and worst of matters are known.

The second point: The benefits of God's command to the Messenger to consult them are several:

First: The Messenger's consultation of them (ﷺ) raises their status and elevates their rank. This requires intense love for him and sincerity in obedience to him. If he had not done so, it would have been a humiliation of them, and that would produce bad character and harshness.

Second: Although he (peace be upon him) was the most intelligent of people, the knowledge of creatures is limited. It is not unlikely that a person might think of aspects of benefit that did not occur to him, especially in matters of worldly affairs. He (peace be upon him) said: "You are more knowledgeable about the affairs of your worldly life, and I am more knowledgeable about the affairs of your religion." For this reason he (peace be upon him) said: "No people have ever consulted together except that they were guided to the most right of their affairs."

Third: Al-Hasan and Sufyan ibn 'Uyaynah said: he was commanded to do this so that others would follow him in consultation and it would become a sunnah (practice) in his community.

Fourth: He (peace be upon him) consulted them at the Battle of Uhud, and they advised him to go out. He was inclined to go out, and when he went out what happened happened. If he had then abandoned consulting them, that would indicate that some residue of effect remained in his heart from their advice. So God commanded him after that event to consult them, to show that no trace of that event remained in his heart.

Fifth: ﴿and consult them in the matter﴾ not so that you might benefit from them in opinion and knowledge, but so that you may know the measures of their intellects and understandings, and the measures of their love for you and their sincerity in obeying you. Then the superior would be distinguished from the inferior in your sight, so explain to them according to their ranks.

Sixth: ﴿and consult them in the matter﴾ not because you are in need of them, but because when you consult them in a matter, each one of them strives to extract the most suitable course in that event. Thus the spirits become aligned and harmonious in achieving the most suitable courses in it. The alignment of pure spirits upon one thing helps in its attainment. This is the secret behind gathering in prayers, and it is the secret of why congregational prayer is superior to praying alone.

Seventh: When God commanded Muhammad (peace be upon him) to consult them, this indicated that they have a rank and value with God. This implies that they have a rank with God, a rank with the Messenger, and a rank with creation.

Eighth: A great king does not consult in great matters except his select companions and those closest to him. When these people sinned, God pardoned them. It might occur to them that although God pardoned them out of His grace, the great rank they had was no longer theirs. So God made clear that this rank was not diminished after repentance; rather, I increase it. This is because before this event I did not command My Messenger to consult you, and after this event I commanded him to consult you, so that you would know that you are now greater in standing than you were before. The reason is that before this event you relied upon your deeds and obedience, but now you rely upon My grace and My pardon. Therefore your rank and station must now become greater than before, so that you would know that My pardon is greater than your deeds, and My generosity is more abundant than your obedience.

The first three aspects are mentioned, and the rest is what occurred to my mind at this point. God knows best His intent and the secrets of His Book.

[Page 55]

The third point: They agreed that whatever has a revelation from God concerning it, it is not permissible for the Messenger to consult the community about it, because when the explicit text (nass) comes, opinion and analogy (qiyas) are nullified. As for what has no explicit text concerning it, is consultation permissible in all matters or not? Al-Kalbi and many scholars said: this command is specific to consultation in wars. Their argument is that the definite article "al-" in the word "al-amr" (the matter) is not for comprehensiveness (istighraq). When He made clear that what has a revelation concerning it is not to be consulted upon, it becomes necessary to take the definite article here as referring to what was previously known. The previously known matter in this verse is only what relates to war and meeting the enemy, so His saying ﴿and consult them in the matter﴾ is specific to that. Then those who held this view said: Al-Hubab ibn al-Mundhir advised the Prophet (ﷺ) on the day of Badr to descend at the water, and he accepted from him. And the two Sa'ds, Sa'd ibn Mu'adh and Sa'd ibn 'Ubadah, advised him on the day of the Trench to abandon reconciling Ghatafan with some of Medina's produce so that they would withdraw, and he accepted from them both and tore up the document. Others among them said: the wording is general, and what has a revelation concerning it is excluded from it, so his argument remains valid regarding the rest. The verified view on this is that God commanded those with insight to take lessons, saying: ﴿So take warning, O people of vision﴾ [al-Hashr: 2], and he (peace be upon him) was the master of those with vision. He also praised those who derive conclusions, saying: ﴿would have known it from those among them who draw correct conclusions﴾ [al-Nisa': 83], and he was the most intelligent and insightful of people. This indicates that he was commanded to exercise independent reasoning (ijtihad) when no revelation came down to him, and ijtihad is strengthened through debate and discussion; for this reason he was commanded to consult. He consulted them on the day of Badr regarding the prisoners, and that was among the matters of religion. The evidence that it is not permissible to restrict an explicit text by analogy is that the text was addressed to all the angels regarding the prostration to Adam, and then Iblis restricted himself by analogy, saying: ﴿You created me from fire and created him from clay﴾ [al-A'raf: 12], and so he became accursed. Had restricting an explicit text by analogy been permissible, he would not have deserved the curse for this reason.

The fourth point: The apparent meaning of a command is obligation. So His saying ﴿and consult them﴾ requires obligation. Al-Shafi'i, may God have mercy on him, interpreted this as recommendation (nadb). He said: this is like His statement, peace and blessings be upon him: "A virgin is to be consulted about herself." If her father were to compel her into marriage, it would be permissible, but it is better for her to have her soul pleased; likewise here.

The fifth point: Al-Wahidi narrated in al-Wasit from 'Amr ibn Dinar, from Ibn 'Abbas, that he said: The one whom the Prophet (ﷺ) was commanded to consult in this verse is Abu Bakr and 'Umar, may God be pleased with them both. But I have a difficulty with this, because those whom God commanded His Messenger to consult in this verse are the very ones He commanded him to pardon and ask forgiveness for, and they were those who fled. Suppose 'Umar was among the fleeing ones and so falls under the verse; but Abu Bakr was not among them, so how does he fall under this verse? And God knows best.

* * *

Then He said: ﴿So when you have decided, rely upon God﴾. On this there are several points:

The first point: The meaning is that when a firm opinion is reached through consultation, it is not necessary for reliance to be placed upon that opinion; rather, reliance must be placed upon God's help, His guidance, and His protection. The intent is that a servant should place no reliance upon anything except God in all affairs.

The second point: The verse indicates that trust in God (tawakkul) does not mean that a person neglects himself, as some ignorant people claim. Otherwise, the command to consult would contradict the command to rely upon God. Rather, trust in God means that a person observes the apparent causes but does not depend on them in his heart; he relies upon the protection of the Truth.

[Page 56]

Third issue: It is related from Jabir ibn Zayd that he recited ﴿فَإذا عَزَمْتَ﴾ (fa-idha 'azamta, "when you have resolved") with a damma on the ta', as though God, exalted is He, said to the Messenger: "When I have resolved, then put your trust [in Me]." This is weak for two reasons.

The first: ascribing resolve ('azm) to God is not permissible. It may be said that this resolve means decisiveness and binding determination, and the meaning is: "Consult them in the matter; then when I have resolved for you upon something and guided you to it, put your trust in Me, and do not consult anyone after that."

The second: a reading that none of the Companions recited may not be added to the Qur'an. And God knows best.

* * *

Then He, exalted is He, said: ﴿إنَّ اللَّهَ يُحِبُّ المُتَوَكِّلِينَ﴾ (Indeed, God loves those who rely upon Him), and the purpose of this is to encourage the responsible servants to turn to God, exalted is He, and to turn away from everything other than God.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 3, verse 160:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿If Allah helps you, none can overcome you; and if He forsakes you, who is there that can help you after Him? And upon Allah let the believers rely.﴾

Ibn ʿAbbas said: "If Allah helps you" as He helped you on the day of Badr, then no one will overcome you; "and if He forsakes you" as He forsook you on the day of Uhud, then no one will help you. And in this are several issues:

The first issue: It has been said that the purpose of the verse is to encourage obedience and to warn against disobedience. This is because He, exalted is He, explained earlier that whoever guards against the disobedience of Allah, Allah helps him, and this is His saying: ﴿Yes, if you are patient and mindful of God, and they come upon you suddenly, your Lord will reinforce you with five thousand angels﴾ [Al ʿImran: 125]. Then in this verse He explained that whoever Allah helps, none can overcome him. From the combination of these two premises it follows that whoever fears Allah has attained the happiness of this world and the Hereafter, for he attains a happiness with no misery accompanying it and a might with no humiliation accompanying it, and he becomes one who overcomes, whom no one can defeat. As for whoever commits disobedience, Allah forsakes him, and whoever is forsaken by Allah has fallen into a misery with no happiness accompanying it and a humiliation with no might accompanying it.

The second issue: The companions (al-Ashab, i.e., the Ashʿari theologians) argued by this verse that faith does not arise except by the help of Allah, and disbelief does not arise except by His forsaking, and the reason for this is clear, because the verse indicates that the whole affair belongs to Allah.

The third issue: ʿUbayd ibn ʿUmayr read ﴿wa-in yukhdhilkum﴾ from akhdhalahu, when he makes him one forsaken.

The fourth issue: His saying ﴿min baʿdihi﴾ (after Him) has two interpretations:

The first: it means "after His forsaking."

The second: it is like your saying: "There is no one for you who would do good to you after so-and-so."

* * *

Then He said: ﴿And upon Allah let the believers rely.﴾ Meaning: since it has been established that the whole affair is in the hand of Allah, and that none can repel His decree or avert His judgment, it is necessary that the believer rely on none but Him. His saying ﴿And upon Allah let the believers rely﴾ conveys restriction (al-hasr, exclusivity), i.e., upon Allah alone let the believers rely, and not upon other than Him.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 3, verse 161 (part 1 of 2):

Allah the Exalted said: ﴿It is not for a prophet to embezzle. And whoever embezzles will bring what he embezzled on the Day of Resurrection. Then every soul will be paid in full what it has earned, and they will not be wronged.﴾

Know that when Allah the Exalted had greatly urged jihad, He followed it with mention of the rulings of jihad. Among them is the prohibition of ghulul (embezzlement), so He mentioned this verse on this topic. It contains several issues:

The first issue: ghulul is treachery (khiyanah). Its root meaning is taking something secretly. It is said: aghalla al-jazzar and al-salikh, when they leave some meat in the hide by way of treachery. Al-ghill is the resentment hidden in the breast. Al-ghilalah is the garment worn beneath the clothes. Al-galal is the water that flows beneath the roots of a tree, because it is concealed by the trees. And taghallala the thing means it penetrated and became hidden. The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Whomever We send on a task and he embezzles anything will come on the Day of Resurrection carrying it on his neck." He (ﷺ) also said: "The gifts of rulers are ghulul." He (ﷺ) said: "There is no liability on the borrower except the one who embezzles (al-mughill)." And he (ﷺ) said: "There is no ighlal and no islal." Also it is said: aghallahu, meaning he found him to be a ghall (embezzler), like your saying abkhaltuhu and afhamtuhu, meaning I found him to be such.

The second issue: Ibn Kathir, Asim and Abu 'Amr read ﴿yaghulla﴾ with a fathah on the ya and a dammah on the ghayn, meaning: it is not for the Prophet to betray. The rest of the seven read ﴿yughalla﴾ with a dammah on the ya and a fathah on the ghayn, meaning: it is not for the Prophet to be betrayed.

They differed concerning the occasions of revelation, and some of them agree with the first reading and some with the second reading.

As for the first type, there are narrations:

The first: that he (ﷺ) took spoils in some campaign and gathered the booty, and the division was delayed for some reasons. Some people came and said: "Will you not divide our spoils?" The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "If you had gold equal to Uhud, I would not withhold from you a single dirham. Do you think I would embezzle your spoils from you?" So Allah revealed this verse.

The second: that this verse was revealed concerning the delivery of revelation. He (ﷺ) would recite the Qur'an, in which was the defect of their religion and the reviling of their gods, so they asked him to leave that, and this verse was revealed.

The third: Ikrimah and Sa'id ibn Jubayr narrated that the verse was revealed concerning a red woolen cloak that was lost on the day of Badr, and some ignorant people said: "Perhaps the Prophet (ﷺ) took it." So this verse was revealed.

The fourth: it is narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him and his father, through another route, that the nobles of the people hoped that the Prophet (ﷺ) would single them out with an extra share of the spoils, so this verse was revealed.

The fifth: it is narrated that he (ﷺ) sent out advance parties, who gained spoils; he divided them but did not give a share to the advance parties, so this verse was revealed.

The sixth: al-Kalbi and Muqatil said: this verse was revealed when the archers left their position on the day of Uhud seeking booty, saying: "We fear the Prophet (ﷺ) will say: whoever takes something, it is his," and that he would not divide the spoils as he had not divided them on the day of Badr. The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "You thought that we would embezzle, so we would not divide for you?" So this verse was revealed.

Know that according to the first narration, the meaning of the verse is the prohibition of the Messenger concealing any part of the spoils from his companions for himself. According to the three narrations, the intended meaning is the prohibition of him from embezzlement, by giving to some and not to others.

Page 58

As for what agrees with the second reading: it is narrated that when the spoils of Hawazin came into his possession on the day of Hunayn, a man embezzled a needle, and so this verse was revealed. Know that the Prophet (ﷺ) magnified the matter of embezzlement and made it one of the grave sins. From Thawban, from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), that he said: "Whoever his soul departs from his body while he is free of three things enters Paradise: pride, embezzlement, and debt." And from Abdullah ibn Amr: that a man who was in charge of the baggage of the Prophet (ﷺ), called Kirkirah, died, and the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "He is in the Fire." They went to look and found on him a cloak and a robe which he had embezzled. The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Return the thread and the needle, for it is shame, fire, and disgrace on the Day of Resurrection." Ruwayfi' ibn Thabit al-Ansari narrated from the Prophet (ﷺ) that he said: "It is not lawful for anyone who believes in Allah and the Last Day to ride a beast from the spoils of the Muslims until, when he has made it lean, he returns it, and it is not lawful for anyone who believes in Allah and the Last Day to wear a garment until, when he has worn it out, he returns it." It is narrated that he (ﷺ) appointed Salman over the spoils, and a man came to him and said: "O Salman, there was a tear in my garment, so I took a thread from these goods and sewed it with it. Is there any blame on me?" Salman said: "Everything has its measure." So the man pulled the thread out of his garment and threw it into the goods. It is narrated that a man came to the Prophet (ﷺ) with one or two sandal straps from the booty, and said: "I got this on the day of Khaybar." The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "One or two straps of fire." "A man was struck by an arrow at Khaybar, and the people said when he died: 'Congratulations to him on martyrdom!' The Prophet (ﷺ) said: 'No! By Him in whose hand is the soul of Muhammad, the cloak which he took from the spoils before their division will blaze upon him as fire.'"

Know that two situations are excepted from this prohibition:

The first situation: taking food and fodder for animals to the extent of need. Abdullah ibn Abi Awfa said: "We got food on the day of Hunayn, and a man would come and take from it the amount sufficient for him, then depart." And from Salman: that on the day of al-Mada'in he obtained loaves, cheese, and a knife, and he began to cut from the cheese and say: "Eat in the name of Allah."

The second situation: when one is in need of it. It is narrated from al-Bara' ibn Malik that he struck a man of the polytheists on the day of Yamamah, and he fell on his back; so he took his sword and killed him with it.

The third issue: as for the reading with a fathah on the ya and a dammah on the ghayn, meaning "it is not for a prophet to betray," it has two interpretations:

The first: that the meaning is that prophethood and treachery do not combine. This is because treachery is a cause of shame in this world and fire in the next, so the soul that desires it is at the utmost baseness, while prophethood is the highest of human positions and suits only a soul in utmost majesty and nobility. Combining the two qualities in one soul is impossible, so it is established that prophethood and treachery do not combine. The parallel to this verse is His saying: ﴿It is not for Allah to take a son﴾ [Maryam: 35], meaning divinity and taking a son do not combine. It has also been said that the lam is transferred, and the estimate is: "And the Prophet would not embezzle," like His saying: ﴿It is not for Allah to take a son﴾ [Maryam: 35], meaning Allah would not take a son.

The second interpretation of this verse on this reading: it may be said that the people had asked him to single them out with an extra portion of the spoils, and there is no doubt that if he had done so, it would have been ghulul. So Allah the Exalted revealed this verse as an emphatic prohibition for him from that. Its parallel is His saying: ﴿If you associate others with Allah, your deeds will surely be lost﴾ [al-Zumar: 65], and His saying: ﴿And if he had fabricated against Us some sayings, We would have seized him by the right hand﴾ [al-Haqqah: 44]. So His saying "It is not for a prophet to embezzle" means: it would not be lawful for him to do that, and if it is not lawful for him, he would not do it. Its parallel is His saying: ﴿And why, when you heard it, did you not say: it is not for us to speak of this﴾ [al-Nur: 16], meaning: it is not lawful for us.

Now that you know the interpretation of the verse on this reading, we say: the argument for this reading is several points:

One: most of the narrations concerning the occasion of revelation of this verse say that they attributed embezzlement to the Messenger (ﷺ), so Allah clarified through this verse that this trait does not befit him.

Page 59

Two: what is of this kind in the revelation has the verb attributed to the doer, such as His saying: ﴿It is not for us to associate anything with Allah﴾, and ﴿It was not for him to seize his brother﴾ [Yusuf: 76], ﴿No soul can die except by Allah's permission﴾ [Al 'Imran: 145], ﴿Allah would not lead a people astray after He had guided them﴾ [Yusuf: 38], ﴿Allah would not reveal to you the unseen﴾ [Al 'Imran: 179]. It is rare to say: "It was not for Zayd to be struck." Since this is so, this verse must be classed with the more general and more common usage. This is reinforced by what Abu 'Ubaydah related from Yunus, that he used to prefer this reading and said: "There is no expression in speech: 'It was not for you to be struck,'" with a dammah on the ta'.

Three: this reading was the choice of Ibn 'Abbas. It was said to him: "Ibn Mas'ud reads ﴿yaghulla﴾," and Ibn 'Abbas said: "The Prophet was intended to be killed, so how would they not attribute to him betrayal?"

As for the second reading, ﴿yughalla﴾ with a dammah on the ya and a fathah on the ghayn, it has two interpretations:

The first: the meaning is: it is not for a prophet to be betrayed.

Know that betrayal toward anyone is forbidden, and singling out the Prophet for this prohibition has benefits:

One: the more exalted and greater in rank the one wronged, the more heinous the betrayal against him, and the Messenger is the best of mankind, so betrayal against him is more heinous.

Two: revelation came to him moment by moment, so whoever betrays him, revelation may descend concerning him, and he would incur, along with the punishment of the Hereafter, the disgrace of this world.

Three: the Muslims at that time were in extreme poverty, so betrayal there was more heinous.

The second interpretation: it may be from ighlal, meaning to be betrayed, i.e., to be attributed to betrayal. Al-Mubarrad said: the Arabs say "akfartu al-rajul," meaning I made him a disbeliever and attributed disbelief to him. Al-'Utbi said: if this were the intended meaning, it would be said "yughallal," as it is said "yufassaq," "yufajjar," and "yukaffar." The more appropriate view is that it is from aghlaltuhu, meaning I found him to be a ghall (embezzler), just as one says abkhaltuhu and afhamtuhu, meaning I found him to be such. The author of al-Kashshaf said: this reading with this interpretation is close in meaning to the first reading, because the meaning of this reading is that it is not valid for the Prophet to be found an embezzler, since one is found an embezzler only if he is an embezzler.

The fourth issue: we have mentioned that ghulul is treachery, but in common usage it became specific to treachery concerning the spoils. This has also come in other than spoils. He (ﷺ) said: "Shall I not inform you of the greatest ghulul? Two men who share a house or land, and if one of them takes from the other the size of a stone's place, it will be hung around his neck from the seven earths." According to this interpretation, the meaning is that he, may the blessings and peace of Allah be upon him, is free of all forms of treachery. And how could we not say so, when the disbelievers offered him great wealth to abandon his claim to prophethood? How then would it befit one who was like this, and who was trustworthy with Allah concerning the revelation descending to him from above the seven heavens, to betray people?

* * *

Then the Exalted said: ﴿And whoever embezzles will bring what he embezzled on the Day of Resurrection﴾. There are two interpretations of this:

The first, which is the view of most exegetes, is to take this verse according to its apparent meaning. They said: it is similar to His saying concerning those who withhold zakat: ﴿On the Day when it will be heated in the fire of Hell, and their foreheads, their sides, and their backs will be branded with it: "This is what you hoarded for yourselves, so taste what you used to hoard"﴾ [al-Tawbah: 35]. It is supported by his saying: "Let me not find any one of you coming on the Day of Resurrection with a camel on his neck making a groaning sound, or a cow lowing, or a sheep bleating, and he calls out: 'O Muhammad, O Muhammad!' and I will say: 'I possess nothing for you against Allah; I have delivered the message to you.'" It is also narrated from Ibn 'Abbas that he said: that thing will be represented to him in the depths of Hell, then it will be said to him: "Go down to it and take it," so he goes down to it, and when he reaches it he carries it on his back, and it is not accepted from him.

The scholars who verify said: the benefit of this is that when he comes on the Day of Resurrection with that embezzlement upon his neck, his disgrace increases.

The second aspect: it may be said that the intended meaning is not its apparent sense; rather, the purpose is to intensify the threat by way of illustration and depiction. A parallel to this is the words of the Exalted: ﴿Indeed, if it be an atom's weight within a rock or in the heavens or in the earth, Allah will bring it forth﴾ [Luqman: 16]. The intended meaning here is not the apparent sense itself; rather, the purpose is to establish that Allah, exalted is He, is not absent from His knowledge or His preservation, not even the weight of an atom, on earth or in the sky. Likewise here, the purpose is to intensify the threat. Then, those who hold this view have mentioned two explanations.

The first: Abu Muslim said: the meaning is that Allah, exalted is He, preserves this act of embezzlement against him and will hold him accountable for it on the Day of Resurrection and recompense him, since nothing is hidden from Him.

The second: Abu al-Qasim al-Ka'bi said: the meaning is that he will become known for that, just as one who carries that thing becomes known. Know that this interpretation is possible, but the established principle in the science of the Qur'an is that the word must be taken in its literal sense unless there is a proof that prevents it, and here there is no barrier to this apparent sense, so it is obligatory to affirm it.

* * *

Then the Exalted said: ﴿Then every soul will be paid in full what it earned﴾, and concerning this there are two questions.

The first question: Why was it not said "then he will be paid in full what he earned," so that it would connect to what precedes it?

The answer: The benefit of mentioning this generality is that the one who embezzles, when he knows that there is a Recompenser here who recompenses everyone for his deed, whether good or evil, knows that he will not escape from among them, along with the enormity of what he has acquired.

The second question: The Mu'tazilah cling to this in establishing that the servant is the agent, and in establishing the threat against sinners.

As for the first: because He, exalted is He, established the recompense for what one earns; so if his earning were a creation of Allah, then Allah would be recompensing him for what He created in him.

As for the second: because He, exalted is He, said concerning the one who kills deliberately: ﴿But his recompense is Hell﴾ [An-Nisa: 93], and in this verse He established that every doer will receive his recompense; thus from the combination of the two verses there results a certainty of the threat against sinners.

The answer: As for the question of the act, its answer is the counter-argument from knowledge. As for the question of the threat, this generality is specified in the case of repentance; similarly it must be specified in the case of pardon, due to the proofs indicating pardon.

* * *

Then the Exalted said: ﴿and they will not be wronged﴾. The judge (al-Qadi) said: this indicates that injustice is possible in the acts of Allah, namely by diminishing from the reward or increasing in the punishment. He said: this is not conceivable except according to our view, not according to the view of those among the Mujbirah who say that whatever Allah, exalted is He, does is just and wise, because He is the Owner.

The answer: Negating injustice from Him does not indicate its validity regarding Him, just as His words: ﴿Neither drowsiness nor sleep overtakes Him﴾ [Al-Baqarah: 255] do not indicate that these are valid regarding Him.

[Page 61]

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Is one who follows the pleasure of Allah like one who incurs wrath from Allah?﴾

Know that when Exalted Allah said, ﴿Then every soul will be paid in full what it has earned﴾, He followed it with a detailed explanation of this statement. He made clear what the reward of the obedient is and what the recompense of the wrongdoers is. So He said: ﴿Is one who follows the pleasure of Allah﴾. There are several matters concerning this verse.

First matter: the commentators have several interpretations of it.

The first: ﴿Is one who follows the pleasure of Allah﴾ means one who avoids ghulul (embezzlement of war spoils), ﴿like one who incurs wrath from Allah﴾ means one who commits ghulul. This is the view of al-Kalbi and al-Dahhak.

The second: ﴿Is one who follows the pleasure of Allah﴾ by believing in Him and acting in obedience to Him, ﴿like one who incurs wrath from Allah﴾ by disbelieving in Him and being occupied with disobeying Him.

The third: ﴿Is one who follows the pleasure of Allah﴾ refers to the emigrants (muhajirun), and ﴿one who incurs wrath from Allah﴾ refers to the hypocrites (munafiqun).

The fourth: al-Zajjaj said: When the polytheists charged against the Muslims, the Prophet (ﷺ) called on his companions to charge against the polytheists. Some of them did so, and others abstained. So He said: ﴿Is one who follows the pleasure of Allah﴾, meaning those who obeyed his command, ﴿like one who incurs wrath from Allah﴾, meaning those who did not accept his word. Al-Qadi said: Each of these interpretations is correct, but it is not permissible to restrict the wording to any one of them. Everyone who inclines toward following the self and its desire is included under His saying, ﴿like one who incurs wrath from Allah﴾. At most, the verse was revealed concerning a specific event, but you know that the generality of the wording is not nullified by the specificity of the occasion of revelation.

Second matter: His saying, ﴿Is one who follows﴾. The interrogative particle (hamza) here expresses denial (inkar), and the fa' (فاء) is a conjunction joining it to an implied preceding clause, whose sense is: Is one who fears (Allah) and then follows the pleasure of Allah (like one who incurs wrath)?

Third matter: His saying, ﴿incurs wrath﴾ (باء بسخط), meaning he bore it and returned with it. We have mentioned this in Surat al-Baqarah.

Fourth matter: Asim, in one of the two transmissions from him, read (رُضْوانَ اللَّهِ) with a ḍammah on the rāʾ, while the rest read it with a kasrah. Both are verbal nouns (maṣdar): the ḍammah form is like al-kufran (كُفْرانِ), and the kasrah form is like al-hisban (حِسْبانِ).

Fifth matter: His saying, ﴿and his abode is Hell﴾, is a continuation of what precedes it, and the sense is: like one who incurs wrath from Allah and whose abode is Hell. As for His saying, ﴿and wretched is the destination﴾, it is separate from what precedes it and is an independent statement, as if, when He mentioned Hell, He followed it with a mention of its description.

Sixth matter: Similar to this verse are His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Or do those who commit evil deeds think that We will make them like those who believe and do righteous deeds, equal in their living and their dying?﴾ [al-Jathiyah: 21], His saying: ﴿Is one who is a believer like one who is defiantly disobedient? They are not equal﴾ [al-Sajdah: 18], and His saying: ﴿Or shall We make those who believe and do righteous deeds like corrupters on earth? Or shall We make the righteous like the wicked?﴾ [Sad: 28]. The (Mu'tazilite) people have used this verse to argue that it is not permissible for Allah, Exalted is He, to cause the obedient to enter the Fire or to cause the sinners to enter Paradise. They said: He, Exalted is He, mentioned this by way of rejecting it as unlikely, and if it were not impossible according to reason, this rejection would not be fitting. Al-Qaffal affirmed this, saying: It is not permissible in wisdom that the evildoer be equated with the one who does good, for that would encourage sins, permit them, and neglect acts of obedience.

Then He, exalted is He, said: ﴿They are degrees with Allah﴾, and on this there are several issues.

The first issue: The full sense of the sentence is "For them are degrees with Allah," but this omission is good (ḥasuna hādhā al-ḥadhf), because the difference in their deeds has made them like things that differ in their very natures. Thus this metaphor (majāz) is more eloquent than the literal expression (ḥaqīqa). The philosophers (ḥukamā') say that human souls differ in their essence and reality: some are clever and some are dull, some are luminous and light-filled, some are dark and murky, some are good and some are base. The difference in these qualities is not due to differences in bodily temperaments, but to differences in the essences of the souls. For this reason, peace and blessings be upon him said: "People are mines like the mines of gold and silver," and he said: "Spirits are armies gathered in ranks." Since this is so, it is established that people are in themselves degrees, not that they have degrees.

The second issue: The pronoun "hum" (they) refers back to the word "man" (whoever) in His saying: ﴿Is one who follows the pleasure of Allah﴾. The word "man" conveys plurality in meaning, so it is correct for His saying ﴿they﴾ to refer back to it. A parallel is His saying: ﴿Is one who was a believer like one who was a defiant sinner? They are not equal﴾, where His saying ﴿they are not equal﴾ is in the plural form and refers back to "man."

The third issue: The pronoun "hum" refers to something previously mentioned. Both the one who followed the pleasure of Allah and the one who incurred wrath from Allah have been mentioned, so this pronoun may refer to the first, or to the second, or to both together, and the possibilities are only these three.

The first aspect: that it refers to ﴿Is one who follows the pleasure of Allah﴾. Its implied meaning is: "Is one who follows the pleasure of Allah equal [to one who incurred wrath]? No! Rather, they are degrees with Allah according to their deeds." The following points show that this pronoun refers to those who follow the pleasure and that this is preferable:

First: In common usage, "darajāt" (degrees) is used predominantly for the people of reward, and "darakāt" (lower degrees) for the people of punishment.

Second: He, exalted is He, described the one who incurred wrath from Allah, that their refuge is Hell and an evil destination. Therefore His saying ﴿they are degrees﴾ must be a description of the one who followed the pleasure of Allah.

Third: The custom of the Qur'an for the most part is that whatever is of reward and mercy, Allah attributes to Himself, and whatever is of punishment He does not attribute to Himself. He, exalted is He, said: ﴿Your Lord has prescribed for Himself mercy﴾ [al-An'ām: 54], and He said: ﴿Retribution is prescribed for you﴾ [al-Baqarah: 178], ﴿Fasting is prescribed for you﴾ [al-Baqarah: 183]. So when He attributed these degrees to Himself, saying ﴿they are degrees with Allah﴾, we know that this is the attribute of the people of reward.

Fourth: It is reinforced by His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Behold how We have favoured some of them over others, and the Hereafter is greater in degrees and greater in favour﴾ [al-Isrā': 21].

The second aspect: that His saying ﴿they are degrees﴾ refers to ﴿like one who incurred wrath from Allah﴾. The argument is that the pronoun refers to the nearer antecedent, and this is the view of al-Ḥasan, who said: the meaning is that the people of the Fire vary in their levels of punishment. This is like His saying: ﴿And for each there are degrees according to what they did﴾ [al-An'ām: 132]. And it is reported from the Messenger of Allah ﷺ: "In it (the Fire) there is a shallow part and a deep part, and I hope that Abū Ṭālib will be in its shallowest part." He, peace and blessings be upon him, also said: "The least punished of the people of the Fire on the Day of Resurrection is a man who will be given two sandals of fire, from whose heat his brain will boil. He will call out: 'O my Lord, is there anyone who is punished more severely than I?!'"

The third aspect: that His saying ﴿they﴾ refers to all of them. This is because the degrees of the people of reward vary, and the degrees of the people of punishment also vary according to the variation in people's deeds, since He, exalted is He, said: ﴿So whoever does an atom's weight of good will see it, and whoever does an atom's weight of evil will see it﴾ [al-Zalzalah: 7–8]. Since the ranks of creation vary in their deeds of disobedience and obedience, it is necessary that their ranks vary in the degrees of punishment and reward.

The fourth issue: His saying ﴿with Allah﴾ means "in the judgment and knowledge of Allah." It is like saying: "This issue, according to al-Shāfi'ī, is such-and-such, and according to Abū Ḥanīfa, such-and-such." By this, the weakness of the argument of the Mushabbiha (anthropomorphists) is made clear, from His saying: ﴿And those who are with Him do not disdain﴾ [al-Anbiyā': 19] and His saying: ﴿In the seat of truth, with a mighty King﴾ [al-Qamar: 55].

* * *

Then He, exalted is He, said: ﴿And Allah is Seeing of what they do﴾. The purpose is that, since He mentioned that He gives each person the recompense of their deeds in full, this cannot be complete unless He knows all the actions of the servants in detail, free of doubt, suspicion and conjecture. He followed it with a statement that He knows everything, as an emphasis of that meaning, namely His saying: ﴿And Allah is Seeing of what they do﴾.

Muhammad ibn Isḥāq, the author of the Maghāzī (military campaigns), mentioned in interpreting His saying ﴿It is not for a Prophet to deceive (an-yaghulla)﴾ another aspect. He said: "It is not for a Prophet to deceive" means it is not for a Prophet to conceal from the people what Allah has sent him with to them, out of desire for people or fear of them. Then He said: ﴿Is one who follows the pleasure of Allah﴾, meaning: one who prefers the pleasure of Allah over the pleasure of creation and the wrath of Allah over the wrath of creation, ﴿like one who incurred wrath from Allah﴾, who prefers the wrath of creation over the wrath of Allah and the pleasure of creation over the pleasure of Allah. The connection of the verses according to this explanation is that when He said: ﴿So pardon them, ask forgiveness for them, and consult them in the matter﴾, He made clear that this is only valid when it accords with the religion. As for when it goes against the religion, it is not permissible. How, then, can one who follows the pleasure and obedience of Allah be equated with one who follows the pleasure of creatures? This explanation is plausible, because we have shown that ghulūl is a term for betrayal in a secret way. As for restricting this word to betrayal in the spoils of war, that is a newly arisen usage.

The commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on Surah 3, verse 164:

Allah the Exalted said: ﴿Indeed, Allah conferred a favour upon the believers when He sent among them a Messenger from among themselves, reciting to them His verses, purifying them, and teaching them the Book and the wisdom, although before that they had been in clear error.﴾

Know that there are several aspects to the connection (wajh al-nazm, the way this verse links to what precedes it):

The first: when Allah explained the error of those who attributed to him misappropriation (ghulul, taking booty dishonestly) and betrayal, He confirmed that refutation with this verse. This is because this Messenger was born among them and grew up among them, and nothing was seen from him throughout his life except truthfulness, trustworthiness, calling to Allah, and turning away from the world. How, then, could betrayal befit one whose condition is this?

The second: when He explained their error in ascribing betrayal and misappropriation to him, He said: I am not content with that, nor do I suffice, regarding his right, with clearing him of betrayal and misappropriation. Rather, I say: his presence among you is among the greatest of My blessings upon you, for he purifies you from the false ways and teaches you knowledge beneficial to you in your worldly life and in your religion. So what sensible person would think of attributing betrayal to such a man?

The third: it is as if He, the Exalted, were saying: he is from you, from your land and from your kin, while you are people of obscurity and baseness. When Allah, the Exalted, honours him and singles him out with the qualities of excellence and beneficence above all the worlds, great honour accrues to you because he is among you. So your slandering him and your striving to attribute foul things to him is contrary to reason.

The fourth: since he possesses such nobility and distinction that Allah bestows favour through him upon His servants, it is obligatory upon every sensible person to help him with the utmost of his ability. Therefore it is incumbent upon you to fight his enemies, and to stand with him with hand, tongue, sword and spear. The purpose of this return to the theme is to encourage the Muslims to strive against the disbelievers.

In the verse there are several issues:

The first issue: al-Wahidi, may Allah have mercy on him, said: The word mann (favour) has several meanings in the Arabic language:

One of them: that which falls from the sky, as in His saying: ﴿And We sent down upon you the manna and the quails﴾ [al-Baqarah: 57].

The second: to bestow upon someone and reproach them for it, as in His saying: ﴿Do not nullify your charities by reminding of favour and causing hurt﴾ [al-Baqarah: 264].

The third: cutting off, as in His saying: ﴿For them is a reward that will never be cut off﴾ [Fussilat: 8], and ﴿Indeed, for you is a reward never cut off﴾.

The fourth: bounty and kindness to one from whom you do not seek recompense. From this is His saying: ﴿This is Our gift, so grant [favour] or withhold, without account﴾ [Sad: 39], and His saying: ﴿And do not give [in order] to receive more﴾. As for al-Mannan as an attribute of Allah, the Exalted, it means the One who gives at the outset without seeking any return from them. And His saying: ﴿Allah conferred a favour upon the believers﴾ means: He bestowed blessing and kindness upon them by sending this Messenger.

The second issue: sending the Messenger is a kindness to all the worlds. This is because the aspect of kindness in his mission is that he calls them to what saves them from the punishment of Allah and brings them to the reward of Allah. This applies generally to all the worlds, since he was sent to all the worlds, as Allah the Exalted said: ﴿And We have not sent you except as a comprehensive [bearer of good tidings and warner] to mankind﴾ [Saba': 28]. However, since only the people of Islam benefited from this blessing, for this reason Allah the Exalted restricted this favour to the believers. A parallel to this is His saying: ﴿a guidance for those who fear Allah﴾ [al-Baqarah: 2], although it is guidance for all, as He said: ﴿a guidance for mankind﴾ [al-Baqarah: 185], and His saying: ﴿You are only a warner for those who fear it﴾ [al-Nazi'at: 45].

* * *

The third issue: know that the sending of a Messenger is a kindness from Allah to creation. Then, since benefit from the Messenger is greater, the aspect of favour in the sending of messengers is greater. The mission of Muhammad (ﷺ) comprised both matters:

One of them: the benefits arising from the very fact of his mission.

The second: the benefits arising from the qualities that he possessed, which did not exist in anyone else.

As for the benefit due to the very fact of the mission, it is what Allah mentioned in His saying: ﴿Messengers as bearers of good tidings and as warners, so that people will have no argument against Allah after the messengers﴾ [al-Nisa': 165]. Abu 'Abd Allah al-Halimi said: The aspect of benefit from the sending of messengers lies only in the path of religion, and it has several aspects:

The first: that creation was made with deficiency, little understanding and lack of insight. So he, peace and blessings be upon him, presented to them the aspects of proofs and refined them, and whenever a doubt or a misgiving occurred to them, he removed it and answered it.

The second: that although creation knew that they must serve their Master, they did not know the manner of that service. So he explained that manner to them, so that they might undertake the service secure from error and from doing what is not befitting.

The third: that creation was made inclined to laziness, heedlessness, slackness and weariness. So he presented to them various kinds of encouragement and warning, so that whenever laziness or lethargy overtook them, he would reinvigorate them for obedience and encourage them towards it.

The fourth: that the lights of the intellects of creation are like the lights of sight. It is known that benefit from the light of sight is not complete except when the light of the sun shines. His light is intellectual and divine, and it operates like the rising of the sun. It strengthens intellects with the light of his intellect, and there appear to them from the signs of the unseen what had been hidden from them before his appearance. This is a true indication of the benefits of the very fact of the mission.

As for the benefits arising from the qualities that were in Muhammad (ﷺ), these are matters which Allah mentioned in this verse, the first of which is His saying: ﴿from among themselves﴾.

* * *

Know that the aspect of benefit in this has several aspects:

The first: he, peace be upon him, was born among them and grew up among them. They knew his circumstances and were acquainted with all his actions and words. They witnessed from him, from the beginning of his life to its end, only truthfulness and chastity, indifference to the world, distance from lying, and constancy in truth. Whoever knows of a man, from the beginning of his life to its end, that he consistently maintained truthfulness and trustworthiness and kept far from betrayal and lying, and then claimed prophethood and messengership, in which lying is the foulest kind of lie, will be inclined in the mind of everyone to believe that he is truthful in this claim.

The second: they knew that he had not studied under anyone, had not read a book, and had not engaged in lessons or repetition. Until the age of forty he never spoke at all of prophethood or messengership. Then, after forty, he claimed messengership, and there appeared on his tongue knowledge such as had not appeared on the tongue of anyone among the worlds. Moreover, he recounted the stories of earlier peoples and the circumstances of the past prophets in the manner that existed in their books. Everyone with sound intellect knows that this cannot be achieved except through heavenly revelation and divine inspiration.

The third: after he claimed prophethood, they offered him abundant wealth and wives in order that he would abandon this claim, but he did not turn to any of that. Rather, he was content with poverty and endured hardship. When his affair became elevated, his station became great, he conquered lands, and the spoils became abundant, he did not change his path of distance from the world and of calling to Allah. The liar only commits lying in order to obtain the world; when he obtains it, he enjoys it and expands in it. Since he did none of that, it is known that he was truthful.

The fourth: the Book he brought contains nothing but affirmation of monotheism, transcendence (of Allah), justice and prophethood, establishment of the Return, explanation of acts of worship, and confirmation of acts of obedience. It is known that human perfection lies in knowing the truth for its own sake and the good for the sake of acting upon it. Since his Book is solely concerned with affirming these two matters, every sensible person knows that he is truthful in what he says.

The fifth: before his coming, the religion of the Arabs was the basest of religions, namely the worship of idols, and their morals were the basest of morals, namely raiding, plunder, killing, and eating foul foods. Then, when Allah sent Muhammad (ﷺ), by the blessing of his coming Allah raised them from that state, which is the lowest of states, until they became the best of nations in knowledge, asceticism, worship, and indifference to the world and its good things. There is no doubt that in this is the greatest favour.

Having understood these aspects, we say: Muhammad, upon him be prayer and peace, was born among them and grew up among them, and they were witnessing these circumstances and were acquainted with these proofs. Thus their belief, while witnessing these circumstances, was easier than it would have been had they not been acquainted with these circumstances. For these meanings Allah conferred His favour upon them by making him sent from among them, so He said: ﴿when He sent among them a Messenger from among themselves﴾. There is in this another aspect of favour: it became an honour for the Arabs and a source of pride for them, as He said: ﴿And indeed, it is a reminder for you and for your people﴾ [al-Zukhruf: 44]. This is because pride in Ibrahim, peace be upon him, was shared among the Jews, the Christians and the Arabs. Then the Jews and the Christians used to take pride in Musa, Isa, the Torah and the Gospel, while the Arabs had nothing equivalent to that. So when Allah sent Muhammad, peace be upon him, and revealed the Qur'an, the honour of the Arabs through that became greater than the honour of all nations. This is the aspect of the benefit in His saying: ﴿from among themselves﴾.

[p. 66]

Then Allah the Exalted said after that: ﴿reciting to them His verses, purifying them, and teaching them the Book and the wisdom﴾.

Know that the perfection of the human condition lies in two matters: in knowing the truth for its own sake, and the good for the sake of acting upon it. In other words, the human soul has two powers: theoretical and practical. Allah the Exalted sent down the Book upon Muhammad, peace be upon him, so that it would be a means of perfecting creation in these two powers. So His saying: ﴿reciting to them His verses﴾ indicates his being a conveyor of that revelation from Allah to creation. His saying: ﴿and purifying them﴾ indicates the perfecting of the theoretical power through the attainment of divine knowledge. "The Book" indicates knowledge of the interpretation (ta'wil, the inner meaning and ultimate reality). In other words, "the Book" indicates the outward meanings of the Shari'ah, and "the wisdom" indicates the excellences of the Shari'ah, its secrets, its underlying causes and its benefits. Then Allah explained what completes this blessing: that before this they had been in clear error. This is because when a blessing comes after a trial, its anticipation is greater. So if the nature of the blessing is knowledge and instruction, and it comes after ignorance and departure from religion, it is greater. A parallel to this is His saying: ﴿And He found you lost and guided you﴾ [al-Duha: 7].

**Verse 3:165**

"Why, when a calamity afflicted you, although you had inflicted twice as much (on the enemy), do you say, 'How is this?' Say, 'It is from yourselves.' Indeed, Allah is over all things competent."

Know that when Allah, exalted is He, informed about the hypocrites that they reproached the Messenger ﷺ by attributing to him embezzlement and betrayal, He related from them another doubt in this verse, which is their saying: "If he were a messenger from Allah, his army would not have been defeated by the disbelievers on the Day of Uhud." This is what is meant by their saying, "How is this?" Allah answered it with His words, "Say, 'It is from yourselves'," meaning: this defeat only occurred due to the ill omen of your disobedience. This is the explanation of the connection of the verse. Regarding the verse there are several issues:

**First issue: the explanation of the verse, "When a calamity afflicted you"**, the intended meaning is the event of Uhud. Regarding His words, "although you had inflicted twice as much (on the enemy)," there are two opinions:

The first, which is the view of most scholars, is that its meaning is: "you had inflicted (such losses) on the Day of Badr." This is because the polytheists killed seventy of the Muslims on the Day of Uhud, while the Muslims killed seventy of them on the Day of Badr and captured seventy.

The second: the Muslims defeated the disbelievers on the Day of Badr, and they also defeated them at the beginning of the Day of Uhud; then, when they disobeyed, the polytheists defeated them. Thus the defeat of the polytheists occurred twice, and the defeat of the Muslims occurred once. This is the choice of al-Zajjaj. al-Wahidi criticized this view, saying: just as the Muslims inflicted harm on the polytheists on the Day of Badr, the polytheists likewise inflicted harm on the Muslims on the Day of Uhud, but they did not defeat the Muslims at all. As for the Day of Uhud, the Muslims first defeated the polytheists, then the situation reversed.

**Second issue: the benefit in His words, "you had inflicted twice as much"**, is to alert that the affairs of this world do not remain on one course. Since you defeated them twice, what is improbable about them defeating you once?

As for His words, "you say, 'How is this?'", there are two issues:

**First issue: the reason for their astonishment** is that they said: "We support Islam, which is the religion of truth, and the Messenger is with us, while they support the religion of polytheism and disbelief. How then have they become victorious over us?"

Know that Allah, exalted is He, answered this doubt in two ways:

The first is what He included when relating the question, namely His words, "you had inflicted twice as much," meaning that the states of this world do not remain on one course. So when you inflicted twice such an event upon them, how do you find this event improbable?

The second is His words: "Say, 'It is from yourselves'," and regarding it there are issues:

**First issue: the explanation of this answer in two ways:**

The first: you fell into this calamity only due to the ill omen of your disobedience, for they disobeyed the Messenger in several matters:

First: the Messenger, peace be upon him, said: "The best course is that we do not go out of Medina but remain here," but they insisted on going out. When they opposed him, he set out toward Uhud.

Second: what Allah related of their cowardice.

Third: the dispute that arose among them.

Fourth: they left their position and split the ranks.

Fifth: their preoccupation with seeking spoils and their turning away from obeying the Messenger, peace be upon him, in fighting the enemy. All these aspects are sins and acts of disobedience, and Allah promised them victory only on condition of abandoning disobedience, as He said: "If you are patient and fear Allah, and they come upon you suddenly this very moment, your Lord will reinforce you" (Qur'an 3:125). So when the condition was lost, the conditioned outcome was inevitably lost.

The second way of interpretation: what has been related from Ali, may Allah be pleased with him, that he said: "Gabriel, peace be upon him, came to the Prophet ﷺ on the Day of Badr and said: 'O Muhammad, Allah has disliked what your people did in taking ransom from the captives, and He has commanded you to offer them a choice between bringing the captives forward to have their necks struck, or taking ransom on condition that an equal number of them be killed.' The Messenger of Allah ﷺ mentioned that to his people, and they said: 'O Messenger of Allah, they are our clans and brothers; we take ransom from them and strengthen ourselves thereby in fighting the enemy, and we accept that an equal number of us be martyred.' So seventy men were killed on the Day of Uhud, equal to the number of the captives of the people of Badr." This is the meaning of His words, "Say, 'It is from yourselves'," i.e., by taking ransom and your choosing killing.

* * *

**Second issue:** The Mu'tazilah cited His words, "Say, 'It is from yourselves'," as evidence that the actions of the servant are not created by Allah, exalted is He, in several ways:

The first: if that were produced by the creation of Allah with no effect of the servant's power in it, then His words, "from yourselves," would be a lie.

The second: the people were amazed how Allah would let the disbeliever dominate the believer; Allah removed the amazement by mentioning that you only fell into this disliked outcome due to the ill omen of your own deed. Had their act been the creation of Allah, this answer would not be valid.

The third: the people said, "How is this?", meaning, "From where is this?", which is a request for the cause of the occurrence. So if the one who originated it were not the servant, the answer would not correspond to the question.

The reply: it is countered by the verses indicating that the actions of the servant are by the origination of Allah, exalted is He.

* * *

Then Allah, exalted is He, said: "Indeed, Allah is over all things competent," meaning that He is capable of granting you victory if you stand firm and are patient, just as He is capable of leaving you to yourselves if you oppose and disobey. Our companions used this to argue that the act of the servant is created by Allah, exalted is He. They said: the act of the servant is a thing, so it is created by Allah, exalted is He, and He is capable of it. If Allah is capable of bringing it into existence, and then the servant brings it into existence, it becomes impossible for Allah to be capable of bringing it into existence, because once the servant has brought it into existence, its origination by Allah becomes impossible, since bringing an existent into existence is impossible. Since the servant's being its originator leads to this impossibility, it must be that the servant is not its originator. And Allah knows best.

**Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on Surah 3, verse 166:**

The Exalted said: ﴿And whatever afflicted you on the day the two hosts met, it was by the permission of Allah, and that He might know the believers﴾ ﴿and that He might know those who became hypocrites. It was said to them, "Come, fight in the way of Allah, or repel the enemy." They said, "If we knew there would be fighting, we would certainly follow you." They were nearer to disbelief that day than to faith, saying with their mouths what is not in their hearts. And Allah knows best what they conceal﴾.

Know that this is connected to what preceded it, His saying: ﴿Why, when a calamity afflicted you, though you had inflicted twice as much, do you say, "From where is this?"﴾. In the first verse He mentioned that the calamity befell them because of their own sin and from themselves. In this verse He mentioned that it befell them for another reason, namely that the believer be distinguished from the hypocrite. There are several issues in the verse:

**The first issue:** His saying, ﴿the day the two hosts met﴾. It refers to the Day of Uhud. The two hosts are:

First: the host of the Muslims, the companions of Muhammad (ﷺ).

Second: the host of the polytheists who were with Abu Sufyan.

**The second issue:** Concerning His saying, "by the permission of Allah" (*fa-bi-idhni llah*), there are several interpretations:

The first: The permission of Allah is an expression for leaving free and abandoning resistance. He used the word "permission" metaphorically for leaving the disbelievers free, for He did not prevent them from them in order to test them, because permission to do something does not turn the one permitted away from his purpose. So when abandoning resistance was a necessary consequence of permission, the term was applied to abandoning resistance by way of metaphor (*majaz*, figurative usage).

The second interpretation: "by the permission of Allah" means "by His knowledge," as in His saying: ﴿And a proclamation from Allah﴾ [al-Tawbah: 3], meaning a notification, and His saying: ﴿We have informed You that none of us is a witness﴾ [Fussilat: 47], and His saying: ﴿then be informed of war from Allah﴾ [al-Baqarah: 279]. All of these have the meaning of knowledge. al-Wahidi criticized this view, saying: The verse is a consolation to the believers for what befell them, and consolation can only occur if it happened by His knowledge, because His knowledge encompasses all known things, as evidenced by His saying: ﴿No female conceives or gives birth except with His knowledge﴾ [Fatir: 11].

The third interpretation: The intended meaning of "permission" is command, as evidenced by His saying: ﴿Then He turned you away from them in order to test you﴾ [Al 'Imran: 152]. The meaning is that when He commanded fighting, and that fighting then led to that defeat, it is correct, by way of metaphor, to say that it occurred by His command.

The fourth interpretation, which is related from Ibn 'Abbas: The intended meaning of "permission" is Allah's decree concerning that and His judgment regarding it. This is preferable, because the verse is a consolation to the believers for what afflicted them, and consolation is only achieved when it is said that this occurred by the decree and destiny of Allah, and then they will be content with what Allah has decreed.

* * *

Then He said: ﴿and that He might know the believers﴾ ﴿and that He might know those who became hypocrites﴾. The meaning is that He would distinguish the believers from the hypocrites. There are several issues in the verse:

**The first issue:** al-Wahidi said: It is said, "The man became a hypocrite (*munafiq*)" if he displays the word of faith and conceals its opposite. Hypocrisy (*nifaq*) is an Islamic term whose derivation has been disputed in several interpretations:

The first: Abu 'Ubayda said: It is from *nafiqa'* of the jerboa (*yarbu'*). That is because the burrow of the jerboa has two openings: the *qasi'a'* and the *nafiqa'*. If one is pursued from one of them, it exits from the other. So the hypocrite is called a hypocrite because he has set for himself two paths: displaying Islam and concealing disbelief. Whichever of them you pursue him by, he will exit by the other.

The second: Ibn al-Anbari said: The hypocrite (*munafiq*) is from *nafaq*, which is a tunnel (*sirb*). Its meaning is that he conceals himself with Islam, just as a man hides himself in a tunnel.

The third: It is derived from *nafiqa'*, but in a way other than the one that Abu 'Ubayda mentioned. The *nafiqa'* is a burrow that the jerboa digs inside the earth, then it thins out the part above the burrow, so that when it senses a threat it pushes away the dirt with its head and exits. The hypocrite is called a hypocrite because he conceals disbelief within himself, and when he is examined he casts off that disbelief and holds fast to Islam.

**The second issue:** His saying, ﴿and that He might know the believers﴾. Its apparent meaning suggests that He permitted that affliction in order that this knowledge might come about. This implies a renewal of Allah's knowledge, and this is impossible with respect to the knowledge of Allah, the Exalted. Therefore, "knowledge" here means the object of knowledge (*ma'lum*), and the sense is: that the believer might be made clear from the hypocrite, and that one of them might be distinguished from the other, the permission for that affliction occurred. This meaning has already been explained in the preceding verses, and Allah knows best.

**The third issue:** There is an ellipsis (*hadhf*) in the verse. Its estimated form is: "and that He might know the faith of the believers and the hypocrisy of the hypocrites."

If it is asked: Why did He say, ﴿and that He might know the believers﴾ ﴿and that He might know those who became hypocrites﴾, and not say, "and that He might know the hypocrites"?

We say: The noun (*ism*) indicates the affirmation of that meaning, while the verb (*fi'l*) indicates its renewal. His saying, ﴿and that He might know the believers﴾, indicates that they are steadfast in their faith and firm in it. As for "became hypocrites" (*nafaqu*), it indicates that they only began to undertake the actions appropriate to hypocrisy at that time.

[p. 69]

Then He, exalted is He, said: ﴿And it was said to them, "Come, fight in the way of Allah or repel [the enemy]."﴾ On this verse there are several issues:

The first issue: Concerning who this speaker was, there are two views.

The first: al-Asamm said: it was the Messenger (ﷺ), peace be upon him, who was calling them to fight.

The second: It is narrated that when 'Abdullah ibn Ubayy ibn Salul set out with his army toward Uhud, they said: "Why should we throw ourselves into killing?" So they turned back, and they were three hundred of the thousand with whom the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) had set out. Then 'Abdullah ibn 'Amr ibn Haram, father of Jabir ibn 'Abdullah al-Ansari, said to them: "I remind you of Allah, do not forsake your Prophet and your people at the presence of the enemy." This is what is meant by His saying, ﴿and it was said to them﴾, that is, the saying of this 'Abdullah.

The second issue: His saying, ﴿Fight in the way of Allah or repel﴾, means: if there is in your hearts love of the religion and Islam, then fight for the religion and Islam; and if you are not like that, then fight to repel [the enemy] from yourselves, your families and your wealth. That is, be either among the men of religion or among the men of this world. al-Suddi and Ibn Jurayj said: "Repel the enemy from us by increasing our numbers, if you do not fight with us." They said: "Because multitude is one of the causes of awe and majesty." The first view is the more apparent.

The third issue: His saying, exalted is He, ﴿Fight in the way of Allah or repel﴾, is an explicit statement that they gave precedence to seeking the religion over seeking the world, and this indicates that a Muslim must give precedence to religion over the world in all important matters.

* * *
Then He, exalted is He, said: ﴿They say, "If we knew there would be fighting, we would have followed you." They were nearer to disbelief that day than to faith﴾. This is the answer that the hypocrites mentioned, and in it there are two views:
The first: that the meaning is that the two groups will not fight at all, therefore we turned back.

The second: that the meaning is: "If we knew what could be called fighting, we would have followed you." That is, what they were advancing toward is not called fighting; rather it is casting oneself into destruction, because 'Abdullah's opinion was to remain in Madinah, and he did not think going out was the right course.
