Know that if the intended meaning of this statement is the first view, then it is corrupt, because conjecture in worldly matters takes the place of knowledge, and the signs of the coming of battle were manifest on that day. If it were said to this hypocrite who gave this answer: "You should, if you saw someone who had drawn his sword in war, not advance to fight him because you do not know that he will fight," and likewise in all other worldly affairs. Rather, the truth is that jihad is obligatory when the signs of warfare appear, and there is no sign stronger than their nearness to Madinah at the mountain of Uhud. So the mention of this answer indicates the utmost disgrace and hypocrisy, and that their purpose in giving this answer was either deception or mockery. As for the intended meaning of the hypocrite being the second view, it too is false, because when Allah, exalted is He, had promised them victory and help, going out to that battle was not casting oneself into destruction.

* * *
Then He, exalted is He, explained their condition when they gave this answer, saying: ﴿They were nearer to disbelief that day than to faith﴾. On this there are issues:
The first issue: concerning the interpretation there are two views:

The first: that before this incident they used to show faith outwardly, and no sign of their disbelief had appeared from them. When they turned back from the army of the believers, they distanced themselves thereby from being thought to be believers.

Know that their withdrawal from aiding the Muslims indicates that they were not among the Muslims. Also, their saying, ﴿If we knew there would be fighting, we would have followed you﴾, indicates that they were not among the Muslims, because we have shown that this speech indicates either mockery of the Muslims or lack of trust in the words of the Prophet (ﷺ), and each of these is disbelief.

The second view of interpretation: that the meaning is that they were nearer in support to the people of disbelief than to the people of faith, because their reducing the numbers of the Muslims by withdrawing leads to strengthening the polytheists.

The second issue: Most scholars said: this is an explicit statement from Allah, exalted is He, that they were disbelievers. al-Hasan said: when Allah, exalted is He, says "nearer" (aqrab), it is certainty that they are polytheists, and it is like His saying: ﴿a hundred thousand or more﴾ [al-Saffat: 147], for that excess is beyond doubt. Also, the accountable person cannot be free of either faith or disbelief, so when the verse indicates nearness, the occurrence of disbelief is necessary. al-Wahidi said in al-Basit: this verse is evidence that whoever utters the word of tawhid does not become a disbeliever, and the statement of his disbelief is not made absolute, because He, exalted is He, did not make absolute the statement of their disbelief, even though they were disbelievers, due to their outward profession of "There is no god but Allah, Muhammad is the Messenger of Allah."

* * *
Then He, exalted is He, said: ﴿They say with their mouths what is not in their hearts﴾. The meaning is that their tongues oppose their hearts; though they show faith with the tongue, they conceal disbelief in their hearts.
* * *
Then He said: ﴿And Allah knows best what they conceal﴾.

Page 71
If it is said: when two knowers know a known thing, neither of them knows it more than the other, so what is the meaning of His saying: ﴿And Allah knows best what they conceal﴾?
We say: the meaning is that Allah, exalted is He, knows from the details of those states what no one else knows.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Those who said of their brothers, while they themselves sat back, "If they had obeyed us, they would not have been killed." Say: "Then avert death from yourselves, if you are truthful."﴾

Know that those whom God related as having said ﴿If we knew there would be fighting, we would certainly have followed you﴾ are described by God, exalted is He, as having stayed behind and argued for their staying behind. Likewise, they discouraged others and argued for that too. So God related that they said to their brothers that the ones who went out, if they had obeyed us, would not have been killed. Thus they frightened whoever intended to agree with the Messenger (ﷺ) in fighting the disbelievers, by means of killing, when they knew what had happened at the Battle of Uhud, where the disbelievers killed the Muslims. This is because what is known of human nature is the love of life. So the occurrence of this doubt in the hearts operated like the whisperings that Satan inserts. In the verse there are several issues.

The first issue: concerning the grammatical position of ﴿alladhina﴾ (those who), there are several possibilities.

The first: the accusative, as a *badal* (substitution, apposition) of ﴿alladhina nafaqu﴾ (those who were hypocrites).

The second: the nominative, as a *badal* of the pronoun in ﴿yaktumuna﴾ (they conceal).

The third: the nominative, as the predicate of an inchoative (*mubtada'*), with the implied sense: "They are those who."

The fourth: that it be in the accusative, as an expression of blame (*dhamm*).

The second issue: The exegetes said: the intended referent of ﴿those who said﴾ is Abdullah ibn Ubayy and his companions. Al-Asamm said: this is not valid, because Abdullah ibn Ubayy went out with the Prophet (ﷺ) in the jihad on the day of Uhud. This statement applies to those who had stayed behind, because He said ﴿those who said to their brothers while they sat back, "If they had obeyed us"﴾, meaning in the sitting back, ﴿they would not have been killed﴾. So it is a statement subsequent to the jihad, said to those who went out to jihad and to those whose intention in that was strong, so that it would become a doubt for them afterward, diverting them from jihad.

The third issue: ﴿They said to their brothers﴾ means they said for the sake of their brothers. The meaning of this brotherhood has already been explained: whether brotherhood by lineage, or brotherhood through sharing a dwelling, or in enmity toward the Messenger (ﷺ), or in the worship of idols. And God knows best.

The fourth issue: Al-Wahidi said: the *waw* in His saying ﴿wa qa'adu﴾ (and they sat back) is for the circumstantial (*hal*). The meaning of this sitting is sitting back from jihad, meaning: those who were killed at Uhud, if they had stayed back as we stayed back, and done as we did, they would have been safe and would not have been killed. Then God answered this with His saying: ﴿Say: "Then avert death from yourselves, if you are truthful."﴾

If it is said: What is the basis for the argument with this, given that the difference is obvious? For avoiding being killed is possible, whereas avoiding death is absolutely impossible?

The answer: This argument which God mentioned holds only if we acknowledge *al-qada' wa'l-qadar* (divine decree and predestination). For when we say that nothing comes into existence except by God's decree and predestination, we acknowledge that the disbeliever does not kill the Muslim except by God's decree. Then there is no difference between being killed and dying, and so the argument is valid. But if we say that the act of the servant is not by God's decree and determination, then the difference between death and killing would be obvious in the respect you mentioned, and this would lead to the invalidity of the argument God mentioned. It is known that what leads to that is false. Thus it is established that this verse indicates that everything is by God's decree.

His saying ﴿if you are truthful﴾ means: if you are truthful in being occupied with guarding against what is disliked and in attaining what is sought.

[Page 72]

Commentary of al-Razi (*Mafatih al-Ghayb*) on surah 3, verses 169–170 (part 1 of 2):

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Do not think of those who were killed in the way of Allah as dead. Rather, they are alive with their Lord, being provided for,﴾ ﴿rejoicing in what Allah has given them of His bounty, and rejoicing for those who have not yet joined them from behind them, that no fear will be upon them, nor will they grieve.﴾

Know that when the people [the hypocrites] discouraged those who were eager for jihad by saying, "Jihad leads to killing," as they said concerning those who went out to jihad on the day of Uhud, and killing is a disliked thing, then it was necessary to avoid jihad. Then Allah, exalted is He, made clear that their saying "jihad leads to killing" is false, because killing happens only by the decree and predestination of Allah, just as death happens by the decree and predestination of Allah. So whoever Allah has destined to be killed cannot guard against it, and whoever Allah has not destined to be killed has nothing to fear from killing. Then, in this verse, He answered that doubt with another answer, namely: we do not accept that killing in the way of Allah is a disliked thing. And how can that be said, when the one killed in the way of Allah has been given life by Allah after being killed, has been singled out with degrees of nearness and honour, has been given the best kinds of provision, and has been brought to the highest levels of joy and delight? So what intelligent person would say that such a killing is disliked? This is the manner of the arrangement (*nazm*) of the verses. And in the verse there are several issues:

**The first issue:** This verse was revealed concerning the martyrs of Badr and Uhud, because at the time this verse was revealed, none of the martyrs was other than those killed on these two famous days. The hypocrites were only discouraging the fighters from jihad so that they would not become killed like those Muslims who were killed on these two days. Allah, exalted is He, mentioned the virtues of those killed on these two days, so that this would become a call for the Muslims to imitate those who fought on these two days and were killed. The summary of the matter is that whoever abandons jihad may or may not reach the bliss of this world, and even if he does reach it, it is small and trivial. But whoever turns to jihad will certainly attain the bliss of the Hereafter, which is a great bliss, and despite its greatness it is lasting and enduring. When this is the case, it becomes clear that turning to jihad is better than abandoning it.

* * *

**The second issue:** Know that the apparent meaning of the verse indicates that these killed ones are alive. Either the intended meaning is literal or figurative. If the intended meaning is literal, then either the meaning is that they will become alive in the Hereafter, or the meaning is that they are alive now. And assuming that this is the intended meaning, either the intended meaning is the affirmation of spiritual life, or the affirmation of bodily life. This is the account of the possible views that can be mentioned concerning this verse.

**The first possibility:** That the interpretation of the verse is that they will become alive in the Hereafter. This was held by a group of the Mu'tazilite theologians (*mutakallimun al-Mu'tazilah*), among them Abu al-Qasim al-Ka'bi, who said: "That is because the hypocrites about whom Allah related what He related used to say: 'The companions of Muhammad ﷺ expose themselves to killing, so they get killed and lose their life and gain no good.' They used to say this because they denied the Resurrection and the promise. So Allah rejected them and made clear by this verse that they will be resurrected, provided for, and that joy, delight and good tidings will reach them."

Know that this view, in our opinion, is false, and the following points indicate that:

**The first proof:** His saying ﴿but alive﴾ apparently indicates that they are alive at the time of the revelation of the verse. So taking it to mean that they will become alive after that is a departure from the apparent meaning.

**The second proof:** There is no doubt that the side of mercy, bounty and kindness is weightier than the side of punishment and retribution. Then Allah, exalted is He, mentioned concerning the people of punishment that He gave them life before the Resurrection for the sake of punishment, for He, exalted is He, said: ﴿They were drowned, then they were made to enter a fire﴾ [Nuh: 25]. The particle *fa* (then) indicates sequence, and punishment is conditioned upon life. Also, Allah, exalted is He, said: ﴿The Fire, they are exposed to it morning and evening﴾ [Ghafir: 46]. And when Allah makes the people of punishment alive before the establishment of the Resurrection for the sake of punishment, then it is more fitting that He makes the people of reward alive before the Resurrection for the sake of kindness and recompense.

**The third proof:** If He had intended that He would make them alive at the resurrection in Paradise, He would not have said to the Messenger, upon him be blessings and peace: ﴿Do not think﴾, since he knew that all the believers are like that. But when we take it to mean the reward of the grave, the saying "Do not think" is fitting, because perhaps he, upon him be blessings and peace, did not know that Allah honours the obedient and the sincere with this honour, namely that He gives them life before the establishment of the Resurrection in order to deliver the reward to them.

If it is said: He, upon him be blessings and peace, although he knew that they would become alive with their Lord at the resurrection, did not know that they were among the people of Paradise. So it was permissible for Allah to give him good tidings that they would become alive and reach the reward and delight.

We say: His saying "Do not think" concerns only death, because He said: ﴿Do not think those who were killed in the way of Allah to be dead﴾. So what removes this supposition is that they are alive now, because there is no supposition there concerning their becoming alive on the Day of Resurrection. And His saying ﴿being provided for﴾ ﴿rejoicing﴾ is the predicate of a subject, and it has no connection with that supposition. So this objection is removed.

**The fourth proof:** His, exalted is He, saying: ﴿and rejoicing for those who have not yet joined them from behind them﴾. Those who have not yet joined them must necessarily be in this world, so their rejoicing for those who are in this world must necessarily be before the establishment of the Resurrection. And rejoicing must necessarily be together with life. So this indicates that they are alive before the Day of Resurrection. There is a discussion concerning this argument that will come later.

**The fifth proof:** What has been related from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him and his father: "The Prophet ﷺ said concerning the description of the martyrs: 'Their souls are in the crops of green birds, and they come to the rivers of Paradise and eat of its fruits, and they roam wherever they wish, and they take refuge in lamps of gold beneath the Throne. When they saw the goodness of their dwelling, their food and their drink, they said: "Would that our people knew what we are in of bliss and what Allah has done with us, so that they would be eager for jihad." Then Allah, exalted is He, said: "I will inform about you and convey to your brothers." So they rejoiced at that and were delighted, and Allah, exalted is He, revealed this verse.'" And Ibn Mas'ud, may Allah be pleased with him, was asked about this verse, and he said: "We asked about it, and it was said to us: The martyrs are at a river at the gate of Paradise, in a green dome." And in another narration: "in a green garden." And from Jabir ibn 'Abd Allah, who said: The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "Shall I not give you good tidings that your father, when he was struck at Uhud, Allah gave him life, then said: 'What do you want, O servant of Allah, that I should do for you?' He said: 'O my Lord, I love that You return me to the world so that I may be killed for You a second time.'" The reports on this subject have almost reached the level of *tawatur* (mass transmission). So how can they be denied? Al-Ka'bi criticized these reports and said: They are not permissible, because the souls do not experience bliss; rather, only the body experiences bliss when there is life in it, not the soul. The position of the soul in relation to the body is like the position of strength. Also, the apparent meaning of the transmitted report requires that these souls are in the crops of birds. Also, its apparent meaning requires that they come to the rivers of Paradise, eat of its fruits and roam, and this contradicts their being in the crops of birds.

The answer: As for the first criticism, it is based on the premise that the soul is an accident subsisting in the body, and we will show that this is not the case. As for the second criticism, it is rejected, because the purpose of such expressions is metaphors for attaining comforts and delights and the removal of fears and calamities. This is the summary of the discussion regarding this possibility.

As for the second of the possible views concerning this verse: that the martyrs are alive now. Among those who hold this view, some affirm this life for the soul, and some affirm it for the body. Before entering into this subject, it is necessary to present a preliminary point, namely that the human being is not merely the sum of this bodily structure. Two things indicate this:

The first: the parts of this structure are in constant melting, dissolution and change, while the particular human being is one thing that remains from the beginning of his life to its end, and what remains is different from what changes. What confirms what we have said is that he sometimes becomes fat and sometimes thin, and that at the beginning he is small in body, then he grows and increases. There is no doubt that every human being finds in himself that he is one thing from the beginning of his life to its end. So what we have said is established.

The second: the human being may know himself while being unaware of all his limbs and parts, and what is known is different from what is not known. So by these two points it is established that he is a thing different from this perceptible body. Then after that it is possible that it is a particular body permeating this physical form, like the permeation of fire in charcoal, of oil in sesame, and of rose water in roses. And it is possible that it is a substance subsisting by itself, which is neither a body nor inherent in a body. On both views, it is not unlikely that when the body died, that thing separated while alive. And if we say that Allah caused it to die, He will still restore life to it. On this basis, doubts about the reward of the grave are completely removed, as in this verse, and about the punishment of the grave, as in His saying: ﴿They were drowned, then they were made to enter a fire﴾ [Nuh: 25]. So it is established by what we have mentioned that there is no impossibility in this. The apparent meaning of the verse indicates it, so it is necessary to adopt it. What confirms what we have mentioned is the Qur'an, the Hadith and reason.

As for the Qur'an, there are verses:

The first of them: ﴿O soul at rest,﴾ ﴿return to your Lord, well-pleased and pleasing [to Him],﴾ ﴿enter among My servants,﴾ ﴿and enter My Paradise﴾ [al-Fajr: 27–30]. There is no doubt that what is meant by His saying ﴿return to your Lord﴾ is death. Then He said: ﴿enter among My servants﴾ [al-Fajr: 29], and the *fa* of sequence indicates that the occurrence of this state is after death, and this indicates what we have mentioned.

The second: ﴿Until, when death comes to one of you, Our messengers take him, and they do not fail﴾ [al-An'am: 61]. This is an expression for the death of the body.

Then He said: ﴿Then they are returned to Allah, their true Master﴾ [al-An'am: 62]. So His saying "they are returned" refers to that [soul], and it returns with its life and its particular essence. This indicates that it remains after the death of the body.

The third: His saying: ﴿But if he was among those brought near,﴾ ﴿then [for him is] rest and bounty and a Garden of pleasure﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 88–89]. The *fa* of sequence indicates that this rest, bounty and Garden are obtained immediately after death.

As for the Hadith, there is the saying of the Prophet, upon him be blessings and peace: "Whoever dies, his resurrection has already come" (*man mata faqad qamat qiyamatuh*). The *fa* is the *fa* of sequence and indicates that the resurrection of each person occurs after his death. As for the Great Resurrection, it occurs at the appointed time with Allah. Also, his saying, upon him be blessings and peace: "The grave is either a garden from the gardens of Paradise or a pit from the pits of the Fire." Also it has been related that "on the day of Badr the Prophet, upon him be blessings and peace, used to call out to the slain and say: 'Have you found what your Lord promised to be true?' It was said to him: 'O Messenger of Allah, they are dead, so how do you call to them?' He, upon him be blessings and peace, said: 'They hear better than you.'" Or words to this effect. Also, he, upon him be blessings and peace, said: "The friends of Allah do not die, but they are transferred from one abode to another." All of this indicates that souls remain after the death of the body.

As for reason, it is in several respects:

[p. 75 continued]

The first: the time of sleep weakens the body, but this weakness does not require that the soul be weakened. Rather, the soul grows stronger during sleep, witnessing states and gaining knowledge of unseen things. If the weakness of the body does not necessitate the weakness of the soul, then this strengthens the presumption that the death of the body does not entail the death of the soul.

The second: many thoughts (*al-afkar*) cause the brain to dry out, and its drying leads to death. These thoughts are also the means by which the soul is perfected with divine knowledge, which is the ultimate perfection of the soul. Whatever is a cause of the soul's perfection is a cause of the body's deficiency. This strengthens the presumption that the soul does not die with the death of the body.

The third: the states of the soul are the opposite of the states of the body. This is because the soul rejoices and delights only in divine knowledge. The proof is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Surely, in the remembrance of Allah do hearts find rest﴾ [al-Ra'd: 28]. The Prophet, upon him be prayers and peace, said: "I spend the night with my Lord; He feeds me and gives me drink." There is no doubt that this food and drink is nothing but an expression for knowledge, love, and illumination by the lights of the unseen world. Furthermore, we observe that when a person is overcome by the joy of serving a ruler, or of attaining a position, or of reaching his beloved, he may forget food and drink; indeed, he may come to a state where, if he were invited to eat and drink, he would find in his heart a strong aversion to it. The knowers (*al-arifun*) who are deeply immersed in the knowledge of Allah, exalted is He, may find within themselves that when some of those lights appear to them and some of those secrets are revealed to them, they do not feel hunger or thirst at all. In sum, the spiritual happiness of the soul is like the opposite of bodily happiness, and all of this strongly suggests that the soul is independent in its essence and has no attachment to the body. If that is so, the soul must not die with the death of the body. Let these persuasive arguments (*al-iqna'iyyat*) suffice for this discussion.

Know that once this principle is established, all doubts and objections are removed concerning what has been reported in the Qur'an about the reward and punishment of the grave. Now that you know this principle, we say: some of the commentators (*al-mufassirun*) said: the spirits of the martyrs are alive, and they bow and prostrate every night beneath the Throne until the Day of Resurrection. The proof for this is what is related, that the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "When a servant sleeps in his prostration, Allah, exalted is He, boasts of him to His angels and says: 'Look at My servant: his soul is with Me and his body is in My service.'"

Know that the verse indicates this, namely His saying: ﴿alive with their Lord﴾. The word "with" (*'inda*) is mentioned here, and likewise it is mentioned in the description of the angels: ﴿And those who are with Him do not disdain to worship Him﴾ [al-Anbiya': 19]. So when you understand the happiness attained by the angels through being with Allah, you understand the happiness attained by the martyrs through being with Allah. These are words that open to the intellect the doors of knowledge of the Hereafter.

The third aspect in interpreting this verse, according to those who affirm this life for the bodies: those who hold this view have differed. Some of them said: Allah lifts up the bodies of these martyrs to the heavens and to lamps beneath the Throne, and delivers all kinds of happiness and honours to them. Others said: He leaves them on earth, revives them, and delivers these blessings to them. Among the people is one who criticised this and said: we see the bodies of these martyrs being eaten by wild beasts. Then either it must be said that Allah revives them while they are in the bellies of these beasts and delivers the reward to them, or it must be said that those parts, after being separated from the bellies of the beasts, are reassembled by Allah, joined together, and life is returned to them, and the reward is delivered to them. All of this is far-fetched. Moreover, we see the slain body remaining for days until its limbs disintegrate and pus and discharge are separated out. If we allow that they are living, enjoying bliss, rational and knowing, it would necessitate adopting sophistry (*al-safsata*).

The fourth aspect in interpreting this verse is to say: the intended meaning of their being alive is not the existence of life in them; rather, the intended meaning is a certain figurative usage (*majaz*). Its explanation is in several ways:

The first: al-Asamm al-Balkhi said: when a deceased person was of great standing in religion, and his end on the Day of Resurrection is joy, happiness, and honour, it is correct to say that he is alive and not dead, just as it is said of an ignorant person who benefits neither himself nor anyone else: he is dead and not alive; and as it is said of a dull person: he is a donkey, and of a harmful person: he is a beast of prey. It is related that when 'Abd al-Malik ibn Marwan saw al-Zuhri and recognised his understanding and his precision, he said to him: "No one has died who has left behind someone like you." In sum, there is no doubt that when a person dies and leaves behind a good reputation and a fine remembrance, it is said figuratively that he has not died but is alive.

The second: some of them said: the figurative meaning of this life is that their bodies remain in their graves, and that they do not decay beneath the earth at all. These people argued with what is related: when Mu'awiyah wanted to run a canal over the graves of the martyrs, he ordered that it be proclaimed: "Whoever has a slain relative, let him bring him out from this place." Jabir said: "We went out to them and brought them out with their bodies still fresh, and a spade struck the finger of one of them, and blood dripped from it."

The third: the intended meaning of their being alive is that they are not washed as the dead are washed.

This is the entirety of what has been said about this verse, and Allah knows best the secrets of created things.

Third issue: the author of al-Kashshaf (*Sahib al-Kashshaf*) said: "Do not think" (*wa la tahsabanna*) is addressed to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), or to everyone. It was also read with the *ya'* (*wa la yahsabanna*), and in this there are several possibilities:

One: "Let not the Messenger of Allah think."

Second: "Let no one who reckons think."

Third: "Let not those who were slain for the sake of Allah think themselves dead." He said: "*Tahsabanna*" was also read with a *fatha* on the *sin*. Ibn 'Amir read "*qutthilu*" with the doubled *ta'*, while the rest read it with the single *ta'*.

Fourth issue: His saying: ﴿But they are alive﴾. Al-Wahidi said: the estimated (grammatical) reading is: "Rather, they are alive." The author of al-Kashshaf said: "*ahya'an*" was also read with the accusative, in the sense of "Rather, I reckon them to be alive." I say: al-Zajjaj said: if "*ahya'an*" were read with the accusative, it would be permissible in the sense of "Rather, I reckon them to be alive." Abu 'Ali al-Farisi criticised this, saying: that is not permissible, because it would be a command to doubt, and a command to doubt is not permissible for Allah. He also said that interpreting *husban* (reckoning) as knowledge is not permissible, because no scholar of the language has held that. Al-Zajjaj could reply by saying: *husban* is conjecture, not doubt; so why do you say that Allah may not command conjecture? Is it not the case that His obligation in all matters of juristic reasoning (*al-mujtahadat*) is nothing but conjecture?

I say: this debate between al-Zajjaj and Abu 'Ali al-Farisi indicates that "*ahya'an*" was not actually read with the accusative; rather, al-Zajjaj claimed that it has a grammatical justification in the language, and al-Farisi disputed this with him. Not every reading that has a grammatical justification (*wajh fi al-i'rab*) is thereby permissible as a recitation.

As for His saying: ﴿with their Lord﴾, there are several interpretations:

One: in a state where no one possesses benefit or harm for them except Allah, exalted is He.

Second: "they are alive with their Lord" means they are alive in His knowledge and His judgment, just as one says: "This is so according to al-Shafi'i, and according to Abu Hanifa it is otherwise."

Third: "*'inda*" means nearness and honour, as in His saying: ﴿And those who are with Him﴾ [al-Anbiya': 19], and His saying: ﴿Those who are with your Lord﴾ [Fussilat: 38].

As for His saying: ﴿they are provided for﴾, ﴿rejoicing in what Allah has given them﴾: know that the theologians (*al-mutakallimun*) said: reward is a pure and enduring benefit joined with honour. So His saying "they are provided for" points to the benefit, and His saying "rejoicing" points to the joy arising from that honour. As for the philosophers (*al-hukama'*), they said: when the luminous essences of the holy spirits are illumined by divine lights, they are joyful in two respects:

One: that their essences become radiant, shining, and gleaming with those holy manifestations and divine knowledge.

The second: that they are looking toward the fountain of light and the source of mercy and majesty. They said: their joy in this second respect is more complete than their joy in the first. So His saying "they are provided for" points to the first degree, and His saying "rejoicing" points to the second degree. For this reason He said: ﴿rejoicing in what Allah has given them of His bounty﴾, meaning that their joy is not in the provision itself but in the bestowing of the provision, because one occupied with provision is occupied with himself, while one who looks to the bestowing of provision is occupied with the Provider. Whoever seeks the Truth for the sake of something other than it is veiled.

* * *

Then He, exalted is He, said: ﴿and they rejoice in those who have not yet joined them from behind them, that there will be no fear for them, nor will they grieve﴾.

Know that His saying "*that there is no fear*" (*alla khawfun*) is in the position of the genitive as an apposition (*badal*) of "those" (*alladhina*). The estimated meaning is: "they rejoice that there is no fear and no grief, concerning those who have not yet joined them from behind them." In the verse there are several issues:

First issue: *al-istibshar* is the joy arising from good tidings, and the basic meaning of the *istif'al* form is seeking the action; so the one who rejoices is like one who seeks joy and finds it through good tidings.

Second issue: know that those who accepted that the martyrs are alive before the Resurrection have mentioned other interpretations of this verse:

As for the first: it is said that the martyrs say to one another: "We left behind our brothers, so-and-so and so-and-so, in the ranks of those fighting the unbelievers, and they will be killed, if Allah wills, and will attain provision and honour just as we attained." This is His saying: ﴿and they rejoice in those who have not yet joined them﴾.

As for the second: it is said that when the martyrs enter Paradise after the Resurrection, they are provided for, rejoicing in what Allah has given them of His bounty. The meaning of His saying "*those who have not yet joined them from behind them*" is their brothers among the believers who do not have the rank of the martyrs, because the martyrs enter Paradise before them. The proof is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And Allah has preferred those who strive over those who sit back by a great reward, degrees from Him, and forgiveness and mercy﴾ [al-Nisa': 95–96]. They rejoice at what they see of the abodes of the believers and the bliss prepared for them, and at what they hope for of gathering with them, and by this their eyes are comforted. This is the choice of Abu Muslim al-Isfahani and al-Zajjaj.

Know that the first interpretation is stronger than the second, because the result of the second returns to some believers rejoicing in others on account of their being gathered together in Paradise; and this is a general matter concerning all believers, so there is no sense in singling out the martyrs for it. Furthermore: just as they rejoice in those who have not yet joined them from behind them, so too they rejoice in those who preceded them into entry, because the stations of the prophets and the truthful (*al-siddiqun*) are above the stations of the martyrs. He, exalted is He, said: ﴿Those are with those on whom Allah has bestowed favour from among the prophets, the truthful, the martyrs, and the righteous﴾ [al-Nisa': 69]. On this interpretation there remains no benefit in the specification. But when we interpret the verse according to the first aspect, there is the greatest benefit in singling out the fighters for this special quality, so that is preferable, and Allah knows best.

Third issue: fear arises from anticipating a disliked matter that will descend in the future, and grief arises from the loss of benefits that existed in the past. So He, glorified is He, clarified that there is no fear for them regarding what will come upon them of the conditions of the Resurrection, nor is there any grief for them regarding what they have missed of the bliss of this world.

Commentary of al-Razi (*Mafatih al-Ghayb*) on surah 3, verses 169–170 (part 1 of 2):

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Do not think of those who were killed in the way of Allah as dead. Rather, they are alive with their Lord, being provided for,﴾ ﴿rejoicing in what Allah has given them of His bounty, and rejoicing for those who have not yet joined them from behind them, that no fear will be upon them, nor will they grieve.﴾

Know that when the people [the hypocrites] discouraged those who were eager for jihad by saying, "Jihad leads to killing," as they said concerning those who went out to jihad on the day of Uhud, and killing is a disliked thing, then it was necessary to avoid jihad. Then Allah, exalted is He, made clear that their saying "jihad leads to killing" is false, because killing happens only by the decree and predestination of Allah, just as death happens by the decree and predestination of Allah. So whoever Allah has destined to be killed cannot guard against it, and whoever Allah has not destined to be killed has nothing to fear from killing. Then, in this verse, He answered that doubt with another answer, namely: we do not accept that killing in the way of Allah is a disliked thing. And how can that be said, when the one killed in the way of Allah has been given life by Allah after being killed, has been singled out with degrees of nearness and honour, has been given the best kinds of provision, and has been brought to the highest levels of joy and delight? So what intelligent person would say that such a killing is disliked? This is the manner of the arrangement (*nazm*) of the verses. And in the verse there are several issues:

**The first issue:** This verse was revealed concerning the martyrs of Badr and Uhud, because at the time this verse was revealed, none of the martyrs was other than those killed on these two famous days. The hypocrites were only discouraging the fighters from jihad so that they would not become killed like those Muslims who were killed on these two days. Allah, exalted is He, mentioned the virtues of those killed on these two days, so that this would become a call for the Muslims to imitate those who fought on these two days and were killed. The summary of the matter is that whoever abandons jihad may or may not reach the bliss of this world, and even if he does reach it, it is small and trivial. But whoever turns to jihad will certainly attain the bliss of the Hereafter, which is a great bliss, and despite its greatness it is lasting and enduring. When this is the case, it becomes clear that turning to jihad is better than abandoning it.

* * *

**The second issue:** Know that the apparent meaning of the verse indicates that these killed ones are alive. Either the intended meaning is literal or figurative. If the intended meaning is literal, then either the meaning is that they will become alive in the Hereafter, or the meaning is that they are alive now. And assuming that this is the intended meaning, either the intended meaning is the affirmation of spiritual life, or the affirmation of bodily life. This is the account of the possible views that can be mentioned concerning this verse.

**The first possibility:** That the interpretation of the verse is that they will become alive in the Hereafter. This was held by a group of the Mu'tazilite theologians (*mutakallimun al-Mu'tazilah*), among them Abu al-Qasim al-Ka'bi, who said: "That is because the hypocrites about whom Allah related what He related used to say: 'The companions of Muhammad ﷺ expose themselves to killing, so they get killed and lose their life and gain no good.' They used to say this because they denied the Resurrection and the promise. So Allah rejected them and made clear by this verse that they will be resurrected, provided for, and that joy, delight and good tidings will reach them."

Know that this view, in our opinion, is false, and the following points indicate that:

**The first proof:** His saying ﴿but alive﴾ apparently indicates that they are alive at the time of the revelation of the verse. So taking it to mean that they will become alive after that is a departure from the apparent meaning.

**The second proof:** There is no doubt that the side of mercy, bounty and kindness is weightier than the side of punishment and retribution. Then Allah, exalted is He, mentioned concerning the people of punishment that He gave them life before the Resurrection for the sake of punishment, for He, exalted is He, said: ﴿They were drowned, then they were made to enter a fire﴾ [Nuh: 25]. The particle *fa* (then) indicates sequence, and punishment is conditioned upon life. Also, Allah, exalted is He, said: ﴿The Fire, they are exposed to it morning and evening﴾ [Ghafir: 46]. And when Allah makes the people of punishment alive before the establishment of the Resurrection for the sake of punishment, then it is more fitting that He makes the people of reward alive before the Resurrection for the sake of kindness and recompense.

**The third proof:** If He had intended that He would make them alive at the resurrection in Paradise, He would not have said to the Messenger, upon him be blessings and peace: ﴿Do not think﴾, since he knew that all the believers are like that. But when we take it to mean the reward of the grave, the saying "Do not think" is fitting, because perhaps he, upon him be blessings and peace, did not know that Allah honours the obedient and the sincere with this honour, namely that He gives them life before the establishment of the Resurrection in order to deliver the reward to them.

If it is said: He, upon him be blessings and peace, although he knew that they would become alive with their Lord at the resurrection, did not know that they were among the people of Paradise. So it was permissible for Allah to give him good tidings that they would become alive and reach the reward and delight.

We say: His saying "Do not think" concerns only death, because He said: ﴿Do not think those who were killed in the way of Allah to be dead﴾. So what removes this supposition is that they are alive now, because there is no supposition there concerning their becoming alive on the Day of Resurrection. And His saying ﴿being provided for﴾ ﴿rejoicing﴾ is the predicate of a subject, and it has no connection with that supposition. So this objection is removed.

**The fourth proof:** His, exalted is He, saying: ﴿and rejoicing for those who have not yet joined them from behind them﴾. Those who have not yet joined them must necessarily be in this world, so their rejoicing for those who are in this world must necessarily be before the establishment of the Resurrection. And rejoicing must necessarily be together with life. So this indicates that they are alive before the Day of Resurrection. There is a discussion concerning this argument that will come later.

**The fifth proof:** What has been related from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him and his father: "The Prophet ﷺ said concerning the description of the martyrs: 'Their souls are in the crops of green birds, and they come to the rivers of Paradise and eat of its fruits, and they roam wherever they wish, and they take refuge in lamps of gold beneath the Throne. When they saw the goodness of their dwelling, their food and their drink, they said: "Would that our people knew what we are in of bliss and what Allah has done with us, so that they would be eager for jihad." Then Allah, exalted is He, said: "I will inform about you and convey to your brothers." So they rejoiced at that and were delighted, and Allah, exalted is He, revealed this verse.'" And Ibn Mas'ud, may Allah be pleased with him, was asked about this verse, and he said: "We asked about it, and it was said to us: The martyrs are at a river at the gate of Paradise, in a green dome." And in another narration: "in a green garden." And from Jabir ibn 'Abd Allah, who said: The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "Shall I not give you good tidings that your father, when he was struck at Uhud, Allah gave him life, then said: 'What do you want, O servant of Allah, that I should do for you?' He said: 'O my Lord, I love that You return me to the world so that I may be killed for You a second time.'" The reports on this subject have almost reached the level of *tawatur* (mass transmission). So how can they be denied? Al-Ka'bi criticized these reports and said: They are not permissible, because the souls do not experience bliss; rather, only the body experiences bliss when there is life in it, not the soul. The position of the soul in relation to the body is like the position of strength. Also, the apparent meaning of the transmitted report requires that these souls are in the crops of birds. Also, its apparent meaning requires that they come to the rivers of Paradise, eat of its fruits and roam, and this contradicts their being in the crops of birds.

The answer: As for the first criticism, it is based on the premise that the soul is an accident subsisting in the body, and we will show that this is not the case. As for the second criticism, it is rejected, because the purpose of such expressions is metaphors for attaining comforts and delights and the removal of fears and calamities. This is the summary of the discussion regarding this possibility.

As for the second of the possible views concerning this verse: that the martyrs are alive now. Among those who hold this view, some affirm this life for the soul, and some affirm it for the body. Before entering into this subject, it is necessary to present a preliminary point, namely that the human being is not merely the sum of this bodily structure. Two things indicate this:

The first: the parts of this structure are in constant melting, dissolution and change, while the particular human being is one thing that remains from the beginning of his life to its end, and what remains is different from what changes. What confirms what we have said is that he sometimes becomes fat and sometimes thin, and that at the beginning he is small in body, then he grows and increases. There is no doubt that every human being finds in himself that he is one thing from the beginning of his life to its end. So what we have said is established.

The second: the human being may know himself while being unaware of all his limbs and parts, and what is known is different from what is not known. So by these two points it is established that he is a thing different from this perceptible body. Then after that it is possible that it is a particular body permeating this physical form, like the permeation of fire in charcoal, of oil in sesame, and of rose water in roses. And it is possible that it is a substance subsisting by itself, which is neither a body nor inherent in a body. On both views, it is not unlikely that when the body died, that thing separated while alive. And if we say that Allah caused it to die, He will still restore life to it. On this basis, doubts about the reward of the grave are completely removed, as in this verse, and about the punishment of the grave, as in His saying: ﴿They were drowned, then they were made to enter a fire﴾ [Nuh: 25]. So it is established by what we have mentioned that there is no impossibility in this. The apparent meaning of the verse indicates it, so it is necessary to adopt it. What confirms what we have mentioned is the Qur'an, the Hadith and reason.

As for the Qur'an, there are verses:

The first of them: ﴿O soul at rest,﴾ ﴿return to your Lord, well-pleased and pleasing [to Him],﴾ ﴿enter among My servants,﴾ ﴿and enter My Paradise﴾ [al-Fajr: 27–30]. There is no doubt that what is meant by His saying ﴿return to your Lord﴾ is death. Then He said: ﴿enter among My servants﴾ [al-Fajr: 29], and the *fa* of sequence indicates that the occurrence of this state is after death, and this indicates what we have mentioned.

The second: ﴿Until, when death comes to one of you, Our messengers take him, and they do not fail﴾ [al-An'am: 61]. This is an expression for the death of the body.

Then He said: ﴿Then they are returned to Allah, their true Master﴾ [al-An'am: 62]. So His saying "they are returned" refers to that [soul], and it returns with its life and its particular essence. This indicates that it remains after the death of the body.

The third: His saying: ﴿But if he was among those brought near,﴾ ﴿then [for him is] rest and bounty and a Garden of pleasure﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 88–89]. The *fa* of sequence indicates that this rest, bounty and Garden are obtained immediately after death.

As for the Hadith, there is the saying of the Prophet, upon him be blessings and peace: "Whoever dies, his resurrection has already come" (*man mata faqad qamat qiyamatuh*). The *fa* is the *fa* of sequence and indicates that the resurrection of each person occurs after his death. As for the Great Resurrection, it occurs at the appointed time with Allah. Also, his saying, upon him be blessings and peace: "The grave is either a garden from the gardens of Paradise or a pit from the pits of the Fire." Also it has been related that "on the day of Badr the Prophet, upon him be blessings and peace, used to call out to the slain and say: 'Have you found what your Lord promised to be true?' It was said to him: 'O Messenger of Allah, they are dead, so how do you call to them?' He, upon him be blessings and peace, said: 'They hear better than you.'" Or words to this effect. Also, he, upon him be blessings and peace, said: "The friends of Allah do not die, but they are transferred from one abode to another." All of this indicates that souls remain after the death of the body.

As for reason, it is in several respects:

[p. 75 continued]

The first: the time of sleep weakens the body, but this weakness does not require that the soul be weakened. Rather, the soul grows stronger during sleep, witnessing states and gaining knowledge of unseen things. If the weakness of the body does not necessitate the weakness of the soul, then this strengthens the presumption that the death of the body does not entail the death of the soul.

The second: many thoughts (*al-afkar*) cause the brain to dry out, and its drying leads to death. These thoughts are also the means by which the soul is perfected with divine knowledge, which is the ultimate perfection of the soul. Whatever is a cause of the soul's perfection is a cause of the body's deficiency. This strengthens the presumption that the soul does not die with the death of the body.

The third: the states of the soul are the opposite of the states of the body. This is because the soul rejoices and delights only in divine knowledge. The proof is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Surely, in the remembrance of Allah do hearts find rest﴾ [al-Ra'd: 28]. The Prophet, upon him be prayers and peace, said: "I spend the night with my Lord; He feeds me and gives me drink." There is no doubt that this food and drink is nothing but an expression for knowledge, love, and illumination by the lights of the unseen world. Furthermore, we observe that when a person is overcome by the joy of serving a ruler, or of attaining a position, or of reaching his beloved, he may forget food and drink; indeed, he may come to a state where, if he were invited to eat and drink, he would find in his heart a strong aversion to it. The knowers (*al-arifun*) who are deeply immersed in the knowledge of Allah, exalted is He, may find within themselves that when some of those lights appear to them and some of those secrets are revealed to them, they do not feel hunger or thirst at all. In sum, the spiritual happiness of the soul is like the opposite of bodily happiness, and all of this strongly suggests that the soul is independent in its essence and has no attachment to the body. If that is so, the soul must not die with the death of the body. Let these persuasive arguments (*al-iqna'iyyat*) suffice for this discussion.

Know that once this principle is established, all doubts and objections are removed concerning what has been reported in the Qur'an about the reward and punishment of the grave. Now that you know this principle, we say: some of the commentators (*al-mufassirun*) said: the spirits of the martyrs are alive, and they bow and prostrate every night beneath the Throne until the Day of Resurrection. The proof for this is what is related, that the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "When a servant sleeps in his prostration, Allah, exalted is He, boasts of him to His angels and says: 'Look at My servant: his soul is with Me and his body is in My service.'"

Know that the verse indicates this, namely His saying: ﴿alive with their Lord﴾. The word "with" (*'inda*) is mentioned here, and likewise it is mentioned in the description of the angels: ﴿And those who are with Him do not disdain to worship Him﴾ [al-Anbiya': 19]. So when you understand the happiness attained by the angels through being with Allah, you understand the happiness attained by the martyrs through being with Allah. These are words that open to the intellect the doors of knowledge of the Hereafter.

The third aspect in interpreting this verse, according to those who affirm this life for the bodies: those who hold this view have differed. Some of them said: Allah lifts up the bodies of these martyrs to the heavens and to lamps beneath the Throne, and delivers all kinds of happiness and honours to them. Others said: He leaves them on earth, revives them, and delivers these blessings to them. Among the people is one who criticised this and said: we see the bodies of these martyrs being eaten by wild beasts. Then either it must be said that Allah revives them while they are in the bellies of these beasts and delivers the reward to them, or it must be said that those parts, after being separated from the bellies of the beasts, are reassembled by Allah, joined together, and life is returned to them, and the reward is delivered to them. All of this is far-fetched. Moreover, we see the slain body remaining for days until its limbs disintegrate and pus and discharge are separated out. If we allow that they are living, enjoying bliss, rational and knowing, it would necessitate adopting sophistry (*al-safsata*).

The fourth aspect in interpreting this verse is to say: the intended meaning of their being alive is not the existence of life in them; rather, the intended meaning is a certain figurative usage (*majaz*). Its explanation is in several ways:

The first: al-Asamm al-Balkhi said: when a deceased person was of great standing in religion, and his end on the Day of Resurrection is joy, happiness, and honour, it is correct to say that he is alive and not dead, just as it is said of an ignorant person who benefits neither himself nor anyone else: he is dead and not alive; and as it is said of a dull person: he is a donkey, and of a harmful person: he is a beast of prey. It is related that when 'Abd al-Malik ibn Marwan saw al-Zuhri and recognised his understanding and his precision, he said to him: "No one has died who has left behind someone like you." In sum, there is no doubt that when a person dies and leaves behind a good reputation and a fine remembrance, it is said figuratively that he has not died but is alive.

The second: some of them said: the figurative meaning of this life is that their bodies remain in their graves, and that they do not decay beneath the earth at all. These people argued with what is related: when Mu'awiyah wanted to run a canal over the graves of the martyrs, he ordered that it be proclaimed: "Whoever has a slain relative, let him bring him out from this place." Jabir said: "We went out to them and brought them out with their bodies still fresh, and a spade struck the finger of one of them, and blood dripped from it."

The third: the intended meaning of their being alive is that they are not washed as the dead are washed.

This is the entirety of what has been said about this verse, and Allah knows best the secrets of created things.

Third issue: the author of al-Kashshaf (*Sahib al-Kashshaf*) said: "Do not think" (*wa la tahsabanna*) is addressed to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), or to everyone. It was also read with the *ya'* (*wa la yahsabanna*), and in this there are several possibilities:

One: "Let not the Messenger of Allah think."

Second: "Let no one who reckons think."

Third: "Let not those who were slain for the sake of Allah think themselves dead." He said: "*Tahsabanna*" was also read with a *fatha* on the *sin*. Ibn 'Amir read "*qutthilu*" with the doubled *ta'*, while the rest read it with the single *ta'*.

Fourth issue: His saying: ﴿But they are alive﴾. Al-Wahidi said: the estimated (grammatical) reading is: "Rather, they are alive." The author of al-Kashshaf said: "*ahya'an*" was also read with the accusative, in the sense of "Rather, I reckon them to be alive." I say: al-Zajjaj said: if "*ahya'an*" were read with the accusative, it would be permissible in the sense of "Rather, I reckon them to be alive." Abu 'Ali al-Farisi criticised this, saying: that is not permissible, because it would be a command to doubt, and a command to doubt is not permissible for Allah. He also said that interpreting *husban* (reckoning) as knowledge is not permissible, because no scholar of the language has held that. Al-Zajjaj could reply by saying: *husban* is conjecture, not doubt; so why do you say that Allah may not command conjecture? Is it not the case that His obligation in all matters of juristic reasoning (*al-mujtahadat*) is nothing but conjecture?

I say: this debate between al-Zajjaj and Abu 'Ali al-Farisi indicates that "*ahya'an*" was not actually read with the accusative; rather, al-Zajjaj claimed that it has a grammatical justification in the language, and al-Farisi disputed this with him. Not every reading that has a grammatical justification (*wajh fi al-i'rab*) is thereby permissible as a recitation.

As for His saying: ﴿with their Lord﴾, there are several interpretations:

One: in a state where no one possesses benefit or harm for them except Allah, exalted is He.

Second: "they are alive with their Lord" means they are alive in His knowledge and His judgment, just as one says: "This is so according to al-Shafi'i, and according to Abu Hanifa it is otherwise."

Third: "*'inda*" means nearness and honour, as in His saying: ﴿And those who are with Him﴾ [al-Anbiya': 19], and His saying: ﴿Those who are with your Lord﴾ [Fussilat: 38].

As for His saying: ﴿they are provided for﴾, ﴿rejoicing in what Allah has given them﴾: know that the theologians (*al-mutakallimun*) said: reward is a pure and enduring benefit joined with honour. So His saying "they are provided for" points to the benefit, and His saying "rejoicing" points to the joy arising from that honour. As for the philosophers (*al-hukama'*), they said: when the luminous essences of the holy spirits are illumined by divine lights, they are joyful in two respects:

One: that their essences become radiant, shining, and gleaming with those holy manifestations and divine knowledge.

The second: that they are looking toward the fountain of light and the source of mercy and majesty. They said: their joy in this second respect is more complete than their joy in the first. So His saying "they are provided for" points to the first degree, and His saying "rejoicing" points to the second degree. For this reason He said: ﴿rejoicing in what Allah has given them of His bounty﴾, meaning that their joy is not in the provision itself but in the bestowing of the provision, because one occupied with provision is occupied with himself, while one who looks to the bestowing of provision is occupied with the Provider. Whoever seeks the Truth for the sake of something other than it is veiled.

* * *

Then He, exalted is He, said: ﴿and they rejoice in those who have not yet joined them from behind them, that there will be no fear for them, nor will they grieve﴾.

Know that His saying "*that there is no fear*" (*alla khawfun*) is in the position of the genitive as an apposition (*badal*) of "those" (*alladhina*). The estimated meaning is: "they rejoice that there is no fear and no grief, concerning those who have not yet joined them from behind them." In the verse there are several issues:

First issue: *al-istibshar* is the joy arising from good tidings, and the basic meaning of the *istif'al* form is seeking the action; so the one who rejoices is like one who seeks joy and finds it through good tidings.

Second issue: know that those who accepted that the martyrs are alive before the Resurrection have mentioned other interpretations of this verse:

As for the first: it is said that the martyrs say to one another: "We left behind our brothers, so-and-so and so-and-so, in the ranks of those fighting the unbelievers, and they will be killed, if Allah wills, and will attain provision and honour just as we attained." This is His saying: ﴿and they rejoice in those who have not yet joined them﴾.

As for the second: it is said that when the martyrs enter Paradise after the Resurrection, they are provided for, rejoicing in what Allah has given them of His bounty. The meaning of His saying "*those who have not yet joined them from behind them*" is their brothers among the believers who do not have the rank of the martyrs, because the martyrs enter Paradise before them. The proof is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And Allah has preferred those who strive over those who sit back by a great reward, degrees from Him, and forgiveness and mercy﴾ [al-Nisa': 95–96]. They rejoice at what they see of the abodes of the believers and the bliss prepared for them, and at what they hope for of gathering with them, and by this their eyes are comforted. This is the choice of Abu Muslim al-Isfahani and al-Zajjaj.

Know that the first interpretation is stronger than the second, because the result of the second returns to some believers rejoicing in others on account of their being gathered together in Paradise; and this is a general matter concerning all believers, so there is no sense in singling out the martyrs for it. Furthermore: just as they rejoice in those who have not yet joined them from behind them, so too they rejoice in those who preceded them into entry, because the stations of the prophets and the truthful (*al-siddiqun*) are above the stations of the martyrs. He, exalted is He, said: ﴿Those are with those on whom Allah has bestowed favour from among the prophets, the truthful, the martyrs, and the righteous﴾ [al-Nisa': 69]. On this interpretation there remains no benefit in the specification. But when we interpret the verse according to the first aspect, there is the greatest benefit in singling out the fighters for this special quality, so that is preferable, and Allah knows best.

Third issue: fear arises from anticipating a disliked matter that will descend in the future, and grief arises from the loss of benefits that existed in the past. So He, glorified is He, clarified that there is no fear for them regarding what will come upon them of the conditions of the Resurrection, nor is there any grief for them regarding what they have missed of the bliss of this world.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 3, verse 171:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿They rejoice in a blessing from Allah and bounty, and that Allah does not waste the reward of the believers﴾. And concerning this there are several issues:

The first issue: He, may He be exalted, has explained that just as they rejoice over those who have not yet joined them, as He mentioned, they also rejoice for themselves over the blessings they have been given. The word "yastabshirun" (they rejoice/receive glad tidings) is repeated because the first rejoicing was over the states of those who had not yet joined them from behind them, while the second rejoicing was specifically over their own states.

If it is said: Did He not mention their joy over their own states, and is joy not the very same as istibshar (rejoicing with glad tidings)?

We say: The answer is in two respects:

The first: istibshar is complete joy, so there is no necessary repetition.

The second: Perhaps what is meant is the attainment of joy over what has already occurred, and the attainment of istibshar over what they came to know, that a great blessing will be theirs in the Hereafter.

The second issue: His saying ﴿a blessing from Allah and bounty﴾. The "ni'mah" (blessing) is the reward, and the "fadl" (bounty) is the additional favour beyond it.

The third issue: The verse indicates that their rejoicing over the happiness of their brethren is more complete than their rejoicing over their own happiness, because the first istibshar mentioned is over the states of their brethren. This is an admonition from Allah, may He be exalted, that a person's joy at the good state of his brethren and those connected to him ought to be more complete and perfect than his joy at the good state of his own self.

* * *

Then He said: ﴿and that Allah does not waste the reward of the believers﴾. And concerning this there are several issues:

The first issue: al-Kisa'i read "wa-inna Allah" with a kasra on the alif, as a new sentence (isti'naf). The rest read it with a fatha, meaning "and that Allah," and the estimate is: they rejoice in a blessing from Allah and bounty, and that Allah does not waste the reward of the believers. The first reading is more complete and perfect, because on this reading the istibshar is over Allah's bounty and mercy alone, whereas on the second reading the istibshar is over bounty, mercy, and the seeking of reward. There is no doubt that the first station is more complete, because a servant's being occupied with seeking Allah is more complete than his being occupied with seeking the reward of his deed.

The second issue: The purpose of the verse is to explain that what preceded of the conveying of reward and great joy to the martyrs is not a ruling specific to them. Rather, every believer deserves some portion of reward and recompense, and Allah, glorified is He, conveys that reward and recompense to him and does not waste it at all.

The third issue: According to us, the verse indicates the pardoning of the sinful among the people of prayer, because by his faith he has earned Paradise. So if, because of his sinfulness, he remained in the Fire forever and eternally, the reward of his faith would not reach him, and then the reward of the believers for their faith would be wasted, and that contradicts the verse.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 3, verse 172:

His statement, exalted is He: ﴿Those who responded to Allah and the Messenger after the wound had afflicted them—for those among them who did good and had taqwa there is a great reward.﴾

Know that Allah, exalted is He, praised the believers for two military expeditions. One is known as the expedition of Hamra' al-Asad (Hamra' al-Asad), and the second is known as the expedition of the Lesser Badr (Badr al-Sughra). Both are connected to the Battle of Uhud. As for the expedition of Hamra' al-Asad, it is the one intended by this verse, as we will mention, God willing. In the verse there are several issues:

The first issue: concerning the position of (alladhina) there are several views:

The first, which is the view of al-Zajjaj, is that it is in the nominative case as the subject of a nominal sentence, and its predicate is ﴿for those among them who did good﴾ to the end of this verse.

The second: that its position is in the genitive case as a qualifier (na't) of "the believers."

The third: that it is in the accusative case by way of praise (madh).

The second issue: concerning the occasion of revelation (sabab al-nuzul) of this verse there are two views:

The first, and it is the more correct: when Abu Sufyan and his companions turned back from Uhud and reached al-Rawha', they regretted and said: "We have killed most of them and only a few remain. Why did we leave them? Rather, it is necessary that we return and eradicate them." So they resolved to return. This reached the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), so he wished to frighten the disbelievers and show them strength from himself and his companions. He called his companions to set out in pursuit of Abu Sufyan and said: "I do not want anyone to go out with me now except those who were with me in the fighting." So the Messenger (ﷺ) went out with a group of his companions—it is said they were seventy men—until they reached Hamra' al-Asad, which is three miles from Madinah. Then Allah cast terror into the hearts of the polytheists and they fled. It is reported that among them there was one who carried his companion on his neck for a while, then the one carried would carry the carrier for another while, and all of that was because of the severity of their wounds. Among them was one who would lean on his companion for a while, and his companion would lean on him for a while.

The second: Abu Bakr al-Asamm said: this verse was revealed concerning the Day of Uhud, when people returned to the Prophet (ﷺ) after the defeat, and he pressed with them against the polytheists until he drove them back. They had intended to mutilate the bodies, and he prevented them from that after they had mutilated Hamzah. Then Allah cast terror into their hearts and they fled. He (ﷺ) prayed over them and buried them in their blood. It is mentioned that Safiyyah came to look at her brother Hamzah, and the peace and blessings of Allah be upon him said to al-Zubayr: "Turn her back, lest she grieve over the mutilation of her brother." She said: "I have heard what was done to him, and that is small in comparison with obedience to Allah, exalted is He." Then he said to al-Zubayr: "Let her look at him." She said good words and asked forgiveness for him. A woman came whose husband, father, brother and son had been killed, and when she saw the Prophet (ﷺ) alive she said: "Every calamity after you is insignificant." This is what was said concerning the occasion of revelation of this verse, and most of the reports follow the first view.

The third issue: "istajaba" means "ajaba" (to respond), and from it is His saying: (fa-liyastajibu li) ("so let them respond to Me"). It was said: "ajaba" means to perform the response, and "istajaba" means to seek to perform the response, because the basic meaning of the form istif'al is seeking the act. The meaning is: they responded and obeyed Allah in His commands and obeyed the Messenger after the severe wounds had afflicted them.

**Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 3, verses 173–174:**

As for His saying, ﴿Those among them who did good and guarded themselves (against evil) will have a great reward,﴾ there are two issues.

**The first issue:** Regarding His saying, ﴿those among them who did good and guarded themselves will have a great reward,﴾ there are several aspects.

**First:** "Did good" (*ahsanu*) includes complying with all the commands, and "guarded themselves" (*ittaqaw*) includes refraining from all the prohibitions. A person who fulfils these two matters deserves the great reward.

**Second:** They did good by obeying the Messenger at that time, and they guarded themselves against disobeying the Messenger. This indicates that it is obligatory for them to respond to the Messenger even if their injuries were severe, after they were able to rise with him.

**Third:** They did good in what they did of obeying the Messenger ﷺ, and they guarded themselves against committing any of the prohibited acts after that.

**The second issue:** The author of al-Kashshaf (al-Zamakhshari) said: the *min* (from/among) in His saying, ﴿those among them who did good,﴾ is for specification (*tabyin*), because all those who responded to Allah and the Messenger did good and guarded themselves, not merely some of them.

﴿Those to whom the people said, "Indeed the people have gathered against you, so fear them." But it increased them in faith, and they said, "Allah is sufficient for us, and He is the best Disposer of affairs."﴾ ﴿So they returned with favour from Allah and bounty, no harm touched them, and they followed the pleasure of Allah. And Allah is the Possessor of great bounty.﴾

* * *

His saying, ﴿Those to whom the people said, "Indeed the people have gathered against you, so fear them." But it increased them in faith, and they said, "Allah is sufficient for us, and He is the best Disposer of affairs."﴾ ﴿So they returned with favour from Allah and bounty, no harm touched them, and they followed the pleasure of Allah. And Allah is the Possessor of great bounty.﴾

There are several issues concerning the verse.

**The first issue:** This verse was revealed concerning the Expedition of Badr al-Sughra (the Lesser Badr). Ibn Abbas narrated that when Abu Sufyan resolved to return from Madinah to Makkah, he called out: "O Muhammad, our appointment is the season of Badr al-Sughra, so we shall fight there, if you wish." The Prophet ﷺ said to Umar: "Say to him: That is between us and you, if Allah wills." When the appointed time arrived, Abu Sufyan set out with his people until he reached Marr al-Zahran, and Allah cast terror into his heart, so he decided to turn back. He met Nu'aym ibn Mas'ud al-Ashja'i, who had come to perform *umrah*, and said: "O Nu'aym, I promised Muhammad that we would meet at the season of Badr, but this is a year of drought, and only a year in which we graze the trees and drink milk would suit us. It has become clear to me that I should return. But if Muhammad goes out and I do not, that will embolden him. So go to Madinah and dissuade them, and I will give you ten camels." Nu'aym set out and found the Muslims preparing, so he said to them: "This is not a sound opinion. They have come to you in your homes and killed most of you; if you go out to them, not one of you will return." This statement entered the hearts of some of them. When the Messenger ﷺ learned of this, he said: "By Him in whose hand is the soul of Muhammad, I will certainly go out to them, even if I am alone." Then the Prophet ﷺ went out with about seventy men, including Ibn Mas'ud, and they proceeded until they reached Badr al-Sughra. It is water belonging to the Banu Kinanah, and it was the site of a market where they gathered every year for eight days. The Messenger of Allah ﷺ and his companions did not meet any of the polytheists, and they arrived at the time of the market. They had expenses and merchandise with them, so they sold and bought, traded skins and raisins, and gained profit, earning two dirhams for every one dirham, and they returned to Madinah safe and laden with gain. Abu Sufyan returned to Makkah, and the people of Makkah named his army "the Army of Sawiq" (parched barley), saying: "You only went out to drink sawiq." This is the account of the cause of revelation of this verse.

**The second issue:** Concerning the position of *alladhina* (those who) there are several aspects:

**One:** It is in the genitive case, as an adjective (*sifah*) of "the believers," with the implied meaning: "And Allah does not waste the reward of the believers who were told by the people..."

**Two:** It is a substitute (*badal*) for His saying, "for those who did good."

**Three:** It is in the nominative case as the subject (*mubtada'*), and its predicate is ﴿it increased them in faith.﴾

**The third issue:** The intended meaning of His saying, "those (*alladhina*)," is those previously mentioned, namely those who responded to Allah and the Messenger.

Concerning the intended meaning of His saying, ﴿the people said to them,﴾ there are several views:

**First:** This speaker was Nu'aym ibn Mas'ud, as we mentioned in the cause of revelation of this verse. The word "people" (*al-nas*) may be applied to a single person because, when one person says a statement and has followers who say the same as he says or are pleased with his statement, it is then fitting to attribute that action to all of them. Allah the Exalted says: ﴿And when you killed a soul and disputed over it﴾ [al-Baqarah: 72], and ﴿And when you said, "O Musa, we will not believe you until we see Allah openly"﴾ [al-Baqarah: 55], though they themselves did not do that; rather, their forefathers did it, but it was attributed to them because they followed them and approved of their actions. Likewise here, it is permissible to attribute the statement to the group who were pleased with that one person's statement.

**Second:** This is the view of Ibn Abbas and Muhammad ibn Ishaq: a caravan from Abd al-Qays passed by Abu Sufyan, so he sent them to the Muslims to frighten them, and he guaranteed them a reward for doing so.

**Third:** Al-Suddi said: they were the hypocrites. They said to the Muslims when they were preparing to march to Badr for the appointment with Abu Sufyan: "The people have come to you in your homes and killed most of you. If you go to them, not one of you will remain."

**The fourth issue:** His saying, ﴿Indeed the people have gathered against you,﴾ the intended "people" are Abu Sufyan, his companions, and the leaders of his army. His saying, ﴿they have gathered against you,﴾ means they gathered the hosts against you. The object is omitted because the Arabs call an army *jam'*, and they make its plural *juyush*. His saying, ﴿so fear them,﴾ means: be afraid of them. Then He the Exalted informed that when the Muslims heard this statement, they did not pay attention to it and did not give it any weight. So He the Exalted said, ﴿But it increased them in faith.﴾ There are several issues concerning this:

**The first issue:** To what does the pronoun in His saying "it increased them" refer? There are two views. The first: it refers to those who spoke these frightening statements. The second: it refers to the statement itself, and the meaning is: "that statement increased them in faith." This attribution is fitting because this increase in faith occurred upon hearing this statement, so it is fitting to attribute it both to the statement and to its speaker. A parallel is His saying: ﴿but my call only increased them in flight﴾ [Nuh: 6], and His saying: ﴿But when a warner came to them, it increased them only in aversion﴾ [Fatir: 42].

**The second issue:** The meaning of the increase in faith is that when they heard this frightening statement, they did not pay attention to it. Rather, a firm resolve arose in their hearts to fight the disbelievers and to obey the Messenger ﷺ in everything he commanded and forbade, whether that was heavy or light for them. Among them were those who had severe injuries and needed treatment. And a conviction arose in their hearts that Allah would grant them victory over their enemies and support them in this fighting. This is the intended meaning of His saying, ﴿but it increased them in faith.﴾

**The third issue:** Those who say that faith is not merely affirmation (*tasdiq*) but consists of acts of obedience, and that it admits increase and decrease, took this verse as evidence, since He the Exalted explicitly stated that an increase occurred. Those who do not hold this view said: the increase only occurred in the degrees of faith and in its rites, so it is valid to speak of an increase in faith figuratively (*majazan*).

* * *

**The fourth issue:** This event clearly indicates that everything occurs by the decree and destiny of Allah. The Muslims had been defeated by the polytheists on the day of Uhud, and it is customary that when one of two opponents defeats the other, strength and a sense of dominance arise in the heart of the victor, while breaking and weakness arise in the heart of the vanquished. Yet here, He the Glorified reversed the situation: He placed fear and terror in the hearts of the victors, who were the polytheists, and He placed strength, zeal, and steadfastness in the hearts of the vanquished. This indicates that the motives and the deterrents come from Allah the Exalted, and whenever they arise in the hearts, actions occur in accordance with them.

* * *

Then He the Exalted said, ﴿and they said, "Allah is sufficient for us, and He is the best Disposer of affairs."﴾ The meaning is that whenever their faith increased in their hearts, they manifested what corresponds to it, so they said: "Allah is sufficient for us, and He is the best Disposer of affairs." Ibn al-Anbari said: ﴿Allah is sufficient for us﴾ means Allah is enough for us. A similar expression is the saying of Imru' al-Qays:

*"Enough for you of wealth is contentment and satisfaction."*

meaning: contentment and satisfaction suffice you. As for *al-Wakil* (the Disposer of affairs), there are several views:

**One:** It means *al-kafil* (the guarantor). The poet said:

*"I remembered Abu Arwa, so I spent the night as if I were a guarantor (wakil) for the return of the past affairs."*

He meant: as if I were a guarantor for returning the affairs.

**Two:** Al-Farra' said: *al-Wakil* means *al-Kafi* (the Sufficient).
