The evidence for the soundness of this view is that the construction *ni'ma* requires that what follows it agree with what precedes it. You say: "Our Provider is Allah, and the best Provider," and "Our Creator is Allah, and the best Creator." This is better than the one who says: "Our Creator is Allah, and the best Provider." Likewise here, the meaning of the verse is: "Allah is sufficient for us, and the best Sufficient."

**Three:** *Wakil* is of the form *fa'il* in the sense of *maf'ul* (passive), meaning one to whom affairs are entrusted (*mawkul ilayhi*). The sufficient one and the guarantor may be called *wakil*, because affairs are entrusted to the sufficient one, and likewise affairs are entrusted to the guarantor.

* * *

Then He the Exalted said, ﴿So they returned with favour from Allah and bounty.﴾ This is because the Prophet ﷺ went out, and the meaning is: they went out and returned. The going out was omitted because the returning indicates it, as in His saying: ﴿Strike with your staff the sea, and it parted﴾ [al-Shu'ara': 63], meaning: it was struck, and it parted. As for His saying, ﴿with favour from Allah and bounty,﴾ Mujahid and al-Suddi said: "favour" here means well-being, and "bounty" means trade. It was also said: "favour" means the benefits of this world, and "bounty" means the reward of the Hereafter. His saying, ﴿no harm touched them,﴾ means no killing or wounding touched them, according to the consensus. ﴿And they followed the pleasure of Allah﴾ by obeying His Messenger. ﴿And Allah is the Possessor of great bounty﴾ — He has graciously bestowed on them success in what they did. In this there is a casting of regret into the hearts of those who stayed behind, and a demonstration of the error of their opinion, for they deprived themselves of what these people achieved. It is narrated that they said: "Would this be considered a military expedition (*ghazw*)?" So Allah gave them the reward of a military expedition and was pleased with them.

Know that the scholars of the military campaigns (*ahl al-maghazi*) differed. Al-Waqidi held that the first verse refers to the event of Hamra' al-Asad, and the second verse refers to Badr al-Sughra. Others held that both verses refer to the battle of Badr al-Sughra. The first view is preferable, because His saying, ﴿after the wound had befallen them﴾ [Al 'Imran: 172] seems to indicate the recency of the wound, so the praise for going out against the enemy immediately after the wound was sustained is greater. The other view is also possible. According to this view, "wound" (*qarh*) must be interpreted as "defeat." It is as if it were said: those who were defeated, then did good by repenting, and guarded themselves in all their affairs, then responded to Allah and the Messenger, resolved on reward, and prepared themselves to meet the enemy, such that when they learned of the multitude of their enemies, they did not falter or lose heart, and they relied upon Allah and were content with Him as sufficient and helper. For them is a great reward, which the defeat they had suffered does not prevent them from attaining, since they had repented of it. And Allah knows best.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 3, verse 175:

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿That is only the Shaytan (Satan) who frightens you of his allies, so do not fear them, but fear Me, if you are believers.﴾

Know that His saying "al-Shaytan" (the Shaytan) is the predicate (khabar) of "dhalikum" (that), meaning: "That one who discourages you is only the Shaytan." And "yukhawwifu awliyaahu" (he frightens his allies) is a resumptive clause (jumla mustaanifa) explaining his discouragement. Or "al-Shaytan" is an attribute (sifa) of the demonstrative noun (ism al-ishara), and "yukhawwifu" is the predicate. The intended meaning of "al-Shaytan" is the caravan (al-rakb). It was also said that it refers to Nu'aym ibn Mas'ud, and he was called a shaytan because of his obstinacy and rebelliousness in disbelief, like His saying: ﴿the shayatin of mankind and jinn﴾ [al-An'am: 112]. It was also said that it is the Shaytan himself, who frightens through whispering (waswasa).

As for His saying, the Exalted: ﴿yukhawwifu awliyaahu (he frightens his allies)﴾, there is a question about it: the ones God named "Shaytan" were only frightening the believers, so what is the meaning of His saying "the Shaytan frightens his allies"? The exegetes mentioned three aspects regarding it:

The first: the estimated sense of the speech is: "That Shaytan frightens you through his allies," so the second object is omitted and the preposition is omitted. An example of omitting the second object is His saying, the Exalted: ﴿When you fear for him, then cast him into the sea﴾ [al-Qasas: 7], i.e., "when you fear for him from Pharaoh." An example of omitting the preposition is His saying, the Exalted: ﴿to warn of a severe punishment﴾ [al-Kahf: 2], meaning: "to warn you of a punishment," and His saying: ﴿to warn of the Day of Meeting﴾ [Ghafir: 15], i.e., "to warn you of the Day of Meeting." This is the view of al-Farra', al-Zajjaj, and Abu 'Ali. They said: what indicates it is the recitation of Ubayy ibn Ka'b: "yukhawwifukum bi-awliyaihi" (he frightens you through his allies).

The second view: this is according to the saying of the speaker: "I frightened Zayd, Amr," and the estimated sense of the verse is: "he frightens you his allies," so the first object is omitted, just as you say: "I gave the wealth," i.e., "I gave the people the wealth." Ibn al-Anbari said: this is better than a claim that runs without evidence. And His saying "to warn of a punishment" means "to warn you of a punishment," and His saying "to warn of the Day of Meeting" means "to warn you of the Day of Meeting." And "takhwif" (frightening) transitively takes two objects without a preposition; you say: "Zayd feared the fighting" and "I frightened him the fighting." This view is indicated by the recitation of Ibn Mas'ud: "yukhawwifukum awliyaahu" (he frightens you his allies).

The third view: the meaning of the verse is: "he frightens his allies, the hypocrites, so that they sit back from fighting the polytheists." The meaning is: the Shaytan frightens his allies who obey him and prefer his command. As for the allies of God, they do not fear him when he frightens them, and they do not submit to his command or his purpose for them. This is the view of al-Hasan and al-Suddi. So the first view has two omitted elements, the second has one omitted element, and the third has no omission. As for "the allies" (awliya'), they are the polytheists and the disbelievers. His saying ﴿so do not fear them﴾: the pronoun in the first two views refers to the allies, and in the third view it refers to "the people" in His saying: ﴿Indeed, the people have gathered against you﴾ [Al 'Imran: 173], ﴿so do not fear them﴾, so that you sit back from fighting and become cowardly. ﴿But fear Me﴾, so fight alongside My Messenger and hasten to what he commands you ﴿if you are believers﴾, meaning: faith requires that you prefer the fear of God over the fear of people.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 3, verse 176:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And let not those who hasten to disbelief grieve you. Indeed, they will not harm Allah at all. Allah intends not to give them a share in the Hereafter, and for them is a great punishment.﴾ And in this are several issues:

The first issue: Nafi' recited "yuhzinka" (يُحْزِنْكَ) with a damma on the yaa' and a kasra on the zaay, and likewise in every instance in the Qur'an except His saying ﴿The greatest terror will not grieve them﴾ [al-Anbiya': 103] in Surat al-Anbiya', where he read the yaa' with a fatha and the zaay with a damma. All the others read it with a fatha on the yaa' and a damma on the zaay. Al-Azhari said: the good (fasih) usage is "hazanahu yahzunuhu" (حَزَنَهُ يَحْزُنُهُ), which is what most of the reciters recited. The argument of Nafi' is that both are dialects: "hazana yahzunu" like "nasara yansuru," and "ahzana yuhzinu" like "akrama yukrimu" are two dialects.

The second issue: The scholars differed regarding the occasion of revelation of the verse, in several views:

The first: It was revealed concerning the disbelievers of Quraysh, and Allah, exalted is He, made His Messenger secure from their evil. The meaning is: let not grieve you those who hasten to disbelief by intending to gather armies to fight you; for by this act they only harm themselves and do not harm Allah. It is necessary to interpret this as meaning that they will not harm the Prophet and his companions among the believers at all; and if it is interpreted this way, it is necessary to interpret it as a specific harm, because it is well known that afterwards they inflicted various kinds of harm upon the Prophet, peace be upon him. The better view is that this is to be understood as meaning that their aim in gathering armies was to nullify this religion and eliminate this Shari'ah, and this aim will not be achieved for them; rather their affair will dwindle, their might will vanish, and your affair will grow great and your status will rise.

The second: It was revealed concerning the hypocrites, and their hastening was that they used to frighten the believers because of the battle of Uhud and despair them of victory and triumph, or because they used to say that Muhammad seeks kingship: sometimes the matter is his, and sometimes it is against him; and if he were a messenger from Allah he would not be defeated. This used to repel the Muslims from Islam, so the Messenger would grieve because of it. Some said: a group of the disbelievers embraced Islam and then apostatized out of fear of Quraysh, so grief fell upon the heart of the Messenger ﷺ because of that cause, for he, peace be upon him, thought that they would, by that apostasy, inflict harm upon him; so Allah made clear that their apostasy does not affect the infliction of harm upon you. The judge (al-Qadi) said: this view may be strengthened by several matters:

The first: one who persists in disbelief is not described as "hastening in disbelief"; rather this description applies only to one who disbelieves after faith.

The second: Allah's intention that He not give them a share in the Hereafter befits only one who had believed, so that this was deserved, and then it was nullified.

The third: grief is only over the loss of an intended matter. When the Prophet ﷺ assumed benefit from their faith, and then they disbelieved, he ﷺ grieved at that for the loss of increasing numbers through them; so Allah secured him from that and informed him that the existence of their faith is like its absence in that his condition does not change.

The fourth view: The intended ones are the leaders of the Jews: Ka'b ibn al-Ashraf and his companions, who concealed the description of Muhammad ﷺ for the sake of the goods of this world. Al-Qaffal, may Allah have mercy on him, said: It is not far-fetched to take the verse as referring to all categories of disbelievers, based on the saying of Allah, exalted is He: ﴿O Messenger, let not grieve you those who hasten into disbelief﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 41] up to His saying: ﴿and among those who are Jews﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 41]. This verse indicates that his grief was from all these disbelievers.

The third issue: There is a question regarding the verse: grief over the disbelief of the disbeliever and the disobedience of the disobedient is an act of obedience, so how did Allah forbid an act of obedience?

The answer is in two parts:

The first: he used to exceed the limit and be excessive in grief over his people's disbelief, to the point that it nearly led to harm befalling him, so Allah forbade him from excess in it. Do you not see His saying, exalted is He: ﴿So let not your soul go out in pursuit of them in regret﴾ [Fatir: 8].

The second: the meaning is "let them not grieve you by fear that they will harm you and help against you." Do you not see His saying: ﴿Indeed, they will not harm Allah at all﴾, meaning that by their hastening in disbelief they harm none but themselves, and the consequence of that never returns to anyone else at all.

* * *
Then He said: ﴿Indeed, they will not harm Allah at all﴾, and the meaning is that they will not harm the Prophet and his companions at all. Ata' said: He means: they will not harm the friends of Allah at all.

* * *
Then He, exalted is He, said: ﴿Allah intends not to give them a share in the Hereafter﴾, and in this are several issues:

The first issue: This is a refutation of the Mu'tazilah and an explicit statement that good and evil are by the will of Allah, exalted is He. The judge said: what is meant is that He intends to inform of that and to judge it.

Know that this answer is weak for two reasons:

The first: it is a departure from the apparent meaning.

The second: even supposing the matter is as he said, bringing the opposite of what Allah has informed of and judged is impossible, so the difficulty returns.

The second issue: The Mu'tazilah said: will does not attach to non-existence. Our companions said that this is permissible, and the verse is evidence for the view of our companions, because He said: ﴿Allah intends not to give them a share in the Hereafter﴾, so He made clear that His will is attached to this non-existence. The Mu'tazilah said: the meaning is that He, exalted is He, did not will that, as in His saying: ﴿and He does not will hardship for you﴾ [al-Baqarah: 185]. We say: this is a departure from the apparent meaning.

The third issue: The verse indicates that an indefinite noun in a context of negation is general, for if generality were not achieved, the threat to the disbelievers by this verse would not be achieved. Then He said: ﴿and for them is a great punishment﴾, and this is a new independent statement, and the meaning is that just as they have absolutely no share of the benefits of the Hereafter, so they have a great share of its harms.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 3, verse 177:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, those who have exchanged disbelief for faith will never harm Allah at all, and they will have a painful punishment.﴾

Know that if we take the previous verse as referring to the hypocrites and the Jews, and take this verse as referring to the apostates, it is not far-fetched either to take the previous verse as referring to the apostates and this verse as referring to the Jews. The meaning of "exchanging disbelief for faith" with regard to them is that they used to know the Prophet (ﷺ) and believe in him before his mission, and seek victory through him over their enemies. But when he was sent, they disbelieved in him and abandoned what they had been upon. So it is as if they gave up faith and took disbelief in its place, just as a buyer gives something and takes another thing in exchange for it. It is also not far-fetched to take this verse as referring to the hypocrites, because whenever they were with the believers they showed faith, but when they went off to their devils they disbelieved and abandoned faith, so that is as if they had exchanged disbelief for faith.

Know that He, exalted is He, said in the previous verse: (Those who race to disbelief will never harm Allah at all), and said in this verse: ﴿Indeed, those who have exchanged disbelief for faith will never harm Allah at all﴾. The benefit in this repetition is several matters:

The first: that those who exchanged disbelief for faith were without doubt disbelievers at first, then they believed, then they disbelieved after that. This indicates severe instability, weakness of judgment and lack of steadfastness, and such a person is not to be feared, has no dignity, and has absolutely no ability to inflict harm upon others.

The second: that the matter of religion is the most important and greatest of matters, and such a matter is one that a person does not undertake, whether to act or to refrain, except after deep reflection and much thought. Yet these people undertake to act or to refrain in such an important, great matter for the most trivial reasons and the weakest motives, and that indicates little intellect and extreme foolishness. Such people are not worth a sensible person's attention.

The third: that most of them dispute with you about the religion not on the basis of doubts, but on the basis of envy and rivalry over worldly position. Whoever has this degree of intellect, that he sells great felicity in the Hereafter for a little of this world, is in the utmost folly, and one like him has no power to inflict harm upon others. This is the benefit of repeating this verse, and Allah knows best what He intends.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 3, verse 178 (part 1 of 2):

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And let not those who disbelieve suppose that Our giving them respite is good for them. We only give them respite so that they may increase in sin, and for them is a humiliating punishment.﴾

Know that He, exalted is He, related about those who went to Medina to discourage the Companions of the Prophet ﷺ that they only discouraged them because they frightened them that they would be killed as the Muslims had been killed on the Day of Uhud. God, exalted is He, made clear that the words of these devils are not accepted by the believer, and he does not pay attention to them. What is obligatory for the believer is to rely upon the grace of God. Then in this verse He made clear that the survival of these who stayed behind is not better than the killing of those who were killed at Uhud, because this survival has become a means to disgrace in this world and to constant punishment on the Day of Resurrection, while the killing of those who were killed on the Day of Uhud has become a means to beautiful praise in this world and great reward in the Hereafter. Therefore, encouraging those who discourage others toward this kind of life and deterring them from that kind of killing is accepted only by an ignorant person. This is the explanation of the connection of the arrangement (wajh al-nazm), and in the verse there are several issues.

[Page 87]

The first issue: Ibn Kathir and Abu Amr recited "wa la tahsabanna alladhina kafaru" ("and let not those who disbelieve suppose"), "wa la tahsabanna alladhina yabkhalun" ("and let not those who are stingy suppose"), "la tahsabanna alladhina yafrahun" ("let not those who rejoice suppose"), and "fa-la tahsabannahum" ("so do not suppose them") in these four places with the ta' (the second-person form) and a damma on the ba' in the phrase "tahsabunnahum." Nafi' and Ibn Amir recited with the ya' (the third-person form) except in the phrase "fa-la tahsabannahum" (Al Imran: 188), which they recited with the ta'. Hamza recited all of them with the ta'. The difference among the reciters regarding the fatha and kasra of the sin (in yahsabanna/tahsabanna) we have already discussed in surah al-Baqarah. As for those who recited with the ya' with a dot below it: the word "yahsabanna" is a verb, and "alladhina kafaru" is its subject, which requires two objects, or an object that takes the place of two objects, as in "hasibtu" (I supposed) and "hasibtu anna Zaydan muntaliqun" (I supposed that Zayd is departing) and "hasibtu an yaqum 'Amrun" (I supposed that 'Amr would stand). So His saying in the verse, "annama numli lahum khayrun li-anfusihim" ("that Our giving them respite is good for them"), takes the place of the two objects. A parallel to this is His saying: ﴿Or do you suppose that most of them hear?﴾ (al-Furqan: 44). As for the recitation of Hamza with the ta' with a dot above it, the best of what has been said about it is what al-Zajjaj mentioned, namely that "alladhina kafaru" is in the accusative as the first object, and "annama numli lahum" is an apposition (badal) to it, and "khayrun li-anfusihim" is the second object. The meaning is: "And do not suppose, O Muhammad, that the respite of those who disbelieve is good for them." A similar case in which "anna" with its verb is made an apposition for the object is His saying: ﴿And when God promised you that one of the two groups would be yours﴾ (al-Anfal: 7). So His saying "annaha lakum" ("that it would be yours") is an apposition for "ihda al-ta'ifatayn" ("one of the two groups").

The second issue: The "ma" in "annama" may have two meanings:
One of them: that it means "alladhi" (which), so the meaning would be: "Let not those who disbelieve suppose that what We give them respite with is good for them." The ha' is omitted from "numli" because it is permissible to omit the ha' from the relative clause of "alladhi," as in your saying: "alladhi ra'aytu Zaydun" (the one whom I saw, Zayd).
The other: it may be said that "ma" together with what follows it is in the sense of a verbal noun (masdar). The meaning would be: "Let not those who disbelieve suppose that My giving them respite is good for them."

The third issue: The author of al-Kashshaf said: "ma" is a verbal (masdariyya) particle. If that is so, then by the rules of orthography it should have been written separately, but it was written joined in the Qur'an of Uthman. Following the orthography of the Qur'anic copies of that codex is obligatory. As for His saying "annama numli lahum," here it must be written joined, because it is a restrictive (kaffa) particle, unlike the first.

The fourth issue: The meaning of "numli" is "we prolong and delay." And al-Imhal (giving respite) means granting time and postponing. Al-Wahidi, may God have mercy on him, said: its derivation is from al-malwa, which is a period of time. It is said: "malawtu min al-dahr malwatan wa mulwatan wa milawatan wa mulawatan" (meaning: I had a period of time from the age), with one meaning. Al-Asma'i said: it is said: "amla 'alayhi al-zaman," meaning the time lengthened over him, and "amla lahu," meaning he extended for him and gave him time. Abu Ubayda said: from this comes "al-mala" for a wide, long land, and "al-malawan," meaning the night and the day.

* * *

The fifth issue: Our companions (the Ash'arites) argued with this verse in the question of divine decree and predestination (al-qada' wa al-qadar) in several respects. The first: this giving of respite is an expression for prolonging the period, and there is no doubt that it is an act of God, exalted is He, and the verse is explicit in showing that this respite is not good, and this indicates that He, glorified is He, is the doer of good and evil.

The second: He, exalted is He, stated explicitly that the purpose of this respite is that they increase in sin, transgression and aggression, and this indicates that disbelief and disobedience are by the will of God. Then He, exalted is He, emphasized this by His saying: ﴿And for them is a humiliating punishment,﴾ meaning: "We only give them respite so that they may increase in sin, and so that for them there may be a humiliating punishment."

The third: He, exalted is He, informed about them that there is no good for them in this respite, and that they only attain an increase in transgression and insolence. Bringing about the opposite of God's report while that good remains is a combination of two contradictories, which is impossible. And if they were not able, with that respite, to do good and obey, although they are obligated to do so, it follows that the position of this people is invalid.

The Mu'tazilah (the rationalist school that affirms human free will and divine justice) said:
As for the first respect: the intended meaning of this verse is not that this respite is not good in itself. Rather, the intended meaning is that this respite is not better for them than that they should die as the martyrs died on the Day of Uhud, because all these verses concern Uhud and the hypocrites' discouraging of the believers from jihad, as explained earlier in the preceding verses. So God made clear that leaving the disbelievers alive in this world and giving them respite is not good for them compared with dying as the martyrs died. It does not follow from denying that this respite is better than that killing, that this respite is not in itself good.

[Page 88]

As for the second respect: they said: the intended meaning of the verse is not that the purpose of the respite is their committing disbelief and wickedness, based on His saying: ﴿And I did not create the jinn and humankind except that they should worship Me﴾ (al-Dhariyat: 56), and His saying: ﴿And We did not send any messenger except that he be obeyed by God's permission﴾ (al-Nisa': 64). Rather, the verse admits of several interpretations:
One of them: this lam is to be taken as lam al-'aqibah (the lam of consequence, indicating the outcome rather than the purpose), like His saying: ﴿So the family of Pharaoh picked him up, that he might become for them an enemy and a grief﴾ (al-Qasas: 8), and His saying: ﴿And We have certainly created for Hell﴾ (al-A'raf: 179), and His saying: ﴿And they set up rivals to God in order to lead astray from His way﴾ (Ibrahim: 30). They did not do that in order to seek misguidance, but in order to seek guidance. And one may say: "My admonition to you was only for an increase in your persistence in wickedness," if the outcome of the admonition is that.
The second: the speech may be in inverted order (taqdim wa ta'khir), and the meaning is: "And let not those who disbelieve suppose that We only give them respite so that they may increase in sin; We only give them respite because it is good for them."
The third: since He, exalted is He, granted them respite while knowing that they would not increase during this respite except in persistence in error and transgression, this resembled the situation of one who did the giving of respite for this purpose, and resemblance is one of the causes of the beauty of a metaphor (majaz).

The fourth: which is the question I put to the people: the lam in His saying "li-yazdadu ithman" ("so that they may increase in sin") is not understood as indicating purpose, by the consensus of the Muslim community. As for the position of the people of the Sunnah (Ahl al-Sunnah), it is because they deny that God's acts are explained by purposes. And as for our position, it is because we do not say that the act of God is caused by the purpose of inflicting suffering and pain; rather, in our view He, exalted is He, has done no act except for the purpose of benevolence. If that is so, then there is consensus that this lam is not to be understood as indicating causation or purpose. At this point what you have cited as evidence falls away. Moreover, after this, the question of one who asks, "What is the intended meaning of this lam?" is not worth considering, because the one who argues from it based his argument on the premise that this lam indicates causation. If that is invalid, his argument falls.

As for the third respect, which is the reporting and knowledge (of God): it is countered by the argument that if this (divine knowledge) prevented the servant from acting, it would prevent God from (acting), and it would follow that God is an obliger (mujib, acting by necessity) and not a chooser (mukhtar), and this is by consensus invalid.

The answer to the first (objection) is that His saying: ﴿And let not those who disbelieve suppose that Our giving them respite is good for them﴾ means the negation of goodness in reality itself, and its meaning is not that it is not good compared with something else. This is because the construction of comparative superiority (al-mubalagha) may not be used except when mentioning the preferred and the less preferred. Since God mentioned here only one of the two matters, we know that it is for negating goodness, not for negating that it is better than something else.

As for the second objection, which is their clinging to His saying: ﴿And I did not create the jinn and humankind except that they should worship Me﴾ and to His saying: ﴿And We did not send any messenger except that he be obeyed﴾: the answer is that the verse on which we relied is specific (khass), and the verse you cited is general (amm), and the specific takes precedence over the general.

As for the third objection, which is taking the lam as the lam of consequence: this is a departure from the apparent meaning. Furthermore, rational proof invalidates it, because when God knew that they would necessarily become characterized by an increase in error and transgression, that was necessarily going to occur, since the occurrence of what God knows is necessary, and the non-occurrence of it is impossible, and willing the impossible is impossible. So it is impossible that He would will faith from them, and it is necessary that He would will from them an increase in error and transgression. At that point it is established that the intended meaning is causation, and that it is not permissible to turn to the lam of consequence.

As for the fourth objection, which is the inversion of order: the answer to it is from three aspects:
One of them: inversion of order is an abandonment of the apparent meaning.
The second: al-Wahidi, may God have mercy on him, said:

[Page 89]

This would only be good if the recitation "innama numli lahum khayrun li-anfusihim" with the kasra on "inna" were permissible, and the recitation "innama numli lahum li-yazdadu ithman" with the fatha. This recitation has never been found at all.
The third: we have demonstrated by decisive rational proof that God's purpose in this giving of respite must be the occurrence of transgression, not the occurrence of faith. So the claim of inversion of order is an abandonment of the apparent meaning and an adherence to what is contrary to decisive proof.

As for the fifth objection, which is his saying: "this lam cannot be taken as indicating causation": the answer is that in our view it is impossible to explain God's acts by a purpose that issues from the servants. But that God, exalted is He, should do an act in order that something else may result from it, this is not impossible. Also, His saying: ﴿Indeed, We give them respite only so that they may increase in sin﴾ is an explicit statement that the purpose of this respite is not to deliver good to them and to bestow benevolence upon them, and the (Mu'tazilite) people do not say that. So the verse becomes a proof against them from this aspect.

As for the sixth objection, which is the counter-argument from God's act: the answer is that the effect of God's power in bringing created things into existence precedes the relation of His knowledge to their non-existence, so it is not possible that knowledge should be an obstacle to power. As for the servant, the effect of his power in bringing the act into existence comes after the relation of God's knowledge to its non-existence, so it is appropriate that this knowledge should be an obstacle to the servant from the act. This is the complete debate on this verse.

Sixth issue: Our companions (the Ash'arites) agreed that God has no blessings of religious kind (al-ni'am al-diniyyah) for the unbeliever. As to whether He has any worldly blessings (al-ni'am al-dunyawiyyah) for him, the opinions of our companions differed. Those who said that He has no worldly blessings for him relied on this verse and said: this verse indicates that prolonging life and enabling a person to attain his desires in this world are not blessings at all, because God explicitly stated that none of that is good. Reason also confirms this, for whoever feeds a person poisoned sweetmeat (khabis masmum) is not considered to have done him a favor. Therefore, when the purpose of giving the blessings of this world is the punishment of the Hereafter, none of them is a true blessing. As for the verses that speak of multiplying blessings for the unbelievers, they are to be understood as referring to what is a blessing outwardly. And there is no way to reconcile this verse with those verses except to say: those blessings are blessings outwardly, but in reality they are calamities and afflictions. And God knows best.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 3, verse 179:

Allah the Exalted said: ﴿Allah would not leave the believers in the state you are in until He distinguishes the wicked from the good. Nor would Allah disclose the unseen to you, but Allah chooses of His messengers whom He wills. So believe in Allah and His messengers. If you believe and are mindful of Allah, you will have a great reward.﴾

Know that this verse is part of the continuing discourse about the story of Uhud. Allah, the Exalted, informed that the circumstances that occurred in that incident, namely the killing and the defeat, then the Prophet's (ﷺ) call to them, despite their wounds, to go out to pursue the enemy, and then his calling them a second time to Badr al-Sughra (Badr the Lesser) for the appointment with Abu Sufyan, all of these circumstances

[Page 90]

became a proof of the distinction between the believer and the hypocrite (munafiq). This is because the hypocrites feared, turned back, rejoiced at the large number of your dead, and then discouraged and dissuaded the believers from returning to jihad. So Allah, Glorified and Exalted, informed that it is not permissible in His wisdom to leave you in the state you are in, with the hypocrites mixed among you and showing that they are from you and from the people of faith. Rather, it was necessary in His wisdom that these events and incidents occur until this distinction is achieved. This is the connection (wajh al-nazm) of the verse. There are several issues concerning the verse:

The first issue: Hamzah and al-Kisa'i read ﴿حَتّى يُمَيِّزَ الخَبِيثَ﴾ with the doubled (intensive) form, and likewise in the verbs of this kind. The others read ﴿يَمِيزَ﴾ with the single form, with a fatha on the first yā' (ي), a kasra on the mīm, and a sukūn on the final yā'. Al-Wahidi, may Allah have mercy on him, said: Both are dialects. It is said: "mizt al-shay'a ba'dahu min ba'd" (I separated the thing, part from part), so I "umayyizuhu" (distinguish it) "mayzan" or "umayyizuhu tamyizan." From this is the hadith: "Whoever removes harm from a road, it is a charity for him." The argument of those who read the single form with the fatha on the yā' is that mayz gives the meaning of tamyiz (distinction), and it is lighter in pronunciation, so it is preferable. Abu Zayd related from Abu 'Amr that he used to say: The doubled form is for multiplicity; as for one thing from one thing, it is distinguished with the single form. Allah, the Exalted, said: ﴿حَتّى يَمِيزَ الخَبِيثَ مِنَ الطَّيِّبِ﴾, mentioning two things, and this is like what some said regarding "al-farq" (separation) and "al-tafriq" (dividing). Also, Allah, the Exalted, said: ﴿وامْتازُوا اليَوْمَ﴾ [Ya-Sin: 59], which is the reflexive form (mutawa'i') of mayz. The argument of those who read the doubled form is that the doubling is for multiplicity and intensity, and among the believers and the hypocrites there is multiplicity, so the word "tamyiz" here is preferable. And the words "al-tayyib" and "al-khabith," although they are singular in form, are used for the genus (li-l-jins), so what is meant by them is all the believers and all the hypocrites, not two individuals from among them.

The second issue: We have mentioned that the meaning of the verse is: Allah would not leave you, O assembly of believers, in the state you are in, with the believer mixed with the hypocrite and their like, until He distinguishes the wicked from the good, that is, the hypocrite from the believer. They differed about what it was by which He would distinguish between them, and they mentioned several aspects:

The first: By sending trials, afflictions, killing and defeat. Whoever was a believer remained steadfast in his faith and in his affirmation of the Messenger (ﷺ), and whoever was a hypocrite, his hypocrisy and disbelief became manifest.

The second: Allah promised the support of the believers and the humbling of the disbelievers. When Islam grew strong, its dominion became great and disbelief and its people were humbled. At that point this distinction was achieved.

The third: The indications that point to this, such as the Muslims rejoicing at the support and strength of Islam, while the hypocrites were distressed because of that.

The third issue: Here there is a question: If this distinction appears and becomes manifest, then the disbelief of the hypocrites has become apparent, and the manifestation of disbelief from them negates their being hypocrites. And if it does not appear, the promise of Allah is not fulfilled.

Its answer: It appears to the extent that it yields a conjectural (zanni) distinction, not a certain (qat'i) distinction.

* * *

Then Allah, the Exalted, said: ﴿Nor would Allah disclose the unseen to you﴾. Its meaning is that He, Glorified, decreed that this distinction would become manifest. Then through this verse He explained that this distinction cannot be achieved by Allah informing you of His unseen, so that He says: "So-and-so is a hypocrite, and so-and-so is a believer, and so-and-so is among the people of Paradise, and so-and-so is among the people of the Fire." For the way of Allah is established that He does not make the common people aware of His unseen. Rather, there is no way for you to know that distinction except through tests, like what we have mentioned of the occurrence of trials and calamities, so that by them the one who agrees is distinguished from the hypocrite. As for knowing that through informing from the unseen, that is among the special attributes of the prophets. Therefore He said: ﴿but Allah chooses of His messengers whom He wills﴾, that is, but Allah selects from among His messengers whom He wills, so He singles them out by informing them that this one is a believer and that one is a hypocrite. It is also possible that it means: but Allah chooses of His messengers whom He wills, and then tests His creatures through the laws (shara'i') upon their hands, until the two groups are distinguished by the test. It is also possible that the meaning is: Allah would not make all of you knowers of the unseen in the manner in which He informs the Messenger, so that you would become independent of the Messenger. Rather, Allah singles out whom He wills of His servants with prophethood, then He obligates the rest to obey these messengers.

* * *

Then He said: ﴿So believe in Allah and His messengers﴾. The purpose is that the hypocrites cast doubt on the prophethood of Muhammad (ﷺ) by the occurrence of the disliked events in the story of Uhud. So Allah, the Exalted, made clear that there were benefits in them, among them the distinction of the wicked from the good. When He answered this doubt that you mentioned, He said: ﴿So believe in Allah and His messengers﴾, meaning: since the proofs have indicated his prophethood, and this doubt that you mentioned, regarding the attack on his prophethood, we have answered, there remains nothing except that you believe in Allah and His messengers. He said "(and His messengers)" and did not say "and His messenger" because of a subtle point: the way by which one reaches acknowledgment of the prophethood of any of the prophets, peace be upon them, is nothing but the miracle (mu'jiz), and it is present in the case of Muhammad (ﷺ). Therefore it is obligatory to acknowledge the prophethood of each of the prophets. For this subtle reason He said "(and His messengers)." The purpose is to draw attention to the fact that the way of establishing the prophethood of all the prophets is one, so whoever acknowledges the prophethood of one of them is obliged to acknowledge the prophethood of all. When He commanded them to this, He joined to it the promise of reward, saying: ﴿If you believe and are mindful of Allah, you will have a great reward﴾, and this is evident.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 3, verse 180:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And let not those who withhold of what Allah has given them of His bounty think that it is better for them. Rather, it is worse for them. They will have a collar of that about which they were stingy placed around their necks on the Day of Resurrection. And to Allah belongs the inheritance of the heavens and the earth, and Allah is Acquainted with what you do.﴾

Know that when He, exalted is He, had emphasized the exhortation to sacrifice oneself in jihad in the preceding verses, He began here to exhort to spending wealth in jihad, and He made clear the severe threat for whoever is stingy in spending wealth in the way of Allah. There are several issues in this verse:

The first issue: Hamzah recited ﴿وَلَا تَحْسَبَنَّ﴾ with the taa' (tā'), and the rest with the yā' (yā'). As for Hamzah's recitation with the taa' dotted from above, al-Zajjaj said: its meaning is "and do not think that the stinginess of those who are stingy is good for them," so the object was omitted because ﴿يَبْخَلُونَ﴾ indicates it. As for the one who recited with the yā' dotted from below, there are two possibilities:

The first: the subject of ﴿يَحْسَبَنَّ﴾ is a pronoun referring to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ or to someone, and the implied meaning is: "Let not the Messenger of Allah think," or "Let not anyone think, that the stinginess of those who are stingy is good for them." The omission was permissible because ﴿يَبْخَلُونَ﴾ indicates it, as in His saying: "Whoever lies, it is worse for him," meaning lying; and similarly:

"When the foolish one is admonished, he proceeds toward it,"

meaning foolishness. Al-Farra' recited:

"They are the kings and the sons of kings, and they are the takers of it, and the first masters,"

so His saying "bihi" (by it) means by kingship, but he dispensed with mentioning it by mentioning the kings.

Page 92
The second issue: The pronoun in His saying ﴿هُوَ خَيْرًا لَهُمْ﴾ is called a *fasl* (separator) by the Basrans and an *'imad* (support) by the Kufans. This is because when He mentioned ﴿يَبْخَلُونَ﴾, it stands in the position of mentioning stinginess, as if it were said: "Let not those who are stingy think stinginess to be good for them." The verification of this matter is that the subject has an essence, and the predicate has an essence, and the subject's essence being described by the predicate's essence is an additional matter beyond the essence of the subject and the essence of the predicate. So when this being-described is an additional matter beyond the two essences, there must be a third form indicating this being-described, and it is the word "huwa" (it/he).

* * *
The third issue: Know that the verse indicates the blame of stinginess with regard to some of the goods and benefits, and that good may be wealth or knowledge.

The first opinion: this threat was directed at stinginess with wealth, and the meaning is: let not these stingy people suppose that their stinginess is good for them; rather it is worse for them, because the punishment for their stinginess remains upon them. This is what is meant by His saying: ﴿They will have a collar of that about which they were stingy placed around their necks on the Day of Resurrection﴾, even though those wealths do not remain with them. This is what is meant by His saying: ﴿And to Allah belongs the inheritance of the heavens and the earth﴾.

The second opinion: that what is meant by this stinginess is stinginess with knowledge, because the Jews used to conceal the description and attributes of Muhammad ﷺ, so that concealment was stinginess. It is said: "So-and-so is stingy with his knowledge." There is no doubt that knowledge is a bounty from Allah, exalted is He. Allah, exalted is He, said: ﴿And He taught you what you did not know, and the bounty of Allah upon you has been great﴾ [An-Nisa: 113]. Then He, exalted is He, taught the Jews and Christians what is in the Torah and the Gospel, so when they concealed what is in these two books of the glad tidings of the sending of Muhammad ﷺ, that was stinginess.

Know that the first opinion is preferable, and two things indicate it:

The first: He, exalted is He, said: ﴿They will have a collar of that about which they were stingy﴾. If we interpreted the verse as knowledge, we would need to bear the burden of metaphor in interpreting this verse; if we interpreted it as wealth, we would not need metaphor, so this is preferable.

The second: If we take this verse as referring to wealth, it is an encouragement to spend wealth in jihad, and then this verse together with what precedes it has a fine coherence; if we take it to mean that the Jews concealed what they knew of the Torah, the coherence is broken except by way of artificiality, so the first is preferable.

The fourth issue: Most scholars hold that stinginess is an expression for withholding what is obligatory, and that withholding voluntary charity is not stinginess. They argued for this with several points:

The first: the verse indicates a severe threat regarding stinginess, and a threat is only fitting for what is obligatory.

The second: He, exalted is He, blamed stinginess and censured it, and withholding voluntary charity is not such that its doer should be blamed and censured for it.

The third: He, exalted is He, does not cease from leaving off bestowal, because there is no end to His capacities for bestowal, and everything that enters existence is finite; so He is inevitably one who leaves off bestowal. If leaving off bestowal were stinginess, it would follow that Allah, exalted is He, would necessarily be described as stingy, and Allah, exalted and magnified, is far above that by a great exaltation.

The fourth: He, upon whom be blessings and peace, said: "And what disease is more harmful than stinginess?" It is known that the one who withholds voluntary charity does not deserve this description.

The fifth: If the one who leaves off bestowal were stingy, it would be obligatory for the one who possesses all of a great wealth not to be freed from stinginess except by expending all of it.

The sixth: He, exalted is He, said: ﴿And from what We have provided them they spend﴾ [Al-Baqarah: 3], and the word "min" (from) is for partition, so the meaning of this verse is: those who spend part of what Allah has provided them. Then He, exalted is He, said of them: ﴿Those are upon guidance from their Lord, and those are the successful﴾ [Al-Baqarah: 5].

Page 93
Thus He described them with guidance and success, and if the one who leaves off voluntary charity were a stingy, blameworthy person, that would not be correct. So it is established by this verse that stinginess is an expression for leaving off what is obligatory, except that obligatory spending has many categories. Among them is spending on oneself and on one's relatives whose maintenance is incumbent upon him; among them is what relates to the sections of zakat; and among them is when Muslims need to repel an enemy who intends to kill them and seize their wealth, in which case it becomes obligatory upon them to spend wealth on those who will repel him from them, because that goes under the category of repelling harm from the self; and among them is when one of the Muslims becomes compelled, in which case it is obligatory upon him to give him the amount by which he can preserve his life. So all these expenditures are obligatory, and withholding them falls under stinginess. And Allah knows best.

* * *
Then He, exalted is He, said: ﴿They will have a collar of that about which they were stingy placed around their necks on the Day of Resurrection﴾. And there are issues in this:

The first issue: In the interpretation of this threat there are several opinions:

The first: that it be taken according to its apparent meaning, namely that He, exalted is He, will encircle them with a collar that will be a cause of their punishment. It is said that He will transform those wealths into live serpents around their necks, coiling around their necks like collars; and it is also possible that those serpents coil around the rest of their bodies. As for what becomes around their necks, it is because they had committed themselves to paying zakat and then refrained from it; and as for what coils around the rest of their bodies, it is because they used to add those wealths to themselves, so they were recompensed by having serpents coil around them as though they had committed themselves to them and added them to themselves. It is also possible that the collar is a collar of fire placed around their necks; and its parallel is His saying: ﴿On the Day when it will be heated in the fire of Hell and their foreheads, their sides, and their backs will be branded with it﴾ [At-Tawbah: 35]. And from Ibn Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both: That zakat which was withheld is made into a collar around the neck, like a bald-headed poisonous snake with two black spots, which bites at his two cheeks and says: "I am the zakat about which you were stingy in the world."

The second opinion: regarding His saying "sa-yutawwaqun" (they will be encircled). Mujahid said: they will be obligated to bring what they were stingy with on the Day of Resurrection. Its parallel is what is reported from Ibn Abbas that he used to recite "And upon those who are able to fast (yutawwaqunahu), a ransom" and the commentators said: they will be burdened with it and will not be able to bear it. So likewise His saying: ﴿They will have a collar of that about which they were stingy placed around their necks on the Day of Resurrection﴾, meaning they will be commanded to pay what they withheld at a time when it is impossible for them to bring it, so that will be a rebuke, in the sense: "Why did you not do that when it was possible?"

The third opinion: that His saying ﴿They will have a collar of that about which they were stingy﴾ means they will be bound to its sin in the Hereafter, and this is by way of illustration, not that there are actual collars. It is said of it: "So-and-so is like a collar on the neck of so-and-so." The Arabs express the emphasis of binding a thing by placing it on the neck, and from this one says: "I have entrusted you with this matter," and "I have placed this matter on your neck." He, exalted is He, said: ﴿And every person We have fastened his omen to his neck﴾ [Al-Isra: 13].

The fourth opinion: If we interpret this stinginess as stinginess with knowledge, the meaning of "they will be encircled" is that Allah, exalted is He, will place a collar of fire around their necks. He, upon whom be blessings and peace, said: "Whoever is asked about a knowledge which he knows and conceals it, Allah will bridle him with a bridle of fire on the Day of Resurrection." The meaning is that they are punished in their mouths and tongues with this bridle, because they did not speak with their mouths and tongues what indicates the truth.

Know that interpreting this stinginess as the concealing of the proofs of the prophethood of Muhammad ﷺ is not far-fetched, because the Jews and Christians

Page 94
are described in the Qur'an as stingy and censured for it. He, exalted is He, said of them: ﴿Or do they have a share of the kingdom? Then they would not give the people even a speck﴾ [An-Nisa: 53], and He also said about them: ﴿Those who are stingy and enjoin upon people stinginess﴾ [An-Nisa: 37]. Also, after this verse He mentioned: ﴿Allah has certainly heard the statement of those who said, "Indeed, Allah is poor, and we are rich"﴾ [Al Imran: 181], and that is among the sayings of the Jews. It is also not far-fetched that the verse is general, covering both stinginess with knowledge and stinginess with wealth, and the threat applies to both together.

* * *
The second issue: The Mu'tazilah said: this verse indicates the certainty of the threat against the wrongdoers (fussaq), because whoever is obligated by these rights and they do not fall from him is one who affirms the Messenger and the Sharia. As for His saying ﴿Rather, it is worse for them﴾, it is because it leads to the deprivation of reward and the attainment of the Fire. As for His saying ﴿They will have a collar of that about which they were stingy placed around their necks on the Day of Resurrection﴾, it is explicit in the threat.
Know that the discussion of this issue has preceded in Surat al-Baqarah.

* * *
Then He, exalted is He, said: ﴿And to Allah belongs the inheritance of the heavens and the earth﴾, and in it there are two opinions:

The first: To Him belongs what is in them of what their inhabitants inherit, of wealth and other things. So why do they withhold from Him His own possession and not spend it in His way? A parallel to this is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And spend of that in which He has made you successors﴾ [Al-Hadid: 7].

The second, which is the view of the majority: The meaning is that the inhabitants of the heavens and the earth will perish, and the possessions will remain with no owner except Allah. So this takes the place of inheritance, since people leave possessions behind; when they die and leave no one to succeed them, He is the inheritor of them. The purpose of the verse is that the ownership of the multitude of owners will vanish except the ownership of Allah, glorified and exalted, so it becomes like an inheritance. Ibn al-Anbari said: It is said "so-and-so inherited the knowledge of so-and-so" when he became sole possessor of it after having shared it. And He, exalted is He, said: ﴿And Solomon inherited David﴾ [An-Naml: 16], and the meaning was his being sole possessor of that matter after David had shared it with him and dominated it.

* * *
Then He, exalted is He, said: ﴿And Allah is Acquainted with what you do﴾. Ibn Kathir and Abu 'Amr recited "bi-ma ya'malun" (with what they do) with the yā', in the third person, as a reference to those who are stingy; the meaning being: Allah is Acquainted with what they do of withholding the rights, so He will recompense them for it. The rest recited with the tā', in the second person, because what precedes this verse is an address, namely His saying: ﴿And if you believe and fear Allah, you will have a great reward﴾, and "Allah is Acquainted with what you do, so He will recompense you for it." The third person is closer to it than the second person. The author of al-Kashshaf said: the yā' is according to the method of iltifat (shift of grammatical person), and it is more forceful in threat.

[p. 95]

Allah, exalted is He, says: ﴿Allah has certainly heard the saying of those who said, "Indeed, Allah is poor and we are rich." We will record what they have said and their killing of the prophets without right, and We will say, "Taste the punishment of the burning."﴾ ﴿That is for what your hands have put forward, and [because] Allah is not ever unjust to [His] servants.﴾

Know that there are two aspects regarding the manner of the arrangement (naẓm) of the verses:

The first: When Allah, exalted is He, commanded the responsible persons in these verses to sacrifice their lives [in His cause]
[p. 95 continues]
and to spend their wealth in the way of Allah, and emphasized this, He then began to relate the doubts of the people in their attack on his prophethood.

The first doubt: When He commanded spending wealth in His way, the disbelievers said: If He, exalted is He, sought to achieve His aim through spending, He would be poor and powerless, because whoever seeks wealth from another is poor. And since poverty is impossible for Allah, exalted is He, His seeking wealth from His servants is impossible. This indicates that Muhammad is lying in attributing this demand to Allah, exalted is He.

The second aspect of the arrangement: The community of Moses, peace be upon him, when they wanted to draw near to Allah, exalted is He, with their wealth, a fire would come down from the sky and consume it. So when the Prophet (ﷺ) asked them to spend wealth in the way of Allah, they said to him: "If you were a prophet, you would not have asked for wealth for this purpose. He, exalted is He, is not poor such that He would need our wealth to set right His religion. Rather, if you were a prophet, you would seek our wealth so that a fire would come from the sky and consume it. Since you have not done that, we know that you are not a prophet." This is the aspect of the arrangement. In the verse there are issues:

The first issue: Know that it is far-fetched for a sensible person to say, "Indeed, Allah is poor and we are rich." Rather, a person mentions this either by way of mockery or by way of argument (ilzām). Most of the narrations state that this statement came from the Jews. It was narrated that the Prophet (ﷺ) wrote, along with Abu Bakr, to the Jews of Banu Qaynuqa', inviting them to Islam, to establishing prayer, to giving zakat, and to lending Allah a goodly loan. Finḥāṣ the Jew said: "Indeed Allah is poor, so that He asks us for a loan." Abu Bakr slapped him on the face and said: "Were it not for the covenant between us and you, I would strike your neck." So [Finḥāṣ] complained to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and he denied what he had said. So this verse was revealed confirming Abu Bakr (may Allah be pleased with him).

Others said: When Allah, exalted is He, revealed, ﴿Who is it that will lend Allah a goodly loan so He will multiply it for him many times over?﴾ [al-Baqara: 245], the Jews said: "We see the god of Muhammad asking to borrow from us. So we are rich and He is poor. And He forbids us from usury, then He gives us usury," and they meant His saying, ﴿so He will multiply it for him many times over﴾.

Know that the verse does not specify who this speaker was, but the scholars attributed this statement to the Jews and argued for it with several points:

One: Allah, exalted is He, related about them that they said, "The hand of Allah is chained," meaning that He is stingy with giving, and that ignorance is suitable to the ignorance mentioned in this verse.

Second: What is reported in the narration that they spoke this way, as we have related in the story of Abu Bakr.

Third: Anthropomorphism (tashbīh) is predominant among the Jews, and whoever holds to anthropomorphism cannot establish that He, exalted is He, is capable of all things. And if he is unable to establish this principle, he is unable to demonstrate that He is rich and not poor.

The fourth aspect: When Moses, peace and blessings be upon him, asked them to join him in striving against the enemies, they said: ﴿So go you and your Lord and fight, indeed we are sitting here.﴾ So when Moses, peace be upon him, asked them to strive with their lives, they said: "Since the God is capable, what need does He have for our striving?" Likewise here: when Muhammad, peace and blessings be upon him, asked them to strive by spending wealth, they said: "Since the God is rich, what need does He have for our wealth?" So attributing this doubt to the Jews is appropriate from this aspect, although it is not impossible that other ignorant people also said this. The more apparent view is that they said it by way of attacking the prophethood of Muhammad (ﷺ), meaning: if Muhammad were truthful that God seeks wealth from His servants, He would be
[p. 96]
poor; and since that is impossible, it is established that he is lying in this report. Or they mentioned it by way of mockery and derision. As for a sensible person saying such a statement out of conviction, that is far-fetched.

* * *

The second issue: This verse indicates that He, exalted is He, hears statements. A parallel to it is His saying, ﴿Allah has certainly heard the saying of her who pleads with you﴾ [al-Mujadila: 1].

The third issue: The apparent meaning of the verse indicates that those who said this were a group, because He, exalted is He, said: "﴿Those who said﴾," and the apparent meaning of this expression conveys plurality. As for what is reported, that the speaker of this statement was Finḥāṣ the Jew, this indicates that no one else said it. But since the Book testifies that the speakers were a group, it is necessary to affirm this with certainty.

* * *

Then He, exalted is He, said: ﴿We will record what they have said﴾, and in it are issues:

The first issue: Ḥamza read "sayuktabu" with the yāʾ and a ḍamma, in the passive form (for which the subject is not named), and "wa-qatlahumu al-anbiyāʾa" with a raised lām, meaning "their killing of the prophets will be recorded." The rest read it with nūn and a fatḥa on the lām, attributed to Him, exalted is He. The author of al-Kashshāf said: al-Ḥasan and al-Aʿraj read "sayaktubu" with yāʾ and the active form.

The second issue: This is a threat regarding that statement, and it may have several meanings:

One: The meaning of His recording it against them is to establish it against them, so that it is not nullified or discarded. This is because when people want to establish a matter in a way that it will not be removed, forgotten, or changed, they write it down. And Allah, exalted is He, made "writing" a metaphor for establishing the ruling of that against them.

Second: "We will record what they have said" in the books in which their deeds are written, so that they may read it in the registers of their deeds on the Day of Resurrection.

Third: In my view there is another possibility, which is that the meaning is: We will record this ignorance of theirs in the Qur'an, so that people until the Day of Resurrection will know the extent of the obstinacy and ignorance of these people, and their exertion in attacking the prophethood of Muhammad (ﷺ) with everything they were able to.

* * *

Then He said: ﴿and their killing of the prophets without right﴾, meaning: and We will record their killing of the prophets without right. In it are two issues:

The first issue: The benefit of adding that they killed the prophets to their describing Allah, exalted is He, as poor, is to show that the ignorance of these people is not specific to this time; rather, since they existed they have been persistent in ignorance and folly.

The second issue: Regarding attributing the killing of the prophets to these people, there are two views:

One of them: "We will record what these people said, and We will record what their predecessors did, and We will recompense both groups according to what they deserve," like His saying: ﴿And when you killed a soul﴾ [al-Baqara: 72], meaning, "your predecessors killed it"; ﴿and when We delivered you from the people of Pharaoh﴾ [al-Baqara: 49]; ﴿and when We divided the sea for you﴾ [al-Baqara: 50]. The doer of these things was their predecessors, and the meaning is that He will preserve for both groups together their statements and their deeds.

The second view: "We will record against these people what they said themselves, and We will record against them their approval of the killing of their fathers, the prophets, may the blessings of Allah be upon them all." It is reported from al-Shaʿbī that a man mentioned Uthmān (may Allah be pleased with him) in his presence and praised his killing. Al-Shaʿbī said: "You have become a partner in his blood." Then al-Shaʿbī recited: ﴿Say: "There have certainly come to you messengers before me with clear proofs and with what you have said. So why did you kill them?"﴾ [Āl ʿImrān: 183]. So he attributed to these people the killing [of the prophets], and between them there were about seven hundred years.

* * *

Then He, exalted is He, said: ﴿And We will say, "Taste the punishment of the burning."﴾ In it are issues:
[p. 97]

The first issue: Ḥamza read "sayuktabu" in the passive form, "wa-qatlahumu al-anbiyāʾa" with a raised lām, and "wa-yaqūlu, dhūqū" with a yāʾ below (the dotted yāʾ), while the rest read "sanaktubu wa-naqūlu" with nūn.

The second issue: The meaning is that He, exalted is He, takes vengeance upon this speaker by saying to him: "Taste the punishment of the burning," just as you made the Muslims taste distress. "Al-ḥarīq" is "the burning one," like "al-alīm" in the sense of "al-mu'lim" (the painful).

The third issue: It is possible that this statement is said to him at death, or at the gathering (al-ḥashr), or at the reading of the Book; and it is possible that this is a metaphor for the realization of the threat, even if there is no actual saying.

The fourth issue: Someone may say: They raised a question, which is that whoever seeks wealth from another is poor and needy; so if Allah sought wealth from His servants, He would be poor, and that is impossible. Therefore it must be said: He did not seek wealth from His servants. And that undermines the truthfulness of Muhammad, peace be upon him, in claiming prophethood. This is the doubt of the people; so where is the answer to it? And how is it good to mention the threat upon mentioning it before mentioning the answer to it?

We say: If we base ourselves on the view of our companions from among the People of the Sunna and the Community (Ahl al-Sunna wa'l-Jamāʿa), we say: Allah does what He wills and rules as He desires. So it is not far-fetched that Allah, exalted is He, commands His servants to spend wealth while He is the richest of the rich.

And if we base ourselves on the view of the Muʿtazila (the Muʿtazila, who hold that He observes what is best for His servants), it is not far-fetched that in this obligation there are kinds of benefits returning to the servants:

Among them: Spending wealth necessitates the removal of love of wealth from the heart, and that is among the greatest benefits. For when a person dies, if the love of wealth remained in his heart while he had left the wealth, that would be a cause of pain to his soul at that separation.

Among them: That one may use that spending as a means to everlasting, perpetual reward.

Among them: That because of spending the heart becomes empty of love for other than Allah, and to the degree that love of other than Allah departs from the heart, to that degree love of Allah grows stronger; and that is the head of all felicities. All these aspects Allah has mentioned in the Qur'an and clarified them repeatedly and in various ways, as He said: ﴿And the enduring good deeds are better in the sight of your Lord for reward﴾ [al-Kahf: 46]; and He said: ﴿And the Hereafter is better and more enduring﴾ [al-A'lā: 17]; and He said: ﴿And approval from Allah is greater﴾ [al-Tawba: 72]; and He said: ﴿So let them rejoice in that; it is better than what they accumulate﴾ [Yūnus: 58]. So when mention of these aspects has preceded in complete detail, raising this doubt after the preceding clear proofs is pure obstinacy. Therefore Allah, exalted is He, when mentioning it, limited Himself to mere threat.

* * *

Then He, exalted is He, said: ﴿That is for what your hands have put forward, and [because] Allah is not ever unjust to [His] servants.﴾ In the verse there are issues:

The first issue: When He mentioned the severe threat, He mentioned its cause, saying: ﴿That is for what your hands have put forward﴾, meaning: this burning punishment is the recompense of your act, in that you described Allah and went ahead to kill the prophets; so this punishment is justice, not oppression.

The second issue: Al-Jubbāʾī (Abū ʿAlī al-Jubbāʾī, a Muʿtazilī scholar) said: The verse indicates that inflicting punishment upon them would have been injustice, on the assumption that these sins did not occur from them. In this is the refutation of the view of the Mujbira (those who affirm complete divine compulsion), who say that Allah punishes children without any crime, and may punish adults without any sin; and it indicates that the servant is the doer; otherwise injustice would have occurred.

The answer: What you have mentioned is countered by the issue of the motive (dāʿī) and the issue of knowledge (ʿilm), as we have explained repeatedly and in various ways.
[p. 98]

The third issue: Someone may say: ﴿And your Lord is not ever unjust to the servants﴾ [Fuṣṣilat: 46] indicates the negation of His being unjust, and negating an attribute gives the impression that the root remains; so this implies the affirmation of the root of injustice.

Al-Qāḍī (ʿAbd al-Jabbār) answered this by saying: If the punishment He threatened to inflict upon them were injustice, it would be great; so He negated it according to the extent of its greatness, were it established. And this confirms what we have mentioned: that inflicting punishment upon them would be injustice if they were not sinners.

The fourth issue: Know that the mention of "hands" here is figurative, because the one who acts is the human being, not the hand. However, since the hand is the instrument of action, it is appropriate to attribute the action to it figuratively. Then in this verse He mentioned the hand in the plural form, saying: ﴿Because of what your hands have sent forward﴾, and in another verse it is mentioned in the dual form, saying: ﴿That is for what your two hands have sent forward﴾ [al-Hajj: 10]. All of this is good and customary in the language.

[p. 95]

Allah, exalted is He, says: ﴿Allah has certainly heard the saying of those who said, "Indeed, Allah is poor and we are rich." We will record what they have said and their killing of the prophets without right, and We will say, "Taste the punishment of the burning."﴾ ﴿That is for what your hands have put forward, and [because] Allah is not ever unjust to [His] servants.﴾

Know that there are two aspects regarding the manner of the arrangement (naẓm) of the verses:

The first: When Allah, exalted is He, commanded the responsible persons in these verses to sacrifice their lives [in His cause]
[p. 95 continues]
and to spend their wealth in the way of Allah, and emphasized this, He then began to relate the doubts of the people in their attack on his prophethood.

The first doubt: When He commanded spending wealth in His way, the disbelievers said: If He, exalted is He, sought to achieve His aim through spending, He would be poor and powerless, because whoever seeks wealth from another is poor. And since poverty is impossible for Allah, exalted is He, His seeking wealth from His servants is impossible. This indicates that Muhammad is lying in attributing this demand to Allah, exalted is He.

The second aspect of the arrangement: The community of Moses, peace be upon him, when they wanted to draw near to Allah, exalted is He, with their wealth, a fire would come down from the sky and consume it. So when the Prophet (ﷺ) asked them to spend wealth in the way of Allah, they said to him: "If you were a prophet, you would not have asked for wealth for this purpose. He, exalted is He, is not poor such that He would need our wealth to set right His religion. Rather, if you were a prophet, you would seek our wealth so that a fire would come from the sky and consume it. Since you have not done that, we know that you are not a prophet." This is the aspect of the arrangement. In the verse there are issues:

The first issue: Know that it is far-fetched for a sensible person to say, "Indeed, Allah is poor and we are rich." Rather, a person mentions this either by way of mockery or by way of argument (ilzām). Most of the narrations state that this statement came from the Jews. It was narrated that the Prophet (ﷺ) wrote, along with Abu Bakr, to the Jews of Banu Qaynuqa', inviting them to Islam, to establishing prayer, to giving zakat, and to lending Allah a goodly loan. Finḥāṣ the Jew said: "Indeed Allah is poor, so that He asks us for a loan." Abu Bakr slapped him on the face and said: "Were it not for the covenant between us and you, I would strike your neck." So [Finḥāṣ] complained to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and he denied what he had said. So this verse was revealed confirming Abu Bakr (may Allah be pleased with him).

Others said: When Allah, exalted is He, revealed, ﴿Who is it that will lend Allah a goodly loan so He will multiply it for him many times over?﴾ [al-Baqara: 245], the Jews said: "We see the god of Muhammad asking to borrow from us. So we are rich and He is poor. And He forbids us from usury, then He gives us usury," and they meant His saying, ﴿so He will multiply it for him many times over﴾.

Know that the verse does not specify who this speaker was, but the scholars attributed this statement to the Jews and argued for it with several points:

One: Allah, exalted is He, related about them that they said, "The hand of Allah is chained," meaning that He is stingy with giving, and that ignorance is suitable to the ignorance mentioned in this verse.

Second: What is reported in the narration that they spoke this way, as we have related in the story of Abu Bakr.

Third: Anthropomorphism (tashbīh) is predominant among the Jews, and whoever holds to anthropomorphism cannot establish that He, exalted is He, is capable of all things. And if he is unable to establish this principle, he is unable to demonstrate that He is rich and not poor.

The fourth aspect: When Moses, peace and blessings be upon him, asked them to join him in striving against the enemies, they said: ﴿So go you and your Lord and fight, indeed we are sitting here.﴾ So when Moses, peace be upon him, asked them to strive with their lives, they said: "Since the God is capable, what need does He have for our striving?" Likewise here: when Muhammad, peace and blessings be upon him, asked them to strive by spending wealth, they said: "Since the God is rich, what need does He have for our wealth?" So attributing this doubt to the Jews is appropriate from this aspect, although it is not impossible that other ignorant people also said this. The more apparent view is that they said it by way of attacking the prophethood of Muhammad (ﷺ), meaning: if Muhammad were truthful that God seeks wealth from His servants, He would be
[p. 96]
poor; and since that is impossible, it is established that he is lying in this report. Or they mentioned it by way of mockery and derision. As for a sensible person saying such a statement out of conviction, that is far-fetched.

* * *

The second issue: This verse indicates that He, exalted is He, hears statements. A parallel to it is His saying, ﴿Allah has certainly heard the saying of her who pleads with you﴾ [al-Mujadila: 1].

The third issue: The apparent meaning of the verse indicates that those who said this were a group, because He, exalted is He, said: "﴿Those who said﴾," and the apparent meaning of this expression conveys plurality. As for what is reported, that the speaker of this statement was Finḥāṣ the Jew, this indicates that no one else said it. But since the Book testifies that the speakers were a group, it is necessary to affirm this with certainty.

* * *

Then He, exalted is He, said: ﴿We will record what they have said﴾, and in it are issues:

The first issue: Ḥamza read "sayuktabu" with the yāʾ and a ḍamma, in the passive form (for which the subject is not named), and "wa-qatlahumu al-anbiyāʾa" with a raised lām, meaning "their killing of the prophets will be recorded." The rest read it with nūn and a fatḥa on the lām, attributed to Him, exalted is He. The author of al-Kashshāf said: al-Ḥasan and al-Aʿraj read "sayaktubu" with yāʾ and the active form.

The second issue: This is a threat regarding that statement, and it may have several meanings:

One: The meaning of His recording it against them is to establish it against them, so that it is not nullified or discarded. This is because when people want to establish a matter in a way that it will not be removed, forgotten, or changed, they write it down. And Allah, exalted is He, made "writing" a metaphor for establishing the ruling of that against them.

Second: "We will record what they have said" in the books in which their deeds are written, so that they may read it in the registers of their deeds on the Day of Resurrection.

Third: In my view there is another possibility, which is that the meaning is: We will record this ignorance of theirs in the Qur'an, so that people until the Day of Resurrection will know the extent of the obstinacy and ignorance of these people, and their exertion in attacking the prophethood of Muhammad (ﷺ) with everything they were able to.

* * *

Then He said: ﴿and their killing of the prophets without right﴾, meaning: and We will record their killing of the prophets without right. In it are two issues:

The first issue: The benefit of adding that they killed the prophets to their describing Allah, exalted is He, as poor, is to show that the ignorance of these people is not specific to this time; rather, since they existed they have been persistent in ignorance and folly.

The second issue: Regarding attributing the killing of the prophets to these people, there are two views:

One of them: "We will record what these people said, and We will record what their predecessors did, and We will recompense both groups according to what they deserve," like His saying: ﴿And when you killed a soul﴾ [al-Baqara: 72], meaning, "your predecessors killed it"; ﴿and when We delivered you from the people of Pharaoh﴾ [al-Baqara: 49]; ﴿and when We divided the sea for you﴾ [al-Baqara: 50]. The doer of these things was their predecessors, and the meaning is that He will preserve for both groups together their statements and their deeds.

The second view: "We will record against these people what they said themselves, and We will record against them their approval of the killing of their fathers, the prophets, may the blessings of Allah be upon them all." It is reported from al-Shaʿbī that a man mentioned Uthmān (may Allah be pleased with him) in his presence and praised his killing. Al-Shaʿbī said: "You have become a partner in his blood." Then al-Shaʿbī recited: ﴿Say: "There have certainly come to you messengers before me with clear proofs and with what you have said. So why did you kill them?"﴾ [Āl ʿImrān: 183]. So he attributed to these people the killing [of the prophets], and between them there were about seven hundred years.
