Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 3, verse 183:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Those who say, "Indeed, Allah has taken a covenant with us that we not believe in any messenger until he brings us an offering which the fire consumes." Say, "There have certainly come to you messengers before me with clear proofs and with what you have spoken. So why did you kill them, if you should be truthful?"﴾

Know that this is the second doubt of the disbelievers in casting doubt on his prophethood (ﷺ). Its formulation is that they said: ﴿Indeed, Allah has taken a covenant with us that we not believe in any messenger until he brings us an offering which the fire consumes﴾, and you, O Muhammad, did not do that; therefore you cannot be one of the prophets. This is the explanation of the connection of the discourse. In the verse there are several issues:

The first issue: Ibn 'Abbas said: this verse was revealed concerning Ka'b ibn al-Ashraf, Ka'b ibn Asad, Malik ibn al-Sayf, Wahb ibn Yahudha, Zayd ibn al-Tabut, Finhas ibn 'Azura' and others. They came to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and said: "O Muhammad, you claim that you are the Messenger of Allah and that He, exalted is He, has sent down a Book to you. Indeed He has given us a covenant in the Torah that we not believe in any messenger until he brings us an offering which the fire consumes, and which has a light rumbling sound, descending from the sky. If you bring us this, we will confirm you." So this verse was revealed. 'Ata' said: The Children of Israel used to slaughter for Allah, and they would take the fats and the choicest meat and place them in the middle of a house whose roof was open. The prophet would stand in the house and commune with his Lord, while the Children of Israel stood outside around the house, and a white fire would descend with a light rumbling sound and no smoke, and it would consume all that offering.

Know that the scholars have two views concerning what the Jews claimed:

The first, which is the view of al-Suddi: this condition did come in the Torah, but with a qualification. For He, exalted is He, said in the Torah: "Whoever comes to you claiming to be a prophet, do not confirm him until he brings you an offering which the fire consumes, except for al-Masih and Muhammad, peace be upon them both. For if they come, believe in them, for they come without an offering which the fire consumes." He said: This custom remained until the mission of al-Masih, peace be upon him. When Allah sent al-Masih, it was lifted and removed.

The second view: that the claim of this condition is a lie upon the Torah, and several points show this:

One: If that were true, the miracles of all the prophets would have been this offering, and it is known that the matter was not so, for the miracles of Musa, peace be upon him, before Pharaoh were things other than this offering.

Second: The descent of this fire and its consuming of the offering is a miracle, and so it was equal to all other miracles; there was no benefit in specifying and particularizing this miracle. Rather, when the overpowering miracle appeared at the hand of Muhammad, peace be upon him, it became necessary to be certain of his prophethood, whether or not this miracle appeared.

Third: It is either said that the Torah states that a claimant to prophethood, even if he brings all the miracles, must not be accepted unless he brings this specific miracle, or it is said that the Torah states that a claimant to prophethood must be asked for a miracle, whether the miracle is the coming of the fire or something else. The first is false, because on this assumption bringing all other miracles would not indicate truthfulness, and if it is permissible to dispute all other miracles, it is permissible to dispute this specific miracle as well.

As for the second: it requires that truthfulness be conditioned on the appearance of a miracle in general, not on the appearance of this specific miracle; so taking this miracle into account would be pointless and vain. Thus it has become clear from what we have mentioned that this doubt collapses entirely. And Allah knows best.

The second issue: concerning the position of "alladhina" (those who) there are several views:

First: al-Zajjaj said: it is in the genitive, and it is an attribute of "al-'abid" (the servants), and the estimate is: "Your Lord is not unjust to the servants who said such and such."

Second: the estimate is: "Allah has indeed heard the saying of those who said, 'Indeed Allah is poor,' and the saying of those who said, 'Indeed Allah has taken a covenant with us.'"

Third: that it is in the nominative by way of the inchoative, and the estimate is: "They are those who said that."

* * *

The third issue: al-Wahidi, may Allah have mercy on him, said: The qurban is the act of goodness by which one draws near to Allah. Its origin is the verbal noun from your saying "qariba qurbanan," like "kufran," "rujhanan," and "khusran." Then the name was applied to the very thing by which one draws near. From this is the saying of the Prophet, peace be upon him, to Ka'b ibn 'Ujrah: "O Ka'b, fasting is a shield, and prayer is a qurban," meaning by it one draws near to Allah and seeks intercession for a need in His presence.

Know that He, exalted is He, answered this doubt, saying: ﴿Say, "There have certainly come to you messengers before me with clear proofs and with what you have spoken. So why did you kill them, if you should be truthful?"﴾ And in this there are issues:

The first issue: Know that He, exalted is He, showed by these proofs that they seek this miracle not as a means of guidance but as a means of obstinacy. That is because the forefathers of these Jews sought this kind of miracle from earlier prophets such as Zakariyya, 'Isa and Yahya, peace be upon them, and those prophets did show this miracle. Then the Jews strove to kill Zakariyya and Yahya, and they claim that they also killed 'Isa, peace be upon him. This indicates that those people only sought this miracle from those prophets as a means of obstinacy, for otherwise they would not have striven to kill them. Moreover, the later ones are content with the deeds of those earlier ones and approve of them in everything they did, and this requires that these people, in seeking this miracle from Muhammad, peace be upon him, are obstinate. When it is established that their seeking this miracle was an act of obstinacy and not of guidance, it is not required by the wisdom of Allah to grant them it, especially since many miracles have already come to Muhammad (ﷺ). This answer is sufficient to dispel this doubt.

The second issue: He said "قَدْ جاءَكم رُسُلٌ مِن قَبْلِي" and did not say "جاءتكم رسل", because the verb for a feminine plural subject is made masculine when it precedes its subject.

The third issue: What is meant by His saying "وبِالَّذِي قُلْتُمْ" is what they asked of him, namely the offering which the fire consumes.

Know that He, exalted is He, did not say "قد جاءكم رسل من قبلي بالذي قلتم" alone, but said "قَدْ جاءَكم رُسُلٌ مِن قَبْلِي بِالبَيِّناتِ وبِالَّذِي قُلْتُمْ". The point is this: the people said that Allah, exalted is He, made confirmation of prophethood conditional on the appearance of the offering which the fire consumes. So if the Prophet, peace be upon him, had said to them, "The earlier prophets brought this offering," it would not have followed from this alone that it is obligatory to acknowledge their prophethood, since it is possible that bringing this offering is a condition of prophethood and not its cause. A condition is such that when it is absent, the conditioned thing is absent; but when it is present, the conditioned thing is not necessarily present. Thus it is established that had he been content with this much, the argument would not have been binding. But when he said "قَدْ جاءَكم رُسُلٌ مِن قَبْلِي بِالبَيِّناتِ وبِالَّذِي قُلْتُمْ", the argument became binding, because when they brought the clear proofs, they brought what necessitates confirmation, and when they brought this offering, they brought the condition; and upon bringing both, acknowledging prophethood becomes obligatory. Thus it is established that were it not for his saying "(جاءكم بالبينات)", the argument would not have been binding upon the people. And Allah knows best.

**Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 3, verse 184:**

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And if they deny you, then messengers before you were denied, who came with clear proofs, the scriptures, and the illuminating Book.﴾ ﴿Every soul will taste death, and you will only be paid your rewards on the Day of Resurrection. Whoever is drawn away from the Fire and admitted to Paradise has triumphed. And the life of this world is nothing but the enjoyment of delusion.﴾

Regarding His saying, "And if they deny you," there are several interpretations.

The first: "And if they deny you" in your statement that the earlier prophets came to these Jews with the offering that fire consumes, and they denied and killed them, then messengers before you were denied: Noah, Hud, Salih, Abraham, Shu'ayb, and others.

The second: the meaning is, if they deny you regarding the essence of prophethood and the law, then messengers before you were denied. This interpretation is perhaps the more likely, because He did not specify, because their denial of the essence of prophethood is greater, and because the denial in that dispute is included within it. The purpose of this statement is to console the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and to show that this denial is not something specific to him among the prophets. Rather, it is the way of all the disbelievers to deny all the prophets and to slander them, even though their situation regarding the manifestation of miracles upon them and the descent of scriptures to them was like yours. Despite this, they were patient with what they suffered from those nations and bore their harm for the sake of conveying the message. So be someone who follows their example and takes their path in this respect. This became consolation because when a calamity is widespread, it becomes easier and lighter.

As for "clear proofs" (al-bayyinat), these are the arguments and miracles. As for "the scriptures" (al-zubur), these are books. It is the plural of zabur (psalter, or written scripture), and zabur means a book, in the sense of "the written" (al-mazbur), meaning what is written. One says "I zabarta the book," meaning I wrote it, and every book is a zabur. Al-Zajjaj said: "The zabur is every book containing wisdom." On this basis:

**Page 101**

It is more likely that the meaning of zabur derives from zabr, which is restraint or rebuke. One says "zabartu al-rajul" when you rebuke a man from falsehood. A book was named zabur because of the restraint from opposition to the truth it contains, and by this the Psalms of David were named, because of the large number of rebukes and admonitions in it. Ibn 'Abbas read "wa-bi-l-zubur" (with the ba' repeated), repeating the preposition for emphasis. As for "al-munir" (the illuminating), it derives from your saying "anartu al-shay'," meaning I made the thing clear.

There are two issues in the verse:

The first issue: what is meant by "clear proofs" is the miracles. Then He conjoined the scriptures and the Book after them. This requires saying that their miracles were distinct from their books, and this indicates that none of the prophets had books that were themselves miracles for them. The Torah, the Gospel, the Psalms, and the scrolls: none of them was a miracle. As for the Qur'an, it alone is both a book and a miracle, and this is one of the special qualities of the Messenger, upon whom be prayers and peace.

The second issue: the conjoining of "the illuminating Book" to "the scriptures," although the illuminating Book must be among the scriptures. This conjunction is good because the illuminating Book is the most noble of books and the best of scriptures. So the conjunction is fine, as in His saying: ﴿And [recall] when We took from the prophets their covenant, and from you, and from Noah﴾ [al-Ahzab: 7], and He said: ﴿Whoever is an enemy to Allah and His angels and His messengers and Gabriel and Michael﴾ [al-Baqarah: 98]. The reason for the increase in its nobility is either that it comprises the whole of the law, or that it remains until the end of time. It is possible that what is meant by "the scriptures" is the scrolls, and by "the illuminating Book" the Torah, the Gospel, and the Psalms.

[Page 102]

Allah Most High says: ﴿Every soul shall taste death﴾.

Know that the purpose of this verse is to affirm the consolation of the Messenger, upon him be prayers and peace, and to go to great lengths to remove sorrow from his heart. This is in two respects:

The first: the end of all things is death, and these griefs and sorrows pass and vanish, and nothing of them remains. Sorrow that is like this is not given attention by the sensible person.

The second: after this abode there is an abode in which the good-doer is distinguished from the evildoer, and each person's deeds are fully repaid with the recompense that befits them. Each of these two considerations is extremely powerful in removing sorrow and distress from the hearts of the wise. In the verse there are several issues:

The first issue: Concerning His saying ﴿every soul shall taste death﴾ there is an objection: Allah Most High is called "nafs" (self/soul), as He said: ﴿You know what is in my self, and I do not know what is in Yours﴾. Also, nafs and dhat (essence) are one and the same. On this basis, inanimate things would fall under the term nafs, and it would follow that death is general to inanimate things. Also, Allah Most High said: ﴿And whoever is in the heavens and whoever is on the earth will swoon, except whom Allah wills﴾ [al-Zumar 39:68], which indicates that those excepted in this exception do not die; and this generality indicates the death of all. Also, it would imply that death befalls the people of Paradise and the people of Hell, since all of them are souls.

Its answer: the intended meaning of the verse is the mukallafun (those charged with obligation) present in the abode of obligation, as evidenced by Allah Most High saying after this verse: ﴿So whoever is drawn away from the Fire and admitted into Paradise has succeeded﴾. This meaning can apply only to them. Also, a general term remains a proof after its specification.

The second issue: "dhaʾiqah" (tasting) is an active participle from dhawq (tasting). When the active participle is annexed to a noun and is meant in the past tense, only the genitive (jarr) is permissible in it, as in your saying: Zayd is a striker of ʿAmr yesterday. But if you mean by it the present or future, both the genitive and the accusative (nasb) are permissible, as you say: He is striking Zayd tomorrow, and "ḍārib Zaydan" tomorrow. Allah Most High said: ﴿Are they removers of His harm?﴾ [al-Zumar 39:38], and "kāshifāt ḍurrih" has been read in both ways, because it refers to the future. It is narrated from al-Ḥasan that he read "dhāʾiqatan al-mawt" with tanwin and with the accusative on "al-mawt", and this is the original form. Al-Aʿmash read "dhāʾiqatu al-mawt" by dropping the tanwin together with the accusative, as in the line of poetry:

*"And none remembering God except a little."*

The complete discussion of this issue will come in Surat al-Nisaʾ at His saying: ﴿wronging themselves﴾, if Allah Most High wills.

* * *

The third issue: The philosophers claimed that death is necessarily bound to occur with this bodily life. This is because bodily life is not achieved except through innate moisture (al-ruṭūba al-gharīziyya) and innate heat (al-ḥarāra al-gharīziyya). Then innate heat acts upon dissolving innate moisture, and this condition continues until the original moisture is exhausted, so the innate heat is extinguished and death occurs. By this route, death is necessary within this life. They said: His saying ﴿every soul shall taste death﴾ indicates that souls do not die with the death of the body, because He made the soul a taster of death, and the taster must necessarily remain existing at the time of tasting. The meaning is that every soul tastes the death of the body. This indicates that the soul is other than the body, and that the soul does not die with the death of the body. Also: the word "nafs" is specific to bodies, and this contains an indication that the necessity of death is specific to bodily life, whereas disembodied spirits are not subject to it. Yet there have come in the narrations things contrary to this. For it is narrated from Ibn ʿAbbas that he said: When the saying of Allah Most High was revealed: ﴿Everyone upon it will perish﴾ [al-Raḥmān 55:26], the angels said: "The people of the earth have died." And when His saying ﴿every soul shall taste death﴾ was revealed, the angels said: "We have died."

The fourth issue: His saying ﴿every soul shall taste death﴾ indicates that the one killed is called "dead". It is only that the one properly slaughtered (al-mudhakkā) is not called "dead" because of a specification by custom.

* * *

Then Allah Most High said: ﴿And you will only be given your full rewards on the Day of Resurrection﴾. Allah Most High has made clear that the complete reward and recompense do not reach the mukallaf except on the Day of Resurrection. This is because every benefit that reaches the mukallaf in this world is clouded by griefs and anxieties and by the fear of its ending and passing away. The complete reward and perfect recompense reach the mukallaf only on the Day of Resurrection, because there joy occurs without distress, safety without fear, pleasure without pain, and happiness without fear of cessation. The same applies to the side of punishment: in this world there is no pain purely free of any admixture of pleasure, but rather relief and alleviations are mixed with it. The complete, pure, and lasting pain is only that which will occur on the Day of Resurrection. We seek refuge in Allah from it.

* * *

Then Allah Most High said: ﴿So whoever is drawn away from the Fire and admitted into Paradise has succeeded﴾. Zaḥzaḥa means to move away and remove, and it is the intensive form of zazz, and zazz is pulling with haste. This is an alert that a person, while in this world, is as though he were in the Fire, and that is only because of the abundance of its afflictions and the severity of its trials. For this reason the Prayer and Peace of Allah be upon him said: "The world is the prison of the believer."

Know that a person has no aim beyond these two matters: deliverance from punishment and attainment of reward. So Allah Most High made clear that whoever reaches these two desired things has succeeded in the ultimate aim and the goal beyond which nothing is sought. It is narrated from the Messenger of Allah ﷺ that he said: "A place of a whip in Paradise is better than this world and all that is in it." And he recited His saying Most High: (So whoever is drawn away from the Fire and admitted into Paradise has succeeded). And the Prayer and Peace be upon him said: "Whoever loves to be drawn away from the Fire and to enter Paradise, let his death overtake him while he believes in Allah and the Last Day, and let him treat people with what he loves to be treated with."

* * *

Then He said: ﴿And the worldly life is nothing but the enjoyment of delusion﴾. Ghurūr is a verbal noun from your saying: "gharrartu fulānan ghurūran" (I deceived so-and-so). Allah has likened this world to goods that are concealed (yudallas) from the prospective buyer (al-mustām) and made to appear attractive to him until he buys them, and then their defect and inferiority become evident to him. The deceiver who conceals is Satan. It is narrated from Saʿīd ibn Jubayr that this applies to one who prefers this world over the Hereafter; but as for one who seeks the Hereafter through it, it is an excellent provision. And Allah knows best.

Know that the corruption of this world is from several aspects:

The first: if a person obtained all of his desires, his grief and anxiety would be greater than his joy, because of the shortness of its time, the scarcity of trust in it, and his lack of knowledge whether he will benefit from it or not.

The second: the more a person finds of the worldly things he desires, the greater his greed in seeking them, and the greater his greed, the more intense the heart's anguish from that greed. For a person imagines that if he attains his goal his soul will be at rest, but it is not so; rather his seeking, greed, and desire increase.

The third: to the degree that a person obtains from this world, he remains deprived of the Hereafter, which is the greatest of happinesses and goods. When you have understood these three aspects, you will know that this world is "the enjoyment of delusion," and that it is as Amīr al-Muʾminīn ʿAlī ibn Abī Ṭālib, may Allah be pleased with him, described it when he said: "Its touch is soft, its poison deadly." And some have said: "The world, its outward is a mount of joy, and its inward is a mount of evils."

The Exalted said: ﴿You will surely be tested in your possessions and your selves, and you will surely hear much hurtful talk from those who were given the Scripture before you and from those who associate partners with God. But if you are patient and mindful of God, then that is among the matters requiring resolve.﴾

Know that when God, the Exalted, consoled the Messenger ﷺ with His words ﴿Every soul shall taste death﴾, He increased this consolation with this verse. He explained that the disbelievers, after they had harmed the Messenger and the Muslims on the Day of Uhud, would also harm them in the future by every means available to them, both harm to their persons and harm to their wealth. The purpose of this information is that they should prepare their souls for patience and for abandoning impatience and distress, because a person who does not know that a trial will befall him finds it hard when it does befall him, whereas if he knows it will come, its impact is not so great when it arrives.

As for His words ﴿You will surely be tested in your possessions and your selves﴾, there are several issues concerning it:

The first issue: al-Wahidi (may God have mercy on him) said: the lam is the lam of oath, and the nun was added for emphasis. The waw was given a damma because of its being quiescent and the quiescence of the nun, and it was not given a kasra for the meeting of two quiescent letters, because it is the waw of the plural, so it was moved by the vowel that was required before it, namely the damma. A similar case is ﴿they have bought error﴾ [al-Baqarah: 16].

The second issue: (*latublawunna*) means "you will be tested" (*latukhtabarunna*). It is known that testing (*ikhtibar*) cannot be attributed to God, the Exalted, because it implies seeking knowledge in order to distinguish the good from the bad; rather, its meaning with respect to God, the Exalted, is that He deals with the servant as one who is being tested.

The third issue: they differed about the meaning of this trial. Some said: what is intended is the hardship and poverty they will meet with, and the killing, wounding and defeat they will suffer at the hands of the disbelievers, and the obligation laid upon them to be patient in jihad. Al-Hasan said: what is intended is the severe obligations connected with the body and wealth, namely prayer, zakat and jihad. The judge (al-Qadi) said: the apparent wording admits of each of the two meanings, so there is no barrier to applying it to both.

* * *

As for His words ﴿And you will surely hear much hurtful talk from those who were given the Scripture before you and from those who associate partners with God﴾, what is meant is the various kinds of harm inflicted upon the Muslims by the Jews, the Christians and the polytheists. That is because they used to say "Uzayr is the son of God," "the Messiah is the son of God," and "God is the third of three," and they used to disparage the Messenger, upon him be blessings and peace, by every means they could. Ka'b ibn al-Ashraf satirized him in verse, and they used to incite people against the Messenger ﷺ. As for the polytheists, they used to incite people against the Messenger ﷺ, gather armies to fight the Messenger ﷺ, and discourage the Muslims from supporting him. Therefore the statement must be understood as applying to all of them, since restricting it to some over the others is not preferable to restricting it to the second group.

Then the Exalted said, conjoining the two matters: ﴿But if you are patient and mindful of God, then that is among the matters requiring resolve﴾. Concerning this there are several issues:

The first issue: the commentators said: "The Messenger ﷺ sent Abu Bakr to Finhas the Jew to ask him for a loan. Finhas said: 'Your Lord has become in need that we should lend to Him.' Abu Bakr, may God be pleased with him, resolved to strike him with the sword, but the Messenger of God ﷺ had said to him when he sent him: 'Do not overcome anything until you return to me.' Abu Bakr, may God be pleased with him, remembered that, refrained from striking, and this verse was revealed."

The second issue: the verse has two interpretations.

The first: what is meant is the command to the Messenger ﷺ to endure the trial in self and wealth, and to persevere in bearing harm and in not opposing or retaliating. God, the Exalted, only made this obligatory because it is closer to bringing the opponent into the religion, as He said: ﴿Speak to him gently, perhaps he will remember or fear﴾ [Ta-Ha: 44]; and He said: ﴿Tell those who believe to forgive those who do not expect the days of God﴾ [al-Jathiyah: 14], and the forgiveness meant here is patience and the abandonment of retaliation; and He said: ﴿When they pass by idle talk, they pass by with dignity﴾ [al-Furqan: 72]; and He said: ﴿So be patient as the steadfast of the messengers were patient﴾ [al-Ahqaf: 35]; and He said: ﴿Repel with that which is better, and then the one between you and him who is enmity will be as though he were a devoted friend﴾ [Fussilat: 34]. Al-Wahidi (may God have mercy on him) said: this was before the revelation of the verse of the sword.

Al-Qaffal (may God have mercy on him) said: "What I hold is that this is not abrogated, and the apparent meaning is that it was revealed following the story of Uhud. The meaning is that they were commanded to be patient with what they inflict upon the Messenger ﷺ through the verbal exchanges that take place among them, and to use tact in many situations, and the command to fight does not contradict the command to endure in this manner." Know that al-Wahidi's view is weak, and the correct view is what al-Qaffal said.

The second interpretation: that what is meant by patience and mindfulness is patience in striving against the disbelievers

صفحة ١٠٥
and in opposing them and denouncing them, so they were commanded to be patient in the hardships of jihad and to follow the path of Abu Bakr al-Siddiq, may God be pleased with him, in denouncing the Jews and in guarding against compromise with the disbelievers and against silence about showing denunciation.

The third issue: patience is an expression for enduring what is disliked, and mindfulness (taqwa) is an expression for guarding oneself against what is not fitting. He mentioned patience first and then mentioned mindfulness after it, because a person only undertakes patience in order to guard himself against what is not fitting. There is another point: that what is meant by patience is that returning evil with evil leads to an increase in evil, so he was commanded to be patient in order to lessen the harms of this world, and he was commanded to be mindful in order to lessen the harms of the Hereafter; thus, on this interpretation, the verse comprises the etiquette of both this world and the Hereafter.

The fourth issue: His words ﴿from the resolve of affairs﴾ mean from the sound planning in which there is no doubt about the manifestness of right guidance, and which every intelligent person should resolve upon, so that his soul will inevitably be bound to it. Resolve (*azm*) is, as it were, part of firmness (*hazm*), and its origin is from the saying of a man: "I resolved upon you to do such-and-such," meaning I obligated it upon you without fail, in a way that does not permit leniency in abandoning it. Thus whatever affairs have a praiseworthy outcome and are known for right guidance and correctness are among the resolved affairs, because it is not permissible for an intelligent person to be lenient in abandoning them. It may also bear another meaning: that it is among the matters that have been resolved upon you, i.e., you have been obligated to take hold of it. And God knows best.

[Page 106]

**His statement, may He be exalted:** ﴿And [recall] when God took the covenant of those who were given the Book: "You must make it clear to the people and not conceal it." But they cast it behind their backs and exchanged it for a small price. How wretched is what they buy.﴾

Know that there are two aspects to the manner of the arrangement (*kayfiyyat al-nazm*, the structure and coherence of the verses):

The first: when He, exalted is He, related from the Jews doubtful objections against the prophethood of Muhammad, peace be upon him, and answered them, He followed this with this verse. This is because He, exalted is He, had obligated them in the Torah and the Gospel, given to the community of Moses and Jesus, peace be upon them both, to explain what is in these two books of the proofs that indicate the soundness of his religion and the truth of his prophethood and message. The purpose here is to express wonder at their condition, as if it were said: How is it fitting for you to raise objections to his prophethood and religion, when your books speak and indicate that you are obligated to mention the proofs that indicate the truth of his prophethood and religion?

The second: when He, exalted is He, in the preceding verse, made it obligatory upon Muhammad, peace be upon him, to bear harm from the People of the Book, and among their harm to the Messenger, peace be upon him, was that they concealed what is in the Torah and the Gospel of the proofs indicating his prophethood, and they would distort them and offer corrupt interpretations for them, He made clear that this is part of that category in which patience is obligatory. In the verse there are several issues:

**The first issue:** Ibn Kathir, Abu Bakr, ʿAsim and Abu ʿAmr read *la-yubayyinunnahu* and *wa-la yaktumunahu* with the *ya'* in both, as a reference to the People of the Book. The rest read them with the *ta'* in both, as direct address to the state that existed at the time the covenant was taken, meaning: He said to them, "You must make it clear." Parallel to this verse is His saying: ﴿And [recall] when We took the covenant of the Children of Israel: You shall not worship except God﴾ (al-Baqarah: 83), read with both the *ta'* and the *ya'*. Likewise His saying: ﴿And We decreed to the Children of Israel in the Book that you will surely cause corruption on the earth﴾ (al-Isra': 4).

**The second issue:** The discussion of the manner of taking the covenant has already been given under the preceding verse. This is because the prophets, peace be upon them, presented the proofs in all matters of obligations and obligated them to accept them. So God, glorified and exalted is He, took the covenant from them only through the tongues of the prophets, peace be upon them. That emphasis and obligation is what is meant by taking the covenant. It is related from Saʿid ibn Jubayr that he said to Ibn ʿAbbas: "The companions of ʿAbd Allah read: ﴿And [recall] when God took the covenant of the prophets﴾." He said: "God took the covenant of the prophets concerning their peoples." Know that the obligation of this making clear is undoubtedly specific to the scholars of the people who know what is in the Book. And God knows best.

**The third issue:** To what does the pronoun in His saying ﴿you must make it clear to the people and not conceal it﴾ refer? There are two views. Saʿid ibn Jubayr and al-Suddi said: it refers to Muhammad, peace be upon him. On this interpretation, the pronoun refers to something known but not mentioned. Al-Hasan and Qatadah said: it refers to "the Book" in His saying ﴿those who were given the Book﴾, meaning: We took their covenant that they would make clear to the people what is in the Torah and the Gospel of the indication of the truth of the prophethood of Muhammad, peace be upon him.

**The fourth issue:** The *lam* is the *lam* of emphasis that enters upon an oath. Its implied form is: He made them swear, "You will surely make it clear."

**The fifth issue:** He said *wa-la taktumunahu* and did not say *wa-la taktumnahu*, because the *waw* is the *waw al-hal* (the *waw* of circumstance, indicating a concurrent state) and not the *waw* of conjunction. The meaning is: "You must make it clear to the people while not concealing."

If it is said: Clarification (*al-bayan*) is the opposite of concealment (*al-kitman*). So when He commanded clarification, the command to it was a prohibition of concealment. What, then, is the benefit of mentioning the prohibition of concealment?

We say: What is meant by clarification is the mention of those verses from the Torah and the Gospel that indicate the prophethood of Muhammad, peace be upon him. What is meant by the prohibition of concealment is that they should not insert into them corrupt interpretations and obstructive doubts.

**The sixth issue:** Know that although the apparent meaning of this verse is specific to the Jews and Christians, it is not far-fetched that Muslims are also included in it, because they are the people of the Qur'an, and it is the most noble of books. It is related that al-Hajjaj sent for al-Hasan and said: "What is it that has reached me from you?" He said: "Not everything that has reached you from me did I say, nor did I say everything that I said reached you." He said: "Are you the one who said that hypocrisy had been suppressed, but it has now become so that [a man] wears a turban and carries a sword?" He said: "Yes." He said: "And what moved you to this, when we dislike it?" He said: "Because God took the covenant of those who were given the Book, that they would make it clear to the people and not conceal it." Qatadah said: "The likeness of knowledge that is not spoken of is like the likeness of a treasure from which nothing is spent. And the likeness of wisdom that does not come forth is like an upright idol that neither eats nor drinks." He used to say: "Blessed is the knowledgeable speaker, and the attentive listener. This one knew knowledge and gave it out, and that one heard good and retained it." The Prophet, peace be upon him (ﷺ), said: "Whoever conceals knowledge from its people will be bridled with a bridle of fire." And it is related from ʿAli, may God be pleased with him: "God did not take a covenant from the people of ignorance that they should learn, until He took a covenant from the people of knowledge that they should teach."

\* \* \*

**Then He said, exalted is He:** ﴿But they cast it behind their backs and exchanged it for a small price. How wretched is what they buy.﴾ The meaning is that they did not regard it or pay attention to it. Casting behind the back is like discarding and disregarding. Its opposite is placing it before one's eyes and setting it between one's eyes. His saying ﴿and exchanged it for a small price﴾ means that they concealed the truth so that they might use it to obtain some worldly thing. So whoever does not make the truth clear to the people, and conceals some of it for a corrupt purpose, whether to facilitate matters for the oppressors and to comfort their hearts, or to bring some benefit, or out of taqiyyah (dissimulation) and fear, or out of stinginess with knowledge, falls under this threat.

[Page 107]

**Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 3, verses 188–189:**

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Do not think that those who rejoice in what they have brought and love to be praised for what they did not do, do not think them safe from the punishment; and for them is a painful punishment﴾. ﴿And to Allah belongs the dominion of the heavens and the earth, and Allah is competent over all things﴾.

Know that this is among the things included in His saying: ﴿And from those who associated others with Allah [there will be] much harm﴾. So He, may He be exalted, clarified that among the kinds of this harm is that they rejoice in what they have done of deceit and deception toward the weak among the Muslims, and love to be praised for being people of righteousness, piety, truthfulness and religiosity. There is no doubt that a person is harmed by witnessing such conditions, so He commanded the Prophet (ﷺ) to be patient in the face of them, and clarified what they deserve of severe threat. In the verse there are several points (masa'il, sing. mas'alah, here meaning points of discussion):

**The first point:** Hamzah, 'Asim and al-Kisa'i read the verb with a ta' (ت) dotted from above, while Ibn Kathir, Nafi', Abu 'Amr and Ibn 'Amir read it with a ya' (ي) dotted from below, and likewise in His saying ﴿so do not think them [safe]﴾. As for the first reading, it has two possibilities:

The first: that both are read with a fatha on the ba' (ب).

The second: that both are read with a damma on the ba'. Whoever reads with the ta' and puts a fatha on the ba' in both places makes the implied meaning: "Do not think, O Muhammad, or O listener." Whoever puts a damma on the ba' in both places makes the address to the believers, and makes one of the two objects "those who rejoice," and the second "in safety (bi-mafazah)." His saying ﴿so do not think them in safety﴾ is an emphasis of the first, and its repetition is good because of the length of the speech, as when you say: "Do not consider Zayd, when he comes to you and speaks to you about such and such, to be truthful."

As for the second reading, which is with the ya' dotted from below in His saying "let them not think" (la yahsabanna), it also has two possibilities:

The first: with a fatha on the ba' and a damma on it in both places, making the verb refer to the Messenger (ﷺ), and the rest as you have known.

The second possibility: a fatha on the ba' in the first and a damma on it in the second, which is the reading of Abu 'Amr. Its basis is that he made the verb refer to "those who rejoice," and did not mention either of its two objects. Then he repeated the phrase "so let them not think" with a damma on the ba'. The word "them" (hum) is in the nominative by attaching the verb to it, and the first object is omitted, and the implied meaning is: "And let not those who rejoice think themselves, these people, to be in safety (bi-mafazah) from the punishment."

**The second point:** Know that He, may He be exalted, described these people as rejoicing in their action, and also loving to be praised for what they did not do. The exegetes mentioned several aspects of this:

The first: these Jews distort the texts of the Torah, interpret them with false interpretations, and promote them among the ignorant people. They rejoice in this act, and then love to be praised as people of religion, religiosity, chastity, truthfulness, and distance from lying. This is the statement of Ibn 'Abbas. If you are fair, you will realize that the condition of most people is like this: they employ every kind of trick to obtain worldly gain, and rejoice upon finding what they seek, and then love to be praised as people of chastity, truthfulness and religion.

The second: It is narrated that he (peace be upon him) asked the Jews about something in the Torah, and they concealed the truth and reported the opposite of it, and showed him that they had confirmed him, and they rejoiced in that deception, and they asked the Messenger (peace be upon him) that he praise them for it. So Allah informed His Messenger of this secret. The meaning is that these Jews rejoiced in the deception they had done, and expected from you that you would praise them for truthfulness and fidelity.

The third: they rejoice in what they did of concealing the texts that indicate the mission of Muhammad (ﷺ), and they love to be praised for what they did not do, namely following the religion of Abraham, since they claimed that Abraham (peace be upon him) was on Judaism and that they were upon his religion.

The fourth: It was revealed concerning the hypocrites, for they rejoice in what they did of showing faith to the Muslims in the manner of hypocrisy, since through that they were attaining their worldly interests. Then they expected from the Prophet (peace be upon him) that he would praise them for a faith that was not present in their hearts.

The fifth: Abu Sa'id al-Khudri said: It was revealed concerning men of the hypocrites who would stay behind from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) in the military expedition, and rejoice at their remaining behind from him. When he returned, they apologized to him, and he accepted their excuse. Then they hoped that he would praise them as he used to praise the Muslim fighters.

The sixth: What is meant by it is their concealment of what is in the Torah regarding the covenant taken from them to acknowledge Muhammad (ﷺ), and to affirm his prophethood and his religion. Then they rejoiced at their concealing of that and their turning away from the texts of Allah, the Exalted. Then they claimed that they were the sons of Allah and His beloved, and said: "The Fire will not touch us except for a few numbered days."

Know that the better view is to apply it to all of them, because all these matters share one common aspect, namely that a person performs an act that is not becoming and rejoices in it, and then expects from people that they describe him with uprightness of conduct, straightness of way, asceticism and devotion to obeying Allah.

**The third point:** In His saying ﴿what they have brought﴾ there are two investigations:

The first: al-Farra' said: His saying "what they have brought" (bima ataw) means "what they did," like His saying: ﴿And the two of you who commit it among you﴾ [an-Nisa': 16], and His saying: ﴿You have certainly come up with a monstrous thing﴾ [Maryam: 27], meaning "you did." The author of al-Kashshaf said: atā (to come) and jā'a (to come) are used in the sense of fa'ala (to do). He, may He be exalted, said: ﴿Indeed, His promise is ever fulfilled﴾ [Maryam: 61], and ﴿You have certainly come up with a monstrous thing﴾ [Maryam: 27]. And the reading of Ubayy, "who rejoice in what they did," indicates this.

The second investigation: It was read "ataw" (with the meaning) "they gave," and it is narrated from 'Ali, may Allah be pleased with him, "bima utu" (what they were given).

**The fourth point:** His saying ﴿in safety from the punishment﴾ means: in deliverance from it, from their saying: "So-and-so succeeded (faza)" when he was saved. al-Farra' said: that is, in distance from the punishment, because success (fawz) means distance from what is disliked. He mentioned this in His saying: ﴿then he has indeed succeeded﴾ [Al 'Imran: 185], then He confirmed it with His saying: ﴿and for them is a painful punishment﴾. There is no doubt that the verse was revealed concerning the disbelievers and the hypocrites, whom Allah commanded His Messenger (ﷺ) to be patient with regarding their harm.

* * *

Then He said: ﴿And to Allah belongs the dominion of the heavens and the earth, and Allah is competent over all things﴾. That is: for them is a painful punishment from the One to whom belongs the dominion of the heavens and the earth. So how could one who is punished by this All-Powerful, Dominant One hope for deliverance?

**Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 3, verses 188–189:**

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Do not think that those who rejoice in what they have brought and love to be praised for what they did not do, do not think them safe from the punishment; and for them is a painful punishment﴾. ﴿And to Allah belongs the dominion of the heavens and the earth, and Allah is competent over all things﴾.

Know that this is among the things included in His saying: ﴿And from those who associated others with Allah [there will be] much harm﴾. So He, may He be exalted, clarified that among the kinds of this harm is that they rejoice in what they have done of deceit and deception toward the weak among the Muslims, and love to be praised for being people of righteousness, piety, truthfulness and religiosity. There is no doubt that a person is harmed by witnessing such conditions, so He commanded the Prophet (ﷺ) to be patient in the face of them, and clarified what they deserve of severe threat. In the verse there are several points (masa'il, sing. mas'alah, here meaning points of discussion):

**The first point:** Hamzah, 'Asim and al-Kisa'i read the verb with a ta' (ت) dotted from above, while Ibn Kathir, Nafi', Abu 'Amr and Ibn 'Amir read it with a ya' (ي) dotted from below, and likewise in His saying ﴿so do not think them [safe]﴾. As for the first reading, it has two possibilities:

The first: that both are read with a fatha on the ba' (ب).

The second: that both are read with a damma on the ba'. Whoever reads with the ta' and puts a fatha on the ba' in both places makes the implied meaning: "Do not think, O Muhammad, or O listener." Whoever puts a damma on the ba' in both places makes the address to the believers, and makes one of the two objects "those who rejoice," and the second "in safety (bi-mafazah)." His saying ﴿so do not think them in safety﴾ is an emphasis of the first, and its repetition is good because of the length of the speech, as when you say: "Do not consider Zayd, when he comes to you and speaks to you about such and such, to be truthful."

As for the second reading, which is with the ya' dotted from below in His saying "let them not think" (la yahsabanna), it also has two possibilities:

The first: with a fatha on the ba' and a damma on it in both places, making the verb refer to the Messenger (ﷺ), and the rest as you have known.

The second possibility: a fatha on the ba' in the first and a damma on it in the second, which is the reading of Abu 'Amr. Its basis is that he made the verb refer to "those who rejoice," and did not mention either of its two objects. Then he repeated the phrase "so let them not think" with a damma on the ba'. The word "them" (hum) is in the nominative by attaching the verb to it, and the first object is omitted, and the implied meaning is: "And let not those who rejoice think themselves, these people, to be in safety (bi-mafazah) from the punishment."

**The second point:** Know that He, may He be exalted, described these people as rejoicing in their action, and also loving to be praised for what they did not do. The exegetes mentioned several aspects of this:

The first: these Jews distort the texts of the Torah, interpret them with false interpretations, and promote them among the ignorant people. They rejoice in this act, and then love to be praised as people of religion, religiosity, chastity, truthfulness, and distance from lying. This is the statement of Ibn 'Abbas. If you are fair, you will realize that the condition of most people is like this: they employ every kind of trick to obtain worldly gain, and rejoice upon finding what they seek, and then love to be praised as people of chastity, truthfulness and religion.

The second: It is narrated that he (peace be upon him) asked the Jews about something in the Torah, and they concealed the truth and reported the opposite of it, and showed him that they had confirmed him, and they rejoiced in that deception, and they asked the Messenger (peace be upon him) that he praise them for it. So Allah informed His Messenger of this secret. The meaning is that these Jews rejoiced in the deception they had done, and expected from you that you would praise them for truthfulness and fidelity.

The third: they rejoice in what they did of concealing the texts that indicate the mission of Muhammad (ﷺ), and they love to be praised for what they did not do, namely following the religion of Abraham, since they claimed that Abraham (peace be upon him) was on Judaism and that they were upon his religion.

The fourth: It was revealed concerning the hypocrites, for they rejoice in what they did of showing faith to the Muslims in the manner of hypocrisy, since through that they were attaining their worldly interests. Then they expected from the Prophet (peace be upon him) that he would praise them for a faith that was not present in their hearts.

The fifth: Abu Sa'id al-Khudri said: It was revealed concerning men of the hypocrites who would stay behind from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) in the military expedition, and rejoice at their remaining behind from him. When he returned, they apologized to him, and he accepted their excuse. Then they hoped that he would praise them as he used to praise the Muslim fighters.

The sixth: What is meant by it is their concealment of what is in the Torah regarding the covenant taken from them to acknowledge Muhammad (ﷺ), and to affirm his prophethood and his religion. Then they rejoiced at their concealing of that and their turning away from the texts of Allah, the Exalted. Then they claimed that they were the sons of Allah and His beloved, and said: "The Fire will not touch us except for a few numbered days."

Know that the better view is to apply it to all of them, because all these matters share one common aspect, namely that a person performs an act that is not becoming and rejoices in it, and then expects from people that they describe him with uprightness of conduct, straightness of way, asceticism and devotion to obeying Allah.

**The third point:** In His saying ﴿what they have brought﴾ there are two investigations:

The first: al-Farra' said: His saying "what they have brought" (bima ataw) means "what they did," like His saying: ﴿And the two of you who commit it among you﴾ [an-Nisa': 16], and His saying: ﴿You have certainly come up with a monstrous thing﴾ [Maryam: 27], meaning "you did." The author of al-Kashshaf said: atā (to come) and jā'a (to come) are used in the sense of fa'ala (to do). He, may He be exalted, said: ﴿Indeed, His promise is ever fulfilled﴾ [Maryam: 61], and ﴿You have certainly come up with a monstrous thing﴾ [Maryam: 27]. And the reading of Ubayy, "who rejoice in what they did," indicates this.

The second investigation: It was read "ataw" (with the meaning) "they gave," and it is narrated from 'Ali, may Allah be pleased with him, "bima utu" (what they were given).

**The fourth point:** His saying ﴿in safety from the punishment﴾ means: in deliverance from it, from their saying: "So-and-so succeeded (faza)" when he was saved. al-Farra' said: that is, in distance from the punishment, because success (fawz) means distance from what is disliked. He mentioned this in His saying: ﴿then he has indeed succeeded﴾ [Al 'Imran: 185], then He confirmed it with His saying: ﴿and for them is a painful punishment﴾. There is no doubt that the verse was revealed concerning the disbelievers and the hypocrites, whom Allah commanded His Messenger (ﷺ) to be patient with regarding their harm.

* * *

Then He said: ﴿And to Allah belongs the dominion of the heavens and the earth, and Allah is competent over all things﴾. That is: for them is a painful punishment from the One to whom belongs the dominion of the heavens and the earth. So how could one who is punished by this All-Powerful, Dominant One hope for deliverance?

Commentary of al-Razi (*Mafatih al-Ghayb*) on Surah 3 (Al 'Imran), verse 190:

His statement, exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, in the creation of the heavens and the earth, and the alternation of the night and the day, are signs for those of understanding.﴾

Know that the purpose of this Noble Book is to draw hearts and spirits away from occupation with creation toward complete immersion in the knowledge of the Truth. When the discourse had been long in establishing the rulings and answering the doubts of the falsifiers, it returned to illuminating the hearts by mentioning what indicates divine unity, divinity, majesty and greatness. Thus He mentioned this verse.

Ibn 'Umar said: I said to 'A'isha, "Tell me of the most wondrous thing you saw from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ)." She wept and prolonged her weeping, then said: "All of his affair was wondrous. He came to me on my night, entered under my covering until his skin touched my skin, then said to me: 'O 'A'isha, will you permit me tonight to worship my Lord?' I said: 'O Messenger of Allah, I truly love your nearness and I love what you desire. I have given you permission.' So he rose to a waterskin of water in the house, performed ablution, and did not pour much water. Then he stood to pray, recited from the Qur'an and began to weep. Then he raised his hands and continued weeping until I saw his tears had wet the ground. Bilal came to him to announce the dawn prayer and saw him weeping, and said to him: 'O Messenger of Allah, do you weep when Allah has forgiven you what came before of your sin and what came after?' He said: 'O Bilal, shall I not be a grateful servant?' Then he said: 'Why should I not weep, when Allah has revealed in this night: ﴿Indeed, in the creation of the heavens and the earth…﴾ Then he said: Woe to whoever recites it and does not reflect upon it.'"

It is also narrated: "Woe to whoever chews it between his jaws and does not contemplate it."

And from 'Ali, may Allah be pleased with him: "The Prophet (ﷺ) used to rise at night, brush his teeth with the siwak, then look at the sky and say: ﴿Indeed, in the creation of the heavens and the earth…﴾"

It is related that a man from the Children of Israel, whenever he worshipped Allah for thirty years, a cloud would shade him. One of their youths worshipped Allah, but the cloud did not shade him. His mother said to him: "Perhaps a lapse came from you during your period." He said: "I do not recall." She said: "Perhaps you looked once at the sky and did not take heed." He said: "Yes." She said: "Then you were only afflicted because of that."

Know that He, exalted is He, mentioned this verse in Surah al-Baqarah (chapter 2) and mentioned it here too. In Surah al-Baqarah He concluded this verse with His saying: ﴿Indeed, there are signs for a people who reason﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:164], and here He concluded it with His saying: ﴿Indeed, there are signs for those of understanding.﴾ In Surah al-Baqarah, alongside these three proofs, He mentioned five other kinds, so that the total became eight kinds of proofs. Here He was content with mentioning these three kinds: the heavens and the earth, and the night and the day. So there are three questions:

The first question: What is the benefit of repeating the same verse with the same wording in two surahs?

The second question: Why did He here suffice with repeating three kinds of proofs and omit the remaining five?

The third question: Why did He say there ﴿for a people who reason﴾ and say here ﴿for those of understanding﴾?

I say, and Allah knows best the secrets of His Book: The pupil of insight functions like the pupil of sight. Just as the pupil of the eye cannot thoroughly look at two things, but when the eye fixes its gaze on one thing, it becomes impossible in that state to fix the gaze on another, so too here: when a person fixes the pupil of his intellect upon contemplating one intelligible, it becomes impossible in that state for the pupil of the intellect to fix on another intelligible. Accordingly, whenever the intellect's occupation with turning toward diverse intelligibles is greater, its deprivation of thorough penetration into those conceptions and perceptions is greater. Based on this, the wayfarer to Allah must at the beginning increase the proofs. But when the heart is illuminated by the light of knowledge of Allah, his occupation with those proofs becomes like a veil preventing the heart from being absorbed in knowledge of Allah. So the wayfarer, who at the beginning sought to multiply proofs, when this light falls into his heart, becomes one who seeks to reduce proofs, until the darkness produced by the heart's occupation with other than Allah is removed, and the manifestation of the lights of knowledge of Allah is perfected in him. To this refers His saying: ﴿So take off your sandals; indeed, you are in the sacred valley, Tuwa﴾ [Taha 20:12]. The two sandals are the two premises by which the intellect reaches knowledge. When he reached knowledge, he was commanded to take them off, and it was said to him: You intend to set your feet in the valley of the holiness of Oneness, so abandon occupation with proofs.

Having understood this principle: He mentioned in Surah al-Baqarah eight kinds of proofs, then in this surah He repeated three kinds of them, as an alert that the one who knows, after becoming a knower, must reduce his turning toward proofs so that his absorption in knowledge of the object of knowledge may be complete. Therefore the purpose of repeating three kinds of proofs and omitting the rest was to alert to what we have mentioned. Then He, exalted is He, in this verse elaborated the heavenly proofs and omitted the five remaining proofs, which are the earthly proofs. This is because the heavenly proofs are more overpowering and more dazzling, their wonders are greater, and the heart's transition from them to the greatness and majesty of Allah is more intense. Then He concluded that verse with His saying: ﴿for a people who reason﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:164], and concluded this verse with His saying: ﴿for those of understanding﴾, because intellect has an outward aspect and it has a core (lubb). At the beginning of the matter it is 'aql (intellect), and in the perfection of the state it is lubb (core). This also strengthens what we have mentioned. This is what came to mind, and Allah knows best the secrets of His Great, Noble and Wise speech.

**Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 3, verses 191–192 (part 1 of 3)**

Allah, exalted is He, says: ﴿Those who remember Allah standing, sitting, and on their sides, and reflect upon the creation of the heavens and the earth, saying, "Our Lord, You did not create this in vain. Glory be to You; so protect us from the punishment of the Fire."﴾ ﴿"Our Lord, indeed whoever You admit to the Fire, You have certainly disgraced him, and for the wrongdoers there are no helpers."﴾

Know that when Allah mentioned the proofs of His divinity, power, and wisdom, which relate to establishing His lordship (rububiyya), He mentioned after them what relates to servanthood (ubudiyya). The categories of servanthood are three: affirmation by the heart, acknowledgment by the tongue, and action by the limbs. So His saying ﴿remember Allah﴾ refers to the servanthood of the tongue; His saying ﴿standing, sitting, and on their sides﴾ refers to the servanthood of the limbs and organs; and His saying ﴿and reflect upon the creation of the heavens and the earth﴾ refers to the servanthood of the heart, the thought, and the spirit. A human being is nothing but this whole. So when the tongue is absorbed in remembrance, the limbs in gratitude, and the heart in reflection, this servant is absorbed with all his parts in servanthood. The first verse indicates the perfection of lordship, and this verse indicates the perfection of servanthood. How excellent is this order in drawing souls from creation to the Truth, and in transporting secrets from the realm of delusion to the court of the Forgiving King.

We say: there are several issues in the verse.

**First issue:** The commentators have two opinions regarding this verse.

The first: the intended meaning is that the person is constantly mindful of his Lord, for the states are only these three. Then, when He described them as remembering Him in these states, this was evidence that they were persistent in remembrance and never slackened from it at all.

[p. 111]

The second opinion: the intended meaning of remembrance is prayer (salat). The meaning is that they pray while standing; if they are unable, then while sitting; if they are unable, then while lying down. The meaning is that they do not abandon prayer in any state. Interpreting it according to the first opinion is preferable, because many verses speak of the excellence of remembrance. The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Whoever wishes to graze in the gardens of Paradise, let him increase his remembrance of Allah."

**Second issue:** It is possible that the intended remembrance is remembrance by the tongue, and it is possible that it is remembrance by the heart. The most complete interpretation is that both are intended together.

**Third issue:** Al-Shafi'i, may Allah be pleased with him, said: if a sick person prays lying down, he must pray on his side. Abu Hanifa, may Allah be pleased with him, said: rather, he prays lying on his back, and once he finds some relief, he sits. The proof of al-Shafi'i, may Allah be pleased with him, is the apparent meaning of this verse, namely that Allah praised those who remember Him while lying on their sides, so this position is preferable.

Know that there is a subtle medical point in this: it has been established in medical studies that a person lying on his back prevents complete thinking and reflection, whereas lying on his side does not prevent it. This situation calls for reflection and contemplation. Moreover, lying on the side prevents deep sleep, so this position is preferable, because it is closer to wakefulness and to occupation with remembrance.

**Fourth issue:** The position of ﴿on their sides﴾ is accusative as a circumstantial clause (hal), coordinated with what precedes it, as if it had been said: standing, sitting, and lying down.

* * *

Know that when Allah described them with remembrance, and it is established that remembrance is not complete except together with reflection, He therefore said after it: ﴿and reflect upon the creation of the heavens and the earth﴾. On this there are issues:

**First issue:** Know that Allah encouraged the remembrance of Allah, but when the matter reached reflection, He did not encourage reflection upon Allah Himself; rather, He encouraged reflection upon the states of the heavens and the earth. In accordance with this verse, the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Reflect upon the creation, and do not reflect upon the Creator." The reason for this is that inference from the creation to the Creator cannot take place by way of similarity; it can only take place by way of dissimilarity. So we infer from the origination (huduth) of these perceptible things the eternity (qidam) of their Creator, and from their quantity, quality, and form, the freedom of their Creator from quantity, quality, and form. The saying of the Prophet (ﷺ): "Whoever knows himself knows his Lord" means: whoever knows himself through origination knows his Lord through eternity; whoever knows himself through contingency knows his Lord through necessity; whoever knows himself through need knows his Lord through self-sufficiency. Thus reflection upon creation is possible in this respect. As for reflection upon the Creator, it is absolutely not possible. Therefore, His reality cannot be conceived except through negations (the via negativa). So we say: He is neither a substance nor an accident, neither composite nor compound, and not in a direction. There is no doubt that His particular reality differs from these negations, and the intellect has no way to know that particular reality. So the intellect becomes like one bewildered, astonished, and perplexed in this position. For this reason the Prophet (ﷺ) forbade reflection upon Allah and commanded reflection upon the created beings. Because of this subtle point, Allah in these verses commanded remembrance of Him, and when He mentioned reflection, He did not command reflection upon Him, but commanded reflection upon His creatures.

[p. 112]

**Second issue:** Know that the thing whose particular reality cannot be known can only be known through its effects and actions. Whenever its actions are more noble and exalted, the intellect's grasp of the perfection of that agent is more complete. That is why the layperson greatly esteems the Qur'an, but his belief is imitative (taqlidi) and general. As for the scholarly commentator who continually discovers in every verse wondrous secrets and subtle fine points, his belief in the greatness of the Qur'an is more complete.

Having known this, we say: the proofs of monotheism (tawhid) are confined to two kinds: the proofs of the horizons (afaq) and the proofs of the souls (anfus). There is no doubt that the proofs of the horizons are more majestic and greater, as Allah said: ﴿Certainly, the creation of the heavens and the earth is greater than the creation of mankind﴾ [Ghafir: 57]. Since the matter is so, He therefore commanded in this verse reflection upon the creation of the heavens and the earth, because their indication is more wondrous and their evidences are greater. And how could we not say so? If a person looks at a small leaf from the leaves of a tree, he sees in that leaf one vein extending through its middle, and from that vein many veins branch out to both sides, and from them fine veins branch out, and from each vein other veins continue to branch until they become so fine that the eye cannot see them. At this point he knows that the Creator, in arranging that leaf in this form, has profound wisdoms and wondrous secrets, and that Allah placed in it powers that draw its nourishment from the depths of the earth; then that nourishment flows through those veins until a part of that nourishment is distributed to every part of that leaf, according to the decree of the Mighty, the All-Knowing. If a person wished to know the manner of the creation of that leaf and how the arrangement for its existence was made, and how the nourishing and growing powers were placed in it, he would be unable to do so. When he knows that his intellect is too limited to comprehend the manner of creation of that small leaf, then he compares that leaf with the heavens, together with what is in them of the sun, moon, and stars, and with the earth, together with what is in it of seas, mountains, minerals, plants, and animals. He realizes that that leaf, in relation to these things, is as nothing. When he knows the shortcoming of his intellect in knowing that trivial thing, he knows that there is absolutely no way for him to become aware of the wonders of Allah's wisdom in the creation of the heavens and the earth. And when, by this clear proof, he knows the shortcoming of his intellect and understanding in encompassing this station, nothing remains with him except acknowledging that the Creator is more majestic and greater than that the description of describers or the knowledge of knowers could encompass Him. Rather, he submits that everything He created contains profound wisdoms and great secrets, even though he has no way to know them. At this point he says: ﴿Glory be to You!﴾ What is meant by this is his occupation with glorification (tasbih), declaration of His oneness (tahlil), praise (tahmid), and exaltation (ta'zim). Then at that point he occupies himself with supplication, saying: ﴿so protect us from the punishment of the Fire﴾.

It is reported from the Prophet (ﷺ): "While a man was reclining on his bed, he raised his head and looked at the stars and the sky, and said: 'I bear witness that You have a Lord and a Creator. O Allah, forgive me!' So Allah looked at him and forgave him." The Prophet (ﷺ) also said: "There is no worship like reflection." It has been said: reflection removes heedlessness and draws fear (khashya) into the heart, just as water causes crops to grow. It is reported from the Prophet (ﷺ): "Do not prefer me over Yunus ibn Matta, for every day there was raised for him the equivalent of the deeds of the people of the earth." They said: that deed was reflection upon knowledge of Allah, because no one can perform with his limbs the equivalent of the deeds of the people of the earth.

* * *

**Third issue:** The verse indicates that the highest rank of the truthful (siddiqin) is reflection upon the evidences of the Essence and the Attributes, and that imitation (taqlid) is a false matter, of no value and deserving no regard.

Know that Allah related about these righteous servants, who persist in remembrance and reflection, that they uttered five kinds of supplication:

[p. 113]

**The first kind:** His saying: ﴿Our Lord, You did not create this in vain. Glory be to You; so protect us from the punishment of the Fire.﴾ On this there are issues:

**First issue:** There is an elision (idmar) in the verse, and on it there are two views. Al-Wahidi, may Allah have mercy on him, said: the implied meaning is: they say, "Our Lord, You did not create this in vain." The author of al-Kashshaf (al-Zamakhshari) said: it is in the position of a circumstantial clause, in the sense of "reflecting, saying."

**Second issue:** The word ﴿this﴾ in His saying ﴿You did not create this﴾ is a metonymy for the created thing; the meaning is: You did not create this wondrous creation in vain. The word "this" carries a kind of exaltation, as in His saying: ﴿Indeed, this Qur'an guides to that which is most upright﴾ [al-Isra: 9].

**Third issue:** Regarding the accusative case of His saying ﴿in vain﴾ (batilan), there are several possibilities:
The first: it is an adjective of an elided verbal noun (masdar), meaning: a vain creation.
The second: it is with the preposition removed, its implied form being: "with vanity" or "for vanity."
The third: the author of al-Kashshaf said: it is permissible for "in vain" to be a circumstantial clause from "this."

**Fourth issue:** The Mu'tazila (a rationalist theological school) said: everything Allah does, He does only for the purpose of benefiting His servants and for the sake of wisdom, and by this is meant the safeguarding of the servants' interests. They argued from this verse: if He had not created the heavens and the earth for a purpose, He would have created them in vain, and that is contrary to this verse. They said: this verse also shows that what the Mujbira (the determinists) say, namely that Allah intended by the creation of the heavens and the earth the occurrence of wrongdoing and falsehood from most of His servants, so that they would disbelieve in their Creator, is a rejection of this verse. They said: His saying ﴿Glory be to You﴾ is a declaration of His transcendence above creating them in vain, and above every ugliness. Al-Wahidi mentioned a statement that could serve as a response to this objection. He said: "vain" (batil) refers to what is transient, passing away, having no strength, firmness, or permanence. The creation of the heavens and the earth is a creation that is perfected and firm. Do you not see His saying: ﴿You do not see in the creation of the Most Merciful any imbalance. Return the gaze; do you see any rift?﴾ [al-Mulk: 3], and His saying: ﴿And We built above you seven strong ones﴾ [al-Naba': 12]? So the meaning of His saying ﴿Our Lord, You did not create this in vain﴾ is this meaning, not what the Mu'tazila mentioned.

If it is said: this interpretation is refuted in several ways:
The first: if "vain" meant the flimsy and dissipating, then His saying ﴿Glory be to You﴾ would be a declaration of His transcendence above creating such a creation, and it is known that this is false.

**Second:** The phrase ﴿فَقِنا عَذابَ النّارِ﴾ (*"so protect us from the punishment of the Fire"*) connects well with what precedes only if we read the verse in the sense we have mentioned. The implied meaning is: "You did not create this in vain, without wisdom; rather You created it with a great wisdom, which is that You make it a dwelling for the accountable (*mukallafin*) who occupied themselves with Your obedience and guarded themselves against Your disobedience. So protect us from the punishment of the Fire, for it is the recompense of one who disobeys and does not obey." Thus, when we explain His saying ﴿ما خَلَقْتَ هَذا باطِلًا﴾ (*"You did not create this in vain"*) in the way we have mentioned, the arrangement of the verse is good. But if we explain it as "You created it firm and tightly constructed," the arrangement would not be good.

**Third:** He, exalted is He, mentioned this in another verse, saying: ﴿وما خَلَقْنا السَّماءَ والأرْضَ وما بَيْنَهُما باطِلًا ذَلِكَ ظَنُّ الَّذِينَ كَفَرُوا﴾ (*"We did not create the heaven and the earth and what is between them in vain. That is the assumption of those who disbelieve"*) [Sad 38:27]. He said in another verse: ﴿وما خَلَقْنا السَّماواتِ والأرْضَ وما بَيْنَهُما لاعِبِينَ﴾ ﴿ما خَلَقْناهُما إلّا بِالحَقِّ﴾ (*"We did not create the heavens and the earth and what is between them in play. We did not create them except with truth"*) [al-Dukhan 44:38–39]. He said in another verse: ﴿أفَحَسِبْتُمْ أنَّما خَلَقْناكم عَبَثًا﴾ (*"Did you think that We created you without purpose?"*) [al-Mu'minun 23:115], up to His saying: ﴿فَتَعالى اللَّهُ المَلِكُ الحَقُّ﴾ (*"Exalted is Allah, the True King"*) [al-Mu'minun 23:116]. That is, "Exalted is the True King above His action being purposeless." And if it is impossible that His action be purposeless, then it is all the more impossible that it be vain.

**The answer:** Know that the immediate intuition of reason testifies that the existent is either necessary in its essence (*wajib li-dhatihi*) or possible in its essence (*mumkin li-dhatihi*). The evidence for this is that every possible-in-essence thing must, in its preponderance (*rujhan*), ultimately terminate in the necessary-in-essence. There is no specification in this proposition that the possible thing is distinct from the actions of servants. Rather, this proposition holds in its generality, and reason testifies to its soundness. Since this is so, it follows that good and evil are by the decree of Allah. Since this is so, it is impossible that the intended meaning of this verse be the explanation of Allah's actions by benefits (*masalih*). When you know this, we say: why is it not permissible that the interpretation of the verse be what we have related from al-Wahidi, his saying: "If it were so, then His saying ﴿سُبْحانَكَ﴾ (*"Glory be to You"*) would be a declaration of His transcendence above doing what has no firmness or solidity, and that is false"? We say: why is it not permissible that the intended meaning be: "Our Lord, You did not create this loose, corrupt in construction, but You created it solid and firm." And His saying ﴿سُبْحانَكَ﴾ means that You, although You created the heavens and the earth solid, strong and lasting, are transcendent above needing them and benefiting from them. So His saying ﴿سُبْحانَكَ﴾ means this.

**As for his second statement:** that the connection of ﴿فَقِنا عَذابَ النّارِ﴾ with it is good only if we explain it in our way, we say: we do not concede this. Rather, the manner of the arrangement is that when He said ﴿سُبْحانَكَ﴾, they acknowledged that He is free of need of everything other than Him. When they described Him with independence, they confessed for themselves their weakness and need for Him in this world and the Hereafter, and so they said: ﴿فَقِنا عَذابَ النّارِ﴾. This aspect of the goodness of the arrangement, if it is not better than what you have mentioned, is not less than it. As for the rest of the verses you have cited, they indicate that His actions are exalted above being described as purposeless, playful, or vain. We say in accordance with this: all of Allah's actions are wisdom and rightness, because He, exalted is He, does not dispose except in His own dominion, so His judgment is right absolutely. This is what is in this debate, and Allah knows best.

**The fifth issue:** The philosophers of Islam (*hukama' al-Islam*) argued with this verse that He, glorified is He, created these spheres (*aflak*) and stars, and deposited in each of them specific powers, and arranged that from their movements and the connection of some of them with others there result the benefits of this world and the advantages of the inhabitants of this earthly region. They said: for if they were not so, they would be vain, and that would contradict the verse. They said: no one may say that the benefit in them is to serve as evidence for the existence of the Creator who chooses, because each of the spheres of air and water shares the spheres and stars in this meaning. Then there would be no benefit left in the particular fact that it is a sphere, a sun, or a moon, and so it would be vain, and that is contrary to this text.

The theologians (*mutakallimun*) answered this, saying: why should it not suffice for this meaning that they are causes according to the customary course (*majra al-'adah*), not in the manner of true causality (*'ala sabil al-haqiqah*)?

As for His saying ﴿سُبْحانَكَ﴾ (*"Glory be to You"*), in it there are two issues.

**The first issue:** This is an acknowledgment of the incapacity of minds to comprehend the effects of Allah's wisdom in the creation of the heavens and the earth. That is: when people reflect on these great bodies, they know from them only this much, namely that their Creator did not create them in vain, but created them for marvelous wisdoms and great secrets, even though minds fall short of knowing them.

**The second issue:** The purpose of it is to teach servants by Allah the manner of supplication. Whoever wishes to supplicate must first present praise (*thana'*), and then mention the supplication after it, as in this verse.

* * *

As for His saying ﴿فَقِنا عَذابَ النّارِ﴾ (*"so protect us from the punishment of the Fire"*): know that when He, exalted is He, related about these sincere servants that their tongues are engrossed in the remembrance of Allah, their bodies in obedience to Allah, and their hearts in reflection on the signs of Allah's greatness, He mentioned that, along with these acts of obedience, they ask Allah to protect them from the punishment of the Fire. Had it not been that it is good (*hasan*) for Allah to punish them, this supplication would be purposeless. If the Mu'tazilah (*rationalist school*) thought that the beginning of the verse is a proof for them, let them know that the end of this verse is a proof for us [Page 115] that nothing at all is ugly from Allah. A similar humble entreaty is what Allah related from Abraham in His saying: ﴿والَّذِي أطْمَعُ أنْ يَغْفِرَ لِي خَطِيئَتِي يَوْمَ الدِّينِ﴾ (*"And the one from whom I hope that He will forgive my sin on the Day of Recompense"*) [al-Shu'ara' 26:82].

**The second category of their supplications:** His saying, exalted is He, relating about them: ﴿رَبَّنا إنَّكَ مَن تُدْخِلِ النّارَ فَقَدْ أخْزَيْتَهُ وما لِلظّالِمِينَ مِن أنْصارٍ﴾ (*"Our Lord, indeed, whoever You admit to the Fire, You have disgraced him, and for the wrongdoers there are no helpers"*) [Al 'Imran 3:192]. Concerning it there are several issues:

**The first issue:** Know that when they asked their Lord to protect them from the punishment of the Fire, they followed that with what indicates the greatness and severity of that punishment, namely disgrace (*khizy*), so that the request would have greater weight. For whoever asks his Lord to do something or not to do it, when he explains the greatness and power of that sought matter, his motivation in that supplication is more complete and his sincerity in seeking it is more intense.
