And supplication is not connected with being answered except when it is accompanied by what is most important. So this is a teaching from Allah to His servants about the manner of presenting supplication.

**The second issue:** Al-Wahidi said: the word *ikhza'* (disgracing) in the language occurs in meanings that are close to one another. Al-Zajjaj said: "Allah disgraced the enemy" means He removed him far away. Others said: "Allah disgraced him" means He humiliated him. Shamir ibn Hamdawayh said: "Allah disgraced him" means Allah exposed him. In the Qur'an: ﴿ولا تُخْزُونِي في ضَيْفِي﴾ (*"And do not disgrace me regarding my guests"*) [Hud 11:78]. Al-Mufaddal said: "Allah disgraced him" means He destroyed him. Ibn al-Anbari said: *khizy* in the language is destruction by loss, or by cutting off an argument, or by falling into a trial, and all these meanings are close to one another. Then the author of al-Kashshaf (*al-Zamakhshari*) said: "*faqad akhzaytahu*" means "you have indeed carried disgrace to its utmost," and it is like the saying: "Whoever precedes so-and-so has indeed preceded, and whoever learns from so-and-so has indeed learned."

**The third issue:** The Mu'tazilah said: this verse indicates that the one who commits a major sin (*kabirah*) among the people of prayer is not a believer. That is because the one who commits a major sin, if he enters the Fire, then Allah has disgraced him, by the indication of this verse, and the believer is not disgraced, by His saying: ﴿يَوْمَ لا يُخْزِي اللَّهُ النَّبِيَّ والَّذِينَ آمَنُوا مَعَهُ﴾ (*"On the day when Allah will not disgrace the Prophet and those who believed with him"*) [al-Tahrim 66:8]. So it is necessary from the combination of these two verses that the one who commits a major sin is not a believer.

The answer: His saying ﴿يَوْمَ لا يُخْزِي اللَّهُ النَّبِيَّ والَّذِينَ آمَنُوا مَعَهُ﴾ does not require the negation of disgrace absolutely. It only requires that disgrace not occur at the time when they are with the Prophet. This negation is not contradicted by affirming disgrace in general, since that affirmation may occur at another time. This is what is sound to me in the answer. Al-Wahidi mentioned in *al-Basit* three other answers besides what we have mentioned:

First: he related from Sa'id ibn al-Musayyab, al-Thawri and Qatadah that His saying ﴿إنَّكَ مَن تُدْخِلِ النّارَ فَقَدْ أخْزَيْتَهُ﴾ is specific to those who enter the Fire for eternal abode. This answer, in my view, is weak, because the Mu'tazilah's doctrine is that every wrongdoer who enters the Fire enters it for eternal abode, so this would not be a question about them.

Second: he said: the one admitted into the Fire is disgraced at the time of his entry, even if its outcome is that he comes out of it. This is also weak, because the point of the argument is that His saying ﴿يَوْمَ لا يُخْزِي اللَّهُ النَّبِيَّ والَّذِينَ آمَنُوا مَعَهُ﴾ [al-Tahrim 66:8] indicates the negation of disgrace from believers absolutely, while this verse indicates the occurrence of disgrace for everyone who enters the Fire. So by the ruling of these two verses there is an incompatibility between being a believer and being one of those who enter the Fire who is a disbeliever.

Third: he said: *al-ikhza'* admits two aspects:
One: humiliation and destruction.
The second: shame (*takhjil*). It is said: "He was disgraced (*khaziya khizayah*)" when he felt shame, and "another disgraced him" when he did an act to him that caused him embarrassment and shame.

Know that the upshot of this answer is that the word *ikhza'* is a shared (*mushtarak*) term between shame and destruction, and a shared term cannot be taken in both positive and negative clauses with both of its meanings together. Since this is so, it is possible that what is negated by His saying ﴿يَوْمَ لا يُخْزِي اللَّهُ النَّبِيَّ والَّذِينَ آمَنُوا مَعَهُ﴾ is other than what is affirmed in His saying ﴿إنَّكَ مَن تُدْخِلِ النّارَ فَقَدْ أخْزَيْتَهُ﴾, and by this the argument falls. However, this answer works only if the word *ikhza'* is shared between these two concepts. But if it is a univocal term (*mutawati'*) signifying one meaning, and the two meanings that al-Wahidi mentioned are two species under one genus, then this answer falls, because His saying ﴿يَوْمَ لا يُخْزِي اللَّهُ النَّبِيَّ والَّذِينَ آمَنُوا مَعَهُ﴾ [al-Tahrim 66:8] is for negating the genus, and His saying ﴿فَقَدْ أخْزَيْتَهُ﴾ is for affirming a species, and then there arises an incompatibility between them.

**The fourth issue:** The Murji'ah (*a sect holding that faith is not diminished by sin*) argued with this verse to assert with certainty that the one who commits a major sin is not disgraced, and everyone who enters the Fire is disgraced, so it necessarily follows with certainty that the one who commits a major sin does not enter the Fire. We say that the one who commits a major sin is not disgraced because the one who commits a major sin is a believer, and the believer is not disgraced. We say that he is a believer by His saying, exalted is He: ﴿وإنْ طائِفَتانِ مِنَ المُؤْمِنِينَ اقْتَتَلُوا فَأصْلِحُوا بَيْنَهُما فَإنْ بَغَتْ إحْداهُما عَلى الأُخْرى فَقاتِلُوا الَّتِي تَبْغِي حَتّى تَفِيءَ إلى أمْرِ اللَّهِ﴾ (*"And if two groups among the believers fight, then make peace between them. But if one of them oppresses the other, then fight the one that oppresses until it returns to the command of Allah"*) [al-Hujurat 49:9]. He called the rebel, while he is rebelling, a believer, and rebellion (*baghy*) is among the major sins by consensus (*ijma'*). Also, He, exalted is He, said: ﴿ياأيُّها الَّذِينَ آمَنُوا كُتِبَ عَلَيْكُمُ القِصاصُ في القَتْلى﴾ (*"O you who believe, retaliation is prescribed for you regarding the slain"*) [al-Baqarah 2:178]. He called the one who kills intentionally and unjustly a believer. So it is established that the one who commits a major sin is a believer. And we say that the believer is not disgraced by His saying: ﴿يَوْمَ لا يُخْزِي اللَّهُ النَّبِيَّ والَّذِينَ آمَنُوا مَعَهُ﴾ and by His saying: ﴿ولا تُخْزِنا يَوْمَ القِيامَةِ﴾ (*"And do not disgrace us on the Day of Resurrection"*) [Al 'Imran 3:194].

* * *

Then He, exalted is He, said: ﴿فاسْتَجابَ لَهم رَبُّهُمْ﴾ (*"So their Lord responded to them"*) [Al 'Imran 3:195]. This response indicates that He, exalted is He, does not disgrace the believers. Thus it is established by what we have mentioned that the one who commits a major sin is not disgraced by the Fire. And we say that everyone who enters the Fire is disgraced by His saying, exalted is He: ﴿إنَّكَ مَن تُدْخِلِ النّارَ فَقَدْ أخْزَيْتَهُ﴾. From these two premises there then follows, with certainty, that the one who commits a major sin does not enter the Fire.

The answer to this is what preceded: that His saying ﴿يَوْمَ لا يُخْزِي اللَّهُ النَّبِيَّ والَّذِينَ آمَنُوا مَعَهُ﴾ [al-Tahrim 66:8] does not indicate the negation of disgrace absolutely, but indicates the negation of disgrace at the time when they are with the Prophet, and that does not preclude the occurrence of disgrace at another time.

The Fifth Issue: His saying, ﴿Indeed, whoever You cause to enter the Fire, You have certainly disgraced him﴾, is general, and particularization (al-khusus) has entered it in several places. Among them: the saying of the Exalted, ﴿And there is none of you but will pass over it. That is upon your Lord an absolute decree. Then We will save those who feared Allah﴾ [Maryam: 71, 72], indicates that all the believers enter the Fire, while the people of reward are protected from disgrace.

The second: the angels who are the guardians of Hell (khazanat Jahannam) will be in the Fire, and they too are protected from disgrace. The Exalted said, ﴿Over it are angels, harsh and severe﴾ [al-Tahrim: 6].

The Sixth Issue: The philosophers of Islam (hukama' al-Islam) used this verse to argue that spiritual punishment is more severe and more powerful than physical punishment. They said: because the verse indicates a threat, after the punishment of the Fire, with disgrace (al-khizy), and disgrace is an expression for humiliation (al-takhjil), which is a spiritual punishment. So were it not that spiritual punishment is stronger than physical punishment, it would not be fitting to threaten one who is punished with the Fire with the punishment of disgrace and shame.

Page 117

The Seventh Issue: The Mu'tazilah used this verse to argue that the sinners (al-fussaq) who enter the Fire do not leave it, but remain there eternally. They said: disgrace (al-khizy) is destruction (al-halak), so His saying, ﴿Indeed, whoever You cause to enter the Fire, You have certainly disgraced him﴾ means "You have certainly destroyed him." And if they were to come out of the Fire into Paradise, it would not be correct that everyone who enters the Fire has been destroyed. The answer: we do not interpret disgrace as destruction, but rather interpret it as humiliation and shaming, and with this your argument falls away.

* * *

As for His saying, the Exalted, ﴿And for the wrongdoers there are no helpers﴾, there are two issues in it:

The First Issue: The Mu'tazilah held fast to it in negating intercession (shafa'ah) for the sinners, because intercession is a type of support (nusrah), and negating a genus (jins) necessitates negating its species (naw').

The answer has several aspects:

The first: the Qur'an indicates that the wrongdoer, in the absolute sense, is the disbeliever. The Exalted said, ﴿And the disbelievers, they are the wrongdoers﴾ [al-Baqarah: 254]. What confirms this is that He related of the disbelievers that they restricted themselves to the negation of intercessors and helpers, when they said, ﴿So we have no intercessors, nor any sincere friend﴾ [al-Shu'ara': 100].

The second: the intercessor cannot intercede except by the permission of Allah. The Exalted said, ﴿Who is it that can intercede with Him except by His permission?﴾ [al-Baqarah: 255]. If that is the case, the intercessor is not able to give support except after permission, and when permission is granted, there is in reality no benefit in his intercession. At that point it becomes clear that the pardon came only from Allah, the Exalted, and that intercession had no effect in reality, and judgment belongs only to Allah. So His saying, ﴿And for the wrongdoers there are no helpers﴾ indicates that there is no judgment except for Allah, as He said, ﴿Unquestionably, to Him belongs judgment﴾ [al-An'am: 62], and He said, ﴿And the command that Day belongs entirely to Allah﴾ [al-Infitar: 19]. It may be said: according to this interpretation, there remains no benefit in specifying the wrongdoers with this ruling. We say: rather, there is a benefit in it, because He promised the believers, the God-fearing, in this world, success with reward and deliverance from punishment, so for them on the Day of Resurrection there is this proof; as for the sinners, they do not have that. Thus it is correct to specify them with the negation of helpers in the absolute sense.

The third: this verse is general, while the establishment of intercession is specific, and the specific takes precedence over the general. And Allah knows best.

The Second Issue: The Mu'tazilah held fast to the claim that the sinner does not leave the Fire. They said: if he were to leave the Fire, then whoever brought him out would be a helper to him, and the verse indicates that he has no helper whatsoever.

The answer: it is countered by the verses that indicate pardon, as we mentioned in Surat al-Baqarah.

The Third Type of Their Supplications:

**Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 3, verses 191–192 (part 1 of 3)**

Allah, exalted is He, says: ﴿Those who remember Allah standing, sitting, and on their sides, and reflect upon the creation of the heavens and the earth, saying, "Our Lord, You did not create this in vain. Glory be to You; so protect us from the punishment of the Fire."﴾ ﴿"Our Lord, indeed whoever You admit to the Fire, You have certainly disgraced him, and for the wrongdoers there are no helpers."﴾

Know that when Allah mentioned the proofs of His divinity, power, and wisdom, which relate to establishing His lordship (rububiyya), He mentioned after them what relates to servanthood (ubudiyya). The categories of servanthood are three: affirmation by the heart, acknowledgment by the tongue, and action by the limbs. So His saying ﴿remember Allah﴾ refers to the servanthood of the tongue; His saying ﴿standing, sitting, and on their sides﴾ refers to the servanthood of the limbs and organs; and His saying ﴿and reflect upon the creation of the heavens and the earth﴾ refers to the servanthood of the heart, the thought, and the spirit. A human being is nothing but this whole. So when the tongue is absorbed in remembrance, the limbs in gratitude, and the heart in reflection, this servant is absorbed with all his parts in servanthood. The first verse indicates the perfection of lordship, and this verse indicates the perfection of servanthood. How excellent is this order in drawing souls from creation to the Truth, and in transporting secrets from the realm of delusion to the court of the Forgiving King.

We say: there are several issues in the verse.

**First issue:** The commentators have two opinions regarding this verse.

The first: the intended meaning is that the person is constantly mindful of his Lord, for the states are only these three. Then, when He described them as remembering Him in these states, this was evidence that they were persistent in remembrance and never slackened from it at all.

[p. 111]

The second opinion: the intended meaning of remembrance is prayer (salat). The meaning is that they pray while standing; if they are unable, then while sitting; if they are unable, then while lying down. The meaning is that they do not abandon prayer in any state. Interpreting it according to the first opinion is preferable, because many verses speak of the excellence of remembrance. The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Whoever wishes to graze in the gardens of Paradise, let him increase his remembrance of Allah."

**Second issue:** It is possible that the intended remembrance is remembrance by the tongue, and it is possible that it is remembrance by the heart. The most complete interpretation is that both are intended together.

**Third issue:** Al-Shafi'i, may Allah be pleased with him, said: if a sick person prays lying down, he must pray on his side. Abu Hanifa, may Allah be pleased with him, said: rather, he prays lying on his back, and once he finds some relief, he sits. The proof of al-Shafi'i, may Allah be pleased with him, is the apparent meaning of this verse, namely that Allah praised those who remember Him while lying on their sides, so this position is preferable.

Know that there is a subtle medical point in this: it has been established in medical studies that a person lying on his back prevents complete thinking and reflection, whereas lying on his side does not prevent it. This situation calls for reflection and contemplation. Moreover, lying on the side prevents deep sleep, so this position is preferable, because it is closer to wakefulness and to occupation with remembrance.

**Fourth issue:** The position of ﴿on their sides﴾ is accusative as a circumstantial clause (hal), coordinated with what precedes it, as if it had been said: standing, sitting, and lying down.

* * *

Know that when Allah described them with remembrance, and it is established that remembrance is not complete except together with reflection, He therefore said after it: ﴿and reflect upon the creation of the heavens and the earth﴾. On this there are issues:

**First issue:** Know that Allah encouraged the remembrance of Allah, but when the matter reached reflection, He did not encourage reflection upon Allah Himself; rather, He encouraged reflection upon the states of the heavens and the earth. In accordance with this verse, the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Reflect upon the creation, and do not reflect upon the Creator." The reason for this is that inference from the creation to the Creator cannot take place by way of similarity; it can only take place by way of dissimilarity. So we infer from the origination (huduth) of these perceptible things the eternity (qidam) of their Creator, and from their quantity, quality, and form, the freedom of their Creator from quantity, quality, and form. The saying of the Prophet (ﷺ): "Whoever knows himself knows his Lord" means: whoever knows himself through origination knows his Lord through eternity; whoever knows himself through contingency knows his Lord through necessity; whoever knows himself through need knows his Lord through self-sufficiency. Thus reflection upon creation is possible in this respect. As for reflection upon the Creator, it is absolutely not possible. Therefore, His reality cannot be conceived except through negations (the via negativa). So we say: He is neither a substance nor an accident, neither composite nor compound, and not in a direction. There is no doubt that His particular reality differs from these negations, and the intellect has no way to know that particular reality. So the intellect becomes like one bewildered, astonished, and perplexed in this position. For this reason the Prophet (ﷺ) forbade reflection upon Allah and commanded reflection upon the created beings. Because of this subtle point, Allah in these verses commanded remembrance of Him, and when He mentioned reflection, He did not command reflection upon Him, but commanded reflection upon His creatures.

[p. 112]

**Second issue:** Know that the thing whose particular reality cannot be known can only be known through its effects and actions. Whenever its actions are more noble and exalted, the intellect's grasp of the perfection of that agent is more complete. That is why the layperson greatly esteems the Qur'an, but his belief is imitative (taqlidi) and general. As for the scholarly commentator who continually discovers in every verse wondrous secrets and subtle fine points, his belief in the greatness of the Qur'an is more complete.

Having known this, we say: the proofs of monotheism (tawhid) are confined to two kinds: the proofs of the horizons (afaq) and the proofs of the souls (anfus). There is no doubt that the proofs of the horizons are more majestic and greater, as Allah said: ﴿Certainly, the creation of the heavens and the earth is greater than the creation of mankind﴾ [Ghafir: 57]. Since the matter is so, He therefore commanded in this verse reflection upon the creation of the heavens and the earth, because their indication is more wondrous and their evidences are greater. And how could we not say so? If a person looks at a small leaf from the leaves of a tree, he sees in that leaf one vein extending through its middle, and from that vein many veins branch out to both sides, and from them fine veins branch out, and from each vein other veins continue to branch until they become so fine that the eye cannot see them. At this point he knows that the Creator, in arranging that leaf in this form, has profound wisdoms and wondrous secrets, and that Allah placed in it powers that draw its nourishment from the depths of the earth; then that nourishment flows through those veins until a part of that nourishment is distributed to every part of that leaf, according to the decree of the Mighty, the All-Knowing. If a person wished to know the manner of the creation of that leaf and how the arrangement for its existence was made, and how the nourishing and growing powers were placed in it, he would be unable to do so. When he knows that his intellect is too limited to comprehend the manner of creation of that small leaf, then he compares that leaf with the heavens, together with what is in them of the sun, moon, and stars, and with the earth, together with what is in it of seas, mountains, minerals, plants, and animals. He realizes that that leaf, in relation to these things, is as nothing. When he knows the shortcoming of his intellect in knowing that trivial thing, he knows that there is absolutely no way for him to become aware of the wonders of Allah's wisdom in the creation of the heavens and the earth. And when, by this clear proof, he knows the shortcoming of his intellect and understanding in encompassing this station, nothing remains with him except acknowledging that the Creator is more majestic and greater than that the description of describers or the knowledge of knowers could encompass Him. Rather, he submits that everything He created contains profound wisdoms and great secrets, even though he has no way to know them. At this point he says: ﴿Glory be to You!﴾ What is meant by this is his occupation with glorification (tasbih), declaration of His oneness (tahlil), praise (tahmid), and exaltation (ta'zim). Then at that point he occupies himself with supplication, saying: ﴿so protect us from the punishment of the Fire﴾.

It is reported from the Prophet (ﷺ): "While a man was reclining on his bed, he raised his head and looked at the stars and the sky, and said: 'I bear witness that You have a Lord and a Creator. O Allah, forgive me!' So Allah looked at him and forgave him." The Prophet (ﷺ) also said: "There is no worship like reflection." It has been said: reflection removes heedlessness and draws fear (khashya) into the heart, just as water causes crops to grow. It is reported from the Prophet (ﷺ): "Do not prefer me over Yunus ibn Matta, for every day there was raised for him the equivalent of the deeds of the people of the earth." They said: that deed was reflection upon knowledge of Allah, because no one can perform with his limbs the equivalent of the deeds of the people of the earth.

* * *

**Third issue:** The verse indicates that the highest rank of the truthful (siddiqin) is reflection upon the evidences of the Essence and the Attributes, and that imitation (taqlid) is a false matter, of no value and deserving no regard.

Know that Allah related about these righteous servants, who persist in remembrance and reflection, that they uttered five kinds of supplication:

[p. 113]

**The first kind:** His saying: ﴿Our Lord, You did not create this in vain. Glory be to You; so protect us from the punishment of the Fire.﴾ On this there are issues:

**First issue:** There is an elision (idmar) in the verse, and on it there are two views. Al-Wahidi, may Allah have mercy on him, said: the implied meaning is: they say, "Our Lord, You did not create this in vain." The author of al-Kashshaf (al-Zamakhshari) said: it is in the position of a circumstantial clause, in the sense of "reflecting, saying."

**Second issue:** The word ﴿this﴾ in His saying ﴿You did not create this﴾ is a metonymy for the created thing; the meaning is: You did not create this wondrous creation in vain. The word "this" carries a kind of exaltation, as in His saying: ﴿Indeed, this Qur'an guides to that which is most upright﴾ [al-Isra: 9].

**Third issue:** Regarding the accusative case of His saying ﴿in vain﴾ (batilan), there are several possibilities:
The first: it is an adjective of an elided verbal noun (masdar), meaning: a vain creation.
The second: it is with the preposition removed, its implied form being: "with vanity" or "for vanity."
The third: the author of al-Kashshaf said: it is permissible for "in vain" to be a circumstantial clause from "this."

**Fourth issue:** The Mu'tazila (a rationalist theological school) said: everything Allah does, He does only for the purpose of benefiting His servants and for the sake of wisdom, and by this is meant the safeguarding of the servants' interests. They argued from this verse: if He had not created the heavens and the earth for a purpose, He would have created them in vain, and that is contrary to this verse. They said: this verse also shows that what the Mujbira (the determinists) say, namely that Allah intended by the creation of the heavens and the earth the occurrence of wrongdoing and falsehood from most of His servants, so that they would disbelieve in their Creator, is a rejection of this verse. They said: His saying ﴿Glory be to You﴾ is a declaration of His transcendence above creating them in vain, and above every ugliness. Al-Wahidi mentioned a statement that could serve as a response to this objection. He said: "vain" (batil) refers to what is transient, passing away, having no strength, firmness, or permanence. The creation of the heavens and the earth is a creation that is perfected and firm. Do you not see His saying: ﴿You do not see in the creation of the Most Merciful any imbalance. Return the gaze; do you see any rift?﴾ [al-Mulk: 3], and His saying: ﴿And We built above you seven strong ones﴾ [al-Naba': 12]? So the meaning of His saying ﴿Our Lord, You did not create this in vain﴾ is this meaning, not what the Mu'tazila mentioned.

If it is said: this interpretation is refuted in several ways:
The first: if "vain" meant the flimsy and dissipating, then His saying ﴿Glory be to You﴾ would be a declaration of His transcendence above creating such a creation, and it is known that this is false.

**Second:** The phrase ﴿فَقِنا عَذابَ النّارِ﴾ (*"so protect us from the punishment of the Fire"*) connects well with what precedes only if we read the verse in the sense we have mentioned. The implied meaning is: "You did not create this in vain, without wisdom; rather You created it with a great wisdom, which is that You make it a dwelling for the accountable (*mukallafin*) who occupied themselves with Your obedience and guarded themselves against Your disobedience. So protect us from the punishment of the Fire, for it is the recompense of one who disobeys and does not obey." Thus, when we explain His saying ﴿ما خَلَقْتَ هَذا باطِلًا﴾ (*"You did not create this in vain"*) in the way we have mentioned, the arrangement of the verse is good. But if we explain it as "You created it firm and tightly constructed," the arrangement would not be good.

**Third:** He, exalted is He, mentioned this in another verse, saying: ﴿وما خَلَقْنا السَّماءَ والأرْضَ وما بَيْنَهُما باطِلًا ذَلِكَ ظَنُّ الَّذِينَ كَفَرُوا﴾ (*"We did not create the heaven and the earth and what is between them in vain. That is the assumption of those who disbelieve"*) [Sad 38:27]. He said in another verse: ﴿وما خَلَقْنا السَّماواتِ والأرْضَ وما بَيْنَهُما لاعِبِينَ﴾ ﴿ما خَلَقْناهُما إلّا بِالحَقِّ﴾ (*"We did not create the heavens and the earth and what is between them in play. We did not create them except with truth"*) [al-Dukhan 44:38–39]. He said in another verse: ﴿أفَحَسِبْتُمْ أنَّما خَلَقْناكم عَبَثًا﴾ (*"Did you think that We created you without purpose?"*) [al-Mu'minun 23:115], up to His saying: ﴿فَتَعالى اللَّهُ المَلِكُ الحَقُّ﴾ (*"Exalted is Allah, the True King"*) [al-Mu'minun 23:116]. That is, "Exalted is the True King above His action being purposeless." And if it is impossible that His action be purposeless, then it is all the more impossible that it be vain.

**The answer:** Know that the immediate intuition of reason testifies that the existent is either necessary in its essence (*wajib li-dhatihi*) or possible in its essence (*mumkin li-dhatihi*). The evidence for this is that every possible-in-essence thing must, in its preponderance (*rujhan*), ultimately terminate in the necessary-in-essence. There is no specification in this proposition that the possible thing is distinct from the actions of servants. Rather, this proposition holds in its generality, and reason testifies to its soundness. Since this is so, it follows that good and evil are by the decree of Allah. Since this is so, it is impossible that the intended meaning of this verse be the explanation of Allah's actions by benefits (*masalih*). When you know this, we say: why is it not permissible that the interpretation of the verse be what we have related from al-Wahidi, his saying: "If it were so, then His saying ﴿سُبْحانَكَ﴾ (*"Glory be to You"*) would be a declaration of His transcendence above doing what has no firmness or solidity, and that is false"? We say: why is it not permissible that the intended meaning be: "Our Lord, You did not create this loose, corrupt in construction, but You created it solid and firm." And His saying ﴿سُبْحانَكَ﴾ means that You, although You created the heavens and the earth solid, strong and lasting, are transcendent above needing them and benefiting from them. So His saying ﴿سُبْحانَكَ﴾ means this.

**As for his second statement:** that the connection of ﴿فَقِنا عَذابَ النّارِ﴾ with it is good only if we explain it in our way, we say: we do not concede this. Rather, the manner of the arrangement is that when He said ﴿سُبْحانَكَ﴾, they acknowledged that He is free of need of everything other than Him. When they described Him with independence, they confessed for themselves their weakness and need for Him in this world and the Hereafter, and so they said: ﴿فَقِنا عَذابَ النّارِ﴾. This aspect of the goodness of the arrangement, if it is not better than what you have mentioned, is not less than it. As for the rest of the verses you have cited, they indicate that His actions are exalted above being described as purposeless, playful, or vain. We say in accordance with this: all of Allah's actions are wisdom and rightness, because He, exalted is He, does not dispose except in His own dominion, so His judgment is right absolutely. This is what is in this debate, and Allah knows best.

**The fifth issue:** The philosophers of Islam (*hukama' al-Islam*) argued with this verse that He, glorified is He, created these spheres (*aflak*) and stars, and deposited in each of them specific powers, and arranged that from their movements and the connection of some of them with others there result the benefits of this world and the advantages of the inhabitants of this earthly region. They said: for if they were not so, they would be vain, and that would contradict the verse. They said: no one may say that the benefit in them is to serve as evidence for the existence of the Creator who chooses, because each of the spheres of air and water shares the spheres and stars in this meaning. Then there would be no benefit left in the particular fact that it is a sphere, a sun, or a moon, and so it would be vain, and that is contrary to this text.

The theologians (*mutakallimun*) answered this, saying: why should it not suffice for this meaning that they are causes according to the customary course (*majra al-'adah*), not in the manner of true causality (*'ala sabil al-haqiqah*)?

As for His saying ﴿سُبْحانَكَ﴾ (*"Glory be to You"*), in it there are two issues.

**The first issue:** This is an acknowledgment of the incapacity of minds to comprehend the effects of Allah's wisdom in the creation of the heavens and the earth. That is: when people reflect on these great bodies, they know from them only this much, namely that their Creator did not create them in vain, but created them for marvelous wisdoms and great secrets, even though minds fall short of knowing them.

**The second issue:** The purpose of it is to teach servants by Allah the manner of supplication. Whoever wishes to supplicate must first present praise (*thana'*), and then mention the supplication after it, as in this verse.

* * *

As for His saying ﴿فَقِنا عَذابَ النّارِ﴾ (*"so protect us from the punishment of the Fire"*): know that when He, exalted is He, related about these sincere servants that their tongues are engrossed in the remembrance of Allah, their bodies in obedience to Allah, and their hearts in reflection on the signs of Allah's greatness, He mentioned that, along with these acts of obedience, they ask Allah to protect them from the punishment of the Fire. Had it not been that it is good (*hasan*) for Allah to punish them, this supplication would be purposeless. If the Mu'tazilah (*rationalist school*) thought that the beginning of the verse is a proof for them, let them know that the end of this verse is a proof for us [Page 115] that nothing at all is ugly from Allah. A similar humble entreaty is what Allah related from Abraham in His saying: ﴿والَّذِي أطْمَعُ أنْ يَغْفِرَ لِي خَطِيئَتِي يَوْمَ الدِّينِ﴾ (*"And the one from whom I hope that He will forgive my sin on the Day of Recompense"*) [al-Shu'ara' 26:82].

**The second category of their supplications:** His saying, exalted is He, relating about them: ﴿رَبَّنا إنَّكَ مَن تُدْخِلِ النّارَ فَقَدْ أخْزَيْتَهُ وما لِلظّالِمِينَ مِن أنْصارٍ﴾ (*"Our Lord, indeed, whoever You admit to the Fire, You have disgraced him, and for the wrongdoers there are no helpers"*) [Al 'Imran 3:192]. Concerning it there are several issues:

**The first issue:** Know that when they asked their Lord to protect them from the punishment of the Fire, they followed that with what indicates the greatness and severity of that punishment, namely disgrace (*khizy*), so that the request would have greater weight. For whoever asks his Lord to do something or not to do it, when he explains the greatness and power of that sought matter, his motivation in that supplication is more complete and his sincerity in seeking it is more intense. And supplication is not connected with being answered except when it is accompanied by what is most important. So this is a teaching from Allah to His servants about the manner of presenting supplication.

**The second issue:** Al-Wahidi said: the word *ikhza'* (disgracing) in the language occurs in meanings that are close to one another. Al-Zajjaj said: "Allah disgraced the enemy" means He removed him far away. Others said: "Allah disgraced him" means He humiliated him. Shamir ibn Hamdawayh said: "Allah disgraced him" means Allah exposed him. In the Qur'an: ﴿ولا تُخْزُونِي في ضَيْفِي﴾ (*"And do not disgrace me regarding my guests"*) [Hud 11:78]. Al-Mufaddal said: "Allah disgraced him" means He destroyed him. Ibn al-Anbari said: *khizy* in the language is destruction by loss, or by cutting off an argument, or by falling into a trial, and all these meanings are close to one another. Then the author of al-Kashshaf (*al-Zamakhshari*) said: "*faqad akhzaytahu*" means "you have indeed carried disgrace to its utmost," and it is like the saying: "Whoever precedes so-and-so has indeed preceded, and whoever learns from so-and-so has indeed learned."

**The third issue:** The Mu'tazilah said: this verse indicates that the one who commits a major sin (*kabirah*) among the people of prayer is not a believer. That is because the one who commits a major sin, if he enters the Fire, then Allah has disgraced him, by the indication of this verse, and the believer is not disgraced, by His saying: ﴿يَوْمَ لا يُخْزِي اللَّهُ النَّبِيَّ والَّذِينَ آمَنُوا مَعَهُ﴾ (*"On the day when Allah will not disgrace the Prophet and those who believed with him"*) [al-Tahrim 66:8]. So it is necessary from the combination of these two verses that the one who commits a major sin is not a believer.

The answer: His saying ﴿يَوْمَ لا يُخْزِي اللَّهُ النَّبِيَّ والَّذِينَ آمَنُوا مَعَهُ﴾ does not require the negation of disgrace absolutely. It only requires that disgrace not occur at the time when they are with the Prophet. This negation is not contradicted by affirming disgrace in general, since that affirmation may occur at another time. This is what is sound to me in the answer. Al-Wahidi mentioned in *al-Basit* three other answers besides what we have mentioned:

First: he related from Sa'id ibn al-Musayyab, al-Thawri and Qatadah that His saying ﴿إنَّكَ مَن تُدْخِلِ النّارَ فَقَدْ أخْزَيْتَهُ﴾ is specific to those who enter the Fire for eternal abode. This answer, in my view, is weak, because the Mu'tazilah's doctrine is that every wrongdoer who enters the Fire enters it for eternal abode, so this would not be a question about them.

Second: he said: the one admitted into the Fire is disgraced at the time of his entry, even if its outcome is that he comes out of it. This is also weak, because the point of the argument is that His saying ﴿يَوْمَ لا يُخْزِي اللَّهُ النَّبِيَّ والَّذِينَ آمَنُوا مَعَهُ﴾ [al-Tahrim 66:8] indicates the negation of disgrace from believers absolutely, while this verse indicates the occurrence of disgrace for everyone who enters the Fire. So by the ruling of these two verses there is an incompatibility between being a believer and being one of those who enter the Fire who is a disbeliever.

Third: he said: *al-ikhza'* admits two aspects:
One: humiliation and destruction.
The second: shame (*takhjil*). It is said: "He was disgraced (*khaziya khizayah*)" when he felt shame, and "another disgraced him" when he did an act to him that caused him embarrassment and shame.

Know that the upshot of this answer is that the word *ikhza'* is a shared (*mushtarak*) term between shame and destruction, and a shared term cannot be taken in both positive and negative clauses with both of its meanings together. Since this is so, it is possible that what is negated by His saying ﴿يَوْمَ لا يُخْزِي اللَّهُ النَّبِيَّ والَّذِينَ آمَنُوا مَعَهُ﴾ is other than what is affirmed in His saying ﴿إنَّكَ مَن تُدْخِلِ النّارَ فَقَدْ أخْزَيْتَهُ﴾, and by this the argument falls. However, this answer works only if the word *ikhza'* is shared between these two concepts. But if it is a univocal term (*mutawati'*) signifying one meaning, and the two meanings that al-Wahidi mentioned are two species under one genus, then this answer falls, because His saying ﴿يَوْمَ لا يُخْزِي اللَّهُ النَّبِيَّ والَّذِينَ آمَنُوا مَعَهُ﴾ [al-Tahrim 66:8] is for negating the genus, and His saying ﴿فَقَدْ أخْزَيْتَهُ﴾ is for affirming a species, and then there arises an incompatibility between them.

**The fourth issue:** The Murji'ah (*a sect holding that faith is not diminished by sin*) argued with this verse to assert with certainty that the one who commits a major sin is not disgraced, and everyone who enters the Fire is disgraced, so it necessarily follows with certainty that the one who commits a major sin does not enter the Fire. We say that the one who commits a major sin is not disgraced because the one who commits a major sin is a believer, and the believer is not disgraced. We say that he is a believer by His saying, exalted is He: ﴿وإنْ طائِفَتانِ مِنَ المُؤْمِنِينَ اقْتَتَلُوا فَأصْلِحُوا بَيْنَهُما فَإنْ بَغَتْ إحْداهُما عَلى الأُخْرى فَقاتِلُوا الَّتِي تَبْغِي حَتّى تَفِيءَ إلى أمْرِ اللَّهِ﴾ (*"And if two groups among the believers fight, then make peace between them. But if one of them oppresses the other, then fight the one that oppresses until it returns to the command of Allah"*) [al-Hujurat 49:9]. He called the rebel, while he is rebelling, a believer, and rebellion (*baghy*) is among the major sins by consensus (*ijma'*). Also, He, exalted is He, said: ﴿ياأيُّها الَّذِينَ آمَنُوا كُتِبَ عَلَيْكُمُ القِصاصُ في القَتْلى﴾ (*"O you who believe, retaliation is prescribed for you regarding the slain"*) [al-Baqarah 2:178]. He called the one who kills intentionally and unjustly a believer. So it is established that the one who commits a major sin is a believer. And we say that the believer is not disgraced by His saying: ﴿يَوْمَ لا يُخْزِي اللَّهُ النَّبِيَّ والَّذِينَ آمَنُوا مَعَهُ﴾ and by His saying: ﴿ولا تُخْزِنا يَوْمَ القِيامَةِ﴾ (*"And do not disgrace us on the Day of Resurrection"*) [Al 'Imran 3:194].

* * *

Then He, exalted is He, said: ﴿فاسْتَجابَ لَهم رَبُّهُمْ﴾ (*"So their Lord responded to them"*) [Al 'Imran 3:195]. This response indicates that He, exalted is He, does not disgrace the believers. Thus it is established by what we have mentioned that the one who commits a major sin is not disgraced by the Fire. And we say that everyone who enters the Fire is disgraced by His saying, exalted is He: ﴿إنَّكَ مَن تُدْخِلِ النّارَ فَقَدْ أخْزَيْتَهُ﴾. From these two premises there then follows, with certainty, that the one who commits a major sin does not enter the Fire.

The answer to this is what preceded: that His saying ﴿يَوْمَ لا يُخْزِي اللَّهُ النَّبِيَّ والَّذِينَ آمَنُوا مَعَهُ﴾ [al-Tahrim 66:8] does not indicate the negation of disgrace absolutely, but indicates the negation of disgrace at the time when they are with the Prophet, and that does not preclude the occurrence of disgrace at another time.

The Fifth Issue: His saying, ﴿Indeed, whoever You cause to enter the Fire, You have certainly disgraced him﴾, is general, and particularization (al-khusus) has entered it in several places. Among them: the saying of the Exalted, ﴿And there is none of you but will pass over it. That is upon your Lord an absolute decree. Then We will save those who feared Allah﴾ [Maryam: 71, 72], indicates that all the believers enter the Fire, while the people of reward are protected from disgrace.

The second: the angels who are the guardians of Hell (khazanat Jahannam) will be in the Fire, and they too are protected from disgrace. The Exalted said, ﴿Over it are angels, harsh and severe﴾ [al-Tahrim: 6].

The Sixth Issue: The philosophers of Islam (hukama' al-Islam) used this verse to argue that spiritual punishment is more severe and more powerful than physical punishment. They said: because the verse indicates a threat, after the punishment of the Fire, with disgrace (al-khizy), and disgrace is an expression for humiliation (al-takhjil), which is a spiritual punishment. So were it not that spiritual punishment is stronger than physical punishment, it would not be fitting to threaten one who is punished with the Fire with the punishment of disgrace and shame.

Page 117

The Seventh Issue: The Mu'tazilah used this verse to argue that the sinners (al-fussaq) who enter the Fire do not leave it, but remain there eternally. They said: disgrace (al-khizy) is destruction (al-halak), so His saying, ﴿Indeed, whoever You cause to enter the Fire, You have certainly disgraced him﴾ means "You have certainly destroyed him." And if they were to come out of the Fire into Paradise, it would not be correct that everyone who enters the Fire has been destroyed. The answer: we do not interpret disgrace as destruction, but rather interpret it as humiliation and shaming, and with this your argument falls away.

* * *

As for His saying, the Exalted, ﴿And for the wrongdoers there are no helpers﴾, there are two issues in it:

The First Issue: The Mu'tazilah held fast to it in negating intercession (shafa'ah) for the sinners, because intercession is a type of support (nusrah), and negating a genus (jins) necessitates negating its species (naw').

The answer has several aspects:

The first: the Qur'an indicates that the wrongdoer, in the absolute sense, is the disbeliever. The Exalted said, ﴿And the disbelievers, they are the wrongdoers﴾ [al-Baqarah: 254]. What confirms this is that He related of the disbelievers that they restricted themselves to the negation of intercessors and helpers, when they said, ﴿So we have no intercessors, nor any sincere friend﴾ [al-Shu'ara': 100].

The second: the intercessor cannot intercede except by the permission of Allah. The Exalted said, ﴿Who is it that can intercede with Him except by His permission?﴾ [al-Baqarah: 255]. If that is the case, the intercessor is not able to give support except after permission, and when permission is granted, there is in reality no benefit in his intercession. At that point it becomes clear that the pardon came only from Allah, the Exalted, and that intercession had no effect in reality, and judgment belongs only to Allah. So His saying, ﴿And for the wrongdoers there are no helpers﴾ indicates that there is no judgment except for Allah, as He said, ﴿Unquestionably, to Him belongs judgment﴾ [al-An'am: 62], and He said, ﴿And the command that Day belongs entirely to Allah﴾ [al-Infitar: 19]. It may be said: according to this interpretation, there remains no benefit in specifying the wrongdoers with this ruling. We say: rather, there is a benefit in it, because He promised the believers, the God-fearing, in this world, success with reward and deliverance from punishment, so for them on the Day of Resurrection there is this proof; as for the sinners, they do not have that. Thus it is correct to specify them with the negation of helpers in the absolute sense.

The third: this verse is general, while the establishment of intercession is specific, and the specific takes precedence over the general. And Allah knows best.

The Second Issue: The Mu'tazilah held fast to the claim that the sinner does not leave the Fire. They said: if he were to leave the Fire, then whoever brought him out would be a helper to him, and the verse indicates that he has no helper whatsoever.

The answer: it is countered by the verses that indicate pardon, as we mentioned in Surat al-Baqarah.

The Third Type of Their Supplications:

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 3, verse 193:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Our Lord, indeed we heard a caller calling to faith, "Believe in your Lord," so we believed. Our Lord, forgive us our sins, remove from us our misdeeds, and cause us to die with the righteous.﴾ In the verse there are issues:

The first issue: Concerning the caller (munadi), there are two opinions:

One of them: that he is Muhammad, peace and blessings be upon him, and this is the view of most (scholars),

Page 118

and the evidence for it is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Invite to the way of your Lord﴾ [al-Nahl: 125]. ﴿And as one who invites to Allah by His permission﴾ [al-Ahzab: 46]. ﴿I invite to Allah﴾ [Yusuf: 108].

The second: that he is the Qur'an. They said: Allah, exalted is He, related of the believers among mankind that statement just as He related of the believers among the jinn His saying: ﴿Indeed we have heard a wondrous Qur'an, which guides to righteousness, so we believed in it﴾ [al-Jinn: 1, 2]. They said: The evidence that interpreting the verse in this way is preferable is that not everyone met the Prophet ﷺ, whereas the Qur'an was heard and understood by everyone. They said: This, although it is a metaphor, is a common (conventional) metaphor, because the Qur'an, since it contains guidance, and whoever reflects upon it reaches guidance through it if Allah, exalted is He, grants him success in that, it becomes as though it calls to itself and proclaims through the various kinds of proofs it contains, just as it was said regarding Hell: ﴿It calls one who turns away and withdraws﴾ [al-Ma'arij: 17], since their destiny is toward it. Eloquent speakers and poets describe time as calling and admonishing, and by this they mean the indication of the changing circumstances of time. The poet said:

O you who place the dead in his grave, time has addressed you, yet you did not listen.

The second issue: Concerning His saying ﴿calling to faith (li'l-iman)﴾, there are several aspects:
The first: the lam is in the sense of "ila" (to), like His saying: ﴿Then they return to what they were forbidden﴾ [al-Mujadilah: 8]. ﴿Then they return to what they said﴾ [al-Mujadilah: 3]. ﴿Because your Lord has inspired it﴾ [al-Zalzalah: 5]. ﴿All praise is due to Allah who guided us to this﴾ [al-A'raf: 43]. It is said: "he invited him to such-and-such and to such-and-such," "he urged him for it and to it," "he called him for it and to it," and "he guided him to the path and to it." The reason each of these two words stands in place of the other is that the meaning of the end point (intihaʾ al-ghayah) and the meaning of specification (al-ikhtisas) are both present.

The second: Abu 'Ubaydah said: this is by inversion (al-taqdim wa'l-ta'khir), meaning: "we heard a caller to faith calling that 'believe'," just as one says: "the messenger of the amir came to us calling with such-and-such."

The third: that this lam is the lam of purpose (lam al-ajal), and the meaning is: "we heard a caller whose calling was so that people would believe," i.e., the caller was calling for this purpose. Do you not see that He said: ﴿that believe in your Lord﴾, i.e., so that people would believe? It is like His saying: ﴿And We did not send any messenger except to be obeyed by Allah's permission﴾ [al-Nisa': 64].

The third issue: His saying ﴿we heard a caller calling﴾ is like your saying: "I heard a man saying such-and-such," and "I heard Zayd speaking." The verb is attached to the man and the thing heard is omitted, because you have described him by what he hears and made it a circumstance concerning him, which makes mention of it unnecessary; and because the description or circumstance could not be dispensed with. It is also said: "I heard the speech of so-and-so, or his saying."

The fourth issue: Here there is a question: what is the benefit in combining "caller" (munadi) and "calling" (yunadi)?

Its answer: the calling is mentioned absolutely in one place and then restricted to faith, to magnify the status of the caller, for there is no caller greater than one who calls to faith. Its parallel is your saying: "I passed by a guide who guides to Islam." This is because when "caller" is used absolutely, the mind goes to a caller to war, or to quench a strife, or to relieve one in distress, or for sufficiency in some calamity. Likewise "guide" may be applied to one who guides to the road and who guides to sound judgment. So when you say "one who calls to faith" and "one who guides to Islam," you have elevated and magnified the status of the caller and the guide.

The fifth issue: His saying ﴿that believe﴾ contains an omission or an implied element, and the implied phrase is: "believe," or "by (an) that believe." Then Allah related of them that after that they said: ﴿So forgive us our sins, remove from us our misdeeds, and cause us to die with the righteous﴾. In the verse there are issues:

The first issue: Know that in this supplication they asked Allah, exalted is He, for three things: the first of them: forgiveness of

Page 119

sins.
The second: the removal of misdeeds.

The third: that their death be with the righteous. As for forgiveness (ghufran), it is concealment and covering; and removal (takfir) also is covering. It is said: "a man is muktaffar with weapons," meaning covered with them; and kufr (disbelief) is also from this (root). Labid said:

In a night whose darkness concealed the stars.

Having known this, forgiveness (maghfirah) and removal (takfir) in linguistic terms have one meaning.
As for the exegetes, they mentioned several views on it:

One of them: that by both is meant one thing, and it was only repeated for emphasis, because insistence in supplication and exaggeration in it is recommended.

The second: that by the first is meant the sins already committed, and by the second is meant those yet to come.

The third: that by forgiveness is meant what is removed by repentance, and by removal is meant what is expiated by a great act of obedience.

The fourth: that by the first is meant what a person commits knowing it to be disobedience and sin, and by the second what a person commits while ignorant that it is disobedience and sin.

* * *
As for His saying ﴿and cause us to die with the righteous﴾, there are two discussions:
The first: that al-abrar is the plural of barr or barr, like rabb and arbab, and sahib and ashab.

The second: al-Qaffal mentioned two aspects regarding the interpretation of this "with" (ma'iyyah):

The first: that their death with them is that they die upon the like of their deeds, so that they would be in their ranks on the Day of Resurrection. A man may say, "I am with al-Shafi'i in this issue," meaning that he is equal to him in that belief.

The second: it is said, "so-and-so is with the people of thousands in the giving," meaning he shares with them in giving a thousand.

The third: that what is meant is their being among the followers and partisans of the righteous, and from it is His saying: ﴿Those are with those whom Allah has blessed among the prophets, the truthful, the martyrs, and the righteous﴾ [al-Nisa': 69].

The second issue: Our companions (the Ash'aris) argued for the occurrence of pardon without repentance by this verse, namely His saying, related of them: ﴿So forgive us our sins﴾, and the argument from it is in two ways:

The first: they asked for forgiveness of sins and no mention of repentance was made in it, which indicates that they asked for forgiveness absolutely. Then Allah answered them, for He said at the end of the verse: ﴿So their Lord responded to them﴾ [Al 'Imran: 195], and this is explicit that He, exalted is He, may pardon a sin even if repentance is not present.

The second: He, exalted is He, related of them that when they informed about themselves that they had believed, at this point they said: ﴿So forgive us our sins﴾, and the fa' in His saying ﴿so forgive﴾ is the fa' of consequence, and this indicates that mere faith is a cause for the goodness of asking forgiveness from Allah. Then Allah answered them with His saying: ﴿So their Lord responded to them﴾, and so this verse indicates that mere faith is a cause for obtaining forgiveness, either from the outset, namely that He pardons them and does not admit them to the Fire, or that He admits them to the Fire and punishes them for a period, then pardons them and brings them out of the Fire. Thus the indication of this verse from these two aspects for the occurrence of pardon is established.

The third issue: Our companions argued by this verse that the intercession of Muhammad ﷺ on behalf of the people of major sins is accepted on the Day of Resurrection, because this verse indicates that these believers asked Allah for forgiveness of sins absolutely, without restricting that to repentance, and Allah answered their request and granted them what they sought. So if He accepts the intercession of the believers for pardon of a sin, then it is more fitting that He accept the intercession of Muhammad ﷺ in it.

The fourth type of their supplication:

[Page 121 begins partway through this passage.]

Concerning His saying, relating what they said: ﴿Our Lord, grant us what You promised us through Your messengers, and do not disgrace us on the Day of Resurrection. Indeed, You do not fail in the promise.﴾

There are several issues here.

**The first issue:** His saying ﴿and grant us what You promised us through Your messengers﴾ contains an elision of a noun (ḥadhf al-muḍāf, "the omission of the governed noun"). There are several interpretations of it:

First: "grant us what You promised us through the tongues of Your messengers."

Second: "grant us what You promised us by the confirmation (taṣdīq) of Your messengers." The evidence for this is that the verse is mentioned right after the mention of the one who calls to faith, who is the Messenger, and right after His saying ﴿so we believed﴾, which is confirmation (taṣdīq).

**The second issue:** Here there is a question. Failing to fulfil a promise is impossible for God. So how could they ask in supplication for what they knew would certainly occur?

The answer to this has several aspects.

The first: the purpose of supplication is not merely to request the act. Its purpose is to manifest humility, lowliness and servitude. God has commanded us to supplicate for things that we know with certainty will occur without doubt, as in His saying: ﴿He said: "My Lord, judge with truth."﴾ [al-Anbiyā’: 112] and His saying: ﴿So forgive those who repent and follow Your way.﴾ [Ghāfir: 7].

The second aspect of the answer: God's promise does not extend to each individual member of the community by name, but only to them according to their attributes. God promised the God-fearing (al-muttaqīn) reward and promised the wrongdoers (al-fussāq) punishment. So His saying ﴿and grant us what You promised us﴾ means: "Enable us to do the deeds by which we become worthy of Your promise, and protect us from the deeds by which we become worthy of punishment and disgrace." On this interpretation, the purpose of this verse is to ask for success in obedience and protection from disobedience.

The third aspect: God promised the believers that He would give them victory in this world and subdue their enemy, so they asked for this to be hastened. On this interpretation, the problem disappears.

**The third issue:** The verse indicates that they asked for the benefits of the Hereafter by virtue of the promise, not by virtue of entitlement (istiḥqāq), because they said: ﴿Our Lord, grant us what You promised us through Your messengers﴾, and at the end of the speech they said: ﴿Indeed, You do not fail in the promise.﴾ This shows that what brings about the benefits of the Hereafter is the promise, not entitlement.

**The fourth issue:** Here is another question. Once reward is obtained, the averting of punishment necessarily follows. So His saying ﴿and grant us what You promised us through Your messengers﴾ is a request for reward. After requesting reward, how can the averting of punishment be requested, which is His saying ﴿and do not disgrace us on the Day of Resurrection﴾? Rather, if the averting of punishment had been requested first and then the granting of reward, would the speech not be coherent?

The answer has two aspects.

The first: reward has the condition that it be a benefit accompanied by honour and joy. So His saying ﴿and grant us what You promised us through Your messengers﴾ refers to benefits, and His saying ﴿and do not disgrace us﴾ refers to honour.

The second: we have already explained that the purpose of this verse is to request success in obedience and protection from disobedience. On this interpretation the arrangement is good, as if it were said: "Enable us to perform acts of obedience. And once You have enabled us to perform them, protect us from what would nullify and remove them and bring us into disgrace and destruction." The sum of it is as if it were said: "Enable us to obey You, for we cannot do any act of obedience except by Your enabling. And once You have enabled us to perform it, enable us to maintain it, for we cannot maintain it or continue it except by Your enabling." This is an indication that the servant cannot perform any act, any deed, nor even a glance or a movement, except by God's help and enabling.

**The fifth issue:** His saying ﴿and do not disgrace us on the Day of Resurrection﴾ resembles His saying: ﴿And there will appear to them from Allah what they had not reckoned.﴾ [al-Zumar: 47]. A person may think that he is upon correct belief and righteous action, but on the Day of Resurrection it will become clear to him that his belief was misguidance and his deed was sin. There, great shame, complete regret and intense sorrow will occur. The philosophers of Islam (ḥukamā’ al-Islām) said: "That is the spiritual punishment (al-ʿadhāb al-rūḥānī)." They said: "This punishment is more severe than the physical punishment (al-ʿadhāb al-jismānī)." And among what indicates that God related of these believing servants that in this supplication they asked for several things is that the first of their requests is protection from physical punishment, which is His saying ﴿so protect us from the punishment of the Fire﴾, and the last is protection from spiritual punishment, which is His saying ﴿and do not disgrace us on the Day of Resurrection﴾. This indicates that spiritual punishment is more severe than physical punishment.

[Page 122 of the commentary follows]

God's words: ﴿So their Lord answered them: "I will not waste the work of any worker among you, whether male or female; you are of one another. Those who emigrated, were expelled from their homes, were harmed in My cause, fought, and were killed, I will surely remove their misdeeds from them and admit them into gardens beneath which rivers flow, as a reward from God. And with God is the best of rewards."﴾

Know that when God, may He be exalted, related what they (the people of understanding) had said, that they recognised God through evidence, which is His words: ﴿Indeed, in the creation of the heavens and the earth…﴾ up to His words: ﴿…are signs for people of understanding﴾; then He related their constancy in remembrance, which is His words: ﴿who remember God standing and sitting﴾; and in reflection, which is His words: ﴿and reflect on the creation of the heavens and the earth﴾; then He related that they praised God, may He be exalted, which is their words: ﴿Our Lord, You did not create this in vain; glory be to You﴾; then He related that after praising Him they turned to supplication, which is among their words: ﴿so protect us from the punishment of the Fire﴾ up to His words: ﴿Indeed, You do not break Your promise﴾. In this verse He made clear that He answered their supplication, saying: ﴿So their Lord answered them﴾. The verse contains several issues:

First issue: The verse indicates that the answering of supplication is conditional upon these matters. Since fulfilling these conditions is rare, it follows that the person whose supplication is answered is also rare.

Second issue: The author of al-Kashshaf (al-Zamakhshari) said: it is said *istajabahu* and *istajaba lahu* (both meaning "he answered him"). The poet said:

*"A caller called out, 'O you who answers the call!' but at that moment no one answered him."*

And God, may He be exalted, said: ﴿O you who believe, respond to God and to the Messenger﴾ [al-Anfal: 24].

[Page 122 ends]

Third issue: *Annī lā ughdī'u* (that I do not waste): it is read with a fatha (*bi-annī*, "that I"), with the implied preposition *bi-*; and with a kasra, to indicate the sense of "saying." It is also read *lā uḍayyi'u* with shaddah (intensified form).

Fourth issue: The *min* in His words ﴿min dhakarin﴾ ("male") is said to be explanatory (*li-l-tabyīn*), like His words: ﴿so avoid the abomination of idols﴾ [al-Hajj: 30]. It is also said that it serves to emphasise the negation, meaning: "the work of any worker among you, male or female."

Fifth issue: Know that the intended meaning is not that He does not waste the act itself, because every act, once it exists, vanishes and perishes. Rather, the intended meaning is that He does not waste the reward of the act. Wasting (*iḍā'a*) means withholding the reward. So His words ﴿I do not waste﴾ are a negation of a negation, which yields an affirmation, and the meaning becomes: "I deliver the reward of all your deeds to you." Once this is established, the verse indicates that none of the believers will remain in the Fire forever. The proof is that by his faith he deserves a reward, and by his disobedience he deserves punishment; both must reach him by the ruling of this verse, and combining them is impossible. Either the reward comes first and then is transferred to punishment, which is invalid by consensus (*ijmā'*), or the punishment comes first and then is transferred to reward, which is what is sought.

Sixth issue: Most of the commentators (*mufassirūn*) explained the verse to mean that God accepted from them that He would reward them for their deeds and acts of obedience, and deliver the reward of those deeds to them.

If it is said: "They first asked for forgiveness of sins, and second for the giving of reward. So His words ﴿that I do not waste the work of any worker among you﴾ are an answer to them regarding the giving of reward. Where is the answer regarding the request for forgiveness of sins?"

We say: The removal of punishment does not necessarily entail the attainment of reward, but the attainment of reward necessarily entails the removal of punishment. So His words ﴿that I do not waste the work of any worker among you﴾ become an answer to their supplication regarding what they requested. In my view there is another aspect to the verse: the intended meaning of His words ﴿that I do not waste the work of any worker among you﴾ is "that I do not waste your supplication." Not wasting supplication is an expression for answering it. So the meaning is that the answer to your supplication has been granted in all that you requested and asked for.

* * *

As for His words ﴿male or female﴾, the meaning is that there is no difference in the answering or in the reward between male and female when both of them hold fast to obedience equally. This indicates that merit in matters of religion lies in deeds, not in the other attributes of the doers, because one being male or female, or of a base or noble lineage, has no effect in this matter. Similar is His words: ﴿It is not by your wishes, nor by the wishes of the People of the Book; whoever does evil will be requited for it﴾ [al-Nisa': 123]. It is related that Umm Salama said: "O Messenger of God, I hear God mention men in the emigration but not women," so this verse was revealed.

As for His words ﴿you are of one another﴾, there are several interpretations. The best of them is that *min* here means *ka* (like), i.e., "some of you are like others," and like others in reward for obedience and punishment for disobedience. Al-Qaffal said: this is from their saying: "So-and-so is from me," meaning "of my character and conduct." God said: ﴿Whoever drinks from it is not of me, and whoever does not taste it is of me﴾ [al-Baqarah: 249]. The prayer and peace of God be upon him said: "Whoever deceives us is not of us," and he said: "He is not of us who bears arms against us." So His words ﴿you are of one another﴾ mean: some of you resemble others in deserving reward for obedience and punishment for disobedience. How then is it possible to introduce disparity into this?

* * *

[Page 123]

Then God, may He be exalted, said: ﴿Those who emigrated, were expelled from their homes, were harmed in My cause, fought, and were killed, I will surely remove their misdeeds from them and admit them into gardens beneath which rivers flow, as a reward from God.﴾ The intended meaning of His words ﴿Those who emigrated﴾ is those who chose to emigrate from their homelands in service of the Messenger (ﷺ). The intended meaning of ﴿were expelled from their homes﴾ is those whom the unbelievers forced to leave. There is no doubt that the rank of the former is higher, because they chose to serve the Messenger, peace be upon him, and to remain with him by choice, so they were more excellent. His words ﴿were harmed in My cause﴾ mean: for His sake and because of Him. ﴿Fought and were killed﴾: because fighting comes before being killed. Nafi', Asim and Abu 'Amr read ﴿wa-qātalū wa-qutilū﴾ with the alif in the first (*qātalū*) and *qutilū* unshaddaded, and the meaning is that they fought alongside Him until they were killed. Ibn Kathir and Ibn 'Amir read *wa-qātalū* first and *wa-quttilū* with shaddah. It is said that the shaddah is for emphasis and for the repetition of killing among them, like His words: ﴿with the gates opened for them﴾ [Sad: 50]. It is also said that *quttilū* means "they were cut down," related from al-Hasan. Hamza and al-Kisa'i read *wa-qutilū* without an alif first and *wa-qātalū* with an alif after it. There are several interpretations of this:

The first: the *wāw* does not necessitate sequence, as in His words: ﴿prostrate and bow down﴾ [Al 'Imran: 43].

The second: according to their saying: "We killed, by the Lord of the Ka'ba," when the signs of killing appear, or when his people and kinsmen are killed.

The third: by implying *qad* (already), i.e., "they were killed, having already fought."

Then God, may He be exalted, promised those who do this three things:

The first of them: the erasing of misdeeds and the forgiveness of sins, which is His words: ﴿I will surely remove their misdeeds from them﴾, and that is what they sought: ﴿So forgive us our sins and remove from us our misdeeds﴾.

The second: the giving of a great reward, which is His words: ﴿and admit them into gardens beneath which rivers flow﴾, and that is what they sought by their saying: ﴿and grant us what You promised us through Your messengers﴾.

The third: that this reward be a great reward, accompanied by honour and reverence, which is His words ﴿as a reward from God﴾. That is what they said: ﴿and do not disgrace us on the Day of Resurrection﴾, because He, glory be to Him, is the Great whose greatness has no limit. When a great sultan says to his servant, "I bestow upon you a robe of honour from myself," this indicates that the robe is of the utmost nobility. His words ﴿a reward﴾ are an emphatic verbal noun (*maṣdar*), and the implied meaning is: "I will surely reward them with a reward from God," i.e., "I will reward them with a reward or recompense from God," because His words ﴿I will surely remove their misdeeds from them and admit them﴾ carry the sense of "I will surely reward them." Then He said: ﴿And with God is the best of rewards.﴾ This is an emphasis, so that this reward may be of the utmost nobility, because He, may He be exalted, since He is capable of all things, knows all things, and is free from all needs, is necessarily of the utmost generosity, bounty and beneficence, and so with Him is the best of rewards.

It is related from Ja'far al-Sadiq that he said: "Whoever is afflicted by a matter and says five times, 'Our Lord,' God will save him from what he fears and give him what he wishes," and he recited this verse, and said: "Because God related that they said 'Our Lord' five times, then He informed that He answered them."

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 3, verse 196–197:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Let not the strutting about of those who disbelieve in the land deceive you.﴾ ﴿A brief enjoyment; then their refuge is Hell, and wretched is the resting-place.﴾

Know that when Allah, exalted is He, promised the believers the great reward, and they were in this world in the utmost poverty and hardship while the disbelievers were in blessings, Allah, exalted is He, mentioned in this verse that which consoles them and makes them patient through that hardship. He said: ﴿Let not... deceive you﴾, and in this there are several issues:

Issue one: We have mentioned that al-ghurur (deception) is the verbal noun of your saying: gharartu al-rajul (I deceived the man) with what pleases him outwardly, but then upon examination he finds it contrary to what he loves, so he says: "Its outward appearance deceived me," meaning I accepted it while heedless of testing it. The Arabs also say of a garment, when it is unfolded and then folded back again: radadtuhu ʿala ghirrah (I returned it in heedlessness).

Issue two: The addressee in his saying ﴿Let not... deceive you﴾, who is it? There are two views:

The first: It is the Messenger (ﷺ), but what is meant is the community. Qatadah said: "By Allah, they did not deceive the Prophet of Allah (ﷺ) until Allah took him." And although the address is to him, what is meant is others. It may be said that the reason the Messenger, peace be upon him, was not deceived by this is the continual revelation of these verses to him, as He said: ﴿And had We not strengthened you, you would almost have inclined toward them a little.﴾ [al-Isra: 74]. So Qatadah's view falls. A parallel to this is His saying: ﴿And do not be among the disbelievers.﴾ [Hud: 42] ﴿And do not be among the polytheists.﴾ [al-An'am: 14] ﴿So do not obey the deniers.﴾ [al-Qalam: 8].

The second: This is an address to everyone among the accountable who hears it, as if it were said: "Let it not deceive you, O listener."

Issue three: ﴿The strutting about of those who disbelieve in the land﴾ has two aspects:

The first: It was revealed concerning the polytheists of Makkah, who used to trade and live in luxury. Some of the believers said: "The enemies of Allah, as we see, are in goodness, while we have perished from hunger and hardship." So the verse was revealed.

The second: Al-Farra' said: The Jews used to travel through the land and acquire wealth, so this verse was revealed. What is meant by the strutting about of those who disbelieve in the land is their movement in trade and gain. That is: let not their security for themselves and their free disposal of the land, however they wish, deceive you, while you, O community of believers, are fearful and confined. For that does not last except for a short period, then they will be transferred to a greater punishment.

* * *

Then He said: ﴿A brief enjoyment﴾. It was said: that is, their strutting is a brief enjoyment. Al-Farra' said: that is a brief enjoyment. Al-Zajjaj said: that gain and profit is a brief enjoyment. Allah described it as brief only because the bounties of this world are mixed with calamities and regrets, and in the end it ends and passes away. And how could it not be brief, when it was non-existent from eternity until now, and will become non-existent from eternity to eternity? So when you compare the span of existence with what preceded and what follows, which is eternity without beginning and without end, it is less than what can be described as "brief."

* * *

Then He said: ﴿Then their refuge is Hell﴾, meaning that, despite its brevity, it causes them to fall into the fire of Hell forever and ever. A small blessing, when it is a cause of great harm, is not counted as a blessing. This is like His saying: ﴿We only give them respite so that they may increase in sin.﴾ [Al-Imran: 178] and His saying: ﴿And I give them respite; indeed, My plan is firm.﴾ [al-A'raf: 183].

* * *

Then He said: ﴿And wretched is the resting-place﴾, i.e., the bed. The evidence that it is a wretched resting-place is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿For them there will be canopies of fire above them, and below them canopies﴾ [al-Zumar: 16]. So they are between layers of fires, and above them are coverings, eating fire and drinking fire.

[Page 125]

Know that when He, the Exalted, mentioned the threat, He followed it with the promise of an *nuzul* (a prepared hospitality), and *nuzul* is what is prepared for a guest. His words, ﴿But those who fear their Lord, theirs will be gardens beneath which rivers flow, abiding therein forever, as a hospitality from Allah. And what is with Allah is best for the righteous﴾, cover all acts of obedience, because fear of God includes refraining from what is forbidden and abandoning what is commanded.

Our companions cited this verse as evidence for the *ru'yah* (the vision of Allah in the Hereafter). Since the whole of Paradise is a *nuzul*, there must be the *ru'yah* so that it may be a robe of honour (*khil'ah*). A parallel to this is His saying, ﴿Indeed, those who believe and do righteous deeds, for them are the Gardens of Paradise as a hospitality﴾ [al-Kahf: 107].

As for His saying ﴿nuzulan﴾ (as a hospitality), it is in the accusative as a *hal* (circumstantial qualifier) of ﴿jannat﴾ (gardens), in order to specify them by this description, and the governing element is the *lam* (of the preceding phrase). It is also permissible that it be in the sense of an emphatic verbal noun, because their abiding therein is their being placed therein, or their descent therein. Al-Farra' said: it is in the accusative as an explanatory term, as you say, "It is for you as a gift (*hibah*), as a sale (*bay'*), and as a charity (*sadaqah*)."

Then He said: ﴿And what is with Allah﴾, of the abundant and lasting, ﴿is best for the righteous﴾, compared with what the wicked enjoy of fleeting and little things.

Maslamah ibn Muharib and al-A'mash recited ﴿nuzlan﴾ with the *zay* vowelless (نُزْلًا as نُزْلًا with sukun on the *zay*). Yazid ibn al-Qa'qa' recited ﴿Lakinna alladhina ittaqaw﴾ (لَكِنَّ الَّذِينَ اتَّقَوْا) with a *shaddah* on the *nun*.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 3, verse 199:

﴿And indeed among the People of the Scripture are those who believe in Allah and in what has been revealed to you and what has been revealed to them, humbly submitting to Allah. They do not sell the signs of Allah for a small price. Those will have their reward with their Lord. Indeed, Allah is swift in reckoning.﴾ ﴿O you who have believed, be patient, endure, remain stationed (on the frontier), and fear Allah that you may be successful.﴾

Know that when He, the Exalted, mentioned the state of the believers, and had earlier mentioned the state of the disbelievers, that their destination is the Fire, He clarified in this verse that whoever among them believed was included in the description of those who feared (Allah). So He said: ﴿And indeed among the People of the Scripture﴾. The scholars differed concerning its revelation. Ibn ʿAbbas, Jabir and Qatadah said: it was revealed concerning al-Najashi (the Negus) when he died, and the Prophet (ﷺ) prayed over him. The hypocrites said: "He prays over a Christian whom he never saw." Ibn Jurayj and Ibn Zayd said: it was revealed concerning ʿAbdullah ibn Salam and his companions. It was also said: it was revealed concerning forty men from the people of Najran, thirty-two from Abyssinia, and eight from the Romans, who were upon the religion of ʿIsa (peace be upon him) and then embraced Islam. Mujahid said: it was revealed concerning all the believers among the People of the Scripture. This is the more appropriate view, because when He mentioned the disbelievers and that their destination is punishment, He clarified concerning those among them who believed that their destination is reward.

Know that He, the Exalted, described them with attributes:

The first of them: belief in Allah.

The second: belief in what Allah sent down to Muhammad (ﷺ).

The third: belief in what was sent down to the prophets who came before Muhammad (peace be upon him).

The fourth: that they are "humbly submitting to Allah" (khashiʿīna lillah), and this is a circumstantial clause (ḥāl, a grammatical state describing the subject) from the doer (al-fāʿil, the grammatical subject) of the verb "yu'minu" (يُؤْمِنُ), because "man yu'minu" (مَن يُؤْمِنُ) carries the meaning of the plural.

The fifth: that they do not "sell the signs of Allah for a small price," as the People of the Scripture do, namely those who used to conceal the matter of the Messenger and the truth of his prophethood.

Then He, the Exalted, said concerning them: ﴿Those will have their reward with their Lord. Indeed, Allah is swift in reckoning.﴾ The benefit of His being "swift in reckoning" is that He knows all knowable things, so He knows what each one deserves of reward and punishment.
