Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 3, verse 200:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿O you who have believed, be patient and endure and remain stationed [at the frontiers] and fear Allah that you may be successful.﴾

Know that when He, exalted is He, mentioned in this surah many kinds of the sciences of the foundations (usul) and the branches (furu'), the foundations being what relates to establishing tawhid (Divine oneness), justice, prophethood and the Hereafter, and the branches being what relates to obligations and rulings such as the pilgrimage, jihad and others, He concluded this surah with this verse, which comprises all the etiquettes (adab). This is because the states of a human being are of two kinds: some of them relate to him alone, and some of them are shared between him and others. As for the first kind, patience is necessary in it; as for the second kind, mutual endurance (musabara) is necessary in it.

As for patience (sabr), it encompasses several kinds:

The first: that he be patient in the hardship of reflection and reasoning in knowing tawhid, justice, prophethood and the Hereafter, and in the hardship of deriving answers to the doubts of opponents.

The second: that he be patient in the hardship of performing the obligatory and recommended acts.

The third: that he be patient in the hardship of abstaining from the prohibited acts.

The fourth: patience over the hardships of this world and its calamities, such as illness, poverty, famine and fear. So His saying ﴿be patient﴾ includes these categories, and under each of these three categories there are kinds without end. As for mutual endurance (musabara), it is an expression for bearing the hardships that occur between him and others. It includes bearing bad character from the people of the household, the neighbours and the relatives; it includes leaving retaliation against one who has wronged you, as He said: ﴿And turn away from the ignorant﴾ [al-A'raf: 199], and He said: ﴿And when they pass by idle talk, they pass by it with dignity﴾ [al-Furqan: 72]; it includes preferring others over oneself, as He said: ﴿And they prefer [others] over themselves, even though they themselves are in need﴾ [al-Hashr: 9]; it includes pardoning one who has wronged you, as He said: ﴿And that you pardon is nearer to righteousness﴾ [al-Baqarah: 237]; it includes enjoining good and forbidding evil, for one who undertakes it may be harmed by reason of it; it includes jihad, for it exposes the self to destruction; and it includes mutual endurance with the falsifiers, and resolving their doubts, answering their fallacies, and striving to remove those falsehoods from their hearts. Thus it is established that His saying ﴿be patient﴾ covers everything that relates to him alone, and ﴿and endure﴾ covers everything that is shared between him and others.

Know that although a person may force himself to patience and endurance, he still has blameworthy character traits which must be turned to their opposites, namely lust, anger and greed. A person who has not occupied himself throughout his life with struggling against and subduing these cannot manage to achieve patience and endurance. Therefore He said ﴿and remain stationed﴾. Since this struggle is an act among acts, and a person in every act he performs must have a motive and an aim, it is necessary that in this struggle a person have an aim and an impetus, and that is the fear of Allah in order to attain success and prosperity. Therefore He said: ﴿and fear Allah that you may be successful.﴾ The complete verification of this is that the source of acts is the faculties (quwa). He, exalted is He, commanded patience and endurance, and that is an expression for performing good acts and abstaining from blameworthy acts. And since acts proceed from the faculties, He then commanded the struggle against the faculties which are the sources of blameworthy acts, and that is what is meant by ribat (remaining stationed). Then He mentioned that by which the repelling of these faculties that call to vices and evils is achieved, and that is the fear of Allah. Then He mentioned that for the sake of which it is necessary to prefer the fear of Allah over all other faculties and traits, and that is success. Thus it becomes clear that this verse, which is the conclusion of this surah, comprises treasures of wisdom and spiritual secrets, and that it, despite its brevity, completes everything previously mentioned in this surah of the sciences of the foundations and the branches. This is what I have on this matter.

Let us now mention what the exegetes have said. Al-Hasan said: "Be patient over your religion and do not abandon it because of poverty and hunger, and be patient against your enemy and do not falter because of the defeat that occurred on the day of Uhud." Al-Farra' said: "Be patient along with your Prophet, and endure against your enemy, so that they should not be more patient than you." Al-Asamm said: "When the obligations of Allah in this surah became numerous, He commanded them to be patient in them; and when Allah's exhortation to jihad in this surah became abundant, He commanded them to endure the enemies."

As for His saying ﴿and remain stationed﴾, there are two opinions:

The first: that it is an expression for these people tethering their horses at the frontiers and those people likewise tethering their horses, such that each of the two adversaries is prepared to fight the other. He, exalted is He, said: ﴿And from the tethering of horses, by which you may terrify the enemy of Allah and your enemy﴾ [al-Anfal: 60]. And from the Prophet (ﷺ): "Whoever remains stationed for a day and a night in the way of Allah is like one who fasts and prays a month, not breaking his fast and not departing from his prayer except for a need."

The second: that the meaning of ribat is waiting for prayer after prayer. Two things indicate this:

The first: what is narrated from Abu Salamah ibn Abd al-Rahman that he said: "There was no military campaign in the time of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) in which one would remain stationed, and this verse was only revealed concerning waiting for prayer after prayer."

The second: what is narrated from the hadith of Abu Hurayrah, when he mentioned waiting for prayer after prayer, then said: "That is the ribat," three times.

Know that it is possible to carry the word over all of these meanings. The root of ribat is from rabt, which means binding and tying firmly. It is said of everyone who is patient in a matter: he bound his heart upon it. Others said: ribat is steadfastness and persistence, and this meaning also returns to what we mentioned of patience and binding the self. Then this steadfastness and constancy may be in jihad, and may be in prayer. And Allah knows best.

The Imam, may Allah be pleased with him, said: The commentary on this surah was completed, by the grace and kindness of Allah, on Thursday, the first of Rabi' al-Akhir, in the year five hundred and ninety-five.
